name: Predictive Model
diff_siblings: The root of the entire taxonomy: a predictive model is any formal mathematical mapping f(X) -> Y that uses observed variables X to produce an estimate of an unobserved outcome Y, unifying statistical, machine learning, and deep learning approaches under the shared criterion of generalization to unseen data.
strengths: Encompasses the full spectrum from interpretable parametric models (linear regression) to high-capacity non-parametric ones (deep networks), allowing the right inductive bias to be chosen per problem.
The bias-variance decomposition provides a universal diagnostic framework applicable to every model in the taxonomy, guiding regularization and capacity decisions regardless of algorithm family.
Evaluation is grounded in held-out generalization error, giving a single, comparable criterion across all model families despite their architectural diversity.
weaknesses: No single model dominates across all tasks: the No Free Lunch theorem (Wolpert, 1996) guarantees that gains on one problem class come at the cost of performance on others, so taxonomy navigation is always required.
Conflation of prediction and causal inference is a persistent failure mode: high predictive accuracy does not imply that the model has captured the data-generating mechanism.
Real-world deployment introduces distribution shift between training and inference, a challenge unaddressed by standard empirical risk minimization that affects every family in the taxonomy.
recommended_for: Structured decision problems where a measurable outcome Y (continuous, categorical, or ordinal) must be estimated from a fixed feature matrix X, with enough labeled examples to estimate generalization error reliably.

Comparative model selection studies where multiple algorithm families (e.g., gradient boosting vs. neural networks vs. GLMs) are benchmarked on the same task to trade off accuracy, interpretability, and computational cost.
not_recommended_for: Causal questions requiring intervention estimates (e.g., 'what happens if we change X?'), where predictive fit alone cannot substitute for a causal model or randomized experiment.
Problems with fewer than ~30 labeled examples per feature dimension, where the variance of any empirical risk minimizer dominates and prior-based Bayesian or mechanistic models are more appropriate.
curiosity: The term 'statistical learning' — now used to describe the unified framework bridging classical statistics and machine learning — was popularized in its modern sense by Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman in the first edition of 'The Elements of Statistical Learning' (2001), consolidating decades of parallel development in two scientific cultures that Leo Breiman had diagnosed as fundamentally divided in his landmark paper 'Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures' (2001).

children.name: 1. Machine Learning
children.diff_siblings: Unlike classical statistics (which assumes parametric data distributions and focuses on inference) and deep learning (which learns hierarchical representations end-to-end), classical ML relies on hand-crafted features fed into algorithms with explicit, interpretable structure to optimize a defined loss function.
strengths: Achieves strong predictive performance on tabular data with engineered features without requiring GPU infrastructure or massive datasets (hundreds to low thousands of samples can be sufficient)
Model internals are inspectable: decision boundaries, feature importances, and coefficients can be audited, making compliance and debugging tractable
Training and inference are computationally cheap enough to iterate rapidly on a laptop, enabling fast experimentation cycles on resource-constrained projects
weaknesses: Performance is bounded by the quality of hand-engineered features — raw pixels, audio waveforms, or raw text require domain expertise to transform into useful inputs
Most classical ML models assume a fixed input schema; adding or removing features requires full retraining with no incremental update path
Ensemble and kernel methods scale poorly with sample size (O(n²) to O(n³) for kernel SVMs; tree ensembles slow at inference with millions of trees)
recommended_for: Structured tabular datasets (tens to hundreds of features, thousands to millions of rows) where interpretability is required, such as credit scoring or clinical risk models
Rapid prototyping phases where a strong baseline is needed within hours on a CPU, before committing resources to a deep learning pipeline
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional raw perceptual data (images >64×64, long audio sequences, free-form text) where feature engineering cannot capture the relevant structure and end-to-end representation learning is necessary
Online learning settings with continuous concept drift where the model must update incrementally from a stream without periodic full retraining
children.curiosity: The term 'machine learning' was coined by Arthur Samuel in 1959 in his study of a checkers-playing program on the IBM 701, where he defined it as 'the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed' — the first documented use of the phrase.

children.name: 1.1 Supervised
children.diff_siblings: Unlike unsupervised learning (which infers structure from unlabeled data) and reinforcement learning (which optimizes via environmental reward signals), supervised learning minimizes a loss function defined over explicit input-output pairs, making the target signal fully specified at training time.
strengths: Direct optimization against known labels allows measurable generalization guarantees via empirical risk minimization — validation loss tracks real-world performance reliably.
The full output signal at every training step enables gradient-based optimization to converge with far fewer samples than reward-sparse reinforcement learning requires.

Covers both regression (continuous target) and classification (discrete target) within a single mathematical framework — the same loss-minimization principle applies to linear models through deep networks.
weaknesses: Requires large volumes of correctly labeled data; label noise or systematic annotation bias propagates directly into model predictions with no self-correcting mechanism.
Cannot discover latent structure beyond what the chosen label captures — a model trained on a single target variable is blind to all other patterns in the data.
Closed-world assumption: the model cannot generalize to output classes or value ranges not represented in the training distribution, failing silently on out-of-distribution inputs.
recommended_for: Structured tabular datasets with a well-defined response variable and thousands of labeled examples — e.g., credit scoring with historical approval decisions and known defaults.

Image or text classification tasks where domain experts can annotate a representative sample and the label space is finite and stable — e.g., medical image diagnosis with radiologist-confirmed ground truth.
not_recommended_for: Exploratory settings where no ground-truth label exists or the objective is unknown — customer segmentation or anomaly detection without prior examples of anomalies.
Sequential decision problems where feedback is delayed and actions affect future states — robot navigation or game-playing, where reinforcement learning is the appropriate paradigm.
children.curiosity: The formal statistical framework for supervised learning — empirical risk minimization — was established by Vladimir Vapnik and Alexey Chervonenkis in their 1971 paper on the uniform convergence of relative frequencies, which later became the mathematical foundation for generalization theory and support vector machines.

children.name: 1.1.1 Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Classification, which maps inputs to a finite discrete label set (Y ∈ {1…C}), Regression maps inputs to a continuous real-valued output (Y ∈ ℝ), minimizing a loss over residuals rather than a probability over classes.
strengths: Produces a quantitative magnitude — not just a direction — enabling cost/benefit calculations directly from model output
Loss functions (MSE, MAE, Huber) have well-understood gradient geometry, making optimization behavior predictable and diagnosable
Encompasses a spectrum from closed-form linear estimators to arbitrarily complex nonlinear approximators, all under the same unified residual-minimization objective
weaknesses: Sensitive to outliers when using squared-error loss: a single extreme residual can dominate the gradient and distort the learned surface
Requires the target variable to carry ordinal meaning; applying regression to pseudo-numeric encodings of nominal categories produces mathematically meaningless predictions
Extrapolation outside the training support is unconstrained — the model has no mechanism to detect or bound predictions for inputs far from observed data
recommended_for: Forecasting a numerical quantity with structured tabular inputs and a known measurement scale, such as predicting energy consumption (kWh) from building characteristics and weather readings
Estimating a dose-response or price-elasticity relationship where the signed magnitude and direction of the prediction are both operationally meaningful
not_recommended_for: Problems where the target is a mutually exclusive category without intrinsic order (e.g., disease subtype, product SKU), where classification objectives and calibrated probabilities are required
Survival or time-to-event outcomes with censored observations, where specialized models such as Cox proportional hazards handle the partial-information structure correctly
children.curiosity: The method of least squares — the foundational estimator for regression — was first published by Adrien-Marie Legendre in 1805 in 'Nouvelles méthodes pour la détermination des orbites des comètes'; Carl Friedrich Gauss independently claimed use of the method from 1795 and formalized its probabilistic justification under Gaussian errors in 1809.

children.name: GLM (Generalized Linear Models)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike siblings that assume Gaussian-distributed errors and a direct linear relationship, GLMs generalize regression to any exponential family distribution (Binomial, Poisson, Gamma, etc.) by coupling a linear predictor to the response mean through a monotone link function g(μ) = Xβ.
strengths: Handles non-Gaussian responses natively: the choice of exponential family distribution enforces the correct variance function (e.g., variance proportional to mean for Poisson counts), eliminating the need for variance-stabilizing transforms.
Coefficients remain interpretable on the scale of the linear predictor: a unit increase in x_j changes g(μ) by β_j regardless of the link, enabling auditable inference in regulated domains.
Fitted via iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS), which converges to the exact MLE under the chosen family without requiring gradient tuning or learning-rate selection.
weaknesses: Restricted to a linear predictor on the link scale: feature interactions and non-monotone effects require manual engineering, since no automatic basis expansion is performed.

Overdispersion — when empirical variance exceeds the family's theoretical variance function — violates the model and inflates test statistics; requires ad-hoc fixes such as quasi-likelihood or switching to a more flexible family (e.g., negative binomial).

The choice of distribution family and link function must be specified a priori; a misspecified family yields biased coefficient estimates if the canonical link is used, and there is no AIC-equivalent for quasi-likelihood models to guide selection.
recommended_for: Clinical or actuarial regression where the response is a count or rate (e.g., hospital admissions per 1000 patients) and interpretable, coefficient-level inference with confidence intervals is required alongside prediction.

Insurance or credit scoring with binary or Gamma-distributed outcomes, where regulatory interpretability mandates a parametric model with explicit distributional assumptions and auditable link-scale coefficients.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional data with hundreds of correlated features and no regularization: IRLS optimizes unpenalized MLE, so GLMs overfit when p approaches n and require a separate penalized extension (Ridge GLM, Lasso GLM) to remain stable.

Problems with strongly non-linear, non-monotone feature-response relationships (e.g., image pixel intensities predicting a label), where the fixed link-scale linearity assumption is fundamentally inadequate and tree-based or neural models are more appropriate.
children.curiosity: Introduced by John Nelder and Robert Wedderburn in their 1972 paper 'Generalized Linear Models' (Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A, 135, 370–384), the framework unified apparently unrelated models — normal regression, logistic regression, and Poisson regression — into a single algorithmic form fitted by the same IRLS procedure, a unification that Nelder later called 'the most important statistical idea of the 20th century.'

children.name: Gaussian GLM (identity)
children.diff_siblings: Pairs the Gaussian (normal) error distribution with the identity link g(μ)=μ, making the linear predictor directly equal to the conditional mean — the only GLM variant that reduces exactly to ordinary least squares estimated via maximum likelihood.
strengths: Closed-form coefficient estimates via normal equations (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy — no iterative reweighted least squares needed, unlike all other GLM families.
Gauss-Markov theorem guarantees BLUE (Best Linear Unbiased Estimator) when errors are homoscedastic and uncorrelated, a uniquely strong optimality result.
Residual diagnostics (Q-Q plots, Shapiro-Wilk, Breusch-Pagan) are well-established and directly interpretable because the error distribution is fully specified as N(0, σ²).
weaknesses: Constant variance assumption (homoscedasticity) fails when the response is strictly positive or bounded — in those cases a Gamma or binomial GLM with a non-identity link is more appropriate.
Identity link allows predicted means to go negative, which is nonsensical for count, proportion, or rate responses.
Sensitive to outliers: squared-error loss gives O(n) influence to individual extreme observations, unlike robust alternatives such as quantile regression.
recommended_for: Continuous, unbounded response variables with approximately normal residuals and constant variance, such as predicting housing prices in log-scale or blood pressure change in a randomized controlled trial.

Settings requiring interpretable additive effect sizes (β coefficients as direct unit changes in the mean) and fast computation on large design matrices, such as genome-wide association studies with linear mixed model extensions.
not_recommended_for: Count or rate outcomes (e.g., number of events per time period) where variance grows with the mean — Poisson or negative-binomial GLMs are structurally required.
Binary or multinomial classification targets, where the identity link produces probabilities outside [0, 1] and the Bernoulli log-likelihood is the correct objective.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Nelder and Wedderburn (1972) in 'Generalized Linear Models' (Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A), the Gaussian GLM with identity link was the canonical example used to show that OLS is a special case of the unified exponential-family framework — its variance function V(μ)=1 (constant) is what makes the iterative reweighted least squares algorithm collapse to a single ordinary least-squares step.

target.notes: Conditional mean modeled directly via identity link g(mu)=mu; response should be unbounded (real-valued) with symmetric, approximately normal residuals. Not for strictly-positive, bounded, count, or categorical targets.

data_regime.rows: works on <100 to millions; closed-form normal equations are exact at any n
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n required for unique OLS solution (XtX must be invertible); collinear or p>=n needs regularization, not plain Gaussian GLM

features.interpretability: high: each beta is the additive change in the mean per unit of the feature, on the response scale
features.notes: Categoricals via dummy coding. Scaling not required for fit but matters for coefficient comparison; predictors with near-perfect collinearity inflate variance.

assumptions: linearity of the conditional mean in the predictors
homoscedasticity (constant error variance)
independent, uncorrelated errors
approximately normal residuals (for valid inference/CIs)
no severe multicollinearity (full-rank design matrix)
loss: squared error / Gaussian negative log-likelihood (OLS is the MLE)
contraindicated_when: response is a count or rate with variance scaling with the mean (use Poisson / negative-binomial)
response is strictly positive and right-skewed (use Gamma or log-link)
response is bounded in [0,1] or a proportion (use Beta / binomial logit)
binary or multiclass target (use logistic / multinomial)
heteroscedastic errors or heavy-tailed outliers (consider WLS, robust, or quantile regression)
p >= n or strong collinearity without regularization

children.name: Binomial / Logistic GLM
children.diff_siblings: Uses the logit link function to map a linear predictor to probabilities in (0,1), modeling a Binomial response — unlike Gaussian GLM (identity link, continuous output) or Poisson GLM (log link, count response).
strengths: Coefficients exponentiate directly to odds ratios, giving a statistically rigorous and legally defensible interpretation required in credit scoring and clinical trials.
Estimated via IRLS (Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares), converging in few iterations on datasets with thousands to millions of rows without storing a full kernel matrix.
Calibrated probabilities out of the box: the predicted value is a proper P(Y=1|X) usable directly in decision thresholds, expected-value calculations, and cost-sensitive classification.
weaknesses: Complete or quasi-complete separation — when a predictor perfectly predicts the outcome in the training set — causes MLE to diverge, sending one or more coefficients to infinity.
Decision boundary is a single hyperplane, making it unable to capture XOR-type interactions or non-linear class boundaries without explicit manual feature engineering.
Assumes no multicollinearity among predictors; highly correlated features inflate standard errors, destabilize coefficient estimates, and degrade inference even when predictions remain acceptable.
recommended_for: Binary clinical endpoints (e.g., 30-day hospital readmission) with structured tabular covariates, where regulatory submissions require interpretable odds ratios and calibrated risk scores.

Credit default scoring on thousands of applicants with demographic and financial features, where model transparency is mandated by fair-lending regulations and a probability of default must feed downstream expected-loss calculations.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional genomics data (p >> n) with many near-zero-effect SNPs, where the large number of correlated predictors causes separation and unstable MLE without additional regularization (use Ridge/Lasso-penalized logistic instead).

Multi-class image or text classification where the ground-truth decision boundary is highly non-linear and features are raw pixels or token embeddings (use softmax neural networks or gradient boosting instead).
children.curiosity: The unified GLM framework encompassing Binomial/Logistic regression was formalized by Nelder and Wedderburn (1972) in their paper 'Generalized Linear Models' (Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A), where they showed that logistic, Poisson, and Gaussian regressions share a common fitting algorithm — IRLS — differing only in their link function and variance structure.

target.notes: Models P(Y=1|X) via logit link; supports grouped Binomial counts (successes/trials) as proportion targets.

data_regime.rows: works from a few hundred to millions of rows; IRLS scales without a kernel matrix
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n required for stable unpenalized MLE; fails when p>>n unless regularized

features.interpretability: high: exponentiated coefficients are odds ratios, legally defensible for credit/clinical use
features.notes: Linear-in-logit; non-linear effects and interactions need explicit feature engineering. Benefits from scaling/standardization for optimizer conditioning.

assumptions: log-odds is linear in the predictors
observations conditionally independent
no perfect/quasi-complete separation (drives MLE coefficients to infinity)
low multicollinearity (correlated predictors inflate standard errors and destabilize estimates)
correctly specified link (logit)
loss: log-loss / binomial deviance (maximum likelihood)
supports L1/L2 penalties via Lasso/Ridge-penalized variants
contraindicated_when: p>>n with many correlated near-zero-effect predictors (separation, unstable MLE) -> use penalized logistic
decision boundary is highly non-linear (XOR-type interactions, raw pixels/embeddings) -> use trees/boosting or neural nets
complete or quasi-complete separation present in training data
multi-class targets without extension to multinomial/softmax

children.name: Poisson GLM
children.diff_siblings: Unlike other GLM variants that target binary outcomes (Logistic), continuous skewed values (Gamma), or overdispersed counts (Negative Binomial), Poisson GLM assumes the response follows a Poisson distribution with a log link, enforcing the constraint that mean equals variance — making it the canonical choice strictly for equidispersed count data.
strengths: Log link guarantees strictly positive fitted values, eliminating the need for manual transformations when modeling counts or rates.
Coefficients have a direct multiplicative interpretation on the rate scale (eβ = incidence rate ratio), which is analytically meaningful in epidemiology and ecology.
Efficient maximum likelihood estimation via IRLS (Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares) converges in few iterations for well-specified count data.
weaknesses: The equidispersion constraint (Var = Mean) is violated by most real count datasets, causing underestimated standard errors and anticonservative p-values when overdispersion is present.
Cannot model excess zeros structurally — a high proportion of zero counts (e.g., species absence data) inflates the variance beyond what Poisson allows, requiring zero-inflated extensions.
Sensitive to outlying large counts: a single extreme observation can disproportionately distort the fitted rate because the log link stretches the response scale asymmetrically.
recommended_for: Modeling event counts per fixed exposure unit (e.g., number of insurance claims per policy-year, hospital admissions per 1,000 inhabitants) when a dispersion test confirms Var ≈ Mean.
Rare-event epidemiological studies with a known offset (population size or observation time), such as disease incidence rates across geographic regions where counts are low and equidispersion holds.
not_recommended_for: Datasets where the conditional variance substantially exceeds the mean (overdispersion ratio > 1.5), as inference will be anti-conservative — use Negative Binomial GLM instead.

Count responses with structural excess zeros (e.g., wildlife species counts where many sites are uninhabitable), where a zero-inflated or hurdle model is required to separate the zero-generating process.
children.curiosity: Poisson regression as a GLM was formalized by Nelder and Wedderburn (1972) in their landmark paper 'Generalized Linear Models' (Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A), which unified Poisson, logistic, and Gamma regression under a single iterative fitting algorithm (IRLS), enabling all three to be estimated with the same computational framework for the first time.

target.notes: Non-negative integer counts of events per fixed exposure unit; assumes equidispersion (conditional Var == Mean). Rate modeling via a log-exposure offset.

data_regime.rows: works on <1k; suited to low-count and rare-event settings
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; no built-in regularization (use penalized GLM for p>=n)

features.interpretability: high; exp(beta) is a directly meaningful incidence rate ratio (multiplicative effect on the rate)

assumptions: equidispersion: conditional variance equals the conditional mean
log-linear relationship between predictors and the log mean count
independent observations (no clustering/autocorrelation)
correct exposure encoded as a fixed-coefficient log offset when modeling rates
loss: Poisson negative log-likelihood / Poisson deviance (log link, canonical), fit by IRLS maximum likelihood
contraindicated_when: overdispersion present (dispersion ratio > ~1.5) -> SEs anti-conservative; use Negative Binomial GLM
structural excess zeros -> use zero-inflated or hurdle models
continuous, binary, or proportion targets (use Gamma/Logistic/Beta GLM respectively)
extreme large-count outliers that distort the log-scale fit

children.name: Gamma GLM
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Gaussian GLM (constant variance) or Poisson GLM (discrete counts), Gamma GLM assumes variance proportional to the square of the mean (Var = φμ²), making it the natural choice for strictly positive, continuous, right-skewed responses where dispersion grows with the magnitude of the outcome.
strengths: Log link produces multiplicative effects on the mean, directly interpretable as percentage changes — ideal for claim costs and durations where ratios matter more than differences.
Var = φμ² captures heteroscedasticity intrinsically: residual spread widens with the predicted value without any manual transformation of the response.
Estimates are on the original positive scale via the link function, avoiding the retransformation bias that log-OLS introduces when back-transforming predictions.
weaknesses: Strictly excludes exact zeros: a single zero in the response causes likelihood failure, requiring either zero-truncation or switching to a Tweedie (p=2) or hurdle model.

MLE of the dispersion parameter φ is sensitive to outliers because the Gamma PDF has light tails — a few extreme observations can heavily distort the fit, often requiring robust alternatives like Pearson estimation.
Assumes a single fixed shape for the variance-mean relationship (power = 2); if the true power is between 1 and 2 (e.g., semi-continuous data with zeros), a Tweedie GLM is structurally superior.
recommended_for: Insurance claim severity modeling: positive, right-skewed loss amounts per claim where variance scales with claim size and multiplicative rate factors (territory, age) are interpretable directly.
Healthcare cost prediction for patients with at least one visit: continuous positive expenditures with high dispersion that increase proportionally with the predicted mean.
not_recommended_for: Datasets with exact zero responses (e.g., total insurance losses including zero-claim policies), where the Gamma likelihood is undefined at y=0.
Count data or discrete non-negative integers, where Poisson or Negative Binomial GLMs respect the discrete support structure that Gamma ignores.
children.curiosity: Introduced as part of the unified GLM framework by Nelder and Wedderburn (1972) in their landmark paper 'Generalized Linear Models' (Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A), which showed that Gaussian, Poisson, Binomial, and Gamma regressions are all special cases of a single iteratively reweighted least squares algorithm.

target.notes: Strictly positive continuous response (y>0), right-skewed, with variance proportional to the square of the mean (Var = phi*mu^2), i.e. constant coefficient of variation. Exact zeros are excluded (likelihood undefined at y=0).

data_regime.rows: works on <1k; stable with hundreds of observations per parameter
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n strongly preferred; no built-in regularization unless penalized GLM variant used

features.interpretability: high — with the canonical/log link, coefficients are exponentiated into multiplicative rate factors (percentage change in the mean), directly actuarially interpretable
features.notes: Linear predictor is additive on the link scale; nonlinearities and interactions must be specified manually. Categorical predictors enter as dummy factors.

assumptions: Response is strictly positive and continuous (no exact zeros)
Variance-mean relationship follows the power-2 law (Var = phi*mu^2); if true power is between 1 and 2, a Tweedie GLM is structurally superior
Correct link function (log is typical) so the linear predictor maps to the positive mean
Observations independent; linear predictor correctly specified on the link scale
Light-tailed Gamma errors — sensitive to extreme outliers, especially for dispersion estimation
loss: Gamma deviance / negative log-likelihood (MLE)
Pearson chi-square for dispersion (phi) estimation, more robust than MLE under outliers
contraindicated_when: Response contains exact zeros (e.g. total losses including zero-claim policies) — use Tweedie p in (1,2) or a hurdle/two-part model
Count or discrete non-negative integer responses — use Poisson or Negative Binomial
Symmetric / constant-variance continuous response — use Gaussian GLM or OLS
Heavy-tailed responses with influential outliers, where Gamma's light tail distorts the fit
p >= n or strong collinearity without penalization

children.name: Inverse Gaussian GLM
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Gamma GLM (variance = φμ²) or Gaussian GLM (variance = φ), the Inverse Gaussian GLM uses a variance function of φμ³, meaning dispersion grows cubically with the mean, making it the right choice when extreme right-skew and rapidly accelerating variance are present in positive continuous outcomes.
strengths: Cubic variance function (Var = φμ³) captures heavier right tails than Gamma, fitting data where large values are far more variable than small ones
Canonical link 1/μ² preserves the additive structure of inverse first-passage-time models, enabling interpretable linear predictors for time-to-event rates
Exact IRLS estimation via maximum likelihood; closed-form score equations make parameter inference computationally identical in cost to Gamma GLM
weaknesses: Variance grows faster than in Gamma GLM, so model fit degrades quickly when data are only moderately skewed rather than extremely right-tailed
Canonical link 1/μ² is rarely interpretable in applied settings; log link is safer but sacrifices theoretical optimality
More sensitive to outliers than Gamma because the cubic variance-mean relationship amplifies influence of large observations during IRLS iterations
recommended_for: Modeling right-skewed positive response times or first-passage times (e.g., patient time-to-recovery, machine failure latency) where residual variance grows faster than the square of the mean
Insurance claim severity when exploratory analysis shows Gamma residuals are systematically heteroscedastic and Tweedie power p is estimated near 3
not_recommended_for: Data with moderate right skew where variance scales roughly as μ²: Gamma GLM will fit equally well with fewer numerical stability issues
Zero-inflated or bounded count data: the distribution is strictly positive and continuous, so it cannot model zero masses or discrete outcomes
children.curiosity: The distribution was first derived by Erwin Schrödinger (1915) as the first-passage-time of one-dimensional Brownian motion with positive drift; the name 'Inverse Gaussian' was coined by M.C.K. Tweedie in 1956, who showed it is inverse to the Gaussian in the sense that the cumulant-generating function of 1/X when X is Gaussian yields the IG form.
keywords: variance increases with cube of mean

target.notes: Strictly positive continuous response with extreme right skew. Variance function V(mu)=mu^3, so dispersion accelerates cubically with the mean: heavier right tail than Gamma. Equivalent to Tweedie with power p=3. Cannot represent zeros, negatives, bounded/proportion data, or discrete counts.

data_regime.rows: works on small samples (hundreds); ML/IRLS stable with modest n
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; no built-in regularization, so needs n comfortably exceeding p

features.interpretability: medium with log link (multiplicative effects on mean); low with canonical 1/mu^2 link, which is theoretically optimal but rarely interpretable
features.notes: Standard GLM design matrix. Effects enter linearly through the link; no automatic nonlinearity or interactions.

assumptions: Response follows inverse Gaussian (Wald) distribution: strictly positive, continuous, very heavy right tail
Variance is proportional to the cube of the mean (Var=phi*mu^3); fit degrades fast if true variance scales only as mu^2
Correct link function (canonical 1/mu^2 or log) linearizing the mean
Independent observations; dispersion phi constant across observations
loss: inverse-Gaussian deviance (maximum likelihood via IRLS)
Tweedie deviance at power p=3
contraindicated_when: Outcome can be zero, negative, or bounded (use Tweedie 1<p<2, Beta, or other GLM)
Discrete count or count-with-zeros data (use Poisson/negative-binomial/zero-inflated)
Only moderate right skew with variance ~mu^2 (Gamma GLM fits as well with better numerical stability)
Heavy outlier contamination: cubic variance-mean amplifies leverage of large observations during IRLS
Need for variable selection or p>=n (no native regularization)

children.name: GLM Tweedie
children.diff_siblings: Unlike its siblings (Gaussian, Poisson, Gamma, Inverse Gaussian), Tweedie unifies the entire GLM exponential-dispersion family through a single continuous power parameter p (Var[Y] = φμ^p), and is the only member that naturally produces a point mass at zero combined with continuous positive support — the compound Poisson-Gamma structure that emerges when 1 < p < 2.
strengths: Handles zero-inflated semicontinuous responses in a single model (no separate hurdle stage) by exploiting the compound Poisson-Gamma structure for 1 < p < 2
Variance function Var[Y] = φμ^p adapts to heavy-tailed, right-skewed positive data without log-transforming the target, preserving additive interpretability of the linear predictor
Profile likelihood over p makes distribution selection data-driven rather than analyst-imposed, reducing misspecification risk when the response lies between Poisson and Gamma regimes
weaknesses: Estimating p via profile likelihood requires fitting a grid of models, increasing computation substantially compared to any fixed-distribution sibling
Numerical evaluation of the Tweedie density is intractable in closed form for non-integer p; series and Fourier methods both suffer from unbounded term counts, complicating exact inference

When the zero proportion exceeds roughly 90%, the compound Poisson mass at zero is too dominant for the Tweedie variance structure to capture the zero-generating process accurately, biasing predictions
recommended_for: Insurance pure-premium modeling where a policy portfolio has many zero-claim policyholders and a heavy-tailed continuous claim amount for the rest — exactly the 1 < p < 2 regime
Healthcare expenditure prediction with cost data that is zero for non-users and right-skewed continuous for users, where separating frequency and severity into two models would discard information
not_recommended_for: Bounded or proportion responses (e.g., loss ratios in [0,1]) where the Beta distribution or a logit-linked GLM is the natural choice and Tweedie's positive-unbounded support is misaligned
Count responses with no continuous component (e.g., number of accidents per year), where a Poisson or Negative Binomial GLM is simpler, interpretable, and avoids unnecessary p estimation
children.curiosity: The Tweedie family was formally characterized by Maurice Tweedie in a 1984 conference paper ('An index which distinguishes between some important exponential families'), and the distribution class was subsequently named after him by Bent Jørgensen in his 1987 exponential dispersion model work — making the naming a tribute by a student of the field rather than self-designation by the original author.
keywords: predicting total cost with many zeros

target.notes: Best when 1<p<2: a semicontinuous response with an exact point mass at zero plus right-skewed strictly positive continuous values. Endpoints recover Poisson (p=1) and Gamma (p=2). Support is non-negative and unbounded above.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ to estimate the power parameter p reliably; with the zero proportion above ~90% the zero mass dominates and the variance structure misfits
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; regularized GLM variants extend to higher dimensions but no built-in feature selection

features.interpretability: high: coefficients act on a (usually log) linear predictor with multiplicative interpretation on the mean, standard for actuarial pricing and exposure offsets
features.notes: Typically log link; supports exposure offsets (e.g. policy years). Predictors enter additively on the link scale; nonlinearity must be engineered (splines, interactions).

assumptions: mean-variance relation follows Var[Y]=phi*mu^p with a single global p
correct link (usually log) so the linear predictor is additive on the transformed mean
observations independent given covariates
response non-negative with the zero mass generated by the compound Poisson-Gamma mechanism, not a separate structural-zero process
loss: Tweedie deviance / log-likelihood (exponential dispersion family)
profile likelihood over the power parameter p for distribution selection
contraindicated_when: target is a bounded proportion or rate in [0,1] (use Beta or logit-linked GLM)
pure count with no continuous component (use Poisson or Negative-Binomial GLM)
zero proportion is extreme (>~90%) so the zero-generating process needs an explicit hurdle/zero-inflated two-part model
Gaussian symmetric errors with possible negative values (use ordinary linear/Gaussian GLM)

children.name: GLM Quasi-likelihood
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Poisson, Gaussian, Binomial, or Gamma GLMs — which require a fully specified exponential-family distribution — Quasi-likelihood GLM needs only a mean function and a variance-mean relationship (V(μ)), estimating a free dispersion parameter φ rather than assuming φ=1.
strengths: Handles overdispersion (φ>1) or underdispersion (φ<1) without committing to a full probability distribution, making it robust when the true distribution is unknown.
Preserves the GLM coefficient estimates and their asymptotic normality via quasi-score equations identical in form to the true score equations, so standard IWLS fitting applies unchanged.
Sandwich (Huber-White) standard errors remain valid even if the specified variance function V(μ) is misspecified, providing correct inference at the cost of efficiency.
weaknesses: No true log-likelihood exists, so AIC/BIC cannot be computed directly; model selection requires quasi-AIC (QAIC) or cross-validation, complicating routine comparisons.
Requires the analyst to specify V(μ) (e.g., V=μ for quasi-Poisson, V=μ(1-μ) for quasi-binomial) — a wrong choice inflates or deflates standard errors without flagging the misspecification.
Asymptotic guarantees of the sandwich estimator break down with small sample sizes or few clusters, leading to under-coverage of confidence intervals.
recommended_for: Overdispersed count data where Pearson dispersion φ is between 1 and 5 and the variance is approximately proportional to the mean (e.g., weekly insect trap counts across ecological plots).
Overdispersed proportions (cluster-binomial data) such as litter-effect studies where the observed variance among litter proportions exceeds what pure binomial sampling predicts.
not_recommended_for: Strongly overdispersed counts where variance grows quadratically with the mean (φ>>5), where Negative Binomial GLM provides a proper likelihood and better uncertainty quantification.
Settings requiring exact probability predictions or likelihood-ratio tests between non-nested models, since the absence of a true likelihood makes such tests ill-defined.
children.curiosity: Introduced by R.W.M. Wedderburn in 1974 ('Quasi-likelihood functions, generalized linear models, and the Gauss-Newton method', Biometrika 61:439-447), the method showed that a function with the same first-order optimality properties as a log-likelihood can be constructed from only the mean-variance relationship, predating the formal GEE framework by over a decade.

target.notes: No full distribution assumed; only a mean function g(mu)=Xb and a variance-mean relationship V(mu) are specified. Free dispersion phi is estimated (typ. quasi-Poisson V=mu, quasi-binomial V=mu(1-mu)). Use when 1<phi<~5.

data_regime.rows: works on moderate n (hundreds+); sandwich/dispersion inference unreliable at small n or few clusters
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n required; no built-in regularization for p>n

features.interpretability: high: linear predictor with monotone link, coefficients are interpretable on link scale (log/logit) as in standard GLM

assumptions: correct mean model g(mu)=Xb (link + linear predictor correctly specified)
correct variance function V(mu); misspecification distorts model-based SEs without warning
independent observations (or correctly handled clustering)
variance approximately proportional to V(mu) with constant phi
loss: quasi-score / quasi-deviance estimating equations (Wedderburn); IWLS fitting identical in form to GLM
Pearson-chi-square-based dispersion estimate for phi
contraindicated_when: strong overdispersion with variance growing quadratically in the mean (phi>>5) -> prefer Negative Binomial GLM with a proper likelihood
likelihood-ratio tests, AIC/BIC comparison, or exact probabilistic predictions needed (no true likelihood exists)
very small samples or few clusters where sandwich-estimator asymptotics fail
p>=n or need for variable selection / shrinkage

children.name: Ordinal Regression (Proportional Odds)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike multinomial logistic regression (which ignores category order) or Poisson/negative binomial models (which assume count data), the proportional odds model treats the response as cumulative thresholds on a latent continuous scale, using a single shared coefficient vector across all K-1 cut points — the proportional odds assumption.
strengths: Exploits ordinal structure via cumulative logits, yielding a single interpretable odds ratio per predictor that applies across all category boundaries simultaneously
Far more parsimonious than multinomial logistic regression: fits K-1 intercepts plus p slope parameters instead of (K-1)*p slopes
Produces directly interpretable coefficients as cumulative log-odds ratios, with a clear latent-variable interpretation tied to a threshold model
weaknesses: Proportional odds assumption (parallel lines) is frequently violated in practice and standard tests over-reject it in large samples, requiring model diagnostics on every fit
A single odds ratio per predictor conceals differential effects across thresholds — a predictor that strongly separates only adjacent extreme categories is invisible in the pooled estimate
No closed-form MLE; relies on iterative IRLS and can fail to converge with sparse cells in the cross-tabulation of predictors by ordinal outcome
recommended_for: Clinical trials with ordered severity endpoints (e.g., 7-point WHO ordinal outcome scale for respiratory disease), where the proportional odds ratio provides a single regulatory-grade effect size across all transitions
Customer satisfaction or quality-of-life surveys with 4-7 Likert categories where the latent-variable interpretation is scientifically plausible and parsimony is needed over a multinomial model
not_recommended_for: Outcomes with many ordered categories whose spacing is approximately equal and known a priori (e.g., age groups in equal-width bins), where linear regression on the numeric codes is more efficient and easier to communicate

Settings where the proportional odds assumption is strongly violated and category-specific effects are the scientific question, as the pooled coefficient will be a misleading average across non-parallel log-odds curves
children.curiosity: Introduced by McCullagh (1980) in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B (vol. 42, pp. 109-127), the paper unified cumulative link models under a single framework and demonstrated that the proportional odds model is invariant to the collapsing of adjacent outcome categories — a property no other ordinal model shares.

target.notes: Ordered categorical response with K>=3 levels modeled via cumulative logits on a latent continuous scale. For K=2 reduces to ordinary logistic regression. Category labels must have a meaningful order but no assumed numeric spacing.

data_regime.rows: works on small-to-moderate n (hundreds+); needs enough observations per ordinal category and adequate cell counts in predictor-by-outcome cross-tab to avoid separation/non-convergence
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n strongly preferred; no built-in regularization, so unstable when p approaches n

features.interpretability: high; single cumulative log-odds ratio per predictor (proportional odds), shared across all K-1 thresholds, with a clean latent-variable/threshold interpretation
features.notes: Linear in the predictors on the cumulative-logit scale; nonlinearity needs manual basis expansion. Tabular structured data only.

assumptions: Proportional odds (parallel lines): each predictor's effect is constant across all K-1 cut points; violation biases the pooled coefficient
Correct ordering of response categories
Linearity of predictors on the cumulative-logit scale
Independent observations (no clustering/repeated measures without extension)
loss: cumulative-logit log-likelihood (maximum likelihood via IRLS)
contraindicated_when: Proportional odds assumption is strongly violated and threshold-specific effects are the scientific question (use partial/non-proportional odds or multinomial logit)
Response is nominal/unordered (use multinomial logistic regression)
Categories have known, approximately equal numeric spacing (linear regression on numeric codes is more efficient)
Response is a count rather than ordered grades (use Poisson/negative-binomial)
p>=n or many sparse predictor-by-outcome cells (separation, IRLS non-convergence)

children.name: Multinomial Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Binary Logistic Regression (2 classes) and Ordinal Regression (ordered categories), Multinomial Regression models K unordered nominal classes by estimating K-1 log-odds equations simultaneously against a reference category, using the softmax function to produce a joint probability distribution over all classes.
strengths: Jointly estimates all class probabilities via a single model, ensuring they sum to 1 — unlike fitting K independent binary models, which can yield incoherent probability totals.
No assumption of ordering among outcome categories, making it the correct GLM choice when classes are nominal (e.g., vehicle type, disease subtype).
Coefficients are directly interpretable as log-odds ratios relative to the reference class, preserving the inferential transparency of logistic regression.
weaknesses: Carries the Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives (IIA) assumption: the odds ratio between any two classes is unaffected by the presence or absence of other classes, which fails in substitutable-alternative scenarios (e.g., transport mode choice).
Parameter count scales as (K-1) × p, where p is the number of predictors — large K with moderate n leads to sparse cells and unstable coefficient estimates.
Sensitive to choice of reference category: coefficient magnitudes and signs change with the reference, complicating interpretation when no natural baseline class exists.
recommended_for: Survey or clinical data with a nominal outcome of 3-5 unordered categories and n >> (K-1) × p, such as classifying patient treatment choice among distinct therapies.
Econometric discrete-choice problems where the outcome categories are qualitatively distinct alternatives and relative-risk ratios between pairs of classes are the primary quantity of interest.
not_recommended_for: Outcomes with a natural order (mild/moderate/severe), where Ordinal Regression exploits that structure with fewer parameters and greater statistical power.
High-cardinality nominal targets (K > 10) or sparse datasets, where the (K-1) × p coefficient matrix becomes unreliable and tree-based or neural multiclass models are preferable.
children.curiosity: Henri Theil (1969) independently extended the binary logit to multiple unordered categories in 'A Multinomial Extension of the Linear Logit Model' (International Economic Review, 10, 251-259), applying it to consumer choice theory at roughly the same time Cox (1966) proposed a similar formulation for qualitative responses in statistics.
keywords: categorical outcome with more than two classes

target.notes: K unordered nominal classes (K>=3); softmax over K-1 log-odds equations against a reference category. Use Ordinal Regression instead if classes are ordered.

data_regime.rows: needs n >> (K-1)*p; sparse class-by-predictor cells destabilize MLE
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; parameter count grows as (K-1)*p, so large K or large p needs regularization (e.g. elastic-net)

features.interpretability: high; coefficients are log-odds ratios relative to the reference class, but signs/magnitudes shift with the chosen reference baseline
features.notes: linear in the log-odds; categorical predictors need encoding; benefits from scaling when regularized

assumptions: Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives (IIA): pairwise odds unaffected by other classes — fails with substitutable alternatives
log-odds of each class vs reference is linear in the predictors
independent observations; no severe multicollinearity among predictors
classes are nominal/unordered
loss: multinomial (categorical cross-entropy / multinomial log-likelihood)
optionally L1/L2/elastic-net penalized log-likelihood
contraindicated_when: target categories have a natural order (use ordinal regression for power and fewer params)
high-cardinality target (K>10) or sparse data — coefficient matrix unreliable, prefer tree-based or neural multiclass
strong nonlinear class boundaries or feature interactions not manually specified
IIA clearly violated (discrete-choice with close substitutes — use nested/mixed logit)

target.notes: Response must plausibly come from an exponential-family distribution; the chosen family fixes the mean-variance relationship (e.g. var=mu for Poisson, var=mu^2 for Gamma). Family and link are specified a priori, not learned.

data_regime.rows: works on small samples (hundreds) when p is modest; counts/rare-event families want enough events per coefficient (~10+ events/predictor)
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n strongly preferred; unpenalized IRLS is unstable or non-identifiable as p approaches n; use penalized GLM (Ridge/Lasso) for p>=n or correlated features

features.interpretability: high: each beta_j is the additive change in g(mu) per unit of x_j (log-odds for logit, log-rate for log link), giving auditable, CI-equipped coefficients for regulated domains
features.notes: Effects are linear on the link scale only; interactions, non-monotone effects, and basis expansions must be hand-engineered. Scaling not required for fit but aids IRLS conditioning and coefficient comparability.

assumptions: response distribution belongs to the specified exponential family
correct mean-variance (variance-function) specification; no overdispersion beyond the family
linearity of g(mu) in the predictors on the link scale
independent observations (no clustering/repeated measures unless extended to GEE/GLMM)
low multicollinearity among predictors
loss: maximum likelihood / deviance for the chosen family (squared error=Gaussian, log-loss=Bernoulli/Binomial, Poisson deviance, Gamma deviance)
quasi-likelihood for overdispersed counts/proportions
fit by iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) to the exact MLE
contraindicated_when: empirical variance far exceeds the family variance function (overdispersion) and family is not switched (e.g. use negative-binomial instead of Poisson)
p approaches or exceeds n with no regularization
strongly non-linear or non-monotone feature-response structure on the link scale (e.g. raw image pixels -> label)
high-cardinality categorical features, text, image, or graph inputs without manual featurization
predictive accuracy on complex tabular interactions matters more than coefficient interpretability (tree ensembles dominate)

children.name: GAM (Generalized Additive Models)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike polynomial regression (which forces a single global functional form) and regression splines (which fit piecewise polynomials without penalization), GAM fits a separate penalized smooth function f_i(x_i) per predictor and combines them additively — each smooth is estimated via a roughness penalty on its second derivative, controlling flexibility without fixing the polynomial degree.
strengths: Captures nonlinear predictor-response relationships without specifying a functional form in advance, while remaining fully interpretable through individual f_i(x_i) effect plots.
Supports all exponential-family response distributions (Gaussian, Poisson, Binomial, Gamma) via the link function, making it as flexible as a GLM in distributional assumptions.
Automatic smoothing parameter selection (e.g., GCV or REML in mgcv) balances fit and regularization, reducing the risk of manually over-tuning that affects regression splines.
weaknesses: The additive structure ignores predictor interactions by default; modeling interactions requires explicit tensor-product smooths, which grows combinatorially with the number of features.
Computationally expensive relative to GLM as the number of predictors increases, because each smooth term involves solving a penalized least-squares system with its own basis expansion.
Smoothing parameter estimation can fail or produce oversmoothed fits when sample sizes are small relative to the number of knots, especially with non-Gaussian responses.
recommended_for: Dose-response or exposure-outcome studies in epidemiology where the effect of a continuous variable (e.g., pollutant concentration, age) is expected to be nonlinear but must remain interpretable for clinical or regulatory reporting.

Species distribution modeling in ecology where environmental predictors (temperature, precipitation) have unimodal or asymmetric effects on occurrence probability and n is in the hundreds to low thousands.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional datasets (p >> 50 predictors) where fitting and interpreting a separate smooth per feature is impractical and the additive independence assumption is increasingly untenable.

Problems requiring strong predictive accuracy over interpretability with complex, high-order interactions (e.g., image or text data), where gradient-boosted trees or neural networks consistently outperform the additive structure.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Hastie and Tibshirani in their 1986 paper 'Generalized Additive Models' (Statistical Science, Vol. 1, No. 3), where the backfitting algorithm — an iterative procedure that cycles through predictors fitting residuals with a smoother — was proposed as the estimation engine; later, Wood (2004) replaced backfitting with penalized regression splines and REML-based smoothing selection, which became the default in the widely-used mgcv R package.

children.name: Classic GAM (smoothing splines)
children.diff_siblings: Places a knot at every distinct data point and controls smoothness via a penalty on the integrated squared second derivative, whereas P-splines use evenly spaced B-spline bases with difference penalties and regression splines fix a reduced knot set upfront.
strengths: Smoothness is automatically calibrated per predictor through GCV/REML, requiring no manual knot placement
Exact cubic interpolant at the extremes with guaranteed continuity of derivatives up to order 2 at each knot
Backfitting isolates each smooth function on its partial residuals, making each 1-D sub-problem interpretable and independently diagnosable
weaknesses: O(n^3) memory and compute per smoother because the hat matrix is dense with n knots, making it impractical beyond roughly 10,000 observations per term
GCV score surface can have local minima or flat regions at extreme smoothing parameters, causing automated selection to converge to over- or under-smoothed solutions
Additive structure assumes no interaction between predictors; capturing interaction requires explicitly adding tensor-product terms, expanding model complexity rapidly
recommended_for: Ecology and epidemiology studies with hundreds to low thousands of observations where the functional shape of each covariate effect is unknown and must be data-driven
Dose-response or time-trend analyses where smooth, interpretable marginal curves per predictor are the primary scientific deliverable
not_recommended_for: Datasets with tens of thousands or more rows per smooth term, where the O(n^3) cost of full smoothing splines is prohibitive compared to P-splines or thin-plate regression splines with basis truncation
Problems with strong predictor interactions as the core signal, such as image or tabular data where interaction effects dominate, since the additive assumption will systematically underfit
children.curiosity: Introduced by Hastie and Tibshirani in their 1986 Statistical Science paper 'Generalized Additive Models' (Vol. 1, No. 3, pp. 297-310), which proposed the backfitting algorithm as a general estimation strategy and established GAMs as a bridge between parametric GLMs and fully nonparametric regression.

target.notes: Fits any exponential-family response via a link function (GAM framework); response modeled as a sum of smooth univariate functions of predictors. Gaussian identity-link is the canonical case.

data_regime.rows: best on hundreds to low thousands per smooth term; full smoothing-spline hat matrix is dense with one knot per distinct x, so O(n^3) compute/memory makes it impractical past ~10k obs per term
data_regime.dimensionality: p<<n; designed for a modest number of predictors each entering additively, not high-dimensional p>n
needs: moderate sample size to estimate each 1-D smooth reliably

features.interpretability: high; each predictor's effect is an isolated, plottable marginal smooth curve (partial-dependence by construction), individually diagnosable via backfitting on partial residuals
features.notes: Continuous predictors should have enough spread/resolution to support a smooth; categorical predictors enter as parametric terms, not smooths. No scaling required, but very uneven x-density can destabilize knot-per-point splines.

assumptions: effects are additive across predictors with no interactions unless explicit tensor-product terms are added
true conditional mean is a smooth function of each predictor (penalized second-derivative smoothness)
exponential-family response with correct link and mean-variance relationship
observations conditionally independent given the smooths
loss: penalized log-likelihood with an integrated-squared-second-derivative roughness penalty
smoothing parameter selected by GCV or REML
for Gaussian: penalized least squares; supports Poisson deviance, binomial deviance, gamma deviance via the chosen family
contraindicated_when: predictor-predictor interactions carry the core signal (additive structure systematically underfits)
tens of thousands or more rows per smooth term (use P-splines or thin-plate regression splines with truncated bases instead)
high-dimensional feature sets where per-term smoothing is infeasible
response with heavy non-exponential-family behavior or strong heteroskedasticity not captured by the family's variance function

children.name: GAMLSS (Location, Scale, Shape)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike standard GAMs that model only the conditional mean via a link function, GAMLSS models all parameters of the response distribution simultaneously (location, scale, shape/skewness, kurtosis), each as an additive function of covariates, and extends the eligible response families beyond the exponential family to any distribution with computable derivatives.
strengths: Over 100 built-in response distributions (continuous, discrete, mixed) covering heavy tails, zero-inflation, and bounded responses — selected by AIC/SBC rather than assumed a priori.
Full conditional distribution is estimated, so any distributional functional (quantiles, Gini coefficient, tail probabilities) is derived consistently from one model without separate fits.

Non-linear and smooth covariate effects (splines, random effects, spatial terms) are supported independently for each distributional parameter, enabling heteroscedasticity and skewness to vary with predictors.
weaknesses: Fitting requires iterating between parameter equations via RS or CG algorithms; convergence frequently fails when sample size is small relative to model complexity or covariates are highly collinear.

AIC-based variable selection across multiple distribution parameters is unstable — different subsets of covariates may be chosen for mu, sigma, nu, and tau, making the final model hard to interpret and validate.
Computation time scales sharply with random-effect terms and large samples; execution can be orders of magnitude slower than a comparable GLM or standard GAM.
recommended_for: Growth chart and centile estimation (e.g., pediatric BMI-for-age curves) where the spread and skewness of the outcome change with age and sex, requiring all four distribution moments to vary with predictors.

Insurance claim severity modeling with right-skewed, heavy-tailed continuous losses where the variance and tail behavior depend on policyholder covariates, making a mean-only model systematically miscalibrated.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional settings (p > 100 predictors) where simultaneous penalization across four sub-models is computationally prohibitive and variable selection instability undermines inference.
Problems requiring only conditional mean estimation with a well-supported exponential-family distribution, where a standard GAM or GLM achieves equivalent accuracy at a fraction of the fitting cost.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Rigby and Stasinopoulos (2005) in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C, GAMLSS was originally motivated by the need to construct WHO-style reference centile charts for child growth, a context where modeling skewness and kurtosis as smooth functions of age was essential and no existing regression framework provided it.
keywords: predict full distribution not just mean

target.notes: Models the full conditional response distribution: all parameters (mu/location, sigma/scale, nu/skewness, tau/kurtosis) are regressed on covariates simultaneously. Over 100 families spanning heavy-tailed, bounded, zero-inflated, and mixed discrete-continuous responses; family chosen by AIC/SBC rather than assumed. Use when conditional variance, skewness, or tail shape themselves depend on predictors.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds to thousands; small n relative to the multi-parameter model causes RS/CG convergence failures
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n strongly preferred; not for p>100. Simultaneous penalization across 4 sub-models is computationally prohibitive in high dimensions
needs: moderate-to-large sample to identify scale/shape parameters
CPU (slow with random-effect terms and large n)

features.interpretability: medium: additive smooth/spline terms per distributional parameter are inspectable, but AIC-based selection can pick different covariate subsets for mu, sigma, nu, tau, complicating a single coherent interpretation
features.notes: Smooth (spline), random-effect, and spatial terms supported independently for each parameter, enabling heteroscedasticity and skewness to vary with covariates

assumptions: chosen response family must adequately match the conditional distribution (diagnosed via worm/QQ plots of normalized quantile residuals)
covariates not severely collinear (collinearity breaks RS/CG convergence)
sufficient sample size relative to total parameters across all sub-models
selected distribution has computable first/second derivatives
loss: penalized maximum likelihood of the full distribution (RS and CG backfitting algorithms)
AIC/SBC/GAIC for family and term selection
derived functionals (quantiles, centiles, tail probabilities) computed consistently from the fitted distribution
contraindicated_when: only conditional mean is needed with a well-supported exponential-family response (GLM/standard GAM is far cheaper for equivalent accuracy)
high-dimensional p>100 settings
very small samples where multi-parameter fitting fails to converge
highly collinear predictors
real-time or large-scale fitting where the orders-of-magnitude slowdown vs GLM/GAM is unacceptable

children.name: GAMM (GAM with mixed effects)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike plain GAM, GAMM augments the additive smooth predictor with Gaussian random effects (subject- or cluster-level intercepts and slopes), so that within-cluster correlation is explicitly modeled via the mixed-model covariance structure rather than ignored or absorbed into the residual.
strengths: Handles repeated-measures and nested data without violating independence: random effects soak up between-subject variance, yielding valid standard errors for the smooth terms.
Smooth functions and random effects are estimated jointly via penalized quasi-likelihood (DPQL), so smoothness selection and variance-component estimation happen in a single optimization pass.
Arbitrary exponential-family responses (Gaussian, Poisson, binomial, Gamma) are supported, making it usable for counts, proportions, and skewed outcomes in longitudinal designs.
weaknesses: DPQL estimation is biased for binary or small-count outcomes (binomial/Poisson with low means), where Laplace or quadrature methods give more accurate likelihoods.

Computational cost scales poorly with the number of random-effect levels: fitting large panel datasets (thousands of subjects, many time points) is substantially slower than equivalent GLMM or GAM fits.
Model comparison via AIC is unreliable because the effective degrees of freedom for the smooth terms interact with the random-effect structure, making standard selection criteria approximate.
recommended_for: Longitudinal biomedical data where the response trajectory over time is nonlinear and subjects are measured repeatedly at unequal intervals (e.g., growth curves, repeated blood-pressure readings).
Ecological or environmental studies with hierarchical sampling (sites nested within regions) where the covariate effect on abundance or occurrence is expected to be smooth but non-linear.
not_recommended_for: Cross-sectional i.i.d. data with no clustering structure, where the random-effect layer adds complexity without correcting any bias (a plain GAM is simpler and equally valid).
Binary outcomes in small or moderately sized groups (fewer than ~20 observations per cluster), where DPQL bias is severe and a GLMM with Laplace approximation or Bayesian approach is more reliable.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Lin and Zhang (1999) in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B, the GAMM framework proposed double penalized quasi-likelihood (DPQL) to estimate smooth functions and variance components simultaneously; Simon Wood later implemented it in the R package mgcv (2004), making it the de facto standard tool for fitting GAMMs in practice.

target.notes: Exponential-family response via a link function; the additive smooth predictor models nonlinear covariate effects while Gaussian random effects model cluster structure. DPQL is biased for binary/low-count outcomes with few observations per cluster.

data_regime.rows: hundreds to low thousands of observations; needs multiple clusters (subjects/sites) with repeated observations per cluster (rule of thumb >~20 obs/cluster for stable variance components and unbiased DPQL)
data_regime.dimensionality: p<<n; few smooth covariates plus low-dimensional random-effect structure; not for high-dimensional p>n
needs: enough levels per grouping factor to estimate variance components

features.interpretability: high: per-covariate smooth functions are visualizable partial effects and variance components are interpretable; additivity means no automatic interactions unless specified
features.notes: Continuous covariates entered as penalized splines; grouping factors define random intercepts/slopes. Time can be irregularly spaced. Scaling not required but spline basis dimension (k) is a tuning choice.

assumptions: additivity of smooth covariate effects (no unmodeled interactions)
Gaussian random effects with a correctly specified covariance structure capturing within-cluster correlation
response from the specified exponential-family distribution with correct link and mean-variance relationship
smoothness of the true covariate-response relationship (penalty controls wiggliness)
residual independence conditional on the random effects
loss: penalized quasi-likelihood (DPQL)
exponential-family deviance (gaussian/poisson/binomial/gamma) with a smoothness penalty (wiggliness) on the splines
REML/ML for variance components and smoothing parameters
contraindicated_when: cross-sectional i.i.d. data with no clustering (plain GAM is simpler and equally valid)
binary or low-count outcomes with small clusters (<~20 obs/cluster), where DPQL bias is severe; prefer GLMM with Laplace/quadrature or Bayesian fitting
very large panels (thousands of subjects, many time points) where fitting cost is prohibitive
relationships dominated by strong covariate interactions that violate additivity
high-dimensional feature spaces or pure prediction tasks where tree ensembles dominate

target.notes: Any exponential-family response via a link function (identity, log, logit, etc.); the additive predictor is on the link scale, same distributional flexibility as a GLM.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds to low thousands per smooth term; small n relative to knots causes oversmoothing or unstable smoothing-parameter estimation
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; degrades and loses interpretability beyond ~20-50 predictors
needs: enough samples per smooth to estimate effective degrees of freedom

features.interpretability: high - each predictor's effect is a separate f_i(x_i) curve that can be plotted and read directly; main appeal of the family
features.notes: continuous predictors benefit from smooth basis expansions (penalized regression/smoothing splines); categorical handled as parametric terms; cyclic smooths available for periodic/seasonal inputs

assumptions: effects are additive across predictors unless interactions are added explicitly via tensor-product smooths
response follows the chosen exponential-family distribution with correct link
each smooth function is reasonably smooth (penalty on second derivative / roughness)
observations conditionally independent given the predictors
loss: penalized likelihood / penalized deviance for the chosen exponential-family distribution (squared error for Gaussian, log-loss for binomial, Poisson deviance for counts, gamma deviance)
smoothing parameters chosen by GCV or REML
contraindicated_when: strong high-order interactions dominate and accuracy outweighs interpretability (gradient-boosted trees / neural nets win)
high-dimensional p >> n or many predictors where a smooth per feature is impractical and additivity is untenable
raw image, text, or graph inputs with no engineered tabular features
sample size too small to support the basis dimension, producing unstable or oversmoothed fits

children.name: Linear
children.diff_siblings: Fits a strictly additive linear combination of features to minimize the sum of squared residuals (OLS), producing closed-form coefficients — unlike siblings that relax linearity (Polynomial), add regularization penalties (Ridge, Lasso), or use non-parametric fitting (SVR, Tree-based).
strengths: Coefficients are directly interpretable as the marginal effect of each predictor on the target, in the same units as the target
OLS yields the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE) under Gauss-Markov conditions — no iterative optimization needed, solution is exact
Extrapolates predictably outside the training range because the relationship is globally linear, unlike tree or kernel methods that plateau
weaknesses: Cannot capture non-linear or interaction effects without manual feature engineering, causing systematic underfitting when the true relationship is curved
Coefficient estimates become unstable and variance inflates sharply when predictors are collinear (VIF > 10), making inference unreliable
A single high-leverage outlier can shift the regression plane substantially because OLS penalizes squared errors, giving disproportionate weight to extreme points
recommended_for: Predicting a continuous target from a small set of well-understood, roughly independent predictors where interpretability and inference (p-values, CIs) are required — e.g., clinical dosage response with 3-5 biomarkers
Establishing a fast, transparent baseline in tabular regression tasks where the signal is expected to be monotone and the feature count is well below the sample size (p << n)
not_recommended_for: Datasets with strong non-linear patterns (e.g., exponential growth, periodic signals) where residual plots show clear curvature — the model will have high bias regardless of sample size

High-dimensional settings where p approaches or exceeds n (e.g., genomics with thousands of SNPs and hundreds of samples), as OLS becomes underdetermined and coefficients are not unique without regularization
children.curiosity: The method of least squares was first published by Adrien-Marie Legendre in 1805 in 'Nouvelles méthodes pour la détermination des orbites des comètes'; Carl Friedrich Gauss later claimed (1809) to have used it since 1795, sparking one of the most famous priority disputes in the history of mathematics.

children.name: Simple Linear Regression
children.diff_siblings: Fits exactly one predictor against the response via the closed-form OLS solution β₁ = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)(yᵢ−ȳ)/Σ(xᵢ−x̄)², while Multiple Linear Regression extends the design matrix to p > 1 predictors and requires the matrix inverse (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy.
strengths: Analytical solution requires no iterative optimization, making fitting instantaneous even on large datasets.
The slope coefficient is directly interpretable as the marginal effect of X on Y in the original units.
Minimal data requirements: only n > 2 observations are needed to estimate both parameters and assess fit.
weaknesses: Restricted to a single predictor, so any omitted correlated variable inflates the residual variance and biases β₁.
Assumes a strictly linear conditional mean; nonlinear true relationships yield systematically biased predictions across the range of X.
Sensitive to a single high-leverage outlier because OLS minimizes squared errors and one extreme point can rotate the fitted line substantially.
recommended_for: Establishing a baseline relationship between one continuous driver and a continuous outcome when theory supports a linear mechanism (e.g., dose–response with a single drug concentration).
Teaching and model-audit contexts where full interpretability and a closed-form benchmark are required before adding complexity.
not_recommended_for: Datasets where multiple correlated predictors jointly explain the response, because omitting them produces a biased slope and artificially inflated R².
Responses with heteroscedastic or heavy-tailed residuals (e.g., financial returns), where OLS standard errors are invalid and weighted or robust regression is needed.
children.curiosity: The method of least squares underlying this model was first published by Adrien-Marie Legendre in 1805 and independently claimed by Carl Friedrich Gauss (who asserted use since 1795), sparking one of the most famous priority disputes in the history of science; Francis Galton later coined the term 'regression' in 1886 while studying parent–child height data.
keywords: predict a numeric value from one variable
fit a straight line to data
how does one variable affect another

target.notes: Models the conditional mean E[Y|X] as a linear function of a single predictor; residuals assumed iid Gaussian for valid inference (intervals, t-tests on slope).

data_regime.rows: works from n>2 up to arbitrarily large n (closed-form OLS scales trivially)
data_regime.dimensionality: strictly p=1 (one predictor); p<n by construction

features.interpretability: high: single slope is the marginal change in Y per unit X in original units, plus intercept
features.notes: Single numeric predictor; scaling unnecessary. Encode categorical X only if binary (becomes a two-group mean difference).

assumptions: linearity of the conditional mean in X
homoscedasticity (constant residual variance)
independent residuals
approximately Gaussian residuals for valid standard errors / CIs
predictor measured without large error and free of influential high-leverage outliers
loss: ordinary least squares (squared error)
contraindicated_when: multiple correlated predictors jointly drive Y (omitted-variable bias on the slope; use multiple regression)
true relationship is nonlinear over the range of X
residuals are heteroscedastic or heavy-tailed (use weighted/robust regression)
target is count, binary, proportion, or bounded (use GLM)
strong leverage points or outliers present

children.name: Multiple Linear Regression
children.diff_siblings: Extends simple linear regression by fitting a hyperplane y = β0 + β1x1 + … + βpxp via OLS across p ≥ 2 independent predictors simultaneously, partitioning explained variance among all regressors rather than a single one.
strengths: Coefficients are directly interpretable as the marginal effect of each predictor holding all others constant, enabling causal-style reasoning when assumptions hold.
Under Gauss-Markov conditions (linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, no multicollinearity) OLS estimators are BLUE — minimum variance among all linear unbiased estimators.
Closed-form solution (β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy) makes fitting exact and computationally trivial even for hundreds of predictors on modest hardware.
weaknesses: Multicollinearity inflates coefficient standard errors and can reverse sign of estimates, making individual coefficient interpretation unreliable when predictors are correlated above VIF ≈ 10.
Assumes a strictly linear relationship: any nonlinear signal is captured only through feature engineering, so curved or interaction effects are missed unless manually specified.
OLS is sensitive to leverage points and outliers because the squared-loss objective gives quadratic weight to large residuals, distorting the fitted plane.
recommended_for: Econometric studies with pre-specified theory-driven predictors (e.g., wage as a function of education years, experience, and sector) where coefficient sign and magnitude must be reported and explained.
Low-dimensional tabular datasets (p < n, no strong collinearity) where a fast baseline with confidence intervals on each predictor is required before exploring nonlinear methods.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional settings (p approaching or exceeding n) where (XᵀX) becomes singular or near-singular and regularised alternatives such as Ridge or Lasso are necessary.
