Targets with bounded, count, or categorical distributions (e.g., binary outcomes, Poisson counts) where the linear prediction can fall outside the valid range and residuals violate homoscedasticity.
children.curiosity: The method of least squares underlying multiple linear regression was first published by Adrien-Marie Legendre in 1805 (Nouvelles méthodes pour la détermination des orbites des comètes), though Carl Friedrich Gauss later claimed he had used it privately since 1795 — a priority dispute that made both mathematicians' contributions foundational to modern statistics.
keywords: predict continuous value from multiple variables
effect of multiple inputs on output

target.notes: Unbounded real-valued response; inference (CIs, p-values) assumes conditionally Gaussian, homoscedastic errors. Not for bounded/count/categorical targets.

data_regime.rows: works on <100 to thousands; needs n > p with margin
data_regime.dimensionality: p < n required; (XᵀX) singular as p→n. No GPU/large-data needs.

features.interpretability: high — each coefficient is the marginal effect of a predictor holding others fixed
features.notes: Categoricals need dummy/one-hot encoding; scaling not required for OLS but aids coefficient comparison. Nonlinear/interaction effects only captured via manual feature engineering.

assumptions: linearity in parameters between predictors and mean response
independent, homoscedastic, ~Gaussian errors (for valid inference)
low multicollinearity (VIF below ~10; correlated predictors destabilize coefficients)
no high-leverage points or outliers distorting the fit
p < n (full-rank design matrix)
loss: squared error (OLS / minimizes sum of squared residuals)
contraindicated_when: p approaches or exceeds n, or strong multicollinearity present (use Ridge/Lasso/elastic net)
target is binary, count, proportion, or otherwise bounded (use GLM: logistic/Poisson)
relationship is nonlinear without engineered features
heavy-tailed errors or influential outliers (use robust/quantile regression)

children.name: Ridge (L2)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Lasso (L1), which zeros out coefficients via a non-differentiable penalty, Ridge adds a squared L2 penalty that yields a unique closed-form solution (A^T A + λI)^-1 A^T y, shrinking all coefficients toward zero proportionally but never exactly to zero.
strengths: Closed-form analytical solution makes fitting computationally exact and fast, with no iterative optimization required.
Distributes shrinkage evenly across correlated predictors, stabilizing coefficient estimates instead of arbitrarily selecting one among a correlated group.
Always invertible system: the λI term guarantees (A^T A + λI) is positive definite even when A^T A is singular due to multicollinearity.
weaknesses: Retains all features regardless of λ, producing no sparse model and making interpretation harder when many predictors are irrelevant.
Requires tuning λ via cross-validation; the optimal λ is problem-dependent and has no universal default.
Shrinkage is uniform across all coefficients, so it penalizes large-signal predictors alongside noisy ones, potentially underfitting when a few variables dominate.
recommended_for: Prediction tasks with many correlated numeric predictors (e.g., genomic data with p >> n), where coefficient instability from OLS degrades out-of-sample accuracy.
Linear models where all predictors are believed to contribute and a dense coefficient vector is acceptable, such as financial return forecasting with many correlated macro indicators.
not_recommended_for: Problems requiring automatic feature selection, where a sparse model is needed for interpretability or deployment — Lasso or Elastic Net are more appropriate.
Non-linear relationships: Ridge only regularizes a linear mapping; adding L2 to OLS does not capture interactions or curvature without explicit feature engineering.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Arthur Hoerl and Robert Kennard in two landmark papers in Technometrics (1970), where they proved that there always exists a λ > 0 for which Ridge estimator has strictly lower mean squared error than OLS — the first formal bias-variance tradeoff result for penalized regression.

target.notes: Models conditional mean as a linear function; native objective assumes Gaussian/homoscedastic noise. Extends to GLM families only via kernel/IRLS variants, not in the base estimator.

data_regime.rows: works on <1k; closed-form scales fine to moderate n
data_regime.dimensionality: handles p>n and p>>n well (this is its primary use case vs OLS); also good when p<n but predictors are collinear

features.interpretability: medium-high: coefficients are signed linear weights, but no sparsity so a large p makes the dense vector harder to read; categoricals must be one-hot encoded
features.notes: Predictors MUST be standardized (zero mean, unit variance) before fitting because the L2 penalty is scale-dependent; intercept is conventionally left unpenalized. Nonlinearity requires explicit feature engineering (polynomials, interactions, basis expansion).

assumptions: linear relationship between predictors and conditional mean
additive errors with roughly constant variance (homoscedasticity) for the squared-error objective to be efficient
features standardized to a common scale (penalty is not scale-invariant)
all predictors plausibly contribute (no expectation of an exactly sparse true model)
loss: L2-penalized squared error: ||y - Xb||^2 + lambda*||b||^2 (Tikhonov regularization)
contraindicated_when: automatic feature selection / sparse coefficient vector is required (use Lasso or Elastic Net)
the true relationship is nonlinear or has interactions not encoded as features
a few strong-signal predictors dominate and uniform shrinkage underfits them
target is non-continuous (count, binary, time-to-event) — use the matching GLM/regularized GLM instead

children.name: Lasso (L1)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Ridge (L2), which shrinks all coefficients toward zero continuously, Lasso applies an L1 penalty whose geometry (a diamond constraint) forces some coefficients to land exactly at zero, performing simultaneous estimation and discrete variable selection in a single convex optimization.
strengths: Automatic feature selection: the L1 penalty drives irrelevant coefficients to exactly zero, producing a sparse model that eliminates predictors rather than merely down-weighting them.
Interpretability in high dimensions: when p >> n (e.g., genomics with thousands of SNPs and hundreds of samples), the sparse solution identifies the handful of active predictors explicitly.
Convex objective with efficient solvers: the problem has no local minima and is solved exactly by coordinate descent (e.g., LARS/glmnet), scaling to millions of features.
weaknesses: Arbitrary selection among correlated predictors: when two features are highly correlated, Lasso tends to pick one and zero out the other, with the choice depending on random seed or data ordering.
Biased coefficient estimates: the L1 shrinkage that produces sparsity also biases the non-zero coefficients toward zero, understating true effect sizes compared to OLS on the selected subset.
Single hyperparameter lambda controls both sparsity and shrinkage simultaneously, so the model that selects the right variables may over-shrink their coefficients and vice versa.
recommended_for: High-dimensional genomics or text data (p >> n) where the true signal is believed to involve only a small fraction of features and an interpretable sparse list of predictors is required.
Feature screening pipelines where the goal is to reduce hundreds of candidate regressors to a compact subset before applying a richer model, leveraging Lasso's built-in variable selection.
not_recommended_for: Problems with strongly correlated predictor groups (e.g., collinear sensor readings) where all group members carry genuine signal — Lasso will discard most of the group arbitrarily, losing information.
Settings requiring unbiased effect-size estimates for inference or hypothesis testing, since the L1 shrinkage introduces systematic bias that inflates Type II error in post-selection tests.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Robert Tibshirani in 1996 ('Regression Shrinkage and Selection via the Lasso', JRSS-B 58:267-288), Lasso was initially slower than Ridge to gain traction because no efficient algorithm existed; the LARS algorithm (Efron et al., 2004) later showed that the entire Lasso regularization path across all values of lambda can be computed in the same order of operations as a single OLS fit.

target.notes: Linear-Gaussian response; conditional mean modeled as linear in features. Extends to GLM families via L1-penalized likelihood, but the base node is squared-error regression.

data_regime.rows: works at any n; especially valuable when n is small relative to p
data_regime.dimensionality: handles p>n; shines when p>>n and the true active set is sparse

features.interpretability: high: produces a sparse coefficient vector, exact zeros remove predictors, surviving coefficients are directly readable as linear effects
features.notes: Requires standardizing features (zero mean, unit variance) before fitting because the L1 penalty is scale-dependent; categoricals must be encoded. Penalty applied to coefficients, intercept typically unpenalized.

assumptions: Linear relationship between predictors and conditional mean
Sparsity: only a small fraction of features carry true signal
Approximately uncorrelated relevant predictors (irrepresentable condition for correct support recovery)
Homoscedastic, roughly Gaussian errors for standard inference
loss: squared error (least squares) plus L1 penalty on coefficients
more generally penalized negative log-likelihood with L1 term
contraindicated_when: Groups of strongly correlated predictors all carry signal (Lasso keeps one arbitrarily, drops the rest); prefer Elastic Net or Ridge
Unbiased effect-size estimates needed for inference/hypothesis testing (L1 shrinkage biases nonzero coefficients)
True relationship is dense (most features matter) rather than sparse
Strongly nonlinear target-feature relationships without manual feature engineering

children.name: ElasticNet
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Lasso (pure L1) and Ridge (pure L2), ElasticNet minimizes a loss penalized by a convex combination of both — λ1‖β‖₁ + λ2‖β‖₂² — which explicitly enforces a grouping effect: strongly correlated predictors are shrunk together rather than one being arbitrarily zeroed out.
strengths: Grouping effect: when predictors are highly correlated, ElasticNet tends to include or exclude them as a bloc, avoiding the instability of Lasso's arbitrary single-predictor selection.
Handles p >> n: unlike Lasso, which can select at most n non-zero coefficients, ElasticNet is not limited by the number of observations and can retain all p variables if needed.

Tunable sparsity-stability trade-off: the α mixing parameter continuously interpolates between full Lasso and full Ridge, allowing the practitioner to match the penalty to the actual correlation structure.
weaknesses: Double shrinkage: the naive ElasticNet applies L2 on top of already-L1-shrunken coefficients, inflating bias; the corrected version rescales by (1 + λ2) but adds implementation complexity.
Two hyperparameters (λ and α) require cross-validation on a 2D grid, roughly doubling tuning cost compared to Lasso or Ridge.
Loses the exact sparsity guarantee of Lasso when α < 1: the L2 component prevents some coefficients from reaching exactly zero, so the model may include more predictors than expected.
recommended_for: Genomics or text classification with p >> n (e.g., 20 000 gene expression features, n = 200 samples) where correlated gene clusters must survive selection together rather than be randomly reduced to one.

Financial factor models where dozens of macroeconomic indicators are highly collinear and both sparsity (dropping irrelevant factors) and stability (not discarding an entire correlated group) are required simultaneously.
not_recommended_for: Settings where predictors are known to be near-orthogonal and the true signal is sparse: pure Lasso is sufficient and avoids the overhead of tuning α.

Nonlinear or interaction-heavy problems: the linear additive structure means ElasticNet cannot capture curvature or feature interactions without explicit feature engineering, at which point tree-based regularized models are more appropriate.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Hui Zou and Trevor Hastie (2005) in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B, the elastic net was motivated by the observation that in DNA microarray data the lasso selected at most n genes from p >> n candidates — a hard algebraic limit that the ridge component in ElasticNet circumvents by spreading weight across correlated groups.

target.notes: Squared-error loss implies conditional mean estimation with homoscedastic Gaussian noise; generalizes to GLM family (logistic/Poisson ElasticNet) but the canonical node is linear-Gaussian regression.

data_regime.rows: works on small n; designed to remain stable even when n is small relative to p
data_regime.dimensionality: handles p >> n (no n-cap on selected coefficients unlike Lasso); also fine for p < n

features.interpretability: high - linear additive coefficients; sign and magnitude directly readable, sparsity aids selection
features.notes: Predictors MUST be standardized (zero mean, unit variance) before fitting because both penalties are scale-sensitive; categorical features need one-hot/dummy encoding. Especially suited to highly collinear feature blocks (grouping effect).

assumptions: Linear additive relationship between standardized predictors and the conditional mean of the target
Penalty applied to standardized coefficients - failing to scale features distorts selection
True signal benefits from a mix of sparsity and grouped shrinkage; if signal is dense or perfectly orthogonal, pure Ridge or Lasso is preferable
Effects are not curvature- or interaction-driven (those must be engineered in explicitly)
loss: squared error penalized by lambda1*||beta||_1 + lambda2*||beta||_2^2 (convex elastic-net penalty)
supports log-loss / deviance variants for GLM extensions (logistic, Poisson ElasticNet)
contraindicated_when: Predictors are near-orthogonal and the true model is sparse - pure Lasso suffices with one fewer hyperparameter
Strong nonlinearities or feature interactions dominate - tree ensembles / kernel methods fit better
Exact hard sparsity is required (alpha<1 leaves small nonzero coefficients)
Very heavy-tailed or heteroscedastic residuals violating the squared-error / Gaussian assumption without robust loss

children.name: PCR (Principal Component Regression)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Ridge regression (which shrinks all coefficients continuously) and PLS (which constructs components using the response variable), PCR first performs unsupervised PCA on the predictors alone and then regresses on the top-k principal components, discarding the rest entirely.
strengths: Eliminates multicollinearity exactly: PCA produces orthogonal components, so the regression design matrix has condition number of 1 regardless of original predictor correlations.
Stable coefficient estimates in p >> n settings: by reducing to k < n components before fitting OLS, PCR avoids the rank-deficiency that makes standard least squares undefined.
Separation of concerns: the number of components k is the single regularization hyperparameter, tunable via cross-validation independently of the regression step.
weaknesses: Component selection is unsupervised: PCA ranks components by predictor variance, not by relevance to the response, so high-variance but response-irrelevant directions are kept while low-variance but predictive directions are dropped.
Coefficients lose direct interpretability: each original predictor's effect is spread across all retained components, making it impossible to isolate the contribution of a single variable.

Discards information discontinuously: Ridge shrinks all directions smoothly, while PCR hard-zeros the dropped components, which can cause high variance in predictions when the cutoff k is misspecified.
recommended_for: Spectroscopy and chemometrics calibration (e.g., NIR spectra with hundreds of collinear wavelength channels predicting a single chemical concentration), where predictors are far more numerous than samples and highly intercorrelated.
Genomic prediction across populations where thousands of SNP markers are strongly correlated due to linkage disequilibrium and sample sizes are limited relative to the feature space.
not_recommended_for: Problems where the response is driven by low-variance predictor directions (e.g., rare but critical sensor signals), because PCR will systematically discard those components in favor of high-variance but irrelevant ones.

Situations requiring individual predictor inference or regulatory interpretability, since PCR coefficients map back to rotated combinations of original features rather than to the features themselves.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Massy (1965) in the Journal of the American Statistical Association, PCR predates the widespread availability of computers capable of eigendecomposition at scale; Jolliffe (1982) later provided the formal theoretical justification for when dropping the smallest principal components is statistically justified.

target.notes: Single continuous response; OLS on retained PCs assumes approximately gaussian, homoscedastic errors. Multivariate response possible but uncommon.

data_regime.rows: works with small n, including n < p once reduced to k < n components
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for high-dimensional, highly collinear predictors; handles p >> n by truncating to top-k principal components before OLS
needs: cross-validation to select number of components k

features.interpretability: low: coefficients map to rotated PC combinations of original predictors, so individual variable effects cannot be isolated
features.notes: Predictors must be centered and typically standardized (scaled to unit variance) before PCA, otherwise high-variance/large-scale features dominate the components.

assumptions: Predictive signal lies in high-variance directions of the predictor space (PCA ranks components by predictor variance, ignoring the response)
Linear relationship between retained components and the response
Predictors are numeric and meaningfully correlated (dimensionality reduction adds value)
Approximately gaussian homoscedastic residuals for valid OLS inference
loss: squared error (OLS on the top-k principal component scores)
contraindicated_when: Response is driven by low-variance predictor directions (PCR discards them in favor of high-variance but irrelevant components)
Individual predictor inference or regulatory interpretability is required
Predictors are largely uncorrelated (no redundancy to compress; plain OLS or Ridge is preferable)
Response-aware component construction is needed (use PLS, which builds components using the target)
Smooth continuous shrinkage is preferred over hard component truncation (use Ridge)
Non-numeric / categorical-dominant or nonlinear feature structure

children.name: PLS (Partial Least Squares)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike PCR, which builds latent components solely to maximize variance in X (unsupervised), PLS constructs components by simultaneously maximizing covariance between X and Y, so each component is directly supervised by the response.
strengths: Handles severe multicollinearity (p >> n) without matrix inversion failures, because it projects X onto a low-dimensional latent space before fitting
Requires far fewer components than PCR to achieve equivalent prediction error, since components are chosen to covary with Y rather than explain X variance
Natively handles multiple simultaneous responses (PLS2), decomposing X and Y jointly into shared latent structure in a single model
weaknesses: Assumes a linear mapping between latent components and Y — genuinely non-linear predictor–response relationships require kernel PLS or a different model class entirely
Number of components must be chosen by cross-validation; selecting too many reintroduces overfitting, negating the regularization benefit over OLS
Latent components are linear combinations of all original predictors, making variable-level interpretation harder than in sparse methods like Lasso
recommended_for: NIR/NMR spectroscopy with hundreds of correlated wavelength predictors and a continuous chemical property response (e.g., protein content), where p >> n and multicollinearity is extreme
Metabolomics or genomics studies where dozens of correlated biomarkers must predict multiple clinical outcomes simultaneously, exploiting PLS2's joint decomposition
not_recommended_for: Datasets where predictor–response relationships are known to be non-linear (e.g., enzyme kinetics, pharmacokinetic curves), where standard PLS will systematically underfit

Situations requiring automatic predictor selection or sparse solutions, such as high-dimensional gene expression with a need to identify a handful of causal genes — Lasso or Elastic Net are better suited
children.curiosity: PLS was invented by Herman Wold in 1966 as part of the NIPALS algorithm (Non-linear Iterative Partial Least Squares) for econometric path models, and later adapted to chemometrics by his son Svante Wold in the 1970s–1980s, making it one of the few statistical methods shaped by two generations of the same family.

target.notes: Single (PLS1) or multiple simultaneous continuous responses (PLS2). No native likelihood for count/binary; classification handled only via PLS-DA dummy coding, which is suboptimal.

data_regime.rows: works with small n, including n in tens to hundreds
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for p >> n; handles extreme p>n without matrix inversion

features.interpretability: low-to-medium: latent components are dense linear combinations of all predictors; VIP/loadings give partial insight but no variable selection
features.notes: Predictors should be centered and scaled (unit variance) before fitting; component count chosen by cross-validation. Best when predictors are highly correlated/redundant.

assumptions: linear relationship between latent components and the response
predictive signal lies in directions of X that covary with Y, capturable in a few latent components
homoscedastic gaussian-like residuals for valid inference
loss: squared error / minimized prediction RMSE on continuous response(s)
contraindicated_when: predictor-response relationship is genuinely non-linear (use kernel PLS or non-linear models)
sparse solution or automatic variable selection is required (use Lasso/Elastic Net)
p < n with low multicollinearity, where plain OLS or ridge is simpler and adequate
target is count, binary, or time-to-event with a proper likelihood needed

children.name: Stepwise Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike OLS (which fits all predictors simultaneously) or Ridge/Lasso (which shrink or zero coefficients via a continuous penalty), Stepwise Regression iteratively adds or removes predictors one at a time using F-test or AIC thresholds, making discrete in/out decisions with no penalty term.
strengths: Interpretable subset selection: produces a plain OLS model with a small, named predictor set, making coefficients directly interpretable without any regularization artifact.
Works without tuning a penalty hyperparameter: inclusion threshold (p-to-enter/p-to-remove or AIC delta) has a natural statistical meaning and requires no cross-validated grid search.
Computationally cheap on wide datasets: evaluates O(p) candidate models per step rather than the 2^p combinations of best-subset search, scaling to hundreds of predictors.
weaknesses: Inflated Type I error and biased coefficients: each F-test step is an implicit multiple comparison without correction, so selected variables appear more significant than they are and coefficient magnitudes are systematically overstated.

Greedy path yields unstable selection: a small change in the data can swap which variable enters first, cascading into a completely different final model — variance across bootstrap resamples is high.

Ignores multicollinearity structure: when predictors are correlated, the algorithm may drop an important variable because a correlated substitute entered first, producing an arbitrary and misleading subset.
recommended_for: Exploratory epidemiological studies with ~10–50 candidate predictors where the goal is generating a short, interpretable hypothesis list rather than a production-ready model.
Legacy clinical scoring systems that must output a fixed small set of named lab values or vitals, where a plain OLS coefficient table is the required deliverable format.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional genomic or text data (p >> n): multiple-comparison inflation is severe and the greedy path is computationally wasteful compared to Lasso, which solves the full regularized problem in one pass.

Causal inference settings: the arbitrary variable selection path confounds the estimate of any individual predictor's effect, making stepwise-selected coefficients unsuitable for policy or mechanistic conclusions.
children.curiosity: The combined forward-backward variant was formalized by M. A. Efroymson in a 1960 chapter in 'Mathematical Methods for Digital Computers' (Ralston & Wilf, eds.), making it one of the earliest automated model-selection algorithms designed explicitly for electronic computers.

target.notes: Inherits OLS target assumptions; the response should be approximately conditionally Gaussian for the F-test/AIC selection steps to be meaningful.

data_regime.rows: needs n comfortably larger than the candidate predictor count; unstable when n is small relative to p
data_regime.dimensionality: p < n required; designed for ~10-50 (up to low hundreds) candidate predictors, not p >> n

features.interpretability: high - output is a plain OLS model on a small named subset with directly readable coefficients and no regularization artifact
features.notes: Categoricals dummy-encoded; correlated predictors degrade selection because a substitute may enter first and exclude an important variable.

assumptions: linearity of conditional mean in selected predictors
homoscedastic, approximately Gaussian residuals (F-test validity)
low multicollinearity among candidates (selection path is arbitrary otherwise)
candidate set is modest relative to n so multiple-comparison inflation stays bounded
loss: ordinary least squares (squared error) for the fitted model
selection driven by sequential F-test p-to-enter/p-to-remove or AIC/BIC deltas, not a penalty term
contraindicated_when: p >> n (genomic, text, wide tabular) - severe Type I inflation and wasteful greedy search; prefer Lasso
strong multicollinearity among predictors
causal / effect-estimation goals - data-driven selection biases individual coefficients and standard errors
need for stable, reproducible variable selection (high variance across bootstrap resamples)
valid post-selection inference required - reported p-values are optimistically biased

children.name: Best Subset Selection
children.diff_siblings: Unlike stepwise methods that greedily add or remove one variable at a time, Best Subset Selection exhaustively evaluates all 2^p subsets of predictors and picks the one minimizing a criterion (e.g., Mallows' Cp or BIC), guaranteeing a globally optimal subset for the chosen size k.
strengths: Globally optimal sparse model: among all subsets of size k, it finds the exact minimum-RSS solution, something stepwise heuristics cannot guarantee.
No shrinkage bias on retained coefficients: selected variables are fit by OLS, so coefficient estimates are unbiased unlike LASSO which penalizes all coefficients toward zero.
Dominates regularization methods (LASSO, Ridge) in high-SNR regimes where the true signal is strong relative to noise, producing better predictive accuracy.
weaknesses: Computationally NP-hard: evaluating all 2^p subsets becomes infeasible beyond roughly p=40 variables without branch-and-bound or mixed-integer optimization solvers.
High variance in variable selection: small changes in the training data can yield a completely different chosen subset, making the selection unstable.
Requires a model-size criterion (Cp, AIC, BIC, cross-validation) to choose k; the criterion choice is non-trivial and can lead to over- or under-selection.
recommended_for: Low-dimensional regression (p < 30) where interpretability and exact sparsity matter, such as clinical biomarker studies identifying the minimal set of predictors from a pre-screened panel.
High-SNR scientific settings where the true model is believed sparse and unbiased coefficient estimates are required, such as experimental physics or controlled agricultural trials.
not_recommended_for: Wide data (p >> n or p > 40) such as genomics or text features, where 2^p enumeration is computationally prohibitive even with leaps-and-bounds algorithms.
Low-SNR or noisy observational data where shrinkage from LASSO or Ridge reduces test error more than finding the exact best subset.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Hocking and Leslie (1967) in Technometrics, the paper proposed using Mallows' Cp criterion to compare subsets and developed the leaps-and-bounds algorithm to avoid evaluating all 2^p candidates, making the method practical for the first time on computers of that era.

target.notes: Linear regression target; assumes Gaussian homoskedastic noise for Cp/AIC/BIC criteria to be valid. Selection mechanism is task-agnostic but the underlying fit is OLS on a continuous response.

data_regime.rows: works on <1k; needs n > k for OLS identifiability of each candidate subset
data_regime.dimensionality: strictly p < n; practical only for p <= ~30-40 (2^p enumeration, or up to a few hundred with MIO/branch-and-bound solvers)
needs: model-size criterion (Cp, AIC, BIC, or CV)

features.interpretability: high: yields an exact minimal subset of predictors, each fit by unbiased OLS, directly readable as a parsimonious linear model
features.notes: Categorical predictors must be dummy-encoded; grouped dummies are not handled jointly (a level may be selected without its group). Sensitive to multicollinearity, which destabilizes which subset is chosen.

assumptions: linear relationship between predictors and response
Gaussian, homoskedastic, independent residuals (required for Cp/AIC/BIC to rank subsets correctly)
true model is sparse
high signal-to-noise ratio
low multicollinearity among predictors
loss: squared error / residual sum of squares (RSS) within each subset size
model-selection criteria across sizes: Mallows' Cp, AIC, BIC, cross-validated error
contraindicated_when: p >> n or p > ~40 (enumeration computationally prohibitive)
low signal-to-noise or noisy observational data (shrinkage from LASSO/Ridge lowers test error more)
strong multicollinearity (selection becomes unstable, high variance in chosen subset)
non-linear target-feature relationships
need for a stable, reproducible feature ranking rather than a single optimal subset

target.notes: Conditional mean modeled as linear in coefficients; OLS is the MLE under homoscedastic Gaussian errors. Best for unbounded continuous targets; for counts/proportions/rates prefer GLMs.

data_regime.rows: works on <1k; even tens of rows feasible if p is small
data_regime.dimensionality: requires p < n (ideally p << n); design matrix must be full-rank or coefficients are non-unique

features.interpretability: high - each coefficient is the marginal effect of a predictor on the target in target units, with closed-form standard errors enabling p-values and confidence intervals
features.notes: Categoricals need dummy/one-hot encoding. Scaling not required for fit but aids coefficient comparison. Non-linear/interaction terms must be added manually as derived features (polynomials, products).

assumptions: Linearity of the conditional mean in the coefficients
Independent, homoscedastic errors (constant residual variance)
Approximately Gaussian residuals for valid inference (CIs, p-values)
No perfect or severe multicollinearity among predictors (VIF < 10)
Predictors measured without large error; no influential high-leverage outliers
loss: squared error / ordinary least squares (sum of squared residuals)
contraindicated_when: True relationship is clearly non-linear (residual plots show curvature, periodicity, or exponential growth) - high bias regardless of n
p approaches or exceeds n (e.g. genomics, wide feature sets) - solution underdetermined; use Ridge/Lasso instead
Strong multicollinearity inflates coefficient variance and destabilizes inference
Heavy-tailed targets or influential outliers dominate the squared-error fit - prefer robust/quantile regression
Target is bounded, count, or proportion data where Gaussian-mean assumptions are violated - use the appropriate GLM

children.name: Non-Linear
children.diff_siblings: Unlike linear regression, where parameters enter the model linearly and estimates are computed in closed form via OLS, non-linear regression models encode parameters inside arbitrary functions (exponential, logistic, power, etc.), requiring iterative optimization (e.g., Levenberg-Marquardt) and making convergence dependent on initial values.
strengths: Captures true functional forms (growth curves, saturation, decay) that linear models cannot represent regardless of feature engineering
Model equation retains physical or domain interpretability — each parameter maps to a measurable quantity (rate constant, carrying capacity, half-life)
Fewer parameters than adding polynomial/interaction terms to a linear model to achieve equivalent fit, reducing overfitting risk on small samples
weaknesses: No closed-form solution: iterative solvers can converge to local minima or diverge entirely if initial parameter guesses are poor
Requires the analyst to specify the functional form in advance — misspecifying the equation produces biased estimates even with large n
Standard errors and confidence intervals rely on linearization approximations (delta method), which become unreliable when curvature is high
recommended_for: Pharmacokinetics and dose-response modeling where concentrations follow known exponential or Emax equations and each parameter has a biological meaning
Population growth or decay data (ecology, epidemiology) where the sigmoid or Malthusian form is theoretically motivated and sample sizes are modest (n < 500)
not_recommended_for: Exploratory settings where the true functional form is unknown and the goal is prediction, not mechanism — flexible methods (GAM, gradient boosting) give better fit without a structural assumption
High-dimensional inputs (many predictors): non-linear regression is designed for a small set of parameters in a known equation, not for learning from dozens of features simultaneously
children.curiosity: The dominant algorithm for fitting nonlinear regression models, Levenberg-Marquardt, was first proposed by Kenneth Levenberg in 1944 and independently rediscovered by Donald Marquardt (1963), who showed it interpolates smoothly between gradient descent and the Gauss-Newton method via a damping parameter, making it robust near ill-conditioned Jacobians.

children.name: Polynomial Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike spline or piecewise methods that fit separate low-degree polynomials over regions of X, Polynomial Regression fits a single global polynomial of degree n across the entire input domain, making it a one-piece parametric curve.
strengths: Closed-form OLS solution: no iterative optimization needed; coefficients are computed directly via the normal equations (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy.
Captures smooth, monotone or oscillating curvature with a single interpretable equation — the degree n is the only structural hyperparameter.
Exact multicollinearity between degree-1 and higher terms is handled by standard linear algebra; no kernel trick or distance metric is required.
weaknesses: High-degree polynomials oscillate wildly near the boundaries of the data range (Runge's phenomenon), producing unreliable extrapolation even one step outside the training interval.
The design matrix columns x, x², …, xⁿ are strongly collinear, inflating coefficient variance and making individual coefficient estimates numerically unstable for n ≥ 4.
A single global fit cannot adapt to local structure: a region of near-linearity and a region of sharp curvature in the same dataset force a degree high enough to distort the smooth region.
recommended_for: Physical or engineering relationships known to follow a polynomial law (e.g., projectile height as a function of time, dose-response curves with a clear peak) where a global parametric form is theoretically justified.
Low-dimensional datasets (n < 500, p = 1–3) where the true curvature is mild (degree 2–3) and interpretability of the exact coefficient values is required by stakeholders.
not_recommended_for: Time-series or spatial data with abrupt local changes or regime shifts, where a global polynomial will either overfit the transitions or underfit the flat regions.
High-dimensional feature spaces (p > 10): adding polynomial terms creates p^d interaction features, causing combinatorial feature explosion and severe multicollinearity.
children.curiosity: The use of polynomial curves for empirical data fitting dates to Adrien-Marie Legendre (1805) and Carl Friedrich Gauss (1809), who independently developed the method of least squares — the same ordinary least squares estimator used in polynomial regression today — to fit orbital trajectories with polynomial models.

target.notes: Same target assumptions as OLS: conditional mean is a polynomial in X, errors gaussian/homoscedastic for valid inference. Nonlinearity lives in features, not the link.

data_regime.rows: works on <1k; low n fine since model is parametric with few coefficients
data_regime.dimensionality: p<<n required; effective design width grows as p^d with degree d, so keep p small (1-3 raw features) and degree low (2-3)

features.interpretability: medium: single closed-form equation, but high-degree coefficients are hard to interpret individually and unstable
features.notes: Continuous predictors only; basis is x, x^2, ..., x^d. Center/scale or use orthogonal polynomials to combat severe collinearity among power terms (n>=4). Categorical/text/high-cardinality features not applicable.

assumptions: true conditional mean is a smooth global polynomial of the chosen degree
errors independent, homoscedastic, gaussian for valid OLS inference
no abrupt local regime shifts (single global curve cannot adapt locally)
predictors low-dimensional and well within training range (no extrapolation)
loss: squared error (ordinary least squares via normal equations)
contraindicated_when: extrapolation beyond training range needed (Runge boundary oscillation)
data has local structure / breakpoints / regime shifts (use splines or piecewise models)
p>10 or many predictors (combinatorial p^d feature explosion, severe multicollinearity)
high degree (>=4) required to fit (numerical instability, variance inflation; prefer regularized or spline basis)

children.name: Quantile Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike other non-linear regressors that model the conditional mean, Quantile Regression minimizes an asymmetrically weighted sum of absolute errors (the pinball/check function ρ_τ) to estimate any conditional quantile τ ∈ (0,1) of the response distribution directly.
strengths: Robust to outliers: the check-function loss is based on absolute deviations, so a single extreme observation shifts the estimated quantile by at most one rank position, unlike OLS where squared deviations give outliers quadratic influence.
Full distributional view: fitting multiple quantiles (e.g., τ = 0.10, 0.50, 0.90) reveals heteroscedasticity and skewness patterns that a single conditional-mean estimate would mask.
No distributional assumption on errors: consistency holds under very general error distributions, making it valid when residuals are heavy-tailed, skewed, or mixture-distributed.
weaknesses: Computationally expensive at scale: solving the linear programming problem for each τ is O(n^1.5) per quantile; fitting a full quantile process over many τ values on large datasets is substantially slower than OLS.

Quantile crossing: independently fitted quantile curves for different τ values can cross each other, violating the monotonicity of the true distribution and producing incoherent probability statements.

Inference complexity: standard errors require either bootstrapping or asymptotic sandwich formulas that depend on estimating the error density (sparsity function) at each quantile, which is sensitive to bandwidth choice.
recommended_for: Insurance and credit-risk modeling where the upper tail (e.g., τ = 0.95) of loss severity matters more than the average, and claim distributions are heavily right-skewed.

Wage and income studies where the effect of education or experience differs across low-, median-, and high-earning workers — heterogeneous covariate effects that OLS would collapse into a single average slope.
not_recommended_for: Problems requiring probabilistic forecast coherence across many quantiles simultaneously, where crossing quantiles would produce invalid predictive intervals — prefer isotonic-constrained or distributional regression instead.
Small samples (n < 50) where bootstrapped standard errors for extreme quantiles (τ < 0.10 or τ > 0.90) are highly unstable due to sparse observations in the tails.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Koenker and Bassett (1978) in Econometrica, the paper recast the classical sample quantile as a solution to a weighted absolute-error minimization, unifying quantiles and regression in one framework; Koenker later received the 2021 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences partly for this work.

target.notes: Models a conditional quantile tau of the response, not the mean. Best when the full conditional distribution (tails, spread) is of interest, or when prediction intervals are needed. Applicable to skewed/heavy-tailed targets where mean regression is unrepresentative.

data_regime.rows: works on small-to-moderate n; LP/IRLS solve is O(n^1.5) per quantile and scales worse than OLS on large n; extreme quantiles (tau<0.1 or >0.9) need enough tail observations (n in the hundreds+ for stable tail fits)
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; linear-in-parameters form, no built-in regularization unless penalized variant used

features.interpretability: high: coefficients are slopes on a given quantile, directly readable as covariate effect on that percentile
features.notes: linear quantile regression is parametric in covariates; nonlinearity must be supplied via basis expansion/splines. Scale-sensitive for regularized variants.

assumptions: linearity of the conditional quantile in covariates (for the standard linear form)
conditional independence of observations
sufficient observations near the targeted quantile, especially in the tails
valid inference requires estimating the error sparsity/density at the quantile (bandwidth-sensitive) or bootstrap
loss: pinball / check loss rho_tau (asymmetric absolute deviation); tau=0.5 reduces to least-absolute-deviations / median regression
contraindicated_when: only the conditional mean is of interest and errors are well-behaved (OLS is simpler and more efficient)
coherent multi-quantile predictive intervals are required, since independently fit quantiles can cross (use monotone/distributional regression instead)
very large n where per-quantile LP cost is prohibitive (prefer gradient-boosted quantile models)
very small samples (n<50) for extreme quantiles where bootstrapped SEs are unstable

children.name: Isotonic Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike splines or polynomial regression, which impose smoothness or parametric shape assumptions, isotonic regression enforces only a monotonicity constraint (non-decreasing or non-increasing output), fitting a step-function that is optimal in the least-squares sense via the Pool Adjacent Violators Algorithm (PAVA) in O(n) time.
strengths: No hyperparameters to tune: the degree of smoothing is determined entirely by the data, unlike splines (knots) or kernel regression (bandwidth).
Guaranteed monotone output: enforces the ordering constraint exactly, making it the standard post-hoc calibrator for classifier scores (e.g., Random Forest, gradient boosting).
O(n) exact solution via PAVA: scales linearly with sample size and produces the provably optimal least-squares fit under the monotone constraint.
weaknesses: Produces a step-function, not a smooth curve: the flat plateaus can be a poor fit when the true relationship is strictly increasing without jumps.
Overfits on small samples: with few data points the algorithm may create many small constant segments that do not generalize.
Strictly one-dimensional by default: extending to multiple predictors (partial orders) is NP-hard in general and requires exponentially more complex algorithms.
recommended_for: Probability calibration of binary classifiers whose raw scores are monotone but not well-calibrated (e.g., correcting overconfident Random Forest probabilities on datasets with ≥1000 samples).
Dose-response modeling in clinical or toxicological studies where a biological monotone relationship (higher dose → stronger effect) must be enforced without assuming a parametric form.
not_recommended_for: Relationships with non-monotone shapes (U-curves, humps, oscillations): the monotone constraint is violated by definition, producing a heavily biased fit.

High-dimensional feature spaces with multiple predictors: isotonic regression does not generalize naturally to more than one covariate, requiring a different approach such as GAMs or gradient boosting.
children.curiosity: The Pool Adjacent Violators Algorithm that solves isotonic regression exactly in O(n) was introduced by Ayer, Brunk, Ewing, Reid, and Silverman in 'An empirical distribution function for sampling with incomplete information' (Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 1955), predating its widespread ML use by decades.

target.notes: Fits a monotone (non-decreasing or non-increasing) map y=f(x). Most common production use is recalibrating classifier scores into calibrated probabilities (target in [0,1]).

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds to thousands+; unstable and overfits on <100 points (creates many tiny constant segments)
data_regime.dimensionality: strictly univariate predictor by default (single ordered x); multivariate isotonic on a partial order is NP-hard and rarely used
needs: a single monotone-ordered feature or a 1-D score to recalibrate

features.interpretability: high: output is a monotone step-function, directly inspectable as a calibration/dose-response curve
features.notes: Only the rank order of x matters, so it is invariant to any monotone rescaling of the predictor; no feature scaling needed. Requires the single predictor to be orderable.

assumptions: the true relationship is monotone in the predictor (non-decreasing or non-increasing) over the whole range
errors are well-approximated by least squares (PAVA minimizes weighted squared error)
a single ordering variable captures the signal
loss: weighted squared error (L2) solved exactly by Pool Adjacent Violators Algorithm in O(n)
extensions exist for other Bregman/L1 losses but L2 is the standard implementation
contraindicated_when: the relationship is non-monotone (U-shape, hump, oscillation) — the constraint forces a biased fit
two or more predictors must be combined (no natural multivariate form; use GAMs, splines, or gradient boosting)
a smooth curve is required and plateaus/jumps of a step-function are unacceptable
sample size is small (few hundred or fewer), where it overfits; Platt/sigmoid calibration is steadier
the predictor scores are not even monotonically related to the target (calibration assumption fails)

children.name: Tobit Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike other non-linear regression methods that model the observed outcome directly, Tobit models a latent continuous variable via maximum likelihood under a Gaussian error assumption, mapping it to a censored observed outcome through a known threshold.
strengths: Produces consistent estimates for censored outcomes where OLS coefficients are systematically biased toward zero by the proportion of censored observations.
Simultaneously models the probability of the outcome being censored (probit part) and its conditional magnitude (linear part) within a single likelihood function.
Directly interpretable marginal effects can be decomposed into the probability of being uncensored and the expected value conditional on being uncensored (McDonald-Moffit decomposition).
weaknesses: Parameter estimates are inconsistent under any violation of homoscedasticity or normality of the latent error term, with no robust fallback unlike OLS.
Assumes a single known censoring threshold; unknown or interval censoring requires model extensions (e.g., Tobit II, intrinsic estimator) that add complexity.
Asymptotic MLE standard errors can be unreliable in small samples with a high fraction of censored observations (above ~70-80%), inflating type-I error.
recommended_for: Household expenditure surveys where many respondents report zero spending on a category (left-censoring at zero) but the underlying propensity is continuous.
Labor economics wage equations where wages are top-coded at a legal or administrative cap, creating right-censoring at a known value.
not_recommended_for: Count outcomes with many zeros (e.g., insurance claims frequency), where a zero-inflated Poisson or hurdle model respects the discrete data-generating process.
Survival or time-to-event data with right-censoring from dropout, where Cox proportional hazards handles censoring without the Gaussian latent-variable assumption.
children.curiosity: Introduced by James Tobin in 1958 in 'Estimation of Relationships for Limited Dependent Variables' (Econometrica), the name 'Tobit' was coined by Arthur Goldberger in 1964 as a portmanteau of 'Tobin' and 'probit', reflecting the model's structural link to the probit likelihood.

target.notes: Observed outcome is a censored continuous variable: a latent Gaussian variable y* is observed only when above/below a known threshold, otherwise piled at the censoring point. Requires a substantial mass of observations clustered exactly at a known limit (corner solution at zero, top-coded cap).

data_regime.rows: needs enough observations in BOTH the censored mass and the uncensored region; MLE standard errors unreliable in small n when censored fraction is very high (>70-80%)
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred (no native regularization)

features.interpretability: high: coefficients act on the latent variable, with marginal effects decomposable into P(uncensored) and E[y|uncensored] (McDonald-Moffitt)
features.notes: Tabular data; standard linear-model covariate handling

assumptions: homoscedasticity of the latent error (estimates inconsistent if violated, no robust fallback)
normality of the latent error term (Gaussian)
single known censoring threshold
correct linear specification of the latent index
loss: censored Gaussian log-likelihood (MLE combining probit censoring probability and conditional linear density)
contraindicated_when: target is a count with excess zeros (use zero-inflated/hurdle Poisson or negative-binomial)
time-to-event data censored by dropout (use Cox PH or AFT, which avoid the Gaussian latent assumption)
heteroscedastic or non-normal latent errors
the mass point is a genuine discrete state rather than a censored continuous value
unknown or interval censoring without model extension

children.name: Beta Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike polynomial or spline regression that transform the predictor space while keeping a Gaussian response assumption, Beta Regression models the response itself via the beta distribution — parameterized by mean and precision — making heteroscedasticity and asymmetry intrinsic to the likelihood rather than treated as violations.
strengths: Variance is naturally tied to the mean (var = μ(1−μ)/(1+φ)), so heteroscedasticity in proportions is captured without any correction or transformation.
The logit link yields directly interpretable odds-ratio-style coefficients on the (0,1) scale without requiring a log or arcsine transformation of the response.

Flexible shape: the beta distribution covers symmetric, left-skewed, right-skewed, U-shaped, and J-shaped densities via a single precision parameter φ, adapting to the actual distribution of the proportion.
weaknesses: Strictly requires the response to lie in the open interval (0,1); exact zeros or ones (e.g., 0% or 100% pass rates) break the likelihood and require a zero/one-inflated extension (ZOIB).
Maximum likelihood estimation via Fisher scoring can be slow to converge and numerically unstable when φ is very large (data near a spike) or the sample is small.
Model diagnostics and goodness-of-fit tests are less standardized than for GLMs — pseudo-R² metrics (e.g., Ferrari–Cribari-Neto R²) and residual types vary across software implementations.
recommended_for: Modeling continuous proportions such as credit utilization rates or forest canopy cover percentages, where the response is bounded in (0,1) and visibly skewed or heteroscedastic.
Survey-based indices (e.g., satisfaction scores rescaled to (0,1)) across groups with unequal sample sizes, where variance naturally inflates near the midpoint and shrinks near the boundaries.
not_recommended_for: Outcomes that include exact 0 or 1 values without a zero/one-inflated wrapper, since the beta density is undefined at the endpoints and the MLE diverges.
Binary classification or count data expressed as k/n with small n (e.g., 3/5 correct answers), where the discrete binomial likelihood is more appropriate than the continuous beta approximation.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Ferrari and Cribari-Neto (2004) in the Journal of Applied Statistics, the model was motivated by the inadequacy of the arcsine-square-root transformation then routinely applied to proportions; Ferrari and Cribari-Neto showed that directly modeling the beta likelihood outperformed the transformed-normal approach in both bias and coverage of confidence intervals.

target.notes: Response must be a continuous proportion strictly in the open interval (0,1). Parameterized by mean mu and precision phi; variance = mu(1-mu)/(1+phi), so heteroscedasticity and skew are intrinsic. Exact 0 or 1 are undefined; needs a zero/one-inflated (ZOIB) extension.

data_regime.rows: works on small-to-moderate samples (hundreds); MLE via Fisher scoring can be unstable on very small n or when phi is very large
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred (classical GLM-style estimation, no built-in regularization)

features.interpretability: high: logit-link coefficients read as odds-ratio-style effects on the (0,1) scale; precision sub-model coefficients quantify dispersion drivers

assumptions: response is a continuous proportion in open (0,1), not a discrete k/n count
response follows a beta distribution given covariates (mean modeled via logit link)
correct link specification for mean and precision sub-models
observations conditionally independent
loss: beta log-likelihood (maximum likelihood / Fisher scoring)
optional separate linear predictor for precision phi (variable dispersion)
contraindicated_when: response contains exact 0 or 1 values without a zero/one-inflated wrapper (MLE diverges at endpoints)
outcome is binary classification or a k/n proportion with small n (binomial/logistic likelihood is correct, not the continuous beta approximation)
response is unbounded continuous (use Gaussian/gamma GLM) or a count (use Poisson/negative-binomial)
p>=n or strong collinearity, since there is no native regularization

children.name: MARS (Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike polynomial regression (global basis) or regression trees (step functions), MARS builds piecewise-linear segments using paired hinge functions max(0, x-c) that activate only past a learned knot c, enabling localized, continuous fits without assuming a global functional form.
strengths: Automatically detects knot positions and interaction terms via greedy forward selection followed by GCV-pruned backward elimination, requiring no manual specification of the nonlinear form.
Produces an explicit, inspectable equation of hinge-function terms, making feature importances and partial effects directly readable — unlike kernel or ensemble methods.
Handles mixed continuous and categorical predictors in the same model without preprocessing, because hinge functions operate feature-by-feature.
weaknesses: Piecewise-linear segments cannot fit smooth, globally curved relationships (e.g., sine waves) without an impractical number of knots, leading to jagged approximations.
The greedy forward pass is sensitive to noisy features: a spurious term admitted early can anchor subsequent knot placements and propagate error through the basis.
Does not generalize well beyond the training data range, as hinge functions extrapolate linearly from the last knot with no global smoothing constraint.
recommended_for: Actuarial and engineering regression problems with 3–20 predictors and 200–5000 observations where the response changes slope abruptly at unknown thresholds (e.g., material fatigue vs. load).
Exploratory nonlinear regression when interpretability is required: the resulting equation can be audited by domain experts and directly translated into scoring rules.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional settings with p >> n (e.g., genomics with thousands of SNPs), where the greedy search degrades and GCV-based pruning underestimates complexity.
Problems requiring smooth probability outputs over continuous domains (e.g., density estimation), where the piecewise-linear discontinuities in slope violate smoothness assumptions downstream.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Jerome Friedman in 'Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines' (The Annals of Statistics, 1991), the paper ran 67 pages and introduced Generalized Cross-Validation as the pruning criterion — a choice that made the method self-tuning and directly influenced the design of later boosting algorithms Friedman developed in the following decade.

target.notes: Native form fits a continuous response by least squares; extensions exist for binary/multiclass via classification wrappers but the core is regression. Best when the response has piecewise-linear structure with regime changes at unknown thresholds.

data_regime.rows: 200 to ~5000 typical; works on a few hundred, scales poorly to very large n due to forward-pass search cost
data_regime.dimensionality: p < n required; effective for 3-20 predictors

features.interpretability: high — yields an explicit additive equation of hinge terms max(0, x-c) / max(0, c-x), so partial effects, knot locations, and detected interactions are directly readable and auditable
features.notes: No scaling required; hinge functions act feature-by-feature. Handles mixed numeric/categorical without dummy preprocessing. Interactions are discovered greedily, not specified.

assumptions: Response is well-approximated by a sum of piecewise-linear basis functions (locally linear between knots)
Additive/low-order interaction structure; high-order interactions are hard to recover greedily
Signal-to-noise high enough that the greedy forward pass does not anchor on spurious early terms
Predictions only valid within the training range (linear extrapolation beyond outermost knots)
loss: squared error (GCV used for term pruning)
contraindicated_when: p >> n (e.g. genomics, thousands of SNPs) — greedy search degrades and GCV mis-prunes
true relationship is smoothly curved (sinusoidal/exponential) — piecewise-linear fit needs impractically many knots and looks jagged
extrapolation beyond observed feature ranges is required
very large n where forward knot search is computationally prohibitive
smooth continuous outputs needed downstream (slope discontinuities at knots violate smoothness)

children.name: Spline Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Polynomial Regression (single global polynomial) or Kernel/Locally Weighted Regression (local averaging), Spline Regression partitions the predictor domain at fixed knot points and fits separate low-degree polynomials per segment, enforcing continuity and smoothness constraints at each knot via matching derivatives.
strengths: Avoids the Runge phenomenon: low-degree polynomials per segment remain numerically stable where a single high-degree global polynomial oscillates wildly at the boundaries.
Smooth joins at knots (matching up to the (d-1)-th derivative for a degree-d spline) produce a globally smooth curve without requiring a high polynomial degree across the full domain.
Basis representation (B-splines) yields a sparse, well-conditioned design matrix, making least-squares fitting efficient even with many knots.
weaknesses: Knot number and placement must be chosen manually; uniform spacing misfits regions of high curvature while over-parameterizing flat regions.
Extrapolation beyond the boundary knots is unreliable: the terminal polynomial segment grows unboundedly, unlike natural splines or GAMs with boundary penalties.
Basis coefficients are not directly interpretable; understanding the fitted shape requires plotting predicted values rather than reading parameter estimates.
recommended_for: Dose-response or growth-curve modeling where the relationship changes regime at known or discoverable thresholds (e.g., hormone levels vs. age, drug concentration vs. effect).
Time-series smoothing with a moderate number of observations (~100–10 000) where the analyst can inspect residuals and adjust a small number of knots.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional input spaces: tensor-product splines for p predictors grow as k^p basis functions, making them impractical beyond two or three interacting covariates.

Problems requiring automatic, data-driven flexibility tuning — Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) with penalized splines handle knot density and smoothness selection automatically and should be preferred.
children.curiosity: The mathematical formalization of spline functions as piecewise polynomials with derivative continuity at joints was introduced by Isaac Jacob Schoenberg in his 1946 paper 'Contributions to the problem of approximation of equidistant data by analytic functions,' published in the Quarterly of Applied Mathematics — the same work that coined the term 'spline' in the mathematical sense.
keywords: flexible regression without specifying a formula
model nonlinear trends in tabular data

target.notes: Native form is least-squares regression of a continuous response on one (or few) continuous predictors; conditional mean is modeled as a smooth piecewise-polynomial curve. Extends to GLM-family responses only when embedded in a GAM-style penalized framework.

data_regime.rows: works from ~50 up; sweet spot ~100-10,000 where the analyst can inspect residuals and tune a small number of knots
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n required; effectively 1-2 (at most 3) predictors. Tensor-product bases grow as k^p, so high-dimensional interaction modeling is impractical

features.interpretability: medium: the fitted curve shape is easy to read by plotting, but individual B-spline basis coefficients are not directly interpretable
features.notes: Predictor must be continuous and reasonably densely sampled across its range. Knot count/placement is a manual hyperparameter; uniform knots misfit high-curvature regions. B-spline basis gives a sparse, well-conditioned design matrix

assumptions: Smooth, continuous relationship between predictor and conditional mean (continuity up to (d-1)-th derivative at knots)
Homoscedastic, independent Gaussian-like residuals for ordinary least-squares fitting and valid inference
Knots capture the true regime changes; mis-specified knot density biases the fit
Domain of interest lies within the boundary knots (no reliable extrapolation)
loss: squared error / ordinary least squares
penalized least squares (roughness penalty) in smoothing-spline / P-spline variants
contraindicated_when: Many predictors or many interacting covariates (curse of dimensionality in tensor-product bases)
Extrapolation beyond the observed predictor range is required (terminal segment diverges; use natural splines or boundary-penalized models)
Automatic data-driven smoothness/knot selection is desired (prefer penalized GAMs)
Predictor is categorical or sparse, or the response-predictor relationship is genuinely discontinuous/step-like
Very few observations relative to chosen knots, causing overfitting

children.name: SUR (Seemingly Unrelated Regression)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike siblings that fit a single equation, SUR estimates a system of multiple regression equations jointly via Feasible GLS, exploiting the cross-equation error covariance matrix to gain efficiency when residuals are correlated across equations.
strengths: Efficiency gain over OLS when cross-equation error correlations are non-zero: FGLS achieves lower variance by absorbing shared unobserved shocks across equations.
Allows each equation to have a different set of regressors, unlike multivariate regression which requires identical design matrices for all outcomes.
Enables cross-equation hypothesis testing (e.g., testing whether a coefficient in one equation equals a coefficient in another) within a single framework.
weaknesses: Gains over OLS vanish entirely when equations share identical regressors or when cross-equation error correlations are near zero, making the extra complexity pointless.
Covariance matrix estimation becomes unreliable when the number of equations N approaches the number of observations T; FGLS is rank-deficient when N > T.
Assumes linear relationships and homoscedastic, normally distributed errors within each equation; misspecification in any one equation propagates efficiency loss to all others.
recommended_for: Macroeconomic panel studies where multiple country- or sector-level outcome variables (e.g., investment, consumption) share common unobserved shocks but have different determinants per equation.
Demand system estimation (e.g., Almost Ideal Demand System) where budget shares for multiple goods are modeled jointly and cross-equation adding-up constraints must be imposed and tested.
not_recommended_for: Settings with many equations relative to time periods (N close to or exceeding T), where the covariance matrix estimate is ill-conditioned and FGLS performs worse than equation-by-equation OLS.
Problems where the true relationship is nonlinear or errors are heteroscedastic across observations, since standard SUR has no mechanism to model either without explicit extension.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Arnold Zellner in 1962 in the Journal of the American Statistical Association ('An Efficient Method of Estimating Seemingly Unrelated Regressions and Tests for Aggregation Bias', vol. 57, pp. 348-368), where he showed that joint GLS estimation of equations whose disturbances are contemporaneously correlated is strictly more efficient than OLS applied equation by equation.

target.notes: Multiple continuous outcomes modeled jointly as a system of equations; each equation may have its own outcome and its own regressor set. Designed for the case where the multivariate response vector has correlated errors across equations.

data_regime.rows: needs T (observations) comfortably larger than N (number of equations); efficiency and covariance estimation degrade as N approaches T
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred per equation; FGLS covariance matrix is rank-deficient and ill-conditioned when N>=T

features.interpretability: high; linear coefficients per equation with interpretable cross-equation tests and standard errors
features.notes: Cross-equation adding-up / linear constraints can be imposed and tested (e.g., demand systems).

assumptions: Linear relationship within each equation
Errors homoscedastic and normally distributed within each equation, with a stable cross-equation contemporaneous covariance matrix
Non-zero cross-equation error correlation AND differing regressor sets across equations (otherwise SUR collapses to equation-by-equation OLS)
T large enough relative to N to estimate the NxN error covariance reliably
Regressors exogenous (no simultaneity / endogeneity), otherwise FGLS is inconsistent
loss: Feasible Generalized Least Squares (GLS) minimizing covariance-weighted squared error across the equation system
Equivalent to system MLE under joint normality
contraindicated_when: All equations share identical regressors (gain over OLS vanishes)
Cross-equation error correlations near zero (no efficiency gain; added complexity is pointless)
Number of equations close to or exceeding number of observations (N>=T): covariance estimate ill-conditioned, worse than OLS
True relationships are nonlinear or errors are heteroscedastic across observations
Endogenous regressors / simultaneous determination (use 3SLS or other simultaneous-equation estimators instead)

target.notes: Continuous response modeled as a known parametric function of predictors plus additive (usually homoscedastic Gaussian) noise; non-Gaussian/multiplicative error needs weighting or a GLM/transform instead.

data_regime.rows: works on small samples (n < 500) when the functional form is known; few parameters keep it viable where flexible learners overfit
data_regime.dimensionality: p<<n strongly preferred — designed for a handful of structural parameters in 1-few predictors, not high-dimensional feature sets
needs: reasonable initial parameter values for the iterative solver

features.interpretability: high — each fitted parameter maps to a measurable domain quantity (rate constant, carrying capacity, half-life, asymptote)
features.notes: Predictors typically a single driver (dose, time, concentration); scaling/centering predictors improves solver conditioning and convergence.

assumptions: the chosen functional form (exponential, logistic/sigmoid, power, Emax, Michaelis-Menten) is correctly specified — misspecification biases estimates even at large n
additive, roughly homoscedastic, independent errors
low curvature near the solution so delta-method/linearization-based standard errors and CIs are valid
solver starts near the global optimum (no severe local minima / divergence)
loss: nonlinear least squares (sum of squared residuals via Levenberg-Marquardt / Gauss-Newton)
weighted least squares for heteroscedastic error
maximum likelihood under a specified error distribution
contraindicated_when: the true functional form is unknown and the goal is prediction, not mechanism (use GAM, splines, or gradient boosting)
many predictors / high-dimensional inputs
data span insufficient to identify the curve's nonlinear features (e.g. plateau or inflection not observed), making parameters unidentifiable
good starting values are unavailable and the surface has many local minima

children.name: Mixed Effects
children.diff_siblings: Unlike purely fixed-effects regression (one coefficient per group, consuming a degree of freedom each) or purely random-effects models (no population-level slope), Mixed Effects models partition coefficients into fixed effects (population mean) and random effects (group-level deviations drawn from a Gaussian prior), enabling partial pooling via BLUP shrinkage in a single likelihood.
strengths: Partial pooling via BLUP shrinkage yields more accurate group-level estimates than no-pooling fixed effects when groups are small or imbalanced — each group borrows strength from the population distribution.

Handles repeated-measures and longitudinal data natively by modeling within-subject correlation through random intercepts and slopes, without requiring wide-format pivoting or explicit covariance structures.
Produces valid inference (standard errors, p-values) for both the fixed population effects and the variance components, unlike GLS or pooled OLS which ignore group structure.
weaknesses: Convergence failures are common with complex random-effects structures (e.g., crossed random effects or random slopes with few observations per group), requiring manual simplification of the G matrix.

Assumes random effects are Gaussian and independent of predictors; violation of this exogeneity assumption (group membership correlated with a covariate) causes biased fixed-effect estimates — exactly the failure mode that motivates fixed-effects panel models.

Scales poorly to very large numbers of random-effect levels (e.g., millions of users): the mixed-model equations involve inverting an (N+q) × (N+q) matrix where q is the number of random-effect parameters.
recommended_for: Longitudinal clinical trials with repeated measurements per patient across irregular time points, where patient-level random intercepts absorb baseline heterogeneity and the fixed effect isolates treatment.
Multi-site educational or psychological studies where schools or clinics are sampled from a larger population, and the goal is to generalize beyond the specific sites observed.
not_recommended_for: Panel data where group membership is endogenous (e.g., workers selecting employers based on unobserved ability) — the random-effects exogeneity assumption is violated and a fixed-effects panel model is needed.

Problems with millions of crossed random-effect levels (e.g., user × item in large-scale recommender systems) where the mixed-model equations become computationally intractable; matrix factorization methods scale better.
children.curiosity: The mixed-model equations at the core of every modern LME solver were derived by Charles R. Henderson in 1950 for estimating breeding values in dairy cattle — a context with severely unbalanced designs and thousands of sires — making animal genetics the unlikely birthplace of a method now standard in clinical trials and social science.

children.name: LMM / lmer (Linear Mixed Models)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike GLS (which models only residual correlation) or GLMM (which extends to non-Gaussian responses), LMM decomposes variance into fixed population-level effects and normally-distributed random effects estimated via REML, enabling exact likelihood evaluation and principled shrinkage of group-level parameters.
strengths: REML estimation produces less biased variance component estimates than ML, particularly with small numbers of groups
Handles unbalanced and missing-at-random data without listwise deletion, because the likelihood is evaluated over all observed values
Random effects provide automatic partial pooling across groups, reducing overfitting compared to fitting separate OLS regressions per group
weaknesses: Assumes Gaussian residuals and Gaussian random effects; skewed or heavy-tailed responses cause biased fixed-effect estimates and invalid inference
Requires sufficient number of groups (roughly ≥ 5-6) to estimate variance components reliably; with few groups, REML estimates of random-effect variance collapse to zero
Cannot model non-linear relationships between predictors and response without manual feature engineering, unlike nonparametric mixed-effects extensions
recommended_for: Longitudinal clinical trials with repeated measurements per patient and irregular follow-up intervals, where within-subject correlation must be modeled and dropout is missing at random

Educational or ecological studies with observations nested in groups (students in classrooms, animals in plots) where group-level variability is a nuisance to control rather than the target of inference
not_recommended_for: Binary, count, or survival outcomes, where the Gaussian residual assumption is structurally violated and GLMM or Cox frailty models are the appropriate choice
Cross-sectional data with no clustering or repeated measures structure, where OLS achieves identical point estimates with lower complexity and no REML overhead
children.curiosity: Laird and Ware (1982) formalized the modern LMM in their paper 'Random-Effects Models for Longitudinal Data' (Biometrics, 38:963-974), introducing the two-stage likelihood framework that enabled REML estimation for unbalanced repeated-measures data and became the foundation for the lme4 package's lmer function.

target.notes: Conditional response is Gaussian given fixed + random effects; residuals and random effects both assumed normal. Not for binary/count/time-to-event (use GLMM / Cox frailty).

data_regime.rows: works on small-to-moderate n; needs a sufficient number of GROUPS/clusters (roughly >=5-6) to estimate variance components, not just total rows
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n on fixed effects preferred; designed for low-dimensional, interpretable predictors, not high-dimensional p>n

features.interpretability: high: fixed-effect coefficients are population-level slopes/intercepts; variance components quantify between- vs within-group variability
features.notes: Requires an explicit grouping/cluster id (subject, classroom, plot) for random intercepts/slopes. Relationship to predictors is linear in parameters; nonlinearity needs manual basis expansion.

assumptions: Gaussian, homoscedastic residuals
Gaussian random effects with constant variance
linear relationship between predictors and conditional mean
missingness is missing-at-random (MAR)
enough groups to identify variance components; correct random-effects structure specified
loss: REML (restricted maximum likelihood, default) for variance components
ML log-likelihood (needed for likelihood-ratio tests comparing fixed-effect structures)
contraindicated_when: response is binary, count, proportion, or time-to-event (Gaussian residual assumption structurally violated)
data is cross-sectional with no clustering or repeated measures (plain OLS is equivalent and simpler)
very few groups (<5-6), where random-effect variance estimates collapse toward zero
skewed or heavy-tailed residuals that bias fixed-effect inference
genuinely nonlinear predictor-response relationships without manual feature engineering

children.name: GLMM (Generalized Linear Mixed Models)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike LMM (which requires a Gaussian response with identity link), GLMM combines a non-Gaussian exponential-family response distribution and a link function with Gaussian random effects, making it the most general member of the mixed-effects regression family.
strengths: Handles non-Gaussian grouped data natively: binary (logit/probit link), count (log link), and proportion responses share the same random-effects framework without transforming the outcome.
Subject-specific inference via random effects: captures between-cluster heterogeneity and yields conditional (cluster-level) estimates rather than only population-averaged ones.
Accommodates overdispersion in binomial/Poisson responses by adding observation-level random effects, removing the need for a separate quasi-likelihood workaround.
weaknesses: Marginal likelihood requires integrating out random effects analytically intractable for non-Gaussian links; Laplace, PQL, or adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature are approximations that can bias estimates in sparse or rare-event data.
Computational cost scales badly with the number of random-effect dimensions: adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature becomes prohibitive beyond 2-3 grouping levels.
