children.diff_siblings: Unlike bagging siblings that train trees independently on bootstrap samples and average them to cut variance, boosting fits shallow trees sequentially, each one regressing on the residuals (negative loss gradient) of the current ensemble to systematically drive down bias.
strengths: Each new tree fits the gradient of the loss on prior residuals, so an ensemble of shallow trees reaches a far lower bias than a single tree or a random forest at equal depth
Accepts any differentiable loss (squared error, Huber, quantile/pinball), so swapping the loss turns the same algorithm into robust or interval/quantile regression
Shrinkage (learning rate) combined with row/column subsampling acts as built-in regularization, trading extra trees for markedly lower test error
weaknesses: Sequential dependence between trees blocks the across-tree parallelism that bagging enjoys, so training does not scale across cores the way a random forest does
Because every tree fits the prior residuals, it chases label noise and overfits unless learning rate, tree depth, and number of rounds are jointly tuned with early stopping
Under squared-error loss it is sensitive to outlier targets, since large residuals dominate the next tree's fit and the ensemble bends toward them
recommended_for: Structured tabular regression with mixed numeric/categorical features and nonlinear interactions, where modern variants (XGBoost, LightGBM) are the default strong baseline
Predicting conditional quantiles or prediction intervals by fitting the pinball loss, e.g. demand or price forecasting that needs P10/P90 bounds
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional unstructured data such as images, audio, or raw text, where deep nets capture spatial/sequential structure that axis-aligned tree splits cannot
Datasets with heavy label noise or many mislabeled targets, where the residual-chasing dynamic amplifies the noise and a variance-reducing random forest generalizes better
children.curiosity: The idea began with Schapire's (1990) proof that weak learners can be boosted into strong ones and Freund and Schapire's AdaBoost (1997); Jerome Friedman then recast it as steepest-descent in function space in 'Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine' (Annals of Statistics, 2001), introducing the shrinkage trick standard in every gradient-boosting library today.

children.name: Gradient Boosting Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike AdaBoost's exponential-loss sample reweighting or Random Forest's parallel bagging, it fits each successive shallow tree to the negative gradient (pseudo-residuals) of an arbitrary differentiable loss, framing boosting as stagewise steepest descent in function space.
strengths: Pluggable differentiable loss: swapping squared error for Huber or quantile loss yields robust or interval regression without changing the algorithm.
Depth-limited trees (typically 3-8 splits) capture nonlinear feature interactions automatically, modeling structure a linear regressor misses.
Shrinkage (learning rate) plus row/column subsampling act as built-in regularizers, giving fine bias-variance control by trading more trees for lower variance.
weaknesses: Trees are built sequentially on prior residuals, so boosting rounds cannot be parallelized like Random Forest's independent trees, slowing training on large data.
It keeps chasing residuals, so with too many iterations and no early stopping it progressively memorizes label noise and overfits.
Accuracy hinges on jointly tuning coupled hyperparameters (learning rate, n_estimators, max_depth), so defaults often underperform and grid search is costly.
recommended_for: Structured tabular regression on mixed numeric/categorical features (e.g. house-price or energy-demand forecasting) where nonlinear interactions matter and accuracy outranks training speed.
Heavy-tailed or outlier-prone targets such as insurance-claim amounts, using a Huber or quantile loss to avoid the distortion a squared-error fit suffers.
not_recommended_for: Online or streaming settings needing incremental updates per observation, since the sequential batch fitting requires full retraining to absorb new data.
Very high-dimensional sparse text or genomic data (p >> n), where regularized linear models generalize better and axis-aligned trees overfit without prohibitive tuning.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Jerome H. Friedman in 'Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine' (Annals of Statistics, vol. 29, pp. 1189-1232, 2001), which recast boosting as numerical optimization in function space and later directly inspired XGBoost (Chen & Guestrin, 2016) and LightGBM (Ke et al., 2017).

target.notes: Loss-agnostic: any differentiable regression loss. Squared error assumes symmetric noise; Huber/quantile handle heavy tails and intervals; Poisson/Tweedie deviance for nonneg counts/insurance frequency-severity. No distributional assumption is baked in beyond the chosen loss.

data_regime.rows: hundreds to ~1M; sweet spot 1k-500k tabular rows
data_regime.dimensionality: p < n strongly preferred; degrades when p >> n and features are sparse
needs: CPU adequate (sequential training, not parallel across rounds)
validation set or CV for early stopping and hyperparameter tuning

features.interpretability: medium: feature importances and partial-dependence/SHAP available, but the additive tree ensemble is not directly readable like a linear coefficient
features.notes: Scale-invariant (axis-aligned splits); no standardization needed. Handles nonlinearities and interactions automatically via depth. Categoricals need encoding (this classic sklearn-style GBM has no native categorical handling, unlike LightGBM/CatBoost). Robust to monotone feature transforms.

assumptions: i.i.d. samples; no autocorrelation modeling, so time-series leakage must be avoided by careful splitting
training distribution covers prediction range: trees cannot extrapolate beyond observed target/feature range
sufficient signal-to-noise: with very noisy labels and no early stopping it memorizes noise
loss: squared error (L2)
least absolute deviation (L1)
Huber
pinball / quantile (prediction intervals)
Poisson / Tweedie deviance
custom differentiable loss
contraindicated_when: p >> n sparse high-dimensional data (text, genomics) where regularized linear models generalize better
online/streaming data requiring incremental per-observation updates (needs full batch retrain)
extrapolation required beyond the training target range
strict latency/training-speed constraints on large data where parallel Random Forest or histogram boosters (LightGBM/XGBoost) are preferable
the target-feature relationship is genuinely linear and interpretability of coefficients is required

children.name: XGBoost Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike standard Gradient Boosting (first-order gradients only) and other non-linear regressors, XGBoost minimizes a regularized objective using a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss, incorporating both gradient and Hessian at each boosting step, with explicit L1/L2 penalties on leaf weights and tree complexity built into the objective function.
strengths: Second-order Newton updates converge faster and more stably than first-order gradient descent, requiring fewer trees to reach the same residual
Native L1/L2 regularization on leaf scores directly prevents overfitting without needing a separate validation-based early-stopping heuristic
Built-in sparsity-aware split finding handles missing values and zero-inflated features without preprocessing, using a learned default direction per split
weaknesses: Dozens of interdependent hyperparameters (eta, max_depth, subsample, colsample, lambda, alpha, min_child_weight) make tuning expensive and non-intuitive
Sequential tree construction is inherently serial at the boosting level, so wall-clock training time scales poorly when the number of boosting rounds is large
Predictions are a sum of step functions (piecewise constant trees), so extrapolation beyond the training range is flat and unreliable for regression targets
recommended_for: Tabular regression datasets with mixed feature types, missing values, and moderate size (10k–10M rows) where predictive accuracy is the primary criterion over interpretability
Kaggle-style structured prediction tasks with engineered features where the signal-to-noise ratio is high and hyperparameter tuning budget is available
not_recommended_for: Time-series regression requiring extrapolation beyond observed values, where the piecewise-constant leaf structure produces constant predictions outside the training range
Ultra-high-dimensional sparse text or genomics regression (>100k features) where linear models or neural networks handle sparsity more efficiently and with lower memory overhead
children.curiosity: Introduced by Tianqi Chen and Carlos Guestrin at KDD 2016 (arXiv:1603.02754), XGBoost won or contributed to winning solutions in 17 out of 29 Kaggle competition challenge tracks in 2015, which drove its rapid adoption as the default baseline for structured data competitions.

target.notes: Objective is configurable: squared error for symmetric continuous targets, Poisson/Tweedie deviance for count/zero-inflated insurance-style targets, gamma deviance for positive-skewed. No distributional assumption on residuals; predicts conditional mean.

data_regime.rows: best on thousands to ~10M rows; underperforms vs regularized linear models on <1k rows where it overfits
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n strongly preferred; degrades on p>>n ultra-sparse high-dimensional inputs (>100k features)
needs: CPU sufficient; GPU optional for speed

features.interpretability: medium-low: global feature importance / SHAP available, but the model is a sum of hundreds of trees, not directly inspectable
features.notes: No scaling/normalization needed (split-based, monotone-invariant). Sparsity-aware split finding handles missing values and zero-inflation natively without imputation. Categoricals need encoding (one-hot/target/native categorical support).

assumptions: target signal is captured by axis-aligned feature interactions and thresholds
test inputs lie within the training feature range (piecewise-constant leaves do not extrapolate)
enough rows per leaf for stable gradient/Hessian estimates
loss: squared error (reg:squarederror)
pseudo-Huber
Poisson deviance (count:poisson)
gamma deviance
Tweedie deviance
pinball/quantile (reg:quantileerror)
custom twice-differentiable objectives via gradient+Hessian
contraindicated_when: target requires extrapolation beyond observed range (e.g. trending time-series regression)
n is very small (<1k) relative to model capacity
features are ultra-high-dimensional and sparse (text TF-IDF, genomics >100k dims) where linear/NN models are more efficient
a transparent, coefficient-level interpretable model is mandatory

children.name: LightGBM Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike level-wise boosters (XGBoost) or ordered/symmetric ones (CatBoost), it grows trees leaf-wise (best-first), splitting whichever leaf yields the largest squared-error reduction, and uses GOSS and Exclusive Feature Bundling to shrink the cost of each split search.
strengths: Histogram bucketing of features into discrete bins makes split-finding scan K buckets instead of every sorted value, training up to 20x faster than classic GBDT at near-equal accuracy
GOSS keeps all large-gradient (high-error) rows and subsamples small-gradient ones, so it estimates split gain from less data without biasing the regression fit
Exclusive Feature Bundling merges mutually-exclusive sparse features into one, cutting effective feature count and memory on high-dimensional one-hot inputs
weaknesses: Leaf-wise growth chases deep, asymmetric trees and overfits on small samples unless num_leaves and min_data_in_leaf are tuned
Default histogram binning (255 bins) discretizes continuous predictors, slightly hurting precision on smooth low-noise regression surfaces
Native categorical handling and EFB introduce many interacting hyperparameters, making tuning less intuitive than depth-bounded XGBoost
recommended_for: Tabular regression on hundreds of thousands to millions of rows with many features, where training speed and memory matter
Wide sparse datasets (one-hot or count features) where EFB collapses exclusive columns and accelerates split search
not_recommended_for: Small datasets (a few thousand rows or fewer), where leaf-wise growth overfits and a regularized linear or shallow model generalizes better
Problems needing a transparent, auditable model, since an ensemble of asymmetric leaf-wise trees is hard to interpret directly
children.curiosity: Introduced by Guolin Ke et al. at Microsoft Research in the NeurIPS 2017 paper 'LightGBM: A Highly Efficient Gradient Boosting Decision Tree', which proposed the GOSS and Exclusive Feature Bundling techniques.

target.notes: Default objective is squared error on a continuous target; supports tweedie/poisson/gamma objectives for skewed, non-negative, or insurance-style targets. No distributional assumption on residuals beyond the chosen loss.

data_regime.rows: needs many thousands+; shines from ~1e5 to 1e7+ rows
data_regime.dimensionality: handles wide p including p>n via regularization and feature subsampling; EFB compresses sparse high-dimensional inputs
needs: large tabular data for leaf-wise growth to pay off without overfitting
CPU sufficient; GPU optional for speedup

features.interpretability: low; ensemble of asymmetric leaf-wise trees is not directly auditable (rely on SHAP/gain importances)
features.notes: No scaling/standardization needed; monotone to feature transforms. Native categorical handling (no one-hot required); continuous predictors are binned into ~255 histogram buckets, slightly discretizing smooth surfaces. Captures nonlinearities and interactions automatically.

assumptions: i.i.d. rows; not designed for autocorrelated time series unless lag/temporal features are engineered
sufficient sample size relative to num_leaves/min_data_in_leaf to avoid leaf-wise overfitting
informative signal is in feature interactions/thresholds, not smooth global linear trends
loss: squared error (L2)
L1 / MAE
huber
quantile / pinball (probabilistic intervals)
poisson deviance
gamma deviance
tweedie deviance
custom first/second-order gradient objectives
contraindicated_when: only a few thousand rows or fewer (regularized linear or shallow model generalizes better)
target is a smooth low-noise function where histogram binning loses needed precision (e.g. spline/GP fits better)
a transparent, regulatorily auditable model is required
strong extrapolation beyond the training feature range is needed (trees cannot extrapolate)
pure time-series forecasting without engineered lag/calendar features

children.name: CatBoost Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike XGBoost and LightGBM, which build asymmetric trees with arbitrary split conditions per node, CatBoost uses oblivious (symmetric) trees where every node at the same depth applies the same split, and eliminates target leakage in categorical encoding through ordered boosting on random data permutations.
strengths: Native ordered target statistics for categorical features: replaces one-hot encoding with per-permutation CTRs, avoiding target leakage without manual preprocessing.
Symmetric tree structure makes inference O(depth) via a single lookup table, producing prediction latency significantly lower than asymmetric-tree boosters of the same depth.
Strong out-of-the-box performance on mixed-type tabular data with default hyperparameters, reducing the need for extensive tuning compared to XGBoost or LightGBM.
weaknesses: Ordered boosting maintains multiple auxiliary models per permutation, making CPU training 1.5–2x slower per iteration than standard gradient boosting on the same data.
High-cardinality categoricals (thousands of levels) inflate memory consumption because the CTR statistics table grows with cardinality and the number of permutations.
Symmetric tree splits can underfit complex decision boundaries that require asymmetric partitioning, as every node at a given depth must use the identical feature-threshold pair.
recommended_for: Tabular regression datasets with a mix of numerical and high-cardinality categorical columns (e.g., e-commerce transaction logs with product IDs, user IDs, and city codes) where manual encoding is error-prone.
Production pipelines requiring fast batch inference on CPU, where the symmetric-tree lookup table provides low-latency scoring without GPU dependency.
not_recommended_for: Very large datasets (tens of millions of rows) with tight training-time budgets on CPU, where LightGBM's histogram-based leaf-wise growth is substantially faster.
Purely numerical data with no categorical features, where CatBoost's main architectural advantage is unused and XGBoost or LightGBM typically match or exceed its accuracy.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Prokhorenkova, Gusev, Vorobev, Dorogush, and Gulin (NeurIPS 2018, arXiv:1706.09516), CatBoost was developed at Yandex and its name is a portmanteau of 'Categorical Boosting'; the ordered boosting scheme was specifically designed to eliminate the prediction shift that affects all prior gradient boosting implementations when target statistics are computed naively.

target.notes: Default objective RMSE (squared error). Native support for MAE, MAPE, Quantile, Poisson, Tweedie, and custom objectives. Handles skewed/heavy-tailed targets well via robust loss choices.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ for stable boosting; ordered boosting/permutation overhead makes it best below ~tens of millions of rows on CPU
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; handles moderate-to-high p with built-in regularization, but not p>>n
needs: large labeled data for full benefit
GPU optional (accelerates training; CPU inference is fast via oblivious trees)

features.interpretability: medium: tree-based feature importances, SHAP support, but ensemble of symmetric trees is not directly inspectable
features.notes: Key advantage is native categorical handling via ordered target statistics (CTRs); no manual one-hot/label encoding needed. No scaling required (tree splits are scale-invariant). High-cardinality categoricals inflate memory.

assumptions: No distributional assumption on features; assumes target relationship is learnable via piecewise-constant additive trees
Symmetric (oblivious) trees assume the same split is useful across a depth level, which can underfit boundaries needing asymmetric partitioning
Ordered target statistics assume rows are exchangeable (no leakage-inducing ordering beyond what permutations handle)
loss: squared error (RMSE)
MAE / L1
MAPE
quantile / pinball
Huber
Poisson deviance
Tweedie
log-cosh
custom objectives via gradient/hessian
contraindicated_when: Purely numerical data with no categorical features (architectural advantage unused; XGBoost/LightGBM match or exceed accuracy)
Tens of millions of rows under tight CPU training-time budgets (LightGBM histogram leaf-wise growth is faster)
Very small datasets (<~1k rows) where simpler regularized linear models generalize better
Decision boundaries requiring strongly asymmetric tree structure that symmetric trees underfit

children.name: HistGradientBoosting Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike the exact GradientBoosting sibling that scans every sorted value at each split, it pre-bins continuous features into at most 255 integer histogram bins, dropping split-finding cost from O(n) to O(bins) per feature and using the Hessian (Newton boosting) instead of a line search.
strengths: Orders of magnitude faster than the exact GradientBoostingRegressor past ~10,000 rows, because gain is computed over 255 bins per feature rather than every distinct value.
Native NaN handling: at each node the grower learns whether missing samples route left or right by potential gain, so no imputer is needed and missingness becomes a usable signal.
Native categorical support (no one-hot) plus per-feature monotonic constraints (monotonic_cst), letting you enforce domain rules like 'price rises with size' directly inside the trees.
weaknesses: 255-bin quantization is lossy: features needing very fine cut points (e.g. tiny but meaningful sensor differences) can collapse into one bin and lose signal.
Reported split thresholds are bin boundaries, not original feature units, so they are harder to read for regulatory audits.
Trees are built sequentially like all boosting, so a single fit cannot be parallelized across estimators the way a random forest can.
recommended_for: Large tabular regression with tens of thousands to millions of mixed numeric/categorical rows containing missing values, where training speed and skipping imputation matter.
Problems needing business-logic monotonicity, such as credit risk scoring where predicted default probability must increase with debt-to-income ratio, enforced via monotonic_cst.
not_recommended_for: Small datasets under ~1,000 rows, where coarse 255-bin splits generalize worse than exact-split GradientBoosting or a simple regularized linear model.
Targets needing smooth extrapolation beyond the training range, such as long-horizon trend forecasting, since piecewise-constant leaves stay flat outside observed values.
children.curiosity: Its histogram binning was introduced by Ke et al. (2017) in 'LightGBM: A Highly Efficient Gradient Boosting Decision Tree' (NeurIPS 2017); scikit-learn's HistGradientBoostingRegressor, added experimentally in v0.21 (2019) and stabilized in v1.0 (2021), explicitly credits LightGBM as its inspiration.
keywords: fast gradient boosting on large datasets

target.notes: Native losses: squared error (gaussian), absolute error, gamma deviance, and poisson deviance for nonnegative skewed/count targets. Also supports pinball/quantile loss for conditional-quantile regression.

data_regime.rows: shines at tens of thousands to millions of rows; histogram binning makes it near-linear in n
data_regime.dimensionality: p < n preferred; handles moderate-to-high p but not p >> n sparse regimes well
needs: large tabular data to beat exact GBM and linear baselines

features.interpretability: medium: feature importances and monotonic constraints available, but split thresholds are reported as integer bin boundaries, not raw units, hurting auditability
features.notes: No scaling/imputation needed; continuous features pre-binned into <=255 quantile bins. Native categorical handling (no one-hot). NaN routed by learned gain, so missingness is a usable signal.

assumptions: additive piecewise-constant structure suffices; leaf predictions are flat, so no smooth extrapolation beyond observed feature range
enough rows per region that 255-bin quantization does not erase meaningful fine-grained cut points
loss: squared error
absolute error
pinball/quantile
gamma deviance
poisson deviance
contraindicated_when: n < ~1000, where coarse binning generalizes worse than exact-split GBM or a regularized linear model
target requires smooth extrapolation outside the training range (long-horizon trend forecasting)
features carry signal only in very fine differences that collapse into a single histogram bin
p >> n high-dimensional sparse settings (text/genomics) where linear/regularized models dominate

children.name: AdaBoost Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike gradient-boosting siblings that fit each new tree to the residuals/gradients and sum the outputs, AdaBoost.R2 reweights the training instances by their loss relative to the worst error in the round and aggregates predictions by a weighted median rather than a weighted sum.
strengths: Per-round error is rescaled by the largest error D = max|e_i| so every adjusted loss lands in [0,1], making the reweighting scale-free without manual loss tuning
Final output is the weighted median (weighted by log(1/beta_t)) of the base regressors, so a few wildly wrong learners cannot drag the ensemble's prediction the way a weighted mean would
Offers three selectable loss shapes (linear, square, exponential) so the aggressiveness of reweighting hard cases can be matched to the problem
weaknesses: Because every error is normalized against the single worst instance D, one extreme outlier compresses all other errors toward zero and stalls learning on the rest of the data
Locked to its exponential-family reweighting scheme, so it cannot optimize arbitrary differentiable objectives (Huber, quantile) the way gradient boosting can
Sequential reweighting forbids parallel tree construction and offers none of the regularization (shrinkage, column subsampling) that modern boosters use to curb overfitting
recommended_for: Low-to-moderate-noise tabular regression where short decision-tree stumps need a quick accuracy lift without tuning a learning rate
Small-to-medium datasets where the weighted-median aggregation gives robustness against a handful of badly-predicted points while keeping the model interpretable
not_recommended_for: Datasets with heavy-tailed targets or genuine outliers, since normalizing by the maximum error makes the whole reweighting collapse around those points
Large high-dimensional problems needing custom loss functions or fast training, where regularized gradient boosters (XGBoost, LightGBM) are both faster and more accurate
children.curiosity: Introduced by Harris Drucker (1997) in 'Improving Regressors using Boosting Techniques' (ICML); scikit-learn's AdaBoostRegressor implements exactly this AdaBoost.R2 variant, including its weighted-median aggregation step.

target.notes: Single continuous response. AdaBoost.R2 aggregates base regressors by a weighted median, so it is fairly robust to a few mispredicted points but assumes no extreme outliers (error normalization by the max residual breaks down on heavy tails).

data_regime.rows: small-to-medium; works on <1k to low tens of thousands
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; moderate p

features.interpretability: medium; ensemble of shallow trees, less transparent than a single tree but no opaque deep architecture
features.notes: Tree base learners (commonly stumps/shallow trees) handle nonlinearities and interactions; no scaling required; raw categoricals need encoding.

assumptions: No genuine outliers / heavy-tailed targets: per-round errors are rescaled by the single largest residual, so one extreme point compresses all other losses toward zero and stalls learning
Signal learnable by weak tree learners with low-to-moderate label noise
loss: AdaBoost.R2 adaptive instance reweighting with selectable linear/square/exponential loss shapes (not an arbitrary differentiable objective)
contraindicated_when: Heavy-tailed targets or real outliers (max-error normalization collapses)
Need for custom differentiable losses (Huber, quantile/pinball) — use gradient boosting
Large high-dimensional data needing fast/parallel training and regularization — prefer XGBoost/LightGBM
High label noise (sequential reweighting overfits noisy points)

children.name: NGBoost (probabilistic)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike standard boosting siblings that optimize a single scalar loss to produce point predictions, NGBoost treats the parameters of a conditional probability distribution as the boosting target and uses the natural gradient (Fisher-information-scaled gradient) to correct the multi-parameter update geometry, outputting a full distribution rather than a single value.
strengths: Outputs a calibrated probability distribution (e.g., Normal, LogNormal, Bernoulli) over the target, enabling principled uncertainty quantification without post-hoc calibration.

Modular design: any differentiable proper scoring rule (NLL, CRPS), any parametric distribution, and any regression base learner can be combined, allowing the output distribution to be tailored to the domain (e.g., LogNormal for right-skewed survival times).

Natural gradient update is parameterization-invariant, meaning the learned distribution is stable across equivalent reparameterizations — a property ordinary gradient boosting on distribution parameters lacks.
weaknesses: Training is 5-10x slower than XGBoost or LightGBM on the same data because each boosting round requires computing and applying the Fisher information matrix to scale gradients across all distribution parameters.

Requires selecting the output distribution family in advance; a misspecified family (e.g., Normal for a heavy-tailed target) yields overconfident or biased intervals even if point predictions remain accurate.

Scales poorly to very high-dimensional feature spaces or millions of rows compared to histogram-based boosters (LightGBM, XGBoost), since it inherits standard decision-tree base learner overhead multiplied by the number of distribution parameters.
recommended_for: Medical prognosis or survival analysis where a calibrated predictive interval (not just a point estimate) is required, and the target follows a known parametric family such as LogNormal or Exponential.
Actuarial claim severity modeling with moderate-sized tabular datasets (tens of thousands of rows) where distributional adequacy and coverage of confidence intervals are primary evaluation criteria.
not_recommended_for: Real-time or high-throughput inference pipelines where training speed and prediction latency are critical, as the Fisher-information-scaled multi-parameter boosting is substantially slower than standard gradient boosters.

Problems with a purely ordinal or multiclass classification target where no natural parametric distribution applies, since NGBoost's probabilistic framework requires a well-defined continuous or discrete distribution family.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Duan et al. (2019) from the Stanford ML Group, NGBoost was the first boosting algorithm to generalize gradient boosting to multi-parameter probabilistic prediction using natural gradients, and was formally presented at ICML 2020 — where ablation studies showed that replacing the natural gradient with ordinary gradient updates caused the training to diverge on several benchmark datasets.

target.notes: Predicts the full conditional distribution; the parametric family is chosen in advance and must match the target's shape (e.g. LogNormal/Gamma for right-skewed, Exponential for survival times). Point prediction is the fitted mean.

data_regime.rows: best on hundreds to tens of thousands of rows; degrades past ~100k vs histogram boosters
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; tree base learners handle modest p but cost scales with number of distribution parameters

features.interpretability: low: ensemble of trees over distribution parameters, no closed-form coefficients
features.notes: no feature scaling required (decision-tree base learners); categoricals need encoding

assumptions: chosen output distribution family is correctly specified for the target; misspecification (e.g. Normal on heavy-tailed data) yields miscalibrated intervals
homoscedasticity is NOT assumed (variance is modeled as a function of features)

natural-gradient (Fisher-information-scaled) updates on distribution parameters
contraindicated_when: only a point estimate is needed and training/inference speed matters (5-10x slower than XGBoost/LightGBM)
millions of rows or very high-dimensional features
target is ordinal or multiclass with no natural parametric distribution
no plausible parametric family fits the target distribution

target.notes: Regression family; loss is swappable, so the same algorithm covers symmetric squared-error targets, robust/heavy-tailed targets (Huber), conditional quantiles (pinball), and count/insurance targets (Poisson/Tweedie deviance).

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds to thousands+; shallow-tree sequential fitting underperforms on very small n where a linear/regularized model wins
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; handles moderate p and irrelevant features via split selection, but degrades when p>>n with mostly noise features

features.interpretability: medium; global split-based feature importance and SHAP available, but individual predictions are a sum over hundreds of trees, so not directly inspectable
features.notes: Scale-invariant (axis-aligned splits), handles monotone nonlinearities and feature interactions natively, robust to mixed scales; no standardization required. Native categorical handling in CatBoost/LightGBM.

assumptions: Signal must be capturable by axis-aligned splits on tabular features; no spatial/sequential structure exploited
Targets reasonably clean: residual-chasing amplifies label noise and outliers under squared error
i.i.d. rows; temporal/grouped leakage must be controlled in CV
loss: squared error
Huber / absolute error (robust)
pinball/quantile
Poisson deviance
Gamma / Tweedie deviance
any twice-differentiable custom objective
contraindicated_when: Unstructured data (images, audio, raw text) where deep nets capture structure trees cannot
Heavy label noise or many mislabeled targets, where a variance-reducing random forest generalizes better
Very small n or need for a fully transparent parametric model
Strict low-latency/low-memory inference where a single tree or linear model suffices

children.name: Ensemble — Stacking / Voting
children.diff_siblings: Unlike the homogeneous tree siblings (Random Forest's bagged trees, Gradient Boosting's sequentially fitted trees), stacking/voting combines several already-trained, often heterogeneous base regressors, and stacking adds a second-level meta-learner trained on their out-of-fold predictions instead of growing more trees.
strengths: Meta-learner can correct systematic biases of base models because it sees their out-of-fold prediction errors and learns optimal per-model weights, often beating any single member
Combines model families with uncorrelated errors (e.g. a tree ensemble plus a linear model plus a kNN), so their residuals partly cancel rather than reinforce
Voting variant needs no extra training and gives an instant variance-reduction baseline by averaging the base regressors' outputs
weaknesses: Stacking leaks and overfits if base predictions on the training set are not generated out-of-fold via k-fold CV, inflating validation scores while degrading production accuracy
Inference cost is the sum of every base model plus the meta-model, so latency and memory scale with the number of members
Simple averaging in voting weights all members equally regardless of skill, so a weak base regressor drags the ensemble down
recommended_for: Tabular regression competitions or high-stakes tasks where squeezing the last fraction of RMSE justifies running and tuning several diverse models
Blending models with genuinely different inductive biases (tree ensemble + regularized linear + neural net) whose errors are weakly correlated
not_recommended_for: Low-latency or memory-constrained deployment, since every prediction must pass through all base models plus the meta-learner
Small datasets where the held-out folds needed to build clean meta-features leave too little data, making the meta-learner unstable
children.curiosity: Stacked generalization was introduced by David H. Wolpert (1992), who framed the meta-learner as a way to estimate and correct the biases of the base learners relative to the training set.

children.name: Stacking Regressor
children.diff_siblings: Unlike the Voting Regressor, which combines base predictions with fixed (or user-set) averaging weights, the Stacking Regressor trains a learned meta-model (level-1 estimator) on the out-of-fold predictions of the base regressors to discover the optimal combination.
strengths: Learns data-driven weights via a meta-estimator, so it can exploit complementary error patterns that fixed-weight averaging misses
Out-of-fold (cross-validated) base predictions feed the meta-model, preventing the leakage that would occur if base models scored their own training rows
Mixes heterogeneous learners (e.g. a tree boosting model, a linear model, a kNN regressor) under one estimator, since the meta-model only sees their numeric outputs
weaknesses: Cross-validating every base learner to generate level-1 features multiplies training cost roughly by the number of folds
The two-level pipeline (base regressors plus meta-model, each with its own hyperparameters) is hard to tune and to explain to stakeholders
Easily overfits when base models are correlated or the training set is small, because the meta-model then learns noise in their joint predictions
recommended_for: Kaggle-style tabular regression where several already-strong, diverse models exist and squeezing out the last fraction of RMSE justifies the extra compute
Blending models built on different feature views or algorithm families (linear, tree, distance-based) whose errors are weakly correlated
not_recommended_for: Low-latency or resource-constrained inference, since every base regressor plus the meta-model must run on each prediction
Small datasets or settings needing an interpretable model, where a single regressor matches the accuracy without the leakage risk and opacity
children.curiosity: Stacked generalization was introduced by David Wolpert (1992) in Neural Networks; Leo Breiman (1996) adapted it to regression in 'Stacked Regressions', showing that constraining the level-1 least-squares weights to be non-negative makes the combined estimator interpolating (its predictions stay between the minimum and maximum of the base learners).

target.notes: Regression meta-ensemble; target is a real-valued scalar. No native count/survival/probabilistic handling beyond what base learners and the meta-loss provide.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+; cross-validated out-of-fold meta-features make small-n unreliable and prone to meta-model overfit
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; high-p is delegated to base learners, the meta-model sees only the low-dimensional vector of base predictions
needs: compute budget ~k_folds x base training cost

features.interpretability: low; two-level pipeline (base models + learned meta-estimator) obscures feature attribution and combination logic
features.notes: Raw feature handling is whatever the base learners support; the meta-model's inputs are just the base predictions, so feature engineering happens at the base level. Base predictions should be from out-of-fold folds to avoid leakage.

assumptions: base learners make weakly correlated / complementary errors (diversity is the source of gain)
out-of-fold prediction scheme is respected so meta-features are leakage-free
training set large enough that the meta-model learns signal, not noise in joint base predictions
loss: squared error / RMSE (default and most common meta-objective)
any differentiable regression loss exposed by the chosen meta-estimator (MAE, Huber, quantile/pinball if meta-model supports it)
contraindicated_when: base models are highly correlated or only one strong model exists (no diversity to exploit; added variance hurts)
small datasets (meta-model overfits the joint base predictions)
low-latency or resource-constrained inference (all base models plus meta-model run per prediction)
interpretability is required
a single well-tuned regressor already matches accuracy (marginal RMSE gain rarely justifies the k-fold cost and opacity)

children.name: Voting Regressor
children.diff_siblings: Unlike the StackingRegressor sibling, which trains a meta-learner via cross-validation to learn data-driven combination weights, the VotingRegressor combines base models by a fixed (uniform or pre-specified) weighted average of their predictions, with no second-level model.
strengths: Averaging decorrelated base learners cancels their independent errors, lowering variance without adding a meta-model that could overfit the level-0 predictions
No cross-validation needed to combine: each base regressor is fit once on the full dataset, so it is cheaper to train than stacking and trivially parallelizable
Manual weights let a practitioner encode prior trust in stronger models, and dropping a member is a single estimator removal with no retrained combiner
weaknesses: Fixed weights are not learned from data, so a poorly performing member still drags the average unless the user manually down-weights it
It only averages point predictions, so it cannot exploit nonlinear or input-dependent ways of combining members the way a stacking meta-learner can
Combining highly correlated base regressors yields almost no variance reduction, so the ensemble can barely beat its best single member
recommended_for: Blending a handful of conceptually different, comparably-accurate regressors (e.g. a linear model, a gradient-boosted tree, and a k-NN) whose errors are weakly correlated
Production settings needing a simple, auditable ensemble where a transparent weighted average is preferable to an opaque learned combiner
not_recommended_for: Pools dominated by one clearly superior model or by mutually redundant, correlated learners, where uniform averaging only dilutes the best predictor
Cases where the optimal blend is input-dependent or nonlinear and the extra accuracy of a learned combiner justifies stacking instead
children.curiosity: VotingRegressor was added to scikit-learn in version 0.21 (2019) as the regression counterpart to the older VotingClassifier, generalizing simple prediction averaging into a first-class ensemble meta-estimator.

target.notes: Wrapper that averages the point predictions of several fitted base regressors; target type is whatever the base learners support, in practice real-valued tabular regression.

data_regime.rows: scales to whatever the base learners need; no extra data cost beyond fitting each member once
data_regime.dimensionality: inherits the p/n tolerance of its members; no CV folds so cheaper than stacking
needs: weakly correlated member errors to gain anything

features.interpretability: medium: the combination rule is a transparent fixed weighted average, but each base model's interpretability is its own
features.notes: Feature preprocessing/scaling is delegated to each base estimator; the voter only touches the output predictions.

assumptions: Member errors are approximately decorrelated so averaging cancels independent errors
Members are of comparable accuracy; weights are set a priori rather than learned
loss: minimizes variance of the averaged point prediction; does not optimize a joint loss (weights are fixed, not fitted to data)
contraindicated_when: One base model is clearly superior, so uniform averaging dilutes it
Base regressors are highly correlated, giving negligible variance reduction
The optimal blend is input-dependent or nonlinear (use stacking instead)
You want combination weights learned from data rather than hand-specified

target.notes: Regression meta-strategy; loss/target type is inherited from the chosen base learners and meta-learner. Voting averages base outputs directly; stacking trains a second-level regressor on out-of-fold base predictions.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ for stacking (out-of-fold CV must leave enough data per fold to fit a stable meta-learner); voting works at any n the base models support
data_regime.dimensionality: no intrinsic p/n constraint; inherits whatever each base learner can handle
needs: k-fold CV infrastructure for clean out-of-fold meta-features (stacking)

features.interpretability: low: prediction routes through multiple base models plus a meta-learner, obscuring per-feature attribution beyond what the base models expose
features.notes: Most effective on tabular data; gains depend on base learners having weakly correlated errors (mix tree ensemble + regularized linear + kNN/NN).

base members are highly correlated (e.g. several similar tree ensembles), so combination adds cost with little error cancellation
a single well-tuned model already meets the accuracy bar and the marginal RMSE gain does not justify the operational complexity

children.name: 1.1.2 Classification
children.diff_siblings: Unlike regression, which minimizes a continuous loss (e.g., MSE) over a real-valued output, classification learns a decision boundary that maps inputs to discrete class labels, optimized via losses defined on probability distributions over a finite label set (e.g., cross-entropy, hinge).
strengths: Decision boundaries can be evaluated with threshold-independent metrics (AUC-ROC), enabling calibration of precision/recall trade-offs independently of model retraining.
Probabilistic classifiers output posterior class probabilities P(y|x), making uncertainty quantification and cost-sensitive thresholding directly available without post-hoc calibration methods.
The discrete output space enables exact confusion-matrix decomposition (TP, FP, FN, TN per class), giving fine-grained diagnostic visibility that continuous regression outputs cannot provide.
weaknesses: Ordinal relationships between classes are ignored by default; predicting 'low' vs 'high' treats them as exchangeable, requiring explicit ordinal regression extensions to capture rank structure.
Class imbalance directly distorts decision boundaries toward majority classes, as standard cross-entropy loss weights all samples equally regardless of class frequency.
The hard partitioning of continuous phenomena into discrete bins introduces labeling ambiguity at class boundaries, making performance sensitive to how the target variable was discretized.
recommended_for: Medical diagnosis with discrete outcomes (e.g., disease present/absent, cancer stage I–IV) where the target is a finite, clinician-defined category and class-conditional probabilities drive clinical decisions.

Document or image categorization with a fixed label taxonomy (e.g., spam detection, object recognition in ImageNet-style benchmarks) where exhaustive class enumeration is feasible and training labels are reliably annotated.
not_recommended_for: Predicting inherently continuous quantities (e.g., house price, temperature, patient survival time) where discretizing the output into bins discards information and inflates error at bin boundaries.
Settings with open-set or continuously expanding label spaces (e.g., real-time entity recognition in evolving ontologies) where the closed-world assumption of a fixed class set is violated.
children.curiosity: The formal foundation for linear classification was laid by R.A. Fisher in 1936 ('The Use of Multiple Measurements in Taxonomic Problems', Annals of Eugenics), who derived the linear discriminant that maximizes between-class to within-class variance ratio — a criterion still embedded in modern LDA and used as a geometric interpretation for many classifiers.

children.name: Probabilistic / Bayesian
children.diff_siblings: Unlike siblings that learn a decision boundary directly (SVMs via margin maximization, logistic regression via sigmoid of a linear score, trees via recursive feature partitioning), Probabilistic/Bayesian classifiers model the joint distribution P(x, y) and apply Bayes' theorem to derive the posterior P(y|x), making class assignment an inference step over an explicit generative model of the data.
strengths: Reaches low error with very few training examples because the generative model encodes structural assumptions that substitute for data
Outputs calibrated class-posterior probabilities P(y|x) natively, without requiring post-hoc calibration as needed by SVMs or decision trees
Prior distributions allow injecting domain knowledge directly into the model, acting as a principled form of regularization without a separate hyperparameter tuning step
weaknesses: Conditional-independence assumptions (e.g., Naive Bayes) are rarely true: correlated features inflate confidence and degrade accuracy relative to discriminative models when n is large
Asymptotic accuracy is lower than discriminative classifiers given sufficient data, because misspecified generative assumptions introduce irreducible bias
Estimating the full class-conditional density P(x|y) becomes intractable in high dimensions without strong parametric constraints (Gaussian, multinomial), limiting expressiveness
recommended_for: Text classification with small labeled corpora (hundreds of documents) where bag-of-words features are approximately independent per class, e.g., spam filtering or topic routing
Medical diagnosis with structured tabular data where prior prevalence rates are known and calibrated probability outputs are required by clinical decision protocols
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional continuous features with strong inter-feature correlations (e.g., raw pixel images), where the independence assumption causes severe probability miscalibration

Large-scale benchmark tasks (> 10k samples, complex feature interactions) where discriminative models such as gradient boosting or neural networks consistently outperform generative classifiers on asymptotic accuracy
children.curiosity: Thomas Bayes formulated the theorem underlying this family in a posthumous 1763 paper 'An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances', published by Richard Price; the first practical text classifier based on it, the Naive Bayes model, was independently derived and empirically validated by Maron and Kuhns (1960) for document retrieval at RAND Corporation.

children.name: Gaussian Naive Bayes
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Multinomial and Bernoulli variants, Gaussian Naive Bayes models each feature's class-conditional distribution as a Gaussian, estimating per-class mean and variance via MLE to handle continuous real-valued inputs rather than counts or binary flags.
strengths: Trains in a single pass over data, computing only per-class mean and variance per feature — O(n·d) time and O(k·d) space regardless of dataset size
Naturally handles continuous features without binning or discretization, preserving ordinal information that Bernoulli NB would destroy
Remains effective with very few training samples per class because it needs only two parameters (mean, variance) per feature per class to define its likelihood
weaknesses: The Gaussian assumption fails silently on skewed or multimodal features (e.g., income, pixel intensities), producing miscalibrated posteriors without any warning
The naive conditional independence assumption ignores correlations between features, causing systematic bias when features are linearly or nonlinearly related
Zero-variance features (constant within a class) cause division-by-zero in the Gaussian PDF, requiring variance smoothing workarounds not needed in Multinomial NB
recommended_for: Sensor or biometric data (e.g., accelerometer readings, blood pressure measurements) where each channel is approximately normally distributed within a physiological class
Fast baseline classification over tabular datasets with continuous numeric columns and many classes, where training speed and interpretability of per-class distributions matter
not_recommended_for: Text classification with bag-of-words or TF-IDF features, where feature values are non-negative integer counts — Multinomial NB fits that generative model correctly
Datasets with heavily skewed, heavy-tailed, or bimodal feature distributions (e.g., financial transaction amounts) where the Gaussian PDF assigns grossly wrong likelihoods
children.curiosity: The Gaussian likelihood model for Naive Bayes was formalized and popularized by John Maron and colleagues in early pattern recognition literature, but its modern algorithmic form and the 'naive' label were systematically described by Minsky (1961) in a technical report, making it one of the oldest classifiers still in widespread production use.

target.notes: Class label is categorical; the Gaussian assumption applies to features given the class, not to the target. Outputs class posterior probabilities but they are typically poorly calibrated due to the independence assumption.

data_regime.rows: works on very small n; effective with few samples per class since only mean+variance per feature per class are estimated
data_regime.dimensionality: handles p>n and high p well; parameter count grows linearly with p (no covariance matrix), so no inversion or regularization needed

features.interpretability: high; each class is summarized by per-feature mean and variance, and per-feature contributions to the log-posterior are inspectable
features.notes: Expects continuous real-valued features that are roughly Gaussian within each class. No scaling required (variance is estimated per feature). Skewed features benefit from log/Box-Cox transforms; constant-within-class features need variance smoothing to avoid division by zero.

assumptions: features are conditionally independent given the class (naive assumption)
each feature is Gaussian-distributed within each class (unimodal, symmetric)
homoscedasticity is NOT assumed — variance is estimated separately per class and per feature
loss: maximizes class-conditional Gaussian likelihood via closed-form MLE (per-class mean and variance); predicts via maximum a posteriori, no iterative loss minimization
contraindicated_when: features are non-negative counts or bag-of-words/TF-IDF (use Multinomial NB)
features are binary/boolean flags (use Bernoulli NB)
features are heavily skewed, heavy-tailed, or multimodal within a class, making the Gaussian PDF assign wrong likelihoods
features are strongly correlated, where the independence violation biases posteriors
well-calibrated probability estimates are required without post-hoc calibration

children.name: Multinomial Naive Bayes
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Bernoulli NB (which models binary word presence/absence) and Gaussian NB (which assumes continuous features follow a normal distribution), Multinomial NB models term frequency counts as draws from a multinomial distribution, capturing how often each word appears — not just whether it appears.
strengths: Trains in O(n·d) time and classifies in O(d) per document, making it viable for real-time pipelines with millions of documents.
Laplace (additive) smoothing directly handles zero-frequency terms in the multinomial likelihood, giving a principled solution to vocabulary mismatch between train and test sets.
Outperforms Bernoulli NB on large-vocabulary corpora because term frequency explicitly differentiates a document mentioning 'cancer' once from one mentioning it 40 times.
weaknesses: The conditional independence assumption ignores term co-occurrence (e.g., 'New York' treated as two independent tokens), degrading accuracy on tasks where phrase structure matters.
Heavily imbalanced class priors can overwhelm the likelihood term, causing the model to default to the majority class regardless of content.
Produces poorly calibrated posterior probabilities — the 'naive' factorization drives estimates toward 0 or 1 — making raw outputs unsuitable as confidence scores without isotonic/Platt calibration.
recommended_for: Short-text document classification (news topic routing, support-ticket triage) where bag-of-words term counts are informative and training data reaches tens of thousands of labeled examples.
Spam and phishing email filtering where token frequency (e.g., repeated '$$$' or 'click here') is a direct signal and low-latency inference is required.
not_recommended_for: Sentiment analysis on reviews or social media where negation and word order are critical — 'not good' and 'good' produce identical unigram count vectors.
Tasks with continuous or mixed-type features (e.g., tabular data with numeric measurements), where the multinomial distribution is a fundamental mismatch for the data-generating process.
children.curiosity: Formalized by McCallum and Nigam (1998) in 'A Comparison of Event Models for Naive Bayes Text Classification' (AAAI Workshop on Learning for Text Categorization), where they showed that the multinomial event model consistently outperforms the multi-variate Bernoulli model at large vocabulary sizes because it encodes term frequency rather than mere occurrence.

target.notes: Discrete class label; per-class feature likelihood modeled as a multinomial over the vocabulary. Class prior estimated from label frequencies.

data_regime.rows: works from a few thousand labeled docs; scales linearly to millions
data_regime.dimensionality: handles p>>n (very high-dimensional sparse vocabularies); robust in the sparse-count regime

features.interpretability: high: per-feature log-likelihood ratios give directly readable token weights per class
features.notes: Expects non-negative count or frequency features (bag-of-words term counts, TF or TF-IDF). Sparse matrices ideal. Not for continuous/signed numeric features.

assumptions: Conditional independence of features given the class (ignores term co-occurrence and word order)
Features are non-negative counts/frequencies drawn from a class-conditional multinomial
Class priors are reasonably representative; severe imbalance distorts the posterior toward the majority class
loss: log-loss / maximum likelihood of the multinomial with additive (Laplace/Lidstone) smoothing
contraindicated_when: Continuous or mixed-type tabular features (multinomial is a distributional mismatch; use Gaussian NB or a GBM)
Tasks where negation/word order/phrase structure drives the label (sentiment, intent) since unigram counts collapse 'not good' and 'good'
Well-calibrated probability outputs are required without post-hoc isotonic/Platt calibration
Strong feature correlation makes the naive independence factorization badly biased

children.name: Naive Bayes Bernoulli
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Multinomial NB (which models term frequency) and Gaussian NB (which models continuous values), Bernoulli NB models each feature as a binary variable — term presence vs. absence — and explicitly penalizes the non-occurrence of class-indicative terms during scoring.
strengths: Explicitly penalizes absent features: non-occurring terms that are strong class indicators still pull the posterior toward the competing class, an effect absent in Multinomial NB.
Extremely fast training and inference on high-dimensional binary feature spaces, scaling linearly with vocabulary size and corpus length.
Performs well on short documents where term frequency carries little signal and binary occurrence is the dominant discriminator.
weaknesses: Degrades on long documents: as document length grows, ignoring term frequency loses progressively more signal, increasing misclassification.
Requires binarization of all features, discarding real-valued or count information that may be meaningful in the original data.
On average 27% higher error than Multinomial NB at large vocabulary sizes, as quantified by McCallum and Nigam (1998) across five corpora.
recommended_for: Short-text binary classification (e.g., spam vs. ham email filtering) where each document is represented as a bag-of-words presence vector and vocabulary size is moderate.
Sentiment or topic detection on tweet-length or headline-length text where word counts are rarely above 1 and binary occurrence is the natural feature representation.
not_recommended_for: Long documents (news articles, legal filings) where term frequency carries meaningful signal — Multinomial NB or TF-IDF-based models are more appropriate.
Datasets with continuous or ordinal features (e.g., sensor readings, gene expression levels) where discretizing to binary loses critical information and Gaussian NB is the correct variant.
children.curiosity: McCallum and Nigam (1998) formally named and compared the multivariate Bernoulli and multinomial event models in their AAAI workshop paper, finding that Bernoulli NB excels at small vocabulary sizes but the multinomial model reduces error by an average of 27% as vocabulary grows — a result that remains the standard empirical benchmark for choosing between the two variants.

target.notes: Class-conditional likelihood is a product of per-feature Bernoulli terms; class prior is multinomial over labels. Generative classifier estimating P(class)*prod P(feature_present|class).

data_regime.rows: works on <1k; trivially scales to large corpora
data_regime.dimensionality: handles p>>n (high-dimensional sparse vocabularies); robust as a strong baseline when labeled data is scarce

features.interpretability: high: per-feature log-likelihood-ratio contributions to the posterior are directly inspectable
features.notes: Requires binary/Boolean features (term presence vs absence). Continuous or count features must be binarized, discarding frequency/magnitude. Models BOTH presence and absence of every vocabulary term, so the feature space must be a fixed binary vector.

assumptions: Conditional independence of features given the class (naive assumption); strong correlations among features inflate confidence
Each feature is Bernoulli (binary occurrence); term frequency carries no signal beyond presence
Requires smoothing (e.g. Laplace/Lidstone) to avoid zero-probability for unseen feature/class combinations
loss: maximum likelihood / negative log-likelihood of the Bernoulli class-conditional model (closed-form MLE counts, no iterative optimization)
contraindicated_when: Documents are long or term frequency is informative (Multinomial NB or TF-IDF models fit better)
Features are continuous, ordinal, or count-valued and binarization destroys signal (use Gaussian NB or other variant)
Strong feature dependencies dominate and calibrated probabilities are required (NB posteriors are poorly calibrated, typically overconfident)
Large vocabulary text where ~27% higher error vs Multinomial NB (McCallum & Nigam 1998) is unacceptable

children.name: Complement Naive Bayes
children.diff_siblings: Instead of estimating the likelihood of a word given its target class, CNB estimates the likelihood given all other classes combined (the complement), then uses those complement weights to classify — a contrastive inversion that corrects the systematic bias Multinomial Naive Bayes develops toward majority classes.
strengths: Robust to class imbalance: complement statistics are estimated from the larger, more stable complement set, so minority-class parameters are less noisy than in Multinomial NB
Weight normalization (dividing each feature weight by the L2 norm of its weight vector) further reduces the compounding effect of the conditional-independence violation in long documents
Matches or beats Multinomial NB on standard text benchmarks (Reuters, 20 Newsgroups) while adding zero computational overhead — same O(n·d) training complexity
weaknesses: Offers no advantage over Multinomial NB when classes are perfectly balanced, because the complement set is equally large for every class
Still assumes conditional feature independence, so correlated words (e.g., 'machine' and 'learning' co-occurring) cause probability estimates to be miscalibrated
Outputs are not well-calibrated probabilities — the complement-based log-sums are relative scores, so Platt scaling or isotonic regression is needed when confidence values matter
recommended_for: Multi-class text classification with skewed label distributions (e.g., a 20-category news corpus where some topics have 10x fewer articles than others)
Spam or intent detection pipelines that use bag-of-words or TF-IDF features and need a fast, lightweight baseline that handles class imbalance without oversampling
not_recommended_for: Datasets where feature counts per class are comparable and classes are balanced, since Multinomial NB will perform equally well without the complement correction
Tasks requiring calibrated posterior probabilities (e.g., risk scoring or cost-sensitive decisions), because complement log-sums do not correspond to true class probabilities
children.curiosity: Introduced by Rennie, Shih, Teevan, and Karger at ICML 2003 ('Tackling the Poor Assumptions of Naive Bayes Text Classifiers'), CNB was shown to outperform a linear SVM on the Reuters-21578 benchmark — a result the authors themselves described as surprising given the model's simplicity.

target.notes: Class-conditional feature distribution modeled as multinomial over token counts; designed for skewed/imbalanced label priors where Multinomial NB is biased toward majority classes.

data_regime.rows: works from a few hundred labeled docs; cheap to scale to large corpora
data_regime.dimensionality: handles p>>n well (sparse high-dimensional vocabularies); strong baseline when features vastly outnumber samples

features.interpretability: medium: per-feature complement log-weights are inspectable, but the complement inversion + L2 weight normalization make them less directly readable than plain NB likelihoods
features.notes: Expects non-negative count features (bag-of-words / TF-IDF). Sparse term-frequency vectors are the native input; dense continuous features are not appropriate.

assumptions: conditional independence of features given class (violated by correlated co-occurring words, miscalibrating estimates)
features are non-negative counts/frequencies
multinomial generative model of token occurrence
loss: maximum-likelihood multinomial estimation with Laplace smoothing; decision by complement log-weight score (not a directly optimized differentiable loss)
contraindicated_when: classes are balanced and per-class feature counts are comparable (no gain over Multinomial NB)
calibrated posterior probabilities are required (complement log-sums are relative scores; needs Platt/isotonic post-hoc)
features are dense continuous/negative-valued rather than counts
strong feature correlations dominate and independence is badly violated

children.name: LDA (Linear Discriminant Analysis)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike QDA (which estimates a separate covariance matrix per class) and Gaussian Naive Bayes (which assumes diagonal covariance), LDA constrains all classes to share a single pooled covariance matrix, forcing decision boundaries to be strictly linear hyperplanes.
strengths: Requires estimating only one shared covariance matrix instead of k separate ones, making it statistically efficient with small training sets (e.g., n < 500).
Simultaneously classifies and reduces dimensionality to at most k-1 discriminant axes, which are directly interpretable as directions of maximum class separation.
Closed-form solution via eigendecomposition of S_W^{-1} S_B, with no hyperparameters to tune and no iterative optimization.
weaknesses: Fails when n < p (more features than samples) because the within-class scatter matrix S_W becomes singular and non-invertible.
Shared covariance assumption is systematically wrong when classes have genuinely different spreads or orientations, producing miscalibrated boundaries.
Assumes multivariate Gaussian class-conditionals, so it degrades on skewed, heavy-tailed, or multimodal class distributions.
recommended_for: Face recognition and biometric classification with dozens of labeled images per subject, where the LDA projection to k-1 dimensions compresses within-subject variance while preserving between-subject separation.
Medical diagnosis tasks with continuous biomarker features (e.g., blood panel values), small cohort size (n ~ 100-300), and roughly Gaussian distributions per group.
not_recommended_for: Text or image datasets where p >> n (e.g., bag-of-words with 10,000 features and 200 documents), as S_W is singular and the standard solution breaks down without heavy regularization.
Problems with clearly non-linear class boundaries (e.g., concentric clusters or XOR patterns), where a linear discriminant hyperplane cannot separate the classes regardless of the projection.
children.curiosity: Fisher introduced the two-class version in 1936 ('The Use of Multiple Measurements in Taxonomic Problems', Annals of Eugenics) purely as a geometric projection criterion; C.R. Rao reformulated it as a Bayesian generative model under Gaussian class-conditionals in 1948, which is the probabilistic framing used in modern implementations.

target.notes: Class-conditional features assumed multivariate Gaussian with a single shared (pooled) covariance across classes; class priors multinomial. Yields linear log-posterior, hence linear decision boundaries.

data_regime.rows: works on <1k; statistically efficient at small n because only one pooled covariance is estimated
data_regime.dimensionality: p < n required; S_W singular and non-invertible when p >= n unless shrinkage/regularized (RDA) variant used

features.interpretability: high; closed-form eigendecomposition of S_W^{-1}S_B yields up to k-1 discriminant axes interpretable as directions of maximum class separation
features.notes: Continuous features expected; centering/scaling helps. Categorical/high-cardinality inputs violate the Gaussian assumption. Doubles as supervised dimensionality reduction to k-1 dims.

assumptions: multivariate Gaussian class-conditional densities
homoscedasticity: all classes share one covariance matrix (else use QDA)
p < n so within-class scatter S_W is invertible
features approximately non-collinear (collinearity inflates S_W^{-1})
loss: maximizes Gaussian class-conditional likelihood / posterior under shared covariance (equivalently Fisher between-class vs within-class scatter ratio)
contraindicated_when: p >> n (e.g. bag-of-words 10k features, 200 docs): S_W singular
classes have genuinely different covariance spread/orientation (use QDA)
non-linear class boundaries (concentric, XOR) unreachable by a linear hyperplane
skewed, heavy-tailed, or multimodal class-conditional distributions
predominantly categorical features

children.name: QDA (Quadratic Discriminant Analysis)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike LDA (which pools a single covariance matrix across all classes) or Naive Bayes (which assumes feature independence), QDA fits a separate full covariance matrix per class, producing quadratic decision boundaries via class-specific Mahalanobis distances.
strengths: Captures heteroscedastic class distributions: when classes have different spread or orientation, the per-class Σ_k models the true geometry that a shared matrix would distort.
Closed-form posterior: class probabilities are computed analytically from the multivariate Gaussian likelihood and Bayes' rule — no iterative optimization required.
More expressive than LDA with minimal assumptions: gains quadratic boundaries at the cost of estimating p(p+1)/2 additional parameters per class, a controlled trade-off when n >> p.
weaknesses: Covariance matrix singularity in high dimensions: requires n_k > p per class to invert Σ_k; fails or degrades sharply when features outnumber per-class samples.
Quadratic growth in parameters: p features and K classes demand K·p(p+1)/2 covariance entries, making QDA impractical for even moderately wide feature sets without regularization.
Sensitivity to Gaussian violations: the quadratic boundary is optimal only under multivariate normality; heavy tails, skew, or multimodal classes can yield worse accuracy than simpler models.
recommended_for: Medical biomarker classification with a small number of well-measured continuous features (e.g., 5–15 lab values) and ample per-class samples, where LDA underperforms because disease groups have genuinely different covariance structures.
Sensor-fusion classification tasks (e.g., fault detection from 3–10 physical measurements) where each class corresponds to a distinct physical regime with its own variability pattern.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional feature spaces (e.g., text bag-of-words, gene expression arrays with p > 1000) where per-class covariance matrices are singular and parameter estimation collapses.
Small datasets with many classes: if any class has fewer observations than features, Σ_k is rank-deficient and QDA is undefined without regularization, making LDA or Naive Bayes safer defaults.
children.curiosity: The quadratic form of discriminant analysis was formalized by C. R. Rao in 1948 ('The utilization of multiple measurements in problems of biological classification', Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B), extending Fisher's 1936 linear discriminant by removing the equal-covariance constraint and deriving the class-specific Mahalanobis distance as the optimal Bayes rule under Gaussian class-conditionals.

target.notes: Discrete class label; generative model assumes class-conditional features are multivariate Gaussian with a separate full covariance per class.

data_regime.rows: needs per-class n_k > p to invert each Σ_k; comfortable when n_k >> p(p+1)/2 for stable covariance estimates
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n strongly preferred per class; fails for p>n_k (singular covariance) without shrinkage/regularization

features.interpretability: medium: closed-form Gaussian posteriors and class-specific Mahalanobis distances are inspectable, but quadratic boundaries are less directly readable than LDA coefficients
features.notes: Continuous features only; categorical/high-cardinality inputs violate the Gaussian assumption. Roughly Gaussian, non-collinear features help; standardization not required but extreme scale differences can worsen conditioning of Σ_k.

assumptions: class-conditional multivariate normality of features
each class has its own (heteroscedastic) full covariance matrix
sufficient per-class sample size to estimate and invert Σ_k
features not severely collinear (else near-singular covariance)
loss: maximizes Gaussian class-conditional likelihood; classifies by maximum posterior (Bayes rule)
minimizes class-specific Mahalanobis distance plus log-determinant and prior terms
contraindicated_when: p > n_k for any class (rank-deficient covariance, QDA undefined without regularization)
high-dimensional sparse features (text bag-of-words, gene expression with p>1000)
heavy-tailed, skewed, or multimodal class distributions that break the Gaussian boundary optimality
many classes with few observations each
predominantly categorical features
when classes share covariance structure (LDA is more parameter-efficient)

children.name: Bayesian Network
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Naive Bayes (which forces full conditional independence among features) and Tree-Augmented Naive Bayes (which allows exactly one inter-feature dependency per variable), a Bayesian Network encodes an arbitrary directed acyclic graph of conditional dependencies, letting the structure itself be learned or specified to match the actual causal relationships in the domain.
strengths: Explicit probabilistic structure allows exact marginal and conditional queries on any subset of variables, not just the class label
Domain knowledge can be encoded directly as edges in the DAG, reducing the data needed to learn a useful model
Handles missing features at inference time naturally via marginalization, without imputation
weaknesses: Structure learning over n variables requires searching a super-exponential DAG space, proven NP-hard even under the constraint of at most 2 parents per node
Exact inference is NP-hard in general networks; approximate methods (loopy belief propagation, MCMC) add implementation complexity and may not converge
Conditional probability tables grow exponentially with the number of parents per node, requiring large amounts of data to estimate reliably for densely connected subgraphs
recommended_for: Clinical decision support where causal structure is partially known (e.g., disease -> symptom edges from medical literature) and interpretable probability estimates per variable are required
Fault diagnosis in industrial systems with a small number of discrete, causally related variables where domain experts can specify the DAG topology
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional feature spaces (hundreds of continuous variables) where structure learning becomes computationally intractable and CPT estimation demands prohibitively large datasets

Tasks requiring only a single class prediction with no need for uncertainty quantification or causal reasoning, where simpler discriminative models (logistic regression, SVM) yield better accuracy at lower cost
children.curiosity: Judea Pearl introduced Bayesian networks in 1985 as a model of human probabilistic reasoning and formalized the framework in his 1988 book 'Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems'; this work formed the foundation that earned him the 2011 Turing Award.

target.notes: Generative model of the full joint distribution; class label is just one queryable node. Any subset of variables can be predicted, and the model also answers conditional/marginal queries with no fixed target. Discrete/categorical variables are the native case; continuous variables require discretization or conditional linear-Gaussian CPDs.

data_regime.rows: works on small n when the DAG is expert-specified; structure learning needs thousands+ to estimate CPTs for densely connected nodes
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n strongly preferred; small number of variables (tens, not hundreds). Structure search is super-exponential in p and NP-hard
needs: expert-specified DAG or feasible structure search
enough samples per parent configuration to fill CPTs

features.interpretability: high; the DAG and CPTs are directly readable and edges can carry causal meaning
features.notes: Continuous features need discretization or conditional-Gaussian assumptions. CPT size grows exponentially with parents-per-node, so high-cardinality categoricals and dense connectivity are costly.

assumptions: the dependency structure is well-approximated by a DAG (no cycles, no unmeasured confounders if causal claims are made)
conditional independencies implied by the graph hold (Markov condition)
discrete variables or valid parametric CPDs for continuous ones
sufficient data per parent configuration to estimate CPTs reliably
loss: maximum likelihood / MAP of the joint distribution
Bayesian Dirichlet (BDeu) score for structure learning
BIC/MDL penalized likelihood for structure search
log-loss for the class node at prediction time
contraindicated_when: high-dimensional spaces with hundreds of continuous features (intractable structure learning, unfillable CPTs)
only a single discriminative class prediction is needed with no uncertainty or causal reasoning (logistic regression/SVM/gradient boosting are cheaper and more accurate)
strong feature interactions are dense and unknown, making the DAG and CPTs unidentifiable from available data
large labeled tabular data with many predictive but non-causal features where discriminative learners dominate

target.notes: Generative classifiers: model joint P(x,y) via class priors and class-conditional likelihood P(x|y), then apply Bayes' rule for posterior P(y|x). Likelihood family is chosen to match feature type (multinomial/Bernoulli for counts/indicators, Gaussian for continuous).

data_regime.rows: excels in small-sample regime (hundreds to low thousands); strong-prior structure substitutes for data
data_regime.dimensionality: handles p>>n well under independence/parametric constraints (e.g. high-dim sparse text); full joint density intractable in high dim without those constraints

features.interpretability: high: priors, likelihoods and posterior contributions are explicit and inspectable
features.notes: Naive Bayes variants assume per-class feature independence; works best with sparse count/indicator features (bag-of-words). Continuous features assumed Gaussian per class unless discretized.

assumptions: conditional independence of features given class (Naive Bayes); correlated features inflate posterior confidence
correct parametric form of class-conditional density (multinomial/Bernoulli/Gaussian); misspecification adds irreducible bias
priors reflect true class prevalence for calibration to hold
loss: log-loss / negative log-likelihood (MAP/MLE on the generative model)
outputs natively calibrated class-posterior probabilities
