assumptions: base learners are sufficiently diverse and individually competent (errors decorrelated)
the single holdout split is representative of the full distribution
holdout rows are never seen by base models (no leakage)
loss: log-loss
squared error
any loss supported by the chosen meta-learner (commonly logistic/linear regression or GBM as combiner)
contraindicated_when: dataset below ~1000 rows (holdout too small, base models data-starved)
you need the lowest-variance meta-training signal: prefer full out-of-fold stacking
only one or near-identical base models exist (no diversity to exploit)
single split risks unrepresentative meta-training under class imbalance or temporal drift

children.name: Voting Classifier (hard/soft)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Stacking, which trains a meta-learner to optimally weight base model outputs, Voting aggregates predictions through a fixed rule: majority class count (hard) or argmax of averaged class probabilities (soft), with no second-level learning step.
strengths: Soft voting exploits calibrated probability estimates from each base model, often outperforming hard voting when classifiers assign confident, well-separated probabilities.
Combines heterogeneous algorithms (e.g., SVM + Naive Bayes + Decision Tree) in a single pass, reducing variance from any individual model's bias without requiring cross-validated fold generation.
Trivially parallelizable: each base classifier trains and predicts independently, with no data dependency between models.
weaknesses: Weights in soft voting must be set manually or via grid search — the model has no mechanism to learn optimal combination weights from data, unlike Stacking.
Hard voting is unreliable when base classifiers are correlated or trained on the same feature set, as errors cluster rather than cancel.
Performance is bounded by the quality of base learners: a miscalibrated or underperforming member cannot be down-weighted automatically, contaminating the average.
recommended_for: Classification tasks where 3–5 diverse, already-tuned classifiers of different families (linear, kernel, tree-based) are available and a quick, interpretable ensemble is needed without extra training overhead.

Moderate-sized tabular datasets (thousands to low millions of rows) where soft voting over probability outputs from classifiers with reliable probability calibration (e.g., logistic regression, calibrated SVM) is feasible.
not_recommended_for: Scenarios where base classifiers are strongly correlated or share the same inductive bias, as voting provides negligible variance reduction and adds inference cost.
High-stakes problems where optimal combination weights matter critically — Stacking with cross-validated meta-learning will systematically outperform any fixed voting rule in those settings.
children.curiosity: The theoretical foundation for majority voting ensembles was established by Hansen and Salamon (1990) in 'Neural Network Ensembles', showing that an ensemble of independently trained networks with error rate below 0.5 converges to perfect accuracy as ensemble size grows — the first formal proof that combining classifiers beats any single member.

target.notes: Classification only. Soft voting needs base members that emit calibrated class probabilities (predict_proba); hard voting only needs class labels.

data_regime.rows: inherits base learners' requirements; works from low thousands to low millions of tabular rows
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred (driven by base members); no own dimensionality handling
needs: 3-5 already-tuned base classifiers of diverse model families for the variance reduction to materialize

features.interpretability: medium: fixed aggregation rule is transparent, but the ensemble obscures individual member reasoning
features.notes: No own preprocessing; each base learner handles its own scaling/encoding. Soft voting weights are fixed hyperparameters, not learned.

assumptions: Base learners make decorrelated errors (diverse inductive biases) so mistakes cancel under aggregation
For soft voting, member probabilities are well-calibrated and on a comparable scale
All members are of roughly comparable competence; no single bad member drags the average
loss: no own trainable objective; hard voting = plurality of predicted labels, soft voting = argmax of (optionally weighted) averaged class probabilities
contraindicated_when: Base classifiers are strongly correlated or share the same features/inductive bias (errors cluster, negligible variance reduction)
Optimal combination weights matter (use Stacking with a cross-validated meta-learner instead)
Members are poorly or inconsistently calibrated, making soft-vote probability averaging meaningless
A regression target, or a single strong model already suffices

children.name: SuperLearner
children.diff_siblings: Unlike standard stacking or voting ensembles that combine base learners with heuristic or fixed weights, SuperLearner selects the convex combination of base learners that minimizes cross-validated risk, providing asymptotic oracle optimality guarantees — meaning it converges to the best possible weighted combination as sample size grows.
strengths: Oracle property: asymptotically achieves the lowest cross-validated risk among all convex combinations of the candidate library, proven by van der Laan et al. (2007) under mild conditions.
Seamlessly integrates arbitrarily heterogeneous base learners (parametric, tree-based, neural) without assuming any single one is correctly specified.
Natural fit for doubly-robust causal estimators (TMLE, AIPTW): provides flexible nuisance function estimation while preserving valid statistical inference on the target parameter.
weaknesses: Computational cost scales multiplicatively: K-fold cross-validation runs every candidate learner K times, making large libraries with slow base learners (e.g., boosted trees) expensive.
Convexity constraint on meta-learner weights can prevent negative coefficients, limiting expressiveness when base learners are systematically biased in the same direction.
In small samples or high-dimensional longitudinal settings, many ML base learners fail to converge inside the cross-validation folds, collapsing the effective library to only parametric candidates.
recommended_for: Observational causal inference pipelines (e.g., propensity score or outcome model estimation feeding into TMLE) where no single model class is trusted and doubly-robust guarantees are required.
Biomedical prediction tasks with moderate samples (n ~ 500–5000) and heterogeneous feature types, where blending regularized regression, random forests, and GAMs outperforms any single algorithm.
not_recommended_for: Real-time or low-latency prediction systems: K-fold retraining of a full candidate library at fit time and storing multiple models at inference time is prohibitive.
Very small samples (n < 100) where K-fold cross-validation inside each fold leaves too few observations for complex base learners to train reliably, making weight estimation noisy.
children.curiosity: Introduced by van der Laan, Polley, and Hubbard (2007) in 'Super Learner' (Statistical Applications in Genetics and Molecular Biology), the paper provided the first formal proof — via cross-validation oracle inequalities — that a stacking ensemble can asymptotically match the performance of the single best algorithm in any candidate library, a result that gave stacking a rigorous theoretical foundation it had lacked since Wolpert's original 1992 proposal.
keywords: improve prediction accuracy by combining models

target.notes: Meta-learner is task-agnostic; any base learners predicting the target type can be stacked. Common in binary outcome / propensity-score estimation.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds to low thousands (n ~ 500-5000 ideal); unreliable at n<100 because each CV fold must train complex base learners
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; in p>n or longitudinal settings many ML base learners fail inside folds and the library collapses to parametric candidates
needs: full candidate-library training repeated K times per fold (CPU/compute heavy)
storing all base models at inference

features.interpretability: low: an opaque cross-validated convex blend of heterogeneous base learners; interpretability is only as good as the chosen library
features.notes: Handles heterogeneous feature types by delegating to base learners; no single distributional assumption imposed by the meta-learner.

assumptions: Oracle optimality holds asymptotically and under mild conditions; small samples make CV weight estimation noisy
At least one library member (or their convex blend) approximates the truth well
CV folds large enough for each base learner to converge
loss: minimizes cross-validated risk over the convex combination of base learners (default negative log-likelihood / log-loss for classification, squared error for regression)
any CV risk metric supported by the chosen loss (e.g. AUC, MSE)
contraindicated_when: real-time or low-latency serving (K-fold retraining at fit + multi-model inference is prohibitive)
very small samples (n<100)
base learners are systematically biased in the same direction (convexity forbids negative weights to correct it)
a single simple model already suffices (ensemble overhead unjustified)

target.notes: Combiner family inherits the task of its base learners; primarily applied to classification (probability output via soft voting / meta-learner) but stacking generalizes to regression by combining base regressors.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds+ labeled samples per class; out-of-fold meta-feature generation requires enough data for k-fold splits to leave each fold trainable
data_regime.dimensionality: agnostic at the meta-level (meta-features = number of base models, typically 3-15); base-level dimensionality governed by chosen base learners
needs: k-fold CV for correct out-of-fold predictions (stacking)

features.interpretability: low — combination of multiple models obscures attribution; meta-coefficients only indicate relative trust in base models, not feature effects
features.notes: Meta-features are the base models' out-of-fold predictions/probabilities; base learners should be architecturally heterogeneous (e.g. trees + linear + SVM) so errors are uncorrelated and the meta-learner finds complementarity.

assumptions: base learners make errors that are diverse/uncorrelated — redundant base models give no lift
out-of-fold predictions are generated correctly; predicting on own training data leaks and inflates meta-features
meta-learner is kept simple relative to the few meta-features to avoid second-level overfitting
loss: inherits base-learner objectives; meta-learner natively optimizes log-loss (classification) or squared error (regression)
soft voting averages class probabilities to improve calibration
contraindicated_when: small datasets (under ~500 samples) where k-fold OOF generation starves base learners and both levels overfit
base models are similar/highly correlated, so combination adds compute without accuracy gain
strict low-latency inference, since prediction requires forward passes through all base models before the meta-model
a single strong model already saturates performance and the 2-5% marginal lift does not justify the complexity and maintenance cost

target.notes: Single-tree classifiers. Leaf posteriors are class-frequency step functions, poorly calibrated; use isotonic/Platt if probabilities matter.

data_regime.rows: works on small n (hundreds), but variance grows and pruning/CV needed; not data-hungry
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; degrades as p grows (greedy splits chase noise), no built-in regularization beyond depth/pruning

features.interpretability: high: prediction path is an explicit nested if-else rule set, auditable without post-hoc tools
features.notes: Handles mixed numeric/categorical natively without encoding or normalization; tolerates missing values (surrogate splits); scale/monotone transforms of features are irrelevant

assumptions: axis-aligned (rectangular) decision boundaries suffice; oblique/diagonal separation requires exponential depth
splits assume informative marginal thresholds; XOR-like interactions need depth
sufficient samples per leaf to avoid memorizing noise
loss: Gini impurity
entropy / information gain
gain ratio
misclassification error (for pruning)
contraindicated_when: target is continuous/count/time-to-event (this node is classification; use regression trees)
image, audio, or raw text where structure is spatial/sequential
calibrated probability estimates required
smooth or oblique decision boundary
low-bias high-accuracy goal on its own (prefer bagged/boosted ensembles; a single tree is high-variance)

children.name: Rules
children.diff_siblings: Unlike decision trees (which partition the feature space with a single recursive structure) or geometric classifiers (SVMs, kNN), rule-based classifiers induce an ordered or unordered set of independent IF-THEN rules via sequential covering: each rule is learned, its covered instances removed, and the process repeats — so each rule is a standalone logical clause, not a path in a shared tree.
strengths: Human-readable IF-THEN rules map directly to domain knowledge, making model auditing trivial without post-hoc interpretation tools.
Sequential covering (RIPPER, CN2) handles class imbalance naturally by learning rules for minority classes first, before majority-class instances dominate.
Rules can have different antecedent lengths per class, avoiding the rigid rectangular partitioning that forces decision trees to split on irrelevant features for some branches.
weaknesses: Greedy sequential covering is sensitive to rule ordering: a misclassified instance by early rules is never reconsidered, so errors compound across the rule list.
Does not model continuous feature interactions well — numeric attributes must be discretized into intervals, losing resolution compared to tree splits or kernel methods.
Rule sets grow large on high-dimensional data with many interacting features, degrading both interpretability and generalization relative to regularized alternatives.
recommended_for: Medical or legal decision support where each prediction must be justified by an explicit, auditable logical condition (e.g., 'IF age > 60 AND creatinine > 1.5 THEN high-risk').
Datasets with categorical or discretized features and strong class-specific patterns, such as intrusion detection logs where specific flag combinations define attack signatures.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional continuous feature spaces (e.g., image pixels, raw sensor signals) where meaningful rules require thousands of conjuncts and discretization destroys signal.
Problems requiring soft probability calibration, such as ranking or cost-sensitive decisions, since most rule learners assign a single class label per rule with no reliable confidence estimate.
children.curiosity: RIPPER (Repeated Incremental Pruning to Produce Error Reduction), the canonical rule induction algorithm, was introduced by William W. Cohen at ICML 1995; it improved upon IREP by adding a global optimization pass that revises each rule after the full rule set is built, reducing error by up to 40% on benchmark datasets compared to its predecessor.

children.name: RIPPER (JRip)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike CN2 (which uses beam search with a single covering pass) or PART (which builds rules from partial decision trees), RIPPER applies a two-phase grow-then-prune cycle per rule using Reduced Error Pruning, followed by a global MDL-based optimization pass that revises or discards each rule against the full ruleset.
strengths: Produces compact, ordered rule lists competitive with decision trees in accuracy while remaining fully human-readable, due to the MDL stopping criterion that prevents overfitting without requiring a held-out test set.
The post-generation optimization phase revises each rule in context of the full ruleset, catching interactions that single-rule pruning misses and yielding higher precision on minority classes.

Scales linearly with number of training examples per rule-growing iteration, making it tractable on datasets with tens of thousands of instances where exhaustive covering algorithms become prohibitive.
weaknesses: Rule ordering is fixed by class prevalence (rarest class first, majority class as default else-branch), so the model cannot represent overlapping class regions and misclassifies majority-class instances that also match minority-class rules.
The grow/prune split is deterministic and single-pass per rule; unlike ensemble methods, one noisy training partition can corrupt an entire rule and there is no variance reduction mechanism.
Multiclass extension is sequential one-vs-rest, meaning later classes train on a progressively smaller and more skewed residual set, degrading rule quality for mid-prevalence classes.
recommended_for: Medical or legal audit tasks requiring fully interpretable if-then rules over structured tabular data (e.g., patient risk stratification from lab values) where model transparency is a regulatory requirement.
Text categorization with bag-of-words binary features and strong class imbalance toward one category, where the ordered default rule efficiently handles the majority class without explicit coverage.
not_recommended_for: Datasets with continuous features of high cardinality and no natural discretization boundaries, where the axis-aligned conjunctive rule structure produces overly fragmented rules with many threshold conditions.
Problems requiring probability estimates or calibrated confidence scores, since RIPPER outputs a deterministic rule list with no native posterior probability and calibration post-hoc is non-trivial.
children.curiosity: Introduced by William W. Cohen at ICML 1995, RIPPER was one of the first rule learners to replace simple error rate with the Minimum Description Length principle as the stopping criterion, directly connecting rule induction to information-theoretic model selection.

target.notes: Discrete class labels only. No native probability output; deterministic ordered rule list. Multiclass handled by sequential one-vs-rest, which degrades on mid-prevalence classes as the residual set shrinks.

data_regime.rows: hundreds to tens of thousands; scales near-linearly per rule-growing iteration, more tractable than exhaustive covering algorithms
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; performs internal feature selection via conjunctive rule conditions but degrades when many irrelevant high-cardinality continuous features force fragmented thresholds

features.interpretability: high: outputs a small ordered list of human-readable if-then rules with a default else-branch, suitable for audit/regulatory transparency
features.notes: Best with categorical or naturally discretizable features. Continuous features are handled via axis-aligned threshold splits; high-cardinality continuous features without natural cut points yield many fragmented conditions. No scaling required.

assumptions: Class regions are separable by axis-aligned conjunctive (AND-of-conditions) rules
Classes do not overlap heavily: fixed rule ordering (rarest class first, majority as default) cannot represent overlapping regions
Training partitions are low-noise: single grow/prune pass per rule means one noisy split can corrupt a rule, with no variance-reduction mechanism
loss: sequential covering with reduced-error pruning per rule
global MDL (minimum description length) optimization to revise/discard rules and set stopping point
contraindicated_when: calibrated probabilities or confidence scores are required (output is a hard rule list, no native posterior)
features are high-cardinality continuous with no natural discretization boundaries (rules become overly fragmented)
smooth, oblique, or strongly interacting decision boundaries dominate (axis-aligned conjunctions approximate poorly)
heavy class overlap or many classes of similar prevalence (one-vs-rest residual skew and fixed ordering hurt)
maximum predictive accuracy outweighs interpretability (gradient-boosted trees / random forests typically win)

children.name: OneR
children.diff_siblings: Unlike multi-rule systems (PRISM, RIPPER) that build ordered or unordered rule lists across multiple attributes, OneR selects exactly one attribute and derives a single flat lookup table mapping each of its values to the majority class — the simplest possible non-trivial rule structure.
strengths: Human-readable output: the entire model is one lookup table, trivially auditable without any ML expertise.
Strong baseline signal: Holte (1993) showed it matches or beats 70–90% of more complex classifiers on 16 UCI datasets, revealing how much signal one attribute can carry.
Near-zero training cost: a single pass over the data to count class frequencies per attribute value suffices, O(n·d) with negligible constant.
weaknesses: Cannot model attribute interactions: by design it ignores all but one feature, so any class boundary that requires a conjunction (e.g., age > 40 AND cholesterol > 200) is structurally unrepresentable.
Numeric discretization is naive and overfits: the original binning scheme shrinks bins until error falls, often producing overly specific cuts that do not generalize (Witten & Frank, 2005).

Single-rule constraint collapses under class imbalance: the chosen attribute's majority-class mapping trivially predicts the dominant class for most bins, producing rules nearly equivalent to ZeroR on skewed targets.
recommended_for: Establishing an interpretable baseline on tabular datasets where a domain expert needs to validate that at least one strong single-attribute signal exists before investing in complex models.
Medical or legal triage tables where the entire decision policy must fit on a single printed card and auditability overrides predictive power.
not_recommended_for: Problems where the class boundary is defined by interactions between features, such as XOR-structured data or credit scoring that jointly weighs income, debt, and employment history.
High-cardinality continuous inputs (e.g., sensor time series, image pixel values) where no single feature provides a stable discriminant and discretization produces thousands of nearly empty bins.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Robert C. Holte in 'Very Simple Classification Rules Perform Well on Most Commonly Used Datasets' (Machine Learning, 1993), the paper deliberately challenged the ML community's assumption that model complexity correlates with accuracy, reporting that OneR achieved mean accuracy within 1–2% of C4.5 across 16 benchmark datasets.

target.notes: Classification only; predicts majority class per value of one chosen attribute. No probability calibration beyond per-bin class frequencies.

data_regime.rows: works on <1k; only needs enough counts per attribute-value bin to be stable
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; evaluates each feature independently but uses exactly one in the final rule

features.interpretability: high: model is a single attribute->class lookup table, auditable without ML expertise
features.notes: Numeric features require discretization (naive error-minimizing binning); high-cardinality or continuous inputs degrade to overfit bins. Best when at least one low-cardinality categorical feature carries strong signal.

assumptions: A single attribute carries most of the class-discriminating signal (no required feature interactions)
Class boundary is not defined by conjunctions of features
Reasonably balanced classes; per-value majority is informative
Chosen attribute is low-cardinality after discretization
loss: 0/1 classification error (selects the attribute and per-value mapping minimizing training misclassification)
contraindicated_when: Class boundary requires feature interactions (e.g. XOR, joint income/debt scoring)
Severe class imbalance (collapses toward ZeroR / majority-class prediction)
High-cardinality or continuous inputs where discretization yields thousands of near-empty bins
Calibrated probabilities or strong accuracy are required rather than an interpretable baseline

children.name: PART
children.diff_siblings: Unlike RIPPER (which optimizes rules globally via MDL) or C4.5rules (which post-prunes a full tree), PART builds a partial C4.5 decision tree in each separate-and-conquer iteration and promotes the single best leaf directly into a rule, avoiding both global optimization overhead and full-tree construction.
strengths: Produces ordered decision lists that are more compact than full C4.5 rule sets because each partial tree is pruned before rule extraction, yielding fewer and shorter rules.
Inherits C4.5's reduced-error pruning within each partial tree, making it more robust to noise than sequential covering methods that rely purely on coverage thresholds.
No global optimization pass means training time scales roughly linearly with the number of rules generated, keeping runtime manageable on mid-sized datasets (tens of thousands of instances).
weaknesses: Generates an ordered decision list, so rules later in the list are evaluated only after all preceding rules fail — a structural bias that can obscure interaction patterns visible in unordered rule sets.
Each iteration rebuilds a partial tree from scratch on the remaining instances, making the algorithm significantly slower than RIPPER on large datasets (hundreds of thousands of rows).
Rule quality degrades when classes are severely imbalanced because separate-and-conquer removes covered instances, leaving the minority class underrepresented in later iterations.
recommended_for: Medical or regulatory decision support with tabular data (dozens of features, thousands of patients) where clinicians need auditable if-then rules that can be traced to specific feature thresholds.
Text categorization with bag-of-words features where interpretable rules per category are required and the number of training documents is in the low tens of thousands.
not_recommended_for: High-cardinality continuous feature spaces (e.g., sensor time series with hundreds of channels) where repeated partial tree construction per iteration becomes computationally prohibitive.
Severely class-imbalanced datasets without resampling preprocessing, as later separate-and-conquer iterations see too few minority instances to induce reliable rules.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Eibe Frank and Ian H. Witten (1998) in 'Generating Accurate Rule Sets Without Global Optimization' (ICML-98), the paper demonstrated that building only partial decision trees — stopping as soon as the best leaf is identified — achieves accuracy comparable to C4.5rules and RIPPER while avoiding the expensive global MDL optimization that RIPPER requires.

target.notes: Nominal class label; produces an ordered decision list (rule order matters at prediction time).

data_regime.rows: works from hundreds to low tens of thousands; partial-tree rebuild per iteration makes it slow on hundreds of thousands of rows
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; dozens to low hundreds of features

features.interpretability: high: emits human-readable if-then rules with explicit feature thresholds, auditable per decision
features.notes: Handles mixed numeric/categorical natively via C4.5 splits; no scaling needed. High-cardinality continuous spaces inflate per-iteration tree cost.

assumptions: Class signal is expressible as axis-parallel threshold rules
Reasonably balanced classes; separate-and-conquer starves minority class in later iterations
Moderate feature count so repeated partial-tree induction stays tractable
loss: information-gain / gain-ratio splitting with reduced-error (subtree) pruning per partial tree; coverage-based separate-and-conquer rule selection (not a smooth probabilistic loss)
contraindicated_when: Severe class imbalance without resampling
Very large datasets (hundreds of thousands+ rows) where RIPPER or tree ensembles are far faster
High-dimensional continuous/sensor data where per-iteration tree construction is prohibitive
Need for calibrated class probabilities or smooth decision boundaries rather than discrete rules
Strong feature interactions better captured by unordered rule sets or ensembles

children.name: Decision Table
children.diff_siblings: Unlike rule-list methods (RIPPER, PART) that chain ordered if-then rules, a Decision Table maps every combination of values from a selected feature subset directly to a majority class via a flat lookup table, with no rule ordering or conflict-resolution logic.
strengths: Extremely transparent: the entire model fits in a human-readable table where each row is a feature-value combination and each cell is a majority class label
Built-in feature selection: best-first search over feature subsets discards irrelevant attributes, reducing noise before classification
Competitive accuracy on low-to-mid dimensionality datasets despite simplicity, as demonstrated by Kohavi (1995) against C4.5 on UCI benchmarks
weaknesses: Exponential table growth: the number of rows scales as the product of cardinalities of selected features, making it impractical when selected features have many distinct values
Schema search cost is NP-hard in the number of features; best-first heuristic can miss the optimal subset on wide datasets
Handles only the feature interactions captured by the schema; interactions between non-selected features are entirely invisible to the model
recommended_for: Tabular datasets with a small number of meaningful categorical or discretized features (under ~20 relevant attributes) where full model transparency is required, such as clinical decision support
Business rule validation tasks where stakeholders must audit every decision path, and the label distribution within each feature-value cell needs to be directly inspectable
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional continuous data (e.g., raw text embeddings or image pixel vectors) where the schema search space is intractable and discretization artifacts dominate
Problems requiring fine-grained interaction of many features simultaneously, where a decision tree or ensemble model captures cross-feature structure that a flat table schema cannot represent
children.curiosity: Introduced by Ron Kohavi in 'The Power of Decision Tables' (ECML 1995), the paper showed that this deceptively simple majority-lookup model statistically matched or outperformed C4.5 on 27 of 32 UCI datasets, challenging the then-prevailing assumption that structural complexity was necessary for competitive accuracy.

target.notes: Each cell stores the majority class for a feature-value combination; predicts hard labels (class probabilities only as crude per-cell frequencies).

data_regime.rows: works on small-to-mid datasets; each schema cell needs enough rows for a reliable majority vote, so sparse cells degrade fast
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n strongly preferred; effective only with few selected features (roughly <20 relevant attributes) because table rows scale as the product of selected-feature cardinalities

features.interpretability: high: the whole model is a human-readable lookup table, every decision path auditable
features.notes: Numeric features must be discretized into bins; high-cardinality or continuous features explode the table and introduce discretization artifacts. Best-first feature-subset selection is built in.

assumptions: Relevant feature interactions are captured by a small selected feature subset; interactions among non-selected features are invisible
Features are low-cardinality or can be sensibly discretized
Enough samples per feature-value cell to estimate a stable majority class
loss: 0/1 classification error (majority-vote per cell)
contraindicated_when: High-dimensional or raw continuous inputs (text embeddings, image pixels) where schema search is intractable and binning dominates
Many features must interact simultaneously, exceeding the flat schema's representational reach
Selected features are high-cardinality, causing exponential table growth and sparse, unreliable cells
Calibrated probabilities or ranking scores are required

target.notes: Single hard class label per rule; native discrete classification, not probabilistic. Poor at calibrated class probabilities.

data_regime.rows: works from hundreds to tens of thousands; rule list growth and overfitting on very large noisy data without strong pruning
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n strongly preferred; degrades as p grows or features interact heavily

features.interpretability: high — output is an explicit ordered/unordered set of IF-THEN logical clauses, directly auditable without post-hoc tools
features.notes: Numeric features must be discretized into intervals (resolution loss); best when predictive structure is captured by discrete feature-value conjunctions.

assumptions: predictive signal expressible as short conjunctions of feature conditions (axis-aligned, threshold/category based)
low-order feature interactions; high-order continuous interactions are not modeled well
discretization of numeric features preserves enough signal
rule ordering / coverage sequence is stable — greedy covering does not revisit early misclassifications
loss: accuracy / 0-1 misclassification under sequential covering
information-gain or FOIL-gain rule scoring (CN2, RIPPER)
MDL-based rule pruning
contraindicated_when: high-dimensional continuous feature spaces (image pixels, raw sensor/audio signals) where good rules need thousands of conjuncts
calibrated probabilities, ranking, or cost-sensitive thresholds are required
smooth nonlinear decision boundaries or strong continuous feature interactions dominate
regression / continuous targets
heavy feature interaction where regularized tree ensembles (gradient boosting, random forest) generalize better

target.notes: Discrete categorical target with a finite, closed label set; ordinal targets need explicit ordinal extensions. Outputs are class labels or posterior P(y|x). Multi-label (non-mutually-exclusive) requires a multi-output variant.

data_regime.rows: family spans <1k (linear/SVM/naive Bayes) to thousands+ (trees, ensembles, neural nets)
data_regime.dimensionality: members vary: p<n classical, p>n needs regularized/sparse or kernel members
needs: enough samples in the minority class for reliable boundaries

features.interpretability: varies by member: high for logistic regression / shallow trees, low for ensembles and deep nets
features.notes: scaling matters for margin/distance-based members; tree members are scale-invariant

assumptions: classes are mutually exclusive and the label set is fixed (closed-world)
training class distribution is representative of deployment, or imbalance is corrected via weighting/resampling/threshold tuning
labels at class boundaries are unambiguous
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss (multinomial deviance)
hinge loss (margin classifiers)
exponential loss (boosting)
focal loss (imbalance)
class-weighted variants
contraindicated_when: target is inherently continuous and discretizing it discards information (use regression)
label space is open-set or continuously expanding (closed-world assumption violated)
target has a meaningful rank order that must be modeled (use ordinal regression)
extreme class imbalance with too few minority samples to estimate the boundary

children.name: 1.1.3 Time Series
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Regression and Classification, which treat observations as independent and identically distributed, Time Series models explicitly exploit temporal autocorrelation — the statistical dependency between a value and its own past — making the ordered sequence of observations the primary structural feature of the input.
strengths: Captures autocorrelation and seasonality inherent in sequential data that standard regression ignores, enabling forecasts grounded in the signal's own temporal structure.
Supports multi-step-ahead forecasting by feeding predicted values back as inputs, a pattern that is architecturally natural here but nonsensical in cross-sectional supervised models.

Spans a rich model family — from linear ARIMA (interpretable, low data) to LSTM and Transformers (nonlinear, long-range) — letting practitioners match model complexity to data volume and pattern type.
weaknesses: Requires stationarity or explicit differencing for statistical methods (ARIMA), and distribution-shift handling for neural methods, because the data-generating process itself can change over time (concept drift).
Needs a sufficient historical window per series; short or sparse series (fewer than ~50 observations) make parameter estimation unreliable across almost all time series models.
Cold-start problem: new series with no history cannot be forecast without transfer learning or hierarchical pooling, unlike cross-sectional models that generalize across entities.
recommended_for: Demand or sales forecasting where measurements are taken at regular intervals (daily, weekly) and exhibit trend, seasonality, or cyclic autocorrelation over months or years.
Sensor and IoT monitoring (vibration, temperature, power consumption) where the goal is to predict a future reading or detect anomalies based on recent sequential context.
not_recommended_for: Cross-sectional prediction where each observation is an independent entity (e.g., predicting house prices from structural features) and there is no meaningful temporal ordering between records.
Very high-frequency event streams (sub-millisecond tick data) with irregular timestamps and exogenous shocks dominating the signal, where event-driven or point-process models are more appropriate.
children.curiosity: The modern statistical foundation for time series was formalized by George Box and Gwilym Jenkins in their 1970 book 'Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control', which introduced the systematic ARIMA model-building cycle — identification, estimation, and diagnostic checking — that remains the baseline workflow against which all subsequent approaches are measured.

children.name: Classics (ARMA/ARIMA)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike neural (LSTM) or decomposition-based (Prophet) siblings, ARMA/ARIMA models the series as a finite-order linear combination of its own past values (AR terms) and past forecast errors (MA terms), after differencing to enforce stationarity — no hidden states, no trend decomposition, no nonlinear activation.
strengths: Interpretable parametric structure: each AR/MA coefficient has a direct probabilistic meaning tied to autocorrelation at specific lags, making model diagnostics via ACF/PACF plots straightforward.
Computationally minimal: fitting ARIMA(p,d,q) on hundreds of observations takes milliseconds; no GPU, no large training set, and the Box-Jenkins identification procedure is well-codified.

Statistically rigorous confidence intervals: forecast prediction intervals derive analytically from the model's error variance, not from empirical bootstrapping, giving calibrated uncertainty bounds on short horizons.
weaknesses: Assumes linearity: the current value is modeled as a linear combination of lags and errors, so nonlinear dynamics (regime shifts, multiplicative seasonality) cause systematic forecast bias.
Captures only short memory: ARIMA cannot represent long-range dependence (Hurst exponent > 0.5) — phenomena like hydrology or finance volatility clustering require FARIMA or GARCH extensions.
Manual order selection burden: choosing (p, d, q) requires inspecting ACF/PACF plots or running information-criterion grid searches; misspecification degrades accuracy substantially.
recommended_for: Univariate economic or financial series (monthly CPI, quarterly GDP) with a few hundred observations, where the data show clear autocorrelation structure and the forecasting horizon is short (1–12 steps ahead).

Production pipelines requiring fast, explainable forecasts with analytic confidence intervals and no GPU infrastructure, such as inventory replenishment for hundreds of SKUs run nightly on a CPU server.
not_recommended_for: Multivariate series where external regressors drive the outcome (e.g., energy demand forecasting with weather covariates at hourly resolution) — use ARIMAX cautiously or switch to gradient-boosted trees with lag features.

Long sequences with nonlinear or chaotic dynamics and thousands of training time steps, where LSTM or Temporal Fusion Transformers extract patterns ARIMA's linear filter fundamentally cannot represent.
children.curiosity: Box and Jenkins formalized the unified ARIMA framework in their 1970 book 'Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control', but the underlying AR component traces back to Yule (1927) and the MA component to Slutsky (1927), making the 'Box-Jenkins revolution' largely a methodological codification of 40-year-old mathematics.

children.name: AR (AutoRegressive)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike MA (which regresses on past error terms) or ARMA/ARIMA (which combine both), AR models the current value as a weighted linear combination of its own p past observations only, with no moving-average correction term.
strengths: PACF cuts off sharply at lag p, making order identification unambiguous compared to MA or ARMA where both ACF and PACF taper gradually.
Estimated via OLS or Yule-Walker equations, giving closed-form solutions that are computationally trivial even for large p.
Captures persistent autocorrelation structures (e.g., momentum, mean-reversion cycles) directly through the lag coefficients φ₁…φₚ without needing differencing or error-term modeling.
weaknesses: Requires strict stationarity (constant mean and variance); trending or heteroskedastic series must be pre-processed by differencing or transformation before fitting.
Cannot represent invertible moving-average dynamics: a process driven by exogenous shocks (MA structure) requires an AR of theoretically infinite order to approximate.
Order p must be chosen explicitly via PACF inspection or information criteria (AIC/BIC); misspecification of p produces biased residuals and invalid inference.
recommended_for: Stationary economic or financial series with clear momentum, such as weekly interest rates or log-returns, where PACF shows a sharp cutoff at lag 2-3 and AIC confirms parsimony.
Short-horizon forecasting of physiological signals (EEG, heart rate) that exhibit sustained autocorrelation over a fixed number of lags and where real-time, low-latency computation is required.
not_recommended_for: Non-stationary series with trends or seasonal cycles (e.g., monthly retail sales), where differencing alone is insufficient and ARIMA or SARIMA is the appropriate family.
Processes where abrupt external shocks dominate the dynamics (e.g., event-driven news impact on stock prices), since AR cannot parsimoniously model shock-driven MA structure.
children.curiosity: Introduced by George Udny Yule (1927) to model the annual sunspot cycle, AR was the first formal stochastic difference-equation approach to time series, predating the Box-Jenkins unification of AR and MA into ARIMA by over four decades.
keywords: predict future values from past values

target.notes: Univariate, equally-spaced series. Models y_t as a linear combination of its own p lagged values plus white-noise innovation; Gaussian innovations assumed for ML estimation and forecast intervals.

data_regime.rows: works on short series; needs roughly 50+ observations for stable order/coefficient estimation, more for large p
data_regime.dimensionality: single series (univariate); effective parameter count = p lag coefficients

features.interpretability: high; each lag coefficient phi_k quantifies the direct dependence on observation t-k, and PACF gives clean order identification
features.notes: No exogenous covariates in pure AR (use ARX/SARIMAX for that). Series must be regularly sampled with no gaps; pre-difference or detrend to enforce stationarity.

assumptions: strict (weak) stationarity: constant mean and variance over time
no trend or seasonal structure remaining in the input series
homoskedastic, serially uncorrelated white-noise innovations
linear, additive dependence on past values
correct order p (PACF cutoff / AIC-BIC); misspecification biases residuals
loss: squared error (OLS / conditional least squares)
Yule-Walker equations (method-of-moments)
Gaussian conditional log-likelihood (exact/conditional MLE)
contraindicated_when: series is non-stationary with trend or seasonality not removed by differencing (use ARIMA/SARIMA)
dynamics are dominated by exogenous shocks / moving-average structure (pure AR needs infinite order to approximate)
relationship between past and present is nonlinear or regime-switching
variance is time-varying / heteroskedastic (use ARCH-GARCH family)
multivariate cross-series dependence matters (use VAR)

children.name: MA (Moving Average)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike AR, which regresses on lagged observed values, MA(q) expresses the series as a linear combination of current and q lagged white-noise innovations (unobservable errors), making shocks transient by construction — their influence dies out exactly after q periods.
strengths: Always stationary regardless of parameter values, because it is a finite linear combination of white noise terms with finite variance.
ACF cuts off sharply after lag q, providing a clean diagnostic signal that directly identifies the model order from the correlogram.
Captures short-lived, mean-reverting shock dynamics (e.g., one-time supply disruptions) that AR models can only approximate with many lags.
weaknesses: Lagged innovations are unobservable, so estimation requires iterative nonlinear optimization (e.g., maximum likelihood) instead of closed-form OLS, increasing computational cost and convergence risk.
Invertibility constraints on θ parameters must be imposed to guarantee a unique parameterization; without them, multiple distinct MA models share the same autocorrelation structure.
Shock memory is strictly bounded at q periods — the model cannot represent long-range dependence or slowly decaying autocorrelation without a very high order q.
recommended_for: Economic series driven by transient external shocks (e.g., weekly retail sales after a promotional event), where the ACF shows a sharp cutoff after 1–3 lags confirming low MA order.
Residual modeling inside ARMA/ARIMA pipelines for series where AR terms alone leave correlated residuals with a short-lag ACF signature.
not_recommended_for: Time series with slowly decaying ACF (long memory), such as financial volatility or hydrological flows, where the required q would be impractically large and an AR or ARFIMA structure is more parsimonious.
Non-stationary series with trends or unit roots, where the mean-stationarity assumption is violated and differencing plus ARIMA is needed before any MA component is meaningful.
children.curiosity: The theoretical foundation of the MA model was established by Herman Wold in his 1938 Stockholm dissertation 'A Study in the Analysis of Stationary Time Series', where he proved that every purely non-deterministic covariance-stationary process admits an infinite-order MA representation — a result now known as the Wold decomposition theorem.

target.notes: Single equally-spaced univariate series modeled as a linear combination of current and q past white-noise innovations; assumes a constant (zero after centering) mean. Gaussian innovations underpin the standard MLE/Box-Jenkins inference.

data_regime.rows: needs a moderate run of consecutive observations (~50+ ordered points) to estimate the ACF cutoff and fit MA parameters reliably; very short series make order selection unstable
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate, no exogenous features; only the MA order q and noise variance are estimated

features.interpretability: high; q innovation coefficients (theta) with a clear shock-memory interpretation, each lagged shock dies out exactly after q periods
features.notes: Requires regularly-spaced, ordered observations with no missing gaps; series must be mean-stationary before fitting.

assumptions: weak (covariance) stationarity, achieved after differencing/detrending if needed
innovations are zero-mean white noise with constant variance (homoscedastic), Gaussian for standard MLE
invertibility constraints on theta so the MA process has a unique, AR(infinity)-representable parameterization
shock memory is finite and bounded at exactly q lags
loss: Gaussian conditional/exact maximum likelihood (equivalently one-step-ahead squared forecast error of the innovations); estimated by iterative nonlinear optimization, not closed-form OLS
contraindicated_when: series is non-stationary (trend or unit root) without prior differencing
ACF decays slowly (long-memory / persistent autocorrelation), requiring an impractically large q where AR/ARIMA/ARFIMA is more parsimonious
autocorrelation persists at long lags or volatility clustering dominates (use AR, GARCH, or long-memory models)
irregular sampling, large gaps, or strong heteroscedasticity in the innovations

children.name: ARMA
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ARIMA, ARMA omits the differencing operator entirely, combining only autoregressive (AR) and moving-average (MA) polynomial operators applied directly to the raw series, making it valid exclusively for already-stationary processes.
strengths: Exact maximum-likelihood estimation is tractable in closed form via the Kalman filter state-space representation, yielding efficient parameter estimates even for short series.
ACF and PACF plots provide a principled, interpretable diagnostic for selecting orders p and q before fitting, keeping model specification theory-grounded.
Parsimonious: a low-order ARMA(p,q) can approximate high-order pure AR or MA processes with far fewer parameters, reducing overfitting risk.
weaknesses: Requires strict covariance stationarity (constant mean and autocovariance); non-stationary series must be pre-differenced manually, shifting the burden to the analyst.
Assumes linear conditional mean and Gaussian, iid innovations — it cannot capture volatility clustering or heavy tails common in financial returns (GARCH is needed for that).
Order selection via ACF/PACF is ambiguous for mixed ARMA processes, where both functions tail off gradually and information criteria (AIC/BIC) comparisons across many candidate models are required.
recommended_for: Stationary macroeconomic indicators (e.g., monthly GDP growth rates, industrial production indices) where the series fluctuates around a fixed mean and autocorrelation decays quickly.
Signal processing and control engineering applications (e.g., vibration or EEG data) where the physical process is known to be stationary and a compact linear filter model is desired.
not_recommended_for: Non-stationary series with trends or unit roots (e.g., raw price levels, cumulative sales) — ARIMA or differencing plus ARMA is required before any valid inference.
Multivariate time series with cross-variable dependencies, where VAR or VARMA models are the appropriate generalizations.
children.curiosity: The formal unification of AR and MA into the ARMA framework and its systematic identification-estimation-diagnostic cycle was established by George Box and Gwilym Jenkins in their 1970 book 'Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control', which is why the entire methodology is still commonly called the Box-Jenkins approach.

target.notes: Univariate, equally-spaced, single endogenous series. Models the conditional mean as a linear combination of past values (AR) and past innovations (MA). Innovations assumed Gaussian iid for exact MLE and valid prediction intervals.

data_regime.rows: works on short series (tens to low hundreds of observations); Kalman-filter exact MLE is efficient even for small n
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate single series; only p+q+1 parameters, kept low (typically p,q <= 3)

features.interpretability: high: AR/MA coefficients and the ACF/PACF diagnostics map directly to the lag structure of the process
features.notes: Uses only the series' own lagged values and lagged residuals; no exogenous covariates (use ARMAX/SARIMAX for that). Series must be mean-stationary before fitting.

assumptions: covariance (weak) stationarity: constant mean and autocovariance over time
linear conditional mean in past values and past errors
Gaussian, iid, homoskedastic innovations (no volatility clustering, no heavy tails)
invertibility (MA roots outside unit circle) and causality (AR roots outside unit circle)
loss: exact Gaussian conditional log-likelihood via Kalman filter
equivalently minimizes one-step-ahead squared prediction error of innovations
contraindicated_when: series is non-stationary: has a trend, unit root, or growing variance (use ARIMA / differencing first)
seasonal periodicity present (use SARIMA)
exogenous drivers matter (use ARMAX/SARIMAX)
multivariate / cross-series dependence (use VAR or VARMA)
conditional heteroskedasticity / volatility clustering as in financial returns (pair with or use GARCH)
nonlinear dynamics or regime switching

children.name: ARIMA
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ARMA (which requires pre-stationary input) or SARIMA/ARIMAX (which add seasonal or exogenous components), ARIMA incorporates d-order differencing directly into the model to eliminate trend-induced non-stationarity, keeping the specification purely univariate and non-seasonal.
strengths: Handles non-stationary series with linear trends through explicit differencing (d), removing the need for manual detrending before fitting.
Interpretable parameter structure (p, d, q) with well-established information criteria (AIC/BIC) and ACF/PACF diagnostics for principled order selection.
Exact maximum-likelihood estimation via the Kalman filter yields asymptotically efficient parameter estimates on moderate-length series (n ≈ 50–500).
weaknesses: Cannot model periodic seasonal patterns — monthly or quarterly cycles require SARIMA or seasonal differencing applied separately.
Assumes a linear data-generating process, so non-linear dynamics (volatility clustering, regime switches) are systematically misspecified.
Requires the analyst to identify (p, d, q) manually or via grid search; misspecification of d causes either residual non-stationarity or over-differencing.
recommended_for: Short univariate economic or financial series (e.g., monthly CPI, quarterly GDP growth) where trend is present but seasonality is absent and n < 500.
Baseline forecasting benchmarks in academic studies, where a simple, fully interpretable model is needed to compare against more complex approaches.
not_recommended_for: Time series with strong periodic seasonality (e.g., hourly electricity load, monthly retail sales) — structural seasonal terms are absent and residuals will be autocorrelated.
High-dimensional multivariate settings where interdependencies between multiple series must be captured simultaneously — VAR or state-space models are more appropriate.
children.curiosity: Introduced by George E. P. Box and Gwilym M. Jenkins in their 1970 book 'Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control', the framework unified autoregression, differencing, and moving-average filtering into a single iterative identification-estimation-diagnostic methodology that became the dominant approach to univariate forecasting for two decades.

target.notes: Single equally-spaced univariate series; models the conditional mean of y_t given its own past after d-order differencing. Innovations assumed Gaussian white noise for exact ML / valid AIC-BIC and prediction intervals.

data_regime.rows: best on short-to-moderate series, n approx 50-500 contiguous observations; too few points underdetermines (p,d,q), very long series favor state-space or ML alternatives
data_regime.dimensionality: strictly univariate, no covariates (use ARIMAX/VAR/state-space for exogenous or multivariate)
needs: no missing gaps in the time index

features.interpretability: high — (p,d,q) orders, AR/MA coefficients, and ACF/PACF diagnostics map directly to series dynamics
features.notes: Order selection via ACF/PACF or AIC/BIC grid search; d chosen by unit-root tests (ADF/KPSS). Over-differencing inflates variance, under-differencing leaves residual non-stationarity.

assumptions: series becomes weakly stationary after d-order differencing (constant mean/variance, stable autocovariance)
linear data-generating process — no volatility clustering, regime switches, or non-linear dynamics
no seasonal/periodic component (non-seasonal model)
Gaussian, homoscedastic, serially-uncorrelated residuals
fixed regular sampling interval, no structural breaks over the window
loss: Gaussian conditional log-likelihood (exact ML via Kalman filter)
one-step-ahead squared prediction error / conditional sum of squares
contraindicated_when: strong periodic seasonality present (use SARIMA or seasonal differencing)
multiple interdependent series must be modeled jointly (use VAR / multivariate state-space)
conditional variance is time-varying / volatility clustering (use GARCH-family)
non-linear or regime-switching dynamics dominate
exogenous predictors carry signal (use ARIMAX/regression with ARMA errors)
irregular timestamps or substantial missingness without state-space handling

children.name: SARIMA
children.diff_siblings: Extends ARIMA with a multiplicative seasonal block (P,D,Q)_s — separate AR, differencing, and MA operators applied at lag multiples of the period s — so both within-period autocorrelation and cross-period seasonality are modeled simultaneously without manual deseasonalization.
strengths: Handles strong, stable seasonal cycles (monthly, quarterly, weekly) natively: the seasonal differencing operator (1-L^s)^D removes periodic non-stationarity that non-seasonal differencing cannot reach.
Inherits full ARIMA expressiveness for the non-seasonal component, so trend, drift, and short-range autocorrelation are captured in the same model without preprocessing.
Interpretable parameters with well-established diagnostic tools (ACF/PACF at seasonal lags, Ljung-Box on residuals) that guide order selection rigorously.
weaknesses: Parameter space explodes to six orders (p,d,q,P,D,Q) plus period s, making manual identification laborious and grid search expensive for large seasonal periods.
Assumes linearity and stationarity after differencing; cannot capture nonlinear seasonal interactions or abrupt structural breaks in the seasonal pattern.
Long seasonal periods (e.g., s=52 for weekly data) produce a seasonal AR/MA polynomial of very high lag order, inflating estimation variance and often making the model numerically unstable.
recommended_for: Monthly economic or retail sales series with a clear annual cycle (s=12) and multi-year history, where the seasonal pattern is stable and explainability is required.
Short hourly or daily energy demand series with a well-defined weekly cycle (s=7 or s=24) and no exogenous drivers, where a parsimonious closed-form model is preferred over a neural approach.
not_recommended_for: Time series with multiple overlapping seasonal periods (e.g., hourly data with both daily and weekly cycles), since a single s cannot capture both simultaneously.
High-frequency or very long seasonal-period data (s > 52) where the large number of seasonal lag parameters makes estimation unreliable and computationally prohibitive.
children.curiosity: The SARIMA notation (p,d,q)×(P,D,Q)_s was formalized by Box and Jenkins in their 1970 book 'Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control', where they applied the multiplicative seasonal model to monthly airline passenger counts — a dataset that became the canonical benchmark for seasonal time series methods.

target.notes: Univariate, regularly-spaced series with a single dominant seasonal period s. Models the conditional mean of the differenced series; Gaussian innovations assumed for ML estimation and prediction intervals.

data_regime.rows: needs several full seasonal cycles (rule of thumb >= 3-4 periods, e.g. >= ~36-50 obs for s=12); long histories improve seasonal order estimation
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate (no covariates); exogenous regressors require the SARIMAX extension

features.interpretability: high: explicit AR/MA/differencing orders (p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_s with diagnosable ACF/PACF and Ljung-Box residual tests
features.notes: Single integer seasonal period s must be known/specified; long s (e.g. 52) yields high-lag seasonal polynomials and unstable estimation.

assumptions: Linearity in lagged values and errors
Weak stationarity after non-seasonal (1-L)^d and seasonal (1-L^s)^D differencing
Stable, single seasonal period over the whole history (no shifting/multiple seasonalities)
Homoskedastic, uncorrelated (ideally Gaussian) residuals
No abrupt structural breaks in trend or seasonal pattern
loss: Gaussian conditional log-likelihood (exact/CSS-ML)
equivalently squared one-step-ahead forecast error
contraindicated_when: Multiple overlapping seasonal cycles (e.g. hourly with daily AND weekly periods)
Very long seasonal period (s > ~52) making seasonal lag parameters unreliable/costly
Nonlinear dynamics, regime switching, or conditional heteroskedasticity (use nonlinear/GARCH-type models)
Short history covering fewer than ~2-3 full seasonal cycles
Strong dependence on exogenous drivers (prefer SARIMAX or ML regressors)

children.name: ARIMAX / SARIMAX
children.diff_siblings: Unlike plain ARIMA/SARIMA, which model the series purely from its own past, ARIMAX/SARIMAX adds a linear regression layer on contemporaneous exogenous regressors (e.g., temperature, price) directly inside the state-space equation, keeping the AR/I/MA dynamics intact.
strengths: Captures the effect of known external drivers (e.g., holidays, promotions) without sacrificing the autocorrelation structure that ARIMA already models well.
Seasonal SARIMAX variant handles both intra-cycle seasonality (period S) and the influence of exogenous inputs in a single, unified state-space model estimated by maximum likelihood.
Produces interpretable coefficients for each exogenous regressor alongside the AR/MA parameters, making it easy to quantify how much each external factor shifts the forecast.
weaknesses: Requires future values of all exogenous regressors at forecast time — if those values are not known or accurately predicted in advance, forecast quality degrades proportionally.
Assumes a strictly linear, contemporaneous relationship between exogenous inputs and the target; lagged or nonlinear external effects must be hand-engineered as additional regressors.
Does not allow feedback from the target series back into the exogenous variables — if bidirectional causality exists, a VAR/VARX model is more appropriate.
recommended_for: Hourly electricity demand forecasting where outdoor temperature and time-of-week dummies are known in advance and drive a predictable seasonal load curve.
Retail sales forecasting with planned promotional calendars: promotion flags and price-discount variables are known future regressors that shift the baseline ARIMA trend.
not_recommended_for: Scenarios where future exogenous values are themselves uncertain and must also be forecast, as cascading forecast errors undermine the model's accuracy advantage over plain SARIMA.
Multivariate settings where every series influences every other (e.g., macroeconomic variable systems), because ARIMAX treats exogenous inputs as strictly one-directional drivers.
children.curiosity: The exogenous-input extension of Box-Jenkins ARIMA models was formalized by Box and Jenkins in their 1976 book 'Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control' (2nd ed.), which introduced the transfer-function noise model — the direct precursor to what practitioners now call ARIMAX.
keywords: predict future values from past data

target.notes: Single univariate series indexed by regular time steps; residuals/innovations assumed Gaussian for MLE and prediction intervals. The series is modeled by its own past plus a contemporaneous linear regression on exogenous inputs.

data_regime.rows: works on short-to-moderate series (dozens to low thousands of timestamps); needs at least several full seasonal cycles to identify the S period reliably
data_regime.dimensionality: small number of exogenous regressors (p << n); not for wide feature sets
needs: future/known values of every exogenous regressor at forecast horizon

features.interpretability: high — explicit AR/I/MA + seasonal orders and one linear coefficient per exogenous regressor, each directly readable
features.notes: Exogenous inputs enter linearly and contemporaneously; lagged or nonlinear effects must be hand-engineered as extra columns. Categorical drivers (holiday/promo flags) used as dummies. Differencing (d, D) handles trend/seasonal nonstationarity in the target.

assumptions: target is stationary after (seasonal) differencing
exogenous->target relationship is linear and contemporaneous
exogenous regressors are strictly one-directional drivers (no feedback from target)
future regressor values are known or accurately forecastable
Gaussian, homoscedastic, serially-uncorrelated innovations
stable single seasonal period S
loss: Gaussian log-likelihood (exact MLE via Kalman filter / state-space)
one-step prediction error / squared error
contraindicated_when: future exogenous values are themselves uncertain and must be forecast (cascading error erases the advantage over plain SARIMA)
bidirectional causality among series — use VAR/VARX
many candidate predictors or high-cardinality/nonlinear drivers — use gradient-boosted trees or ML regressors with lag features
multiple or non-integer seasonal periods, or strongly nonlinear dynamics
very long horizons where autocorrelation structure decays to the mean

children.name: VAR (Vector AutoRegression)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ARIMA and SARIMA, which model a single series with scalar lag equations, VAR generalizes the AR structure to k simultaneous equations where each variable regresses on lagged values of all k variables, allowing bidirectional dynamic interdependencies to be estimated jointly.
strengths: Captures bidirectional feedback between series without imposing causal direction a priori, enabling Granger-causality testing across all variable pairs simultaneously.
Each equation is estimable independently by OLS (since regressors are identical across equations), making inference computationally straightforward even for moderately large systems.

Impulse response functions (IRFs) quantify how a one-unit shock in one variable propagates through the entire system over h forecast horizons, providing structural interpretability absent from univariate models.
weaknesses: Parameter count grows as k²p + k (k variables, p lags), so a VAR(2) with 10 variables already requires estimating ~210 coefficients, rapidly exhausting degrees of freedom on typical macroeconomic sample sizes.
All series must be covariance-stationary; nonstationary variables with unit roots require differencing or a VECM reformulation, and misspecifying integration order distorts inference.
Assumes a time-invariant coefficient matrix and constant error covariance, making it ill-suited for systems with structural breaks or regime changes without extensions like TVP-VAR.
recommended_for: Macroeconomic policy analysis with 3-8 quarterly series (e.g., GDP growth, inflation, interest rate, unemployment) where feedback loops are theoretically expected and sample size is T > 100.

Short-horizon joint forecasting of interrelated financial variables (e.g., equity returns and credit spreads) where the cross-variable lag structure improves point forecasts over k independent ARIMA models.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional panels (k > 20 variables) where the k²p parameter explosion makes OLS estimation unreliable without Bayesian shrinkage or factor-model dimension reduction.
Series with known nonlinear dynamics or threshold effects (e.g., asymmetric business cycle responses), where the linear coefficient matrix systematically misspecifies the data-generating process.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Christopher Sims in his 1980 Econometrica paper 'Macroeconomics and Reality', VAR was explicitly designed as a critique of the large-scale structural macroeconometric models then dominant, which Sims argued imposed incredible identifying restrictions; the paper directly shaped how central banks worldwide model monetary policy transmission.

target.notes: Models a k-dimensional vector of endogenous, simultaneously-observed continuous series; each of the k variables is both predictor and target. Gaussian innovations assumed for ML/inference (IRF confidence bands, Granger tests).

data_regime.rows: needs T > ~10x the per-equation parameter count; rule of thumb T > 100 for small systems; T must exceed kp+1 per equation just to estimate
data_regime.dimensionality: k small (3-8 typical); parameters scale as k^2*p so p>n risk appears fast; k>20 needs Bayesian (Minnesota prior) shrinkage or factor reduction

features.interpretability: high: coefficient matrices, Granger-causality tests, and impulse response functions give structural, directional read of cross-series dynamics
features.notes: All variables enter as their own lags; no exogenous-only regressors (use VARX for those). Lag order p chosen by AIC/BIC/HQ.

assumptions: All series covariance-stationary (no unit roots); nonstationary I(1) series need differencing or a VECM/cointegration formulation
Time-invariant coefficient matrix and constant error covariance (no structural breaks/regime shifts without TVP-VAR or Markov-switching extensions)
Linear dynamics; serially uncorrelated, homoskedastic (Gaussian for inference) innovations
Correct lag order p; underfitting leaves autocorrelated residuals, overfitting burns degrees of freedom
Variables genuinely interdependent; if truly independent, k separate ARIMA models are more parsimonious
loss: equation-by-equation OLS / squared error (regressors identical across equations)
Gaussian log-likelihood (equivalent to OLS here) for ML estimation and likelihood-ratio lag/causality tests
contraindicated_when: High-dimensional systems (k > ~20) where k^2*p coefficients exhaust degrees of freedom under plain OLS
Nonlinear or threshold/asymmetric dynamics (regime-dependent business cycles) that a single linear coefficient matrix misspecifies
Nonstationary series with unit roots or cointegration left unaddressed (use VECM)
Univariate problem or series with no meaningful cross-feedback (ARIMA/SARIMA more efficient)
Short samples (T small relative to kp) where estimates are unstable and IRFs uninformative

children.name: VARMA
children.diff_siblings: Unlike VAR, which models multivariate dynamics using only lagged values of the series themselves, VARMA adds matrix-valued moving average terms on lagged error vectors, enabling more parsimonious representations of the same cross-series dynamics at the cost of a non-trivial identifiability problem absent in the purely autoregressive siblings.
strengths: More parsimonious than VAR: the MA component can represent long autoregressive dependencies with fewer parameters, reducing estimation variance when the true DGP has finite-order VARMA structure.
Captures cross-series error propagation explicitly: the MA matrices model how a shock in one series contaminates the forecast errors of others over multiple steps, which VAR cannot express directly.
Theoretically optimal representation: every stationary multivariate process has a finite VARMA(p,q) form, whereas the equivalent pure VAR representation may require infinite lag order.
weaknesses: Identifiability requires non-trivial constraints: without imposing an echelon form or similar canonical structure, the same VARMA(p,q) process has infinitely many observationally equivalent parameterizations, making naive MLE ill-posed.

Numerically fragile estimation: quasi-Newton optimization of the likelihood is sensitive to starting values and frequently diverges for dimensions above 3-4 variables, explaining why VAR dominates in applied work despite VARMA's theoretical superiority.

Specification complexity: determining both the AR order p and the MA order q jointly, along with Kronecker indices for the echelon form, requires sequential hypothesis testing procedures (e.g., Tiao-Box, 1981) that are computationally expensive and error-prone.
recommended_for: Low-dimensional macro or financial systems (2-5 series) where the impulse-response function has a known short MA structure, such as modeling the joint dynamics of interest rate, inflation, and output gap with quarterly data.

Settings where parsimony is critical due to a short sample (T < 200 observations) and a VAR would require more lags than the VARMA(1,1) equivalent, such as monthly industrial production indices across a small set of sectors.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional panels (more than 6-8 series): each additional series multiplies the number of MA matrices, making identification constraints and optimization intractable without sparse regularization frameworks not available in standard software.

Real-time operational forecasting pipelines where model stability and reproducibility matter: numerical sensitivity of VARMA estimation to starting values makes automated re-estimation unreliable, whereas VAR or VAR with Bayesian priors is more robust.
children.curiosity: Tiao and Box (1981) formalized a three-stage iterative procedure (specification, estimation, diagnostic checking) for VARMA models in their paper 'Modeling Multiple Time Series with Applications' (Journal of the American Statistical Association, 76:802-816), establishing the echelon form approach that remains the standard canonical identification strategy for VARMA to this day.
keywords: time series with feedback between variables

target.notes: Multivariate (vector-valued) target: jointly forecasts k>=2 continuous, mutually endogenous series with feedback. Gaussian innovations assumed for MLE. Requires (weak) stationarity; difference first for unit-root/trending series (the VARMA-on-differences route, no native cointegration handling unlike VECM).

data_regime.rows: needs T>=100-200 observations; works in short samples better than high-order VAR because the MA term buys parsimony, but MLE still unstable below ~100
data_regime.dimensionality: low-dimensional only: 2-5 series practical; identification/optimization degrade rapidly past 6-8 series

features.interpretability: medium: AR/MA coefficient matrices and impulse-response functions are interpretable, but echelon/Kronecker canonical form needed for identifiability obscures direct reading
features.notes: Inputs are the lagged series and lagged error vectors themselves; no exogenous design matrix unless extended to VARMAX. All series should be on comparable scales for stable optimization.

assumptions: weak stationarity of the (possibly differenced) vector process
Gaussian, serially uncorrelated, homoskedastic innovation vectors
linear, time-invariant cross-series dynamics
correct joint (p,q) order and identifying constraints (echelon form / Kronecker indices)
invertibility of the MA polynomial and stability of the AR polynomial
loss: Gaussian conditional log-likelihood (exact or conditional MLE)
one-step multivariate squared forecast error
contraindicated_when: more than ~6-8 series, or p>n / wide panels (use sparse VAR, factor models, or regularized methods)
nonstationary cointegrated series where the long-run relations matter (use VECM)
nonlinear cross-series dynamics, regime switching, or volatility clustering as the target (use multivariate GARCH / state-space / ML methods)
automated/real-time re-estimation pipelines needing reproducibility (numerical fragility; prefer VAR or Bayesian VAR)
univariate problems where a single ARIMA suffices
irregularly sampled or short series (T<100)

children.name: VECM
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ARIMA or VAR, VECM explicitly decomposes multivariate dynamics into a long-run equilibrium term (the error-correction term αβ'y_{t-1}) and short-run adjustment terms, making it the only model in this family that can represent cointegrated non-stationary systems without differencing away the long-run relationship.
strengths: Preserves long-run equilibrium information: cointegrated variables are modeled in levels, so the cointegrating vector β captures economically meaningful steady-state ratios (e.g., price-to-income) that pure VAR-in-differences discards.
Estimates adjustment speed explicitly: the loading matrix α quantifies how fast each variable corrects toward equilibrium per period, enabling direct inference on error-correction dynamics.
Handles multiple cointegrating relationships: Johansen's reduced-rank regression allows up to K-1 cointegrating vectors among K variables, each testable via trace or maximum-eigenvalue statistics.
weaknesses: Requires pre-testing for cointegration rank via Johansen or Engle-Granger tests, which have low power in small samples and are sensitive to lag selection, making the rank determination itself a source of model misspecification.

Assumes linear cointegrating relationships and constant adjustment coefficients; structural breaks (e.g., regime changes, policy shifts) violate these assumptions and can produce spurious cointegration evidence.

Computationally and analytically demanding relative to VAR-in-differences: the additional step of estimating β and α matrices increases parameter count and reduces degrees of freedom, worsening performance with fewer than ~50 observations per variable.
recommended_for: Macroeconomic systems where theory predicts long-run equilibria, such as modeling the relationship between GDP, consumption, and investment across 30+ quarterly observations with confirmed I(1) series.

Pairs or groups of financial prices tied by arbitrage constraints (e.g., spot and futures prices, or sovereign bond yields across countries), where the cointegrating spread is the basis for trading or risk analysis.
not_recommended_for: Stationary time series (I(0) processes): applying VECM to already-stationary data is mathematically invalid since there is no unit root to correct, and results reduce to a misspecified VAR.
High-frequency or short data sets (fewer than ~30 observations per variable) where the asymptotic properties of the Johansen rank tests do not hold and cointegration rank estimation is unreliable.
children.curiosity: The error-correction representation was formalized by Engle and Granger (1987) in their Nobel-cited paper 'Co-integration and Error Correction: Representation, Estimation, and Testing' (Econometrica, 55(2):251-276), which proved the Granger Representation Theorem: any set of cointegrated I(1) variables has an ECM representation, and vice versa.

target.notes: Multivariate (K>=2) jointly-modeled time series. Each endogenous variable individually I(1) (non-stationary, unit root), but linear combinations are I(0) (cointegrated). Gaussian innovations assumed for Johansen ML estimation and rank tests.

data_regime.rows: needs >=30-50 observations per variable for reliable Johansen rank inference; asymptotic test properties fail in short samples
data_regime.dimensionality: low K (typically 2-6 variables); parameter count grows with K and lag order, so p<<n required

features.interpretability: high: cointegrating vector beta encodes economically meaningful long-run equilibrium ratios; loading matrix alpha quantifies per-period adjustment speed toward equilibrium
features.notes: All series must be in levels (do NOT difference away the cointegrating relationship). Requires prior unit-root testing (ADF/PP) to confirm I(1), then cointegration rank selection (Johansen trace / max-eigenvalue).
