assumptions: all endogenous series integrated of the same order, typically I(1)
at least one linear cointegrating relationship exists (rank 1<=r<=K-1)
cointegrating relationships are linear and adjustment coefficients constant over the sample (no structural breaks / regime shifts)
innovations are white-noise, homoskedastic, approximately Gaussian
correct lag order specified (misspecification biases rank tests)
loss: Gaussian maximum likelihood via Johansen reduced-rank regression
conditional least squares on the error-correction representation
contraindicated_when: series are stationary I(0): no unit root to correct, model is invalid and reduces to a misspecified VAR
series are integrated but NOT cointegrated: use VAR in differences instead
fewer than ~30 observations per variable: Johansen rank estimation unreliable
structural breaks or regime changes present: can produce spurious cointegration
relationships are nonlinear or adjustment speeds time-varying
univariate problem: use ARIMA

children.name: Naive Forecast / Seasonal Naive
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ARIMA, SARIMA, or Exponential Smoothing siblings that estimate parameters from historical data, Naive/Seasonal Naive requires zero parameter estimation: it copies the last observed value (Naive) or the value from exactly one seasonal period ago (Seasonal Naive), making it the only zero-cost, zero-assumption baseline in the family.
strengths: Zero computational cost and no hyperparameters — fit time is O(1) regardless of series length, making it the fastest possible forecasting method.
Seasonal Naive exactly captures pure seasonal repetition (e.g., weekly retail cycles) with no risk of overfitting when the dominant signal is stable period-over-period repetition.
Statistically optimal under the random walk hypothesis — if prices or demand genuinely follow a random walk, no model can systematically beat the Naive forecast in expectation.
weaknesses: Produces flat (Naive) or purely periodic (Seasonal Naive) forecasts, so any trend component is completely ignored and errors grow unboundedly with horizon.
Seasonal Naive breaks immediately when the seasonal period shifts or a calendar anomaly (holiday, promotion) disrupts the most recent cycle used as the template.
Provides no probabilistic decomposition of error sources — it cannot distinguish signal from noise, making it useless for causal analysis or intervention modeling.
recommended_for: Establishing a mandatory sanity-check baseline in any forecasting competition or production pipeline, particularly for daily or weekly retail sales data with strong, stable weekly seasonality.
Short-horizon forecasting of financial instrument prices where the random walk hypothesis holds and sophisticated models consistently fail to beat this benchmark after transaction costs.
not_recommended_for: Series with a clear monotonic trend (rising demand, growing user base) where copying the last observation or last-season observation systematically underestimates every future value.
Multi-step forecasts over horizons longer than one seasonal period when external shocks, promotions, or structural breaks make the most recent seasonal cycle unrepresentative of future cycles.
children.curiosity: Makridakis and Hibon (1979) showed in a landmark study that the naive method outperformed the majority of statistically sophisticated methods tested on 111 real series, a result that triggered decades of debate and directly motivated the M-competition series designed to rigorously benchmark forecasting methods against simple baselines.

target.notes: Univariate, evenly-spaced series only. Naive copies the last observation; Seasonal Naive copies the value from one seasonal period ago. No covariates.

data_regime.rows: works with as few as one observation (Naive) or one full season (Seasonal Naive); benefits nothing from large n
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate, p=0 exogenous features

features.interpretability: high - forecast is literally a past observed value, fully transparent
features.notes: Requires a known, fixed seasonal period m for Seasonal Naive (e.g. m=7 daily/weekly, m=12 monthly/yearly). No scaling or transformation needed.

assumptions: Naive assumes a random walk (no trend, last value is best predictor of next).
Seasonal Naive assumes stable, repeating seasonality with a fixed known period and no trend across cycles.
Most recent observation / most recent season is representative of the future.
loss: minimizes expected squared error under the random walk DGP; used as the denominator baseline for scale-free metrics (MASE)
contraindicated_when: Series has a clear monotonic trend - forecasts systematically biased.
Seasonal period is unknown, drifting, or multiple-overlapping seasonalities exist.
Recent observations contaminated by outliers, promotions, holidays, or structural breaks (becomes the template and propagates the anomaly).
Multi-step horizon longer than one season where future cycles diverge from the last one.
Need for probabilistic signal/noise decomposition, intervention or causal analysis.

children.name: Croston (intermittent demand)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ARIMA or exponential smoothing, which apply a single update equation to the raw series, Croston decomposes intermittent demand into two independent series — non-zero demand sizes and inter-demand intervals — and applies separate exponential smoothing to each, deriving the forecast as their ratio.
strengths: Directly handles zero-inflated series: updates only occur at demand events, preventing the dilution of signal that SES suffers when averaging across many zero periods.
Produces a stable per-period demand rate estimate without requiring distributional assumptions on the arrival process, making it robust when demand follows no clean ARMA structure.
Computationally trivial (two scalars updated per event), scaling to catalogues with hundreds of thousands of slow-moving SKUs with negligible overhead.
weaknesses: Proven positively biased by Syntetos and Boylan (2001): the ratio of two exponentially smoothed series is not an unbiased estimator of the true mean, systematically over-forecasting demand.
Freezes forecasts between demand events — inter-event information (e.g., lengthening silence signaling obsolescence) never triggers a downward revision.
Assumes demand sizes and inter-arrival intervals are mutually independent and individually stationary, an assumption violated by seasonal or trend-driven intermittent series.
recommended_for: Spare-parts and MRO inventory with very low demand frequency (average inter-demand interval > 1.32 periods) and stable, non-seasonal demand sizes, such as aircraft or industrial machinery components.

Slow-moving retail or wholesale SKUs with sporadic, size-variable transactions spread across long zero-demand stretches, where service-level targets require a steady mean-rate estimate rather than a point forecast.
not_recommended_for: Products with seasonal or trending demand patterns, where the stationarity assumption breaks down and SARIMA or state-space models capture the structure that Croston ignores.
Items approaching end-of-life or subject to obsolescence risk, since Croston never updates the forecast downward during zero-demand runs, leading to chronic over-stocking.
children.curiosity: Introduced by J.D. Croston in 'Forecasting and Stock Control for Intermittent Demands' (Operational Research Quarterly, 1972), the method remained the standard for over two decades until Syntetos and Boylan (2001) formally proved its positive bias and proposed the Syntetos-Boylan Approximation (SBA) as a corrected variant.

target.notes: Univariate non-negative demand series that is intermittent: many exact-zero periods interspersed with sporadic non-zero demand events. Decomposes into two latent series (non-zero demand size, inter-demand interval) each smoothed separately; forecast = size/interval as a per-period mean demand rate, not a calendar-aligned point forecast.

data_regime.rows: works on short single series; only needs enough demand events to seed two smoothers (effective sample = count of non-zero periods, not total periods)
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate per SKU; scales to hundreds of thousands of independent series (two scalars updated per event)

features.interpretability: high: two interpretable state variables (mean demand size, mean inter-demand interval) with a single smoothing constant; forecast is their ratio

assumptions: Demand sizes and inter-demand intervals are mutually independent
Both component series are individually stationary (no trend or seasonality)
Inter-demand intervals are geometrically distributed / arrivals memoryless
Demand sizes are i.i.d. across events
loss: exponential smoothing of each component (recursive level update minimizing weighted squared error on the non-zero subseries)
produces a mean-rate estimate rather than optimizing a forecast loss directly; not a probabilistic/quantile forecaster
contraindicated_when: demand is seasonal or trending (stationarity broken; use SARIMA or state-space)
items face obsolescence/end-of-life (lengthening zero runs never trigger downward revision; Croston freezes between events)
unbiased mean estimation is required (classic Croston is positively biased per Syntetos-Boylan; prefer SBA/TSB correction)
demand is fast-moving / non-intermittent (no zero-inflation advantage over SES or ARIMA)
demand sizes correlate with interval length (independence assumption violated)

target.notes: Univariate, equally-spaced series. Assumes Gaussian white-noise innovations for analytic prediction intervals and ML/CSS estimation. Models the conditional mean only — not volatility (use GARCH) and not count/integer-valued series directly.

data_regime.rows: works on hundreds of observations; effective sample shrinks with differencing and high (p,q). Long history not required and does not help much beyond stable parameter estimates
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate by design; only exogenous regressors via ARIMAX. Not for wide multivariate panels

features.interpretability: high — each AR/MA coefficient maps to autocorrelation at a specific lag; order chosen via ACF/PACF and information criteria (AIC/BIC)
features.notes: Requires (weak) stationarity after d-order differencing; SARIMA adds seasonal (P,D,Q,s) terms for fixed-period seasonality. Variance-stabilizing transform (log/Box-Cox) needed when variance grows with level

assumptions: stationarity after differencing (constant mean/variance/autocovariance)
linear dependence on past values and past errors
homoskedastic, serially-uncorrelated, approximately Gaussian residuals
fixed and known seasonal period for SARIMA
no structural breaks or regime shifts over the horizon
loss: Gaussian log-likelihood (exact ML or conditional sum of squares)
one-step-ahead squared forecast error
information criteria (AIC/AICc/BIC) for order selection
contraindicated_when: series is nonstationary in a way differencing cannot fix (regime shifts, level breaks)
dynamics are nonlinear, chaotic, or show volatility clustering (use GARCH/LSTM/TFT)
long-range dependence / long memory present (use FARIMA)
forecast horizon is long — intervals widen to the unconditional variance quickly
the outcome is driven mainly by exogenous covariates rather than its own past
irregular sampling, heavy missingness, or count/integer-valued targets

children.name: Exponential Smoothing
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ARIMA (which models autocorrelation structure via lag polynomials) and Moving Average smoothers (which weight past values equally within a window), Exponential Smoothing assigns geometrically decaying weights to all past observations and decomposes the series explicitly into level, trend, and seasonal state variables updated recursively at each step.
strengths: Handles trend and multiplicative seasonality natively through the Holt-Winters triple smoothing equations (α, β, γ), without requiring differencing or stationarity pre-processing.
Performs well on short series (as few as two seasonal cycles) where ARIMA cannot reliably estimate p/d/q parameters from limited data.
The ETS state-space formulation (Hyndman et al., 2008) yields exact likelihood for model selection via AIC, enabling automatic model choice across 30 Error/Trend/Seasonal combinations.
weaknesses: Cannot incorporate exogenous regressors (e.g., promotions, calendar effects) without extensions like ETSX, unlike ARIMAX which handles covariates natively.
Smoothing parameters α, β, γ are optimized globally over the training period, so a structural break mid-series corrupts estimates for all observations before and after it.

Assumes the seasonal pattern has a fixed period (e.g., 12 months); irregular or multi-frequency seasonality (e.g., daily + weekly) requires separate modeling that the standard ETS framework does not support.
recommended_for: Retail demand forecasting at the SKU level with clear annual seasonality and short history (1-3 years), where Holt-Winters multiplicative seasonality captures proportional swings in sales volume.
Operational metrics monitoring (server load, energy consumption) with a stable seasonal cycle and a need for fast, interpretable one-step-ahead forecasts deployable without statistical expertise.
not_recommended_for: Financial return series with heavy tails, volatility clustering, and no meaningful seasonality, where GARCH-family models are required and exponential smoothing produces miscalibrated prediction intervals.

Long-horizon forecasts on series with multiple overlapping seasonal periods (e.g., hourly electricity demand with daily, weekly, and annual cycles), where TBATS or deep learning models handle the multi-seasonality explicitly.
children.curiosity: Charles C. Holt developed the two-parameter (level + trend) variant in 1957 as an unpublished ONR memorandum at Carnegie Institute of Technology; it remained a grey-literature document for nearly 50 years until formally published in the International Journal of Forecasting in 2004.

children.name: Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES)
children.diff_siblings: SES models only the level component via a single smoothing parameter alpha, producing a flat (constant) forecast horizon, whereas Holt adds a trend term and Holt-Winters adds a seasonal term on top of that.
strengths: Requires estimating only one parameter (alpha), making it robust to overfitting on very short time series (as few as 10-15 observations).
Optimal alpha estimated by minimizing one-step-ahead SSE yields forecasts equivalent to ARIMA(0,1,1), giving it a solid statistical grounding.
Computationally trivial and fully incremental: updating the forecast after a new observation costs O(1) time and constant memory, ideal for high-frequency streaming data.
weaknesses: Produces a flat forecast for all horizons beyond t+1 — the predicted value is the same whether forecasting one step or fifty steps ahead.
Cannot capture trend or seasonality; applied to trended or seasonal data it systematically lags, producing biased forecasts.
The optimal alpha is highly sensitive to the initialization of the level S0; poor initialization degrades accuracy on short series.
recommended_for: Stationary demand streams with no discernible trend or seasonality, such as slow-moving spare-parts inventory where daily demand fluctuates randomly around a stable mean.
High-volume, low-latency monitoring pipelines (IoT sensors, server metrics) where a continuously updated single-number baseline is needed with negligible compute cost.
not_recommended_for: Series with a deterministic or stochastic trend (e.g., growing sales, cumulative counts) — use Holt or ARIMA(0,2,2) instead.
Data with recurring seasonal patterns (daily, weekly, annual cycles) — SES will average out the seasonality rather than model it, inflating forecast error.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Robert G. Brown in his 1956 U.S. Navy report 'Exponential Smoothing for Predicting Demand' and later formalized in his 1959 book 'Statistical Forecasting for Inventory Control', SES was originally devised to track moving targets for fire-control systems before being adopted for inventory management.

target.notes: Univariate, evenly-spaced numeric series. Forecast is the smoothed level; constant (flat) for all horizons >1. Equivalent to ARIMA(0,1,1) optimal forecast.

data_regime.rows: works on very short series (10-15 obs); only one parameter (alpha) to estimate
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate only (no exogenous regressors, no cross-series)

features.interpretability: high; single smoothing constant alpha is the exponential decay weight on past observations, level is directly readable
features.notes: O(1) incremental update per new observation, constant memory; suited to high-frequency streaming. Sensitive to initial level S0 on short series.

assumptions: series is locally stationary in mean (no trend, no seasonality)
no deterministic or stochastic trend component
no recurring seasonal cycles
level evolves as a slowly-changing random walk (consistent with ARIMA(0,1,1))
loss: one-step-ahead sum of squared errors (SSE) for alpha/initial-level estimation
contraindicated_when: series has trend (growing/declining or cumulative counts) — use Holt or ARIMA(0,2,2)
series has seasonality (daily/weekly/annual cycles) — use Holt-Winters or SARIMA
multi-step forecasts needed with non-flat profile (SES gives identical value at all horizons)
exogenous drivers must be incorporated

children.name: Holt's Linear Trend
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Simple Exponential Smoothing (which tracks only the level) and Holt-Winters (which adds a seasonal component), Holt's Linear Trend maintains two separate smoothing equations — one for the level (α) and one for the trend slope (β) — producing forecasts that grow linearly into the future at a rate updated at each step.
strengths: Captures non-stationary series with a persistent linear drift without requiring differencing or ARIMA identification; the β parameter adapts the slope estimate as new data arrives.
Only two hyperparameters (α, β), both optimized by minimizing SSE over the training set, making fitting fast and interpretable even on short series (≥15 observations).
Produces multi-step forecasts analytically as ℓ_t + h·b_t, with exact prediction-interval formulas available under the ETS(A,A,N) state-space representation.
weaknesses: The trend is projected indefinitely as a constant slope, causing systematic over-forecasting on long horizons when true growth decelerates — Gardner & McKenzie (1985) showed this empirically across 1,001 business series.
No seasonal component: applying it to series with annual, weekly, or intra-day cycles yields biased level and slope estimates because the seasonal signal is absorbed into β.
Assumes the trend is additive (linear growth in absolute units); multiplicative/exponential growth series require log-transforming the data before fitting, adding a manual preprocessing step.
recommended_for: Monthly or quarterly sales/demand series with a clear upward or downward linear drift and no recurring seasonal pattern, where forecasts are needed 3–12 periods ahead.

Short to medium-length industrial time series (20–200 observations) where model parsimony is required and only trend — not seasonality — is present, such as equipment wear-rate or cumulative defect counts.
not_recommended_for: Series with strong seasonality (e.g., retail weekly sales, energy consumption with daily cycles) where omitting the seasonal equation produces structurally biased forecasts regardless of α and β tuning.

Very long forecast horizons (h > 2× the series length) where the constant-slope extrapolation diverges from reality; the damped-trend variant (Gardner & McKenzie, 1985) is the appropriate replacement.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Charles C. Holt in a 1957 ONR Research Memorandum at Carnegie Institute of Technology — a report that circulated unpublished for decades and was only formally published in the International Journal of Forecasting in 2004, nearly 50 years after it was written.

target.notes: Univariate, equally-spaced series with a persistent linear (additive) trend and NO seasonal component. Single series at a time; not for cross-sectional regression.

data_regime.rows: works on short series (>=15 obs); typical sweet spot 20-200 observations
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate only (1 series, no exogenous regressors)

features.interpretability: high: two state equations (level, slope) with two readable smoothing weights (alpha, beta); forecast = l_t + h*b_t
features.notes: Requires evenly-spaced timestamps. Multiplicative/exponential growth must be log-transformed before fitting. Equivalent to ETS(A,A,N) state-space model.

assumptions: Trend is additive and locally linear (constant-per-step slope around the smoothed estimate)
No seasonal cycle present (seasonality otherwise leaks into the slope and biases it)
Series is regularly sampled with no large gaps
Growth is in absolute units; exponential growth violates additivity unless log-transformed
loss: sum of squared errors (SSE) of one-step-ahead forecast residuals, minimized over alpha and beta
contraindicated_when: Series has strong seasonality (weekly/daily/annual cycles) -> use Holt-Winters/ETS with seasonal term
Long horizons (h > ~2x series length) where constant-slope extrapolation diverges -> use damped-trend (Gardner & McKenzie)
Multivariate forecasting or need for exogenous predictors -> use ARIMAX/regression or ML forecasters
Series is stationary/flat with no trend -> Simple Exponential Smoothing suffices
Forecasting many unrelated short series jointly where global/ML models pool information better

children.name: Holt-Winters (Seasonal)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Simple Exponential Smoothing (level only) and Holt's Double Exponential Smoothing (level + trend), Holt-Winters adds a third smoothing equation for a periodic seasonal component, which can be formulated additively (constant amplitude) or multiplicatively (amplitude proportional to level).
strengths: Adapts the seasonal factors recursively each period via the γ parameter, so the seasonal pattern evolves with the series instead of being fixed.
Handles both additive and multiplicative seasonality, making it suitable for series where seasonal swings grow with the level (e.g., retail sales that scale with volume).
Low computational cost and interpretable decomposition into level, trend, and seasonal components, enabling fast retraining on streaming data.
weaknesses: Requires at least two full seasonal cycles of historical data to initialise the seasonal indices reliably.
Assumes a single, fixed seasonal period (e.g., 12 months); mixed or irregular seasonality (e.g., double seasonality in hourly electricity data) cannot be captured by a single model.
Smoothing parameters α, β, γ are estimated by minimising in-sample SSE, which can overfit short series and produce poor out-of-sample forecasts when the optimisation landscape is flat.
recommended_for: Monthly retail or e-commerce sales with a strong 12-period annual cycle and a growing trend, where the seasonal amplitude increases proportionally with sales volume (multiplicative variant).

Short-horizon operational forecasting (1-12 steps ahead) on weekly or monthly time series with stable, well-defined seasonality and limited historical data, where lightweight models are preferred over SARIMA or neural networks.
not_recommended_for: High-frequency time series with multiple nested seasonal periods (e.g., hourly energy demand with daily, weekly, and annual cycles), where TBATS or Prophet handle multi-seasonality explicitly.

Series with abrupt structural breaks or irregular calendar effects (promotions, holidays, COVID shocks), since the smoothing equations cannot absorb sudden level shifts without parameter re-estimation.
children.curiosity: Peter R. Winters formalised the seasonal extension in 'Forecasting Sales by Exponentially Weighted Moving Averages' (Management Science, 1960), building on Charles Holt's unpublished 1957 ONR report; the method thus predates Box-Jenkins ARIMA by over a decade and was for years the dominant approach in industry inventory management.

target.notes: Univariate, equally-spaced series with a single fixed seasonal period m. Additive variant for constant-amplitude seasonality; multiplicative for amplitude proportional to level (requires strictly positive values).

data_regime.rows: needs at least 2 full seasonal cycles to initialise seasonal indices; works on short series (dozens to hundreds of points)
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate; no exogenous regressors
needs: regular time index with known seasonal period m

features.interpretability: high; explicit decomposition into level, trend, and seasonal components with smoothing weights alpha/beta/gamma
features.notes: Multiplicative seasonality/trend require strictly positive data; log transform an alternative for additive fit on multiplicative data.

assumptions: single fixed and known seasonal period
trend is locally linear (damped option for flattening long-horizon trend)
no covariates needed; recent observations more informative than distant ones
no abrupt structural breaks or level shifts within the smoothing window
seasonal pattern stable in shape (it evolves slowly via gamma but the period itself is constant)
loss: in-sample sum of squared errors (SSE) minimised over alpha, beta, gamma and initial states
Gaussian likelihood under the equivalent ETS state-space form, enabling AIC-based selection and prediction intervals
contraindicated_when: multiple nested/complex seasonalities (e.g. hourly demand with daily+weekly+annual cycles) -> use TBATS, Prophet, or SARIMA with Fourier terms
abrupt structural breaks, regime shifts, or irregular calendar/holiday effects without re-estimation
need to incorporate exogenous predictors (use SARIMAX or regression-based methods)
fewer than two seasonal cycles of history
no seasonality and no trend (Simple Exponential Smoothing suffices) or non-stationary behaviour better modelled by differencing in ARIMA

children.name: ETS (Error, Trend, Seasonality)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike named exponential smoothing methods (Simple, Holt, Holt-Winters) that fix the error-trend-season structure, ETS formalizes all 30 combinations as explicit state-space models with observation and transition equations, enabling maximum likelihood estimation and AIC-based automatic selection across the full family.
strengths: Principled model selection: AIC comparison across all 30 ETS(E,T,S) variants picks the statistically best structure without manual specification

Native multiplicative seasonality: ETS(M,*,M) handles series where seasonal amplitude grows proportionally to the level, producing calibrated prediction intervals that ARIMA requires differencing tricks to approximate
Interpretable decomposition: the fitted level, trend, and seasonal states are readable quantities that map directly to business intuitions about baseline, growth, and periodic swings
weaknesses: Assumes a single fixed smoothing structure for the entire series, so it cannot adapt to structural breaks or regime changes mid-series without refitting
Multiplicative error variants (M error) can produce explosive prediction intervals when the level approaches zero, making them unsuitable for sparse or near-zero demand series
No exogenous regressors: unlike ARIMAX or regression with ARIMA errors, pure ETS cannot incorporate calendar effects, promotions, or covariates without extending the framework
recommended_for: Retail or supply-chain demand forecasting where seasonal amplitude scales with volume (multiplicative seasonality) and series length is 2-5 full seasons, enabling AIC to distinguish additive from multiplicative components reliably
Automated batch forecasting of hundreds of univariate series (e.g., SKU-level inventory) where a single pipeline must select an appropriate smoothing structure per series without manual intervention
not_recommended_for: Series driven by external shocks or known covariates (e.g., electricity demand with temperature), where the inability to include regressors leaves systematic variance unexplained
Intermittent or count demand series with frequent zeros, where multiplicative error formulations become numerically unstable and additive variants underestimate the spike-and-zero pattern
children.curiosity: Hyndman, Koehler, Snyder, and Grose (2002) showed in the International Journal of Forecasting that the then-disparate zoo of exponential smoothing heuristics could all be derived as special cases of 30 state-space models with a common likelihood, resolving decades of debate about which method was 'correct' and enabling formal statistical comparison for the first time.

target.notes: Single univariate equally-spaced series. Additive-error variants assume homoscedastic Gaussian innovations; multiplicative-error variants model variance scaling with the level. No multivariate/panel support.

data_regime.rows: needs at least 2 full seasonal cycles; 2-5+ seasons for AIC to reliably distinguish additive vs multiplicative seasonality
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate only (p=1, the series itself); no covariates

need for multivariate or hierarchical cross-series dependence

children.name: BATS
children.diff_siblings: Unlike TBATS, which represents each seasonal period via Fourier series (requiring only 2 seed states per season), BATS stores one seed state per time step of each seasonal period, making it exact for short integer-period seasonality but computationally intractable for long or non-integer periods.
strengths: Handles multiple simultaneous seasonal periods (e.g., weekly + annual) within a single state space framework, unlike classic ETS which supports only one.
Box-Cox transformation is selected automatically by AIC, stabilizing variance in count-like or right-skewed series without manual pre-processing.
ARMA(p,q) error structure absorbs residual autocorrelation that exponential smoothing alone cannot capture, reducing systematic forecast bias.
weaknesses: State space grows linearly with seasonal period length: a period of m requires m seed states, making hourly or sub-daily data (m = 8760 for annual) computationally infeasible.
Cannot incorporate exogenous regressors (promotions, holidays, weather), unlike SARIMAX or regression-with-ARMA-errors approaches.
Automatic model selection via AIC over the full combinatorial space of Box-Cox, trend, damping, and ARMA orders is slow on long series.
recommended_for: Weekly retail sales with dual seasonality (day-of-week + week-of-year) where periods are short integers and no external regressors are available.
Monthly or quarterly economic indicators with trend and heteroscedastic variance, where the Box-Cox parameter needs data-driven selection.
not_recommended_for: High-frequency data (hourly or finer resolution) with long annual cycles, where the per-step seed states make fitting computationally prohibitive — use TBATS instead.
Forecasting problems where external drivers (price, promotions, temperature) are known and available, since BATS has no mechanism to include covariates.
children.curiosity: Introduced by De Livera, Hyndman, and Snyder (2011) in the Journal of the American Statistical Association (vol. 106, pp. 1513-1527), the paper simultaneously presented both BATS and its Fourier-based successor TBATS, positioning BATS as the exact-seasonality baseline against which TBATS demonstrated superior scalability.

target.notes: Univariate single-series forecasting. Box-Cox auto-selection accommodates right-skewed or heteroscedastic series (count-like positive values), but the model is not a true count/GLM model; it transforms to approximate Gaussian innovations rather than modeling a discrete distribution.

data_regime.rows: needs enough history to estimate each seasonality (rule of thumb >= 2 full cycles of the longest period); short integer seasonal periods only
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate; one endogenous series, no covariate matrix

features.interpretability: medium: decomposable into level/trend/seasonal + ARMA error components, but Box-Cox + ARMA + multiple seasonal states make the full state vector hard to read directly
features.notes: Input is the raw univariate series only; no engineered exogenous features can be supplied. State space dimension grows linearly (m seed states per seasonal period m), so memory/compute scale with period length.

assumptions: Seasonal periods are short and integer-valued (one seed state per step is feasible)
Seasonal pattern is stable / additive in the Box-Cox-transformed scale
Innovations are homoscedastic after Box-Cox transform
No relevant external drivers omitted (closed univariate system)
loss: Gaussian likelihood / one-step-ahead squared prediction error in the Box-Cox scale
AIC for automatic selection over Box-Cox, trend, damping, and ARMA(p,q) orders
contraindicated_when: High-frequency data (hourly/sub-daily) with long cycles where per-step seasonal seed states make fitting intractable (use TBATS with Fourier seasonality instead)
Non-integer or very long seasonal periods
Known, available exogenous regressors matter (use SARIMAX or regression with ARMA errors)
Multivariate / many parallel series requiring cross-series learning (use global ML forecasters)
True discrete count targets requiring a count likelihood rather than a Box-Cox-transformed Gaussian approximation

children.name: TBATS
children.diff_siblings: Unlike standard ETS models that represent seasonality via additive or multiplicative state components requiring integer periods, TBATS encodes each seasonal cycle as a Fourier series of trigonometric terms within the state space, allowing non-integer and multiple simultaneous seasonal periods (e.g., period 365.25) with only 2k seed states per seasonality regardless of cycle length.
strengths: Handles non-integer seasonal periods (e.g., daily data with period 365.25) that break standard ETS/Holt-Winters formulations requiring integer lags
Jointly estimates Box-Cox transformation, ARMA(p,q) residual correction, trend damping, and Fourier seasonal orders in a single state space model via maximum likelihood
Allows each seasonal component to evolve slowly over time through stochastic state updates, capturing gradual drift in seasonal shape unlike static Fourier regression
weaknesses: Estimation is computationally expensive — fitting scales poorly with long series because the Kalman filter runs over the full history for each candidate model in the automatic order-selection grid search
Prediction intervals are systematically over-wide due to high parameter uncertainty when many Fourier harmonics and ARMA orders are selected simultaneously
Cannot incorporate exogenous regressors or fixed calendar effects (holidays, promotions), making it inferior to dynamic regression or Prophet when such covariates are available
recommended_for: Sub-daily demand or sensor data with both weekly (period 7) and annual (period 365.25) cycles simultaneously, where standard Holt-Winters would require integer approximations that accumulate phase error over years

Electricity load forecasting with intraday (period 48 for half-hourly) and intraweek (period 336) seasonality, where the slowly-evolving seasonal state captures shifting consumption habits across seasons
not_recommended_for: Short series (fewer than 2 full seasonal cycles) where the Kalman filter cannot identify trigonometric state parameters reliably, yielding degenerate or near-flat forecasts

Forecasting problems that require incorporating known external drivers (promotions, weather, holidays), since TBATS has no covariate input mechanism and ignoring such structure produces avoidable bias
children.curiosity: Introduced by De Livera, Hyndman, and Snyder (2011) in the Journal of the American Statistical Association (vol. 106, no. 496), TBATS was motivated by Australian electricity demand data that exhibited three overlapping seasonal cycles — intraday, intraweek, and intra-year — none of which could be handled by any existing exponential smoothing formulation at the time.

target.notes: Univariate continuous series; Box-Cox transform inside the model handles right-skew and multiplicative/variance-changing structure, so strict Gaussianity of raw data is not required.

data_regime.rows: needs at least 2 full cycles of the longest seasonal period; long high-frequency histories preferred but fitting cost grows with series length (Kalman filter over full history per candidate model in the order-selection grid)
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate single series, no feature matrix
needs: sufficiently long history to identify trigonometric seasonal states

features.interpretability: medium - decomposes into trend, multiple Fourier seasonal components, and ARMA residual, but Fourier harmonic states are not directly meaningful
features.notes: No exogenous regressor or calendar/holiday input; only the target series and its seasonal periods. Designed for one or more seasonal periods including non-integer ones (e.g., 365.25, 48, 336).

assumptions: seasonal periods are known and roughly stable in length (slow stochastic drift in shape is allowed, abrupt regime/period changes are not)
at least two full seasonal cycles observed per declared period
no important driver is external; relevant structure is captured by trend + seasonality + ARMA autocorrelation
errors approximately Gaussian after Box-Cox transform
loss: Gaussian log-likelihood via Kalman filter / maximum likelihood (state space innovations)
contraindicated_when: series shorter than ~2 full cycles of the longest period (states unidentifiable, near-flat forecasts)
known exogenous drivers matter (promotions, weather, holidays) - no covariate mechanism, use dynamic regression or Prophet
single simple integer seasonality where ETS/Holt-Winters or SARIMA is cheaper and competitive
very long series where the per-candidate Kalman filtering over full history makes grid-search fitting prohibitively slow
calibrated prediction intervals are critical (intervals tend to be over-wide when many harmonics/ARMA orders are selected)

children.name: STL (Seasonal-Trend Decomposition)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Holt-Winters and other exponential smoothing methods that forecast directly by updating level, trend, and seasonal state equations, STL is a pure decomposition filter: it uses iterative LOESS (locally weighted regression) passes in inner and outer loops to separate a series into trend, seasonal, and remainder components without producing a forecast model itself.
strengths: Seasonal component can vary in shape over time — the LOESS window controls how fast it is allowed to change, which no fixed exponential smoothing seasonal equation can do.
Robust outer loop down-weights outliers during smoothing, so a single anomalous spike does not distort the extracted trend or seasonal pattern.
Seasonal period is an arbitrary integer (7, 52, 365, etc.) set by the user, whereas classical additive decomposition requires even-length periods for centered moving averages.
weaknesses: Only additive decomposition is supported natively; multiplicative seasonality requires a prior log transformation and back-transformation of residuals, adding steps and potential error propagation.
Requires manual tuning of two bandwidth parameters (trend window and seasonal window) — wrong choices produce over-smoothed or under-smoothed components with no automatic selection built in.
Produces no forecast on its own; a second model (ARIMA, ETS, etc.) must be fitted to the remainder and trend components separately, increasing pipeline complexity.
recommended_for: Weekly retail sales with evolving seasonal peaks (e.g., holiday patterns that shift year to year), where the changing-seasonality capability of the LOESS window is essential.

Anomaly detection in long daily sensor streams (temperature, electricity load) where the robust outer loop isolates the true seasonal baseline from spike contamination before residuals are thresholded.
not_recommended_for: Short series with fewer than two full seasonal cycles, where the LOESS smoother has too little data to estimate stable trend and seasonal windows without severe boundary effects.

Series with multiplicative heteroscedastic seasonality (amplitude growing proportionally with level, e.g., airline passengers) where a log transform is inadvisable due to near-zero values or interpretability constraints.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Cleveland, Cleveland, McRae, and Terpenning (1990) in the Journal of Official Statistics, STL was developed at Bell Labs and originally applied to decompose monthly CO2 measurements from Mauna Loa — the same dataset used by Keeling to document rising atmospheric CO2 — demonstrating that the secular trend and annual seasonal cycle could be cleanly separated even as the seasonal amplitude evolved over decades.

target.notes: Not a forecaster: decomposes a univariate equally-spaced series into trend + seasonal + remainder. No predictive target is fit; output components feed downstream forecasting or residual thresholding.

data_regime.rows: needs at least two full seasonal cycles; long series (hundreds to thousands of points) preferred for stable LOESS windows
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate single series only; no exogenous regressors or multivariate input

features.interpretability: high — components (trend, seasonal, remainder) are directly inspectable and additive
features.notes: Single value column indexed by time; requires regular sampling and a user-specified seasonal period m (e.g. 7, 52, 365). Two bandwidth parameters (trend/seasonal window) tuned manually.

assumptions: additive structure: series = trend + seasonal + remainder (multiplicative requires prior log transform)
fixed, known integer seasonal period
regularly-spaced observations with no large gaps
seasonal shape evolves slowly relative to the LOESS seasonal window
contraindicated_when: fewer than two complete seasonal cycles available
multiplicative/heteroscedastic seasonality with amplitude scaling on the level and values near zero (log transform unsafe)
irregular or missing timestamps
a direct forecast is required without an added downstream model
multiple or non-integer/fractional seasonal periods (use MSTL or TBATS instead)

target.notes: Univariate equally-spaced series. ETS state-space form assumes additive or multiplicative Gaussian errors; prediction intervals presume normal innovations. No exogenous regressors in standard form.

data_regime.rows: works on short series (as few as 2 full seasonal cycles); does not need thousands of points
data_regime.dimensionality: strictly univariate (single target series), p=0 covariates
needs: a known seasonal period if seasonality is modeled

features.interpretability: high; level/trend/seasonal states are explicit and the smoothing weights decay geometrically with interpretable meaning
features.notes: No feature engineering needed; consumes the raw series. Multiplicative seasonality requires strictly positive values.

assumptions: single fixed seasonal period (no multiple overlapping cycles like daily+weekly+annual)
no structural breaks (global smoothing parameters corrupt all estimates around a break)

Gaussian likelihood / AIC for automatic ETS model selection across Error/Trend/Seasonal combinations

exogenous regressors are essential (use ARIMAX/regression-with-ARIMA-errors)

children.name: Volatility (ARCH/GARCH)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ARIMA/SARIMA (which model the conditional mean assuming constant variance) and state-space models (which model latent dynamics), ARCH/GARCH explicitly models the conditional variance as an autoregressive process of past squared residuals and past variances, making it the only family in this group designed to capture time-varying volatility.
strengths: Captures volatility clustering: periods of high variance follow high variance, a persistent empirical pattern in financial returns that constant-variance models miss entirely.
Parsimonious parameterization: GARCH(1,1) needs only 3 parameters (omega, alpha, beta) yet fits the volatility dynamics of most financial assets as well as ARCH models with 10+ lags.
Directly yields conditional variance estimates usable for Value-at-Risk (VaR) and option pricing without auxiliary simulation.
weaknesses: Assumes a symmetric response to shocks: a negative return of magnitude x raises future variance exactly as much as a positive return of x, which contradicts the well-documented leverage effect in equities.
Slow mean-reversion after regime shifts: when volatility jumps to a structurally new level (e.g., a market crisis), the conditional variance catches up only gradually over many periods.
Requires residuals from a pre-fitted mean model (e.g., ARIMA); misspecification of the mean equation contaminates variance estimates.
recommended_for: Daily or intraday financial return series (equity indices, FX, commodities) where volatility clustering is confirmed by a significant Ljung-Box test on squared residuals.
Risk management pipelines computing rolling 1-day or 10-day VaR, where a closed-form conditional variance forecast is needed without Monte Carlo overhead.
not_recommended_for: Series where the variance process is asymmetric to positive vs. negative shocks (e.g., individual equities with leverage effect); use EGARCH or GJR-GARCH instead.
Non-financial time series with no volatility clustering (e.g., temperature, demand forecasting), where the conditional heteroskedasticity assumption adds complexity without fit improvement.
children.curiosity: Robert Engle introduced ARCH in 1982 (Econometrica, 50:987-1007) to model UK inflation uncertainty; the work earned him the 2003 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, shared with Clive Granger.

children.name: ARCH
children.diff_siblings: Unlike GARCH, which models conditional variance as a function of both past squared errors AND past conditional variances, ARCH(q) models conditional variance exclusively as a linear combination of q lagged squared residuals, requiring no feedback from its own variance history.
strengths: Parsimonious for short-memory volatility: when volatility bursts decay quickly, a low-order ARCH(q) captures the pattern without the parameter proliferation of higher-order GARCH.
Directly interpretable coefficients: each α_i weight quantifies exactly how much a shock q periods ago contributes to today's variance, with no indirect variance-lag terms obscuring the attribution.
Computationally simpler likelihood estimation than GARCH because the conditional variance depends only on observable past residuals, not on recursively estimated past variances.
weaknesses: Requires a large q (many lags) to model long-memory volatility persistence common in financial returns, leading to overparameterization and unstable estimates.
Treats positive and negative shocks symmetrically via squared residuals, so it cannot capture the leverage effect where negative returns amplify volatility more than positive ones of equal magnitude.
No feedback loop from past variances means ARCH cannot efficiently represent the high volatility persistence (near-unit-root in variance) routinely observed in daily asset returns.
recommended_for: Short-horizon volatility modeling in high-frequency data (e.g., intraday returns over minutes) where volatility clusters are brief and decay within a small number of lags, making ARCH(1) or ARCH(2) sufficient.

Econometric research contexts requiring a transparent baseline model, such as testing for conditional heteroskedasticity via the Lagrange Multiplier test before deciding whether to use GARCH extensions.
not_recommended_for: Daily or weekly financial return series with persistent volatility clustering (autocorrelation in squared returns lasting dozens of lags), where GARCH(1,1) captures the same structure with far fewer parameters.
Equity markets subject to asymmetric volatility responses to news, where leverage-effect models such as EGARCH or GJR-GARCH are required for unbiased variance forecasting.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Robert F. Engle in 'Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity with Estimates of the Variance of United Kingdom Inflation' (Econometrica, 1982), the paper earned Engle the 2003 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, shared with Clive Granger.

target.notes: Models the conditional variance (volatility) of a univariate, (weakly) stationary, mean-zero return/residual series; the mean process is assumed handled separately (e.g. constant or ARMA). Conditional distribution of innovations is typically Gaussian but can be Student-t for fat tails. Not a point-forecaster of the level.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds to thousands of regularly-spaced observations for stable QMLE of q lag coefficients
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate single series; only parameter count is the order q

features.interpretability: high: each alpha_i directly quantifies the contribution of a shock i periods ago to current variance, with no variance-lag terms
features.notes: Operates on lagged squared residuals of an equally-spaced series; no exogenous features. Requires demeaning/mean-model first.

assumptions: conditional variance is a finite linear function of q lagged squared residuals only (no variance feedback)
innovations are serially uncorrelated and stationary
non-negativity of variance coefficients (alpha_i >= 0)
volatility shocks are symmetric (squared residuals ignore sign)
short-memory volatility: clustering decays within a small number of lags
loss: Gaussian (quasi-)maximum-likelihood / conditional log-likelihood of the variance equation
Student-t MLE variant for heavy tails
contraindicated_when: persistent volatility clustering (squared-return autocorrelation over dozens of lags) where GARCH(1,1) is far more parsimonious
asymmetric/leverage effects present (negative shocks raise variance more) requiring EGARCH or GJR-GARCH
target is the conditional mean/level rather than the variance
series is non-stationary in mean or has structural breaks in volatility regime

children.name: GARCH
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ARCH, which models conditional variance using only past squared residuals, GARCH adds lagged conditional variance terms (σ²ₜ₋ⱼ) to the equation, achieving ARCH(∞)-equivalent memory with far fewer parameters — typically just three in the GARCH(1,1) specification.
strengths: Parsimonious volatility persistence: GARCH(1,1) captures long-memory volatility clustering with only 3 parameters (ω, α, β), whereas an equivalent ARCH model would require dozens of lags.
Closed-form conditional variance: σ²ₜ is computed recursively from past residuals and past variances, making inference via maximum likelihood tractable and fast even on long daily return series.

Empirically well-calibrated for daily returns: the persistence parameter α+β typically falls near 0.99 for equity returns, quantifying how slowly volatility mean-reverts — a directly interpretable risk metric.
weaknesses: Symmetric shock response: positive and negative residuals of equal magnitude produce identical variance updates, so GARCH systematically underestimates volatility after negative price shocks (leverage effect).
Non-negativity constraints: ω > 0, α ≥ 0, β ≥ 0 must be imposed during estimation; near-boundary solutions cause numerical instability and can produce degenerate variance paths.

Gaussian tail assumption by default: MLE under normality underestimates tail risk; heavy-tailed distributions (Student-t, GED) are needed but add complexity and are not always accounted for by practitioners.
recommended_for: Daily equity or FX return series where volatility clustering is evident and a simple, interpretable model is needed for VaR computation or option pricing with time-varying volatility.
Short-horizon volatility forecasting (1–10 days) in liquid markets where symmetric shocks are acceptable and the priority is a fast, robust estimate rather than capturing leverage asymmetry.
not_recommended_for: Asset return series with strong leverage effects (e.g., individual equities after earnings shocks), where asymmetric models such as EGARCH or GJR-GARCH are demonstrably superior.
High-frequency intraday data (tick or minute level), where microstructure noise violates the i.i.d. innovation assumption and realized-volatility-based models are more appropriate.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Tim Bollerslev in 1986 ('Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity', Journal of Econometrics), GARCH(1,1) can be rewritten as an ARCH(∞) with geometrically decaying weights — a fact Bollerslev used to prove that a single β parameter replaces infinitely many ARCH lags.

target.notes: Models the conditional variance (volatility) of a mean-zero return series, not the level. Innovations assumed conditionally Gaussian by default; Student-t/GED used to fit heavy tails. Target is typically log returns with little/no autocorrelation in the mean but strong autocorrelation in squared residuals.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds+ observations; daily financial series of 500-5000+ points are typical for stable MLE
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate (single series); low parameter count (GARCH(1,1) = 3 params)

features.interpretability: high — alpha (shock impact), beta (volatility persistence), and alpha+beta (mean-reversion speed) are directly interpretable risk quantities
features.notes: Operates on the residual/return series itself; no exogenous features required. Often layered on top of an ARMA mean model.

assumptions: conditional variance depends linearly on past squared residuals and past variances
symmetric response to positive and negative shocks (violated under leverage effect)
innovations are i.i.d. with the assumed distribution (violated by microstructure noise at intraday frequency)
covariance-stationary volatility process: alpha+beta < 1
non-negativity: omega>0, alpha>=0, beta>=0
loss: Gaussian (quasi-)maximum likelihood of conditional variance
Student-t / GED log-likelihood for heavy tails
contraindicated_when: strong leverage/asymmetry present (use EGARCH or GJR-GARCH)
high-frequency intraday/tick data dominated by microstructure noise (use realized-volatility models)
no volatility clustering (squared residuals show no autocorrelation)
non-stationary or very short series where MLE is unstable
interest is in forecasting the return level rather than its variance

children.name: EGARCH
children.diff_siblings: Unlike GARCH and GJR-GARCH, EGARCH models the logarithm of conditional variance rather than the variance itself, eliminating non-negativity constraints on parameters and capturing asymmetric leverage effects through an explicit sign term in the shock function.
strengths: No positivity constraints on coefficients: modeling log(σ²) means variance forecasts are always positive by construction, even with unrestricted parameter signs.
Explicit leverage effect parameterization: the γ term directly measures whether negative shocks amplify volatility more than positive shocks of equal magnitude.
Exponential response to shocks: large innovations have an exponentially larger impact on volatility than in standard GARCH, matching heavy-tailed financial return distributions.
weaknesses: Harder to interpret coefficients: parameters act on log(σ²), so their economic magnitude is less intuitive than in the linear GARCH variance equation.
Estimation is more sensitive to starting values and can converge to local optima, especially in short samples or during structural breaks.
Asymmetric persistence can be overfit: the additional γ parameter may capture sample-specific noise in short series, inflating apparent leverage effects.
recommended_for: Daily equity or index return series where the leverage effect is documented (e.g., S&P 500), and the goal is precise volatility forecasting for options pricing or Value-at-Risk.
Cryptocurrency return series with extreme positive and negative spikes, where unconstrained log-variance dynamics better accommodate sudden volatility jumps than standard GARCH.
not_recommended_for: Low-frequency data (monthly or quarterly) with few observations, where the additional asymmetry parameter cannot be reliably identified and standard GARCH suffices.
Processes where volatility is known to be symmetric (e.g., some commodity spreads or interest rate differentials), making the leverage term unnecessary and wasteful of degrees of freedom.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Daniel B. Nelson in 'Conditional Heteroskedasticity in Asset Returns: A New Approach' (Econometrica, 1991), EGARCH was the first GARCH-family model to guarantee non-negative variance forecasts without imposing sign restrictions on any coefficient, solving a fundamental estimation problem that had plagued practitioners since Engle's original 1982 ARCH paper.

target.notes: Models the conditional variance (volatility) of a univariate return/innovation series, not the conditional mean. Target is the series whose time-varying variance is forecast; mean is typically a constant or ARMA filter. Conditional distribution of standardized residuals is Gaussian by default but Student-t or GED is preferred for heavy tails.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds to thousands of observations; high-frequency (daily) financial data preferred. Asymmetry (leverage) parameter is poorly identified in short samples.
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate single-series model; not a feature-matrix method

features.interpretability: medium: log-variance dynamics with an explicit leverage term, but coefficients act on log(sigma^2) so economic magnitude is less intuitive than linear GARCH
features.notes: Input is the (de-meaned) return series itself; volatility clustering and serial dependence in squared returns are the modeled structure. No exogenous features required.

assumptions: returns are (weakly) stationary with conditional heteroskedasticity (volatility clustering)
standardized innovations are i.i.d. from the assumed distribution
presence of an asymmetric leverage effect (negative shocks raise volatility more than positive ones) justifies EGARCH over symmetric GARCH
no structural breaks/regime shifts within the estimation window
loss: Gaussian quasi-maximum-likelihood
Student-t / GED maximum likelihood for heavy-tailed standardized residuals
contraindicated_when: volatility is symmetric (no leverage effect) so the extra asymmetry parameter wastes degrees of freedom and standard GARCH suffices
low-frequency (monthly/quarterly) or short series where the leverage parameter cannot be reliably identified
the modeling goal is the conditional mean / point forecast rather than the variance
non-stationary series with trends or regime changes
cross-sectional or multivariate-dependence problems (single-series variance model only)

children.name: GJR-GARCH
children.diff_siblings: GJR-GARCH extends standard GARCH by adding an indicator-function term (I_{t-1}=1 when ε_{t-1}<0) that scales past squared innovations separately for negative shocks, capturing the leverage effect additively in the variance equation — unlike EGARCH, which models asymmetry in log-variance, or TGARCH, which applies the threshold to conditional standard deviation rather than variance.
strengths: Captures the leverage effect directly: negative return shocks increase next-period variance by (α+γ)ε² while positive shocks only contribute αε², with γ statistically testable via a simple t-test on a single parameter.
Retains the interpretive clarity of GARCH — all parameters remain in the variance domain, so conditional variance forecasts are computed without exponentiating a log-equation as required in EGARCH.
Widely supported in estimation packages (rugarch in R, arch in Python, MATLAB Econometrics Toolbox) with well-established MLE asymptotics and standard Wald/LR tests for the leverage coefficient γ.
weaknesses: Non-negativity of conditional variance is not guaranteed by construction — requires the constraint α+γ≥0 alongside ω>0 and β≥0 to be enforced explicitly during estimation.
Uses a single threshold at zero, so it cannot model more complex asymmetry patterns where large positive and large negative shocks both increase volatility differently from small ones.

Assumes innovations enter variance quadratically; in heavy-tailed distributions this can overweight extreme observations, and the model may underfit when the actual leverage decay is exponential as EGARCH assumes.
recommended_for: Daily equity-index or individual-stock return series where the leverage effect is empirically documented and γ>0 is expected — e.g., S&P 500 or individual blue-chip stocks where negative price shocks visibly spike implied volatility.

Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall estimation for portfolios with asymmetric downside risk, where distinguishing the variance response to losses vs. gains is necessary for regulatory capital calculations.
not_recommended_for: High-frequency intraday return data (tick or minute-level) where the binary threshold on the sign of lagged innovations is too coarse — realized-variance models or HAR-RV handle the persistent intraday volatility structure better.

Commodity or crypto return series with positive-shock asymmetry (supply squeezes, short-squeeze rallies), where γ<0 would violate non-negativity constraints or where the leverage effect operates in the opposite direction from equities.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Glosten, Jagannathan, and Runkle (1993) in 'On the Relation between the Expected Value and the Volatility of the Nominal Excess Return on Stocks' (Journal of Finance, 48(5): 1779–1801), the paper's primary goal was testing the ICAPM risk-return tradeoff — the asymmetric variance specification was proposed as a by-product to fit the empirical finding that market volatility responds more strongly to negative return innovations than to positive ones of equal magnitude.

target.notes: Models the conditional variance (volatility) of a univariate return/innovation series, not a conditional mean. Mean process is typically a constant or ARMA; the residuals epsilon_t are assumed mean-zero with time-varying variance h_t. Standardized innovations z_t = epsilon_t/sqrt(h_t) are i.i.d. with a chosen distribution (gaussian, or fat-tailed Student-t / GED for heavy tails).

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds to thousands of observations for stable MLE; volatility/asymmetry parameters (alpha, beta, gamma) are weakly identified in short series. Typical use: several years of daily returns (>=500-1000 obs).
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate single series; very low parameter count (~ omega, alpha, gamma, beta + distribution params). No high-dimensional feature space.

features.interpretability: high — all coefficients live in the variance domain; gamma directly quantifies the leverage effect and is testable with a single-parameter t/Wald/LR test.
features.notes: Input is the return series itself (one lagged-innovation channel); no exogenous covariates required, though GARCH-X extensions allow them. Returns should be de-meaned via the mean model.

assumptions: Returns exhibit volatility clustering / conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH effects present — check via Ljung-Box on squared residuals or ARCH-LM test).
Asymmetric leverage: negative shocks raise next-period variance more than positive shocks of equal size, with gamma>0.
Innovations enter the variance equation quadratically and asymmetry has a single threshold at zero.
Variance process is covariance-stationary (alpha + gamma/2 + beta < 1) with omega>0, beta>=0, alpha>=0, alpha+gamma>=0 for non-negative conditional variance.
Standardized innovations are i.i.d. from the assumed distribution; mis-specified mean model contaminates the variance estimate.
loss: Gaussian (quasi-)maximum likelihood on conditional variance
Student-t / GED maximum likelihood for fat-tailed innovations
produces full conditional-variance and density forecasts usable for VaR and Expected Shortfall quantiles
contraindicated_when: High-frequency intraday data — the single zero threshold on lagged innovation sign is too coarse; prefer realized-variance / HAR-RV.
Series with positive-shock asymmetry (some commodities/crypto) where gamma<0 would violate non-negativity constraints or reverse the leverage direction.
No measurable ARCH effect (homoskedastic residuals) — GARCH-family modeling is unnecessary.
Multivariate/cross-asset volatility and correlation needs — use DCC/BEKK multivariate GARCH instead.
Very short samples where alpha/gamma/beta cannot be identified.
Exponentially-decaying leverage in log-variance is better captured by EGARCH.

target.notes: Models the conditional variance of a stationary, mean-zero (or pre-meaned) return series, not the level. Innovations are typically standardized gaussian or fat-tailed (Student-t / GED) to capture excess kurtosis in returns.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds to thousands of regularly-spaced observations for stable (omega, alpha, beta) estimates; long samples preferred for high-persistence (alpha+beta near 1)
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate per series (p=1); multivariate extensions (DCC/BEKK-GARCH) scale poorly past a handful of series

features.interpretability: high: omega/alpha/beta map directly to baseline variance, shock sensitivity, and volatility persistence; alpha+beta is the mean-reversion speed of variance
features.notes: Operates on residuals of a fitted mean model (constant or ARIMA), not on raw covariates; no exogenous feature engineering by default (GARCH-X needed for regressors). Requires regularly-spaced series; sensitive to outliers and structural breaks in variance.

assumptions: Conditional mean correctly specified and removed first; mean misspecification contaminates variance estimates
Volatility clustering present (ARCH effect confirmable via Ljung-Box on squared residuals or Engle's LM test)
Stationary, regularly-spaced series with weak-stationary variance (alpha+beta < 1 for finite unconditional variance)
Symmetric response of variance to positive vs negative shocks (plain GARCH; violated by leverage effect)
loss: Gaussian quasi-maximum-likelihood (QMLE)
Student-t / GED maximum likelihood for fat tails
log-likelihood of conditional variance
contraindicated_when: No volatility clustering / homoskedastic series (e.g. temperature, smooth demand) — adds parameters without fit gain
Asymmetric shock response / leverage effect — use EGARCH or GJR-GARCH
Abrupt regime shifts in variance level — slow mean-reversion lags the new regime; consider Markov-switching GARCH
Irregularly-sampled or very short series where (alpha, beta) cannot be identified
Goal is forecasting the level/mean rather than the variance

children.name: ML for Time Series
children.diff_siblings: Converts the temporal sequence into a tabular supervised problem via sliding-window feature engineering (lag values, rolling statistics, calendar features), then applies any standard ML regressor — unlike classical statistical siblings that model autocorrelation structure directly and unlike deep learning siblings that learn temporal representations end-to-end.
strengths: Captures non-linear feature interactions between lags and exogenous covariates that ARIMA-family models cannot express without manual linearisation
Gradient boosted tree variants (XGBoost, LightGBM) routinely cut RMSE by 30-50% over ARIMA baselines on short-to-medium horizon tasks with rich exogenous features
Mature ecosystem of tabular ML tooling (hyperparameter search, feature importance, SHAP) applies directly once the window transformation is done
weaknesses: Requires manual or heuristic selection of window size and lag depth; a misspecified window discards autocorrelation signal beyond its horizon
Standard ML regressors have no built-in notion of temporal ordering, so naive train-test splits leak future information into training if not done with strict time-based cutoffs
Accumulates error quickly in multi-step recursive forecasting because each prediction is fed back as a lag feature for the next step
recommended_for: Short-to-medium horizon demand or energy forecasting where many exogenous tabular features (price, weather, calendar) are available alongside the target series
Anomaly detection in industrial sensor streams where labeled fault windows exist and the problem reduces to binary classification over fixed-length lag vectors
not_recommended_for: Very long-range forecasting (hundreds of steps ahead) where recursive error accumulation in lag-based inputs degrades predictions faster than sequence models
Raw high-frequency signals (e.g., ECG at 1 kHz) where the window would require thousands of features and the tabular representation becomes intractably wide
children.curiosity: The framing of time series as a supervised regression via lag features was systematically popularised by Ben Taieb and Hyndman (2012) in their study on recursive vs. direct multi-step strategies, establishing the sliding-window tabular transformation as a formal benchmark methodology.

children.name: Prophet (Meta)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ARIMA/SARIMA (which model autocorrelation structure in residuals) or ETS (exponential smoothing of levels), Prophet decomposes the series into trend, seasonality, and holiday components via a generalized additive model with Fourier-series seasonality and automatic piecewise-linear or logistic-growth trend changepoint detection.
strengths: Handles multiple human-calendar seasonalities simultaneously (weekly + yearly + custom holidays) without manual Fourier-order tuning, using a single Stan-based posterior fit.
Automatic changepoint detection via sparse Laplace prior on trend slope changes identifies structural breaks with no stationarity preprocessing or differencing required.
Robust to missing observations and irregular time spacing — no interpolation step needed before fitting, because the GAM is fit directly on the observed timestamps.
weaknesses: Poor on high-frequency or short-horizon forecasts (minutes, hours): the additive decomposition assumes smooth trend and periodic seasonality, missing fine-grained autocorrelation that ARIMA captures.
Changepoint detection can hallucinate structural breaks in short or noisy series, causing the trend to overfit transient fluctuations rather than genuine regime shifts.
No native multivariate support: exogenous regressors are added only as linear extra terms, so complex lag-dependent relationships between covariates cannot be modeled.
recommended_for: Business KPI forecasting (daily sales, app DAU) with known annual and weekly seasonality patterns and irregular holiday effects that must be explicitly enumerated.
Long-horizon trend projection (weeks to months ahead) on series with at least 2 full seasonal cycles of history, where human interpretability of the trend and seasonality decomposition is required.
not_recommended_for: High-frequency trading or sensor data at sub-hourly resolution, where autocorrelation at short lags dominates and the Fourier seasonality provides no useful structure.
Multivariate problems where the target depends causally on several external time series with complex lag structures — a VAR or ML model with lag features is better suited.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Sean J. Taylor and Benjamin Letham of Facebook Core Data Science in their 2018 paper 'Forecasting at Scale' (The American Statistician, 72(1):37–45); the name 'Prophet' reflects their goal of enabling non-expert analysts to produce reliable forecasts at scale without time-series expertise.

target.notes: Univariate target observed at timestamps. Additive (or multiplicative) decomposition with Gaussian observation noise; supports logistic-growth saturating targets when a capacity is supplied. Non-negative counts are modeled as continuous, not via a count likelihood.

data_regime.rows: needs at least 2 full seasonal cycles of history for seasonality to be identifiable; comfortable from hundreds to tens of thousands of timestamps
data_regime.dimensionality: single target series; exogenous regressors enter only as additive linear terms

features.interpretability: high: trend + seasonal + holiday components are separately plotted and read off; changepoints are explicit
features.notes: Primary input is the timestamp itself plus the target; calendar/holiday tables and optional linear extra regressors. No lag-feature engineering or scaling required.

assumptions: trend is smooth and piecewise-linear or logistic with sparse changepoints
seasonality is periodic on human calendar cycles and well-approximated by a low-order Fourier series
residuals are roughly Gaussian and serially uncorrelated after decomposition (no short-lag autocorrelation modeling)
history covers enough seasonal cycles to identify the periodic components
loss: MAP/posterior fit of a Gaussian additive GAM (squared-error style likelihood); L1 sparse Laplace prior on changepoint slope deltas
contraindicated_when: sub-hourly / high-frequency data where short-lag autocorrelation dominates (use ARIMA/SARIMA)
short or very noisy series where automatic changepoint detection overfits transient fluctuations
multivariate targets with complex lag-dependent covariate relationships (use VAR or ML with lag features)
no clear calendar seasonality, where the Fourier components add nothing
count or strictly-bounded targets requiring a non-Gaussian likelihood

children.name: Theta Model
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ARIMA or state-space models that fit parameters to an explicit generative process, Theta decomposes the series into 'theta-lines' by scaling the second differences with a coefficient θ, suppressing or amplifying local curvature, then forecasting each line separately (typically with SES) and combining the results.
strengths: Won the M3 Competition across 3003 heterogeneous series by combining a θ=0 straight-line trend with a θ=2 double-curvature line — two forecasts, equal weights — achieving lower sMAPE than ARIMA, Holt-Winters and most other entrants.

Mathematically equivalent to SES with drift (proved by Hyndman and Billah, 2003), so parameter estimation reduces to a single smoothing parameter α optimized by MLE, with no risk of over-parameterization.
Robust to short series: because the θ=0 line is a simple linear regression and the θ=2 line is SES, the method needs far fewer observations than seasonal ARIMA to produce stable forecasts.
weaknesses: Does not model seasonality internally — the standard implementation requires a separate multiplicative seasonal adjustment (STL or classical decomposition) before applying Theta, assuming stable and periodic seasonality.
Long-horizon forecasts revert to a linear trend (the θ=0 component dominates), making the method unreliable when the true long-run dynamic is nonlinear or subject to structural breaks.

The two-line combination (θ=0, θ=2) is fixed by convention from the M3 entry; optimizing θ values or using more theta-lines requires cross-validation and adds complexity that erodes the method's simplicity advantage.
recommended_for: Monthly or quarterly business KPIs (sales, demand, revenue) with stable multiplicative seasonality and series length between 24 and 120 observations, where SES-based methods are competitive and training time must be minimal.

Large-scale automated forecasting pipelines (thousands of SKUs) where a single robust univariate model must run without manual tuning, exploiting Theta's single-parameter estimation and consistent M3-validated accuracy.
not_recommended_for: Series with abrupt level shifts or irregular interventions (e.g., product launches, policy changes), because neither theta-line captures sudden structural breaks and residuals will be systematically biased.
Multivariate settings where external regressors (price, promotions, weather) drive the target, since Theta is strictly univariate and ignores all covariate information by design.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Assimakopoulos and Nikolopoulos (2000) in the International Journal of Forecasting, the Theta method won the M3 Competition outright; three years later Hyndman and Billah (2003) proved algebraically that the winning variant — combining θ=0 and θ=2 lines with equal weights — is mathematically identical to simple exponential smoothing with a drift term equal to half the overall trend slope.

target.notes: Strictly univariate point forecasting of a single numeric series h steps ahead; no covariates.

data_regime.rows: works on short series (≈12-24+ obs); stable up to a few hundred; no GPU/large data needed
data_regime.dimensionality: univariate (single series); scales to thousands of independent series in batch pipelines
needs: enough observations to estimate seasonality if present (≥2 full periods)

features.interpretability: medium: decomposes into θ=0 linear trend line + θ=2 curvature line forecast via SES; equivalent to SES-with-drift so a single smoothing parameter α
features.notes: No exogenous features. Multiplicative seasonality must be removed beforehand (STL/classical decomposition) and re-applied.

assumptions: No internal seasonality handling: assumes seasonality is stable/periodic and pre-adjusted externally
Long-run dynamic is approximately linear; reverts to linear trend at long horizons
No structural breaks or level shifts within the series
Series is univariate and target is driven by its own history, not external drivers
loss: squared error (SES smoothing parameter α optimized by MLE / SSE minimization)
contraindicated_when: Abrupt level shifts, interventions, or structural breaks (launches, policy changes) bias residuals
External regressors (price, promotions, weather) drive the target — Theta ignores all covariates
Long-horizon forecasts of genuinely nonlinear long-run dynamics
Complex/changing seasonality that cannot be captured by a single pre-adjustment

children.name: Hierarchical Forecasting (reconciliation)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike standalone time series models that forecast each series independently, reconciliation methods impose linear summing constraints across a hierarchy so that forecasts at every aggregation level are mutually consistent (coherent) by construction.
strengths: Minimum Trace (MinT) reconciliation provably minimizes the total forecast error variance across all levels simultaneously, outperforming both bottom-up and top-down baselines in empirical benchmarks.
Pooling information across all hierarchy levels corrects individually biased base forecasts: a noisy disaggregate series benefits from the signal present at higher, more stable aggregations.
Reconciliation is model-agnostic: any base forecaster (ARIMA, ETS, LightGBM, neural nets) can be used per series and then reconciled in a post-processing step without retraining.
weaknesses: The full MinT estimator requires inverting the W covariance matrix of base-forecast errors, which is rank-deficient when the number of series exceeds the length of the training window, forcing shrinkage or diagonal approximations.

Reconciliation is a linear mapping: if the hierarchy is misspecified (e.g., a series belongs to two groups simultaneously without proper cross-sectional grouping), the summing matrix S is wrong and the reconciled forecasts inherit structural bias.
Computational cost scales with the square of the total number of series; hierarchies with tens of thousands of SKUs at the leaf level make exact MinT impractical without sparse approximations.
recommended_for: Retail demand planning with a product-location hierarchy (e.g., SKU > store > region > national), where inventory decisions are made at multiple levels and coherence between the store-level order and the national budget is mandatory.
