Energy load forecasting across a grid hierarchy (substation > zone > country), where regulatory reporting requires that zonal totals exactly match the national aggregate without manual post-hoc adjustment.
not_recommended_for: Flat, single-series forecasting tasks with no aggregation structure: reconciliation adds computational overhead and a reconciliation step that changes nothing when S is a 1×1 identity.

Very short time series (fewer than ~30 observations per node) where the covariance matrix of forecast errors cannot be estimated reliably, making any reconciliation estimator noisier than a simple bottom-up sum.
children.curiosity: The optimal combination framework for hierarchical reconciliation was introduced by Hyndman, Ahmed, Athanasopoulos, and Shang (2011) in Computational Statistics & Data Analysis; the subsequent MinT (Minimum Trace) estimator by Wickramasuriya et al. (2019) in JASA proved that minimizing the trace of the reconciled forecast error covariance is the unique solution that is both unbiased and variance-optimal across the entire hierarchy.
keywords: demand forecasting across stores and regions

target.notes: Post-processing layer over base forecasts; applies to whatever target the base models produce. Requires a set of series linked by linear aggregation constraints (a summing matrix S), not a single series.

data_regime.rows: needs per-node history long enough to estimate base-forecast error covariance; weak below ~30 obs/node
data_regime.dimensionality: scales with number of series m; full MinT cost is O(m^2)+matrix inversion, impractical for tens of thousands of leaf series without sparse/diagonal/shrinkage approximations
needs: a defined cross-sectional and/or temporal hierarchy
base forecasts (and their in-sample errors) for every node

features.interpretability: high; reconciliation is a transparent linear projection (S (S'W^-1 S)^-1 S'W^-1) of base forecasts onto the coherent subspace
features.notes: Inputs are the base forecasts and their residual covariance W, not raw features; the hierarchy structure (S) must be specified correctly and exhaustively.

assumptions: the aggregation structure is correctly and uniquely specified (each series maps cleanly into S; no overlapping groups without proper cross-sectional grouping)
base-forecast errors are unbiased and their covariance W is estimable / well-conditioned
the coherence constraints are exactly linear (forecasts must sum)
base forecasts at each node are individually reasonable (garbage base forecasts propagate)
loss: minimum trace: minimizes total forecast-error variance summed across all hierarchy levels (MinT)
least-squares projection onto the coherent subspace (OLS / WLS / structural-scaling variants)
contraindicated_when: flat single-series forecasting with no aggregation structure (S is 1x1 identity; reconciliation is a no-op with overhead)
very short series (<~30 obs/node) where W cannot be estimated reliably
number of series greatly exceeds training-window length, making W rank-deficient (forces shrinkage/diagonal fallback)
hierarchy is misspecified or non-linear constraints are required; reconciled forecasts inherit structural bias

target.notes: Umbrella for the sliding-window-to-tabular family: target is the future value(s) of a series (forecasting) or a label over a fixed-length lag window (time-series classification/anomaly detection). Distribution is whatever the chosen downstream regressor/classifier optimizes; no intrinsic distributional assumption on the series itself.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds+ usable windows; tree-ensemble variants scale to millions of rows
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred but tolerates p>=n via tree regularization; window width inflates p (lag depth + rolling stats + exogenous + calendar features)
needs: strict time-ordered train/test splits to avoid leakage
exogenous covariates to outperform classical baselines

features.interpretability: medium: SHAP/feature importance on engineered lags and covariates explain drivers, but the window transformation obscures direct autocorrelation interpretation
features.notes: Core derivation is the feature engineering step: lag values, rolling mean/std, calendar (day-of-week, month, holiday), and exogenous regressors. Window size and lag depth are manual hyperparameters that bound the captured memory.

assumptions: informative lags/covariates exist within the chosen window horizon
no temporal leakage in the train/test split (time-based cutoffs mandatory)
relationship between window features and target is reasonably stationary or covariate-shift is captured by features
stationarity-like regularity within the window; abrupt regime changes outside training degrade fit
loss: squared error / RMSE
MAE
pinball/quantile loss (for probabilistic forecasts via gradient boosting)
log-loss (classification variants)
poisson deviance (count targets)
custom objectives supported by the downstream regressor
contraindicated_when: very long-horizon forecasting where recursive multi-step prediction accumulates error faster than end-to-end sequence models
raw high-frequency signals (e.g. 1 kHz ECG) where the window becomes intractably wide
very short series with too few windows to train a flexible learner
the only signal is linear autocorrelation/seasonality with no exogenous features, where ARIMA/ETS are simpler and competitive
strong extrapolation beyond the training range is required (tree ensembles cannot extrapolate trend)

children.name: State Space
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ARIMA (which models autocorrelation directly in the observed series) or recurrent networks (which learn latent dynamics through gradient-based training), State Space Models decompose the series into explicit unobserved state variables governed by a transition equation and an observation equation, enabling closed-form recursive inference via the Kalman filter.
strengths: Handles missing observations natively: the Kalman filter update step is simply skipped for missing timesteps, leaving the state estimate intact without imputation.
Decomposes a series into interpretable structural components (trend, seasonality, noise) whose parameters have direct physical or statistical meaning.
Provides exact online updates in O(d³) per timestep (d = state dimension), making real-time filtering feasible even on embedded hardware.
weaknesses: Kalman filter optimality holds only under Gaussian noise and linear dynamics; nonlinear or heavy-tailed settings require approximate variants (EKF, UKF, particle filters) that add implementation complexity.
Model structure (state dimension, transition matrix parameterization) must be specified by the analyst; misspecification leads to systematically biased estimates that cross-validation may not detect.
Parameter estimation via maximum likelihood over the Kalman smoother (EM or gradient-based) is sensitive to local optima and can be slow for long series with many latent states.
recommended_for: Sensor fusion or tracking problems where observations arrive asynchronously, contain known measurement noise variances, and the physical dynamics can be written as a linear system (e.g., GPS + accelerometer integration).
Macroeconomic time series with structural breaks (e.g., quarterly GDP with regime changes) where explicit trend-cycle-seasonal decomposition and interpretable parameter estimates are required.
not_recommended_for: High-frequency, highly nonlinear series (e.g., limit-order book mid-price at millisecond resolution) where the linear-Gaussian assumption is severely violated and a neural sequence model will generalize better.
Short series (fewer than ~50 observations) with many latent states, where the likelihood surface is nearly flat and maximum-likelihood parameter estimation is unreliable.
children.curiosity: Rudolf E. Kalman introduced the state-space formulation for optimal linear filtering in his 1960 paper 'A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems' (Journal of Basic Engineering); NASA adopted it within months for Apollo trajectory estimation, making it one of the fastest transitions from academic paper to critical engineering deployment in history.

children.name: Kalman Filter
children.diff_siblings: Unlike other state space models that require batch processing or Monte Carlo sampling, the Kalman Filter produces the exact closed-form Bayesian update for linear-Gaussian systems by propagating only the mean and covariance of the state distribution, making it computationally O(n³) per step with no approximation.
strengths: Optimal estimator (minimum mean squared error) when the system is truly linear and noise is Gaussian, guaranteed by the Kalman-Bucy theorem
Recursive one-pass algorithm: processes each new observation in constant memory without storing or reprocessing the full history
Naturally handles missing observations by skipping the update step, leaving only the prediction step active for that timestep
weaknesses: Degrades to a biased, inconsistent estimator when state transitions or observation equations are nonlinear, requiring EKF/UKF approximations that lose optimality guarantees
Assumes Gaussian process and observation noise; heavy-tailed or multimodal noise distributions cause the covariance-based representation to misrepresent true uncertainty
Requires explicit specification of the state transition matrix F, observation matrix H, and noise covariance matrices Q and R, which are often unknown and must be tuned manually or estimated
recommended_for: Real-time sensor fusion in navigation systems (GPS + IMU) where observations arrive sequentially, latency is constrained, and motion dynamics are well-modeled by linear ODEs
Tracking smoothly evolving economic or financial state variables (e.g., time-varying beta in a factor model) where the latent state follows a known linear transition with Gaussian shocks
not_recommended_for: Systems with strongly nonlinear dynamics or non-Gaussian noise (e.g., robot localization with range-bearing sensors), where particle filters or UKF achieve materially lower RMSE
Discrete or categorical latent states (e.g., regime-switching models), where the continuous Gaussian state representation is structurally inappropriate and Hidden Markov Models are the correct family
children.curiosity: Introduced by Rudolf E. Kalman in his 1960 paper 'A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems' (ASME Journal of Basic Engineering), the algorithm was adopted by NASA for the Apollo guidance computer within two years of publication, providing real-time trajectory estimation under the strict memory constraints of 1960s onboard hardware.

target.notes: Estimates a continuous latent state vector evolving over time; observations are noisy linear functions of that state. Output is the filtered/smoothed state mean plus its covariance, not a class or count.

data_regime.rows: works online from the first observation; no training set needed, processes one timestep at a time in constant memory
data_regime.dimensionality: state dimension small to moderate; per-step cost O(d^3) in state dimension d from the covariance matrix inversion, so very high-dimensional states are expensive
needs: explicit state-space specification: transition matrix F, observation matrix H, process noise Q, observation noise R

features.interpretability: high: latent state has physical/economic meaning and the model is a fully specified linear-Gaussian generative process
features.notes: Observations must be continuous numeric measurements linearly related to the latent state; handles irregular sampling and missing observations by running prediction-only steps.

assumptions: linear state transition and linear observation equations
Gaussian (unimodal, light-tailed) process and observation noise
known/correctly-specified F, H, Q, R matrices
Markov state: current state depends only on the previous state
continuous-valued latent state
loss: minimum mean squared error state estimation (BLUE/optimal under linear-Gaussian)
equivalently maximizes the Gaussian likelihood of observations; matrices can be fit by maximum likelihood via the prediction-error decomposition
contraindicated_when: dynamics or observation map are strongly nonlinear (use EKF/UKF/particle filter)
noise is heavy-tailed, skewed, or multimodal so a single mean+covariance misrepresents uncertainty
latent state is discrete/categorical or regime-switching (use HMM)
no credible parametric state-space model is available and you only have a generic regression/forecasting task

children.name: Hidden Markov Model (HMM)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike the Kalman Filter, which assumes a continuous Gaussian state space and linear transitions, HMM operates over a finite set of discrete hidden states, modeling the sequence as emissions from unobserved categorical regimes with transition probabilities between them.
strengths: Exact inference via the Forward-Backward algorithm yields the probability of any hidden state at each timestep without approximation, given a fixed number of states.
The Viterbi algorithm decodes the globally most probable hidden-state sequence in O(N²T) time, making it tractable for real-time sequential labeling tasks.
Training via Baum-Welch (EM) is unsupervised — it learns transition and emission parameters from unlabeled sequences, requiring no annotated state data.
weaknesses: The first-order Markov assumption limits memory to one step: the probability of the next state depends only on the current state, making it unable to capture long-range temporal dependencies without model extensions.
The number of hidden states K must be fixed before training; model selection (choosing K) has no closed-form solution and requires heuristics or information criteria like BIC.

Computational and statistical complexity scales as O(K²T) per training iteration, and with continuous emissions the model requires strong distributional assumptions (typically Gaussian mixtures) that may not match the data.
recommended_for: Phoneme-level speech recognition where the acoustic signal can be segmented into a small number of discrete phonetic states each producing spectrally distinct observations.
Financial regime detection in daily return series where the market alternates between a small number of distinct volatility regimes (e.g., bull, bear, crash) and the regime itself is unobserved.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional continuous state spaces (e.g., robot localization in 3D) where the required number of states to approximate the continuous manifold becomes computationally intractable.
Time series with strong long-range dependencies (e.g., language modeling over paragraphs) where the first-order Markov property forces irrelevant historical context to be discarded.
children.curiosity: The foundational statistical framework for HMMs was laid by Leonard E. Baum and colleagues in a series of papers from 1966 to 1972 at the Institute for Defense Analyses; the Baum-Welch parameter estimation algorithm, later recognized as a special case of the EM algorithm formalized by Dempster, Laird, and Rubin (1977), was derived in Baum et al. (1970), 'A maximization technique occurring in the statistical analysis of probabilistic functions of Markov chains,' Annals of Mathematical Statistics.

target.notes: Models an observed sequence as emissions from a discrete latent state chain. Used unsupervised (Baum-Welch learns states from unlabeled sequences) or for supervised sequence labeling (Viterbi decodes a hidden-state path). Emission distribution is configurable: multinomial/categorical for discrete observations, Gaussian or GMM for continuous; the latent state itself is categorical.

data_regime.rows: needs many sequences or one long sequence (hundreds to thousands of timesteps) to estimate K^2 transition + emission params reliably
data_regime.dimensionality: best with low-dimensional emissions; continuous high-dim emissions force restrictive GMM assumptions and blow up parameter count
needs: a pre-specified number of hidden states K

features.interpretability: high: hidden states, transition matrix, and emission params are directly inspectable and often map to meaningful regimes
features.notes: Observations must be a single sequence (or set of sequences); features are per-timestep emissions. Continuous emissions typically require Gaussian/GMM and benefit from scaling.

assumptions: first-order Markov property: next state depends only on current state, so long-range dependencies are lost
conditional independence of emissions given the hidden state
stationary transition and emission distributions over the sequence
correct choice of K (number of hidden states) and emission family
discrete, finite latent state space adequately captures the underlying dynamics
loss: maximizes data likelihood via Baum-Welch (EM)
Forward-Backward for exact posterior state probabilities
Viterbi for MAP hidden-state sequence decoding
contraindicated_when: target dynamics have strong long-range temporal dependencies that violate first-order Markov
the underlying state is continuous and high-dimensional (e.g. 3D localization), making discrete-state approximation intractable
transition/emission distributions are nonstationary over time
no natural notion of a small set of discrete latent regimes exists

children.name: Structural Time Series (STS)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike generic state-space models that treat the latent state as an undifferentiated vector, STS explicitly partitions the state into named, semantically meaningful components — trend, seasonal, cycle, and irregular — each governed by its own stochastic equation, making the model structure directly interpretable.
strengths: Trend and seasonality are separately estimable and plottable, enabling decomposition of forecasts into human-readable components without post-hoc analysis.
Handles missing observations natively through the Kalman filter recursion, which propagates uncertainty forward without imputation.
Supports inclusion of exogenous regressors with time-varying coefficients, allowing the model to adapt when the relationship between covariates and the target shifts over time.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter estimation via maximum likelihood on the Kalman filter likelihood surface is prone to local optima, especially when signal-to-noise ratios for trend vs. seasonal variances are low.
Computational cost scales as O(n * d^3) where d is the state dimension — adding seasonal harmonics or regressors quickly makes fitting expensive.
Assumes Gaussian, linear dynamics; non-Gaussian noise (heavy tails, discrete counts) or nonlinear transitions require approximations that undermine the exact Kalman filter guarantees.
recommended_for: Business KPIs (weekly revenue, daily active users) with known seasonal periods and occasional marketing interventions, where explainable component decomposition is required by stakeholders.
Causal impact estimation after a policy change or campaign, using the pre-intervention STS fit as a counterfactual baseline (as in Google's CausalImpact framework).
not_recommended_for: High-frequency financial returns where the Gaussian linearity assumption fails and volatility clustering (ARCH effects) dominates the signal.
Short series (fewer than 2 full seasonal cycles) where the Kalman filter cannot reliably estimate seasonal variance parameters, leading to degenerate or overfit components.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Andrew Harvey in his 1989 book 'Forecasting, Structural Time Series Models and the Kalman Filter' (Cambridge University Press), the framework was later popularized in the Bayesian setting by Scott and Varian (2014) as the engine behind Google's CausalImpact package, which estimates the causal effect of interventions on time series at scale.

target.notes: Single univariate (or low-dimensional) continuous series observed on a regular interval; conditional observation noise assumed Gaussian. Counts/proportions need a non-Gaussian observation model that breaks the exact Kalman filter.

data_regime.rows: needs at least 2-3 full seasonal cycles to identify seasonal variance; works on moderate series, not millions of steps (O(n*d^3))
data_regime.dimensionality: latent state dimension d should stay small; cost scales as d^3, so many seasonal harmonics + regressors get expensive

features.interpretability: high — state is partitioned into named components (level, trend, seasonal, cycle, irregular), each separately estimable and plottable
features.notes: Supports exogenous regressors, optionally with time-varying coefficients; handles missing observations natively via the Kalman recursion (no imputation).

assumptions: linear, Gaussian state-space dynamics
additive decomposition of trend + seasonal + cycle + irregular
stable / slowly-varying noise variances (homoscedastic, no volatility clustering)
seasonal period is known and series spans enough cycles to estimate it
loss: Gaussian Kalman-filter log-likelihood (maximum likelihood)
Bayesian posterior via MCMC/variational in probabilistic implementations
produces forecasts with calibrated uncertainty intervals
contraindicated_when: series shorter than ~2 full seasonal cycles (degenerate/overfit seasonal variance)
non-Gaussian targets: counts, heavy tails, or discrete data
volatility clustering / ARCH effects dominate (e.g. high-frequency financial returns)
nonlinear dynamics or abrupt regime switches
very long series where O(n*d^3) cost is prohibitive and a simpler model suffices

children.name: Dynamic Linear Models (DLM)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike generic state space models that may use nonlinear or non-Gaussian evolution equations, DLMs restrict both the observation and state transition equations to be linear with Gaussian noise, enabling exact closed-form filtering and smoothing via the Kalman recursions rather than requiring approximation methods.
strengths: Discount factors replace explicit tuning of error covariance matrices, reducing a hard estimation problem to a single scalar per component and making fitting orders of magnitude faster than EM-based state space estimation.
Arbitrary components (trend, seasonality, regression effects with time-varying coefficients) are stacked by superposition into a single model without altering the Kalman recursion structure.
Handles irregular sampling and missing observations natively: the Kalman filter skips the update step for missing time points, yielding valid posteriors without imputation.
weaknesses: Linearity and Gaussianity are structural assumptions — count data, heavy-tailed noise, or multiplicative dynamics violate them and require warped or approximate extensions.
Discount factor selection is empirical and can be misspecified: too low causes the model to chase noise; too high makes it ignore genuine structural breaks.
Computational cost scales cubically with the state dimension, making high-dimensional multivariate DLMs expensive without additional graphical or low-rank structure.
recommended_for: Online forecasting of economic or financial indicators (e.g., monthly sales, inflation) where the signal-to-noise ratio and trend slope change gradually over time and rapid sequential updating is required.

Environmental or epidemiological surveillance where observations arrive irregularly, some weeks have missing reports, and the underlying trend plus seasonal pattern must be decomposed in interpretable components.
not_recommended_for: Count or categorical time series (e.g., daily event counts, ordinal survey responses) where the Gaussian observation assumption is structurally invalid and a generalized state space model is needed.
Systems with abrupt regime switches between qualitatively different dynamics, where a Hidden Markov Model or Markov-switching model captures discrete state transitions that a DLM cannot represent.
children.curiosity: The DLM framework was systematized by Mike West and Jeff Harrison in their 1989 monograph 'Bayesian Forecasting and Dynamic Models' (Springer); the discount factor technique they introduced — replacing variance matrix estimation with a single scalar parameter per block — became the standard practice and remains the default in the R package 'dlm' released by Petris (2010).

target.notes: Univariate or low-dimensional multivariate continuous series observed sequentially over time; observation equation is linear-Gaussian. Decomposes into latent trend/seasonal/regression states.

data_regime.rows: works on short-to-medium series; benefits from regular or near-regular sampling but tolerates gaps
data_regime.dimensionality: scales O(d^3) per step in state dimension d, so keep latent state low-dimensional; not for high-dimensional multivariate without low-rank/graphical structure

features.interpretability: high: additive components (level, slope, seasonality, time-varying regression coefficients) are individually inspectable with filtered/smoothed posteriors and credible intervals
features.notes: Exogenous regressors enter via a time-varying-coefficient regression block; missing observations handled natively by skipping the Kalman update step (no imputation).

assumptions: linear state-transition and observation equations
Gaussian state and observation noise
additive (not multiplicative) component structure
smoothly/gradually evolving states rather than abrupt regime switches
approximately correct discount-factor specification for state evolution variance
loss: Gaussian log-likelihood / one-step-ahead predictive density
Bayesian sequential filtering (Kalman) and smoothing posteriors
produces full predictive distributions enabling CRPS / interval scoring
contraindicated_when: target is count, categorical, ordinal, or proportion data where Gaussian observation is structurally invalid (use a generalized/non-Gaussian state space model)
noise is heavy-tailed or dynamics are multiplicative
series exhibits abrupt regime switches between qualitatively distinct dynamics (prefer HMM or Markov-switching models)
state dimension is large, making cubic per-step cost prohibitive

target.notes: Models one or more observed series as noisy projections of latent state variables; classic linear-Gaussian form (Kalman filter) assumes Gaussian observation and process noise. Non-Gaussian/nonlinear targets need EKF/UKF/particle-filter variants.

data_regime.rows: works on short-to-medium univariate or low-dimensional multivariate series; needs roughly 50+ observations for stable MLE of transition/noise parameters, and more as latent state dimension grows
data_regime.dimensionality: low state dimension preferred; O(d^3) per timestep in state dim d. Not for wide cross-sectional p>n feature problems

features.interpretability: high: explicit trend/seasonality/noise components and state variables carry direct statistical or physical meaning
features.notes: Operates on the sequential signal itself plus known measurement-noise variances; handles missing timesteps natively (filter update skipped) and irregular/asynchronous observations (sensor fusion).

assumptions: linear transition and observation equations for exact Kalman optimality
Gaussian (and often homoscedastic) process and observation noise
correctly specified state dimension and transition-matrix parameterization (misspecification biases estimates)
known or identifiable noise covariances
loss: Gaussian log-likelihood maximized via Kalman filter/smoother (EM or gradient-based)
minimum-mean-squared-error recursive state estimation (filtering/smoothing)
contraindicated_when: series is highly nonlinear or noise is heavy-tailed and linear-Gaussian assumptions are severely violated (e.g. millisecond limit-order-book dynamics)
very short series (<~50 obs) combined with many latent states: near-flat likelihood, unreliable MLE
the analyst cannot specify a plausible state structure and a black-box sequence learner is preferred
purely cross-sectional data with no temporal ordering

keywords: predicting next value in a sequence

target.notes: Target is a value indexed by time; observations are ordered and serially dependent (autocorrelated), not i.i.d. Forecasts are multi-step or single-step ahead. Counts (sales, events) are common and may need Poisson/NB treatment in some family members.

data_regime.rows: Per-series history matters more than total rows; statistical methods (ARIMA, ETS) work on a single short series (~50-200 obs) while neural methods (LSTM, Transformer, N-BEATS) need long or many series (thousands+ of steps or a large panel)
data_regime.dimensionality: Univariate or low-dimensional multivariate (a few exogenous regressors); deep methods handle higher-dimensional and multi-series panels
needs: GPU only for deep sequence models

features.interpretability: high for linear/statistical members (ARIMA coefficients, decomposed trend/seasonality) to low for deep sequence models (black-box, attention only partially interpretable)
features.notes: Primary feature is the lagged target itself plus engineered calendar/seasonal terms and lag/rolling features; exogenous covariates optional. Differencing or detrending often required to stabilize mean; scaling helps neural variants.

assumptions: temporal ordering is meaningful and observations are autocorrelated (i.i.d. assumption deliberately rejected)
stationarity after differencing for classical methods (ARIMA/ETS)
the data-generating process is reasonably stable; concept drift / regime change degrades forecasts
timestamps are regular or have been resampled to a fixed frequency
loss: squared error / MSE-RMSE
MAE
MAPE / sMAPE / MASE
pinball / quantile loss for probabilistic forecasts
Gaussian or Poisson likelihood for state-space members
CRPS for distributional forecasts
contraindicated_when: observations are cross-sectional independent entities with no meaningful time order
series are extremely short or sparse (<~50 obs) with no pooling/transfer source
new series with zero history (cold start) and no hierarchical or transfer support
irregular sub-millisecond event streams dominated by exogenous shocks, better served by point-process models

children.name: 1.1.4 Survival (Survival Analysis)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike regression (predicts a continuous scalar) and classification (predicts a class label), survival models operate on a (time, event_indicator) target pair and are trained with a loss that correctly handles right-censored observations — instances for which the event had not yet occurred at last follow-up — rather than discarding or mislabeling them.
strengths: Handles right-censored data natively via partial-likelihood or censored loss functions, so no observations need to be discarded or imputed.
Outputs an interpretable survival function S(t) and hazard h(t) over time, enabling risk stratification at any desired time horizon from a single model.
Scales from simple non-parametric estimators (Kaplan-Meier) to high-capacity ML models (Random Survival Forests, DeepHit) without changing the prediction target or evaluation metric (C-index).
weaknesses: Requires the non-informative censoring assumption — that censoring is independent of the true event time — which cannot be tested and is frequently violated when patients drop out precisely because they are deteriorating.
Most classical models (Cox PH) assume a constant hazard ratio across time (proportional hazards); violations of this assumption produce biased coefficient estimates and misleading risk scores.
Survival datasets tend to be small and heavily censored (30-80% in clinical trials), so high-capacity ML survival models are prone to overfitting and yield poorly calibrated probability estimates.
recommended_for: Clinical trials with patient dropout, where right-censoring is unavoidable and the goal is to estimate time to relapse, death, or discharge — the defining use case since Kaplan and Meier (1958).

Predictive maintenance of industrial equipment where each machine is monitored until failure or end-of-study, and the objective is to predict remaining useful life under irregular observation schedules.
not_recommended_for: Problems where every unit is fully observed (no censoring) and the outcome is a fixed continuous value — standard regression is simpler, faster to train, and loses no information in that setting.

High-frequency event streams (e.g., click-through prediction at millisecond intervals) where the event is certain to occur for every unit and timing differences are negligible; classification or point-process models are more appropriate.
children.curiosity: The Kaplan-Meier estimator, still the most cited method in clinical oncology (used in over 70% of oncology papers), was published in June 1958 by Edward L. Kaplan and Paul Meier after the Journal of the American Statistical Association initially rejected the paper; Cox's proportional hazards extension followed in 1972, together forming the two pillars of modern survival analysis.

children.name: Kaplan-Meier
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Cox regression (which models covariate effects on hazard) and Nelson-Aalen (which estimates cumulative hazard), Kaplan-Meier directly estimates the survival function via the product-limit formula S(t) = ∏(Y(tᵢ) - d(tᵢ))/Y(tᵢ), requiring no distributional or proportional-hazards assumptions.
strengths: Handles right-censored observations exactly without assuming a parametric distribution for event times
Produces a step-function survival curve that is directly interpretable as empirical event-free probabilities at each observed failure time
Comparison of two or more groups via the log-rank test requires only the KM curves, no covariate modeling
weaknesses: Cannot incorporate continuous covariates or confounders — group comparison is univariable only
Curve confidence bands widen rapidly in the tail where few subjects remain at risk, making late-time estimates unreliable
Assumes censoring is non-informative (independent of the true event time); informative censoring biases the survival estimate
recommended_for: Clinical trials comparing two treatment arms on a time-to-event endpoint (e.g., overall survival in oncology) where no covariate adjustment is needed and the primary output is a survival curve
Reliability engineering datasets where exact failure times and right-censored run times are recorded and the goal is an empirical estimate of component survival probability over time
not_recommended_for: Studies with multiple confounders that must be adjusted for simultaneously — Cox regression or parametric AFT models handle this; KM cannot
Competing-risks settings (e.g., death from other causes before the primary event) where standard KM overestimates the cumulative incidence of the event of interest
children.curiosity: Introduced by Edward L. Kaplan and Paul Meier (1958) in 'Nonparametric Estimation From Incomplete Observations' (JASA 53:457–481), the paper was initially rejected; after the two statisticians independently submitted near-identical manuscripts, the editor asked them to merge their work — making it one of the most-cited papers in all of scientific literature.

target.notes: Estimates the survival function S(t) nonparametrically; no parametric event-time distribution assumed. Requires a duration variable plus a censoring indicator (event=1 / right-censored=0).

data_regime.rows: works on small samples (tens to hundreds of subjects); tail estimates degrade once few subjects remain at risk
data_regime.dimensionality: no covariate dimensionality — univariable only (at most one grouping factor)

features.interpretability: high — output is an empirical step-function survival curve readable as event-free probability at each failure time; group differences tested with log-rank
features.notes: Does not accept continuous covariates or multiple predictors; stratification is limited to a single categorical group variable.

assumptions: Censoring is non-informative / independent of true event time (informative censoring biases the estimate)
No competing risks — standard KM overestimates cumulative incidence when competing events exist
Subjects censored or entering are representative of those remaining at risk
loss: product-limit (Kaplan-Meier) nonparametric MLE of the survival function
log-rank statistic for between-group comparison
contraindicated_when: Multiple confounders must be adjusted simultaneously (use Cox regression or parametric AFT)
Continuous covariate effects on hazard/survival are of interest
Competing risks are present (use cumulative incidence / Aalen-Johansen)
Reliable late-time / tail survival estimates are needed but the at-risk set is small
Censoring depends on prognosis (informative)

children.name: Cox Proportional Hazards
children.diff_siblings: Unlike fully parametric siblings (Weibull, Exponential, Log-Normal) that specify the baseline hazard distribution, Cox uses partial likelihood to estimate covariate effects while leaving the baseline hazard completely unspecified — making it semiparametric and distribution-free at the cost of not producing absolute survival time predictions.
strengths: Estimates hazard ratios for multiple covariates simultaneously without assuming a baseline hazard shape, giving robust covariate effects even when the underlying time distribution is unknown.
Handles right-censored observations natively via partial likelihood, which is the dominant data type in clinical follow-up studies where patients drop out or the study ends.
Well-established inference framework: confidence intervals, Wald tests, and log-rank-equivalent score tests are all derived analytically, with no need for bootstrapping.
weaknesses: The proportional hazards assumption — that the hazard ratio between any two individuals is constant over all time — is violated in many real studies (e.g., immunotherapy trials with delayed treatment effect), leading to biased hazard ratio estimates.
Cannot produce individual survival time predictions or absolute risk curves without a separate nonparametric estimate of the baseline hazard (Breslow estimator), adding a second modeling step.
Ties in event times require approximations (Breslow or Efron) that degrade accuracy when a large fraction of subjects share the same event time, common in discrete-time data.
recommended_for: Randomized clinical trials with right-censored time-to-event outcomes and multiple baseline covariates (age, treatment arm, biomarkers) where the goal is estimating adjusted hazard ratios rather than predicting individual survival curves.

Epidemiological cohort studies linking binary exposures (smoking, drug use) to time-to-disease onset, where event rates are low, follow-up lengths vary, and no strong distributional assumption can be justified.
not_recommended_for: Trials with known delayed or crossing hazards (e.g., immunotherapy vs. chemotherapy), where the proportional hazards assumption fails and the resulting hazard ratio is a weighted average that has no clinical interpretation.

Settings requiring fully probabilistic survival time forecasts (e.g., predicting median time-to-failure for warranty planning), where a fully parametric AFT or Weibull model yields direct, interpretable quantile estimates.
children.curiosity: Introduced by David R. Cox in 'Regression Models and Life-Tables' (Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 1972), the paper is one of the most cited in all of statistics; Cox deliberately left the baseline hazard unspecified and used partial likelihood — a concept he invented in that same paper — to sidestep the need to estimate it.

target.notes: Outcome is a (time, event-indicator) pair with right-censoring. Semiparametric: models the hazard via h(t|x)=h0(t)exp(x'beta) with the baseline hazard h0(t) left unspecified, so no parametric distribution is assumed for event times. Estimates relative risk (hazard ratios), not absolute survival times; absolute survival curves require a separate Breslow baseline-hazard estimate.

data_regime.rows: works on <1k; needs enough observed (uncensored) events, not just rows. Rule of thumb >=10-15 events per covariate to avoid biased/overfit coefficients
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; standard partial likelihood breaks down when p>=n (requires ridge/lasso-penalized Cox for high-dimensional/genomic settings)

features.interpretability: high: exp(beta) is a directly interpretable hazard ratio per covariate with analytic CIs and Wald/score tests
features.notes: Effect is multiplicative and linear on the log-hazard scale; continuous covariates assumed to have a log-linear effect unless splines/transformations are added. Time-varying covariates supported via counting-process (start,stop) formulation. No distributional assumption on event times themselves.

assumptions: Proportional hazards: hazard ratio between any two subjects is constant over time (no crossing/converging hazards; check via Schoenfeld residuals)
Log-linear additive covariate effects on the log-hazard (violations from nonlinearity/interactions bias estimates)
Non-informative censoring: censoring independent of the event process given covariates
Few tied event times (heavy ties degrade Breslow/Efron approximations; favors discrete-time models instead)
loss: Cox partial likelihood (negative log partial likelihood); penalized variants add L1/L2 (lasso/ridge/elastic-net) for high-dimensional data
contraindicated_when: Hazards cross or treatment effect is delayed (e.g. immunotherapy vs chemo) — PH assumption fails and the single hazard ratio is uninterpretable
Goal is absolute survival-time / quantile forecasts (median time-to-failure, warranty planning) — use a parametric AFT/Weibull model
Discrete time scale with many ties in event times
p>=n without penalization, or too few events relative to covariates
Informative/covariate-dependent censoring or competing risks (use competing-risks / Fine-Gray models)

children.name: Weibull Regression
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Cox (semi-parametric, no baseline hazard assumption) or Exponential regression (constant hazard, shape fixed at 1), Weibull Regression fully parameterizes the baseline hazard via a shape parameter k that lets the hazard monotonically increase (k>1), decrease (k<1), or stay constant (k=1), enabling direct estimation of survival time ratios (AFT formulation).
strengths: Shape parameter k captures monotonic hazard dynamics (aging or burn-in effects) that Cox suppresses and Exponential cannot represent
Dual interpretation as both a proportional hazards and an accelerated failure time model allows estimation of event time ratios, not available in Cox
Fully parametric likelihood yields more efficient parameter estimates and valid survival-time extrapolation beyond the observed follow-up window
weaknesses: Shape parameter constrains the hazard to be strictly monotonic, making it unfit for bathtub-shaped or unimodal hazard curves common in chronic disease data
Requires correct distributional assumption; misspecifying the Weibull family inflates bias more than the semi-parametric Cox model would
Maximum likelihood estimation is sensitive to small censored samples, producing wide confidence intervals for k when fewer than ~50 events are observed
recommended_for: Industrial reliability studies (e.g., component fatigue life) where physical theory predicts a monotonically increasing wear-out hazard and median time-to-failure must be estimated with confidence intervals
Clinical trials with administratively censored endpoints where the investigator needs event time ratios (ETR) alongside hazard ratios and the Kaplan-Meier curve shows a smooth, monotonic hazard trend
not_recommended_for: Populations with early high mortality followed by a stable period then late-life increase (bathtub hazard), where the Weibull shape cannot accommodate the non-monotonic pattern
Exploratory analyses on heterogeneous registry data where the true baseline hazard shape is unknown and misspecification risk outweighs the efficiency gain over Cox
children.curiosity: The distribution was formally introduced to the statistics community by Swedish engineer Waloddi Weibull in his 1951 paper 'A Statistical Distribution Function of Wide Applicability' (Journal of Applied Mechanics), though the same functional form had been identified independently by Fréchet (1927) and applied to particle-size data by Rosin and Rammler (1933).

target.notes: Outcome is a duration until an event with right-censoring; baseline hazard parameterized as monotonic via shape k (k>1 increasing/wear-out, k<1 decreasing/burn-in, k=1 exponential). Supports both PH and AFT interpretations, yielding hazard ratios and event-time ratios.

data_regime.rows: needs ~50+ observed (uncensored) events for stable shape estimate; small/heavily-censored samples give wide CIs for k
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; no built-in regularization, so high-dimensional p>n needs penalized extension

features.interpretability: high - coefficients map to interpretable hazard ratios (PH) or time-acceleration factors (AFT); shape parameter directly describes aging dynamics
features.notes: Requires (time, event-indicator) target encoding censoring; covariates enter log-linearly so monotone/log-scale relationships fit best

assumptions: Baseline hazard is monotonic and follows the Weibull family (correct distributional specification)
Proportional hazards across covariate levels (or equivalently AFT log-linear time scaling)
Censoring is non-informative / independent of event time
Covariate effects are log-linear and constant over time
loss: parametric maximum likelihood with right-censoring (Weibull log-likelihood)
supports left/interval censoring in standard implementations
contraindicated_when: Hazard is non-monotonic (bathtub or unimodal) - shape parameter cannot represent it
True baseline shape unknown and misspecification risk outweighs efficiency gain - prefer semi-parametric Cox
Very few events or heavy censoring make k poorly identified
Time-varying covariate effects violate proportional hazards / AFT scaling

children.name: AFT (Accelerated Failure Time)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Cox (which leaves the baseline hazard unspecified and models covariates multiplicatively on the hazard) and Weibull Regression (a special AFT case restricted to the Weibull distribution), the general AFT framework models covariates as multiplicative scalars directly on the time axis — log(T) = Xβ + σε — admitting log-normal, log-logistic, or Weibull error distributions and producing coefficients interpretable as time-acceleration factors.
strengths: Coefficients are directly interpretable as time ratios: a coefficient of 0.5 means the event occurs at half the expected time, without invoking hazard ratios
Valid when the proportional hazards assumption fails — the acceleration factor is constant even when the hazard ratio changes over time
Parameter estimates are robust to omitted covariates in a way that Cox PH estimates are not, because the log-linear form avoids multiplicative hazard confounding
weaknesses: Requires committing to a parametric error distribution (log-normal, log-logistic, Weibull, etc.) — misspecification of this distribution biases all coefficients and survival estimates
The constant-acceleration-factor assumption breaks down under time-varying treatment effects (e.g., a drug whose efficacy wanes), making the model structurally inadequate

Semiparametric AFT estimators (Buckley-James, rank-based) have iterative algorithms that may fail to converge due to discontinuities in the estimating equations, and they are computationally heavier than fitting a Cox model
recommended_for: Randomized clinical trials with unequal follow-up periods where the proportional hazards assumption is violated and results must be communicated to clinicians in intuitive time units (e.g., median survival extended by N months)

Industrial reliability studies requiring extrapolation beyond the observed time window, where a fully parametric form (e.g., log-normal for fatigue failures) is justified by engineering knowledge and life-test data
not_recommended_for: Observational studies where reviewers, regulatory agencies (FDA, EMA), or journal standards mandate the hazard ratio as the primary effect measure — AFT outputs acceleration factors, requiring additional derivation
Settings with time-varying covariates measured at irregular intervals, as the AFT log-linear formulation assumes fixed covariate effects that uniformly stretch or compress the entire time axis
children.curiosity: Buckley and James (1979, Biometrika) proposed the first semiparametric AFT estimator by imputing censored residuals using the Kaplan-Meier distribution and iterating least squares — a landmark that preceded widespread use of the model by two decades, as the instability of the algorithm in small samples kept AFT in the shadow of Cox PH until robust rank-based alternatives were developed in the 1990s.

target.notes: Models log(T) = Xβ + σε for a possibly right/left/interval-censored positive duration; requires a (time, event-indicator) pair. The chosen parametric error distribution sets the baseline; coefficients are time-acceleration (time-ratio) factors, not hazard ratios.

data_regime.rows: fully parametric AFT works on small samples (<1k events) and even few hundred when distribution is justified; semiparametric variants (Buckley-James, rank-based) need more events to converge
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; no built-in regularization, so p approaching n inflates variance and harms MLE stability

features.interpretability: high — coefficients are directly readable as time ratios (0.5 = event at half the expected time)
features.notes: Assumes fixed (baseline) covariates that uniformly stretch/compress the time axis; not designed for time-varying covariates measured at irregular intervals.

assumptions: correct specification of the parametric error distribution (log-normal/log-logistic/Weibull/...) — misspecification biases all coefficients and survival estimates
constant acceleration factor over time (no time-varying treatment effect; efficacy must not wane/grow)
log-linear additive effect of covariates on log survival time
censoring independent of the event time (non-informative censoring)
loss: censored maximum likelihood under the assumed parametric distribution
rank-based / Buckley-James estimating equations for semiparametric AFT
contraindicated_when: the hazard ratio is the mandated primary effect measure (regulatory/journal standards) — AFT outputs time ratios and requires extra derivation
treatment or covariate effects vary over time, violating the constant-acceleration assumption
time-varying covariates measured at irregular intervals
no defensible parametric form for the survival distribution and the proportional-hazards assumption actually holds (Cox is then preferable)

children.name: Fine-Gray (competing risks)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike cause-specific hazard models, which remove subjects from the risk set upon any competing event, Fine-Gray models the subdistribution hazard by keeping subjects who experienced a competing event in a weighted risk set, directly linking covariates to the cumulative incidence function (CIF) of the event of interest.
strengths: Direct CIF modeling: regression coefficients map unambiguously to the probability of the target event over time, unlike cause-specific hazards where the CIF depends on all competing hazards simultaneously.

Interpretable absolute risk: delivers subject-level predicted probabilities of the event of interest at any time horizon in the presence of competing events, without needing a separate model per event type.
Standard in transplant and oncology trials: embedded in EBMT statistical guidelines and widely supported in R (cmprsk, riskRegression) and SAS PHREG, enabling straightforward peer-reviewed reporting.
weaknesses: Artificial risk set: subjects who died from a competing cause are kept in the risk set with decreasing weights, producing a latent population with no clinical interpretation and complicating coefficient interpretation.
Multiple-outcome inconsistency: fitting one Fine-Gray model per competing event can yield sum-of-CIFs exceeding 1 for certain covariate patterns, violating probability axioms.

Proportional subdistribution hazards assumption is restrictive and hard to verify; when true CIFs cross over time, the model cannot capture that crossing and is outperformed by cause-specific approaches.
recommended_for: Clinical prognosis where the goal is estimating the absolute probability of a single event (e.g., cancer-specific death) by a fixed horizon in the presence of a clearly defined competing event (e.g., non-cancer death), such as building risk nomograms from registry data.

Hematopoietic cell transplant studies comparing relapse incidence across treatment arms when death in remission is a competing risk and the primary estimand is the observable incidence in the real-world population.
not_recommended_for: Etiological or causal inference about covariate effects on the biological event mechanism, where cause-specific hazard models are more appropriate because subdistribution hazard ratios conflate the effect on the event of interest with the effect on competing events.

Simultaneously modeling all competing events: fitting a Fine-Gray model for each outcome independently is mathematically inconsistent and should be replaced by a cause-specific or multi-state framework when absolute risks of multiple outcomes are all needed.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Jason Fine and Robert Gray (1999) in the Journal of the American Statistical Association, the paper went virtually unnoticed for several years before becoming one of the most cited articles in biostatistics; by the 2010s it had been adopted as the reference competing-risks method in the European Group for Blood and Marrow Transplantation statistical guidelines.
keywords: mortality risk with competing causes of death

target.notes: Right-censored time-to-event with >=2 mutually exclusive competing event types; models the subdistribution hazard / cumulative incidence function (CIF) of ONE event of interest. Requires an event-type indicator (event of interest / competing event / censored), not just binary event-vs-censored.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds+ of subjects with adequate numbers of the event of interest; coefficient stability degrades with few events relative to covariates
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n; classical regression, not regularized for p>n without penalized extensions (riskRegression)

features.interpretability: medium: subdistribution hazard ratios map directly to CIF/absolute risk of the target event, but conflate effects on the event of interest with effects on competing events, so are NOT clean etiological effects

assumptions: proportional subdistribution hazards over time (restrictive; fails when CIFs of event vs competing event cross)
competing events are well-defined and mutually exclusive
independent/non-informative censoring (IPCW weighting of those who had competing events)
log-linear covariate effects on the subdistribution hazard
loss: partial likelihood of the subdistribution hazard with inverse-probability-of-censoring weights (IPCW)
contraindicated_when: no competing risks present (use standard Cox / cause-specific hazard)
goal is etiological/causal effect on the event mechanism (use cause-specific hazards)
absolute risks of ALL competing outcomes are needed jointly (fitting one Fine-Gray per event is inconsistent; sum of CIFs can exceed 1; use cause-specific or multi-state models)
subdistribution hazards are clearly non-proportional / CIFs cross over time

children.name: Random Survival Forest
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Cox, Kaplan-Meier, or AFT models, RSF is an ensemble of survival trees that selects splits via the log-rank statistic on random feature subsets and estimates the cumulative hazard at each leaf with Nelson-Aalen, imposing no proportional hazards or distributional assumption.
strengths: Captures non-linear covariate effects and high-order interactions without any model specification — the log-rank splitting criterion finds them automatically.
Natively handles right-censored survival data without requiring the proportional hazards assumption that Cox regression imposes.
Outputs variable importance (VIMP) scores by permuting each feature and measuring the increase in prediction error, giving a ranked measure of predictor relevance.
weaknesses: Produces a black-box ensemble: individual tree paths are not interpretable, and the forest gives no closed-form hazard ratio like Cox does.
Performance degrades with high censoring rates (>80%), where terminal nodes contain few observed events and the Nelson-Aalen leaf estimates become unstable.
Computationally expensive: growing B deep trees on n bootstrap samples with m random features at each node scales poorly for very large n compared to fitting a single Cox model.
recommended_for: Clinical prognosis datasets (e.g., cancer registry or cardiac surgery data) with suspected non-linear or interaction effects among 10–50 clinical variables and moderate sample sizes (n > 300).
High-dimensional genomic survival studies where hundreds of candidate biomarkers exist and no prior knowledge justifies preselecting covariates for a Cox model.
not_recommended_for: Settings requiring a single, auditable hazard ratio per covariate for regulatory or clinical reporting — Cox regression yields the explicit coefficient and confidence interval that RSF cannot.
Very small survival datasets (n < 100 events) where bootstrapping yields insufficient events per terminal node, making the Nelson-Aalen leaf estimates highly variable.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Ishwaran, Kogalur, Blackstone, and Lauer (2008) in The Annals of Applied Statistics, the paper also proposed 'ensemble mortality' — a scalar summary of predicted risk derived from the forest's cumulative hazard — as a simple, interpretable alternative to the full survival curve.

target.notes: Right-censored survival outcome (event time + event/censor indicator). Outputs full estimated cumulative hazard and survival function per observation, not a single risk score; nonparametric, no assumed event-time distribution.

data_regime.rows: needs n>300 with adequate observed events; weak when <100 events
data_regime.dimensionality: handles p>n and high-dimensional genomic covariates; can screen hundreds of features without preselection
needs: sufficient uncensored events per terminal node

features.interpretability: low — black-box ensemble, no hazard ratios; provides permutation VIMP rankings only
features.notes: No scaling required; tree splits are invariant to monotone transforms of numeric features.

assumptions: non-informative (random) right censoring
enough events per leaf for stable Nelson-Aalen leaf estimates
loss: log-rank splitting statistic
harrell concordance index (C-index) for evaluation
integrated brier score
contraindicated_when: a single auditable hazard ratio + confidence interval per covariate is required (use Cox)
very high censoring rate (>80%) starves terminal nodes of events
small samples (<100 events) make bootstrapped leaf estimates highly variable
proportional-hazards covariate effects are genuinely linear and a parsimonious Cox model suffices

children.name: DeepSurv
children.diff_siblings: Unlike DeepHit (which discretizes time into bins and uses a softmax classification head) and Cox-Time (which removes the proportional hazards assumption entirely), DeepSurv retains the Cox partial likelihood as its training objective but replaces the linear risk score with a fully connected deep neural network, outputting a single scalar log-risk while preserving the semi-parametric Cox structure.
strengths: Learns non-linear covariate interactions automatically — capturing U-shaped or threshold effects that the linear Cox model misses — without abandoning the partial likelihood framework.

Produces a continuous, unbounded risk score that ranks patients by relative hazard; ranking quality (C-index) directly optimized during training, unlike methods that minimize cross-entropy on time bins.

Can double as a treatment recommender: computing the difference in predicted log-risk under treatment vs. control identifies patients who benefit most, a use case validated in the original paper on SUPPORT and Rotterdam tumor datasets.
weaknesses: Inherits the proportional hazards assumption — if the hazard ratio between groups changes over time (non-proportional hazards), DeepSurv will produce a single misleading risk score.
Does not natively model competing risks; when multiple distinct failure causes exist, a single output scalar conflates them, requiring a separate model per risk.

Training requires Breslow-style sorting of event times inside each mini-batch to compute the partial likelihood, making it harder to parallelize than standard classification losses and sensitive to batch size relative to the number of events.
recommended_for: Clinical prognosis datasets with right-censored continuous follow-up time, moderate sample sizes (hundreds to low thousands of patients), and covariates suspected to have non-linear or interaction effects on survival (e.g., gene expression panels, multi-biomarker panels).
Personalized treatment selection studies where the goal is to rank patients by differential risk under two treatment arms using the log-hazard difference as a benefit score.
not_recommended_for: Settings with competing events (e.g., cancer-specific mortality vs. cardiovascular death) where a single hazard score is theoretically invalid and DeepHit or cause-specific models are required.

Very short discrete follow-up windows (e.g., 30-day readmission with few time points) where a simpler logistic regression or DeepHit's binned classification head is more natural and avoids the partial likelihood overhead.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Katzman et al. (2018) in BMC Medical Research Methodology, DeepSurv was one of the first works to show that replacing the linear predictor in Cox regression with a deep network and back-propagating through the Cox partial likelihood achieves state-of-the-art C-index on five clinical datasets, including the SUPPORT study of 9,105 critically ill patients.

target.notes: Right-censored survival time; outputs a single scalar log-risk (relative hazard), not absolute survival probabilities. Baseline hazard recovered non-parametrically (Breslow). Models a single event type only; no competing risks.

data_regime.rows: hundreds to low thousands of subjects; needs enough observed (uncensored) events, not just rows, since the partial likelihood is driven by event pairs
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; deep net can overfit when p approaches n without regularization/dropout
needs: adequate event count relative to covariates
GPU helpful but not required at typical clinical n

features.interpretability: low — neural risk score is a black box; loses the per-covariate hazard ratios that plain Cox gives
features.notes: Standardize/normalize numeric covariates; one-hot or embed categoricals. Time-varying covariates not natively supported (assumes baseline covariates).

data_regime.dimensionality: spans the whole range depending on member model: regularized linear handles p>n; tree ensembles prefer p<n with informative features

features.notes: Choice of member model depends on feature type and scaling needs; this node selects the supervised paradigm, not a specific estimator.

hinge
