target.notes: Unsupervised soft clustering / density estimation; no label. Assigns each row a posterior distribution over an unbounded set of Gaussian components and infers the number of clusters.

data_regime.rows: works on small-to-moderate n (hundreds to low tens of thousands); full Bayesian inference (Gibbs/MCMC or variational) scales poorly to very large n
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n strongly preferred; full-covariance Gaussian components degrade in high dimensions (covariance estimation, curse of dimensionality), favor low-to-moderate p
needs: choice of concentration parameter alpha and conjugate base/hyperpriors (e.g. Normal-Inverse-Wishart)

features.interpretability: medium; components are interpretable Gaussians with posterior over assignments, but inferred cluster count and uncertainty require Bayesian literacy
features.notes: Continuous numeric features; standardize/scale features since Gaussian components and the base measure are scale-sensitive. Categorical/text/high-cardinality features need a different mixture base.

assumptions: Clusters are approximately Gaussian (elliptical) in the chosen feature space; heavy-tailed or strongly non-Gaussian components break the base measure
Dirichlet Process prior on weights: implies geometrically decaying (rich-get-richer) cluster sizes, biasing toward one large cluster plus many small ones
Mean-field variational inference assumes posterior factorization, underestimating posterior variance and component count
loss: maximizes marginal likelihood / posterior under a DP mixture (stick-breaking / Chinese restaurant process); optimized via collapsed Gibbs sampling or variational lower bound (ELBO), not a single point loss
contraindicated_when: Clusters are genuinely balanced and equal-sized (DP size prior penalizes the correct partition; finite GMM with BIC is better)
High-dimensional data where full-covariance Gaussians cannot be estimated reliably
Fast deterministic real-time inference is required (MCMC/VI over unbounded components is heavy)
Cluster shapes are non-elliptical, heavy-tailed, or manifold-structured (use density-based or kernel methods instead)
Features are categorical/mixed-type rather than continuous numeric

children.name: LDA Topics (Latent Dirichlet Allocation)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Gaussian Mixture Models and k-means, LDA is a three-level hierarchical Bayesian model that places a Dirichlet prior over per-document topic distributions, enabling it to model each document as a mixture of latent topics rather than assigning it to a single cluster.
strengths: Dirichlet prior prevents overfitting and allows probability assignment to unseen documents, unlike its predecessor pLSA which fits parameters per document and cannot generalize
Produces two interpretable output matrices simultaneously: per-document topic proportions and per-topic word distributions, enabling both document clustering and vocabulary-level topic inspection
Inference via collapsed Gibbs sampling scales to corpora with millions of documents through parallelizable implementations such as Online LDA (Hoffman et al., 2010)
weaknesses: Number of topics K must be fixed before training; no closed-form criterion selects the optimal K, requiring heuristics like perplexity or coherence scores on held-out data
Bag-of-words assumption discards word order and inter-topic correlations, making it blind to semantic relationships that co-occur across topics (e.g., 'bank' in finance vs. river contexts)
Performs poorly on short documents (tweets, product reviews) where per-document word counts are too sparse to estimate a stable topic mixture
recommended_for: Large corpora of long documents (news archives, academic papers, legal filings) where the goal is to discover latent thematic structure and group documents by dominant topic
Exploratory analysis of unlabeled text collections where human-interpretable topics — defined as ranked word lists — are needed to guide downstream labeling or retrieval
not_recommended_for: Short-text collections (fewer than ~50 words per document) where document-level word co-occurrence is too sparse to estimate meaningful topic proportions
Tasks requiring awareness of word order or syntactic structure, such as sentiment analysis or named-entity-driven categorization, where the bag-of-words assumption discards critical signal
children.curiosity: Introduced by Blei, Ng, and Jordan in their 2003 JMLR paper, LDA was the first topic model to place a Dirichlet prior over document-topic distributions, resolving the fundamental generalization failure of pLSA, which had no mechanism to assign probabilities to documents outside the training set.

target.notes: Unsupervised generative model; no labels. Recovers latent per-document topic proportions (theta) and per-topic word distributions (phi). Word counts modeled as multinomial under Dirichlet priors.

data_regime.rows: needs a large corpus (thousands+ documents) for stable topic estimates
data_regime.dimensionality: high-dimensional sparse vocabulary (p = vocab size, often 10k-100k+); handles p>>n in the word-feature sense
needs: documents long enough for reliable per-doc word co-occurrence (~50+ words)

features.interpretability: high - topics are ranked word lists and documents are mixtures over topics, both human-inspectable
features.notes: Input is a bag-of-words document-term count matrix. Requires tokenization, stopword removal, and pruning of very rare/common terms. Order and syntax are discarded.

assumptions: bag-of-words exchangeability: word order within a document is irrelevant
each document is a mixture of a fixed number K of topics
topics are independent (Dirichlet prior imposes no topic correlation; violated when themes co-occur)
documents long enough that word co-occurrence estimates a stable topic mixture
vocabulary is shared and discrete across the corpus
loss: maximizes marginal log-likelihood of the corpus under the generative model (via collapsed Gibbs sampling or variational/online EM)
evaluated by held-out perplexity or topic coherence
contraindicated_when: short texts (tweets, queries, product titles, <~50 words) with sparse per-document co-occurrence
K cannot be reasonably chosen and topic count is unknown with no held-out tuning budget
word order, syntax, or named entities carry the signal (sentiment, NER-driven tasks)
strongly correlated topics where the independence assumption distorts structure (consider correlated topic models)
goal is supervised prediction rather than exploratory latent-structure discovery
dense contextual semantics matter (polysemy/synonymy) where embedding-based topic models fit better

children.name: NMF (Non-negative Matrix Factorization)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike GMM or pLSA, NMF constrains both factor matrices (W and H) to be strictly non-negative, which forces an additive parts-based decomposition where each component represents a latent 'part' that can only combine constructively — no cancellation of signals is permitted.
strengths: Produces inherently interpretable components: non-negativity means each factor represents an additive part (e.g., facial features, topic word distributions) rather than an abstract direction that can cancel others out.
Equivalent to pLSA under KL-divergence loss, giving it a probabilistic grounding without requiring full Bayesian inference overhead.
Naturally induces sparsity in the learned representations, often achieving near-orthogonal components without explicit regularization.
weaknesses: The joint optimization over W and H is non-convex; standard multiplicative update rules (Lee & Seung, 2000) guarantee only convergence to a stationary point, not the global minimum.

Multiplicative updates suffer from a plateau phenomenon — extended epochs of near-zero gradient progress — making convergence substantially slower than projected-gradient or coordinate-descent alternatives.
Rank k must be specified a priori; there is no principled built-in criterion analogous to BIC/AIC, and wrong k produces entangled or duplicated components.
recommended_for: Hyperspectral or audio source separation where physical intensities are non-negative and the signal is truly a mixture of additive parts (e.g., separating instrument tracks from a mixed spectrogram).
Text topic modeling on bag-of-words matrices where word counts are non-negative and each document should be expressible as a weighted sum of a small number of coherent topics.
not_recommended_for: Data with meaningful negative values or signed residuals (e.g., financial returns, centered gene-expression log-ratios), where the non-negativity constraint distorts the true structure.
Scenarios requiring probabilistic uncertainty estimates or model selection via likelihood: NMF provides a point factorization with no posterior, making it inferior to LDA or GMM for those needs.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Lee and Seung in their 1999 Nature paper 'Learning the parts of objects by non-negative matrix factorization', NMF gained widespread attention when the authors demonstrated that it recovered part-like facial features (eyes, nose, mouth) while SVD and VQ produced holistic, non-interpretable bases from the same face images.

target.notes: Unsupervised matrix factorization X (n x p) approx W (n x k) H (k x p); no response variable. Used for soft clustering, topic extraction, source separation, dimensionality reduction.

data_regime.rows: works from low hundreds up to large sparse matrices; scales to high-dimensional sparse bag-of-words / spectral data
data_regime.dimensionality: handles p>n and very high p (vocabulary, spectral bins); rank k << min(n,p) chosen a priori
needs: no GPU required (multiplicative or coordinate-descent updates on CPU)

features.interpretability: high; non-negativity yields additive parts-based components (topics as word distributions, spectral sources, image parts) with no sign cancellation
features.notes: all entries must be >= 0 (counts, intensities, TF/TF-IDF non-negative). Sensitive to feature scaling since reconstruction error is unweighted; column normalization affects which parts dominate.

assumptions: data generated as a non-negative additive (purely constructive) mixture of k latent components
the chosen rank k matches the true number of parts; wrong k entangles or duplicates components
no meaningful negative or signed values in the data
components combine linearly without cancellation
loss: squared Frobenius reconstruction error
generalized KL-divergence (equivalent to pLSA under Poisson likelihood)
Itakura-Saito divergence (for audio/spectral, multiplicative noise)
contraindicated_when: data contains meaningful negative values or signed residuals (financial returns, centered/log-ratio gene expression)
probabilistic uncertainty, posteriors, or likelihood-based model selection (AIC/BIC) is required (prefer LDA/GMM)
global optimum guarantees needed (objective is non-convex; updates reach only stationary points)
the true latent structure involves subtractive/cancelling effects rather than additive parts

target.notes: Unsupervised clustering / density estimation via a latent generative model; output is a soft posterior over K components per point plus a fitted density, not a supervised label.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ for stable per-component covariance estimation; full-covariance GMMs are data-hungry as K and d grow
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n strongly preferred; full covariance costs O(n·K·d^2) per EM step and breaks down when d is large or n per component is small — reduce dimensionality (PCA) first or use diagonal/spherical covariance
needs: multiple EM restarts to escape local optima

features.interpretability: medium — components have explicit mean/covariance parameters and per-point membership probabilities, but K and component meaning are not given a priori
features.notes: Best on continuous, roughly elliptically-distributed features; standardize features since covariance estimation is scale-sensitive. Categorical/sparse/text features violate the Gaussian-component assumption (use diagonal-Bernoulli or latent-class variants instead of GMM).

assumptions: each cluster is generated by a parametric component (Gaussian for GMM) — clusters are unimodal and elliptical
mixture-of-known-family is a realistic local approximation to the data density
components are well-separated enough that EM can identify them; sufficient points per component for covariance estimation
i.i.d. samples; for time-series, requires HMM/temporal mixture rather than plain GMM
loss: maximizes data log-likelihood under the mixture via EM (lower bound / expected complete-data log-likelihood)
model selection by BIC/AIC over number of components K
Bayesian variants (variational / Dirichlet-process mixtures) optimize an ELBO and infer K
contraindicated_when: very high-dimensional sparse data (raw TF-IDF / one-hot) where full covariance collapses and diagonal GMM degrades toward k-means
clusters are non-Gaussian, heavy-tailed, or lie on curved manifolds — component assumption misrepresents geometry (prefer density-based or spectral clustering)
only hard one-of-K assignments are needed and clusters are spherical (k-means is cheaper)
K is large relative to n, or too few points per component for reliable covariance
categorical-dominated feature space with no meaningful Euclidean covariance

children.name: Graph-based
children.diff_siblings: Unlike density-based methods (which grow clusters from high-density cores) or centroid-based methods (which minimize intra-cluster variance), graph-based clustering converts the dataset into a similarity graph and partitions it by optimizing a graph cut criterion — typically the normalized cut — using the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian.
strengths: Detects arbitrarily shaped clusters that centroid-based methods (k-means) cannot find, because cluster shape emerges from the graph topology rather than Euclidean distance to a centroid.

The normalized cut criterion (Shi & Malik, 2000) prevents degenerate singleton partitions by penalizing cuts proportional to total edge weight, producing balanced partitions without specifying cluster geometry.
Encodes pairwise relationships directly in the affinity matrix, making it natural for relational data (social networks, molecular graphs) where no feature-space embedding is available.
weaknesses: Constructing the n×n affinity matrix costs O(n²) memory and O(n²d) time, making the method impractical for datasets above ~50,000 points without approximations (Nystrom, landmark points).

Eigendecomposition of the Laplacian costs O(n³) in the general case; even with sparse approximations, tuning the similarity kernel bandwidth (σ in a Gaussian kernel) critically determines cluster quality and has no principled automatic selection.

The final step embeds eigenvectors into a reduced space and applies k-means, inheriting k-means' sensitivity to initialization and its requirement that the number of clusters k be specified in advance.
recommended_for: Image segmentation where pixels with similar intensity/texture form non-convex regions — the graph encodes spatial and photometric similarity simultaneously, and normalized cuts find perceptually meaningful boundaries.

Community detection in citation or social networks where nodes are already naturally represented as a graph with weighted edges, making affinity-matrix construction trivial and the graph-cut objective directly interpretable.
not_recommended_for: Datasets with more than ~100,000 samples when memory is constrained, because the dense affinity matrix alone requires gigabytes of RAM and sparse approximations introduce hyperparameters that are difficult to tune.
Problems where clusters are globular and well-separated in feature space — standard k-means or GMMs are faster, simpler, and produce equally good results without the O(n²) overhead.
children.curiosity: The normalized cut formulation was introduced by Jianbo Shi and Jitendra Malik in their 2000 IEEE TPAMI paper 'Normalized Cuts and Image Segmentation'; they showed that minimizing the normalized cut criterion is equivalent to a generalized eigenvalue problem on the graph Laplacian, directly connecting graph partitioning to spectral methods.

children.name: Spectral Clustering
children.diff_siblings: Unlike other graph-based methods that operate directly on edge weights or density, Spectral Clustering embeds data into a low-dimensional Euclidean space defined by the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian, then applies k-means in that spectral domain to find clusters with arbitrary shapes.
strengths: Recovers non-convex and ring-shaped clusters that k-means cannot find, because the Laplacian eigenvectors encode global connectivity rather than Euclidean distance
Works naturally on any pairwise similarity matrix, including pre-computed affinity graphs from text, molecules, or networks, without requiring coordinates in feature space
Principled choice of k: the eigengap in the spectrum of the Laplacian reveals the natural number of clusters as the gap between the k-th and (k+1)-th eigenvalues
weaknesses: Eigendecomposition of the n×n affinity matrix costs O(n³) time and O(n²) memory, making it impractical for datasets with more than ~10,000 points without approximations
Results are sensitive to the RBF bandwidth parameter σ: too small isolates every point; too large collapses all pairwise similarities toward the same value, and there is no universal rule to set it
After embedding, k-means is applied in spectral space, inheriting its sensitivity to initialization and tendency to produce equal-sized clusters even when true cluster sizes differ greatly
recommended_for: Image segmentation where pixels form irregular, non-convex regions connected by local texture similarity, and a precomputed pixel-adjacency affinity matrix is available
Community detection in small-to-medium social or citation networks (up to ~5,000 nodes) where edges encode relational strength and clusters have complex topological boundaries
not_recommended_for: Large tabular datasets with tens of thousands of rows and well-separated, roughly spherical clusters, where k-means runs 15-50x faster and produces equivalent results
Streaming or online settings where new data points arrive continuously, because re-eigendecomposing the full affinity matrix from scratch is required for each update
children.curiosity: The two foundational algorithms were published almost simultaneously: Shi and Malik (2000) introduced the normalized cut criterion and its spectral relaxation for image segmentation in IEEE TPAMI, while Ng, Jordan, and Weiss (2002) proved convergence guarantees for the symmetric Laplacian variant at NeurIPS, cementing spectral clustering as a theoretically grounded method.

target.notes: Unsupervised clustering; no labeled target. Produces a hard partition into k groups; requires k (or eigengap heuristic) to be set.

data_regime.rows: small-to-medium only: practical up to ~5k-10k points; dense eigendecomposition is O(n^3) time and O(n^2) memory. Larger n needs Nystrom/landmark approximation or a sparse k-NN affinity graph
data_regime.dimensionality: operates on an n-by-n pairwise affinity matrix, so it is largely insensitive to feature dimensionality p; works when only similarities/distances are available, not coordinates
needs: number of clusters k (or eigengap heuristic)

features.interpretability: low: cluster assignments live in an abstract spectral (eigenvector) embedding with no direct mapping back to original feature contributions
features.notes: RBF/Gaussian affinity is highly sensitive to bandwidth sigma and to feature scaling; standardize numeric features first. Accepts precomputed affinity/adjacency graphs directly (text, molecules, networks).

assumptions: clusters correspond to well-connected components / low-conductance cuts in the similarity graph (connectivity, not Euclidean compactness)
an appropriate similarity kernel and bandwidth encode meaningful neighborhood structure
the number of clusters k is approximately known or revealed by a clear eigengap
affinity matrix is small enough for n-by-n eigendecomposition to be feasible
contraindicated_when: n is large (tens of thousands+) and clusters are roughly spherical and well-separated, where k-means is 15-50x faster with equivalent results
streaming/online data where points arrive continuously, since the full affinity matrix must be re-eigendecomposed
no good similarity metric or bandwidth is available, or the spectrum has no clear eigengap (k ambiguous)
true clusters differ greatly in size, since the final k-means step in spectral space biases toward equal-sized clusters
very high n with no tolerance for graph sparsification/approximation (O(n^2) memory blows up)

children.name: Affinity Propagation
children.diff_siblings: Unlike graph-based clustering methods such as Spectral Clustering that partition a similarity graph via eigenvectors, Affinity Propagation operates by iteratively passing 'responsibility' and 'availability' messages directly between all data points on a factor graph, causing actual data points (exemplars) to emerge as cluster centers rather than computed centroids.
strengths: Determines the number of clusters automatically from the data via the 'preference' hyperparameter, eliminating the need to specify k a priori.
Cluster centers are real data points (exemplars), making them directly interpretable and meaningful in domains like bioinformatics or image retrieval.
Works with any pairwise similarity measure, not just Euclidean distance, allowing application to non-metric spaces such as sequence alignment scores.
weaknesses: Time and memory complexity of O(N^2) per iteration makes it impractical for datasets beyond ~10,000 points without sparse approximations.
Sensitive to the 'preference' parameter: a uniform preference value forces all points to have equal prior probability of becoming exemplars, often producing suboptimal cluster counts.
Can oscillate indefinitely without convergence if the damping factor (range 0.5 to 1.0) is not tuned, requiring trial-and-error to stabilize message updates.
recommended_for: Gene expression profiling where the number of functional gene groups is unknown and exemplars (representative genes) carry biological meaning.
Face recognition or image exemplar selection tasks where clusters must be represented by an actual image from the dataset, not an averaged synthetic centroid.
not_recommended_for: Large-scale datasets with hundreds of thousands of records, where the O(N^2) memory requirement for the full similarity matrix becomes prohibitive.
Problems with clearly spherical, well-separated clusters of known count, where k-means converges faster and produces equally good results.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Brendan J. Frey and Delbert Dueck in Science (2007), the algorithm was derived from belief propagation on a factor graph; their original experiments showed it found better clusterings than k-means with random restarts in less than one-hundredth of the computation time on benchmark datasets.

target.notes: Unsupervised exemplar-based clustering; no labeled target. Assigns each point to a cluster represented by an actual data point (exemplar).

data_regime.rows: practical only up to ~few thousand to ~10k points; O(N^2) time and memory per iteration; needs sparse similarity matrix or landmark approximation beyond that
data_regime.dimensionality: operates on a precomputed NxN pairwise similarity matrix, so raw feature dimensionality p is decoupled from the algorithm cost (cost driven by N, not p)

features.interpretability: high: cluster centers are real data points (exemplars), not synthetic centroids, so each cluster has a concrete representative
features.notes: Requires a pairwise similarity (negative squared Euclidean by default, but any symmetric or non-metric similarity works, e.g. sequence-alignment or kernel scores); no centroid averaging means no requirement that features live in a vector space.

assumptions: clusters are well-represented by a single member point (exemplar) rather than a region mean
the 'preference' (self-similarity) values appropriately encode the prior likelihood of each point being an exemplar; uniform preference biases cluster count
damping factor (0.5-1.0) chosen to avoid oscillation/non-convergence
contraindicated_when: N is large (hundreds of thousands+): full O(N^2) similarity matrix is prohibitive
clusters are spherical, well-separated, and k is known: k-means is faster and equally good
a synthetic mean centroid is acceptable or desired (no need for real exemplars)
the desired number of clusters is fixed and must be controlled exactly (AP controls k only indirectly via preference, often unstably)

children.name: SOM (Self-Organizing Map)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike graph-based clustering methods that operate on explicit graph structures (edges and adjacency), SOM projects high-dimensional data onto a fixed discrete 2D lattice of neurons, preserving topological neighborhood relations through a competitive learning rule that updates both the Best Matching Unit and its spatial neighbors on the grid.
strengths: Topology preservation: data points close in input space map to adjacent neurons, making the 2D grid a readable visualization of high-dimensional structure
Single-pass dimensionality reduction and clustering simultaneously, without requiring a predefined distance metric between clusters
Smooth density estimation across the map: high-density input regions produce denser activation patterns, revealing data distribution gradients that k-means centroids cannot show
weaknesses: Number of neurons and grid shape (m x n) must be fixed before training, and a poorly sized grid either merges distinct clusters or fragments homogeneous ones
Convergence is sensitive to the learning rate schedule and neighborhood radius decay; wrong schedules produce topological defects (folded maps) that invalidate the spatial interpretation
No probabilistic output or uncertainty estimate: cluster assignment is deterministic (nearest neuron by Euclidean distance), giving no confidence measure per point
recommended_for: Exploratory visualization of high-dimensional tabular data (e.g., gene expression matrices with hundreds of features) where the goal is to map and inspect continuous cluster gradients rather than return hard labels
Customer segmentation in CRM datasets where the 2D map layout serves as a navigable interface for analysts to label regions by domain knowledge after training
not_recommended_for: Datasets with arbitrarily shaped or elongated clusters, where the fixed rectangular lattice topology forces incorrect topology preservation and yields distorted cluster boundaries
Pipelines requiring probabilistic cluster membership or downstream likelihood-based inference, since SOM produces only hard nearest-neuron assignments with no density model
children.curiosity: Introduced by Teuvo Kohonen (1982) in 'Self-organized formation of topologically correct feature maps' (Biological Cybernetics, 43:59-69), SOM was directly inspired by the topology-preserving organization observed in the mammalian cerebral cortex, where neighboring neurons respond to similar stimuli.

target.notes: Unsupervised clustering and topology-preserving 2D projection; no labels used during training.

data_regime.rows: works from hundreds to large n; online/competitive updates scale to large datasets
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for high p (many features) projected onto a fixed 2D lattice; p>n tolerable but feature scaling critical
needs: fixed grid size (m x n) chosen a priori
learning-rate and neighborhood-radius decay schedules tuned

features.interpretability: medium: 2D map is directly readable as a topology-preserving visualization, but neuron weights are not feature-attributed
features.notes: Euclidean distance on input vectors, so features must be standardized/normalized; raw categorical or unscaled features distort the BMU competition. Best on continuous numeric vectors (e.g., gene expression, scaled tabular).

assumptions: meaningful Euclidean geometry in input space after scaling
cluster structure compatible with a fixed rectangular (or hexagonal) lattice topology
appropriate grid size relative to number of true clusters
loss: competitive vector quantization error (distance to Best Matching Unit) with neighborhood-weighted weight updates
no probabilistic/likelihood objective
contraindicated_when: probabilistic cluster membership or uncertainty per point is required (output is hard nearest-neuron assignment)
arbitrarily shaped or highly elongated clusters where the fixed lattice forces distorted boundaries
supervised prediction is the goal (no target modeling)
features are unscaled or dominated by mixed/categorical types incompatible with Euclidean distance
a downstream density model or generative likelihood is needed

target.notes: Unsupervised clustering; partitions points by graph-cut criteria, no labels or target variable.

data_regime.rows: best <10k points with a dense affinity matrix; O(n^2) memory and O(n^3) eigendecomposition force Nystrom/landmark approximations beyond ~50k; impractical >100k without sparse graphs
data_regime.dimensionality: operates on a pairwise n x n affinity matrix, so feature dimension p only affects similarity computation, not the partition; high p degrades Euclidean kernels (curse of dimensionality on distances)
needs: full or sparse affinity/Laplacian matrix in memory
number of clusters k specified in advance

features.interpretability: medium; cluster assignments map to graph cuts and Laplacian eigenvectors (Fiedler vector), but the spectral embedding itself is not directly interpretable
features.notes: requires a similarity/affinity definition; for feature-space data needs a kernel (typically Gaussian RBF) whose bandwidth sigma critically controls results and has no principled auto-selection. Scale/standardize numeric features before computing distances. Native fit for data already given as a weighted graph (no feature embedding needed).

assumptions: clusters correspond to weakly-connected components / low-conductance cuts in the similarity graph, not to compact Euclidean balls
an appropriate similarity kernel and bandwidth are chosen so within-cluster edges dominate between-cluster edges
the chosen number of clusters k matches the eigengap structure of the Laplacian
affinity matrix fits in memory and graph is connected enough for stable eigenvectors
loss: normalized cut / ratio cut objective relaxed to a graph Laplacian eigenvalue problem
final k-means step on the spectral embedding minimizes squared error in eigenvector space
contraindicated_when: n is large (>100k) and memory/compute are constrained without sparse-graph or landmark approximation
clusters are globular and well-separated in feature space (k-means or GMM are faster and equally good)
the true number of clusters is unknown and no clear eigengap exists
no meaningful pairwise similarity can be defined, or similarity is dominated by noise in high dimensions
streaming/online data requiring incremental updates (requires recomputing the eigendecomposition)

target.notes: Unsupervised partitioning: no target variable. Output is a discrete cluster label per row (or a dendrogram), not a prediction; cluster ids are nominal (no order/magnitude).

data_regime.rows: centroid/density methods scale to 10k-1M+ rows; agglomerative hierarchical is O(n^2) memory/time and impractical beyond ~10k-50k rows
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n strongly preferred; distance-based methods degrade as p grows (distance concentration). Apply dimensionality reduction (PCA/UMAP) before clustering when p is large or features are sparse

features.interpretability: medium: cluster membership is inspectable and centroids/medoids describe groups, but labels carry no inherent semantics, order, or magnitude
features.notes: Numeric features must be scaled (z-score/min-max) so no single feature dominates Euclidean distance. Mixed-type or categorical data needs an appropriate metric (e.g. Gower) or encoding; raw one-hot high-cardinality inflates dimensionality.

assumptions: a distance/similarity metric reflects true semantic similarity in the chosen feature space
centroid-based methods assume roughly convex, isotropic, comparably-sized clusters
features are on comparable scales (else scaling required)
the number of clusters k or a density threshold is specifiable or tunable; no universally reliable auto-selection
loss: within-cluster sum of squares / inertia (k-means)
minimized within-cluster variance via linkage criteria (Ward)
density-connectivity objectives (DBSCAN/HDBSCAN)
silhouette / Davies-Bouldin as external selection criteria (not optimized directly)
contraindicated_when: the goal is to predict a specific outcome for new unseen rows (clustering does not generalize without an added assignment step; use supervised learning)
ground-truth labels exist and the task is genuinely supervised
high-dimensional sparse data (e.g. raw TF-IDF >10k features) where distances become uninformative without prior reduction
clusters are highly elongated/non-convex and only centroid methods are considered
k is unknown and no domain prior or validation budget exists to tune it

children.name: 1.2.2 Dimensionality Reduction
children.diff_siblings: Unlike clustering (which partitions samples into discrete groups) or density estimation (which models the full joint distribution), dimensionality reduction seeks a low-dimensional latent representation that preserves geometric or statistical structure of the original high-dimensional space.
strengths: Directly counters the curse of dimensionality (Bellman, 1957): sparse high-dimensional spaces make distance metrics meaningless, and projecting to a lower manifold restores their discriminative power.
Reduces storage and compute cost quadratically or more — a drop from 1000 to 20 dimensions cuts a kernel Gram matrix from 10^6 to 400 entries.
Enables 2D/3D visualisation of datasets with hundreds of features, making cluster structure and outliers humanly interpretable without any label.
weaknesses: The chosen latent dimension d is a hyperparameter with no closed-form optimal value; too small loses structure, too large leaves noise intact.
Linear methods (PCA, ICA) cannot capture manifold-shaped structure; non-linear methods (t-SNE, UMAP) are computationally expensive and non-parametric (no out-of-sample transform without refit).
Reduced representations are often not interpretable: a principal component or UMAP axis rarely maps back to a single meaningful feature.
recommended_for: Preprocessing for supervised models on datasets with hundreds of correlated numerical features (e.g., genomics, spectroscopy), where collinearity inflates variance and slows training.
Exploratory analysis of high-dimensional embeddings (e.g., word vectors, image features) to spot clusters, anomalies, or class separability before choosing a downstream algorithm.
not_recommended_for: Datasets where the number of features is already small (fewer than ~10) and features are not correlated — reduction adds complexity with no geometric benefit.

Tasks where full probabilistic inference on the original feature space is required (e.g., Bayesian anomaly scoring), since the invertibility from reduced space to original is generally approximate or undefined.
children.curiosity: The mathematical motivation for dimensionality reduction was formalized when Richard Bellman coined 'the curse of dimensionality' in his 1957 book Dynamic Programming, showing that the data volume needed to densely sample a space grows exponentially with the number of dimensions — making reduction a necessity, not a convenience, for high-dimensional learning.

children.name: Linear
children.diff_siblings: Reduces dimensions by learning a global linear projection matrix W such that the low-dimensional representation is Y = WX, preserving structure (variance, class separability, or correlation) as a closed-form or convex optimization over matrix manifolds — contrasted with nonlinear methods that model curved manifolds and have no single global projection matrix.
strengths: Projection is a single matrix multiply at inference time, making transformation of new points O(d·k) with no approximation error
Solutions are exact and reproducible: PCA and LDA reduce to eigendecompositions with a unique global optimum, unlike iterative nonlinear methods
Preserved axes remain interpretable as weighted linear combinations of original features, enabling direct feature-importance analysis
weaknesses: Cannot unfold curved manifolds: Swiss-roll or clustered data on a nonlinear surface loses structure when flattened by a hyperplane
LDA is bounded to at most C−1 discriminant components for C classes, making it unusable when the number of classes is small relative to desired dimensionality
Sensitive to outliers in PCA because variance maximization gives outsized weight to extreme points, distorting the principal components
recommended_for: High-dimensional tabular data with approximately Gaussian, linear structure (e.g., gene-expression arrays with thousands of features) where interpretable axes and fast projection of new samples are required

Multi-class classification preprocessing when labeled data are abundant and between-class separability in a low-dimensional subspace is the explicit goal (LDA for pipelines with tens of classes and thousands of features)
not_recommended_for: Image and text embeddings that lie on highly curved, nonlinear manifolds — a linear projection collapses the intrinsic geometry that t-SNE or UMAP would preserve for visualization or clustering
Datasets dominated by discrete, categorical, or heavily skewed features where covariance-based objectives (variance maximization, class scatter) are not meaningful summary statistics
children.curiosity: Cunningham and Ghahramani (2015) showed in the Journal of Machine Learning Research that every linear dimensionality reduction method — PCA, LDA, CCA, Factor Analysis, and others — can be cast as a single unified optimization program of the form min f_X(M) subject to M on a matrix manifold, reducing the entire family to a common algorithmic solver.

children.name: PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
children.diff_siblings: PCA finds a new orthogonal basis by eigendecomposing the covariance matrix, ordering axes strictly by variance explained — unlike ICA (which maximizes statistical independence) or LDA (which maximizes class separability using label information).
strengths: Optimal linear reconstruction: the first k principal components minimize mean squared reconstruction error among all k-dimensional linear projections, a guarantee no other linear method provides.
Decorrelated features: the resulting components have zero pairwise covariance by construction, removing multicollinearity that destabilizes downstream linear models.
Computationally tractable via truncated SVD: extracting only the top-k components costs O(n·d·k) rather than O(d³), making it feasible on wide datasets where a full eigendecomposition would not be.
weaknesses: Assumes linearity: it cannot capture variance along curved manifolds (e.g., Swiss rolls, concentric circles), because components are constrained to be linear combinations of the original features.
Sensitive to outliers: since variance is the objective, a single distant point can rotate PC1 toward itself, misrepresenting the bulk structure of the data.
Components are uninterpretable by default: each component is a dense linear combination of all original features, making it hard to assign domain meaning to any single axis.
recommended_for: High-dimensional tabular datasets (e.g., genomics with p > 10,000 features, n ~ 500 samples) where multicollinearity is severe and a compact linear subspace is needed before fitting a regression or classifier.

Preprocessing for noise reduction in sensor or spectral data (e.g., hyperspectral imaging, EEG) where most signal energy concentrates in the first few components and remaining components capture instrument noise.
not_recommended_for: Datasets with intrinsic nonlinear structure (e.g., image manifolds, molecular conformations) where t-SNE, UMAP, or autoencoders will preserve geometry that PCA collapses.

Supervised tasks where class separation matters more than total variance: a direction of high variance may be orthogonal to the class boundary, causing PCA to discard the most discriminative features before the classifier even sees them.
children.curiosity: PCA was introduced by Karl Pearson in 1901 ('On lines and planes of closest fit to systems of points in space', Philosophical Magazine) as a geometric fitting problem; the covariance-eigenvalue formulation used today was developed independently by Harold Hotelling in 1933.

target.notes: Unsupervised linear dimensionality reduction; no target. Ignores labels, so directions of maximum variance may not align with any downstream target.

data_regime.rows: works on small n; even n in the hundreds is fine if d is moderate
data_regime.dimensionality: handles p>n well via truncated SVD; especially valued when p is large and features are collinear
needs: mean-centering (and usually standardization when features differ in scale/unit)

features.interpretability: low: each component is a dense linear combination of all original features, so individual axes lack direct domain meaning
features.notes: Requires continuous/numeric features on comparable scales. Standardize when units differ, else high-variance features dominate. Categorical/sparse-count features should not be fed raw.

assumptions: Relevant structure is linear and lies in a low-dimensional linear subspace
Variance equals importance (informative signal has higher variance than noise)
Features are roughly elliptically distributed; heavy outliers distort the principal axes
Second-order statistics (covariance) capture the structure of interest
loss: minimizes mean squared reconstruction error of the top-k linear projection (equivalently maximizes retained variance)
contraindicated_when: Data lies on a nonlinear manifold (use kernel PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, or autoencoders)
Goal is class separation rather than total variance (use LDA; high-variance directions can be orthogonal to the decision boundary)
Goal is statistically independent sources rather than decorrelated ones (use ICA)
Heavy outliers or non-elliptical/heavy-tailed distributions dominate variance (use robust PCA)
Features are categorical, count, or otherwise non-numeric without suitable transformation
Sparse, interpretable per-feature axes are required (use sparse PCA or NMF for non-negative parts-based factors)

children.name: ICA (Independent Component Analysis)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike PCA (maximizes variance) or NMF (enforces non-negativity), ICA finds a linear transformation whose components are mutually statistically independent by maximizing non-Gaussianity via negentropy, making it the only linear method designed specifically for blind source separation.
strengths: Recovers statistically independent sources from linear mixtures without any prior knowledge of the mixing process (blind source separation)
Uniquely suited to non-Gaussian signals: exploits higher-order statistics (kurtosis, negentropy) that PCA discards entirely
FastICA converges in cubic time per component via a fixed-point iteration, making it practical for high-channel biosignal data (EEG, fMRI)
weaknesses: Fails when sources are Gaussian: statistical independence becomes indistinguishable from uncorrelatedness, making the model unidentifiable
Component order and sign are arbitrary — there is no canonical ranking analogous to PCA's explained variance, complicating interpretation
Requires at least as many observed mixtures as underlying sources; underdetermined settings (more sources than sensors) are not handled by standard ICA
recommended_for: EEG/fMRI artifact removal where eye-movement, cardiac, and muscle signals mix linearly with neural activity across many channels
Audio blind source separation (cocktail party problem) where multiple speakers are recorded simultaneously by multiple microphones and sources must be disentangled without reference signals
not_recommended_for: Data with Gaussian-distributed sources, such as many financial return series under normality assumptions, where ICA components are statistically unidentifiable

Datasets with non-negative, parts-based structure (e.g., document-term matrices, pixel intensities), where NMF's non-negativity constraint produces more interpretable and physically meaningful components
children.curiosity: The information-maximization (Infomax) algorithm, the first practical ICA method, was introduced by Bell and Sejnowski (1995) in Neural Computation; Hyvärinen and Oja later published FastICA (1999), which became the standard implementation by replacing gradient descent with a Newton-based fixed-point iteration that converges an order of magnitude faster.

target.notes: Unsupervised linear latent-variable model for blind source separation; no labels. Estimates an unmixing matrix W so that components s = Wx are maximally statistically independent.

data_regime.rows: works with hundreds to thousands of samples per channel; needs enough samples to estimate higher-order moments stably
data_regime.dimensionality: requires #observed mixtures (sensors) >= #latent sources; standard ICA is square/overdetermined only, not p>n underdetermined
needs: no GPU; FastICA is cubic per component and CPU-cheap

features.interpretability: medium: recovered components are independent sources but have arbitrary order, sign, and scale, so there is no canonical ranking like PCA explained variance
features.notes: Data must be centered and whitened (PCA pre-whitening) first; assumes a linear, instantaneous, noise-free mixing model x = As.

assumptions: sources are mutually statistically independent
at most one source is Gaussian (non-Gaussianity is what makes the problem identifiable)
mixing is linear, instantaneous and stationary
number of sensors >= number of sources
loss: maximize non-Gaussianity via negentropy / kurtosis (FastICA fixed-point)
minimize mutual information between components
maximum-likelihood / infomax objective
contraindicated_when: sources are Gaussian-distributed (e.g. financial returns under normality) — components become unidentifiable, equivalent to mere decorrelation
data has non-negative parts-based structure (document-term matrices, pixel intensities) where NMF is more meaningful
fewer sensors than sources (underdetermined / single-channel separation)
goal is variance-maximizing compression or ranked components — use PCA instead
strong sensor noise or nonlinear/convolutive mixing violating the linear instantaneous model

children.name: SVD (Singular Value Decomposition)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike PCA or LDA, SVD factorizes the raw data matrix A directly into U·Σ·Vᵀ without ever forming a covariance matrix, making it numerically stable even on uncentered or sparse inputs.
strengths: Works on sparse matrices without mean-centering, preserving sparsity — critical for TF-IDF and count-based text features where centering destroys zeros
Truncated SVD computes only the top-k singular triplets in O(mnk) time, avoiding the full O(min(m,n)³) cost of exact decomposition
Singular values directly quantify each component's contribution to total variance, giving an exact low-rank approximation guarantee (Eckart–Young theorem)
weaknesses: Captures only linear structure; nonlinear manifolds in the data are flattened and distorted in the reduced space
Sign indeterminacy: the signs of singular vectors are arbitrary and can flip between runs or implementations, breaking reproducibility of downstream pipelines
Number of components k must be chosen before fitting; there is no intrinsic stopping criterion, and a wrong k either loses information or defeats the dimensionality reduction goal
recommended_for: Latent Semantic Analysis on large sparse document-term matrices (hundreds of thousands of tokens, millions of documents) where PCA's covariance step is infeasible
Low-rank matrix approximation in collaborative filtering (e.g., user-item rating matrices with >90% missing entries) where the truncated reconstruction directly serves as the recommendation score
not_recommended_for: Data with nonlinear structure such as Swiss roll or concentric rings, where methods like UMAP or Isomap recover the true manifold while SVD collapses it
Real-time online learning settings with streaming data, since recomputing or incrementally updating SVD as new samples arrive is computationally expensive and numerically delicate
children.curiosity: The practical algorithm for computing SVD was published by Golub and Reinsch in 1970 ('Singular value decomposition and least squares solutions', Numerische Mathematik) and remains the basis of LAPACK's DGESDD routine used in NumPy and scikit-learn today.

target.notes: Unsupervised linear decomposition; no target. Used for dimensionality reduction, latent-factor extraction, low-rank approximation, and matrix completion.

data_regime.rows: scales to millions of rows/columns via truncated (top-k) SVD; full SVD is O(min(m,n)^3) and only viable for small/medium dense matrices
data_regime.dimensionality: handles p>n and very high-dimensional sparse data (term-document, user-item)
needs: choice of rank k before fitting
sparse-aware solver (e.g. randomized/Lanczos truncated SVD) for large matrices

features.interpretability: medium: singular values give exact variance contribution per component (Eckart-Young), but individual latent dimensions are linear mixtures and not directly meaningful; sign of singular vectors is arbitrary
features.notes: Operates on the raw data matrix without mean-centering, preserving sparsity (TF-IDF, count matrices). Scale-sensitive: features on disparate scales dominate components, so column scaling/normalization matters when units differ.

assumptions: latent structure is linear; a low-rank linear subspace captures the signal
components are orthogonal (uncorrelated linear directions)
for reconstruction guarantees, error is measured in Frobenius/spectral norm (squared-error optimality)
loss: Frobenius-norm (squared-error) low-rank reconstruction — optimal rank-k approximation by Eckart-Young
spectral-norm approximation error
contraindicated_when: data lies on a nonlinear manifold (Swiss roll, concentric rings) — use UMAP, Isomap, kernel PCA
streaming/online settings requiring incremental updates as samples arrive
intrinsic rank is unknown and no principled way to fix k
downstream pipeline requires reproducible component signs without sign-fixing
non-Gaussian / heavy-tailed noise where squared-error reconstruction is dominated by outliers (consider robust PCA)

children.name: Factor Analysis
children.diff_siblings: Unlike PCA or ICA, which decompose observed variance directly, Factor Analysis posits an explicit generative model: each observed variable is a linear combination of a small number of unobserved latent factors plus an independent Gaussian noise term unique to that variable, separating shared covariance from measurement error.
strengths: Models only shared variance (communality), leaving out unique error per variable — making recovered factors stronger candidates for real latent constructs than PCA components.
Supports both exploratory (EFA) and confirmatory (CFA) modes, allowing hypothesis testing about which observed variables load on which factors, not just blind decomposition.
Rotation of the loading matrix (Varimax, Promax) is mathematically valid and improves interpretability without changing model fit, a degree of freedom unavailable in PCA.
weaknesses: The loading matrix is not uniquely identified: any orthogonal rotation of the factors yields the same data likelihood, so the 'true' factor structure is not recoverable without external constraints.
Requires pre-specifying the number of factors k; choosing k incorrectly leads to either under-extracted structure or spurious factors with no reliable automatic criterion.
Assumes multivariate normality of the latent factors and Gaussian unique errors; with ordinal, skewed, or heavy-tailed data the MLE solution is biased and fit indices mislead.
recommended_for: Psychometric scale construction where observed items (e.g., questionnaire responses) are theorized to reflect a small set of unobserved traits (intelligence, anxiety) and measurement error must be explicitly modeled.

Multi-collinear tabular datasets in econometrics or social science where the goal is to identify a handful of interpretable latent drivers (e.g., economic factors from correlated macro indicators) and then use factor scores as inputs to downstream regression.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional settings where p >> n (e.g., genomics with thousands of genes and dozens of samples), since MLE of the loading matrix becomes ill-conditioned and the unique variances may converge to zero (Heywood cases).

Tasks where the goal is purely predictive variance compression with no interest in latent constructs, such as preprocessing image pixels for a classifier — PCA or SVD are computationally cheaper and impose no distributional assumptions.
children.curiosity: Factor Analysis was introduced by Charles Spearman in 1904 ('General Intelligence, Objectively Determined and Measured', American Journal of Psychology) to support his two-factor theory of intelligence, making it one of the oldest latent variable models in quantitative science — predating PCA's formalization by Hotelling in 1933.

target.notes: Unsupervised latent-variable model; no response. Produces k factor scores per observation and a loadings matrix relating observed variables to latent factors.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ for stable MLE; rule-of-thumb >=5-10 observations per observed variable and per estimated parameter
data_regime.dimensionality: p < n required; MLE ill-conditioned when p approaches or exceeds n, producing Heywood cases (unique variances -> 0)

features.interpretability: high — loadings are interpretable as factor-to-variable weights, especially after Varimax/Promax rotation; factors aim to recover real latent constructs
features.notes: Operates on the correlation/covariance matrix of continuous variables. Variables should be standardized; expects roughly continuous interval-scale inputs. Ordinal or binary items need polychoric/tetrachoric correlations or specialized estimators.

assumptions: linear relationship between observed variables and latent factors
multivariate normality of latent factors and Gaussian unique (error) variances — required for MLE estimation and fit indices
substantial shared covariance among variables (low Bartlett's test p, high KMO); near-orthogonal variables yield no meaningful factors
homoscedastic, mutually independent unique errors
correct choice of k
loss: maximum-likelihood (minimize discrepancy between observed and model-implied covariance matrix)
principal-axis factoring / least-squares on reduced correlation matrix
contraindicated_when: p >> n (e.g. genomics, thousands of features, dozens of samples) — ill-conditioned loadings and Heywood cases
goal is pure predictive variance compression with no interest in latent constructs (use PCA/SVD — cheaper, no distributional assumptions)
data is ordinal, skewed, or heavy-tailed and standard Pearson-based MLE is used — biased solution and misleading fit
observed variables are nearly uncorrelated — no shared variance to extract
nonlinear latent structure

children.name: Random Projections
children.diff_siblings: Unlike PCA or Factor Analysis, which require data-dependent decompositions (eigen/SVD), Random Projections use a data-oblivious random matrix whose entries are drawn from a sub-Gaussian distribution, reducing dimensionality in O(nd) time with no training step and provable distance-preservation guarantees via the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma.
strengths: Projection matrix construction is O(nd) and embarrassingly parallelizable, since entries are sampled i.i.d. with no data pass required before the transform.
Distortion is bounded by the JL lemma: for N points, a target dimension of O(log N / ε²) guarantees all pairwise distances preserved within factor (1 ± ε), regardless of original dimensionality.

Achlioptas (2003) sparse variant (entries 0 with probability 2/3, ±1 with probability 1/6) reduces multiply-accumulate operations by ~3x over the dense Gaussian version with equivalent theoretical guarantees.
weaknesses: Target dimension is governed by O(log N / ε²), which depends on the number of points N, not on intrinsic data structure; when true intrinsic dimension is low, PCA reaches the same distortion in far fewer dimensions.
Provides no interpretability: projected axes have no semantic meaning and cannot be ranked by explained variance, making downstream analysis or feature attribution impossible.

Distance preservation fails to help when classes overlap closely in the original space; the transform does not exploit label information, so classification accuracy can degrade when inter-class margin is small relative to intra-class spread.
recommended_for: Approximate nearest-neighbor search preprocessing on corpora with millions of high-dimensional vectors (e.g., TF-IDF matrices with d > 100,000 features), where a single matrix-multiply replaces an expensive SVD.

Sketching step before distance-based clustering (k-means, DBSCAN) on streaming or out-of-core datasets where the full data matrix never fits in memory and a fixed random matrix can be applied chunk by chunk.
not_recommended_for: Tasks requiring interpretable components or variance attribution (e.g., gene expression analysis where each axis must map back to biological features), since projected dimensions carry no meaning.
Low-sample regimes (N < 1,000) where O(log N / ε²) yields a target dimension comparable to the original, eliminating any computational benefit over exact PCA.
children.curiosity: The theoretical foundation was established by William B. Johnson and Joram Lindenstrauss in their 1984 paper 'Extensions of Lipschitz mappings into a Hilbert space', which proved that N points in any Euclidean space can be embedded into O(log N / ε²) dimensions with pairwise distance distortion at most ε — a result that predates its widespread use in machine learning by over a decade.

target.notes: Unsupervised, data-oblivious linear dimensionality reduction; ignores labels and target entirely.

data_regime.rows: needs many points (N in the tens of thousands+) for the O(log N / eps^2) target dimension to be small relative to original p
data_regime.dimensionality: handles very high p (p>>n), e.g. d>100k; best when ambient dimension is large and distance structure must be preserved cheaply
needs: large N for the JL bound to pay off vs exact PCA

features.interpretability: low: projected axes are random linear combinations with no semantic meaning, no variance ranking, no feature attribution
features.notes: Operates on numeric vectors (e.g. TF-IDF, embeddings); apply same fixed random matrix to all chunks. Sparse (Achlioptas) variant cuts MACs ~3x. Distance-based, so scale features comparably.

assumptions: downstream task depends only on pairwise Euclidean/inner-product distances, which JL approximately preserves within (1 +/- eps)
target dimension k = O(log N / eps^2) is materially smaller than original p
data has no exploitable low intrinsic dimension that PCA could capture in far fewer dims
loss: none; no objective optimized: data-independent random sub-Gaussian projection matrix with JL distance-preservation guarantee, no training step
contraindicated_when: interpretable components or explained-variance attribution required
N < ~1000, where k approaches p and the speed benefit over exact PCA vanishes
true intrinsic dimension is low, where PCA reaches equal distortion in far fewer dimensions
class margin is small relative to intra-class spread, since the transform is label-agnostic and can blur separation

target.notes: Umbrella for linear dimensionality reduction (PCA, factor analysis, classical MDS, CCA). Mostly unsupervised; LDA is the supervised exception, requiring a multiclass label to maximize between/within-class scatter.

data_regime.rows: works on <1k; eigendecomposition is exact and cheap at any n
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for high p; PCA handles p>n (rank capped at min(n-1,p)); LDA capped at C-1 components for C classes

features.interpretability: high: each component is an explicit weighted linear combination of original features, enabling loadings/feature-importance analysis
features.notes: Covariance/correlation based, so requires continuous numeric features on comparable scales. Standardize (z-score) before PCA when feature variances differ; one-hot categoricals and heavily skewed features break the covariance objective.

assumptions: Structure of interest is linear: data lies near a linear subspace, not a curved manifold
Variance (PCA) or class scatter (LDA) is a meaningful summary, i.e. roughly elliptical/Gaussian second-order structure
Features are continuous and on comparable scales
LDA: classes are Gaussian with equal covariance and labels are abundant
loss: reconstruction squared error / variance maximization (PCA)
Fisher between-class vs within-class scatter ratio (LDA)
Gaussian likelihood of low-rank-plus-noise covariance (factor analysis)
pairwise distance preservation (classical MDS)
contraindicated_when: Data lies on a curved/nonlinear manifold (Swiss-roll, image/text embeddings) where a hyperplane projection collapses intrinsic geometry; use UMAP/t-SNE/autoencoders
Features are mostly categorical, discrete, or heavily skewed so covariance is not a meaningful statistic
Outliers dominate (PCA variance maximization is non-robust to extreme points)
Desired output dimensionality exceeds C-1 for LDA with few classes

children.name: Non-Linear (Manifold Learning)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike linear methods (PCA, SVD) that project data onto a flat subspace maximizing variance, manifold learning assumes data lie on or near a curved low-dimensional manifold embedded in high-dimensional space, and recovers that intrinsic geometry by preserving either local neighborhood relationships (LLE, t-SNE) or global geodesic distances (Isomap, UMAP).
strengths: Uncovers meaningful low-dimensional structure in data where the true geometry is curved — such as image pose variations or single-cell RNA expression trajectories — where any linear projection collapses distinct clusters into the same subspace.

Algorithms like UMAP and t-SNE produce 2D/3D embeddings that visibly separate high-dimensional clusters with no manual feature engineering, making them the standard tool for exploratory visual analysis of genomics, NLP embeddings, and imaging datasets.
Isomap and UMAP can preserve global topology (relative distances between clusters) in addition to local structure, something PCA achieves only when clusters are linearly separable.
weaknesses: No native out-of-sample extension: the embedding is computed only for training points; mapping a new observation requires costly re-fitting of the full graph (Isomap, LLE) or approximate parametric extensions (UMAP).

Hyperparameters (k-nearest neighbors, perplexity, min_dist) directly control what geometry is preserved — small k emphasizes local structure and fractures global layout; large k blurs cluster boundaries — and there is no principled automatic selection.

Computational cost scales as O(n² ) to O(n² log n) for graph construction and eigendecomposition, making exact manifold learning impractical beyond ~100 000 samples without approximation (landmark Isomap, approximate nearest-neighbor graphs).
recommended_for: Single-cell RNA-seq or mass cytometry data (10 000–500 000 cells × thousands of genes) where the goal is 2D visualization to identify cell-type clusters that are not linearly separable in gene-expression space.

Anomaly detection preprocessing for high-dimensional sensor or image data where normal samples form a tight low-dimensional manifold and anomalies appear as outliers far from that manifold in the embedding.
not_recommended_for: Predictive pipelines that must score new, unseen samples in real time — the lack of a closed-form projection function means each new point requires re-running or approximating the full embedding.

Datasets with heavy noise or many irrelevant features (e.g., raw text bag-of-words with thousands of sparse dimensions), where neighborhood graphs built on Euclidean distance are meaningless and the manifold assumption itself breaks down.
children.curiosity: Manifold learning as a field was effectively launched by two back-to-back papers in Science (vol. 290, Dec 2000): Tenenbaum, Silva, and Langford introduced Isomap on p. 2319, and Roweis and Saul introduced LLE on p. 2323 — both arguing that human perception of faces, handwriting, and motion lives on low-dimensional nonlinear manifolds, not in the full pixel space.

children.name: t-SNE
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Isomap (geodesic distances), LLE (local linear reconstruction), or MDS (global pairwise distances), t-SNE models pairwise similarities as probability distributions in both spaces and minimizes their KL-divergence, using a heavy-tailed Student-t distribution in the low-dimensional space to counteract the crowding problem.
strengths: Exceptional local cluster separation: the asymmetric KL-divergence objective heavily penalizes mapping nearby high-dimensional points far apart, producing tight, visually distinct clusters in 2D/3D

Crowding problem solved by design: the Student-t (df=1) low-dimensional kernel has heavier tails than the Gaussian input kernel, giving moderate-distance pairs room to spread without collapsing into a single mass
De facto standard for single-cell RNA-seq visualization: captures the fine-grained local topology of thousands of cell types across tens of thousands of genes better than any linear method
weaknesses: Distances between clusters are not interpretable: the ratio of inter-cluster to intra-cluster distances in the 2D map has no correspondence to the original space, making cluster proximity meaningless

Non-convex optimization with stochastic initialization: each run can produce a topologically different embedding; results are not reproducible without a fixed random seed and identical hyperparameters
O(n²) memory and time complexity in the exact form; even the Barnes-Hut approximation (O(n log n)) becomes prohibitive for n > 1M points compared to UMAP
recommended_for: High-dimensional biological data (scRNA-seq, flow cytometry, >10k cells, >5k genes) where tight local cluster visualization is the primary goal and global distances are secondary
Word embedding inspection (e.g., GloVe/Word2Vec vectors, ~300 dims) where semantically similar words should form visually separated neighborhoods for qualitative validation
not_recommended_for: Datasets where inter-cluster spatial relationships must be preserved, such as temporal or hierarchical structures, because t-SNE distorts global geometry by design
Pipelines requiring deterministic, reproducible projections for downstream ML features, since the non-convex loss yields run-to-run variation even with fixed seeds across library versions
children.curiosity: Introduced by Laurens van der Maaten and Geoffrey Hinton in their 2008 JMLR paper 'Visualizing Data using t-SNE'; the key insight was replacing the symmetric SNE Gaussian in the low-dimensional space with a Student-t distribution with one degree of freedom, which turned out to be equivalent to a Cauchy distribution and required no additional hyperparameter.

target.notes: Unsupervised manifold learning for visualization; no target variable. Output is a 2D/3D embedding for inspection, not features for downstream supervised models.

data_regime.rows: hundreds to ~100k; exact form O(n^2), Barnes-Hut O(n log n) practical to ~1M but slow; prefer UMAP beyond that
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for high p (hundreds to thousands of input dims); typically run on PCA-reduced (~30-50 dims) input to denoise and speed up

features.interpretability: low: embedding axes have no meaning; only local neighborhood structure is trustworthy
features.notes: Requires numeric vectors with a meaningful distance metric (Euclidean default); scale/standardize features and usually pre-reduce with PCA. Categorical/text/graph data must be embedded into numeric vectors first.

assumptions: Data lies on a low-dimensional manifold with locally meaningful (Euclidean) distances
Only local structure is preserved; inter-cluster distances and global geometry are not meaningful by design
Perplexity must roughly match expected local neighborhood size; bad perplexity fragments or merges clusters
loss: Kullback-Leibler divergence between high-dim Gaussian-based and low-dim Student-t (df=1) pairwise similarity distributions, minimized by gradient descent (non-convex)
contraindicated_when: Global/inter-cluster distances, hierarchy, or temporal ordering must be preserved
Deterministic, reproducible projections are required (stochastic, non-convex, run-to-run variation)
Embedding is needed as features for a downstream supervised model rather than for visualization
n in the millions where UMAP or PCA scale far better
Quantitative density or distance claims will be read off the map

children.name: UMAP
children.diff_siblings: Unlike t-SNE, which minimizes KL divergence between probability distributions, or Isomap/LLE, which rely on geodesic distances or local linear patches, UMAP constructs fuzzy topological representations grounded in Riemannian geometry and algebraic topology, optimizing cross-entropy between high- and low-dimensional fuzzy simplicial sets.
strengths: Scales to millions of points via approximate nearest-neighbor graphs (NN-descent), running 5-10x faster than t-SNE at equivalent dataset sizes.
Preserves more global structure than t-SNE because its cost function penalizes both attraction of near neighbors and repulsion of distant points with balanced weight.
Supports arbitrary output dimensionality — not limited to 2D or 3D — making it viable as a preprocessing step for downstream ML pipelines.
weaknesses: Embeddings are stochastic: different random seeds or n_neighbors values can yield topologically distinct layouts, undermining run-to-run reproducibility more than t-SNE.
Distances in the low-dimensional embedding are not interpretable as true metric distances — relative cluster sizes and inter-cluster gaps carry no guaranteed geometric meaning.
Sensitive to the n_neighbors hyperparameter: small values fragment global structure into disconnected islands; large values blur fine-grained local clusters.
recommended_for: Single-cell RNA-seq with tens of thousands of cells and hundreds of genes, where preserving both cell-type clusters and developmental trajectories simultaneously is required.
Preprocessing before HDBSCAN or k-means when the original feature space exceeds ~50 dimensions and cluster geometry is nonlinear.
not_recommended_for: Tasks requiring stable, reproducible embeddings across runs without fixing a random seed, such as regulated clinical reporting pipelines.
Datasets where the manifold assumption fails — purely random high-dimensional noise or data lying on a linear subspace, where PCA or kernel PCA is more appropriate and interpretable.
children.curiosity: Introduced by McInnes, Healy, and Melville (2018, arXiv:1802.03426), UMAP was the first manifold learning method to ground its construction explicitly in category theory: the fuzzy simplicial sets it builds are objects in a category of extended-pseudo-metric spaces, giving the algorithm a mathematically rigorous justification absent from t-SNE.

target.notes: Unsupervised non-linear dimensionality reduction / manifold embedding; no response variable. Optional supervised/metric mode can use labels to guide the embedding, but it is not a predictor.

data_regime.rows: hundreds to millions; ANN graph (NN-descent) scales far better than t-SNE at large n
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for high p (tens to thousands of input dims); typically reduces to 2-50 output dims for visualization or as input to downstream clustering/ML
needs: meaningful distance metric in input space
enough samples to estimate the local neighborhood graph (n_neighbors)

features.interpretability: low: embedding axes have no semantic meaning and low-dim distances are not true metric distances; inter-cluster gaps and relative cluster sizes are not reliable
features.notes: Numeric features should be scaled/standardized since UMAP depends on a distance metric. Raw categorical/text/graph data needs an upstream embedding or an appropriate custom metric. Works best when data lies on a low-dimensional non-linear manifold.

assumptions: Data lies on a locally connected Riemannian manifold (the manifold hypothesis)
The chosen distance metric is locally meaningful and the manifold is locally uniformly sampled
n_neighbors is set appropriately for the structure scale of interest (too small fragments global structure, too large blurs local clusters)
loss: cross-entropy between high- and low-dimensional fuzzy simplicial set membership (attraction of near neighbors + repulsion of distant points)
contraindicated_when: Reproducible, deterministic embeddings are required without fixing a seed (stochastic; sensitive to seed and n_neighbors)
Data lies on a (near-)linear subspace or is high-dimensional noise with no manifold structure (PCA/kernel PCA more appropriate and interpretable)
Downstream analysis needs preserved true global geometry or metric distances
A supervised prediction target is the goal (use a model with a defined response)

children.name: Isomap
children.diff_siblings: Unlike LLE, which reconstructs local linear patches, Isomap approximates geodesic distances along the manifold via shortest paths in a k-NN graph and then applies classical MDS to that distance matrix, preserving global pairwise geometry rather than only local neighborhoods.
strengths: Preserves global manifold geometry: points far apart on the surface stay far apart in the embedding, unlike LLE which only guarantees local fidelity.
Provably convergent to the true isometry as sample density grows, provided the manifold is geodesically convex and isometric to a convex Euclidean domain.
Produces a single coherent low-dimensional coordinate system (via eigendecomposition of the geodesic distance matrix), avoiding the locally inconsistent patches that LLE can produce.
weaknesses: Fails on manifolds with holes or non-convex boundaries: shortest graph paths detour around voids, systematically overestimating geodesic distances and distorting the embedding.
Quadratic memory and O(n² log n) time for the all-pairs shortest path (Floyd-Warshall or Dijkstra over n nodes), making it impractical beyond ~10,000 points.
Sensitive to the choice of k in the neighbor graph: too small disconnects the graph, too large creates short-circuit edges that corrupt geodesic estimates across distant manifold regions.
recommended_for: Continuous, densely sampled manifolds without holes, such as pose or viewpoint variation in computer vision where a single latent parameter smoothly controls the data (e.g., rotating 3D objects with thousands of images).
Exploratory visualization where global structure matters, such as mapping the full diversity of a molecular conformation space where relative distances between conformations must be meaningful.
not_recommended_for: Datasets with multiple disconnected clusters or manifolds with holes, since the k-NN graph either fragments or routes paths around voids, producing grossly distorted embeddings.
Large datasets (n > 20,000) where the O(n²) distance matrix and all-pairs shortest path computation become memory- and time-prohibitive compared to landmark Isomap variants or UMAP.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Tenenbaum, de Silva, and Langford in Science (2000), Isomap was demonstrated on the 'faces' dataset, where it recovered a three-dimensional embedding (pose, lighting, expression) from 698 64×64 grayscale face images — a result PCA could not achieve because the true manifold is nonlinear.

target.notes: Unsupervised nonlinear dimensionality reduction; produces low-dimensional embedding coordinates, no target variable.

data_regime.rows: needs dense sampling of the manifold for geodesic estimates to converge; impractical beyond ~10k points (O(n^2) distance matrix, O(n^2 log n) all-pairs shortest path) unless landmark/L-Isomap is used
data_regime.dimensionality: high ambient p reduced to a few intrinsic dims; assumes low intrinsic dimensionality embedded in high-D space

features.interpretability: low: embedding axes are eigenvectors of the geodesic distance (MDS) matrix with no direct feature meaning
features.notes: Requires a meaningful Euclidean/metric distance between points to build the k-NN graph; scale/standardize features beforehand. Output dimension chosen via residual-variance elbow.

assumptions: data lies on a single connected, low-dimensional manifold that is isometric to a convex region of Euclidean space (geodesically convex, no holes)
manifold is densely and roughly uniformly sampled so k-NN graph distances approximate true geodesics
an appropriate neighborhood size k exists that neither disconnects the graph nor creates short-circuit edges
loss: minimizes residual between geodesic (graph shortest-path) distances and embedded Euclidean distances via classical MDS (eigendecomposition of the centered squared-geodesic-distance matrix)
contraindicated_when: manifold has holes, non-convex boundaries, or multiple disconnected clusters (paths detour around voids, distances overestimated, embedding distorted)
n is large (>~20k) without landmark approximation, due to O(n^2) memory and all-pairs shortest-path cost
noisy data or poorly chosen k creates short-circuit edges that corrupt global geodesic estimates
categorical/non-metric features where no meaningful neighbor distance exists
only local neighborhood fidelity is needed (LLE/t-SNE/UMAP scale better and handle non-convex/clustered structure)

children.name: LLE (Locally Linear Embedding)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Isomap, which preserves geodesic (global) distances, LLE preserves local geometry by computing per-point linear reconstruction weights from k nearest neighbors and then finding a low-dimensional embedding that exactly respects those weights — no global distance matrix is ever built.
strengths: Handles strongly curved manifolds where global distance metrics (Isomap) break down, because only local linearity is assumed per neighborhood
Computationally lighter than t-SNE/UMAP for moderate n: the weight-solving step is a sparse least-squares system, not an iterative optimization over all pairs
Produces a global embedding in a single eigensolver pass after weights are fixed, making the result deterministic (no random initialization)
weaknesses: No out-of-sample extension: embedding a new point requires re-running the full algorithm on the augmented dataset
Fails on manifolds with holes or strong global curvature because the local-linearity assumption breaks when k neighbors straddle a topological gap
Ill-conditioned eigenproblem when neighborhoods are nearly coplanar or k is too large relative to local intrinsic dimensionality, causing degenerate embeddings without regularization
recommended_for: Visualizing or pre-processing sensory data (e.g., 64×64 face images under varying pose/lighting) where the manifold is smoothly curved and densely sampled
