children.diff_siblings: Unlike QMIX (value decomposition, cooperative-only, discrete actions) and COMA (single shared critic, counterfactual advantage), MADDPG assigns each agent its own centralized critic that observes all agents' actions and states, while keeping actors decentralized and operating on local observations, enabling continuous action spaces in cooperative, competitive, and mixed settings simultaneously.
strengths: Works natively with continuous action spaces via deterministic policy gradient, whereas value-decomposition siblings (QMIX, VDN) require discrete actions or workarounds
Per-agent centralized critics see the full joint action space during training, stabilizing learning against the non-stationarity caused by simultaneously adapting agents
Applicable to cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive environments with no architectural change, since each agent's critic models opponents' behavior independently
weaknesses: Critic input size grows linearly with agent count (each critic receives all N agents' observations and actions), making training cost prohibitive beyond roughly 10-20 agents
Inherits DDPG's sensitivity to hyperparameters and replay buffer size; off-policy training with deterministic policies can diverge in highly stochastic or non-stationary environments
Assumes full observability of other agents' actions at training time, which is impractical when opponents' action spaces are unknown or partially observable
recommended_for: Robotics swarms or multi-vehicle control with continuous joint torques/velocities where discrete-action methods cannot represent the action space faithfully
Mixed cooperative-competitive games (e.g., predator-prey, multi-team sports simulation) where a single shared critic cannot correctly assign credit across opposing teams
not_recommended_for: Environments with dozens to hundreds of agents, where the O(N) critic input growth makes per-agent networks computationally intractable compared to factored methods like QMIX
Purely cooperative tasks with discrete actions and tight communication constraints, where QMIX or MAPPO achieve equivalent or better performance with lower memory and compute cost
children.curiosity: Introduced by Lowe et al. (OpenAI, 2017) in 'Multi-Agent Actor-Critic for Mixed Cooperative-Competitive Environments' (NeurIPS 2017); the authors also released the Multi-Agent Particle Environment (MPE) benchmark alongside the paper, which became the de facto standard testbed for continuous-action MARL research for several years.

target.notes: No labeled target. Learns per-agent deterministic policies from a scalar reward signal per agent via interaction with a multi-agent environment (Markov game). Not a supervised fitter.

data_regime.rows: needs millions of environment transitions (sample-inefficient off-policy RL); not a fixed dataset method
data_regime.dimensionality: actor on local per-agent observation; each centralized critic input scales O(N) with agent count (all agents' obs+actions), tractable only for ~2-20 agents

features.interpretability: low: deep neural actor-critic policies, no closed-form decision rule
features.notes: Continuous state/action vectors; observations should be scaled/normalized as in DDPG. Reward shaping strongly affects convergence.

assumptions: Continuous (or relaxable discrete via Gumbel-Softmax) action spaces
Full observability of all agents' observations and actions during centralized training (decentralized at execution)
Stationary environment dynamics aside from co-adapting agents; Markov game structure
Reward signal is informative and well-shaped per agent
loss: per-agent deterministic policy gradient (maximize each agent's centralized Q)
TD / Bellman squared error for each centralized critic
off-policy actor-critic with target networks and replay
contraindicated_when: agent count exceeds ~20 (O(N) critic input becomes intractable; prefer QMIX/MAPPO/factored methods)
purely cooperative discrete-action tasks with communication limits (QMIX/MAPPO are cheaper and as strong)
no simulator / only a static dataset (use offline RL or supervised learning instead)
highly stochastic or partially observable settings where deterministic off-policy training diverges
single-agent problems (DDPG/SAC/PPO suffice without joint critics)

children.name: QMIX
children.diff_siblings: Unlike VDN (which sums per-agent Q-values linearly) and MADDPG/COMA (which use centralized critics without structural decomposition), QMIX enforces a monotonicity constraint via a hypernetwork-generated mixing network whose weights are non-negative, ensuring that the joint Q-value is a monotonic function of each agent's individual Q-value — preserving the IGM property without assuming linearity.
strengths: Scalable cooperative training: the mixing network complexity grows linearly with agent count, making it tractable for dozens of agents where fully centralized Q-tables are exponential.

Allows rich non-linear factorization: by conditioning mixing-network weights on the global state via hypernetworks, it can represent strictly larger classes of joint Q-functions than VDN's additive decomposition.
CTDE (Centralized Training, Decentralized Execution): each agent acts using only its local observation at execution time, requiring no inter-agent communication at runtime.
weaknesses: Monotonicity constraint is sufficient but not necessary for IGM, so QMIX cannot represent joint Q-functions where a globally optimal joint action requires one agent's local Q-value to decrease — it fails on non-monotonic payoff matrices.
Poorly handles competitive or mixed-motive settings: the architecture assumes full cooperativity and a shared reward; applying it to heterogeneous-reward scenarios yields undefined behavior.

Hypernetwork conditioning on the global state is unavailable at execution time — any state information used during training cannot assist decentralized decision-making, creating a train/test information gap.
recommended_for: Cooperative multi-robot or multi-drone tasks (e.g., StarCraft II micromanagement) where agents share a single team reward and must coordinate without runtime communication.
Decentralized sensor networks or warehouse robotics where each unit has only local partial observations but a centralized simulator is available during training to supply global state to the mixer.
not_recommended_for: Games or problems with non-monotonic payoff structures (e.g., coordination tasks with 'miscoordination penalties') where the optimal joint Q-function cannot be expressed as a monotonic combination of individual utilities.
Mixed cooperative-competitive environments (e.g., general-sum games) where agents have individual reward signals that conflict, as QMIX's architecture presupposes a single shared team reward.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Rashid et al. (ICML 2018) and later extended in JMLR (2020), QMIX was the first method to prove that enforcing non-negative mixing-network weights is sufficient to guarantee the IGM property, enabling tractable greedy action selection in joint action spaces that would otherwise be exponential in the number of agents.

target.notes: No labeled target. Learns from a scalar shared team reward signal in a cooperative Markov game (Dec-POMDP); objective is maximizing expected discounted team return, not fitting a target distribution.

data_regime.rows: needs millions of environment-interaction transitions; sample-inefficient like all deep RL
data_regime.dimensionality: scales to dozens of agents (mixing network grows linearly with agent count)
needs: centralized global state available at training time

features.interpretability: low: deep recurrent Q-networks plus hypernetwork-generated mixing network; joint value is a learned non-linear monotonic composition
features.notes: Per-agent inputs are local partial observations (typically vectorized state/sensor features); a separate global state vector feeds the mixer only during training. Recurrent (GRU) agent nets handle partial observability over time.

assumptions: Fully cooperative setting with a single shared team reward (homogeneous-reward)
Individual-Global-Max (IGM) holds via a MONOTONIC factorization: argmax of joint Q equals per-agent argmax
Centralized Training, Decentralized Execution: global state usable in training but agents act on local obs only at execution
Discrete action spaces (value-based Q-learning)
loss: TD error / Bellman squared-error on the joint (mixed) Q-value, optimized end-to-end through the monotonic mixing network
contraindicated_when: Non-monotonic payoff structures where the optimal joint action requires an agent's local utility to decrease (e.g. miscoordination-penalty matrix games) — monotonicity is sufficient but not necessary for IGM
Mixed cooperative-competitive or general-sum games with conflicting per-agent rewards
Continuous action spaces (use policy-gradient MARL like MADDPG instead)
Single-agent problems (use DQN/PPO)
No simulator or centralized global state available during training
Low interaction budget where sample efficiency matters

children.name: MAPPO (Multi-Agent PPO)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike value-decomposition siblings (QMIX, VDN) that factorize a joint Q-function, and unlike off-policy siblings (MADDPG), MAPPO uses a shared centralized critic with global state access under the on-policy PPO clipped-surrogate objective, giving each agent's actor a trust-region update grounded in joint observations without ever storing a replay buffer.
strengths: Centralized critic conditioned on global state provides accurate credit assignment in partial-observability settings where each agent sees only a local observation
On-policy clipped surrogate objective (epsilon=0.2) prevents destructive policy updates without requiring a replay buffer, making training stable across heterogeneous agent populations
Empirically matches or exceeds off-policy baselines (QMIX, MADDPG) on SMAC benchmarks with identical hyperparameters across tasks, as shown by Yu et al. (2022)
weaknesses: On-policy data collection discards all experience after each update, requiring far more environment interactions than off-policy methods when the environment is slow or expensive to simulate
Centralized critic requires access to the global state at training time, which is unavailable in fully decentralized real-world deployments where agents cannot share raw observations
Shared global reward broadcast to all agents does not distinguish individual contributions, causing credit-assignment ambiguity in teams where agents have asymmetric roles
recommended_for: Cooperative tasks with a simulator that can be parallelized cheaply (e.g., StarCraft micromanagement, multi-robot navigation in MuJoCo) where the global state is observable during training
Research baselines for cooperative MARL: the algorithm's minimal hyperparameter sensitivity and open-source implementation make it the standard reference point when comparing new CTDE methods
not_recommended_for: Real-world multi-robot systems where training interactions are costly and sample efficiency is critical, as on-policy rollouts cannot reuse past experience
Competitive or mixed-cooperative-competitive settings, since MAPPO's centralized critic and shared reward formulation assume a fully cooperative team objective
children.curiosity: Introduced by Chao Yu, Akash Velu, Eugene Vinitsky et al. (NeurIPS 2022) under the title 'The Surprising Effectiveness of PPO in Cooperative Multi-Agent Games'; the paper showed that five implementation details (value normalization, input representation, data reuse epochs, PPO clipping, and death masking) were sufficient for vanilla PPO to match or outperform specialized off-policy MARL algorithms that had been the field's standard for years.

target.notes: Sequential decision-making, not supervised prediction. No labeled target; the learning signal is a scalar reward from environment transitions. Optimizes a joint cooperative team return for N agents acting under partial observability.

data_regime.rows: needs millions of environment steps; on-policy so each batch is discarded after one update, making it sample-inefficient
data_regime.dimensionality: scales to small-to-moderate agent counts (typically 2-30 cooperative agents); per-agent observation and joint global-state dimensionality both matter
needs: global/joint state observable at training time (CTDE)
GPU helpful but not mandatory for small nets

features.interpretability: low: learned actor and centralized critic networks are black-box policies with no parameter-level explanation
features.notes: Inputs are per-agent local observations (decentralized execution) plus a concatenated/structured global state fed only to the centralized critic during training. Observation normalization and reward scaling materially affect PPO stability.

assumptions: fully cooperative team objective with a shared reward (no competitive or mixed-motive incentives)
global state is accessible during centralized training
stationary or slowly-changing environment dynamics across rollouts
on-policy data freshness: experience cannot be safely reused once the policy moves
loss: PPO clipped surrogate objective (epsilon=0.2) on the per-agent policy
value-function (squared-error / GAE-target) loss on the shared centralized critic
entropy regularization bonus to maintain exploration
contraindicated_when: environment interactions are expensive or slow (real-robot, costly simulator) — off-policy MARL (QMIX, MADDPG) reuses experience and is far more sample-efficient
competitive or mixed cooperative-competitive settings — the shared-reward centralized critic assumes a common objective
fully decentralized training where no agent can access global state
single-agent problems — plain PPO is simpler and sufficient
very large agent populations where a centralized critic over the joint global state becomes intractable

target.notes: No supervised target. The learning signal is one scalar reward stream per agent emitted by an environment; agents optimize expected discounted return, not a labeled response variable. Framework is a Markov/stochastic game (N coupled MDPs with joint transitions and per-agent rewards).

data_regime.rows: No fixed dataset; requires an interactive (often simulated) multi-agent environment generating millions to billions of joint-action steps. Sample efficiency degrades sharply with agent count and non-stationarity.
data_regime.dimensionality: Joint action space scales as product of per-agent action spaces (exponential in N); centralized value methods intractable beyond ~a handful of agents without factorization (VDN, QMIX, mean-field).
needs: reward signal per agent or shared global reward

features.interpretability: low: learned joint/decentralized policies are opaque; emergent coordination is hard to attribute, and the multi-agent credit-assignment problem obscures each agent's contribution under a shared reward.
features.notes: Observations are per-agent (often partial/local) state vectors, pixels, or relational/graph structure over agents; centralized-training-decentralized-execution (CTDE) lets the critic see global state while actors use only local observations.

assumptions: Environment expressible as a Markov game with well-defined per-agent reward and (joint) transition dynamics.
A solution concept exists and is targeted (Nash/correlated equilibrium for general-sum, minimax for zero-sum, joint optimum for fully cooperative); guarantees are weak when agents learn concurrently.
Sufficient interaction budget to overcome non-stationarity from co-adapting agents.
Reward shaping/credit assignment available when only a shared global reward is observed.
loss: expected discounted return (per-agent or team) via policy gradient / actor-critic (MADDPG, MAPPO)
TD / Bellman error on factorized joint value (VDN, QMIX)
minimax / equilibrium objectives for competitive games (minimax-Q, Nash-Q)
self-play regret minimization
contraindicated_when: A single decision-maker faces a stationary environment: single-agent RL converges faster with stronger guarantees and no non-stationarity overhead.
The problem is a static prediction/labeling task with a fixed dataset: supervised learning is the correct tool, not RL.
No interactive environment or simulator exists to generate the required volume of joint-action experience.
Thousands+ of homogeneous interacting entities: mean-field RL or classical operations-research methods (LP for traffic assignment) are more tractable than explicit joint multi-agent modeling.
Sparse shared global reward with no mechanism for credit assignment, making cooperative training fail to attribute contributions.

target.notes: No fixed target/label. The learning signal is a scalar reward emitted by an environment, optimized over trajectories (sequences of state-action-reward), not a labeled response variable. Problem is framed as a Markov Decision Process (states, actions, transition dynamics, reward, discount).

data_regime.rows: Needs very large interaction budgets (often 1e5-1e8+ environment steps); sample efficiency is the central bottleneck
data_regime.dimensionality: State/action spaces range from small discrete (tabular) to high-dimensional continuous (deep RL with function approximation)
needs: a queryable environment or simulator (or logged interaction data for offline RL)
GPU for deep RL function approximators
many trials / cheap rollouts for on-policy methods

features.interpretability: low: learned policies/value functions are typically opaque, and credit assignment over long horizons is hard to inspect
features.notes: Inputs are states/observations that can be raw sensors, pixels, or engineered features; the agent must handle sequential, non-i.i.d. data generated by its own policy.

assumptions: Environment is (approximately) Markovian: next state and reward depend only on current state and action
Stationary transition dynamics and reward during training
Reward signal faithfully encodes the intended objective (misspecification leads to reward hacking)
Adequate exploration of state-action space; sufficient simulator fidelity if sim-to-real transfer is intended
loss: expected discounted cumulative reward (return) maximization
temporal-difference error (value/Q-learning, e.g. Bellman residual)
policy gradient objectives (REINFORCE, actor-critic, PPO clipped surrogate)
entropy-regularized return (maximum-entropy RL)
contraindicated_when: A static labeled dataset exists and the task is single-step prediction (supervised learning converges faster and more reliably)
No reward signal or environment/simulator can be defined
Safety-critical settings where online trial-and-error exploration is unacceptable and no high-fidelity simulator exists
Interaction is expensive and only a small fixed sample budget is available (sample inefficiency dominates)
Reward is extremely sparse/delayed with no shaping or curriculum available

children.name: 1.5 Causal / Heterogeneous Inference
children.diff_siblings: Unlike other ML subcategories that minimize predictive loss on outcomes, causal/heterogeneous inference methods target the estimation of individual or conditional average treatment effects (CATE) by explicitly modeling the counterfactual gap between treated and untreated potential outcomes.
strengths: Produces valid confidence intervals for treatment effects even when high-dimensional nuisance functions (propensity score, outcome model) are fit by ML — achieved via Neyman-orthogonal scores and cross-fitting (Double ML, Chernozhukov et al. 2018)
Meta-learner decomposition (S/T/X/DR-learner) allows any off-the-shelf ML model to be repurposed for CATE estimation without rewriting the base algorithm
Causal forests provide honest, asymptotically normal point estimates of heterogeneous effects at the individual level, enabling statistically rigorous subgroup discovery
weaknesses: All methods assume unconfoundedness (no unmeasured confounders) — an untestable assumption that, if violated, produces biased CATE estimates regardless of model sophistication
Positivity violations (subgroups where one treatment arm is nearly absent) cause extreme propensity weights and high-variance estimates, collapsing the effective sample size for those subgroups

CATE evaluation is fundamentally hard: the true individual treatment effect is never observed, so standard cross-validation on held-out outcomes does not measure causal accuracy — specialized proxies (R-loss, plug-in DR) are needed
recommended_for: Randomized experiments or quasi-experiments (observational studies with rich covariate adjustment) where the goal is to find which patient or customer subgroups benefit most from a treatment — e.g., personalized medicine RCT data with hundreds of baseline covariates

Policy evaluation pipelines where both the average effect and its heterogeneity across subgroups must be reported with confidence intervals, such as labor-market program evaluation using administrative records
not_recommended_for: Pure prediction tasks where the causal direction is irrelevant — using a CATE estimator to forecast an outcome wastes the orthogonalization overhead and yields no benefit over standard supervised learning

Settings where treatment assignment is fully deterministic for large subgroups (zero propensity overlap), since positivity is violated and no causal estimator can recover unbiased effects without strong extrapolation assumptions
children.curiosity: The foundational guarantee for this field was established by Chernozhukov et al. (2018) in 'Double/Debiased Machine Learning for Treatment and Structural Parameters' (The Econometrics Journal), proving that cross-fitted Neyman-orthogonal estimators achieve root-n convergence and valid inference even when the nuisance models converge at slower ML rates.

children.name: Causal Forest
children.diff_siblings: Unlike meta-learners (S/T/X-learner) that plug any base estimator into a multi-step recipe, Causal Forest builds trees that split directly on treatment-effect heterogeneity using Neyman-orthogonal scores and honest sample splitting, producing asymptotically normal, pointwise confidence intervals without a separate CATE modeling stage.
strengths: Honest splitting (separate subsamples for tree structure and leaf estimation) eliminates in-sample overfitting bias, enabling valid confidence intervals for each individual CATE estimate.
Double-robustness via residualization of both outcome and treatment on covariates before splitting makes estimates consistent even if one nuisance model is misspecified.

Variable importance is derived directly from splitting frequency on treatment-effect gradients, yielding interpretable covariate rankings tied causally to effect heterogeneity rather than to outcome prediction.
weaknesses: Honest splitting halves the effective sample for both structure search and estimation, requiring roughly 4x more observations than a standard random forest to achieve comparable precision.
Assumes unconfoundedness (no unmeasured confounders); unlike IV-based siblings, it has no identification strategy for settings with endogenous treatment selection.

Confidence intervals are pointwise and asymptotic; simultaneous inference over many subgroups requires additional corrections (e.g., Bonferroni or bootstrap), which are not built into the standard grf implementation.
recommended_for: Randomized experiments or observational studies with a rich covariate set (50-500 features) where the goal is to rank subgroups by treatment response for policy targeting (e.g., which patients benefit most from a drug).
Policy evaluation datasets with 5,000+ observations where heterogeneous treatment effects must come with valid uncertainty quantification rather than just point estimates.
not_recommended_for: Small samples (n < 500): honest splitting leaves too few observations per leaf for reliable CATE estimation and valid coverage of the confidence intervals.

Settings with strong unmeasured confounding where treatment assignment cannot be plausibly treated as ignorable given observed covariates, as the orthogonalization step does not correct for latent selection.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Wager and Athey (2018) in the Journal of the American Statistical Association, the paper proved that individual tree predictions are asymptotically Gaussian and unbiased under honesty — the first formal statistical inference guarantee for a forest-based CATE estimator.

target.notes: Estimand is the conditional average treatment effect (CATE), not the outcome itself; requires an observed treatment/intervention indicator W in addition to outcome Y. Outcome can be continuous or binary (effect on a probability scale); survival/time-to-event needs the dedicated causal survival forest variant.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ (5,000+ recommended); honest splitting halves the effective sample, so ~4x the data of a plain RF for comparable precision; n<500 unreliable
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n; handles 50-500 covariates well, robust to many irrelevant features via splitting
needs: sufficient overlap (propensity bounded away from 0 and 1)

features.interpretability: medium-high: split-frequency variable importance ranks covariates by their role in effect heterogeneity, and per-unit CATE estimates come with pointwise confidence intervals
features.notes: Tree-based, scale-invariant; no standardization needed. Tabular covariates only.

assumptions: unconfoundedness / ignorability of treatment given observed covariates (no unmeasured confounders)
overlap / positivity in propensity score
SUTVA (no interference between units)
nuisance models (outcome and propensity) at least one correctly specified for double-robust consistency
loss: Neyman-orthogonal (doubly-robust / R-loss) score on residualized outcome and treatment
splits chosen to maximize heterogeneity in the treatment-effect gradient
contraindicated_when: goal is plain outcome prediction rather than treatment-effect estimation
no observed treatment variable
strong unmeasured confounding or endogenous treatment selection (use IV / structural methods instead)
small samples (n<500)
poor overlap / near-deterministic treatment assignment
valid simultaneous inference over many subgroups is required without added multiplicity correction

children.name: Double ML (DML)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike meta-learners (T/S/X-Learner) that directly fit conditional outcome models, and unlike Causal Forests that estimate heterogeneous effects non-parametrically, DML targets a single low-dimensional causal parameter by residualizing both outcome and treatment on covariates via Neyman-orthogonal moment conditions and K-fold cross-fitting, which removes first-order regularization bias from the ML nuisance estimators.
strengths: Valid frequentist confidence intervals for the ATE/LATE even when nuisance functions (outcome and propensity) are estimated with high-dimensional ML — asymptotic normality holds under root-n rate conditions.
Doubly robust by construction: consistent if either the outcome model or the propensity score model is correctly specified, providing a safeguard against one misspecified nuisance.
Cross-fitting eliminates own-observation overfitting bias without sacrificing sample size, allowing any black-box ML learner (XGBoost, Lasso, neural nets) as plug-in for nuisance estimation.
weaknesses: Targets only a single global causal parameter (ATE or LATE); heterogeneous treatment effects require a further second-stage model (e.g., Causal Forest on residuals), adding complexity.
Highly sensitive to inclusion of endogenous 'bad controls': even a few post-treatment or collider variables among confounders cause substantial bias that Neyman-orthogonalization does not correct.
Requires strong overlap (positivity) and unconfoundedness; under limited overlap, propensity residuals blow up, inflating variance and breaking the root-n guarantees.
recommended_for: Policy evaluation in economics or medicine where the goal is a valid confidence interval around a single average treatment effect from observational data with 50+ confounders (e.g., wage effect of job training using administrative records).
A/B experiment analysis with imperfect randomization and many pre-treatment covariates, where residualization removes covariate imbalance and tightens standard errors without model-selection bias.
not_recommended_for: Problems requiring personalized treatment rules or individual-level effect estimates across many subgroups — DML alone produces a scalar estimate, not a CATE surface.

Settings where confounders cannot be pre-specified and automated variable selection is used from a mixed pool of controls, as endogenous regressors silently bias the estimate despite orthogonalization.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Chernozhukov, Chetverikov, Demirer, Duflo, Hansen, Newey, and Robins (2018) in 'Double/Debiased Machine Learning for Treatment and Causal Parameters' (The Econometrics Journal, 21: C1–C68); the preprint circulated as arXiv:1608.00060 in 2016 and is among the most-cited works combining econometrics with modern ML, credited with reviving Neyman's 1959 orthogonality concept in a high-dimensional inference context.

target.notes: Estimand is a low-dimensional causal parameter (ATE/ATT/LATE), not the outcome itself; outcome Y can be continuous, binary, or count and treatment D can be binary, continuous, or instrumented. The fitted quantity is a scalar effect with a valid standard error, not a predictive surface.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds+; root-n inference and cross-fitting want enough observations to estimate flexible nuisance models on each fold
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for high-dimensional confounder sets (p large, even p>n) where naive regression adjustment overfits; the causal parameter stays low-dimensional

features.interpretability: high for the target estimate (a single interpretable effect with CI) but low for the nuisance ML models, which are black-box plug-ins
features.notes: Confounders must be pre-treatment and pre-specified; the nuisance learner (Lasso, XGBoost, NN) handles scaling/encoding, but variable choice is a substantive causal decision, not a tuning step.

assumptions: unconfoundedness / conditional ignorability given the controls
overlap / positivity (propensity bounded away from 0 and 1)
no bad controls (no post-treatment, collider, or mediator variables among confounders)
nuisance estimators converge at o(n^-1/4) rate so the orthogonal score yields root-n asymptotic normality
SUTVA / no interference
loss: Neyman-orthogonal moment conditions (orthogonalized/partialled-out score)
K-fold cross-fitting to remove own-observation overfitting bias
nuisance models optimize their own losses: squared error for outcome regression, log-loss for propensity
contraindicated_when: personalized treatment rules or individual/subgroup CATE are required (DML yields a scalar; pair with Causal Forest or X-Learner instead)
confounders cannot be pre-specified and are auto-selected from a mixed pool that may include endogenous/collider variables
limited overlap inflates propensity residuals, breaking root-n variance guarantees
goal is pure prediction of Y rather than an interpretable causal effect
sample is too small to estimate flexible nuisance functions reliably per fold

children.name: Synthetic Control
children.diff_siblings: Unlike DiD (which assumes parallel trends across all control units) or ITS (which models a single unit's trend), Synthetic Control builds a counterfactual by solving a constrained optimization to find a convex combination of donor-pool units that replicates the treated unit's pre-intervention trajectory across multiple predictors simultaneously.
strengths: Transparent counterfactual: the synthetic unit is a named, inspectable weighted average of real donor units, making the comparison concrete and auditable.
Does not require a large number of treated units — valid for N=1 case studies (single country, state, or firm) where DiD is inapplicable.
Convex-hull constraint (weights sum to 1, each ≥ 0) prevents extrapolation beyond the observed donor space, bounding interpolation bias.
weaknesses: Requires a long, stable pre-intervention period (typically 10+ time points) to credibly fit donor weights; short pre-periods lead to overfitting.
Inference relies on permutation (placebo) tests over the donor pool, which have low power when the donor pool is small (fewer than ~20 units).
Sensitive to donor pool composition: a poorly chosen or contaminated donor pool (units also exposed to the intervention) invalidates the counterfactual.
recommended_for: Evaluating a policy applied to a single aggregate unit (e.g., one state's tax reform) with 15+ years of pre-treatment panel data on 20–50 comparable untreated units.
Cross-country or cross-market comparative case studies where randomization is impossible and the treated case is sui generis, requiring a data-driven composite control.
not_recommended_for: Settings where the treated unit lies outside the convex hull of donor units in covariate space — the method cannot extrapolate and will produce a poor pre-period fit.
High-frequency, noisy outcomes (daily stock returns, hourly sensor data) where pre-period volatility makes weight optimization unstable and placebo tests lose interpretability.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Abadie and Gardeazabal (2003) to estimate the economic cost of terrorism in the Basque Country, the method was formalized and given its current optimization framework by Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller (2010) in the Journal of the American Statistical Association, accumulating over 4,000 citations within a decade.
keywords: estimate impact of a policy or intervention
construct synthetic counterfactual from control units
what would have happened without the intervention

target.notes: Estimates a treatment effect as the gap between an observed treated unit's outcome trajectory and a synthetic counterfactual. Target is a panel outcome (typically continuous aggregate metric) observed over time for one treated unit; the estimand is the post-intervention divergence, not a per-row prediction.

data_regime.rows: panel of N donor units x T time points; needs a long pre-intervention window (typically 10+, ideally 15+ time periods) and a donor pool of ~20-50 untreated units for credible placebo inference
data_regime.dimensionality: very few treated units (often N=1); donor weights solved by constrained optimization, so works when classic DiD/regression has too few treated units

features.interpretability: high — the counterfactual is a named, inspectable convex combination of real donor units with non-negative weights summing to 1
features.notes: Predictors should be measured consistently across treated and donor units; outcome and covariates used to match the pre-period trajectory.

assumptions: Treated unit lies inside (or near) the convex hull of donor units in outcome/covariate space — no extrapolation possible
A long, stable pre-intervention period exists to fit donor weights without overfitting
Donor pool is uncontaminated: no donor unit exposed to the same or a similar intervention or spillover
No anticipation effects before the intervention date
Pre-period fit quality transfers to a valid post-period counterfactual
loss: weighted pre-intervention prediction error minimized under simplex constraints (weights >= 0, sum to 1)
inference via permutation / placebo tests over the donor pool rather than parametric standard errors
contraindicated_when: Treated unit is an outlier outside the donor convex hull (poor pre-period fit, cannot extrapolate)
Short pre-intervention series (few time points) causing overfit donor weights
Small donor pool (<~20 units), which leaves placebo tests underpowered
High-frequency, noisy outcomes (daily returns, hourly sensor data) where volatility destabilizes weight optimization
Many treated units available, where DiD or panel fixed-effects estimators are more appropriate
Goal is row-level prediction or classification rather than a single-unit causal counterfactual

children.name: PSM (Propensity Score Matching)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike DiD (which requires panel data and parallel trends) and IV (which requires a valid instrument uncorrelated with unmeasured confounders), PSM collapses all observed covariates into a single scalar — the conditional treatment probability — and matches treated to control units on that scalar alone, without exploiting time variation or external variation.
strengths: Reduces high-dimensional covariate adjustment to a 1-D scalar, making matching feasible when there are dozens of confounders that would cause the curse of dimensionality in direct covariate matching.

Balancing treated and control groups on the propensity score is provably sufficient to eliminate confounding from all included covariates (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983), without specifying an outcome model.

Transparent diagnostic: the standardized mean difference (SMD) before vs. after matching is a model-agnostic balance check that does not require access to outcome data, preserving the separation between design and analysis.
weaknesses: Cannot balance unobserved confounders — if any unmeasured variable jointly predicts treatment assignment and outcome, the ATT estimate remains biased regardless of how well the propensity score is estimated.
Matching discards unmatched treated units (and controls), reducing effective sample size, which increases variance and can introduce selection bias when overlap between groups is limited.

The propensity score itself must be estimated (usually via logistic regression), and misspecification of that model — wrong functional form, missing interactions, or collinearity — produces a biased score and poor balance.
recommended_for: Retrospective observational studies in epidemiology or economics where treatment was not randomized but a rich set of pre-treatment covariates (demographics, prior health measures, baseline outcomes) is recorded for both treated and untreated subjects.

Program evaluation with a large administrative dataset where the treatment group is small relative to a large control pool, allowing tight 1:k nearest-neighbor matching with a narrow caliper (e.g., 0.02 SD of the logit score) without depleting controls.
not_recommended_for: Settings with strong unmeasured confounding (e.g., patient self-selection based on unrecorded severity) where IV or DiD can exploit an exogenous source of variation to purge the bias that PSM cannot touch.

High-dimensional genetic or text data where hundreds of potential confounders make propensity score model specification unreliable; doubly-robust estimators (AIPW) or targeted learning (TMLE) are better suited because they combine outcome and propensity models with error-correction guarantees.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983) in 'The Central Role of the Propensity Score in Observational Studies for Causal Effects' (Biometrika, 70(1):41-55), the paper proved the balancing property — that conditioning on the propensity score renders treatment assignment independent of all observed covariates — which gave theoretical justification for replacing multivariate matching with a single estimated probability.

target.notes: Estimand is a causal contrast (ATT/ATE), not predictive accuracy. The treatment must be binary (or coarsened to binary); the outcome can be any type and is analyzed only after matching. A binary treatment-assignment indicator is required.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds+ per arm; works best when the control pool is much larger than the treated group so 1:k nearest-neighbor matching with a tight caliper does not deplete controls
data_regime.dimensionality: p (confounders) collapsed to a 1-D propensity score, so moderate dozens of covariates are fine; fails when p is very large (hundreds+) because the logistic propensity model becomes unreliable

features.interpretability: high — design (balancing) is separated from outcome analysis; standardized mean difference before/after matching is a transparent, outcome-blind balance diagnostic
features.notes: Requires rich PRE-treatment covariates measured for both treated and control units. Propensity model (usually logistic regression) needs correct functional form, relevant interactions, and no severe collinearity.

assumptions: Unconfoundedness / conditional ignorability: all confounders jointly affecting treatment and outcome are observed and included
Common support / overlap: treated and control propensity-score distributions overlap (positivity)
Correctly specified propensity model — misspecification (wrong form, missing interactions) yields a biased score and poor balance
SUTVA: no interference between units and a single well-defined version of treatment
contraindicated_when: Unmeasured confounding is plausible (e.g., self-selection on unrecorded severity) — use IV or DiD which exploit exogenous variation PSM cannot touch
Poor overlap / limited common support — matching discards many units, shrinking effective sample and risking selection bias
Very high-dimensional confounders (genomic, text) make propensity specification unreliable — prefer doubly-robust AIPW or TMLE
Panel data with parallel-trends structure available — DiD is more appropriate
No measured pre-treatment covariates, or treatment is continuous rather than binary

children.name: IPW (Inverse Probability Weighting)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike meta-learners (S/T/X-learner) that directly model outcome functions, IPW re-weights observations by the inverse of the propensity score P(T=1|X) to create a pseudo-population where treatment assignment is independent of confounders, estimating the ATE without fitting a separate outcome model.
strengths: Non-parametric in the outcome model — correct propensity score estimation yields unbiased ATE even when the outcome-covariate relationship is complex or unknown.
Naturally handles multi-valued and time-varying treatments by extending weights to each treatment level or time point without re-specifying an outcome model.
Doubly robust when combined with outcome regression (AIPW): consistent if either the propensity model or the outcome model is correctly specified, not necessarily both.
weaknesses: Extreme weights when propensity scores are near 0 or 1 (near-violation of positivity) inflate variance sharply and can cause numerical instability.
Requires a correctly specified propensity score model — misspecification (wrong functional form or omitted confounders) produces biased ATE estimates.

Inefficient relative to doubly robust estimators in large samples; the Horvitz-Thompson estimator in particular has higher variance than regression-adjusted alternatives when the outcome model is available.
recommended_for: Observational studies with binary treatment and rich covariate data where the selection-into-treatment mechanism is well understood and can be modeled (e.g., clinical database studies with documented eligibility criteria).
Settings requiring marginal (population-level) treatment effect estimates across the full covariate distribution, such as policy evaluation where the target population differs from the treated group.
not_recommended_for: Data with very low treatment prevalence (< 5%) or near-deterministic assignment, where propensity scores near 0 or 1 produce unstable, high-variance weights.
Problems where unconfoundedness is implausible (unmeasured confounders exist) and no instrumental variable or sensitivity analysis can address the gap — IPW offers no protection against hidden bias.
children.curiosity: The propensity score foundation of IPW was established by Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983) in 'The central role of the propensity score in observational studies for causal effects' (Biometrika, 70(1):41-55), which proved that conditioning on P(T=1|X) alone is sufficient to remove confounding from all observed covariates simultaneously.

target.notes: Target is the potential outcome Y; IPW estimates the marginal treatment effect (ATE) of a treatment T on Y, not Y itself. Requires an observed treatment/exposure indicator T (typically binary, extensible to multi-valued or time-varying). Outcome type is flexible because IPW does not model the outcome.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds+; variance grows sharply in small samples or when effective sample size is reduced by extreme weights
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred for the propensity model; high p requires regularized/ML propensity estimation and good overlap
needs: common-support/overlap region between treated and control

features.interpretability: medium — ATE is interpretable, but estimate validity hinges on the unverifiable unconfoundedness assumption
features.notes: Covariates must include all confounders of treatment and outcome. Propensity score P(T=1|X) can be estimated by logistic regression or any ML classifier; check positivity by inspecting the propensity distribution and weight extremes.

assumptions: Unconfoundedness / ignorability: no unmeasured confounders given X
Positivity / overlap: 0 < P(T=1|X) < 1 for all X
Correctly specified propensity model (functional form and included covariates)
SUTVA: no interference between units, single version of treatment
Treatment assignment mechanism is well understood and modelable
loss: Horvitz-Thompson / inverse-probability-weighted estimating equations for the ATE
stabilized weights to reduce variance
augmented IPW (AIPW) combining propensity and outcome models for double robustness
contraindicated_when: Treatment prevalence very low (<5%) or near-deterministic assignment producing propensity scores near 0 or 1 and unstable extreme weights
Poor covariate overlap / positivity violations between treated and control
Plausible unmeasured confounding with no IV or sensitivity analysis available — IPW gives no protection against hidden bias
Goal is purely predictive (predict Y) rather than estimating a causal effect
Propensity model is likely misspecified and no doubly robust augmentation is used

children.name: TMLE (Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike IPW (which relies solely on the propensity score) or G-computation (which relies solely on the outcome model), TMLE adds a semiparametric 'targeting' fluctuation step after initial nuisance estimation that projects the initial plug-in estimate onto the tangent space of the target parameter, achieving asymptotic efficiency and double robustness simultaneously.
strengths: Double robustness: consistent if either the outcome regression or the propensity score model is correctly specified, not necessarily both
Plug-in estimator structure respects the parameter space (e.g., probabilities stay in [0,1]) unlike one-step AIPW corrections that can violate bounds
Natively integrates SuperLearner ensemble for nuisance parameters, reducing reliance on a single parametric model and lowering empirical bias
weaknesses: Sensitive to practical positivity violations: near-zero propensity scores inflate the clever covariate and cause variance instability or systematic bias in the fluctuation step
Computational complexity is substantially higher than IPW or G-computation due to the iterative targeting loop and the need to fit two separate nuisance models plus a fluctuation model

Correct inference requires cross-fitting (sample splitting) when using data-adaptive learners; omitting it introduces Donsker-class violations that invalidate asymptotic normality of the confidence intervals
recommended_for: Observational studies with moderate confounding where the analyst can credibly specify either the outcome model or the exposure model but not both, and sample size is large enough (n > 500) for the semiparametric efficiency bound to be relevant

Policy evaluation pipelines that must report valid 95% confidence intervals for average treatment effects under flexible, non-parametric covariate adjustment without sacrificing inferential guarantees
not_recommended_for: Settings with near-violation of positivity (e.g., treatment essentially deterministic for a subgroup), where extreme propensity weights destabilize the targeting step regardless of truncation heuristics
Small samples (n < 200) where the cross-fitting folds are too small for SuperLearner to estimate nuisance functions reliably, negating the efficiency advantage over simpler doubly robust estimators
children.curiosity: Introduced by van der Laan and Rubin (2006) in the International Journal of Biostatistics, TMLE was the first general method to combine semiparametric efficiency theory with a plug-in estimator that automatically satisfies the score equation of the target parameter, a property that one-step estimators like AIPW achieve only asymptotically and not in finite samples.

target.notes: Target is not a prediction but an estimand: average treatment effect (ATE/ATT), risk difference/ratio, or other low-dimensional causal parameter. Requires a defined binary or categorical treatment/exposure variable plus an outcome (commonly binary or bounded-continuous; survival variants exist). Not a generic predictor of new observations.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds+; semiparametric efficiency bound and cross-fitting fold sizes matter mainly at n>500. Poor at n<200
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n in the practical sense; handles moderate-to-high covariate dimension via the SuperLearner nuisance step but the estimand stays low-dimensional

features.interpretability: high at the estimand level (a single interpretable causal effect with valid CIs); low for the internal nuisance fits when SuperLearner/ML learners are used
features.notes: Two nuisance models required: outcome regression Q(A,W) and propensity/treatment model g(A|W). Confounder set W must be chosen on causal grounds, not by predictive fit.

assumptions: No unmeasured confounding (conditional ignorability/exchangeability given W)
Positivity/overlap: every covariate stratum has nonzero probability of each treatment level
Consistency / SUTVA (well-defined treatment, no interference)
Correct specification of AT LEAST one nuisance model (outcome or propensity) for consistency; both for full efficiency
Cross-fitting required when data-adaptive learners are used, else Donsker-class conditions are violated and CIs are invalid
loss: targeted log-likelihood fluctuation (logistic submodel on the clever covariate) to solve the efficient influence function estimating equation
negative log-likelihood / cross-entropy and squared error inside nuisance learners
contraindicated_when: Practical positivity violations: near-zero or near-one propensity scores (treatment near-deterministic for a subgroup) destabilize the clever covariate
n<200, where cross-fitting folds are too small for reliable nuisance estimation
Goal is pure outcome prediction rather than effect estimation (use a standard supervised learner)
Key confounders are unmeasured, or treatment is poorly defined (no valid causal estimand)

children.name: DiD (Differences-in-Differences)
children.diff_siblings: DiD identifies the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) by subtracting pre-post changes in a control group from pre-post changes in a treated group, relying on the parallel trends assumption rather than matching on levels (Synthetic Control) or modeling treatment assignment explicitly (IV or RD).
strengths: Allows non-random treatment assignment based on outcome levels, as long as unobserved unit characteristics are time-invariant and absorbed by the two-way fixed effects (unit + time) in the OLS specification.

Scales naturally to large panel datasets with millions of observations; estimation reduces to OLS on a regression with unit and time dummies, requiring no matrix inversion beyond standard linear algebra.
Pre-treatment parallel trends can be partially tested via event-study plots, giving researchers a falsifiability check before the post-treatment period.
weaknesses: TWFE DiD is biased under staggered treatment adoption when treatment effects are heterogeneous across cohorts: early-treated units act as implicit controls for later-treated units, producing sign-reversals documented by Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021).
The parallel trends assumption is not directly testable in the post-period; passing pre-trend tests is neither necessary nor sufficient for the assumption to hold after treatment.

Sensitive to functional form: parallel trends in levels does not imply parallel trends in logs or any nonlinear transformation, so the choice of outcome scale can determine whether identification holds.
recommended_for: Policy evaluation with a clear treatment date and a large panel of untreated units that plausibly share time trends with the treated group, such as minimum-wage laws across US states.

Labor economics studies using administrative earnings records where units self-select into programs but selection is driven by fixed individual characteristics (e.g., region, firm size) rather than anticipatory trend changes.
not_recommended_for: Staggered rollout designs with heterogeneous treatment effect dynamics without applying cohort-specific estimators (Callaway & Sant'Anna or Sun & Abraham), as vanilla TWFE will produce weighted averages contaminated by negative weights.

Settings where only one or very few treated units exist, since the parallel trends assumption cannot be credibly assessed and variance is dominated by the small-sample noise of the treated group; Synthetic Control is preferable there.
children.curiosity: The modern DiD framework was formalized by Ashenfelter and Card (1985) in 'Using the Longitudinal Structure of Earnings to Estimate the Effect of Training Programs' (Review of Economics and Statistics, 67:648-660), which used pre-post earnings comparisons between trainees and non-trainees to evaluate a federal job-training program -- a design that became the template for three decades of applied microeconomics.

target.notes: Estimand is the ATT, not a prediction. Outcome is observed over time for treated and control units; canonical case is continuous. Binary/count outcomes are supported via linear probability or transformations, but parallel trends must hold on the chosen scale.

data_regime.rows: panel/repeated cross-section with at least 2 time periods (pre + post) and many control units; works from moderate panels up to millions of unit-by-time observations
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n; few regressors (treatment indicator, fixed effects, optional controls). Identification needs adequate untreated units, not high p
needs: panel or repeated cross-sectional data with a defined treatment date
a never-treated or not-yet-treated control group sharing time trends

features.interpretability: high: coefficient on treatment-x-post interaction is the causal ATT; two-way fixed effects via OLS dummies
features.notes: Requires a binary treatment indicator, a post-period indicator, and unit + time identifiers. Time-varying confounders correlated with treatment timing bias the estimate.

assumptions: parallel trends: treated and control outcomes would have moved identically absent treatment
no anticipation effects before the treatment date
time-invariant unobserved unit heterogeneity (absorbed by unit fixed effects)
stable composition / no differential selection into the panel over time (SUTVA, no spillovers to controls)
parallel trends is scale-dependent: holds in levels does not imply it holds in logs
loss: squared error via OLS on a two-way fixed-effects regression
clustered standard errors (typically by unit) for inference on the ATT
contraindicated_when: staggered treatment adoption with heterogeneous, dynamic effects under plain TWFE (negative weighting; use Callaway & Sant'Anna or Sun & Abraham)
diverging pre-treatment trends or anticipatory behavior
only one or very few treated units (parallel trends untestable, high variance; prefer Synthetic Control)
treatment timing correlated with time-varying confounders or contemporaneous shocks hitting groups differently
goal is point prediction or forecasting rather than estimating a treatment effect

children.name: IV / 2SLS (Instrumental Variables)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike DID or RDD, which exploit assignment rules or time-based discontinuities, IV/2SLS isolates causal effects by routing identification through a third variable (the instrument) that affects the treatment but has no direct path to the outcome — enabling identification even without a clean natural experiment cutoff.
strengths: Handles endogeneity from unmeasured confounders, simultaneity, or measurement error without requiring the confounder to be observed
Two-stage structure separates exogenous variation (first stage) from outcome estimation (second stage), keeping each stage interpretable via standard OLS diagnostics
Yields a LATE (Local Average Treatment Effect) for compliers, which is policy-relevant when the instrument mirrors an actual policy lever (e.g., draft lottery, distance to hospital)
weaknesses: Finding a valid instrument — one that satisfies both relevance and the exclusion restriction — is empirically difficult and the exclusion restriction is untestable by construction
Weak instruments (first-stage F-statistic below ~10) cause 2SLS estimates to be biased toward OLS and inflate standard errors, undermining the entire causal claim
LATE applies only to compliers, so external validity to always-takers or never-takers requires additional assumptions that are often unjustified
recommended_for: Estimating the return to education using proximity to college as an instrument, where endogeneity arises because ability simultaneously drives schooling and wages
Clinical trials with non-compliance where randomized assignment is used as instrument for actual treatment received, recovering the effect among those who comply with assignment
not_recommended_for: Settings where a plausible instrument cannot be justified on substantive grounds — running 2SLS with a weak or invalid instrument produces estimates worse than biased OLS
Panels with many endogenous regressors and few instruments, where the just-identified or over-identified system becomes unstable and first-stage fit collapses
children.curiosity: The first application of instrumental variables is credited to Philip G. Wright (1928) in 'The Tariff on Animal and Vegetable Oils', where he used supply-side shifters to separately identify supply and demand elasticities — predating the formal econometric literature on simultaneous equations by nearly two decades; Theil (1953) and Basmann (1957) later derived the two-stage computational form still used today.

target.notes: Outcome is typically continuous (linear 2SLS); the estimand is a causal coefficient on an endogenous regressor, not predictive fit. Treatment/endogenous regressor may be continuous or binary; binary treatment yields a LATE (compliers only).

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ for stable first stage; weak-instrument bias and inflated SEs worsen in small samples
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n required; just- or over-identified system needs at least one valid instrument per endogenous regressor
needs: one or more valid instruments (relevant + satisfying the exclusion restriction)

features.interpretability: high — two OLS stages with standard coefficient/diagnostic interpretation
features.notes: Requires an instrument Z correlated with the endogenous regressor but with no direct path to the outcome. First-stage strength must be checked (F-statistic ~>10).

assumptions: Instrument relevance: instrument strongly predicts the endogenous regressor (strong first stage)
Exclusion restriction: instrument affects outcome only through the treatment, untestable by construction
Instrument exogeneity / independence from unobserved confounders
Monotonicity (no defiers) for LATE interpretation with binary treatment
Linearity of the structural equation in standard 2SLS
loss: two-stage least squares (squared error in both stages)
GMM (efficient estimator under over-identification)
contraindicated_when: No substantively justifiable instrument exists — weak/invalid instruments yield estimates worse than biased OLS
First-stage F-statistic below ~10 (weak instruments bias toward OLS and inflate SEs)
Many endogenous regressors with few instruments (unstable, first-stage fit collapses)
Goal is pure prediction rather than identifying a causal effect
Exclusion restriction is implausible (instrument has a direct outcome path)

children.name: Regression Discontinuity (RD)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike DiD (which requires parallel trends across time) or IV (which requires an external instrument uncorrelated with confounders), RD identifies causal effects purely from a known assignment cutoff in a continuous running variable, without needing pre-treatment data or an instrument.
strengths: Credible local causal identification with minimal assumptions: only continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff is required, not parallel trends or instrument validity.
Built-in falsification tests: manipulation of the running variable can be detected via density tests (McCrary, 2008), and placebo cutoffs verify the absence of spurious discontinuities.
Works in sharp and fuzzy variants: when treatment compliance is imperfect at the cutoff, the fuzzy RD recovers the LATE for compliers via a Wald-type IV ratio estimator.
weaknesses: Estimates are strictly local: the LATE applies only to units near the cutoff, making extrapolation to the full population unjustified without strong additional assumptions.
Sensitive to bandwidth choice: the bias-variance tradeoff in local polynomial fitting means over- or under-smoothing around the cutoff directly distorts the treatment effect estimate.
Requires sufficient density near the cutoff: sparse observations at the threshold inflate variance and make the nonparametric local regression unreliable.
recommended_for: Policy evaluation where assignment follows a hard administrative threshold, such as estimating the effect of scholarship eligibility on graduation rates when a test score cutoff determines award.
Healthcare or regulatory studies with score-based eligibility rules, such as measuring the causal impact of a clinical intervention triggered at a specific biomarker threshold.
not_recommended_for: Settings where agents can precisely manipulate their score to sort above or below the cutoff, since sorting invalidates the local randomization assumption.
Studies requiring population-average treatment effects: RD inherently estimates a local effect at the cutoff and cannot generalize to units far from the threshold.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Thistlethwaite and Campbell (1960) to study the effect of merit scholarships on students' academic careers, RD was largely ignored for three decades until Hahn, Todd, and Van der Klaauw (2001) provided its formal nonparametric identification theory.
keywords: estimate causal effect without randomized trial
impact of policy at a threshold

target.notes: Estimand is a treatment effect (LATE at the cutoff), not a prediction. Outcome can be continuous, binary, or count; the running variable assigning treatment must be continuous with a known sharp threshold.

data_regime.rows: needs sufficient density near the cutoff; effective sample is only the bandwidth window, so thousands+ total observations are typically required for a credible local fit
data_regime.dimensionality: low-dimensional by design; identification rests on one continuous running variable and the cutoff, not on many covariates
needs: a known assignment threshold on a continuous running variable
dense observations on both sides of the cutoff

features.interpretability: high: estimate is the jump in the outcome at a single known cutoff, directly interpretable as a local causal effect
features.notes: Requires a continuous forcing/running variable with a deterministic (sharp) or probabilistic (fuzzy) treatment rule at a fixed threshold. Estimation is local-polynomial regression within a chosen bandwidth; bandwidth selection (e.g. CCT/IK) drives the bias-variance tradeoff.

assumptions: continuity of potential outcomes in the running variable at the cutoff
no precise manipulation/sorting of the running variable around the threshold (testable via McCrary density test)
treatment assignment determined by the cutoff (sharp) or discontinuous in compliance probability at the cutoff (fuzzy)
covariates continuous through the cutoff (placebo balance check)
loss: local weighted least squares (local linear/polynomial within bandwidth)
fuzzy RD: Wald/IV ratio of outcome jump to treatment-probability jump
contraindicated_when: agents can precisely manipulate their score to sort across the cutoff (local randomization fails)
no sharp threshold exists or assignment is continuous/gradual rather than discontinuous
the goal is a population-average treatment effect rather than a local effect at the cutoff
sparse data near the threshold inflate variance and make the local regression unreliable
predictive accuracy on new units is the objective rather than causal effect estimation

children.name: Front-Door Criterion (Causal Mediation)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike the Back-Door Criterion (which adjusts for observed confounders blocking back-door paths) and Instrumental Variables (which require an exogenous instrument), the Front-Door Criterion identifies causal effects by exploiting a fully observed mediator that intercepts all causal paths from treatment to outcome, allowing identification even when treatment-outcome confounders are entirely unobserved.
strengths: Identifies average causal effects in the presence of unmeasured treatment-outcome confounders, a scenario where back-door adjustment fails entirely
Requires no instrument — the mediator is on the causal pathway itself, so the identifying variation comes from the mechanism rather than an external lever
Produces nonparametric identification: the front-door formula P(Y|do(X)) = ΣₘP(M=m|X)ΣₓP(Y|X=x,M=m)P(X=x) holds without parametric assumptions on functional form
weaknesses: Complete mediation is required — any direct effect of treatment on outcome not passing through the mediator breaks identification, and this assumption is untestable from observational data alone
The mediator must itself be unconfounded with respect to the treatment (no back-door path from X to M), which can be as restrictive as observing all confounders in the first place
Common support restriction demands that for every value of the mediator, both treated and untreated units exist, failing in datasets with sparse or deterministic treatment assignment
recommended_for: Epidemiological studies where a biological intermediate (e.g., tar deposits, biomarker expression) fully mediates exposure effects and genetic/behavioral confounders cannot be measured
Econometric settings where a policy mechanism (e.g., firm adoption of a technology as mediator between regulation and productivity) is observable and plausibly free of confounding with the treatment
not_recommended_for: Settings where the treatment plausibly affects the outcome through multiple pathways, making complete mediation by a single observed variable scientifically implausible
Small samples with sparse mediator-treatment cells, where the common support restriction fails and the weighted estimator becomes unstable or undefined
children.curiosity: Introduced by Judea Pearl in 'Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research' (Biometrika, 1995), the criterion was illustrated with the smoking-tar-lung cancer DAG, where unmeasured genetic confounding between smoking and cancer is circumvented by measuring tar deposits in the lungs as the sole mediator — an example that became the canonical textbook demonstration of identification under unmeasured confounding.
keywords: identify causal effect with hidden confounder

target.notes: Estimand is a causal effect P(Y|do(X)), not a predictive fit; outcome Y can be of any type since identification is nonparametric. Requires a discrete or low-cardinality observed mediator M and a treatment X with overlapping support across M.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ for stable estimation; the front-door formula sums/weights over mediator-treatment cells, so each (X,M) cell must be well-populated
data_regime.dimensionality: low-dimensional by design: a single (or small set of) fully-observed mediator on the causal path; not a high-p method
needs: a causal DAG specifying X, M, Y structure
fully observed mediator intercepting all X->Y paths
common support across all mediator values

features.interpretability: high: yields an identified, interpretable average causal effect with an explicit estimator; coefficients are not the goal, the do-effect is
features.notes: Requires a designated treatment, mediator, and outcome with a credible structural model; covariate scaling is irrelevant since identification is structural not parametric.

assumptions: Complete mediation: no direct X->Y effect bypassing the mediator (untestable from observational data)
No unblocked back-door path from X to M (mediator unconfounded w.r.t. treatment)
All back-door paths from M to Y are blocked by conditioning on X (and observed covariates)
Common support / positivity: every mediator value occurs under both treated and untreated units
Correctly specified causal DAG
loss: not loss-driven: nonparametric identification via the front-door adjustment formula; estimation typically by plug-in/weighting or doubly-robust/influence-function estimators of the do-effect
contraindicated_when: Treatment plausibly affects outcome through multiple or unobserved pathways (complete mediation implausible)
No credible fully-observed mediator on the causal path
Sparse or deterministic treatment-mediator cells violating positivity
Goal is prediction/forecasting rather than causal-effect identification
Mediator itself is confounded with the treatment

target.notes: Target is not the outcome itself but the treatment effect (CATE/ITE): the counterfactual contrast E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X]. Requires an observed outcome Y plus a treatment/intervention indicator T (binary or multi-arm) per unit; outcome can be continuous, binary, or survival. Estimand is unobservable at the unit level.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+; heterogeneity detection and orthogonal nuisance fitting are data-hungry, and effective sample size shrinks in low-overlap subgroups
data_regime.dimensionality: handles high-dimensional covariates p (hundreds+) via ML nuisance models; Double ML/cross-fitting gives valid inference even when p grows with n
needs: covariates rich enough to plausibly satisfy unconfoundedness

features.interpretability: medium; effect estimates and subgroup CATEs are interpretable with confidence intervals (causal forests, DR-learner), but the meta-learner base models can be black-box
features.notes: Must separate the treatment variable from confounders; covariates should be pre-treatment to avoid collider/mediator bias. Scaling follows whatever base learner is used.

assumptions: Unconfoundedness / conditional ignorability: no unmeasured confounders given covariates (untestable; bias is irrecoverable if violated)
Positivity / overlap: every covariate stratum has nonzero probability of each treatment arm
SUTVA: no interference between units and a single well-defined version of treatment
Correct enough nuisance estimation (propensity and outcome models) for orthogonal scores to remove first-order bias
loss: Neyman-orthogonal / doubly-robust scores (Double ML)
R-loss (Robinson residual-on-residual objective)
DR-learner / plug-in doubly-robust pseudo-outcome regression
causal-forest honest splitting on effect heterogeneity
transformed-outcome (Horvitz-Thompson / IPW) loss for uplift
contraindicated_when: Goal is pure outcome prediction with no intervention question (orthogonalization overhead yields no gain over supervised learning)
No measured treatment variable, or treatment is deterministic for large subgroups (zero overlap / positivity violation)
Strong unmeasured confounding with no instrument or design-based identification
Sample too small to fit nuisance models and detect heterogeneity reliably
Standard held-out outcome cross-validation is the only available metric (does not measure causal accuracy)

children.name: 1.6 Transfer Learning (Classic ML)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ensemble methods (which combine multiple learners on the same distribution) or semi-supervised learning (which exploits unlabeled data from the same distribution), Transfer Learning explicitly bridges two different data distributions by reusing knowledge from a source domain—via instance reweighting (TrAdaBoost), feature alignment (TCA/MMD), or parameter sharing—to improve learning on a target domain with scarce labeled data.
strengths: Drastically reduces labeled data requirements in the target domain by reusing statistical structure already learned from abundant source data
Algorithms like TCA use Maximum Mean Discrepancy in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space to provably align source and target distributions without requiring target labels

Instance-reweighting variants (e.g., Kernel Mean Matching) selectively upweight source samples whose covariate distribution matches the target, making the transfer theoretically grounded under covariate shift
weaknesses: Negative transfer: when source and target tasks are sufficiently dissimilar, transferred knowledge degrades target performance below baseline with no transfer
Requires explicit distribution similarity assessment—no automatic mechanism detects when source-target divergence is too large to transfer safely
Classic (non-deep) methods struggle with high-dimensional, heterogeneous tabular data where feature spaces differ between domains, limiting applicability outside structured, homogeneous datasets
recommended_for: Sentiment analysis on a new product category (target) when labeled reviews exist only for a different category (source) sharing the same vocabulary and label semantics
Industrial fault detection where a new machine (target) has few labeled fault cycles but a related machine (source) has thousands—instance reweighting exploits shared failure physics
not_recommended_for: Problems where source and target feature spaces are disjoint or semantically unrelated (e.g., medical records transferred to financial fraud), as negative transfer is near-certain
Tasks with ample labeled target data (hundreds or more per class), where a model trained directly on target data outperforms any transfer approach at lower complexity
children.curiosity: The term 'transfer learning' as a formal ML category was systematized by Sinno Jialin Pan and Qiang Yang in their landmark 2010 IEEE TKDE survey, which introduced the now-standard taxonomy of inductive, transductive, and unsupervised transfer—a framework still used to classify methods today.

children.name: Domain Adaptation
children.diff_siblings: Addresses distribution shift between a labeled source domain and an unlabeled (or scarce-label) target domain via reweighting or feature alignment — whereas Multi-Task Learning trains jointly on several tasks with no domain gap, Domain Adaptation assumes a single target task whose input distribution P(X) differs from the training distribution.
strengths: Operates without target labels: unsupervised variants (KMM, TCA, CORAL) align distributions using unlabeled target samples only, making it viable when annotation is costly
Grounded theoretical guarantees: Ben-David et al. (2010) bound target error by source error plus H-divergence, giving an explicit measurable criterion for when adaptation is safe
Lightweight classical methods (CORAL aligns second-order statistics in closed form; KMM solves a QP) add near-zero computational overhead over the base classifier
weaknesses: Assumes shared label space and identical task: if P(Y|X) also shifts (concept drift), importance-weighting and marginal alignment methods fail without access to target labels
H-divergence and importance-ratio estimation degrade sharply when source and target overlap is small, making the theoretical bound vacuous and adaptation potentially harmful (negative transfer)
Classical methods (TCA, CORAL) capture only up to second-order statistics; they miss higher-order distributional differences that deep adversarial approaches handle but at greater cost
recommended_for: Sensor-based fault detection across machines: a classifier trained on one machine's vibration data is adapted to a new machine with different operating conditions using CORAL or MMD, with no re-labeling of the new machine

NLP domain shift with fixed feature pipelines: a sentiment model trained on product reviews is reweighted via KMM to match the marginal distribution of social-media text, preserving the same label space
not_recommended_for: Tasks where the label space changes between source and target (e.g., new defect classes in the target factory) — the core covariate-shift assumption is violated and adaptation will degrade performance

Scenarios with no overlap between domains (e.g., medical imaging to satellite imagery) — importance weights become numerically unstable and H-divergence is so large that the error bound offers no guarantee
children.curiosity: The foundational theoretical framework for Domain Adaptation was established by Ben-David, Blitzer, Crammer, Pereira, and Shai Shalev-Shwartz in 'A theory of learning from different distributions' (Machine Learning, 2010), proving that the target error is bounded by the source error plus half the H-divergence between domains — a quantity estimable from unlabeled data alone.
keywords: train on one dataset test on another

target.notes: Not a model itself but a meta-strategy wrapping a downstream classifier/regressor; the base task can be any supervised type. The defining property is in P(X), not P(Y).

data_regime.rows: classical variants (CORAL, KMM, TCA) work from hundreds to thousands per domain; deep adversarial DA needs large unlabeled target sets
data_regime.dimensionality: TCA/CORAL operate on moderate p; high p inflates covariance/kernel estimation variance and destabilizes importance ratios
needs: an unlabeled or scarce-label target domain
non-trivial support overlap between source and target P(X)

features.interpretability: low to medium: alignment (CORAL covariance whitening, TCA subspace projection) obscures original feature semantics; importance weights (KMM) are inspectable per-sample
features.notes: classical methods assume features in a fixed shared representation; CORAL aligns second-order statistics, KMM reweights via kernel mean matching, TCA learns a domain-invariant subspace

assumptions: covariate shift: P(X) differs but P(Y|X) is invariant across domains
shared, identical label space and task between source and target
sufficient density overlap of source and target supports for importance ratios to be finite and estimable
classical variants assume distributional difference is captured up to first/second moments
loss: base learner's loss (log-loss, squared error, etc.) reweighted by source-to-target importance ratios
distribution-discrepancy objectives: MMD (KMM/TCA), second-order CORAL alignment loss, H-divergence / adversarial domain-confusion loss
contraindicated_when: P(Y|X) shifts (concept drift) rather than only P(X) — marginal alignment and reweighting cannot recover it without target labels
label space differs between domains (new classes in target)
source and target supports barely overlap — importance weights blow up and the H-divergence bound becomes vacuous (negative transfer risk)
higher-than-second-order distributional differences dominate and only classical (CORAL/TCA) methods are available

children.name: Multi-Task Learning (Classic ML)
