children.diff_siblings: Unlike domain adaptation (which transfers a single task across data distributions) or pre-training/fine-tuning (which sequentially adapts one model), Multi-Task Learning jointly optimizes multiple related tasks sharing a common representation or parameters, using auxiliary task signals as structured inductive bias during training.
strengths: Auxiliary tasks act as implicit regularizers: joint optimization reduces overfitting on the primary task because the shared parameters must generalize across all task losses simultaneously.
Exploits label correlations across tasks — when labeled data for the primary task is scarce, related tasks supply gradient signal that improves convergence and final accuracy.

Compatible with classic ML models (linear classifiers, SVMs) via regularization terms (e.g., shared covariance penalty, trace-norm) that couple task-specific weight vectors without requiring a neural architecture.
weaknesses: Negative transfer: if tasks have conflicting optimal representations, shared parameters settle at a suboptimal compromise that underperforms independent single-task models on individual tasks.
Task-relatedness must be established a priori or via costly cross-validation; no standard metric determines whether tasks are compatible, and wrong groupings reliably hurt performance.
Gradient imbalance when task datasets differ greatly in size — the larger task dominates updates and starves the smaller task of effective learning signal.
recommended_for: Clinical risk scoring where a primary outcome (e.g., 30-day readmission) shares biological predictors with auxiliary outcomes (length of stay, ICU transfer), and labeled data for the primary label is limited.

NLP classification pipelines where multiple linguistically related labels (sentiment, subjectivity, irony) are annotated on the same corpus, enabling shared feature representations across label types.
not_recommended_for: Tasks drawn from unrelated domains (e.g., predicting equipment failure and customer churn simultaneously) where feature correlations are absent and joint training introduces destructive gradient interference.

High-stakes single-task settings with abundant labeled data, where the regularization benefit of auxiliary tasks is negligible and the added hyperparameter complexity (task weights, shared vs. private layer split) increases tuning cost without accuracy gain.
children.curiosity: Formally introduced by Rich Caruana (1997) in 'Multitask Learning' (Machine Learning, 28:41–75), who demonstrated on a road-following task that training a network simultaneously on auxiliary outputs — road edges and lane count — reduced error on the primary steering prediction by providing corrective inductive bias from related signals.

target.notes: Multi-output by design: requires 2+ related target variables/tasks jointly predicted. Targets may be heterogeneous (mix of regression and classification heads), each with its own per-task loss. Single-target problems gain nothing from this framework.

data_regime.rows: Most valuable when the PRIMARY task has scarce labels (hundreds to low thousands); auxiliary tasks supply extra gradient signal. Of little benefit when every task already has abundant labels.
data_regime.dimensionality: Handles p>n better than single-task because shared-representation/trace-norm coupling pools statistical strength across tasks, effectively regularizing high-dimensional weight estimation.
needs: multiple related labeled tasks on overlapping or shared feature space
balanced or reweighted per-task sample sizes to avoid the large task dominating updates

features.interpretability: medium — classic-ML realizations (regularized linear models, multi-task SVM) keep per-task weight vectors inspectable, but the cross-task coupling penalty obscures which signal is shared vs. task-specific.
features.notes: Tasks should share the same (or strongly overlapping) input feature space so a common representation is meaningful.

assumptions: Tasks are genuinely related — their optimal representations or weight vectors lie in a shared/low-rank subspace.
A common feature representation can serve all tasks without a destructive compromise.
Per-task losses are commensurable after weighting so no single task monopolizes the shared parameters.
loss: weighted sum of per-task losses (e.g., squared error for regression heads + log-loss for classification heads)
coupling regularizers: trace/nuclear-norm on stacked weight matrix, shared-mean or shared-covariance penalty across task weight vectors, group-sparse penalties
contraindicated_when: tasks are unrelated (no shared feature correlations) — joint training causes negative transfer and gradient interference, underperforming independent single-task models
single primary task with abundant labeled data, where auxiliary regularization adds tuning cost (task weights, shared/private split) for negligible gain
task dataset sizes differ by orders of magnitude with no reweighting, starving the smaller task
task relatedness cannot be assessed and wrong groupings cannot be validated cheaply

target.notes: Family is task-agnostic; the defining trait is two distinct domains (source and target), not the target type. Applies wherever a target domain has scarce labels but a related source domain has abundant ones. Label space is typically assumed shared or aligned between domains.

data_regime.rows: Target domain has few labeled rows (tens to low hundreds per class); source domain has thousands+. Justified only when direct training on target data is data-starved.
data_regime.dimensionality: Classic (non-deep) variants assume shared/comparable feature spaces (p_source ~ p_target). Methods like TCA project into a low-dim shared subspace; degrade when feature spaces are disjoint or very high-dimensional/heterogeneous.

features.interpretability: medium; transfer mechanism (instance weights, projected subspace) is inspectable but the aligned feature space is less interpretable than the raw model.
features.notes: Best on structured/homogeneous data where source and target share vocabulary or measurement semantics. MMD/kernel-based alignment (TCA, KMM) needs scaled, comparable numeric features.

assumptions: Source and target share related structure (overlapping feature support, shared label semantics)
Covariate shift: P(X) differs across domains but P(Y|X) is approximately stable (instance-reweighting validity)
Distribution divergence between domains is small enough that transfer helps rather than harms
loss: MMD-based distribution alignment loss (TCA)
importance-weighted empirical risk (KMM, instance reweighting)
reweighted boosting loss (TrAdaBoost)
downstream task loss (log-loss / squared error) on the aligned/reweighted data
contraindicated_when: Source and target feature spaces are disjoint or semantically unrelated (negative transfer near-certain)
Ample labeled target data exists (hundreds+ per class) — direct training beats transfer at lower complexity
Concept shift where P(Y|X) differs across domains, violating covariate-shift reweighting
High-dimensional heterogeneous tabular data with mismatched feature spaces (use deep transfer instead)

target.notes: Umbrella for classical (non-deep) ML: covers supervised regression/classification, plus unsupervised (clustering, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection) where target is none. No single target distribution; family supports both parametric (GLM-style) and distribution-free (tree/kernel/instance-based) members.

data_regime.rows: hundreds to low millions; sweet spot thousands to hundreds of thousands. Kernel methods degrade O(n^2)-O(n^3); tree ensembles and linear models scale to millions
data_regime.dimensionality: best when p<n with informative engineered features; regularized linear and tree methods tolerate moderate p>n, but raw very-high-dimensional perceptual data is out of scope
needs: moderate labeled data for supervised members

features.interpretability: medium to high: coefficients, feature importances, and decision rules are inspectable for most members (tree ensembles and kernel methods less so, but still auditable via SHAP/importances)
features.notes: Performance bounded by feature quality. Linear/kernel/distance methods need scaling and explicit encoding of categoricals; tree-based methods are scale-invariant and handle mixed types natively. Raw pixels/audio/free text require feature extraction first.

assumptions: fixed input schema (adding/removing features forces full retraining; no native incremental update)
i.i.d. samples with stationary distribution (concept drift / online streams hurt batch-trained members)
relevant signal is recoverable from the supplied/engineered features rather than from raw high-dimensional structure
loss: squared error
log-loss / cross-entropy
hinge loss
exponential loss (boosting)
Gini / entropy splitting criteria
absolute error
within-cluster sum of squares (unsupervised)
contraindicated_when: raw perceptual inputs (images >64x64, long audio, free-form text) where end-to-end representation learning is needed
online setting with continuous concept drift requiring incremental updates from a stream
feature engineering is infeasible and the relevant structure is hierarchical/spatial/sequential in raw data

children.name: 2. AI / Deep Learning
children.diff_siblings: Unlike classical statistics (which fits parametric models to human-specified distributions) and traditional ML (which learns shallow mappings over hand-engineered features), this branch groups architectures that learn hierarchical representations directly from raw data through stacked nonlinear transformations — making feature engineering largely unnecessary.
strengths: Learns task-specific feature hierarchies automatically from raw inputs (pixels, tokens, waveforms), removing the need for domain-driven feature engineering.
Scales performance predictably with more data and compute: validation loss keeps dropping as dataset size and parameter count grow, unlike shallow models that plateau.
Achieves state-of-the-art on perception tasks (image classification, speech recognition, machine translation) where the input structure is high-dimensional and locally compositional.
weaknesses: Requires large labeled datasets (typically tens of thousands to millions of examples) to outperform simpler baselines; data-hungry by design.
Training is computationally expensive and energy-intensive — large architectures demand GPU/TPU clusters and significant wall-clock time.
Models are largely non-interpretable: the learned representations are distributed across millions of parameters with no direct semantic mapping to input features.
recommended_for: Unstructured, high-dimensional raw inputs (images, audio, natural language) where meaningful features cannot be defined by hand and sufficient labeled data (>10k samples) is available.
Sequence-to-sequence or generative tasks (translation, image synthesis, speech synthesis) where the output space is complex and structured.
not_recommended_for: Small tabular datasets (<1k rows) with well-understood numeric features, where gradient-boosted trees or logistic regression outperform and train in seconds.
Applications requiring auditable, legally defensible predictions (medical diagnosis coding, credit decisions under ECOA) where model transparency is a regulatory requirement.
children.curiosity: The term 'deep learning' was coined by Geoffrey Hinton, Simon Osindero, and Yee-Whye Teh in their 2006 Science paper demonstrating layer-wise pretraining of deep belief networks — the breakthrough that restarted neural network research after more than a decade of relative dormancy.

children.name: 2.1 Classic Networks
children.diff_siblings: Unlike sibling families that introduce structural inductive biases (local receptive fields in CNNs, recurrence in RNNs, self-attention in Transformers), Classic Networks are fully-connected or energy-based architectures with no built-in spatial or temporal assumption, making them the foundational, general-purpose tier of deep learning.
strengths: Universal approximation with a single hidden layer (Cybenko, 1989): an MLP with enough hidden units can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain, giving theoretical coverage without architectural constraints.

Energy-based models (Hopfield, Boltzmann Machine, RBM) can store and retrieve patterns via gradient descent on a scalar energy function, enabling associative memory and generative modeling without label supervision.
Autoencoders learn compact, nonlinear representations in a single unsupervised pass, producing embeddings directly usable for downstream tasks without defining explicit class boundaries.
weaknesses: No built-in translation invariance or weight sharing: a fully-connected layer treating a 224x224 image requires ~150k parameters per neuron, making raw pixel inputs computationally and statistically intractable compared to CNNs.
Boltzmann Machines and RBMs require Markov Chain Monte Carlo (Gibbs sampling) for exact gradient computation, which is slow to mix and scales poorly beyond a few hundred hidden units.
Vanishing gradient in deep MLPs: without residual connections or normalization, gradients shrink exponentially with depth, limiting practical depth to roughly 3-5 layers before training stalls.
recommended_for: Tabular datasets with heterogeneous features (mix of continuous and categorical columns, no spatial or sequential structure), where an MLP outperforms architecturally biased models that assume local correlations.

Unsupervised pre-training on unlabeled data using Stacked RBMs or Autoencoders to initialize weights before fine-tuning on a small labeled set, as demonstrated by Hinton and Salakhutdinov (2006) on MNIST and Reuters.
not_recommended_for: Image, video, or volumetric data where spatial locality and translation invariance matter: CNNs achieve orders-of-magnitude better parameter efficiency by sharing convolutional filters across positions.

Long sequences (text, audio, time series) where dependencies span hundreds of steps: without recurrence or attention, MLPs require fixed-length inputs and cannot capture variable-range temporal structure.
children.curiosity: Rosenblatt demonstrated the Mark I Perceptron in 1958 at Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory using a 400-photocell retina and hardware potentiometers for weights; it was arguably the first machine to learn from experience without explicit programming, predating software-based neural networks by nearly a decade.

children.name: MLP (Multilayer Perceptron)
children.diff_siblings: Uses globally-connected layers with all weights trained end-to-end via gradient descent — unlike RBF Networks whose hidden activations are local Gaussians anchored to fixed prototypes, and unlike ELM whose hidden weights are random and frozen from initialization.
strengths: Universal approximation: a single hidden layer with sigmoid activations can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain (Cybenko, 1989), given sufficient neurons.
End-to-end gradient learning allows every weight to be jointly optimized, letting the network discover task-specific feature combinations that fixed-prototype or random-weight networks cannot.
Architecture is data-agnostic — the same training procedure applies to regression, multi-class classification, and multi-output problems by changing only the output activation and loss function.
weaknesses: Treats every input dimension symmetrically with full connectivity, so it cannot exploit spatial locality or translation invariance — a 256x256 image requires 65,536 input weights per first-layer neuron before any feature is extracted.

Depth amplifies the vanishing-gradient problem: with sigmoid activations, gradients shrink by a factor of at most 0.25 per layer, stalling learning in early layers beyond 4–5 hidden layers without ReLU or residual connections.

No inductive bias toward sequence order or neighborhood structure means it requires far more training examples than CNNs or RNNs to reach equivalent accuracy on structured inputs like images or time series.
recommended_for: Tabular datasets with tens to hundreds of features and nonlinear class boundaries, where tree ensembles plateau and the added expressivity of learned hidden representations recovers accuracy.

Low-dimensional sensor fusion or scientific regression tasks (e.g., predicting material properties from spectral measurements) where input variables have no spatial arrangement and full cross-feature interactions are physically meaningful.
not_recommended_for: Image classification or object detection, where CNNs achieve the same function with ~100x fewer parameters by sharing convolutional filters across spatial positions.

Variable-length sequence modeling such as language or time-series forecasting, where RNNs and Transformers encode temporal order structurally rather than forcing the network to re-learn positional relationships from scratch.
children.curiosity: Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams published 'Learning representations by back-propagating errors' in Nature in 1986 — the paper that made MLP training practical — but the backpropagation algorithm had already been derived independently by Werbos in his 1974 Harvard PhD thesis, over a decade earlier.

target.notes: Target-agnostic: choose output activation + loss to match (linear for continuous, softmax for multiclass, sigmoid for binary). Supports multi-output regression/classification. No native handling of censoring or count overdispersion without a custom loss.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ to outperform tree ensembles; underfits or overfits on <1k without heavy regularization
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n strongly preferred; degrades when p>n without dropout/weight decay; struggles in very high-p sparse settings
needs: large labeled data for structured inputs
GPU helpful for wide/deep nets but optional for tabular

features.interpretability: low: distributed weights across layers, no per-feature coefficients; needs post-hoc tools (SHAP, permutation importance)
features.notes: Requires input standardization/normalization (zero-mean unit-variance) for stable gradient descent; categoricals must be one-hot or embedded; no built-in handling of missing values or monotonic constraints.

assumptions: i.i.d. samples (no structural prior for spatial/temporal/graph dependence)
sufficient training data relative to parameter count
inputs scaled to comparable ranges for well-conditioned optimization
smooth enough target surface for gradient-based optimization to converge
loss: squared error (regression)
log-loss / cross-entropy (binary and multiclass)
any differentiable custom loss (e.g. Huber, quantile/pinball, focal) via the output layer
contraindicated_when: inputs have spatial structure (images) -> use CNN for parameter sharing
variable-length or ordered sequences (text, time-series) -> use RNN/Transformer
small tabular datasets where gradient-boosted trees match or exceed accuracy with less tuning
very high-cardinality sparse categorical features without embeddings
strict interpretability or regulatory transparency is required
p>>n with limited samples, where regularized linear models generalize better

children.name: RBF Network (Radial Basis Function)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike MLPs that use inner-product activations (sigmoid, ReLU) applied globally, RBF Networks use locally-supported Gaussian kernels centered in input space, so each hidden neuron fires only for inputs near its center, and the output layer is a purely linear combination of those local responses.
strengths: Two-stage training (unsupervised center placement via k-means + closed-form linear output weights via least squares) converges orders of magnitude faster than backpropagation-trained MLPs of equivalent depth.

Exact function interpolation is guaranteed when the number of centers equals the number of training points, because the Gaussian kernel matrix is positive definite (Micchelli 1986), making RBF ideal for surrogate modeling of expensive simulations.
Universal approximation with a single hidden layer and interpretable geometry: each center is a prototype in input space, so the learned representation can be directly inspected and pruned.
weaknesses: Number of centers required to cover an m-dimensional input space grows exponentially with m, making the architecture impractical beyond roughly 10 to 15 input features without aggressive dimensionality reduction first.

Performance is highly sensitive to center placement and kernel width (sigma): randomly chosen centers that do not cover the data manifold yield poor generalization, and there is no gradient signal to correct them.

Gaussian activations saturate to near-zero far from centers, causing numeric underflow and effectively dead hidden units when input dimensionality is high, a failure mode that ReLU-based MLPs do not share.
recommended_for: Scattered data interpolation in low-dimensional spaces (2 to 8 features), such as terrain elevation modeling from irregular GPS samples or aerodynamic coefficient tables from CFD simulation runs.

Online or real-time control tasks where fast, incremental training is required: the linear output layer can be updated in closed form as new observations arrive, without retraining the entire network.
not_recommended_for: Tabular classification problems with more than 15 features, where the exponential growth in required centers and the flattening of Gaussian distances make the model both computationally intractable and statistically unreliable.

Image or text tasks where spatial or sequential structure requires convolutional or attention-based inductive biases; an RBF hidden layer cannot exploit locality or positional relationships across pixels or tokens.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Broomhead and Lowe (1988) in 'Radial Basis Functions, Multi-Variable Functional Interpolation and Adaptive Networks' (RSRE Memorandum 4148), the architecture was originally motivated by numerical analysis rather than neuroscience — specifically by Powell's scattered-data interpolation theory from the 1970s — making it one of the few neural network families with a rigorous approximation-theoretic foundation predating its neural interpretation.

target.notes: Primarily a regression/interpolation tool; output layer is linear least squares so it natively fits continuous targets. Classification via one-hot least-squares or thresholding works but is not its strength.

data_regime.rows: works on small-to-moderate samples; exact interpolation when n_centers = n; with k-means centers needs enough points to populate clusters
data_regime.dimensionality: strongly p<n; degrades sharply above ~10-15 input features (curse of dimensionality on center coverage)

features.interpretability: medium-high: each hidden unit is a prototype/center in input space, directly inspectable and prunable
features.notes: Inputs must be standardized; Gaussian distances assume comparable feature scales. Kernel width (sigma) and center placement dominate performance and require tuning.

assumptions: target is a smooth function of inputs (local Gaussian responses interpolate smoothly)
data lies on a low-dimensional manifold well covered by chosen centers
features are scaled to comparable ranges so Euclidean distance is meaningful
loss: squared error (closed-form least squares on output weights)
contraindicated_when: input dimensionality exceeds ~15 features (centers needed grow exponentially; Gaussian distances flatten and saturate)
data has spatial/sequential structure (images, text, time series with long dependencies) requiring convolutional or attention inductive biases
high-cardinality categorical or sparse features without dense low-dimensional numeric embedding
centers cannot be placed to cover the data manifold (no gradient signal corrects poor placement)

children.name: ELM (Extreme Learning Machine)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike MLP (which tunes all weights via backpropagation) and RBF networks (which learn centers iteratively), ELM randomly fixes input-to-hidden weights and biases at initialization, then solves for output weights analytically via least squares — eliminating gradient descent entirely.
strengths: Training reduces to a single matrix pseudoinverse, completing in milliseconds even for thousands of samples where backprop-based SLFNs take minutes.
Avoids local minima and vanishing gradients by construction: no iterative weight update means no gradient computation at all.
OS-ELM variant updates output weights sequentially chunk-by-chunk via recursive least squares, enabling true online learning without retraining from scratch.
weaknesses: Requires far more hidden neurons than a fully trained SLFN to achieve equivalent accuracy, since random projections waste representational capacity on directions irrelevant to the task.
Random initialization of input weights introduces non-deterministic variance in performance across runs — the same architecture can yield substantially different generalization errors.
Scales poorly with input dimensionality: the hidden-layer matrix grows as O(N × H) and must fit in RAM for the pseudoinverse, becoming memory-prohibitive before gradient-based methods do.
recommended_for: Embedded or edge inference systems where training must complete in real time (e.g., adaptive industrial sensor calibration updating every few seconds on a microcontroller).
Rapid prototyping benchmarks on tabular datasets up to ~50k samples where a non-iterative baseline is needed before committing to hyperparameter search for deeper models.
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional structured inputs such as raw images or audio: random projections do not exploit spatial or temporal locality, so ELM needs exponentially more neurons to match CNN or RNN accuracy.
Production systems where reproducibility is contractually required: the random hidden layer produces different models on every run unless the seed is explicitly fixed and validated.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Huang, Zhu, and Siew (2004) at IJCNN and formalized in Neurocomputing (2006), ELM was originally conceived as a theoretical proof that SLFNs do not need to tune all parameters — the hidden-layer randomness alone provides sufficient basis functions for universal approximation, given enough neurons.

target.notes: Single-hidden-layer feedforward net for regression and classification; multiclass via one-hot output with argmax decoding. No native probabilistic output or uncertainty.

data_regime.rows: works from hundreds up to ~50k samples; pseudoinverse of the N x H hidden matrix must fit in RAM, so very large N becomes memory-bound
data_regime.dimensionality: p < n strongly preferred; high input dimensionality inflates required hidden width and degrades random-projection efficiency
needs: enough hidden neurons (often far more than a trained SLFN) to compensate for random, untuned projections

features.interpretability: low: random fixed input weights and a least-squares output layer give no meaningful feature attribution
features.notes: Inputs should be standardized/scaled since random projection magnitude is sensitive to feature ranges; categorical features must be encoded numerically. No spatial/temporal locality exploited.

assumptions: fixed feature representation adequately captured by random projections plus a nonlinear activation
target is a (nonlinear) function of tabular inputs without structured locality (no image/audio/sequence structure)
sufficient hidden width relative to sample size and noise for the least-squares fit to generalize
loss: squared error / ridge-regularized least squares on output weights (closed-form pseudoinverse; regularized ELM adds an L2 penalty)
contraindicated_when: raw images, audio, or sequences where spatial/temporal locality matters (CNN/RNN dominate)
p comparable to or exceeding n, or very high N where the hidden matrix pseudoinverse is memory-prohibitive
calibrated class probabilities or uncertainty quantification are required
reproducibility is mandated and the random hidden layer seed is not fixed and validated
a compact, parameter-efficient model is needed (ELM wastes capacity on random directions)

target.notes: Umbrella family. Supervised MLPs handle binary/multiclass classification (softmax) and continuous regression (linear output). Energy-based members (Hopfield, Boltzmann, RBM) and autoencoders are unsupervised: target is none, used for associative memory, density/generative modeling, and representation learning.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ for supervised MLPs to beat regularized linear/tree baselines; energy-based models scale poorly past a few hundred hidden units due to MCMC/Gibbs mixing
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; no weight sharing means dense layers blow up parameter count, so raw high-dimensional pixel/sequence inputs are intractable
needs: large labeled data for supervised tier
GPU helps but not mandatory at small width

features.interpretability: low: distributed weights across hidden units, no per-feature coefficient; saliency/probing needed
features.notes: Best on flat, fixed-length tabular feature vectors with heterogeneous continuous+categorical columns (categoricals encoded/embedded). Requires input standardization; sensitive to feature scale. No native handling of spatial, graph, or variable-length sequential structure.

assumptions: i.i.d. fixed-length feature vectors with no exploitable spatial/temporal locality
sufficient labeled data relative to dense parameter count
features standardized to comparable scale for stable gradient training
shallow depth (~3-5 layers) absent residual/normalization tricks to avoid vanishing gradients
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss (classification)
squared error (regression)
reconstruction error (autoencoders)
contrastive divergence / energy-based negative log-likelihood (RBM, Boltzmann)
contraindicated_when: data has spatial locality / translation invariance (images, volumes) where CNNs are far more parameter-efficient
long or variable-length sequences with long-range dependencies (text, audio, time series) needing recurrence or attention
small n with high p where a regularized linear model or gradient-boosted trees generalizes better
strong interpretability or per-feature effect estimates are required

children.name: 2.2 Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike RNNs (which process sequences recurrently) and Transformers (which use global self-attention), CNNs apply learned filters via discrete convolution across fixed local receptive fields, enforcing translational equivariance through weight sharing without any recurrence or attention mechanism.
strengths: Parameter efficiency via weight sharing: the same convolutional filter is applied across the entire input, so a 3×3 filter detects the same edge regardless of position without duplicating weights.
Hierarchical spatial feature extraction: stacked conv layers compose low-level features (edges, textures) into high-level semantic patterns, matching the inductive bias of natural images.
Highly parallelizable at inference: convolutions are matrix multiplications with no sequential dependency, enabling efficient execution on GPUs and dedicated hardware (TPUs, NPUs).
weaknesses: Lacks true translation invariance: standard max-pooling provides only coarse invariance; small sub-pixel shifts can change activations, as shown empirically by Zhang (2019) with aliasing analysis.

Blind to global context without deep stacking: receptive field grows linearly with depth, so capturing long-range dependencies (e.g., object relationships across an image) requires many layers or dilated convolutions.

High data hunger for rotation and scale generalization: the architecture has no built-in equivariance to rotation or scale, so generalizing to those requires large augmented datasets or auxiliary mechanisms.
recommended_for: Image classification and object detection tasks where the input is a fixed 2D spatial grid (e.g., photos, medical scans, satellite imagery) and the signal of interest is locally structured.
1D time-series with short-range local patterns (e.g., ECG anomaly detection, audio waveform classification) where the relevant features are local and translation-equivariant by nature.
not_recommended_for: Tabular datasets with unordered, heterogeneous features (e.g., customer demographics mixed with financial ratios), where there is no spatial locality to exploit and gradient-boosted trees typically outperform.

Long-document or long-sequence modeling where dependencies span hundreds of tokens, since the receptive field grows only O(depth) and transformers with O(1) global attention are architecturally superior.
children.curiosity: Yann LeCun et al. (1989) trained the first convolutional network with backpropagation on handwritten zip codes for the US Postal Service, showing that weight sharing across spatial positions could be learned end-to-end — a result that preceded the term 'deep learning' by nearly two decades.

children.name: LeNet
children.diff_siblings: LeNet uses shallow stacks of 5x5 convolutions with average pooling and tanh activations — the foundational pattern all sibling architectures later deepened, widened, or replaced with max pooling and ReLU.
strengths: Extremely low parameter count (~60K in LeNet-5) makes it trainable from scratch on CPU with small datasets like MNIST in minutes.
End-to-end gradient-based training (backprop through conv + pooling + FC layers) pioneered by LeCun et al. (1998) — the exact pipeline still used in every modern CNN.
Deterministic, well-understood architecture with no skip connections or complex branching — ideal as a baseline or for embedded/low-resource inference.
weaknesses: Average pooling discards spatial peak activations, reducing discriminative power on complex textures compared to max pooling used in AlexNet onward.
Tanh saturates at large activations, causing vanishing gradients in deeper variants and slower convergence than ReLU-based successors.
Designed for 32x32 grayscale inputs; performance degrades sharply on high-resolution or multi-channel images without architectural changes.
recommended_for: Grayscale digit or character recognition on small normalized images (e.g., MNIST 28x28, USPS digits), where simplicity and speed matter more than top accuracy.
Educational or resource-constrained deployments where a fully interpretable CNN baseline is needed and inference must run on hardware without GPU support.
not_recommended_for: Natural image classification benchmarks (ImageNet, CIFAR-10) where depth, ReLU activations, and max pooling are required to reach competitive accuracy.
Transfer learning pipelines — LeNet's capacity is too small to encode general visual features reusable across tasks, unlike VGG or ResNet.
children.curiosity: Introduced by LeCun, Bottou, Bengio, and Haffner in 'Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition' (1998), LeNet-5 was deployed commercially by AT&T and NCR to read millions of handwritten checks per day in the United States — making it one of the first deep learning models used at industrial scale.

target.notes: Image classification head; softmax over a small label set. Originally 10-class digit recognition.

data_regime.rows: trains from scratch on small labeled sets (tens of thousands of images, e.g. MNIST 60k); ~60K params so no large-data requirement
data_regime.dimensionality: fixed small input grid (designed for 32x32, single channel); not for high-resolution or many-channel inputs

features.interpretability: low; learned conv filters are not directly interpretable, though the architecture is small and fully transparent structurally
features.notes: Expects small grayscale rasters, intensity-normalized and center-cropped/resized to the fixed input dimensions; no built-in scale/rotation invariance beyond local pooling.

assumptions: Discriminative signal is local and translation-tolerant (captured by small 5x5 convolutions + pooling)
Inputs share a fixed resolution and channel count
Object of interest is roughly centered and at consistent scale
loss: categorical cross-entropy / log-loss over softmax (modern training)
originally MSE / RBF Euclidean output loss in LeCun et al. 1998
contraindicated_when: natural high-resolution or multi-channel image benchmarks (ImageNet, CIFAR) where depth, ReLU and max pooling are needed
transfer-learning / feature-reuse pipelines (capacity too small for general visual features)
non-image / tabular / sequence data
fine texture discrimination where average pooling loses peak activations

children.name: AlexNet
children.diff_siblings: Unlike LeNet's sigmoid activations and ZFNet's smaller 7x7 first-layer kernels, AlexNet introduced the CNN-scale use of ReLU activations alongside local response normalization and dual-GPU split training, with an 11x11 first-layer kernel capturing coarse spatial features across 227x227 RGB input.
strengths: ReLU activations train 6x faster than tanh equivalents at equal accuracy, as demonstrated empirically by Krizhevsky et al. on CIFAR-10.
Dropout (p=0.5) applied to the two 4096-unit fully connected layers halves co-adaptation between neurons, acting as an implicit ensemble of 2^4096 network architectures.
Data augmentation via random 224x224 crops and horizontal reflections from 256x256 images multiplies training set size by a factor of 2048, directly reducing test error.
weaknesses: 60 million parameters concentrated in the three fully connected layers demand roughly 240 MB of weight storage in float32, making inference heavy for edge or mobile deployment.
The 11x11 stride-4 first convolution loses fine-grained spatial detail early; ZFNet (2013) showed that shrinking this to 7x7 stride-2 visibly improves feature maps.

Local response normalization (LRN), a key regularizer in the original design, was later shown by VGGNet authors (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014) to add complexity without measurable accuracy benefit on deeper nets.
recommended_for: Large-scale image classification benchmarks where training sets contain hundreds of thousands of labeled RGB images at roughly 224x224 resolution and 1000 or more target classes.

Transfer learning baselines for natural image domains (medical imaging, satellite imagery) where convolutional feature maps from the first five layers are fine-tuned on a new classification head with limited target-domain data.
not_recommended_for: Small datasets (fewer than ~10,000 samples) where 60 million parameters cause severe overfitting even with dropout and augmentation, making compact architectures like MobileNet or EfficientNet-B0 preferable.

Tasks requiring localization or dense pixel-level prediction (segmentation, detection), where AlexNet's stride-4 first layer and absence of skip connections discard spatial resolution needed for precise output maps.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Krizhevsky, Sutskever, and Hinton at NeurIPS 2012, AlexNet reduced the ImageNet ILSVRC top-5 error from 26.2% (second place) to 15.3% — a margin so large that the runners-up were all traditional hand-crafted feature pipelines, effectively ending their dominance in large-scale vision benchmarks.

target.notes: Image classification head producing categorical labels; softmax over 1000+ classes in the original ImageNet setting.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds of thousands of labeled images to train from scratch; small target sets only viable via transfer learning / fine-tuning of pretrained features
data_regime.dimensionality: fixed-size raster input (227x227 RGB); 60M parameters dominated by the three FC layers

features.interpretability: low; deep convolutional feature stack with no explicit feature semantics
features.notes: Expects 224/227 spatial RGB input with per-channel mean subtraction; learned conv filters serve as transferable feature extractors for natural-image domains.

assumptions: spatial locality and translation structure in pixel grid (convolutional inductive bias)
sufficient labeled data plus augmentation to constrain the large FC parameter count
input is a single fixed-resolution RGB raster, not sequential or tabular
loss: categorical cross-entropy / log-loss (softmax)
contraindicated_when: dataset is small (fewer than ~10k samples) where 60M params overfit even with dropout/augmentation; prefer compact nets (MobileNet, EfficientNet-B0) or pretrained transfer
task requires dense pixel-level output (segmentation, detection) where stride-4 first conv and lack of skip connections destroy spatial resolution
input is tabular, text, or time-series rather than images
edge/mobile inference with tight memory budget (~240MB float32 weights)
modern accuracy/efficiency is the priority; superseded by ResNet/EfficientNet/ViT on natural-image benchmarks

children.name: VGG
children.diff_siblings: VGG achieves depth (16–19 weight layers) exclusively through stacking uniform 3×3 convolutions with stride 1 and 2×2 max-pooling, rejecting the varied filter sizes of AlexNet or the parallel inception modules of GoogLeNet, making depth itself the sole architectural variable under study.
strengths: Uniform 3×3 filter stacks approximate one large receptive field with more non-linearities and fewer parameters per layer than a single 7×7 conv — two 3×3 layers replace one 5×5 with 28% fewer weights.

Pretrained VGG features transfer exceptionally well to small datasets: the fully convolutional interpretation of its dense layers allows arbitrary input sizes at inference with no architectural change.
Architectural simplicity makes it a reliable baseline — no hyper-parameters for inception branch ratios or residual skip patterns, so ablation studies on depth are unambiguous.
weaknesses: 138M parameters (VGG-16) — roughly 35× more than GoogLeNet — make storage, inference latency, and fine-tuning on constrained hardware prohibitive without pruning or quantization.

Three large fully connected layers (4096→4096→1000) account for ~90% of the parameter count yet contribute no spatial reasoning, a design that ResNet and GoogLeNet abandoned with global average pooling.
No skip connections mean gradients must traverse all 16–19 layers unassisted; training VGG-19 from scratch on new domains risks vanishing gradients and requires careful learning-rate scheduling.
recommended_for: Transfer learning on medical or satellite image datasets with fewer than 10k labeled samples, where VGG's highly generic intermediate feature maps (trained on 1.2M ImageNet images) outperform shallower models without requiring custom architecture design.

Research benchmarks requiring a well-understood, architecture-stable CNN baseline — e.g., evaluating a new regularization technique or data augmentation strategy where controlling for architectural complexity is essential.
not_recommended_for: Edge or mobile deployment (embedded MCUs, smartphones) where model size must stay under a few MB: VGG-16 at ~528 MB FP32 exceeds the memory budget of virtually any constrained device.

Training from scratch on large-scale video or 3D volumetric data, where the absence of residual connections makes convergence unreliable beyond ~16 layers and modern architectures (ResNet, EfficientNet) achieve higher accuracy with a fraction of the parameters.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Karen Simonyan and Andrew Zisserman (arXiv:1409.1556, 2014) from Oxford's Visual Geometry Group, VGG secured 1st place in localization and 2nd place in classification at ILSVRC-2014 — yet the authors' primary goal was not to win the competition but to rigorously isolate depth as the single variable responsible for accuracy gains in deep CNNs.

target.notes: Supervised image classifier head (softmax over classes); the convolutional trunk is also used label-free as a fixed feature extractor / perceptual backbone.

data_regime.rows: from-scratch training needs ~1M+ labeled images; via ImageNet-pretrained transfer learning works on <10k labeled samples
data_regime.dimensionality: fixed-size raster input (canonically 224x224x3); high raw pixel dimensionality handled by convolution + pooling
needs: ~528 MB FP32 storage (VGG-16); high inference latency

features.interpretability: low - 16-19 stacked conv layers, distributed feature representation with no inherent attributions
features.notes: Expects fixed-grid RGB images; standard ImageNet channel-mean subtraction / normalization. Spatial locality and translation structure must hold (natural images).

assumptions: Input is a 2D spatial grid with local correlation (translation-equivariant structure)
Target classes are visually separable from pixel-level features
Train/inference image distribution and preprocessing match the pretraining domain for transfer to help
loss: softmax cross-entropy / categorical log-loss
binary cross-entropy for multi-label heads
contraindicated_when: Tabular, sequence, text, or graph data with no spatial grid structure
Edge/mobile deployment under tight memory or latency budgets (138M params, ~528 MB)
Training very deep from scratch on new domains - no residual connections, vanishing-gradient risk; ResNet/EfficientNet give higher accuracy at a fraction of the parameters
Tiny labeled sets with no access to pretrained weights

children.name: ResNet
children.diff_siblings: Unlike VGGNet (plain stacked convolutions) or Inception (parallel multi-scale filters), ResNet introduces identity shortcut connections that bypass one or more layers, letting the network learn residual functions F(x) = H(x) - x instead of the full mapping H(x), which solved the degradation problem and enabled training of networks with 100+ layers.
strengths: Skip connections allow gradients to flow directly to earlier layers, making 50–152-layer networks trainable without vanishing gradients
Identity shortcuts add zero extra parameters and negligible FLOPs, so depth scales without proportional cost growth
Pre-trained ResNet weights transfer robustly across domains (medical imaging, remote sensing, fine-grained classification) because deep residual features are general-purpose
weaknesses: Residual addition requires input and output tensors to have identical spatial dimensions and channel counts, forcing 1x1 projection convolutions at dimension changes that add complexity
Sequential block structure limits parallelism within a stage compared to Inception's parallel branches, increasing wall-clock time per layer
Very deep variants (ResNet-152) demand significant GPU memory during training due to storing intermediate activations for backpropagation across all 152 layers
recommended_for: Image classification on large labeled datasets (ImageNet-scale, 100k+ images) where depth is necessary to capture fine-grained features and plain networks degrade
Transfer learning base for tasks with limited data (e.g., medical image segmentation), where pre-trained residual features are fine-tuned with only the final layers updated
not_recommended_for: Real-time inference on edge devices with strict latency or memory budgets, where lightweight architectures like MobileNet are more appropriate
Sequence or graph-structured data, where convolutional inductive bias gives no advantage and the architecture must be entirely replaced
children.curiosity: Introduced by He, Zhang, Ren, and Sun (2015) in 'Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition', ResNet-152 won ILSVRC 2015 with a top-5 error of 3.57%, surpassing human-level performance estimated at approximately 5.1% on the same benchmark.

target.notes: Designed for image classification (softmax over classes); the convolutional backbone is also reused as a feature extractor for detection/segmentation heads.

data_regime.rows: needs large labeled image sets (100k+ images for from-scratch ImageNet-scale training); transfer learning makes it usable with hundreds to a few thousand labeled images by fine-tuning
data_regime.dimensionality: input is raw high-dimensional pixel tensors (e.g. 224x224x3); depth (50-152 layers) is justified only when data volume supports it
needs: high GPU memory for deep variants (ResNet-152 stores activations across all layers)

features.interpretability: low; learned hierarchical convolutional features are opaque, requires saliency/Grad-CAM for post-hoc inspection
features.notes: Expects gridded pixel input with local spatial structure; standard ImageNet normalization (per-channel mean/std) and fixed/cropped input resolution; benefits from data augmentation.

assumptions: Input has 2D spatial/translation-invariant structure exploited by convolution
Sufficient labeled data or a transferable pretrained checkpoint exists
Train and deployment image distributions are similar (sensitive to domain shift)
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss (softmax classification)
any differentiable objective via a custom head when used as a backbone (e.g. for detection/segmentation)
contraindicated_when: Data is sequential, tabular, graph-structured, or lacks spatial grid structure (convolutional inductive bias gives no benefit)
Strict real-time latency or tight memory/edge budgets (prefer MobileNet/EfficientNet-lite)
Very few labeled examples and no suitable pretrained weights for transfer
Inputs are tiny/low-resolution where deep downsampling destroys signal

children.name: EfficientNet
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ResNet (depth scaling), VGG (uniform depth), or Inception (hand-crafted multi-branch), EfficientNet uses compound scaling: a single coefficient φ simultaneously scales depth (α^φ), width (β^φ), and input resolution (γ^φ) under a fixed FLOP constraint, derived via neural architecture search on the MBConv baseline.
strengths: Pareto-optimal accuracy-to-FLOP ratio: EfficientNet-B0 matches ResNet-50 accuracy with 5.3x fewer parameters by avoiding the waste of scaling only one dimension.
Compound scaling generalizes across model sizes: the same φ-parameterized family spans from B0 (5.3M params) to B7 (66M params), all sharing the same principled depth/width/resolution balance.

Strong transfer learning base: MBConv blocks with squeeze-and-excitation attention capture both local and channel-wise features, yielding high-quality representations that fine-tune well on small datasets.
weaknesses: Memory-bound training for large variants: EfficientNet-B6/B7 require high input resolutions (528/600px), forcing small batch sizes on 16 GB GPUs and causing non-linear wall-clock increases due to poor kernel fusion in depthwise separable convolutions.

Slow training throughput despite low FLOP count: fine-grained depthwise operations underutilize GPU tensor cores (designed for dense matrix multiplications), making wall-clock time worse than FLOP count suggests versus ResNet.

Fragile to resolution mismatch at inference: accuracy degrades significantly when inference resolution differs from the resolution used during compound-scaling derivation, since φ was tuned assuming a fixed resolution-depth-width ratio.
recommended_for: Mobile and edge deployment with tight parameter budgets: EfficientNet-B0 to B3 achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 77-81% with under 12M parameters, making them suitable for on-device inference where RAM is limited to 1-4 GB.

Transfer learning on small medical or satellite imaging datasets (500-10,000 images): squeeze-and-excitation blocks provide strong channel attention, and the compact architecture reduces overfitting risk compared to wider ResNet variants.
not_recommended_for: Latency-critical inference on GPU servers: depthwise convolutions in MBConv blocks achieve only 40-60% GPU utilization versus 80-90% for standard convolutions in ResNet, making ResNet or ConvNeXt faster in wall-clock time at equivalent accuracy.

Very high-resolution inputs (above 1024px) such as full-resolution satellite or pathology slides: the compound scaling assumption breaks outside the B0-B7 resolution range (224-600px), and alternatives like ViT with patch embeddings handle arbitrary resolutions more naturally.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Tan and Le at Google Brain (ICML 2019), EfficientNet was discovered by first running neural architecture search to find the baseline B0 and then deriving the compound scaling coefficients via a constrained grid search under the condition α·β²·γ² ≈ 2, ensuring that total FLOPs scale approximately as 2^φ with each step.

target.notes: Supervised image classification head; single-label softmax by default, extensible to multi-label (per-class sigmoid). Also used as a frozen/fine-tuned backbone for detection/segmentation downstream.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ to train from scratch; transfer-learning from ImageNet weights works on 500-10,000 labeled images per task
data_regime.dimensionality: raw pixel input (224-600px depending on B0-B7 variant); compound-scaling assumes fixed resolution-depth-width ratio
needs: large labeled data (or pretrained weights for transfer)

features.interpretability: low; deep conv feature hierarchy is opaque, requires saliency/Grad-CAM for post-hoc explanation
features.notes: Expects RGB images at the variant-specific resolution; degrades if inference resolution differs from training resolution. Standard ImageNet normalization. MBConv + squeeze-and-excitation blocks; depthwise-separable convs underutilize GPU tensor cores.

assumptions: inputs are natural-image-like grids with local spatial structure exploitable by convolution
translation-equivariance / locality is appropriate for the task
inference resolution matches the resolution used during compound-scaling derivation
sufficient labeled data or a transferable pretrained backbone is available
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss (softmax multiclass)
binary cross-entropy (multi-label)
label smoothing commonly used
contraindicated_when: tabular, text, time-series, or non-grid data (no spatial locality to exploit)
latency-critical GPU-server inference where dense-conv backbones (ResNet, ConvNeXt) achieve higher tensor-core utilization at equal accuracy
very high-resolution inputs above ~1024px (pathology/satellite slides) outside the B0-B7 224-600px range; ViT-style patch models handle arbitrary resolutions better
tiny datasets with no usable pretrained weights (overfits)

children.name: YOLO (You Only Look Once)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike two-stage detectors (Faster R-CNN) that first propose regions then classify them, YOLO reframes detection as a single regression problem — one forward pass over a grid divides the image into cells, each predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities simultaneously, yielding real-time throughput at the cost of localization precision.
strengths: Processes full images in a single forward pass through 24 convolutional layers, reaching 45 FPS on standard hardware — roughly 1000x faster than sliding-window pipelines of the same era.
Encodes global image context during training (each cell sees the whole image feature map), reducing false positives on background patches compared to region-proposal methods.
Unified architecture is straightforward to fine-tune end-to-end on new domains, with no separate region-proposal stage to retrain or tune.
weaknesses: Each grid cell predicts only 2 bounding boxes and 1 class, so the model struggles when multiple small objects occupy the same cell — dense scenes degrade sharply in recall.
Fixed 7×7 grid resolution means localization error is higher than two-stage detectors; bounding-box coordinates are predicted by a linear head, limiting sub-cell precision.
Generalizes poorly to objects with unusual aspect ratios not well represented in training, because anchor shapes are learned implicitly from the grid rather than through explicit prior clusters.
recommended_for: Real-time video surveillance or autonomous-driving pipelines where latency below 25 ms per frame is required and objects are predominantly medium-to-large relative to frame size.
Edge deployment on embedded GPU hardware (Jetson-class) where a single-stage, single-network architecture avoids the memory overhead of a separate region-proposal network.
not_recommended_for: Aerial or satellite imagery analysis where targets (vehicles, pedestrians) occupy fewer than 16×16 pixels — the fixed grid resolution causes systematic miss-detections.
Medical imaging tasks (e.g., polyp or microcalcification detection) requiring sub-pixel localization accuracy, where two-stage detectors with RoI pooling consistently outperform single-pass grids.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Redmon, Divvala, Girshick, and Farhadi at CVPR 2016, YOLOv1 was trained and run on a single Titan X GPU and achieved 45 FPS at 63.4 mAP on PASCAL VOC 2007 — the first detector to meet broadcast real-time requirements (≥24 FPS) without hardware-specific approximations.

target.notes: Object detection: per-object output is a class label plus 4 continuous bounding-box coordinates and an objectness/confidence score. Requires bounding-box-annotated images, not just image-level labels.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of annotated images per class; benefits from pretraining/transfer learning when labels are scarce
data_regime.dimensionality: raw pixel grids (high-dimensional); learns features end-to-end

features.interpretability: low; deep CNN with a regression detection head, no per-feature explanation
features.notes: Fixed input resolution (e.g. resized to a square); spatially-coherent RGB pixels. Performance tied to object size relative to frame and to grid/anchor resolution.

assumptions: objects are medium-to-large relative to frame; small/dense objects in one grid cell hurt recall
target object scales and aspect ratios are represented in training data
test-time imagery resembles training domain (resolution, viewpoint, lighting)
loss: multi-part detection loss: bounding-box regression (coordinate/IoU error) + objectness/confidence + class log-loss
contraindicated_when: targets are tiny (e.g. <16x16 px in aerial/satellite imagery) — fixed grid causes systematic misses
sub-pixel localization precision required (e.g. medical microcalcification/polyp detection) — two-stage detectors outperform
task is image-level classification, semantic/instance segmentation, or non-image tabular data
only image-level labels available (no bounding boxes)
very few annotated examples without access to pretrained weights

children.name: GoogLeNet / Inception
children.diff_siblings: Unlike VGGNet (uniform 3x3 stack) or AlexNet (sequential single-scale filters), GoogLeNet applies parallel convolutions of three kernel sizes (1x1, 3x3, 5x5) plus max-pooling inside each Inception module, concatenating their outputs to capture multi-scale spatial features in a single layer while keeping compute budgeted via 1x1 bottlenecks.
strengths: 5x fewer parameters than AlexNet (~5 M vs ~60 M) while achieving lower ILSVRC top-5 error (6.67%), because 1x1 convolutions reduce channel depth before each expensive 3x3/5x5 convolution.
Parallel multi-scale receptive fields within each Inception module let the network simultaneously detect fine textures (1x1) and coarser object parts (5x5) without choosing a fixed kernel size.

Two auxiliary classifiers injected at intermediate depths inject gradients directly into early layers, partially mitigating vanishing-gradient degradation in a 22-layer network trained without residual connections.
weaknesses: The branching topology of Inception modules makes the architecture difficult to modify — changing filter counts in one branch can break the computational budget that justified the design.
No skip connections mean that training deeper variants (beyond 22 layers) still suffers gradient attenuation; ResNets and DenseNets superseded GoogLeNet on very deep configurations for this reason.

The heterogeneous parallel branches complicate hardware utilization: the 1x1, 3x3, and 5x5 paths have different arithmetic intensities, making efficient GPU kernel scheduling harder than for uniform-kernel networks.
recommended_for: Image classification on mid-size datasets (tens of thousands of images, hundreds of classes) where inference budget is constrained — the low parameter count and computational efficiency make it a better fit than VGG when memory or latency matters.

Transfer learning for medical imaging tasks (e.g., histopathology patch classification) where multi-scale feature extraction is important and labeled data is limited, since Inception features generalize well across scales.
not_recommended_for: Tasks requiring very deep networks (50+ layers) for maximum accuracy, where residual architectures like ResNet-50 or DenseNet outperform Inception v1 without the architectural rigidity.

Deployment on edge hardware with highly optimized depthwise-separable kernel libraries (e.g., mobile NPUs tuned for MobileNet), where the irregular parallel-branch structure of Inception modules maps poorly to those optimized paths.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Szegedy et al. at Google (2014) and named 'GoogLeNet' as a tribute to LeNet-5 by LeCun; the 'Inception' name references the internet meme 'we need to go deeper', which the authors acknowledged in the original CVPR 2015 paper 'Going Deeper with Convolutions'.

target.notes: Image classifier with softmax head; supervised single-label classification. Backbone is repurposable for detection/segmentation but the node itself targets categorical image labels.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ labeled images per task when training from scratch; works on hundreds-to-thousands per class via transfer learning from ImageNet weights
data_regime.dimensionality: raw pixel inputs (e.g. 224x224x3); learns features end-to-end so explicit p<n reasoning does not apply
needs: large labeled image data (or pretrained weights for transfer learning)

features.interpretability: low; deep hierarchical conv features are opaque, mitigated only via saliency/CAM-style post-hoc tools
features.notes: Expects spatially-structured pixel grids with standard channel normalization; multi-scale Inception modules (1x1/3x3/5x5 parallel) make it tolerant to objects at varying scales. Inputs should be resized/cropped to fixed resolution.

assumptions: inputs are natural-image-like grids with local spatial correlation (translation-invariance assumption of convolutions)
label semantics match the pretrained feature space when using transfer learning
sufficient labeled data or transferable pretrained weights to fit millions of parameters without overfitting
loss: softmax cross-entropy (log-loss) on class labels
auxiliary cross-entropy heads at intermediate depths during training (v1) to inject gradients
contraindicated_when: data is tabular, sequential, text, or graph-structured rather than gridded images
labeled data is tiny and no pretrained backbone is available
maximum accuracy on very deep configs is required (residual nets like ResNet/DenseNet dominate beyond ~22 layers)
deployment targets edge/mobile NPUs optimized for depthwise-separable kernels, where the irregular parallel-branch topology maps poorly

children.name: DenseNet (Densely Connected CNN)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ResNet, which uses additive skip connections between non-adjacent layers, DenseNet concatenates the feature maps of ALL preceding layers as input to each layer within a dense block, preserving the full feature history rather than merging it by summation.
strengths: Strong feature reuse: every layer has direct access to gradients and features from all prior layers, effectively mitigating the vanishing-gradient problem even in very deep networks.

Parameter efficiency: achieves comparable accuracy to ResNet on ImageNet while using less than half the parameters, because repeated feature extraction is replaced by explicit reuse via concatenation.
Compact learned representations: the dense supervision implicit in the connectivity acts as a regularizer, reducing overfitting on smaller labeled datasets such as CIFAR-10.
weaknesses: Quadratic GPU memory growth during training: a naive implementation stores O(L²) intermediate feature maps for L layers, requiring memory-efficient shared-allocation tricks (Pleiss et al., 2017) to be practical.

Inference latency from concatenation overhead: at each layer the runtime must allocate and copy an ever-growing concatenated tensor, making DenseNet slower per forward pass than ResNet at equal depth.

Fixed spatial resolution within a dense block: all feature maps must share the same height and width, so pooling-based downsampling forces the network to be split into separate dense blocks with transition layers, adding architectural complexity.
recommended_for: Medical image segmentation and classification tasks with limited labeled data (e.g., chest X-ray or histopathology slide datasets of a few thousand images), where gradient flow and feature reuse compensate for scarce supervision.
Fine-grained visual recognition benchmarks (e.g., CIFAR-10/100, CUB-200 birds) where compact, parameter-efficient models are preferred and GPU memory budget is not a primary constraint.
not_recommended_for: Real-time inference on edge devices or mobile hardware, where the concatenation overhead and high peak GPU memory make deployment impractical compared to lightweight architectures like MobileNet.
Very deep networks (>200 layers) without memory-efficient implementations, because naive concatenation of all feature maps causes quadratic memory growth that exceeds typical GPU VRAM budgets.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Huang, Liu, van der Maaten, and Weinberger (2017), DenseNet won the Best Paper Award at CVPR 2017 — one of only a handful of deep learning papers to receive that distinction — and the arXiv preprint (arXiv:1608.06993) had accumulated over 45,000 citations by 2024, making it one of the most cited computer vision papers of the decade.

target.notes: Image-level classification head; backbone also feeds segmentation/detection. No assumption on label distribution beyond categorical.

data_regime.rows: thousands+ labeled images; viable on small sets (a few thousand) via ImageNet transfer learning where dense feature reuse acts as a regularizer
data_regime.dimensionality: raw pixel grids (high-dimensional structured input); learns features end-to-end, no manual p<n control
needs: large labeled data (or pretrained weights for transfer)
high peak VRAM during training due to O(L^2) feature-map storage

features.interpretability: low; deep hierarchical conv features are opaque, requires saliency/CAM for post-hoc explanation
features.notes: Expects fixed-size pixel input with channel normalization; spatial resolution must be constant within a dense block (downsampling only at transition layers). Translation-equivariant via convolution; benefits from standard image augmentation.

assumptions: Inputs have local spatial structure / translation equivariance (grid-like pixel data)
Sufficient labeled data or transferable pretrained features
Train/test images share resolution and intensity normalization
loss: cross-entropy / softmax log-loss (classification)
binary cross-entropy (multi-label)
any differentiable objective via SGD/Adam backprop
contraindicated_when: Real-time or edge/mobile inference under tight latency/memory budgets (concatenation overhead, high peak memory) favor MobileNet/EfficientNet
Non-grid data (tabular, sequence, graph) with no spatial locality
Extreme depth (>200 layers) without memory-efficient concatenation implementations
Tiny datasets with no pretraining where any deep CNN overfits

children.name: MobileNet
children.diff_siblings: Unlike VGG or ResNet, which apply standard 3D convolutions across all channels simultaneously, MobileNet factorizes each convolution into a depthwise step (one filter per input channel) followed by a 1x1 pointwise step, reducing FLOPs by a factor of 8-9x at the cost of some inter-channel mixing capacity.
strengths: Two global hyperparameters — width multiplier α and resolution multiplier ρ — let practitioners reduce FLOPs and parameter count continuously without redesigning the architecture.
Depthwise separable convolutions cut multiply-accumulate operations from DK²·M·N·DF² to DK²·M·DF² + M·N·DF², enabling real-time inference on ARM Cortex-class CPUs without a GPU.

Pretrained weights on ImageNet transfer efficiently to narrow domains: fine-tuning MobileNetV1 on tasks like fine-grained bird classification reaches competitive accuracy with far fewer parameters than ResNet-50.
weaknesses: Depthwise convolutions apply a single filter per channel with no cross-channel interaction until the pointwise step, limiting representational capacity compared to full convolutions at the same layer count.
Accuracy degrades sharply when α drops below 0.25: a 90%-sparse full ResNet can match a 0.25× MobileNet while using the same number of non-zero parameters, exposing a structural efficiency ceiling.
Depthwise convolutions have low arithmetic intensity (few FLOPs per memory access), making them underutilized on hardware optimized for dense matrix multiplication such as server-class GPUs and TPUs.
recommended_for: Real-time image classification or object detection on mobile and embedded devices (ARM CPU, DSP) where memory budget is under 20 MB and latency must stay below 50 ms per frame.

Transfer learning pipelines for domain-specific visual tasks with limited labeled data, where a pretrained MobileNet backbone fine-tuned on a few thousand samples outperforms training a larger network from scratch.
not_recommended_for: High-accuracy benchmarks on server hardware where EfficientNet or ResNet variants achieve 3-5% higher top-1 ImageNet accuracy with no inference-time constraint.

Tasks requiring fine spatial detail such as semantic segmentation of small objects, where the aggressive channel reduction in depthwise layers discards spatial frequency information needed for precise boundary localization.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Howard et al. at Google in 2017 (arXiv:1704.04861), MobileNetV1 showed that replacing all standard convolutions with depthwise separable convolutions reduced VGG-16-level ImageNet accuracy by only ~1% while cutting multiply-accumulate operations from ~15 billion to ~569 million — a 26x reduction.

target.notes: Image classification backbone; with a detection/segmentation head extends to object detection. Predicts categorical labels over visual inputs.

data_regime.rows: Works with a few thousand labeled images when fine-tuning ImageNet-pretrained weights; training from scratch needs hundreds of thousands+
data_regime.dimensionality: High-dimensional pixel input (H x W x 3); convolutional weight sharing makes effective parameter count low
needs: pretrained ImageNet weights for small data
no GPU required for inference (designed for ARM CPU/edge); GPU helpful for training

features.interpretability: low - deep convolutional feature hierarchy, not directly inspectable
features.notes: Expects fixed-resolution RGB images normalized to the pretrained preprocessing scheme. Width multiplier alpha and resolution multiplier rho trade accuracy for FLOPs/latency.

assumptions: Inputs are natural images with local spatial structure exploitable by convolutions (translation equivariance)
Target domain is close enough to ImageNet for transfer/fine-tuning to help
Fixed input resolution; spatial relationships matter
loss: cross-entropy / softmax log-loss for classification
detection losses (e.g. localization + classification) when used as a backbone
contraindicated_when: Deployment is on server GPU/TPU with no latency or memory budget, where EfficientNet/ResNet reach 3-5% higher top-1 accuracy (depthwise convs are bandwidth-bound and underutilize dense matmul hardware)
Task needs fine spatial detail such as precise small-object semantic segmentation, where aggressive channel reduction discards spatial frequency information
Data is non-image tabular, sequential, or graph-structured
Extreme compression (alpha < 0.25) is forced, where accuracy degrades sharply and a sparse full network matches it

children.name: U-Net
children.diff_siblings: Unlike FCN (which sums skip connections) and SegNet (which reuses pooling indices), U-Net concatenates full encoder feature maps to their corresponding decoder layers, preserving both spatial detail and channel depth through a fully symmetric encoder-decoder path.
strengths: Trains effectively on very small annotated datasets (original paper used 30 images) via aggressive elastic deformation augmentation
Pixel-wise localization is highly accurate because concatenated skip connections pass full spatial resolution feature maps to each decoder stage
Overlap-tile inference strategy allows segmenting arbitrarily large images without memory constraints by processing overlapping patches with mirrored border padding
weaknesses: Concatenation of full encoder feature maps roughly doubles channel count at each decoder stage, making GPU memory usage high for deep or high-resolution variants
Symmetric depth means the receptive field is fixed at design time; capturing very large context requires stacking many pooling stages, which degrades fine boundary precision
Performs poorly on multi-class segmentation with severe class imbalance unless custom weighted loss functions (e.g., distance-weighted cross-entropy) are carefully tuned
recommended_for: Biomedical image segmentation where annotated data is scarce (fewer than a few hundred images) and pixel-precise delineation of structures like cells or organs is required
Satellite or microscopy tile segmentation where input images are too large for a single forward pass, exploiting the overlap-tile strategy for seamless boundary-free output
not_recommended_for: Scene understanding tasks with many semantic classes (20+) and rich contextual dependencies, where transformer-based decoders or atrous convolutions capture global context more efficiently
Real-time inference on edge devices where memory bandwidth is limited, since full feature-map concatenation across all skip connections is prohibitively expensive
children.curiosity: Introduced by Ronneberger, Fischer, and Brox (2015) at MICCAI, U-Net won the ISBI cell tracking challenge outright and trained end-to-end in under 10 hours on a single GPU using only 30 electron microscopy images, demonstrating that elastic deformation augmentation could substitute for large labeled datasets in biological imaging.

target.notes: Dense per-pixel labeling: each pixel gets a class. Output is a spatial label map (binary mask or per-class softmax), not a single image-level label.

data_regime.rows: works on very small annotated sets (tens to low hundreds of images) when paired with heavy augmentation (elastic deformation); scales to thousands
data_regime.dimensionality: high-dimensional pixel input; capacity tied to network depth/channels not classical p<n
needs: high GPU memory for high-resolution or deep variants due to skip-connection concatenation

features.interpretability: low: deep convolutional encoder-decoder, predictions not attributable to interpretable features
features.notes: Expects gridded image tensors (2D, extendable to 3D for volumetric medical data). Inputs should be intensity-normalized; overlap-tile inference handles images larger than GPU memory via mirrored-border patches.

assumptions: Targets are spatially structured masks aligned pixel-for-pixel with the input
Local spatial correlation and translation equivariance hold (convolutional inductive bias)
Receptive field fixed at design time is large enough for the relevant context; global/long-range context is poorly captured
loss: pixel-wise cross-entropy (often class-weighted)
distance-weighted cross-entropy for boundary separation
soft Dice / Jaccard loss
binary cross-entropy for single-foreground masks
contraindicated_when: target is a single image-level label (classification) rather than a dense mask
many semantic classes (20+) with strong long-range contextual dependencies, where atrous/transformer decoders capture global context better
severe class imbalance without a tuned weighted or Dice loss
real-time / edge inference under tight memory budgets, since full feature-map concatenation is expensive
input is non-grid data (tabular, sequence, graph)

children.name: ConvNeXt V2
children.diff_siblings: Unlike its predecessor ConvNeXt V1 and other modern CNNs, ConvNeXt V2 is co-designed with a self-supervised learning strategy, incorporating a Global Response Normalization (GRN) layer to prevent feature collapse when pre-training with a fully convolutional masked autoencoder (FCMAE).
strengths: Achieves state-of-the-art performance for pure convolutional networks on major benchmarks, rivaling or exceeding vision transformers.
Scales effectively across a wide range of model sizes, from the small 'Atto' to the 'Huge' 650M+ parameter model.
Co-designed for self-supervised learning, enabling strong performance even with only publicly available training data.
weaknesses: Performance gains are a result of both architectural changes (GRN) and a specific self-supervised pre-training method (FCMAE); simply applying one without the other yields subpar results.
Like other large-scale models, the larger variants have a significant computational footprint, which can be a barrier to deployment on resource-constrained hardware.

The architectural improvements are specifically tailored to overcome issues (feature collapse) that arise during masked autoencoder pre-training, which may be less impactful in purely supervised learning settings.
recommended_for: Image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, where it has demonstrated state-of-the-art or competitive performance.
Scenarios where leveraging large unlabeled datasets through self-supervised pre-training is desirable.
not_recommended_for: Simple vision tasks where smaller, less complex models would be more efficient.
Environments with extremely limited computational resources where even the smaller 'Atto' model may be too demanding.
children.curiosity: The model's key architectural innovation, the Global Response Normalization (GRN) layer, was specifically developed to solve the 'feature collapse' problem observed when applying masked autoencoder pre-training to the original ConvNeXt architecture.

target.notes: Supervised head does image multiclass classification (softmax/cross-entropy); also serves as a backbone for detection/segmentation. Self-supervised FCMAE pre-training stage has no labels (target none).

data_regime.rows: needs large labeled data for supervised fine-tuning; FCMAE lets it exploit large unlabeled image corpora for pre-training
data_regime.dimensionality: high-dimensional raw pixel input; not a tabular p-vs-n method
needs: self-supervised pre-training (FCMAE) to realize full benefit
substantial compute for larger variants (up to 650M+ params)

features.interpretability: low; deep hierarchical conv features, not directly inspectable
features.notes: Consumes raw RGB images (typically 224x224+); requires standard normalization and augmentation. GRN layer is tied to masked-autoencoder pre-training to prevent feature collapse.

assumptions: task is grid-structured 2D visual data with local spatial correlation (translation-equivariant structure)
enough labeled data, or transfer from large-scale pre-trained weights, is available
architectural GRN benefit assumes the FCMAE self-supervised regime; pairing one without the other degrades results
loss: softmax cross-entropy (classification)
masked-image reconstruction loss (FCMAE self-supervised pre-training)
downstream detection/segmentation losses when used as a backbone
contraindicated_when: data is tabular, sequential, or non-image
compute/memory is severely constrained even for the smallest 'Atto' variant
task is simple enough for a small/light CNN
only purely supervised training is intended with no pre-training, where the GRN/FCMAE co-design advantage largely vanishes
