children.name: EfficientNetV2
children.diff_siblings: It improves upon other CNNs by using a training-aware neural architecture search (NAS) and a novel progressive learning technique that adaptively adjusts regularization with image size, leading to faster training and higher parameter efficiency.
strengths: Achieves state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer parameters and faster training times compared to other models like Vision Transformers and its predecessor, EfficientNetV1.
Employs Fused-MBConv blocks in early layers, which better utilize modern hardware accelerators compared to the standard MBConv blocks used in EfficientNetV1.
Uses a progressive learning strategy, starting with small images and weak regularization and gradually increasing both, which accelerates training and improves final accuracy.
weaknesses: The progressive learning technique adds complexity to the training process, requiring careful tuning of image size and regularization schedules.
While efficient, depthwise convolutions in MBConv blocks can be a bottleneck on some hardware accelerators compared to standard convolutions.
The performance gains are a result of a complex interplay of architecture search, scaling, and training methods, making it difficult to replicate or modify without extensive computational resources.
recommended_for: Image classification tasks where high accuracy, fast training, and parameter efficiency are all critical.
Use as a high-performance backbone for transfer learning in other computer vision tasks like object detection and semantic segmentation.
not_recommended_for: Applications on extremely resource-constrained devices where even its smaller variants might be too demanding compared to models like MobileNet.
Tasks where the primary concern is model interpretability, due to its complex, search-generated architecture.
children.curiosity: Developed by Google Research authors Mingxing Tan and Quoc V. Le, the model was found using a neural architecture search that jointly optimized for accuracy, training speed, and parameter efficiency.

target.notes: Supervised image classifier; head outputs softmax over classes. Used as a backbone for downstream CV tasks (detection, segmentation) via transfer learning.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ labeled images per dataset; relies on ImageNet-scale pretraining for transfer to smaller targets
data_regime.dimensionality: raw pixel inputs (RGB), high-dimensional; progressive learning varies image resolution during training

features.interpretability: low; NAS-derived architecture with Fused-MBConv/MBConv blocks, no human-readable feature attributions without post-hoc tools
features.notes: Expects 2D image grids with spatial locality; channel normalization to pretraining statistics required. Not for tabular, sequence, or unstructured non-grid inputs.

assumptions: inputs are natural images with translation-invariant local spatial structure
train and deployment image distributions match (resolution, lighting, domain)
sufficient labeled data or a relevant pretrained checkpoint for fine-tuning

very few labeled images and no relevant pretrained backbone

target.notes: Task-agnostic backbone: pairs with a classification head (softmax/sigmoid), a regression head (e.g. keypoint/bounding-box coordinates), or dense per-pixel outputs (segmentation). Can also be trained label-free as an autoencoder/SSL feature extractor (target=none). Target type is set by the head, not the conv stack.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ labeled examples to train from scratch; transfer learning from a pretrained backbone makes hundreds-to-low-thousands viable
data_regime.dimensionality: thrives in very high raw input dimensionality (megapixel images) because weight sharing keeps parameter count low relative to input size; p>>n in raw pixels is fine
needs: large labeled data or a pretrained backbone

features.notes: Requires inputs on a regular grid with meaningful local spatial/temporal structure: 2D images, 3D volumes (medical/video), or 1D signals (audio, ECG). Inputs should be normalized/standardized per channel. Channel-aligned, fixed-size grids; no native handling of unordered heterogeneous columns.

assumptions: Signal is locally correlated and translation-equivariant (nearby pixels/timesteps are related; patterns are meaningful regardless of position)
Input has a fixed, consistent grid topology and channel ordering
Relevant structure is local or composable through stacked receptive fields rather than dominated by long-range global dependencies

Dice / IoU and focal loss (segmentation, class imbalance)

Long-sequence or long-document modeling where dependencies span hundreds of positions (receptive field grows only O(depth); attention is architecturally superior)
Very small labeled datasets with no pretrained backbone available
Inputs with no consistent grid topology or where feature ordering is arbitrary

children.name: 2.3 Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike gated variants (LSTM, GRU) that add explicit memory cells and forget gates, or Transformers that replace recurrence with global self-attention, vanilla RNNs propagate a single hidden state vector h_t = tanh(W_h * h_{t-1} + W_x * x_t) with no gating mechanism, making them the simplest but most gradient-unstable architecture for sequential data.
strengths: Minimal parameter count per time step — no gate matrices — makes them trainable on short sequences with very limited compute
Natural inductive bias for ordered, step-by-step processes (character-level text, control signals) where each output depends only on the immediately preceding state
Straightforward to implement and debug: the full computational graph unrolls into a simple chain of identical operations, easing analysis of learned representations
weaknesses: Vanishing gradient through BPTT: multiplying Jacobians across T steps causes gradients to decay as O(lambda^T) for eigenvalues lambda < 1, making dependencies beyond ~10–20 steps practically unlearnable
Sequential recurrence prevents parallelization across time — training on long sequences is O(T) in wall-clock time, unlike attention-based models that compute all positions simultaneously
Single fixed-size hidden vector must compress the entire sequence history, creating an information bottleneck that collapses context for sequences longer than a few dozen tokens
recommended_for: Short fixed-length time series (< 30 steps) such as real-time sensor control loops where latency matters and long-range context is irrelevant
Character-level language modeling on small corpora where the simplicity of the architecture aids interpretability and overfitting risk from large gated models is a concern
not_recommended_for: Long document or speech sequence modeling (> 100 time steps) where the vanishing gradient prevents learning dependencies between distant tokens
Production NLP tasks (translation, summarization, named entity recognition) where LSTM, GRU, or Transformer architectures consistently outperform vanilla RNNs with no added training complexity
children.curiosity: The modern formulation of training RNNs via backpropagation through time was established by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams in their 1986 Nature paper 'Learning Representations by Back-propagating Errors', the same work that popularized backpropagation for feedforward networks — making the RNN nearly as old as the general backprop algorithm itself.

children.name: RNN Vanilla (Elman)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Jordan networks (which feed back the output layer) or gated architectures like LSTM and GRU (which use learnable gates to control memory), the Elman network feeds back the hidden layer activations directly into a fixed context layer at the next timestep, making the hidden state itself the sole memory mechanism.
strengths: Minimal parameter count: a single recurrent weight matrix W_h connecting hidden-to-context, making it trainable with standard BPTT on small datasets where LSTM would overfit.
Sufficient for short-range sequential dependencies (lags of 5–20 steps), covering most phoneme-level speech patterns and local syntactic context in NLP.

Transparent hidden-state dynamics: because there are no gates, the context vector is a direct, unfiltered copy of the previous hidden activation, simplifying analysis and visualization of learned representations.
weaknesses: Vanishing gradient degrades exponentially with sequence length: gradients of the recurrent weight matrix shrink as W_h^T is multiplied repeatedly during BPTT, making dependencies beyond ~20 timesteps practically unlearnable.
No gating means the network cannot selectively forget irrelevant context — earlier inputs permanently corrupt the hidden state, causing interference in long sequences.
Sensitive to hyperparameter choices (learning rate, hidden size, initialization): without gradient clipping and careful initialization, training diverges via exploding gradients.
recommended_for: Short fixed-length sequence classification (e.g., phoneme recognition windows of 10–30 frames) where the local temporal context is sufficient and low inference latency is required.
Educational prototyping and ablation studies comparing recurrent architectures, where the simplicity of the Elman cell provides a clean baseline with no gating confounds.
not_recommended_for: Long-document language modeling or machine translation where token dependencies span hundreds of positions, as the vanishing gradient prevents learning those relationships.
Production time-series forecasting with irregular or long seasonal cycles (e.g., yearly patterns in daily data), where LSTM or Transformer-based models capture the required long-range structure.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Jeffrey L. Elman in 'Finding Structure in Time' (Cognitive Science, 1990), the network was originally designed to model human language acquisition, demonstrating that a neural network with no built-in grammar could extract syntactic categories such as noun and verb purely from distributional sequential patterns in raw text.

target.notes: Supervised sequence learning: per-step or whole-sequence labels (sequence classification), next-step prediction, or seq2seq. Output head sets the target type (softmax for class, linear for regression).

data_regime.rows: trainable on small/medium labeled sequence sets; far fewer parameters than LSTM/GRU so less prone to overfit when data is scarce
data_regime.dimensionality: input is a sequence of feature vectors; modest hidden size (tens to low hundreds) typical
needs: GPU optional (small models train on CPU)

features.interpretability: medium: ungated context layer is a direct copy of prior hidden state, so dynamics are easier to inspect than gated cells, but still a distributed black-box representation
features.notes: Inputs must be ordered in time and typically scaled/normalized; categorical/text inputs require embedding or one-hot encoding first.

assumptions: relevant dependencies are short-range (roughly 5-20 timesteps); longer-range structure is not learnable
temporal order is meaningful and stationary enough across the sequence
fixed input feature dimension per timestep
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss for classification heads
softmax cross-entropy for next-token / language-model prediction
squared error (MSE) for regression / forecasting heads
contraindicated_when: dependencies span hundreds of timesteps (long documents, long seasonal cycles) where vanishing gradients prevent learning - prefer LSTM/GRU/Transformer
tasks needing selective memory/forgetting of distant context
very long sequences where training is unstable (exploding/vanishing gradients) without heavy tuning
non-sequential tabular data with no temporal/order structure

children.name: LSTM
children.diff_siblings: Unlike vanilla RNNs (single hidden state) and GRUs (two gates, merged cell/hidden state), LSTM maintains a separate cell state c_t alongside the hidden state h_t, controlled by three independent sigmoid gates (forget, input, output) that allow fine-grained decoupling of what to remember, what to write, and what to expose at each time step.
strengths: Explicit cell state with additive gradient flow prevents vanishing gradients over sequences of hundreds of time steps, where vanilla RNNs fail entirely.
Three-gate decoupling lets the network independently control memory retention and output projection, capturing dependencies at multiple timescales simultaneously.
Bidirectional LSTM stacks (BiLSTM) aggregate past and future context at each position, which boosted state-of-the-art on NER and POS tagging benchmarks throughout 2015-2019.
weaknesses: Strictly sequential hidden-state propagation (h_t depends on h_{t-1}) prevents parallelization across time steps, making training on long sequences an order of magnitude slower than Transformers.
Four weight matrices per layer (W_f, W_i, W_o, W_c) roughly quadruple parameter count versus a comparable vanilla RNN, increasing memory footprint and overfitting risk on small datasets.
Fixed-size cell state is a bottleneck for very long sequences (thousands of steps): information written early is progressively overwritten regardless of gate settings.
recommended_for: Multivariate time series forecasting (e.g., sensor streams with 100-1000 time steps) where temporal order matters and the dataset is too small (~tens of thousands of samples) to train a Transformer from scratch.
Online sequence labeling tasks (speech-to-text forced alignment, real-time ECG anomaly detection) where outputs must be produced incrementally step-by-step rather than over the full sequence at once.
not_recommended_for: Long-document NLP tasks (sequences > 512 tokens) where self-attention Transformers can be fine-tuned from pretrained checkpoints — sequential computation makes LSTM training impractical at that scale.
Tabular or non-sequential structured data with no inherent ordering, where the recurrent inductive bias adds parameters without providing any modeling advantage over MLP or gradient boosting.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber in 'Long Short-Term Memory' (Neural Computation, 1997), the LSTM was designed to solve the vanishing gradient problem that Hochreiter had formally diagnosed in his 1991 diploma thesis — making it one of the rare cases where a foundational problem and its solution were identified by the same researcher six years apart.

target.notes: Sequence-to-one (forecasting/classification of a whole sequence), sequence-to-sequence (per-step labeling/generation), or encoder-only representation. Output distribution set by the task head (linear+MSE for regression, softmax for classification); LSTM itself is the sequence encoder, not a likelihood model.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands to tens of thousands of sequences; trainable on far less data than a from-scratch Transformer but overfits on small sets
data_regime.dimensionality: handles long temporal extent (hundreds of steps); per-step feature dim modest

features.interpretability: low; gating dynamics and hidden state are opaque, no native feature attribution
features.notes: Inputs must be an ordered sequence with a meaningful time/position axis. Numeric features should be scaled/normalized; categorical/text via embeddings. Variable-length sequences handled by padding+masking.

assumptions: data has a genuine sequential/temporal ordering that carries signal
dependencies of interest fit within the cell-state memory horizon (degrades over thousands of steps)
enough labeled sequences to fit the quadrupled gate parameters without overfitting
approximately stationary dynamics, or non-stationarity captured by inputs
loss: squared error / MAE for regression heads
cross-entropy / log-loss for classification and per-step labeling
CTC for unaligned sequence labeling (speech)
any differentiable custom objective via backprop-through-time
contraindicated_when: data is tabular or non-sequential with no inherent ordering (recurrent bias only adds parameters)
very long sequences (>512-1000 steps) where pretrained self-attention Transformers fine-tune better and parallelize
dataset is tiny (sequential model overfits; classical time-series like ARIMA/ETS preferred)
training-time parallelism across the time axis is required

children.name: GRU
children.diff_siblings: Unlike LSTM, which uses three gates (input, forget, output) plus a separate cell state, GRU merges the input and forget gates into a single update gate and exposes the full hidden state directly, reducing the parameter count by roughly 25% while retaining gated control over vanishing gradients.
strengths: Trains faster than LSTM on equivalent datasets because each time-step requires two gate computations instead of three, cutting per-step FLOP count by ~25%.
Matches LSTM accuracy on short-to-medium sequence tasks (speech, sentiment, time-series forecasting up to ~500 steps) with fewer parameters, reducing overfitting risk on smaller corpora.

Simpler gradient flow: the update gate directly interpolates between the previous hidden state and the candidate, producing smoother gradients and making hyperparameter tuning more forgiving than LSTM.
weaknesses: Lacks an explicit output gate, so the full hidden state is always exposed to the next layer — this reduces fine-grained control over what information is passed upward, hurting performance on tasks requiring selective memory readout.
Underperforms LSTM on sequences with very long-range dependencies (>1000 steps), where the separate cell state of LSTM provides a more stable gradient highway.

No built-in mechanism for parallelism across time steps; like all RNNs, it processes tokens sequentially, making it significantly slower to train than Transformer-based models on modern GPU/TPU hardware.
recommended_for: Multivariate time-series forecasting (e.g., sensor streams with windows of 50–500 steps) where training data is limited (<100k samples) and inference latency matters, since GRU reaches competitive accuracy faster than LSTM.

On-device sequence classification (e.g., keyword spotting, EEG gesture recognition) where model size must stay under a few MB, as GRU's lower parameter count per hidden unit fits tight memory budgets better than LSTM.
not_recommended_for: Machine translation or document summarization over long sequences (>1000 tokens), where Transformers with full attention or LSTMs with a dedicated cell state consistently outperform GRU on benchmarks such as WMT.

Scenarios requiring interpretable gating decisions or selective memory readout per output step (e.g., structured attention over a knowledge base), since GRU's lack of an output gate makes such control architecturally unavailable.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Cho et al. (2014) in 'Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder-Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation' (arXiv:1406.1078), the GRU was not proposed as a standalone model but as the recurrent unit inside an encoder-decoder for machine translation — it became widely adopted as a general RNN cell only after Chung et al. (2014) empirically showed it matched LSTM on polyphonic music and speech modeling tasks.

target.notes: Sequence-to-one (classification/regression), sequence-to-sequence, or autoregressive forecasting. Target attaches to last hidden state or per-step outputs; final activation/loss set by task.

data_regime.rows: thousands to ~100k labeled sequences; fewer params than LSTM (~25% less) so less overfitting on smaller corpora
data_regime.dimensionality: handles variable-length sequences; effective for windows ~50-500 steps, degrades vs LSTM beyond ~1000 steps

features.interpretability: low: gating is learned and distributed; no explicit output gate, less inspectable than attention
features.notes: Inputs as fixed-dim vectors per time step (embeddings for tokens, standardized numerics for sensors). Requires standardization; sensitive to input scale.

assumptions: Sequential/temporal ordering carries signal
Relevant dependencies are short-to-medium range (<~500-1000 steps)
Stationary-enough generating process within the modeled window
Sufficient labeled data to fit gated parameters without overfitting

squared error / MAE (regression, forecasting)

any differentiable custom loss via backprop-through-time

Long-sequence translation/summarization benchmarks where Transformers dominate

children.name: Bidirectional RNN/LSTM
children.diff_siblings: Unlike unidirectional RNNs/LSTMs that propagate hidden state only forward in time, Bidirectional RNN/LSTM runs two separate recurrent layers — one forward, one backward — over the same sequence and concatenates their outputs, making every timestep's representation conditioned on both past and future context.
strengths: Full context at every token: each hidden state sees the entire input sequence in both directions, which directly improves disambiguation in tasks like NER where a word's label depends on words that follow it.

Combines well with LSTM's gating mechanism: the forget/input/output gates already mitigate vanishing gradients for long-range dependencies, and bidirectionality doubles the effective receptive field without adding recurrent depth.

Strong baseline for offline sequence labeling: BiLSTM-CRF architectures dominated NER and POS tagging benchmarks before transformers, establishing it as a well-understood, reproducible reference point with modest data requirements.
weaknesses: Incompatible with streaming and real-time inference: the backward pass requires the complete input sequence before any output can be committed, so stable predictions cannot be emitted until the full sequence arrives.
Doubles parameter count and compute relative to a unidirectional LSTM of the same hidden size, since two separate recurrent layers are trained and stored.
Largely superseded for sequence labeling by transformer-based encoders (BERT and variants), which capture global context more efficiently and scale better with pre-training.
recommended_for: Offline NLP sequence labeling — NER, POS tagging, syntactic chunking — where the full sentence is available at inference time and labeled training data is limited (thousands to tens of thousands of sentences).

Offline speech or audio feature encoding where an entire utterance is buffered before decoding, and the task benefits from phoneme-level disambiguation using both preceding and following acoustic frames.
not_recommended_for: Streaming or low-latency applications such as live transcription or real-time translation, where outputs must be emitted incrementally before the full input sequence is available.
Large-scale pre-training or fine-tuning regimes with abundant data, where transformer encoders achieve higher accuracy at similar or lower inference cost once pre-trained representations are reused.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Schuster and Paliwal (1997) in IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing, the original BiRNN was applied to phoneme classification in speech — a domain where the authors showed that knowing future acoustic frames reduced error compared to any causal RNN of equivalent size.
keywords: context from past and future tokens

target.notes: Per-timestep sequence labeling (token-level multiclass/multilabel) or sequence-level classification via pooled final states. Outputs typically passed through softmax or a CRF layer for structured tagging.

data_regime.rows: works with thousands to tens of thousands of labeled sequences; far less data-hungry than transformers
data_regime.dimensionality: input is variable-length sequences of embedding vectors; effective context spans the full sequence
needs: GPU recommended for training speed but trainable on CPU for modest data
full input sequence available at inference (offline only)

features.interpretability: low: distributed hidden representations are opaque; attention/saliency analysis needed to inspect
features.notes: Consumes ordered sequences of token/frame embeddings. Requires the complete sequence before emitting outputs; not causal.

assumptions: both past and future context of a timestep are available at inference (non-streaming)
label of a position can depend on surrounding tokens in both directions
sequential/ordered structure carries signal; order matters
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss for per-token or sequence classification
CRF negative log-likelihood when paired as BiLSTM-CRF for structured tagging
CTC for sequence-to-label alignment in speech
contraindicated_when: streaming or low-latency inference where outputs must be emitted before the full sequence arrives
abundant data and compute available where pretrained transformer encoders (BERT) dominate
non-sequential tabular data with no temporal/positional ordering
very long sequences where vanishing gradients and O(length) recurrence limit range vs. attention

children.name: Encoder-Decoder (Seq2Seq)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike plain RNNs (which map each input step to an output step directly) and attention-augmented or Transformer variants (which give the decoder dynamic access to all encoder states), vanilla Seq2Seq compresses the entire input into a single fixed-length context vector — the final encoder hidden state — that the decoder must reconstruct the output from alone.
strengths: Decouples input and output sequence lengths, enabling true many-to-many mapping without requiring step-by-step alignment between source and target tokens.
LSTM-based encoder retains information across hundreds of tokens through gated memory cells, making it far more capable than plain RNNs on variable-length inputs.

Reversing the input sequence at encoding time (as done by Sutskever et al., 2014) significantly reduces the average distance between corresponding source and target tokens, improving gradient flow during training.
weaknesses: The fixed-length context vector becomes an information bottleneck for sequences longer than ~30 tokens: the encoder must discard detail to fit everything into one vector.
Sequential token-by-token decoding prevents parallelization — inference time scales linearly with output length, making it slow for long outputs compared to Transformer decoders.
Vanishing gradients still affect very deep or very long sequences even with LSTMs, causing the model to forget distant context that attention mechanisms would handle explicitly.
recommended_for: Machine translation of short-to-medium sentences (under ~30 tokens) where a compact, interpretable pipeline is needed and attention adds unwanted complexity.
Structured output generation tasks such as SQL query synthesis or code summarization from short natural-language prompts, where input length is bounded and output follows a fixed grammar.
not_recommended_for: Document-level summarization or translation of long paragraphs, where the fixed context vector cannot retain enough information and attention-based Seq2Seq or Transformers are required.
Latency-sensitive production inference pipelines generating long sequences, since the autoregressive decoder cannot be parallelized and throughput degrades linearly with output length.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Sutskever, Vinyals, and Le (NeurIPS 2014), the model achieved a BLEU score of 34.8 on WMT English-to-French translation — surpassing the then best phrase-based SMT system — despite using no alignment mechanism, purely by reversing the source sentence before encoding.

target.notes: Output is a variable-length sequence of discrete tokens; per-step softmax over a vocabulary (multinomial). Generalizes to any input-sequence to output-sequence mapping where lengths differ.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of paired (source, target) sequences; data-hungry, overfits on small corpora
data_regime.dimensionality: high effective p via embeddings; sequence length matters more than tabular p

features.interpretability: low - distributed hidden states and a single fixed-length context vector are opaque
features.notes: Inputs are tokenized sequences mapped to learned embeddings; reversing source token order improves training. Best when input length is bounded (under ~30 tokens).

assumptions: Output can be generated autoregressively left-to-right conditioned on prior tokens
Entire source meaning is compressible into one fixed-length context vector
Sufficient paired training data exists to learn the mapping
loss: per-token cross-entropy / log-loss (teacher forcing)
sequence-level negative log-likelihood
contraindicated_when: Source sequences are long (document-level); fixed context vector bottlenecks at >30 tokens, use attention/Transformer instead
Low-latency inference on long outputs is required; sequential decoding scales linearly and cannot parallelize
Training data is scarce
Task is not a sequence-to-sequence mapping (fixed-length classification/regression on tabular data)

children.name: Attention Mechanism (Bahdanau)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Luong (multiplicative) attention, which scores using a dot product between the current decoder state and encoder hidden states, Bahdanau uses an additive scoring function — a single-layer feed-forward network applied to the previous decoder state and each encoder state — and pairs it with a bidirectional encoder to produce richer annotations.
strengths: Bidirectional encoder captures both left and right context for each source token, producing stronger annotations than unidirectional RNN encoders.
Per-step dynamic context vector: a distinct weighted sum over all encoder states is computed for each decoder step, letting the model attend to different source positions at each output token.
Additive scorer with learned parameters (W_a, U_a, v_a) can capture non-linear alignment patterns that pure dot-product methods miss on smaller or structurally complex datasets.
weaknesses: Alignment scoring requires computing e_ij = v_a^T tanh(W_a s_{i-1} + U_a h_j) for every (decoder step, encoder step) pair, giving O(T_x * T_y) cost that becomes prohibitive for long sequences.
Still inherits sequential RNN processing: encoder and decoder both step token-by-token, blocking the full parallelization that Transformer self-attention achieves.
The additive feed-forward scorer adds parameters and compute compared to dot-product attention; on high-dimensional hidden states this overhead is non-trivial at inference time.
recommended_for: Sequence-to-sequence tasks with moderate-length inputs (sentences up to ~50 tokens) where alignment interpretability matters, such as neural machine translation with post-hoc word-alignment analysis.

Problems where a bidirectional context over the source is critical and a Transformer would overfit due to limited labeled data, such as low-resource NMT or medical report generation from short structured inputs.
not_recommended_for: Long-document tasks (summaries of book chapters, legal documents) where the O(T_x * T_y) attention cost and RNN sequential bottleneck dominate both time and memory budgets.
Production systems requiring high throughput, since the sequential RNN decoder cannot be parallelized across time steps even with the attention context computed in batch.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio in 'Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate' (arXiv 1409.0473, 2014; ICLR 2015), the paper demonstrated that inspection of the learned attention weights produces a soft alignment matrix between source and target words that closely matches human-annotated word alignments — making attention one of the first neural components to offer built-in interpretability.

target.notes: Architectural component for sequence-to-sequence learning; output is typically a sequence of tokens predicted via per-step softmax (multinomial over vocabulary). Not a standalone estimator; used inside an encoder-decoder RNN.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of aligned sequence pairs to train the encoder, decoder, and additive scorer parameters
data_regime.dimensionality: hidden-state dimensionality typically 256-1024; scorer cost grows with hidden size

features.interpretability: medium: attention weights yield soft source-target alignments inspectable per output step, but the underlying RNN states are opaque
features.notes: Inputs are token sequences embedded into dense vectors; assumes ordered sequential structure with meaningful left/right context (bidirectional encoder).

assumptions: Inputs and outputs are ordered sequences with exploitable alignment structure
Moderate sequence lengths (inputs up to ~50 tokens); alignment quality and tractability degrade as length grows
Sufficient labeled paired data to learn non-linear alignment without overfitting

teacher-forced sequence negative log-likelihood
contraindicated_when: Long documents where O(T_x * T_y) alignment cost and RNN sequential decoding dominate time/memory
High-throughput production needs, since the sequential RNN decoder cannot parallelize across time steps
Non-sequential tabular data with no temporal/ordinal structure
Abundant data and compute where a Transformer (parallel self-attention) strictly dominates

target.notes: Maps ordered input sequences to per-step or sequence-level outputs (seq2seq, seq-to-one, seq labeling). No distributional assumption on the target; output layer (softmax/linear) sets the head. Best when the target genuinely depends on order; not for i.i.d. tabular targets.

sequences short enough (<30-50 steps) that BPTT gradients survive

features.notes: Inputs must be ordered and ideally fixed/short length. Numeric inputs should be scaled; categorical/text needs embedding or one-hot. Order carries the signal.

assumptions: Sequential dependency: output at step t depends mainly on recent preceding state, not on distant context
Relevant dependencies are short-range (within ~10-20 steps) so vanishing gradients do not erase them
Stationary-enough generating process across the sequence (shared weights tied across all time steps)
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss (classification, per-step or sequence)
squared error (continuous regression on sequences)
CTC and teacher-forced sequence loss for seq2seq
any differentiable loss via backpropagation through time
contraindicated_when: Long-range dependencies needed (>100 steps); vanishing gradient prevents learning them — prefer LSTM/GRU/Transformer
Non-sequential i.i.d. tabular data with no meaningful order
Long sequences where O(T) sequential training is too slow and attention parallelism is required
Small data with a complex task where simpler classical models or gated nets generalize better
Production NLP (translation, NER, summarization) where gated/attention models dominate at no extra training cost

children.name: 2.4 Transformers
children.diff_siblings: Unlike RNNs (which process tokens sequentially through a hidden state) and CNNs (which apply fixed local kernels), Transformers compute pairwise attention scores between all positions simultaneously, enabling direct modeling of long-range dependencies in a single layer without sequential bottlenecks.
strengths: Parallelizable training: all positions in the sequence are processed simultaneously via matrix operations, eliminating the sequential dependency that makes RNN training slow on modern GPU/TPU hardware.

Global receptive field from layer one: self-attention connects any two positions in O(1) operations regardless of sequence length, whereas CNNs require O(n/k) convolutional layers to cover the same span.

Transfer learning backbone: a single pre-trained Transformer (e.g., BERT, GPT) can be fine-tuned with few labeled examples across NLP, vision, and tabular tasks, a regime where RNNs and CNNs rarely generalize as broadly.
weaknesses: Quadratic memory and compute in sequence length: the attention matrix scales as O(T²), making naive application to sequences longer than ~4 k tokens prohibitively expensive without sparse or linear attention variants.

No structural inductive bias: the architecture treats inputs as unordered sets and relies entirely on positional encodings to recover order, which means it requires far more data than CNNs or RNNs to learn local patterns such as edges in images or n-gram statistics in text.

High minimum viable dataset size: the attention-based pretraining objective demands large corpora (billions of tokens) to converge to useful representations; on small datasets (<10 k samples) with no pre-trained weights, Transformers typically underperform fine-tuned CNNs or LSTMs.
recommended_for: Long-document understanding and generation tasks (e.g., legal contract analysis, code synthesis) where the relevant context spans hundreds to thousands of tokens and sequential models lose the signal through gradient decay.

Multi-modal tasks (image-text retrieval, video captioning) where cross-attention between different modalities — image patches and word tokens — can be expressed as a unified attention operation without architectural changes.
not_recommended_for: Low-data tabular regression or classification problems where the training set has fewer than ~5 k rows and no suitable pre-trained checkpoint exists; gradient-boosted trees and MLPs will generalize better at this scale.

Real-time inference on edge devices with tight latency and memory budgets (e.g., microcontrollers, embedded sensors), where the minimum viable Transformer is still orders of magnitude heavier than an equivalent CNN or RNN.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Vaswani et al. (Google Brain, 2017) in 'Attention Is All You Need', the original Transformer reached state-of-the-art BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German (28.4) and English-to-French (41.0) translation benchmarks while training in 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs — a fraction of the time required by the recurrent models it displaced.

children.name: Transformers NLP
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Vision or Audio Transformers that adapt the architecture to spatial or temporal signals, NLP Transformers operate on discrete token sequences with subword tokenization (BPE/WordPiece) and learned positional encodings, and split into encoder-only (BERT), decoder-only (GPT), or encoder-decoder (T5) variants depending on whether the task requires bidirectional context, autoregressive generation, or sequence-to-sequence mapping.
strengths: Full bidirectional self-attention captures long-range syntactic and semantic dependencies in a single forward pass, eliminating the vanishing gradient that crippled RNN encoders on sequences longer than ~200 tokens.
Pre-train once on large corpora, fine-tune on a few thousand labeled examples: encoder models like BERT reach state-of-the-art on classification and NER with as little as 1k–10k annotated samples.
Highly parallelizable across tokens during training — no sequential recurrence — allowing efficient use of tensor cores on GPUs/TPUs and enabling scaling to billions of parameters.
weaknesses: Self-attention complexity scales as O(n²) in both memory and compute with sequence length n, making full-attention models prohibitively expensive beyond ~4k–8k tokens without approximation methods.
Sensitive to tokenization vocabulary mismatch: rare languages, domain-specific jargon, or code not well represented in the pre-training corpus yield degraded sub-word splits and poor embeddings.

Autoregressive decoder inference is inherently sequential (each token depends on the previous), creating a latency bottleneck — generating 1k tokens requires 1k serial forward passes regardless of parallelism.
recommended_for: Classification, NER, and extractive QA over documents of up to ~512 tokens where labeled data is scarce: encoder-only models (BERT, RoBERTa) deliver near-human accuracy with minimal fine-tuning.
Sequence-to-sequence tasks such as machine translation or abstractive summarization where both input and output are natural-language text, leveraging encoder-decoder architectures like T5 or BART.
not_recommended_for: Real-time inference on edge or embedded devices with strict latency and memory budgets: a base BERT model (~110M parameters) alone exceeds the RAM of most microcontrollers and adds hundreds of milliseconds per call.

Tasks on very long documents (>100k tokens, e.g., full legal contracts or genomic sequences) where quadratic attention cost makes full-context Transformers impractical without architectural modifications (Longformer, BigBird).
children.curiosity: Introduced by Vaswani et al. (2017) in 'Attention Is All You Need' (NeurIPS), the Transformer was originally designed for machine translation and eliminated recurrence entirely; within two years it had displaced LSTM-based architectures across virtually every NLP benchmark, a pace of adoption without precedent in the field.

children.name: BERT
children.diff_siblings: Unlike GPT (decoder-only, left-to-right autoregressive) and T5 (encoder-decoder), BERT is an encoder-only transformer trained with Masked Language Modeling, which forces every layer to attend jointly to left and right context simultaneously, producing deep bidirectional representations.
strengths: Bidirectional context at every layer: masking 15% of tokens at pretraining forces the model to reconstruct each token from full surrounding context, yielding richer sentence-level representations than any unidirectional model.
Fine-tuning efficiency: a single pretrained checkpoint achieves state-of-the-art on classification, NER, and QA tasks by adding only a lightweight head, with no architectural changes to the encoder.

Strong span-level understanding: the [CLS] and token-level embeddings directly encode relational context across the full 512-token window, making BERT highly effective for extractive tasks like SQuAD-style reading comprehension.
weaknesses: Hard 512-token input ceiling: the positional embedding table is fixed at 512, so documents longer than that require chunking or truncation with no native mechanism to preserve cross-chunk context.

Cannot generate text natively: the masked LM objective creates a train/inference mismatch — the model never learns to produce tokens autoregressively, making open-ended generation impossible without non-trivial adaptation.

Quadratic attention cost: self-attention scales as O(n²) in both time and memory with sequence length n, making inference on even moderately long inputs (>300 tokens) significantly more expensive than linear-attention alternatives.
recommended_for: Extractive question answering over fixed-length passages (e.g., SQuAD-style tasks with paragraphs under 512 tokens) where a span of the input is the answer and bidirectional context is critical for span boundary detection.

Sentence or document classification tasks (sentiment, intent detection, NLI) with labeled datasets of a few thousand examples, where BERT fine-tuning outperforms training from scratch by a large margin.
not_recommended_for: Open-ended or long-form text generation (chatbots, summarization, story writing) where an autoregressive decoder like GPT is required to produce coherent token sequences beyond a single masked position.

Processing full-length documents such as legal contracts or research papers (often 5,000–100,000 tokens) where the 512-token limit forces lossy truncation and linear-scaling sparse-attention models (Longformer, BigBird) are the appropriate choice.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Devlin, Chang, Lee, and Toutanova at Google AI in 2018 (arXiv:1810.04805), BERT set new state-of-the-art records on 11 NLP benchmarks simultaneously upon release, including a 7.7-point absolute improvement on the GLUE benchmark, which at the time was the largest single-model leap ever recorded on that suite.

target.notes: Encoder backbone; with a fine-tuned head supports sequence classification (binary/multiclass/multilabel), token classification (NER/POS), and span extraction (start/end logits for extractive QA). Used headless it produces contextual token/sentence embeddings (target=none) for retrieval/clustering. Not a generative or regression model.

data_regime.rows: pretrained checkpoint enables fine-tuning with a few hundred to a few thousand labeled examples; from-scratch pretraining needs billions of tokens (impractical to reproduce)
data_regime.dimensionality: input capped at 512 tokens (fixed positional table); longer documents must be chunked/truncated

features.interpretability: low — distributed attention-based representations; attention weights are not faithful explanations
features.notes: Consumes raw text via WordPiece subword tokenization (no manual feature engineering or scaling). Single-sequence or sentence-pair input with [CLS]/[SEP] structure. English-language unless a multilingual/domain checkpoint is used.

assumptions: task domain/register is reasonably close to pretraining corpus or covered by domain fine-tuning
relevant signal fits within the 512-token window
enough labeled in-domain examples exist for the fine-tuning head to converge
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss for sequence and token classification
span start+end cross-entropy for extractive QA
masked-language-model cross-entropy at pretraining
contrastive/cosine objectives when adapted for sentence embeddings (e.g. SBERT)
contraindicated_when: open-ended or long-form text generation is required (use an autoregressive decoder)
inputs routinely exceed 512 tokens (use Longformer/BigBird or chunking with cross-chunk modeling)
the target is numeric/tabular rather than text
latency/compute is tight on long sequences (O(n^2) attention) or no GPU is available
labeled data is essentially absent and the task is far from pretraining (zero-shot LLM prompting may fit better)

children.name: GPT / GPT-4
children.diff_siblings: Unlike encoder-only (BERT) or encoder-decoder (T5, BART) transformer siblings, GPT uses a strictly decoder-only stack with causal (left-to-right) masked self-attention, making it natively autoregressive and optimized for open-ended text generation rather than bidirectional understanding or fixed-format sequence transduction.
strengths: Unified pre-train-then-prompt paradigm: a single model handles translation, summarization, QA, and code generation without task-specific heads, because the causal LM objective implicitly learns all these as next-token prediction.

Few-shot and zero-shot generalization at scale (GPT-3/4): with 175B+ parameters the model transfers to unseen tasks purely from in-context examples, eliminating the need for gradient updates at inference time.

RLHF alignment (GPT-4): reinforcement learning from human feedback steers outputs toward instruction-following and safety, achieving measurably lower hallucination rates (~28.6%) than its unaligned predecessor GPT-3.5.
weaknesses: Self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length (O(n²) in memory and compute), making very long contexts expensive and requiring architectural workarounds like sparse attention or chunking.

Prone to confident hallucination: the causal LM objective optimizes token probability, not factual grounding, so the model generates plausible-sounding but false claims with no built-in retrieval or verification.

Closed architecture and API-only access for GPT-4: OpenAI has not published weights or full architectural details, making reproducibility, fine-tuning, and cost control dependent on a proprietary vendor.
recommended_for: Open-ended text generation and instruction-following tasks (chatbots, copilots, document drafting) where a single large model must handle diverse prompt formats without retraining.
Few-shot NLP benchmarking or rapid prototyping where labeled data is scarce and the practitioner can supply 3-10 in-context examples to steer behavior instead of fine-tuning a task-specific model.
not_recommended_for: High-throughput or latency-critical production pipelines where inference cost matters: GPT-4-scale models require dozens of A100 GPUs per request, making them impractical compared to a fine-tuned 7B model for narrow tasks.

Tasks requiring verifiable factual precision (legal evidence retrieval, medical diagnosis, financial auditing) without a retrieval-augmented grounding layer, because the model has no mechanism to distinguish memorized facts from plausible confabulations.
children.curiosity: GPT-1, introduced by Radford, Narasimhan, Salimans, and Sutskever (OpenAI, 2018) in 'Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training', demonstrated for the first time that a single decoder-only transformer pre-trained on BookCorpus could be fine-tuned to achieve state-of-the-art results on 9 out of 12 diverse NLP benchmarks, establishing the pre-train/fine-tune paradigm that all subsequent GPT versions follow.

target.notes: Per-token categorical distribution over a large vocabulary (~50k-100k subword tokens) under an autoregressive factorization P(x_t | x_<t). 'Target' is the next token; downstream tasks (generation, QA, summarization, classification) are all cast as conditional next-token prediction rather than a fixed label space.

data_regime.rows: Pretraining needs trillions of tokens; not trained by the end user. At use time operates zero-/few-shot (0-10 in-context examples) with no gradient updates, so the practitioner needs no labeled training set.
data_regime.dimensionality: Sequence length bounded by context window; self-attention is O(n^2) in length so very long inputs are costly. Model size 175B+ params for GPT-3/4-class behavior.
needs: API access or dozens of A100-class GPUs for GPT-4-scale inference

features.interpretability: low: dense distributed representations, no feature-level attributions, proprietary closed weights for GPT-4 limiting inspection.
features.notes: Input is raw natural-language (or code) text tokenized into subwords; no manual feature engineering, scaling, or tabular encoding. Tabular/numeric/image/graph data are not native inputs.

assumptions: Task is expressible as conditioning on a textual prompt and producing text
Relevant knowledge is captured in pretraining distribution or supplied in-context (no built-in retrieval)
Sequence fits within the context window
loss: causal language-modeling cross-entropy / log-loss on next-token prediction
RLHF reward optimization (PPO-style) for instruction alignment in GPT-4
contraindicated_when: Verifiable factual precision is required without a retrieval/grounding layer (legal, medical, financial) due to confident hallucination
Inputs are tabular/numeric/structured rather than text
Latency- or cost-critical high-throughput pipelines where a fine-tuned small model suffices
Calibrated probabilistic forecasts of a numeric quantity are needed (the model emits text tokens, not a calibrated predictive distribution over a continuous target)
Reproducibility, on-prem control, or fine-tuning of weights is mandatory (closed GPT-4 weights)

children.name: RoBERTa
children.diff_siblings: Unlike BERT (static masking, next-sentence prediction) and XLNet (autoregressive permutation), RoBERTa keeps the exact BERT encoder architecture but removes NSP entirely and applies dynamic masking — regenerating mask patterns each epoch over a 160 GB corpus, 10x larger than BERT's.
strengths: Dynamic masking prevents the model from memorizing fixed mask positions, producing more robust contextual embeddings across epochs
Byte-pair encoding over raw bytes (vs. BERT's WordPiece) handles out-of-vocabulary tokens and non-Latin scripts without an [UNK] token
Removing NSP removes a noisy pretraining objective that empirically degraded single-sentence downstream tasks like SST-2 and QNLI
weaknesses: Rare word sense information is less accessible than in BERT — embeddings conflate polysemous words more aggressively
Pretraining requires ~1000 GPU-hours and 160 GB of text, making domain-specific re-pretraining from scratch prohibitively expensive
Still a bidirectional encoder — unsuitable for autoregressive generation tasks (text completion, story generation) without architectural modification
recommended_for: Fine-tuning on sentence classification, NER, or extractive QA (SQuAD-style) where a bidirectional encoder benefits from long pretraining and robust masking
Transfer learning baselines on English text corpora where BERT underperforms due to limited training data and static masks
not_recommended_for: Open-ended text generation tasks requiring left-to-right autoregressive decoding, where decoder-only models (GPT family) are architecturally appropriate
Extremely low-resource language settings where the 160 GB English pretraining corpus provides minimal cross-lingual transfer and a multilingual model (mBERT, XLM-R) is more suitable
children.curiosity: Introduced by Liu et al. (2019) at Facebook AI, RoBERTa demonstrated that BERT was significantly undertrained — simply extending training time and batch size (8192 sequences), without any architectural change, was sufficient to match or surpass every post-BERT model on GLUE, SQuAD, and RACE at the time of publication.

target.notes: Used via fine-tuning heads: sequence classification (binary/multiclass/multilabel), token classification (NER), and span extraction (extractive QA). No native regression/count/survival objective; target is a label over text spans or sequences. Encoder-only, so no autoregressive generation target.

data_regime.rows: fine-tunes well on hundreds-to-low-thousands of labeled examples thanks to transfer learning; pretraining itself needs a 160 GB corpus (not user-provided)
data_regime.dimensionality: raw text input up to 512 tokens per sequence; long documents must be truncated or chunked
needs: moderate labeled data for the downstream task

features.interpretability: low - dense 768/1024-dim contextual embeddings with no per-feature attribution; attention weights are not faithful explanations
features.notes: Input is raw text tokenized with byte-level BPE; no manual feature engineering, scaling, or OOV handling needed. English-centric pretraining corpus, so weak zero-shot cross-lingual transfer.

assumptions: downstream task is expressible as sequence/token labeling or span extraction over text
input language matches the (English) pretraining distribution; domain not too far from web/book corpus
sequences fit within the 512-token context after truncation
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss for sequence and token classification
binary cross-entropy for multilabel heads
span start/end cross-entropy for extractive QA
custom task heads on top of the [CLS] / token embeddings
contraindicated_when: open-ended autoregressive text generation is required (use decoder-only GPT-family)
low-resource or multilingual text where mBERT/XLM-R fit better
tabular, numeric, image, or graph inputs (not text)
very long documents that cannot be reasonably truncated/chunked to 512 tokens
tiny labeled set with no GPU and a simple TF-IDF + linear baseline would suffice

children.name: T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike encoder-only models (BERT) or decoder-only models (GPT), T5 uses a full encoder-decoder Transformer that recasts every NLP task — classification, translation, summarization, Q&A — as a text-to-text mapping, training all tasks with the same sequence-to-sequence loss.
strengths: Single architecture covers generative and discriminative tasks without task-specific output heads, because every output is a token sequence
Span-corruption pretraining on C4 (750 GB filtered Common Crawl) gives strong context reconstruction ability, outperforming BERT on many GLUE/SuperGLUE benchmarks at comparable parameter counts
Scales predictably from 60 M (Small) to 11 B parameters, with consistent gains on translation and summarization as size grows
weaknesses: Encoder-decoder structure doubles the memory footprint at inference compared to decoder-only models of similar capacity, making deployment on edge hardware impractical
Pretraining on English-dominated C4 makes multilingual performance weaker without retraining on a multilingual corpus (mT5 variant required)
Reformulating classification tasks as text generation introduces decoding overhead and token-sampling variance not present in encoder-only classifiers
recommended_for: Seq2seq tasks where input and output are both variable-length text, such as abstractive summarization of news articles or document-level machine translation
Multi-task fine-tuning pipelines where a single checkpoint must handle heterogeneous tasks (e.g., NER, QA, sentiment) simultaneously via task-prefix prompting
not_recommended_for: Token-level sequence labeling (e.g., NER with BIO tags over hundreds of tokens) where a dedicated encoder + CRF head is faster and more structurally appropriate
Latency-critical inference with very long contexts, since the encoder must fully attend to the source before the decoder generates any token, adding first-token latency
children.curiosity: Introduced by Raffel et al. (2020) at Google Brain in 'Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer' (JMLR 21:140), the paper ran over 50 pretraining and fine-tuning ablations on the same encoder-decoder base to establish which design choices — objective, architecture, dataset, scale — mattered most, making it one of the most systematic empirical studies of transfer learning in NLP.

target.notes: Target is always a token sequence: every task (classification, QA, summarization, translation, NER) is recast as text-to-text, so labels are emitted as generated strings rather than via a task-specific head. No probabilistic target distribution; classification probabilities are implicit in next-token softmax over the vocabulary.

data_regime.rows: Pretrained on C4 (~750 GB); fine-tuning works with hundreds to thousands of labeled examples per task; few-shot/zero-shot weaker than decoder-only LLMs
data_regime.dimensionality: Inputs are variable-length token sequences; effective with limited labeled data via transfer learning from the pretrained checkpoint
needs: moderate-to-large memory (encoder-decoder doubles inference footprint vs decoder-only of similar capacity)

features.interpretability: low - attention weights and generated tokens give limited insight; opaque billions-of-parameters mapping
features.notes: Raw text input via task-prefix prompting (e.g. 'summarize:', 'translate English to German:'); SentencePiece tokenization, no manual feature engineering or scaling. English-dominated pretraining; use mT5 for multilingual.

assumptions: Task is expressible as a text-to-text mapping with variable-length string output
Input/output fit within the model context window
Target language well-represented in pretraining corpus (English-centric unless mT5)
loss: token-level cross-entropy (teacher-forced seq2seq log-loss) over the vocabulary, identical objective across all tasks
contraindicated_when: latency-critical inference (encoder must fully attend to source before any decoder token, adding first-token latency; decoding overhead for tasks that an encoder-only classifier would solve in one pass)
token-level sequence labeling with strict span structure (NER with BIO tags) where encoder + CRF head is faster and structurally cleaner
edge/memory-constrained deployment (encoder-decoder roughly doubles memory vs comparable decoder-only model)
non-text or fixed-width tabular targets where seq2seq generation adds sampling variance without benefit

children.name: Longformer
children.diff_siblings: Unlike BigBird (which adds random attention on top of local+global) or Reformer (which uses locality-sensitive hashing), Longformer uses a static combination of sliding-window local attention (O(n·w) complexity) plus manually designated global tokens — no randomness or hashing, making its sparsity pattern fully deterministic and reproducible.
strengths: Processes sequences up to 4096 tokens (extendable to 16384+ with gradient checkpointing) by reducing self-attention from O(n²) to O(n·w), where w is the window size
Global attention tokens (e.g., [CLS] or question tokens in QA) can attend to the full sequence, enabling task-specific long-range reasoning without paying full quadratic cost
Drop-in replacement for RoBERTa's attention: pretrained RoBERTa weights transfer directly, enabling fine-tuning on long-document tasks without training from scratch
weaknesses: Relies on custom CUDA kernels for the sliding-window operation; the standard HuggingFace implementation is slower than full attention on sequences shorter than ~1024 tokens due to kernel overhead
Global attention must be manually specified per task (CLS for classification, question tokens for QA) — wrong designation degrades performance with no automatic fallback
Window size w is a fixed hyperparameter set before training; if the relevant context exceeds w tokens and no global token covers it, that dependency is silently missed
recommended_for: Legal or scientific document classification where inputs regularly exceed 2048 tokens (e.g., full contracts, research papers) and a single [CLS] global token suffices to aggregate the document
Extractive QA over long documents (e.g., legal NLP, clinical notes) where question tokens can be marked as global, letting the model attend from question to any answer span regardless of distance
not_recommended_for: Short-text tasks (tweets, sentences, paragraphs under 512 tokens) where standard BERT/RoBERTa is faster and equally accurate due to Longformer's kernel overhead on short sequences
Generative long-document summarization without using the LED (Longformer Encoder-Decoder) variant, since the base encoder-only Longformer has no causal decoder and cannot produce free-form text
children.curiosity: Introduced by Iz Beltagy, Matthew E. Peters, and Arman Cohan at the Allen Institute for AI (2020, arXiv:2004.05150); the paper showed that simply pre-training RoBERTa with position embeddings extended to 4096 and replacing standard attention with sliding-window attention achieved state-of-the-art on WikiHop and TriviaQA without any architectural changes to the feed-forward layers.

target.notes: Encoder-only backbone: native heads are sequence/token classification (sentiment, topic, NER) and extractive span QA (start/end token logits). No generative target without the LED encoder-decoder variant.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of labeled examples for fine-tuning; relies on pretrained RoBERTa weights so few-thousand-example fine-tunes are viable
data_regime.dimensionality: sequence length 1024-4096 tokens (extendable to 16384+ with gradient checkpointing); below ~512-1024 tokens offers no benefit over RoBERTa
needs: custom CUDA sliding-window kernel for speed

features.interpretability: low; deep transformer, only attention maps (local window + designated global tokens) offer partial inspection
features.notes: Input is tokenized text (RoBERTa BPE). Window size w and the set of global-attention token positions ([CLS] for classification, question tokens for QA) are fixed pre-training/fine-tuning hyperparameters that must match the task.

assumptions: Relevant long-range dependencies are either within the local window w or covered by a manually designated global token; dependencies beyond both are silently dropped
Document length regularly exceeds standard 512-token limits so the O(n·w) sparse attention pays off
Sufficient labeled long-document data and GPU memory for the chosen sequence length
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss (sequence and token classification)
span start/end cross-entropy (extractive QA)
contraindicated_when: Inputs are short (<512 tokens): standard BERT/RoBERTa is faster and equally accurate; kernel overhead makes Longformer slower
Free-form generation or abstractive summarization is required: encoder-only model has no decoder (use LED instead)
The key long-range dependency exceeds the window and is not assigned a global token
Low-resource / small labeled sets or CPU-only / no-GPU deployment
Non-text tabular, numeric, or low-cardinality categorical data

children.name: BigBird
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Longformer (local + global only) and Reformer (LSH bucketing), BigBird combines three sparse attention patterns — sliding window (local), a fixed set of global tokens, and random token pairs — giving it theoretical guarantees of Turing completeness and universal approximation that the other variants lack.
strengths: Extends effective context to 4096 tokens at O(n) memory cost, enabling tasks that exceed BERT's 512-token hard limit without architectural surgery.
Random attention component preserves long-range dependency modeling even under extreme sparsity, a property proved theoretically in the original paper.
Directly applicable to non-text sequences: the original paper demonstrates state-of-the-art results on genomic DNA classification, where sequences routinely exceed 4000 nucleotides.
weaknesses: Sparse attention pattern requires sequence length divisible by the block size (default 64), forcing padding or truncation that wastes compute on sequences that don't align naturally.
For sequences shorter than ~1024 tokens the sparse approximation offers no throughput benefit over full attention and can hurt accuracy relative to BERT.
Random attention introduces non-determinism across runs unless the random seed is fixed, complicating reproducibility in production pipelines.
recommended_for: Long-document extractive or abstractive summarization (e.g., legal contracts, scientific papers) where the full document exceeds 1024 tokens and answer evidence is spread across distant passages.
Genomic sequence classification tasks (e.g., promoter prediction, splice site detection) with input lengths of 1000–4096 nucleotides where full self-attention is memory-prohibitive.
not_recommended_for: Short-text tasks (sentiment analysis, NLI on single sentences) where sequences fit within 512 tokens, since full-attention BERT variants will match or exceed BigBird accuracy with simpler infrastructure.

Latency-critical real-time inference with strict SLA requirements, as the block-sparse CUDA kernels are significantly harder to optimize than standard dense attention and show higher variance in wall-clock time.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Zaheer et al. (Google Research, NeurIPS 2020), BigBird was proved to be a universal approximator of sequence-to-sequence functions and Turing complete — theoretical properties that full-attention transformers possess and that no prior sparse-attention model had formally established.

target.notes: Pretrained encoder fine-tuned for downstream heads: sequence/token classification, extractive/abstractive summarization, span QA. Target is task-dependent (categorical labels, span indices, or generated text); the model itself produces contextual token representations.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ labeled examples to fine-tune; relies on large-scale pretraining
data_regime.dimensionality: effective context up to 4096 tokens at O(n) attention memory vs O(n^2) for dense; offers no benefit below ~1024 tokens

features.interpretability: low - deep self-attention encoder, no native feature attribution
features.notes: Tokenized sequences; sequence length must be divisible by block size (default 64), forcing padding/truncation. Also applicable to non-text long discrete sequences (e.g. genomic DNA, 1000-4096 nucleotides).

assumptions: Signal is distributed across long-range positions that exceed a 512-token window
Sufficient pretraining-domain overlap for transfer to be effective
Inputs long enough (>~1024 tokens) that sparse attention pays off
contraindicated_when: Sequences fit within 512 tokens - dense BERT variants match or exceed accuracy with simpler infra
Latency-critical real-time SLA - block-sparse CUDA kernels are hard to optimize and have high wall-clock variance
Small labeled datasets with no usable pretrained checkpoint
Strict run-to-run reproducibility needed without fixing the random-attention seed
Tabular or non-sequential data

children.name: Sparse Transformer
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Longformer's dilated sliding window or Reformer's LSH-based dynamic bucketing, Sparse Transformer uses fixed, predetermined strided and local attention masks that factorize the full attention matrix into two complementary sparse patterns, reducing complexity to O(n√n) without any content-dependent routing.
strengths: Reduces self-attention from O(n²) to O(n√n) by decomposing the attention matrix into strided (every √n-th token) and local (contiguous block) sub-patterns, enabling sequences up to 16,384 tokens on the same hardware that limits vanilla Transformers to ~1,024.
Requires no hashing or learned routing at inference time — the sparse masks are statically defined, making latency predictable and the custom block-sparse CUDA kernels highly optimizable.

Demonstrated strong generative quality on images, audio waveforms (raw), and text with the same architecture, proving the fixed-pattern approach generalizes across modalities without task-specific tuning.
weaknesses: Fixed attention patterns must be chosen before training and cannot adapt: if a task requires attending to a token 900 positions back but the stride is 64, that connection is permanently absent from every layer.

Requires custom block-sparse GPU kernels incompatible with standard dense matrix libraries, making it harder to deploy on inference hardware lacking those kernels and impossible to fine-tune from a dense pre-trained checkpoint.

Two-head decomposition (strided + local) means any single layer covers only a subset of positions; full receptive field requires stacking multiple layers, increasing depth and training cost compared to architectures that achieve global reach per layer.
recommended_for: Generative modeling of long sequences with strong spatial or temporal locality (e.g., raw audio at 24 kHz, high-resolution images in raster order) where neighboring tokens dominate relevance and stride patterns naturally capture periodicity.
Research contexts requiring a simple, mathematically transparent sparse baseline — the two fixed masks make ablation studies straightforward compared to learned or hash-based sparsity.
not_recommended_for: Tasks where arbitrary long-range dependencies are semantically critical and unpredictable at design time (e.g., legal contract cross-referencing, multi-hop QA), where fixed stride patterns will systematically miss relevant distant tokens.

Production deployments on standard inference infrastructure (TensorRT, ONNX, TPUs) without custom kernel support, where the block-sparse operation falls back to dense computation and negates all efficiency gains.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Rewon Child, Scott Gray, Alec Radford, and Ilya Sutskever (OpenAI, 2019) in 'Generating Long Sequences with Sparse Transformers', the model trained on raw ImageNet pixels (64×64) and CIFAR-10 achieved state-of-the-art log-likelihood at the time — predating GPT-2's public release by weeks and sharing several authors with it.

target.notes: Autoregressive generative model: predicts next token over a discrete vocabulary (categorical/multinomial) for text/discretized audio, or next pixel/sample value. Trained for density estimation / sequence generation, not for supervised tabular targets.

data_regime.rows: needs large amounts of sequential data (long-sequence corpora, raw audio, raster-ordered images)
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for very long contexts (up to ~16,384 tokens) where vanilla O(n^2) attention is infeasible; complexity O(n*sqrt(n))

features.interpretability: low; deep stacked attention layers with fixed sparse masks
features.notes: Inputs must be ordered sequences with strong spatial/temporal locality so fixed strided + local masks capture relevant structure. Sequence order and stride choice (~sqrt(n)) must match the data's periodicity.

assumptions: Relevant dependencies are either local (nearby tokens) or fall on a fixed stride pattern decided before training
Token relevance has predictable structure (locality/periodicity); arbitrary unpredictable long-range links are not required
Deployment hardware supports block-sparse kernels (otherwise it degrades to dense compute)
loss: autoregressive cross-entropy / log-likelihood (next-token negative log-loss)
contraindicated_when: Arbitrary, design-time-unpredictable long-range dependencies are semantically critical (multi-hop QA, contract cross-referencing) - fixed stride masks systematically miss distant tokens
Sequences are short enough for dense attention (no efficiency benefit)
Production inference on TensorRT/ONNX/TPU without custom block-sparse kernel support (falls back to dense, negating gains)
You need to fine-tune from a dense pre-trained checkpoint (incompatible sparse structure)
Inputs lack inherent sequential order or locality

children.name: XLNet
children.diff_siblings: Unlike BERT (masked autoencoding) and GPT-style models (left-to-right autoregressive), XLNet trains over all permutations of the factorization order via permutation language modeling, capturing bidirectional context without masking tokens, and incorporates segment-level recurrence from Transformer-XL for longer effective context.
strengths: Eliminates BERT's pretrain-finetune discrepancy: no [MASK] tokens are used, so the input distribution at fine-tuning matches pretraining exactly.
Models dependencies between predicted tokens within the same sequence via autoregressive factorization, which BERT's conditional independence assumption over masked positions cannot capture.
Segment recurrence from Transformer-XL extends the effective context window beyond a single fixed-length segment by caching hidden states from previous segments.
weaknesses: Permutation over all factorization orders makes training significantly more computationally expensive than BERT for equivalent model size and data.
The two-stream attention mechanism (query stream + content stream) roughly doubles memory and compute during pretraining compared to standard self-attention.
Has been largely superseded in practice by RoBERTa, DeBERTa, and decoder-only models (GPT family), leaving a narrower niche where its specific advantages matter.
recommended_for: Reading-comprehension and extractive QA tasks (e.g., SQuAD, RACE) where capturing long-range dependencies between question and passage context is critical.
Sentiment analysis and natural language inference on datasets where fine-tuning distribution must closely match pretraining (no artificial [MASK] tokens in input).
not_recommended_for: Open-ended text generation tasks, where pure left-to-right autoregressive models (GPT family) are architecturally better suited and simpler to sample from.
Resource-constrained environments: the two-stream attention and segment recurrence overhead make XLNet impractical when memory or training budget is tight compared to BERT-base.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Zhilin Yang, Zihang Dai, Yiming Yang, Jaime Carbonell, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, and Quoc V. Le (NeurIPS 2019), XLNet outperformed BERT on 20 NLP benchmarks at release, including a +7.6 point gain on the RACE reading-comprehension dataset, using a model pretrained on 32.89 GB of text with 512 TPU v3 chips for 2.5 days.

target.notes: Pretrained encoder fine-tuned for sequence/token classification, NLI, and extractive QA (span start/end). 'none' covers using it purely for contextual text embeddings.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of labeled examples to fine-tune effectively; benefits from large unlabeled pretraining corpus (provided by the pretrained checkpoint)
data_regime.dimensionality: high-dimensional token sequences; effective context extended beyond a single fixed segment via Transformer-XL segment recurrence

features.interpretability: low; deep attention stack with two-stream (query+content) attention, predictions are not directly attributable to inputs
features.notes: Input is raw/tokenized natural-language text (SentencePiece). No artificial [MASK] tokens used, so fine-tuning input distribution matches pretraining exactly.

assumptions: task is monolingual/text-domain matching the pretraining corpus
labeled fine-tuning data is representative of deployment distribution
long-range dependencies between tokens carry the predictive signal (where XLNet's permutation LM and segment recurrence pay off)
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss for classification
span boundary cross-entropy for extractive QA
permutation language modeling objective (pretraining)
contraindicated_when: open-ended autoregressive text generation is the goal (decoder-only GPT-family is better suited and simpler to sample)
memory or training budget is tight (two-stream attention and permutation training roughly double cost vs BERT-base)
small labeled datasets without a suitable pretrained checkpoint
non-text tabular/numeric data
a stronger encoder (RoBERTa, DeBERTa) suffices for the same task with less overhead

children.name: ALBERT
children.diff_siblings: ALBERT reduces BERT's parameter count 18x by factorizing the embedding matrix into two smaller matrices (E << H) and sharing all transformer layer weights across depth, whereas siblings like RoBERTa and XLNet scale parameters freely per layer.
strengths: Cross-layer weight sharing cuts memory footprint dramatically — ALBERT-xxlarge (235M effective parameters) fits where BERT-large (340M) does not, enabling deployment on memory-constrained hardware.

Sentence Order Prediction (SOP) pretraining task directly models inter-sentence coherence by distinguishing swapped consecutive segments, yielding measurable gains (~+2% SQuAD2.0, ~+1.7% RACE) over BERT's Next Sentence Prediction.
Factorized embeddings decouple vocabulary embedding size E from hidden size H, allowing H to scale without proportionally inflating the embedding lookup table.
weaknesses: Cross-layer parameter sharing increases sequential computation per forward pass — inference latency is higher than DistilBERT and MiniLM despite the smaller parameter count.
Sharing weights across all layers constrains representational diversity: each layer applies the same transformation, which can limit the model's ability to learn layer-specialized features.
Pretraining cost remains high; the parameter reduction speeds up training relative to parameter count but ALBERT-xxlarge still requires substantial compute to reach competitive performance.
recommended_for: Memory-constrained on-device or edge NLP deployments (e.g., mobile inference) where peak RAM is the bottleneck and throughput requirements are moderate.

Multi-sentence understanding tasks — reading comprehension (SQuAD), natural language inference, and discourse-level classification — where the SOP pretraining objective directly benefits coherence modeling.
not_recommended_for: Latency-sensitive production APIs requiring sub-10ms inference per request, where DistilBERT or MiniLM are faster despite lower accuracy on benchmarks.
Single-sentence classification tasks (e.g., short-text sentiment) where inter-sentence pretraining provides no benefit and a smaller, faster model trained with MLM alone suffices.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Lan et al. (2020) at ICLR, ALBERT-xxlarge set new state-of-the-art records on GLUE, RACE, and SQuAD benchmarks with 18x fewer parameters than BERT-large, yet its cross-layer sharing made each individual forward pass slower — a counter-intuitive result where fewer parameters do not imply faster inference.

target.notes: Pretrained encoder; fine-tuned with a task head for text classification, NLI, token labeling (NER), or extractive QA (span start/end). Target attaches to the head, not the backbone; also usable as a frozen sentence/token embedding extractor (target=none).

data_regime.rows: self-supervised pretraining needs massive unlabeled corpora (done by provider); fine-tuning works on hundreds to low-thousands of labeled examples per class
data_regime.dimensionality: input is token sequences (typ. <=512 tokens); not a tabular p-vs-n method
