features.interpretability: low — deep contextual transformer; attention weights are not faithful explanations
features.notes: Consumes raw text via SentencePiece tokenization; no manual scaling/feature engineering. Cross-layer weight sharing reduces parameter memory but raises per-forward sequential compute vs distilled models.

assumptions: task benefits from contextual / pretrained language representations
input is natural language within the max sequence length
fine-tuning domain is reasonably close to pretraining corpus distribution
multi-sentence / discourse structure present when leaning on SOP-pretrained coherence
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss (classification, token labeling)
span start+end cross-entropy (extractive QA)
masked language modeling + sentence-order-prediction (pretraining)
contraindicated_when: latency-critical inference (sub-10ms): weight sharing makes it slower than DistilBERT/MiniLM despite fewer params
single-sentence short-text classification where SOP gives no edge and a smaller MLM-only model suffices
tabular/numeric or non-text data
no GPU and no access to a pretrained checkpoint
tasks needing layer-specialized features (shared weights limit representational diversity across depth)

children.name: DistilBERT
children.diff_siblings: Unlike full BERT (same architecture, all 12 layers) or ALBERT (parameter sharing across layers), DistilBERT applies knowledge distillation during pre-training to train a 6-layer student model that mimics BERT's internal representations via a triple loss (MLM + distillation + cosine embedding), discarding token-type embeddings and the pooler.
strengths: Retains 97% of BERT-base GLUE score with 40% fewer parameters (66M vs 110M), because the distillation loss transfers BERT's soft probability outputs, not just labels
60% faster inference than BERT-base on CPU due to halved layer count, making real-time deployment feasible without GPU
General-purpose: distilled at the pre-training stage, so the same checkpoint fine-tunes across tasks (classification, NER, QA) without task-specific re-distillation
weaknesses: Drops ~3 points on fine-grained sentiment (SST-5: 0.532 vs BERT 0.549) because fewer layers reduce capacity for subtle semantic distinctions
Removing token-type embeddings limits direct applicability to sentence-pair tasks (NLI, QA) that rely on segment A/B separation without adaptation
Distillation requires access to the full BERT teacher during pre-training, making custom domain-specific distillation computationally expensive (same corpus, same pre-training budget as BERT)
recommended_for: On-device or latency-sensitive NLP pipelines (e.g., mobile text classification, browser-side inference) where CPU inference under 100ms is required and a 2-3% accuracy trade-off is acceptable
High-throughput production APIs serving thousands of short-text classification or NER requests per second, where BERT's latency creates a bottleneck
not_recommended_for: Tasks demanding maximum accuracy on complex reasoning or fine-grained semantics (e.g., multi-hop QA, SQuAD v2 with unanswerable questions), where the full 12-layer BERT or RoBERTa meaningfully outperforms
Scenarios where the teacher model is unavailable or the target domain is highly specialized (biomedical, legal), and no domain-adapted distilled checkpoint exists
children.curiosity: Introduced by Sanh, Debut, Chaumond, and Wolf at Hugging Face (arXiv:1910.01108, 2019), DistilBERT was trained on the same corpus as BERT-base using a triple loss that combines masked language modeling, a soft-label distillation loss on the teacher's output distribution, and a cosine embedding loss aligning the student's and teacher's hidden-state vectors layer by layer.

target.notes: Fine-tuned for supervised text tasks: sequence classification (binary/multiclass sentiment, topic), token classification/NER, extractive QA span prediction. Without a task head it produces contextual embeddings (target none).

data_regime.rows: leverages massive self-supervised pretraining; fine-tunes well on a few hundred to a few thousand labeled examples
data_regime.dimensionality: fixed 768-dim contextual representations; max 512 tokens per sequence
needs: GPU helpful for fine-tuning but CPU-feasible for inference (a core design goal)

features.interpretability: low; attention weights give partial introspection but predictions are not directly explainable
features.notes: Consumes raw tokenized text (WordPiece); no manual feature engineering or scaling. Dropped token-type embeddings, so sentence-pair tasks (NLI, QA segment A/B) need adaptation.

assumptions: target text language/domain resembles the pretraining corpus (general English); specialized domains (biomedical, legal) degrade without domain-adapted checkpoints
sequences fit within 512 tokens; long documents must be truncated or chunked
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss for classification and token classification
span start/end cross-entropy for extractive QA
pretraining used masked-LM + distillation (KL on soft logits) + cosine embedding loss
contraindicated_when: maximum accuracy on fine-grained semantics or complex multi-hop reasoning is required (full BERT/RoBERTa/larger models outperform)
inputs are non-text (tabular, image, time-series)
very long documents exceeding the 512-token window without chunking
highly specialized domain with no available distilled domain checkpoint and a teacher model is unavailable

children.name: DeBERTa
children.diff_siblings: Unlike BERT (absolute position embeddings, fused content+position attention) and RoBERTa (same architecture, more data/longer training), DeBERTa encodes content and position in two separate vectors and computes three disentangled attention matrices (content-to-content, content-to-position, position-to-content), then restores absolute position only at the final enhanced mask decoder before the MLM softmax.
strengths: Disentangled relative position attention lets the model capture syntactic dependencies (e.g., subject-verb agreement across intervening clauses) that fused absolute-position encodings systematically miss.
Matches or exceeds RoBERTa-Large on MNLI (+0.9%), SQuAD 2.0 (+2.3%) and RACE (+3.6%) while using only half the pre-training data (78 GB vs 160 GB), meaning higher data efficiency per FLOP.
DeBERTa-v3 variants (using ELECTRA-style replaced-token-detection pre-training) achieve strong NLU scores even at the base scale, making fine-tuning practical on a single GPU.
weaknesses: Disentangled attention requires storing separate content and position key/value matrices, increasing the forward-pass memory footprint and adding ~30% latency compared to an equivalently sized RoBERTa.

The enhanced mask decoder that reintroduces absolute position is tightly coupled to masked language modeling; adapting the architecture for autoregressive or encoder-decoder generation requires non-trivial redesign.

Cross-lingual transfer lags behind XLM-RoBERTa: multilingual DeBERTa variants underperform XLM-RoBERTa on cross-lingual benchmarks because the disentangled positional scheme was designed and tuned for monolingual English pre-training.
recommended_for: High-stakes NLU classification tasks (NLI, sentiment, document classification) on English text where label-efficient fine-tuning matters and a fixed context window of 512 tokens is sufficient.

Reading-comprehension and extractive QA (SQuAD-style) where precise span localization benefits from the model's ability to jointly attend to token content and relative distance without conflating the two.
not_recommended_for: Multilingual or cross-lingual settings where the model must transfer to low-resource languages, because XLM-RoBERTa's larger multilingual corpus gives it a decisive advantage in those scenarios.
Text generation tasks (summarization, machine translation, dialogue) that require an autoregressive decoder, since DeBERTa is a pure encoder and has no built-in generation head.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Pengcheng He, Xiaodong Liu, Jianfeng Gao, and Weizhu Chen at Microsoft Research (arXiv 2006.03654, 2020; ICLR 2021), DeBERTa was the first model to surpass human performance on the SuperGLUE benchmark, scoring 90.3 against the human baseline of 89.8, an achievement announced in June 2021.

target.notes: Encoder fine-tuned with a task head: sequence classification (binary/multiclass/multilabel), token classification (NER, sequence labeling), or span extraction (start/end logits for extractive QA). No native regression head but a linear head can output continuous scores. Not for generation (no decoder).

data_regime.rows: label-efficient: usable fine-tuning from a few hundred labeled examples thanks to pretraining; thousands+ for robust high-stakes NLU
data_regime.dimensionality: fixed 512-token context window per example; no tabular p/n notion
needs: GPU for fine-tuning and low-latency inference

features.interpretability: low: attention weights and disentangled position matrices are not faithful explanations; treat as a black box requiring post-hoc tools (SHAP, integrated gradients)
features.notes: Consumes raw English text via subword tokenization; no manual feature engineering, scaling, or distributional preprocessing needed. Best on monolingual English.

assumptions: text fits within the 512-token context window (long documents need chunking or sliding windows)
task is discriminative/extractive, not generative
domain is reasonably close to pretraining text or enough labeled data exists to adapt
predominantly English text
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss (sequence and token classification)
binary cross-entropy (multilabel)
span start/end cross-entropy (extractive QA)
contraindicated_when: multilingual or cross-lingual transfer to low-resource languages (XLM-RoBERTa is the stronger choice)
text generation, summarization, translation, or dialogue (encoder-only, no autoregressive decoder)
inputs far exceeding 512 tokens where long-context modeling is essential
non-text or tabular data
tight latency/memory budgets (~30% slower and heavier than equivalent RoBERTa due to disentangled attention)
tiny datasets with no pretrained-domain overlap and no GPU

children.name: LLaMA / Mistral
children.diff_siblings: Unlike GPT-style or T5-style siblings, LLaMA/Mistral are open-weight decoder-only transformers that replace absolute positional embeddings with RoPE, use SwiGLU activations instead of ReLU/GELU, and apply RMSNorm pre-normalization — a combination that maximizes training stability and inference throughput per parameter.
strengths: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) reduces the KV-cache memory footprint proportionally to the number of groups, enabling longer context at the same hardware budget compared to standard multi-head attention.
Mistral's Sliding Window Attention (SWA) gives O(W) memory cost per layer instead of O(n), making inference on sequences of 8k+ tokens feasible on a single consumer GPU.
Open weights and permissive licenses (LLaMA 3 Community License, Apache 2.0 for Mistral) allow full fine-tuning, quantization, and deployment without API dependencies.
weaknesses: No built-in retrieval or long-term memory: context is bounded by the fixed window (4k–128k depending on variant), and information outside that window is lost entirely.
Pretraining data and alignment details are only partially disclosed, making systematic bias audits difficult and reproducibility of safety properties impossible.
SWA in Mistral can produce unusually high initial loss when fine-tuned at sequence lengths beyond the pretraining window, requiring careful length-matched training to avoid instability.
recommended_for: Instruction-following assistants and chat applications that need full local deployment — LLaMA 3 8B/70B fine-tuned with LoRA on domain-specific QA pairs routinely matches proprietary APIs at a fraction of the cost.

Domain-specific text generation where the base model is fine-tuned on structured corpora (medical, legal, code) with sequence lengths under 8k, exploiting SwiGLU's superior gradient flow over ReLU for faster convergence.
not_recommended_for: Tasks requiring verified factual grounding over very long documents (>128k tokens) where retrieval-augmented architectures outperform pure context-window extension.
Production deployments with strict regulatory auditability requirements where the partial disclosure of training data and RLHF details of LLaMA/Mistral makes compliance certification impractical.
children.curiosity: LLaMA 1 was introduced by Touvron et al. at Meta AI (2023) with the explicit goal of showing that a 7B model trained on more tokens than the Chinchilla-optimal recipe outperforms a 13B model trained on fewer tokens — empirically validating compute-optimal scaling laws for open-weight LLMs.
keywords: running llm on your own gpu

target.notes: Autoregressive next-token prediction over discrete vocabulary; target is the sequence of tokens itself, not a tabular label. Adaptable to classification/extraction via instruction framing, but native objective is generative.

data_regime.rows: Pretrained on trillions of tokens; downstream needs only hundreds-to-thousands of labeled examples for LoRA/SFT (works in low-data downstream regimes by transfer)
data_regime.dimensionality: Fixed context window 4k-128k tokens depending on variant; information outside the window is lost
needs: GPU (consumer-grade feasible for 7B-8B quantized; A100/H100 class for 70B+ full fine-tune)
VRAM scales with KV-cache and sequence length (GQA/SWA mitigate)
for full pretraining: massive labeled+unlabeled text corpus, not realistic to retrain

features.interpretability: low: billions of parameters, attention attribution is not faithful explanation; no native feature importances
features.notes: Input must be tokenized natural language / code; not for tabular numeric/categorical data unless serialized to text. Sliding Window Attention (Mistral) needs length-matched fine-tuning to avoid loss spikes beyond pretraining window.

assumptions: Task expressible as text-in / text-out (prompting or instruction tuning)
Relevant knowledge fits inside the context window or is supplied via RAG; no implicit long-term memory
Pretraining distribution covers the target domain language/jargon, else heavy fine-tuning needed
loss: cross-entropy / token-level log-loss (next-token prediction)
SFT cross-entropy on instruction-response pairs
preference objectives via DPO/RLHF for alignment (post-hoc)
contraindicated_when: tabular prediction with structured numeric/categorical features (gradient-boosted trees dominate)
verified factual grounding over very long documents (>128k tokens) where retrieval-augmented architectures win
strict regulatory auditability: partial disclosure of training data and alignment makes compliance certification impractical
small-data tasks with no transfer benefit and tight latency/cost budgets where a small classifier suffices
needs calibrated probability estimates or deterministic outputs

children.name: ELECTRA
children.diff_siblings: Unlike BERT and RoBERTa (which train on masked language modeling over ~15% of tokens) and GPT (which uses autoregressive generation), ELECTRA trains a discriminator to detect replaced tokens across all input positions using a generator-discriminator framework, making every token contribute to the pre-training loss.
strengths: Compute efficiency: achieves BERT-Large GLUE performance using roughly 1/4 the FLOPs by computing loss over all tokens instead of only the 15% masked subset
Small-model advantage: ELECTRA-Small outperforms GPT and BERT-Base on GLUE despite having far fewer parameters, making it viable for low-resource deployment
Richer contextual signal: the replaced-token-detection objective forces the encoder to model subtle plausibility distinctions rather than just vocabulary reconstruction from a [MASK] surrogate
weaknesses: Generator-discriminator size coupling: if the generator is too strong it makes replacement nearly undetectable, degrading discriminator learning; finding the right size ratio (~1/4 of discriminator capacity) requires tuning
Sentence embedding degradation: the RTD objective causes a representation drop in later layers, leading to poor out-of-the-box semantic similarity scores without additional fine-tuning
Fine-tuning variance: downstream task performance can fluctuate substantially across fine-tuning runs from the same checkpoint, requiring multiple runs and averaging
recommended_for: Text classification and token labeling tasks (NER, sentiment, QA) under tight compute budgets, where ELECTRA-Small or ELECTRA-Base delivers BERT-Large quality at a fraction of the training cost
Domains requiring domain-adaptive pre-training from scratch (e.g., biomedical, legal) where the all-token loss signal accelerates convergence on limited domain corpora
not_recommended_for: Semantic textual similarity or sentence-embedding tasks where cosine distance over raw encoder outputs is required, as the RTD objective distorts the geometry of later-layer representations

Generative tasks such as text completion, summarization, or translation, because ELECTRA's discriminator produces no language generation capability and the generator component is discarded after pre-training
children.curiosity: Introduced by Clark, Luong, Le, and Manning (2020) at ICLR, ELECTRA achieves a GLUE score of 89.4 with ELECTRA-Large trained for 400K steps, matching RoBERTa trained for 2M steps — demonstrating that the replaced-token-detection signal is roughly 4x more sample-efficient than masked language modeling.

target.notes: Pretrained encoder; target depends on fine-tuning head. Sequence classification (binary/multiclass), token classification (NER, per-token multiclass), and span extraction (QA) are the native downstream targets. Pretraining itself (replaced-token-detection) is self-supervised with no labeled target.

data_regime.rows: Fine-tuning works on a few hundred to thousands of labeled examples per task; pretraining or domain-adaptive continued pretraining needs large unlabeled corpora
data_regime.dimensionality: Fixed-length token sequences (typically <=512 tokens); handles high-dimensional sparse text via subword tokenization
needs: pretrained checkpoint (or large unlabeled corpus to pretrain)

features.interpretability: low; deep transformer encoder with attention, no direct feature attribution without post-hoc methods
features.notes: Raw text input via WordPiece/subword tokenization; no manual feature engineering or scaling. More compute-efficient than BERT for equivalent quality, viable on tighter budgets.

assumptions: Input is natural-language text amenable to subword tokenization
Sufficient task-relevant labeled data for fine-tuning, or a domain-matched pretrained checkpoint
Sequence length within the model context window (truncation hurts long documents)
loss: pretraining: replaced-token-detection binary cross-entropy over all positions (discriminator)
fine-tuning: cross-entropy / log-loss for classification and token labeling
span cross-entropy for extractive QA
contraindicated_when: Task requires text generation, summarization, translation, or completion (discriminator has no decoder/generation capability)
Sentence-embedding or semantic-similarity tasks using raw cosine distance over encoder outputs (RTD objective distorts later-layer geometry)
Non-text or short non-linguistic inputs where a transformer LM provides no advantage over simpler models
No GPU available or extremely small labeled data with no usable pretrained checkpoint

target.notes: Umbrella family for text tasks. Encoder-only (BERT/RoBERTa) heads emit categorical labels per sequence/token (classification, NER, extractive QA span indices); encoder-decoder (T5/BART) and decoder-only (GPT) emit token sequences (translation, summarization, generation). Representation use (sentence embeddings, semantic search) has target=none.

data_regime.rows: pre-trained backbone removes the from-scratch data requirement; fine-tuning works with 1k-10k labeled examples, few-shot/zero-shot possible with large decoders
data_regime.dimensionality: very high effective parameter count (110M+ for base); handles p>>n at the task level because representation is transferred, not learned from the task data
needs: GPU/TPU for fine-tuning and low-latency inference
large unlabeled pre-training corpus (provided by the backbone)

features.interpretability: low - distributed attention weights and dense embeddings are not directly attributable to input tokens; post-hoc attribution (attention rollout, integrated gradients) only approximate
features.notes: Input must be subword-tokenized (BPE/WordPiece/SentencePiece); raw discrete token sequences, not tabular numeric. Performance degrades when domain jargon, rare languages, or code are poorly covered by the pre-training vocabulary, causing fragmented sub-word splits. Sequence length is the dominant cost axis.

assumptions: Task text distribution overlaps the pre-training corpus distribution (domain/language coverage); large shift requires continued pre-training
Relevant context fits within the context window (~512 tokens for BERT-class, a few k for many models) given O(n^2) attention
Sufficient labeled data for the supervised head, or a strong enough backbone for zero/few-shot
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss (sequence and token classification)
masked language modeling (MLM) and next-token (causal LM) cross-entropy for pre-training and generative fine-tuning
span boundary cross-entropy (extractive QA)
seq2seq teacher-forced cross-entropy with label smoothing (translation/summarization)
contrastive / cosine objectives for sentence-embedding variants
contraindicated_when: input is tabular numeric/categorical rather than natural-language text - tree ensembles dominate
strict edge/embedded latency or memory budget (base model ~110M params exceeds microcontroller RAM and adds hundreds of ms per call)
very long documents (>100k tokens) where quadratic full attention is infeasible without sparse/long-context variants (Longformer, BigBird)
tiny labeled data with no suitable pre-trained backbone for the language/domain
low-latency autoregressive generation of long outputs (sequential decoding is a throughput bottleneck)

children.name: Vision Transformers
children.diff_siblings: Applies a pure, unmodified Transformer encoder directly to fixed-size non-overlapping image patches with no convolutional inductive bias, relying entirely on global self-attention from the first layer — whereas siblings like Swin introduce local windowed attention hierarchies, DeiT adds distillation tokens, and MAE/BEiT build masked-reconstruction pretraining objectives on top of the same backbone.
strengths: Global self-attention from layer 1 captures long-range spatial dependencies that CNNs only approximate in deep layers, making it superior for tasks where distant regions are semantically related (e.g., medical image anomaly spanning the full scan)
Linear scalability with model size: ViT-L and ViT-H consistently improve with more parameters and pretraining data, unlike CNNs which plateau earlier on ImageNet-scale datasets

Transfer learning with minimal architectural changes — the same patch-embedding + CLS-token design fine-tunes across image classification, dense prediction (with decoder heads), and multimodal tasks without task-specific convolution modules
weaknesses: Requires very large pretraining corpora (JFT-300M or equivalent) to outperform CNNs; on datasets below ~1M samples, the absence of locality and translation-equivariance inductive biases causes overfitting without heavy regularization

Quadratic self-attention complexity O(N²) with respect to the number of patches makes full-resolution dense tasks (segmentation, detection on 1024×1024 inputs) memory-prohibitive without windowing tricks

Fixed patch size (e.g., 16×16) discards sub-patch spatial structure; fine-grained recognition tasks requiring pixel-level precision suffer compared to convolutional backbones that preserve multi-scale local texture
recommended_for: Large-scale image classification with millions of labeled or unlabeled images available for pretraining, where capturing global context (e.g., scene-level features in satellite or medical imaging) is more valuable than local edge detection

Multimodal architectures (vision-language models, CLIP-style contrastive learning) where a unified patch-sequence representation must be aligned with text token embeddings from a sibling Transformer encoder
not_recommended_for: Small datasets (fewer than ~100k images) without access to pretrained weights, where the lack of CNN-style inductive biases leads to poor generalization relative to a ResNet or EfficientNet baseline

Real-time inference on resource-constrained hardware (mobile, edge devices) with high-resolution inputs, since full self-attention over many patches has significantly higher FLOPs and memory footprint than equivalent MobileNet or EfficientNet-Lite models
children.curiosity: Introduced by Dosovitskiy et al. (Google Brain, 2020) in 'An Image is Worth 16x16 Words' (ICLR 2021), the original ViT-L/16 pretrained on JFT-300M achieved 88.55% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet — the first pure-Transformer model to surpass state-of-the-art CNNs on a standard vision benchmark without any convolutional layers.

children.name: ViT (Vision Transformer)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Swin Transformer (shifted local windows, hierarchical feature maps) and DeiT (distillation token, CNN-teacher training), vanilla ViT divides the image into fixed 16x16 patches, encodes each as a flat linear embedding with a learnable [CLS] token, and runs global self-attention across all patches every layer — no locality, no hierarchy.
strengths: Global receptive field from the first layer: every patch attends to every other patch simultaneously, capturing long-range dependencies that CNNs reach only in deep layers.
Scales supralinearly with data and compute: on JFT-300M, ViT-H/14 surpasses ResNet-based models with 4x fewer FLOPS at inference, a gap that widens as pretraining data grows.

Architecture-agnostic patch interface: the same linear projection layer accepts any modality that can be rasterized into fixed-size patches (images, spectrograms, video frames) without structural changes.
weaknesses: No built-in inductive biases (translation equivariance, locality): requires ~14M+ images to learn spatial structure from scratch; on ImageNet alone without pretraining, test accuracy drops ~10–15 pp vs. comparably sized ResNets.

Quadratic attention cost with respect to sequence length: a 224x224 image at patch size 16 yields 196 tokens (manageable), but doubling resolution to 448x448 quadruples the sequence length and 16x the attention matrix memory.

Uniform patch grid ignores object boundaries: patches straddle edges without awareness of semantic content, making dense prediction tasks (segmentation, detection) structurally awkward without architectural add-ons like FPN heads.
recommended_for: Large-scale image classification with a pretraining corpus exceeding 100M images (JFT-300M, LAION-5B), where ViT's capacity and global attention yield state-of-the-art accuracy without locality assumptions.

Transfer learning to downstream vision tasks when a pretrained ViT backbone (e.g., ViT-L/16) is fine-tuned on a target dataset of a few thousand labeled examples, leveraging rich patch-level representations learned at scale.
not_recommended_for: Training from scratch on small datasets (fewer than ~1M images) without strong augmentation: ViT overfits or underfits compared to ResNets of equivalent parameter count due to the absence of spatial inductive bias.

Real-time inference on high-resolution inputs (e.g., 1024x1024 medical images or satellite imagery) where the quadratic attention cost becomes a hard memory and latency constraint without patch-size compromises.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Dosovitskiy et al. at Google Brain in 2020 ('An Image is Worth 16x16 Words', arXiv:2010.11929), ViT was initially outperformed by ResNets on ImageNet when trained from scratch — the paper itself acknowledged this, noting that the advantage emerged only when pretraining on the proprietary JFT-300M (303M images) dataset.

target.notes: Primary use is supervised image classification (softmax over classes); also serves as a backbone producing patch/[CLS] embeddings (target none) for downstream transfer, detection, segmentation.

data_regime.rows: needs very large labeled or weakly-labeled image corpora to train from scratch (~14M+, ideally 100M+ like JFT-300M / LAION); fine-tuning a pretrained backbone works on a few thousand labeled images
data_regime.dimensionality: high-dimensional raw pixel inputs reduced to a fixed token grid (e.g. 196 tokens at 224x224, patch 16); attention cost is quadratic in token count

features.interpretability: low: distributed self-attention representations, no semantic patch boundaries; attention maps give only rough saliency
features.notes: Inputs are fixed-size rasterized patches (images, video frames, spectrograms) linearly embedded; requires consistent input resolution / patch size and standard image normalization. Resolution drives sequence length and memory.

assumptions: Abundant pretraining data to compensate for the lack of locality/translation-equivariance inductive biases
Inputs cleanly tileable into a uniform fixed-size patch grid
Objects/semantics need not align with patch boundaries (uniform grid ignores edges)
loss: cross-entropy / softmax log-loss for classification
self-supervised / contrastive or masked-image objectives when used as a pretrained backbone
distillation loss in DeiT-style training variants
contraindicated_when: Training from scratch on small datasets (<~1M images) without strong augmentation or pretrained weights: underperforms equivalently sized CNNs
Tabular, low-dimensional, or non-rasterizable data with no spatial/patch structure
Real-time or memory-constrained inference on high-resolution inputs (e.g. 1024x1024 medical/satellite) where quadratic attention cost dominates
Strong locality/translation-equivariance is required and data is limited (CNN inductive bias preferable)

children.name: Swin Transformer
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ViT and DeiT, which apply global self-attention across all patches (O(n²) complexity), Swin Transformer partitions the image into non-overlapping local windows and alternates between regular and shifted window partitioning across layers, enabling cross-window connections while keeping complexity linear in image size; it also progressively merges patches to produce hierarchical feature maps at multiple scales, a property absent in isotropic Vision Transformers.
strengths: Linear O(n) computational complexity with respect to image size, achieved by confining self-attention to fixed-size local windows (e.g., 7×7 patches) rather than computing global pairwise attention across all tokens.

Produces multi-scale feature pyramids through staged patch merging (4×, 8×, 16×, 32× downsampling), making it a drop-in convolutional backbone replacement for dense prediction heads like FPN or UperNet.

State-of-the-art on dense prediction benchmarks at the time of release: 58.7 box AP on COCO test-dev (object detection) and 53.5 mIoU on ADE20K (semantic segmentation), outperforming concurrent Vision Transformers on tasks requiring spatial detail.
weaknesses: Shifted window attention requires a specific masking mechanism to handle boundary conditions, adding implementation complexity and making the architecture harder to adapt to non-square or irregular input resolutions.

Window-local attention limits the receptive field per layer; long-range global dependencies accumulate slowly through depth, which can be insufficient for tasks like image retrieval or global scene understanding where ViT's full self-attention is beneficial.

Pre-training on large datasets (ImageNet-21K or JFT) is required to match peak performance; training from scratch on small datasets yields significantly lower accuracy than CNNs of equivalent parameter count.
recommended_for: High-resolution dense prediction tasks (instance segmentation, object detection, medical image segmentation) where multi-scale feature maps and linear complexity with respect to spatial resolution are critical, e.g., 3D CT/MRI volumes processed patch-by-patch.

General-purpose vision backbone replacement in pipelines originally designed for CNNs, particularly when the task benefits from both local texture (window attention) and hierarchical spatial abstractions (patch merging stages).
not_recommended_for: Global image-level representation tasks such as image retrieval or few-shot classification, where full pairwise self-attention across all tokens (as in ViT) captures long-range correlations more directly without the windowing bottleneck.

Latency-critical edge deployment on hardware without optimized window-attention kernels, where a lightweight CNN (MobileNet, EfficientNet) or a distilled isotropic ViT offers a better accuracy-per-millisecond trade-off.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Ze Liu, Yutong Lin, Yue Cao et al. from Microsoft Research Asia (2021), Swin Transformer won best paper (Marr Prize) at ICCV 2021 and accumulated over 15,000 citations within three years, making it one of the fastest-cited computer vision papers in history.

target.notes: Supervised image classification head (softmax over classes), but primarily used as a backbone feeding task-specific heads (detection boxes/masks, segmentation maps); target depends on the head, not the backbone.

data_regime.rows: needs large labeled data; requires ImageNet-1K scale for classification and benefits heavily from ImageNet-21K/JFT pre-training, fine-tunes on smaller downstream sets
data_regime.dimensionality: high-dimensional raw pixel input; scales linearly with image resolution (windowed attention) so handles high-resolution images better than isotropic ViT

features.interpretability: low; deep attention backbone, no per-feature coefficients, only post-hoc attention/saliency maps
features.notes: Consumes raw RGB images partitioned into non-overlapping patches; expects standard normalization and roughly square inputs; produces multi-scale hierarchical feature pyramids (4x/8x/16x/32x) suitable for FPN/UperNet dense-prediction heads.

assumptions: spatial locality: nearby pixels/patches are most informative, so local window attention suffices for early layers
sufficient pre-training data or transfer weights available; training from scratch on small datasets underperforms CNNs of equal size
input is grid-structured image data with roughly square, fixed resolution
loss: cross-entropy / softmax log-loss for classification
task-head losses when used as backbone (e.g., box regression + classification for detection, per-pixel cross-entropy for segmentation)
contraindicated_when: tabular, sequence, or non-grid data (not image-structured)
small labeled datasets with no pre-trained weights, where CNNs (EfficientNet, ResNet) train more sample-efficiently
global image-level tasks like retrieval or few-shot classification where full-image self-attention (ViT) captures long-range correlations better
latency-critical edge deployment lacking optimized window-attention kernels, where lightweight CNNs give better accuracy-per-millisecond

children.name: DETR
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ViT and Swin, which are general-purpose vision backbones, DETR is an end-to-end object detection pipeline that replaces region proposals and NMS with a transformer encoder-decoder and a Hungarian bipartite matching loss that directly predicts a fixed set of bounding boxes as a set prediction problem.
strengths: Eliminates hand-designed post-processing steps (NMS, anchor generation), making the pipeline fully differentiable and end-to-end trainable.
Global self-attention in the encoder captures long-range context across the entire image, enabling strong reasoning about object relationships and scene layout.
Parallel decoding of all object queries at inference time produces a fixed set of predictions in a single forward pass, with no sequential region proposal step.
weaknesses: Requires ~500 training epochs to match Faster R-CNN accuracy because attention weights start uniform and take many iterations to focus on relevant image regions.
Poor detection of small objects in its native form due to operating on a single low-resolution feature map from the CNN backbone, lacking multi-scale feature pyramids.
Fixed number of learned object queries (typically 100) sets a hard ceiling on detectable objects per image, causing missed detections in dense scenes that exceed this count.
recommended_for: Uncluttered scenes with a moderate number of large or medium-sized objects (e.g., autonomous driving street-view with vehicles and pedestrians) where global context aids disambiguation.
Research or production pipelines where eliminating NMS tuning and anchor hyperparameters is a priority, and training compute is not the binding constraint.
not_recommended_for: Detection of small or densely packed objects (e.g., aerial imagery of crowds or satellite imagery of vehicles) where single-scale low-resolution features cause systematic misses.
Low-data or fast-iteration regimes where training from scratch for hundreds of epochs is impractical and convergence speed is critical.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Carion et al. (Facebook AI, 2020) in 'End-to-End Object Detection with Transformers' (arXiv:2005.12872), DETR was the first model to frame object detection purely as a set prediction problem, making it the first detector that requires zero NMS or anchor design — a property no CNN-based detector had achieved at the time.

target.notes: Set-prediction task: each image maps to an unordered set of (class label, bounding box) pairs. Per-query output combines a multiclass class distribution (objects + 'no-object' class) and a 4-vector box regression (normalized cx, cy, w, h). Not a scalar-target estimator; no target distribution moments apply.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of annotated images; native training requires ~500 epochs on COCO-scale data to match anchor-based detectors
data_regime.dimensionality: high-dimensional pixel input via CNN backbone; fixed set of ~100 learned object queries caps detectable objects per image
needs: large labeled detection dataset (per-object bounding boxes + classes)
long training budget unless using deformable/DN variants

features.interpretability: low: end-to-end transformer encoder-decoder; decoder cross-attention maps offer some visual explanation of which image regions each query attends to
features.notes: Consumes raw images through a CNN backbone (e.g., ResNet) producing a single low-resolution feature map plus positional encodings; no multi-scale feature pyramid in vanilla DETR, which drives weak small-object performance.

assumptions: object count per image stays below the fixed number of object queries (~100)
objects are large/medium relative to the single-scale backbone feature map
sufficient training compute and epochs available for attention to converge
loss: Hungarian bipartite matching loss (optimal assignment between predicted and ground-truth sets)
cross-entropy / log-loss on class predictions including the no-object class
L1 box regression loss
generalized IoU (GIoU) box loss
contraindicated_when: detecting small or densely packed objects (aerial/satellite, crowds) where single-scale low-resolution features systematically miss
scenes whose object count exceeds the fixed query budget
low-data or fast-iteration settings where hundreds of training epochs are impractical
tasks needing scalar/tabular prediction rather than spatial object localization

children.name: DINOv2
children.diff_siblings: It is distinguished from other Vision Transformers by its self-supervised pre-training on a massive curated dataset, which produces general-purpose visual features that excel at downstream tasks with minimal or no fine-tuning.
strengths: Produces powerful, general-purpose visual features applicable to many downstream tasks like classification, segmentation, and depth estimation.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance with simple linear classifiers, often outperforming supervised models.
Reduces the need for large labeled datasets and expensive fine-tuning for new tasks.
weaknesses: Extremely high computational cost and data requirements for the initial pre-training phase.
The large, uncurated pre-training dataset may encode societal biases into the learned features.
Performance can be lower on out-of-domain data (e.g., medical images) without further domain-adapted pre-training.
recommended_for: Feature extraction for a wide range of computer vision tasks, especially with limited labeled data.
Establishing strong performance baselines for tasks like image classification, semantic segmentation, and depth estimation.
not_recommended_for: Training from scratch in resource-constrained environments.
Real-time inference on low-power devices, although smaller distilled versions exist.
children.curiosity: Without any explicit 3D supervision, its learned features enabled it to achieve state-of-the-art results on monocular depth estimation benchmarks.

target.notes: Self-supervised feature extractor; produces frozen image embeddings, not predictions. A target enters only via a downstream head (linear probe / kNN) trained on top of the embeddings.

data_regime.rows: pretrained backbone is fixed; downstream tasks work with as few as tens-to-hundreds of labeled images per class via linear probe or kNN
data_regime.dimensionality: outputs dense patch + CLS embeddings (e.g. 384/768/1024-dim per ViT size); p>n at the head is fine since the head is linear and low-capacity
needs: GPU for inference (full feature extraction over images)
no large labeled data for downstream use; labeled data only for the lightweight head

features.interpretability: low - opaque ViT embeddings; downstream linear probe gives some attributability but features themselves are not interpretable
features.notes: Input is natural RGB images; uses ImageNet-style normalization and fixed patch tokenization. Embeddings are general-purpose and used frozen (no fine-tuning needed) as input to classifiers, segmentation heads, retrieval, or depth heads.

assumptions: Inputs resemble the natural-image pretraining distribution; out-of-domain inputs (medical, satellite, microscopy) degrade feature quality without domain-adapted pretraining
downstream task is reachable from frozen general-purpose features (linear separability / simple head sufficient)
contraindicated_when: Data is not images (tabular, text, audio, graph)
domain is far from natural images and no domain-adapted variant is available
real-time/low-power inference required without using distilled smaller variants
training from scratch under tight compute budget - DINOv2 is meant to be used pretrained, not retrained

children.name: MaxViT
children.diff_siblings: It is a hybrid architecture that serially combines convolutional blocks (MBConv) with a novel multi-axis attention mechanism, which decomposes attention into sparse local (blocked) and global (dilated/gridded) forms to achieve linear complexity and a global receptive field at every stage of the network.
strengths: Achieves linear computational complexity with respect to image size, making it scalable to high-resolution inputs.
Combines the local feature extraction strengths of CNNs with the global context modeling of Transformers at every hierarchical level.
Demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of vision tasks, including classification, object detection, and segmentation.
weaknesses: The multi-axis attention blocks can be computationally intensive compared to pure CNNs, especially for larger model variants.
Its performance can be sensitive to the specific arrangement and hyperparameters of the convolutional and attention blocks.
Like other Transformers, it generally requires large datasets for pre-training to achieve its peak performance and generalization.
recommended_for: High-resolution computer vision tasks like object detection, instance segmentation, and medical image analysis.
Use as a powerful and scalable backbone for a broad spectrum of visual recognition and generation tasks.
not_recommended_for: Low-resource settings where training data and computational budgets are highly constrained.
Tasks where pure translational equivariance, a strong inductive bias of CNNs, is critical and not complemented by attention.
children.curiosity: The core Multi-Axis attention module was designed to be so universal that its blocks can be stacked hierarchically, similar to a classic ResNet, allowing it to 'see' globally even in the earliest, high-resolution stages of the network (Tu et al., 2022).

target.notes: Backbone for image-level classification (multiclass/multilabel via head) or dense prediction (detection/segmentation) via task heads; the backbone itself produces visual feature maps, no target distribution assumptions.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ labeled images; peak performance requires large-scale pretraining (ImageNet-1k/21k) then fine-tune
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for high-resolution inputs; multi-axis attention gives linear complexity in image size so it scales where ViT global attention does not
needs: large labeled data or pretrained weights

features.interpretability: low; deep hybrid conv+attention backbone with no inherent feature attribution
features.notes: expects 2D pixel grids with standard normalization; benefits from data augmentation; hierarchical multi-stage feature maps suitable as detector/segmenter backbone

assumptions: Inputs are spatially structured 2D images (grid topology)
Sufficient pretraining data or transfer from a pretrained checkpoint is available
Local + global spatial context both carry signal (block + grid attention)
loss: cross-entropy for classification
task-head losses for detection/segmentation (e.g. focal, box regression, dice/CE)
contraindicated_when: Small datasets with no pretrained backbone (overfits; classical CNNs or smaller models fit better)
Tight compute/latency or edge budgets
Non-image or tabular data with no grid structure
Tasks where strong CNN translational-equivariance inductive bias alone suffices and attention adds no benefit

target.notes: Backbone family: pretrained as label-free or weakly-labeled representation learner, then fine-tuned with task heads. Native head is image-level multiclass/multilabel classification; with decoder heads supports dense prediction (segmentation, detection) and contrastive/multimodal embedding. No target distribution assumptions — optimizes via the attached head's loss.

data_regime.rows: needs very large image corpora to shine: typically >1M images for from-scratch training; below ~100k requires pretrained weights or strong augmentation/distillation (DeiT) to avoid overfitting
data_regime.dimensionality: high-dimensional pixel input flattened to N patches; self-attention is O(N^2) in patch count, so high-resolution dense tasks are memory-bound without windowing
needs: large labeled or unlabeled image data

features.interpretability: low — distributed attention representations; attention maps offer partial saliency cues but not faithful feature attributions
features.notes: Input is fixed-size non-overlapping patches (e.g. 16x16) with learned patch + positional embeddings; requires consistent input resolution and standard image normalization. Lacks CNN translation-equivariance/locality inductive bias, so benefits heavily from augmentation.

assumptions: enough pretraining data (or transferable pretrained weights) to compensate for absent convolutional inductive bias
fixed input resolution / patch grid consistent between pretraining and fine-tuning
global long-range spatial dependencies carry task-relevant signal
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss (classification head)
masked-image-modeling reconstruction (MAE/BEiT-style pretraining)
contrastive InfoNCE (CLIP-style multimodal alignment)
distillation loss (DeiT)
task-head losses for dense prediction (e.g. per-pixel cross-entropy, detection losses)
contraindicated_when: small datasets (<~100k images) with no pretrained weights — a ResNet/EfficientNet generalizes better
real-time/edge inference on high-resolution inputs where O(N^2) attention FLOPs are prohibitive (prefer MobileNet/EfficientNet-Lite)
fine-grained pixel-precise tasks where fixed patching discards sub-patch texture
non-image tabular/sequence data

children.name: Multimodal Transformers
children.diff_siblings: Unlike unimodal transformer variants (NLP-only, vision-only, audio-only), Multimodal Transformers process two or more modalities jointly — text, image, video, audio — through cross-modal attention or shared embedding spaces, enabling representations where information from one modality directly conditions the attention over another.
strengths: Cross-modal attention (co-attention, as in ViLBERT) lets each modality's representations be conditioned on the other at the token level, enabling fine-grained alignment beyond simple feature concatenation.
A single pre-trained backbone covers tasks spanning multiple modalities (VQA, image captioning, video-text retrieval) without task-specific unimodal encoders, reducing total parameter overhead.
Contrastive pre-training (CLIP-style) produces modality-agnostic embedding spaces that support zero-shot transfer: a text query can retrieve images never seen during fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Modality gap persists even after joint training — CLIP's global dot-product fusion lacks token-level alignment, causing failures on compositional or spatially precise queries.
Pre-training data requirements are orders of magnitude larger than unimodal baselines; FLAVA's smaller corpus visibly hurts performance relative to SimVLM trained on 1.8B examples.

Optimization is complex: balancing contrastive, masked-language, and masked-image objectives simultaneously requires careful round-robin sampling and is sensitive to batch size and learning-rate scheduling across modalities.
recommended_for: Visual question answering and image captioning where the answer depends on precise alignment between specific image regions and individual words in the question.
Cross-modal retrieval systems (e.g., searching a video archive with a natural-language query) that require a shared embedding space enabling similarity comparisons across different data types.
not_recommended_for: Purely unimodal tasks (text classification, single-image recognition) where the added cross-modal machinery introduces unnecessary compute cost and training complexity with no accuracy benefit.
Low-resource settings with fewer than tens of thousands of paired multimodal examples, where the cross-modal attention layers remain under-trained and unimodal fine-tuned models outperform.
children.curiosity: ViLBERT (Lu et al., NeurIPS 2019) introduced the co-attention layer — feeding keys and values from the visual stream into the text multi-head attention block and vice versa — establishing the dual-stream cross-modal paradigm that became the template for the subsequent generation of vision-language pre-trained models.

children.name: CLIP
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Florence (hierarchical, multi-resolution) or ALIGN (single dual-encoder with noisy web text), CLIP trains two completely separate encoders — one visual (ViT or ResNet) and one textual (Transformer) — with no cross-modal attention between them, relying solely on InfoNCE contrastive loss over 400 million image-text pairs to align both embedding spaces.
strengths: Zero-shot image classification without any task-specific fine-tuning: a natural-language label set at inference time is enough to define new categories
Embeddings from both modalities live in the same metric space, enabling cross-modal retrieval (image-to-text and text-to-image) by cosine similarity alone
Strong transfer: the shared embedding serves directly as a frozen feature extractor for downstream tasks such as DALL-E conditioning and Stable Diffusion's text encoder
weaknesses: No cross-modal attention inside the model — image and text never interact at intermediate layers, so compositional queries (e.g., 'a red cube left of a blue sphere') are poorly resolved
Fails on fine-grained intra-class distinctions (e.g., aircraft variants, flower species) because contrastive training on web captions favors coarse semantic alignment
Inherits societal biases from web-scraped data, including occupation-gender correlations and demographic misclassification documented in the original 2021 paper
recommended_for: Building zero-shot or few-shot image classifiers where label sets change frequently and collecting labeled training data per category is impractical
Cross-modal retrieval systems (e.g., searching a photo library with text queries) where a shared embedding space is more valuable than task-specific accuracy
not_recommended_for: Tasks requiring spatial or compositional reasoning over image regions, such as visual question answering about object relationships or referring expression comprehension
Fine-grained classification benchmarks (CUB-200 bird species, Stanford Cars) where intra-class visual differences are subtle and indistinguishable from global caption signals
children.curiosity: Introduced by Radford et al. at OpenAI (2021), CLIP matched the zero-shot accuracy of the original supervised ResNet-50 on ImageNet (76.2%) without using a single labeled ImageNet example — a result the authors considered unlikely before training.

target.notes: Pretraining objective is self-supervised contrastive alignment, not a labeled target. At inference it enables open-vocabulary multiclass classification with no training labels: candidate classes are supplied as natural-language prompts and scored by cosine similarity. No fixed label set is learned.

data_regime.rows: as a frozen pretrained model needs zero downstream rows for zero-shot; few-shot/linear-probe works with tens-to-hundreds per class. Pretraining itself required ~400M image-text pairs (not user-facing)
data_regime.dimensionality: outputs a fixed dense embedding (e.g. 512/768-d) per image and per text; downstream classifiers operate in this low-dim shared space
needs: pretrained weights (no user training needed for zero-shot)
paired image-text data only if fine-tuning

features.interpretability: low: dense embedding vectors with no inherently meaningful dimensions; decisions explained only via similarity scores against prompts
features.notes: Inputs are raw images plus free-text class prompts/queries. Prompt wording materially affects zero-shot accuracy (prompt engineering / ensembling). Image and text share one metric space, so cosine similarity is the operative measure.

assumptions: Target categories are describable in natural language and align with coarse web-caption semantics
Distinctions are global/semantic rather than fine-grained intra-class or spatial-compositional
Test distribution is reasonably covered by the broad web pretraining distribution
loss: InfoNCE / symmetric contrastive cross-entropy over image-text similarity matrix (pretraining)
cosine-similarity scoring at inference
log-loss for downstream linear probes
contraindicated_when: task needs fine-grained intra-class discrimination (species, vehicle variants) where caption-level signal is insufficient
task requires spatial/compositional reasoning or region-level grounding (VQA on relations, referring expressions) since there is no cross-modal attention
categories cannot be expressed as text prompts, or a small fixed label set with abundant labels makes a supervised CNN/ViT more accurate
fairness-sensitive deployment without auditing, given documented demographic and occupation-gender biases from web data

children.name: LLaVA
children.diff_siblings: Unlike BLIP-2 (which bridges vision and language via a learned Q-Former with cross-attention query tokens) or Flamingo (which injects visual features through gated cross-attention layers interleaved in the LLM), LLaVA uses a single lightweight linear projection to map frozen CLIP-ViT embeddings directly into the LLM token space, then fine-tunes the whole model end-to-end on GPT-4-generated visual instruction data.
strengths: Instruction-following quality: because training data is generated by GPT-4 as multi-turn dialogues about images, the model follows complex, open-ended visual instructions far better than contemporaries trained on caption-only or VQA pairs.

Training efficiency: only the projection layer is trained in the alignment stage (LLM and ViT both frozen), reducing compute to a single A100-day for the 13B variant while reaching 85.1% of GPT-4 score on multimodal benchmarks.
Modular architecture: swapping the LLM backbone (LLaMA, Vicuna, Mistral) or the vision encoder requires no architectural changes — only re-training the projection layer.
weaknesses: Linear projection bottleneck: the original single-layer projection loses spatial detail and fine-grained visual structure; LLaVA-1.5 had to replace it with a two-layer MLP to recover accuracy on dense tasks.
Hallucination tendency: the model inherits the LLM's propensity to generate plausible but visually unsupported text, especially for counting, spatial relations, and small objects in cluttered scenes.
Fixed image resolution: CLIP-ViT processes images at 224x224 or 336x336 pixels; high-resolution documents, charts, and fine print are severely degraded before the LLM ever sees them.
recommended_for: Open-ended visual dialogue and multimodal chatbots where the input is a natural-language question about a photograph and the answer requires multi-step reasoning or comparison across image regions.

Domain-specific visual assistants (medical imaging, remote sensing) where a small labeled instruction set can be used to fine-tune the projection and LLM on top of the pretrained CLIP-Vicuna backbone in under 24 h of compute.
not_recommended_for: Document understanding or OCR-heavy tasks (invoices, receipts, dense tables) where sub-word text in the image must be read accurately — fixed low-resolution CLIP encoding destroys character-level detail.

Latency-sensitive or on-device deployments: even the 7B variant requires ~14 GB VRAM and produces tokens autoregressively, making real-time interactive use impractical on consumer hardware without aggressive quantization.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Haotian Liu, Chunyuan Li, Qingyang Wu, and Yong Jae Lee (NeurIPS 2023, Oral), LLaVA was the first model to use a language-only GPT-4 prompt — feeding image captions and bounding-box annotations as text — to synthesize 158k multimodal instruction-following examples without any human annotator ever labeling a single image.

target.notes: Generative vision-language model: input is an image plus a natural-language prompt, output is free-form text. Not a fixed-label predictor; framed as autoregressive text generation conditioned on visual tokens. Can be steered to classification/VQA via instructions but does not optimize a discrete-label objective.

data_regime.rows: pretrained foundation model; usable zero-shot. Instruction fine-tuning works with thousands of image-instruction pairs (projection + LLM tuned on GPT-4-style dialogues)
data_regime.dimensionality: n/a in tabular sense; operates on raw images + tokenized text
needs: large pretrained backbones (CLIP-ViT + LLM such as Vicuna/LLaMA)

features.interpretability: low: end-to-end deep multimodal transformer, no human-readable decision path; outputs are free text that can hallucinate visually unsupported content
features.notes: Images encoded by frozen CLIP-ViT at fixed 224x224 or 336x336; high-resolution detail and small text are lost before the LLM sees them. Single linear (or 2-layer MLP in v1.5) projection maps visual embeddings into LLM token space.

assumptions: Salient content is legible at low fixed resolution (224/336 px); fine print, dense tables, and small objects are destroyed by downsampling
Frozen CLIP visual representation captures the relevant semantics for the task
Task can be expressed as a natural-language instruction over a single image
loss: autoregressive next-token cross-entropy (language-modeling loss) over the generated answer tokens, conditioned on projected visual tokens
contraindicated_when: OCR-heavy / document understanding (invoices, receipts, charts, dense tables) requiring accurate sub-word text reading
tasks needing precise counting, spatial relations, or small-object detection in cluttered scenes (hallucination-prone)
latency-sensitive or on-device/consumer-hardware deployment without aggressive quantization
structured numeric prediction with calibrated probabilities or a well-defined loss (use a discriminative classifier/regressor instead)
high-resolution imagery where downscaling to 224/336 px removes the discriminative signal

children.name: Flamingo
children.diff_siblings: Unlike siblings that fine-tune the full model or use a Q-Former bridge, Flamingo keeps both the vision encoder and the LLM completely frozen and inserts gated cross-attention dense layers (XATTN-DENSE) between every fourth frozen LLM block, fed by a Perceiver Resampler that compresses variable-length visual features into a fixed set of 64 latent tokens — enabling true in-context few-shot learning over interleaved image-text sequences without any gradient update to the backbone.
strengths: Few-shot in-context learning over interleaved image-text sequences: the same prompt format used for text-only LLMs works for vision tasks, requiring only 4–32 labeled examples at inference time rather than task-specific fine-tuning.

Handles videos and images uniformly: the Perceiver Resampler accepts a variable number of spatial or temporal feature maps, so the same architecture processes static images and video frames without structural changes.

Preserves the frozen LLM's language capabilities: by training only the cross-attention and Perceiver parameters (~1/4 of LLM size), the model retains strong text generation quality while gaining vision grounding.
weaknesses: Inferior to fine-tuned specialist models on tasks with abundant labeled data: on VQA benchmarks with full training sets, BLIP-2 trained with far fewer parameters surpasses Flamingo by using a Q-Former and full fine-tuning.
High inference cost: the 80B variant stacks a large NFNet-F6 vision encoder, a Perceiver Resampler, and a 70B Chinchilla LLM, making real-time or resource-constrained deployment impractical.

Single visual context per interleaved position: each image slot is encoded independently through the Perceiver; there is no direct attention between multiple image representations, limiting tasks that require fine-grained cross-image comparison.
recommended_for: Few-shot visual question answering or captioning over diverse domains where collecting large labeled datasets is expensive — the model generalizes from 4–32 in-context examples per task without retraining.
Multimodal dialogue over documents or video frames where the input alternates between text and multiple images, exploiting Flamingo's native support for arbitrarily interleaved image-text sequences.
not_recommended_for: Production deployments with strict latency or memory budgets: the smallest Flamingo variant (3B) still requires a non-trivial GPU footprint, and the 80B version needs multi-GPU inference infrastructure.

Tasks with thousands of labeled examples: when sufficient supervision is available, lighter models such as BLIP-2 or LLaVA achieve higher accuracy with far fewer trainable parameters and faster training.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Alayrac et al. at DeepMind (NeurIPS 2022), Flamingo was the first large vision-language model to demonstrate that inserting gated cross-attention layers into a completely frozen 70B language model (Chinchilla) enables few-shot performance surpassing fine-tuned state-of-the-art on 6 of 16 vision-language benchmarks using only 32 task-specific examples.

target.notes: Generative vision-language model: outputs free-form text (answers, captions) conditioned on interleaved image/video and text. Not a fixed-label classifier; framed as open-ended sequence generation.

data_regime.rows: designed for few-shot inference (4-32 in-context examples per task); no task-specific training set required, but pretraining needs web-scale interleaved image-text corpora
data_regime.dimensionality: n/a (in-context, no fitting at deployment)
needs: frozen pretrained vision encoder + LLM backbone

features.interpretability: low: deep frozen backbones plus gated cross-attention; no feature attributions
features.notes: Inputs are arbitrarily interleaved image/video frames and text tokens; visual features compressed by a Perceiver Resampler into 64 latent tokens per image slot. Images encoded independently per slot, so no fine-grained cross-image attention.

loss: autoregressive cross-entropy / next-token log-loss over text, conditioned on visual context (only cross-attention + Perceiver params trained)
contraindicated_when: thousands of labeled examples are available (fine-tuned specialists like BLIP-2/LLaVA win)
strict latency or memory budgets / edge deployment
task needs fine-grained comparison across multiple images simultaneously
target is a structured numeric/tabular prediction rather than text generation
pure unimodal text or unimodal vision task with no need for multimodal grounding

children.name: BLIP / BLIP-2
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Flamingo (gated cross-attention injected into a frozen LLM) or LLaVA (single linear projection from CLIP), BLIP/BLIP-2 introduces a dedicated Q-Former — a lightweight Querying Transformer with 32 learned query vectors — that bridges a frozen ViT encoder and a frozen LLM, training only this adapter module (~188M parameters) while keeping both backbones fully frozen.
strengths: Q-Former decouples vision and language pretraining: with both backbones frozen, only the adapter trains, cutting GPU memory and compute by ~54x compared to Flamingo 80B while matching or exceeding its zero-shot VQA scores.

BLIP's MED (Multimodal Encoder-Decoder) architecture handles understanding and generation in a single model via three objectives (ITC, ITM, LM) with shared weights, eliminating the need for separate retrieval and captioning models.
CapFilt (BLIP's captioner + filter loop) bootstraps noisy web image-text pairs into clean training signal without manual annotation, directly improving downstream task quality.
weaknesses: The 32-token visual bottleneck in Q-Former loses fine-grained spatial information, causing errors on tasks requiring precise counting, reading small text, or localizing objects in cluttered scenes.
BLIP-2 inherits hallucination tendencies from the frozen LLM: the language model can generate fluent but visually ungrounded text when prior language statistics override weak image signals.
Training requires two distinct pretraining stages (vision-language representation learning, then generative LLM alignment), making reproduction and adaptation to new LLM backbones non-trivial.
recommended_for: Image captioning and zero-shot visual question answering pipelines where compute budget is limited and both frozen ViT and a pretrained LLM (OPT, FlanT5) are already available — Q-Former adds minimal overhead.
Multimodal retrieval-augmented systems that need a compact, fixed-length visual embedding (32 tokens) per image for fast similarity search alongside a language model for answer generation.
not_recommended_for: Tasks demanding pixel-level or fine-grained spatial reasoning (e.g., OCR on dense documents, counting objects in crowded scenes) where the 32-token bottleneck provably discards spatial detail.
Few-shot in-context learning settings: BLIP-2 was trained on single image-text pairs and does not support interleaved multi-image context windows the way Flamingo does.
children.curiosity: BLIP-2 was introduced by Junnan Li et al. at Salesforce Research (2023, arXiv:2301.12597) and demonstrated that training only 188M Q-Former parameters achieved an 8.7 percentage point improvement over Flamingo 80B on zero-shot VQAv2 — with 54x fewer trainable parameters.

target.notes: Generative multimodal model: outputs natural-language text (captions, VQA answers) conditioned on an image, and produces fixed-length 32-token image embeddings for retrieval/matching. No scalar target distribution; supervision is image-text pairs, not labeled tabular targets.

data_regime.rows: leverages large-scale web image-text pretraining; adapter (Q-Former) fine-tunes on thousands+ pairs, but typically used zero-shot/few-shot off pretrained checkpoints
data_regime.dimensionality: high-dimensional pixel + token inputs, not p/n tabular
needs: image-text paired data for any fine-tuning

features.interpretability: low; deep transformer with frozen ViT + LLM and a learned Q-Former bottleneck, no per-feature attribution
features.notes: Input is raw RGB images paired with text; the 32-token Q-Former bottleneck yields a compact fixed-length visual embedding but discards fine-grained spatial detail.

assumptions: Task is expressible as image-conditioned text generation or image-text similarity
Image content can be summarized by ~32 visual query tokens (coarse global semantics, not pixel-precise)
Single image per query (no interleaved multi-image context)
loss: image-text contrastive (ITC)
image-text matching (ITM, binary)
language modeling / generative cross-entropy (LM)
contraindicated_when: Task needs pixel-level or fine-grained spatial reasoning (dense OCR, counting in crowded scenes, precise localization) where the 32-token bottleneck loses detail
Few-shot in-context learning with interleaved multi-image prompts (use Flamingo-style models)
Tabular/structured data or any non-image-text modality
Hallucination-sensitive deployments where fluent but visually ungrounded text is unacceptable without grounding checks

children.name: FLUX Kontext
children.diff_siblings: Unlike sibling multimodal transformers that condition on images via cross-attention adapters or fine-tuned encoders, FLUX Kontext conditions on reference images by concatenating their latent tokens directly into the same sequence as the target tokens inside a single flow-matching transformer, requiring no separate conditioning module or inversion step.
strengths: Iterative identity preservation: because reference and target share the same token sequence, object and character features are retained across multiple sequential edits without drift
Unified architecture for T2I and I2I: a single model handles text-to-image generation, local region editing, global style transfer, and character reference without task-specific heads or LoRA swaps

Inference speed: rectified flow matching traces a near-straight path from noise to image, enabling high-quality results in substantially fewer NFE (number of function evaluations) than diffusion-based editing counterparts
weaknesses: Sequence-length cost: concatenating full reference image latents with target latents roughly doubles the token count per forward pass, increasing VRAM and compute proportionally

Prompt sensitivity in local edits: edits that must stay confined to a small region can bleed into surrounding context when the text instruction is ambiguous, since there is no explicit spatial mask in the base architecture
Limited to latent-space resolution of the autoencoder: fine structural details smaller than the VAE's spatial compression factor (typically 8x) are irretrievable regardless of prompt specificity
recommended_for: Character-consistent storyboarding or product-image workflows where the same person or object must appear unmodified across dozens of generated scenes
Iterative image refinement pipelines where an editor applies successive natural-language instructions to a single image and needs each step to preserve all unmentioned regions faithfully
not_recommended_for: Tasks requiring pixel-precise spatial control (e.g., exact inpainting at a specific bounding box) where a dedicated inpainting model with an explicit mask input is more reliable

Deployment on hardware with less than ~20 GB VRAM at full precision, since the concatenated reference-plus-target sequence of the [dev] checkpoint (~24 GB) saturates consumer GPUs without aggressive quantization
children.curiosity: Introduced by Black Forest Labs in June 2025 (arXiv 2506.15742), FLUX.1 Kontext is the first flow-matching model to unify text-to-image generation and reference-image editing through plain sequence concatenation, validated on the authors' KontextBench benchmark of 1,026 image-prompt pairs across five task categories.

target.notes: Generative model: outputs RGB images conditioned on a text instruction and optional reference image(s). No predictive target / label distribution; not for supervised tabular prediction.

data_regime.rows: no per-task training data needed at inference (pretrained foundation model used zero-shot/instruction-driven); fine-tuning/LoRA optional and needs only small image sets
data_regime.dimensionality: operates in VAE latent space (~8x spatial compression); reference latents are concatenated with target latents, roughly doubling sequence length per forward pass
needs: high VRAM (~20+ GB at full precision for [dev] checkpoint; quantization required on consumer GPUs)

features.interpretability: low: end-to-end flow-matching transformer with no exposed feature attributions; control is via natural-language prompts, not interpretable parameters
features.notes: Inputs are a text instruction plus optional reference image(s); conditioning is in-context (reference image latent tokens concatenated into the same sequence as target tokens), so no explicit spatial mask or bounding-box control.

assumptions: Edit region/intent is adequately specifiable in natural language; ambiguous instructions bleed into unmentioned regions due to absence of explicit spatial mask
Required detail is above the VAE compression scale; sub-8x-pixel structure is unrecoverable
Domain/style is within the pretraining distribution of Black Forest Labs FLUX
loss: rectified flow-matching / conditional flow-matching velocity objective (near-straight noise-to-image path; not a discriminative loss)
contraindicated_when: task is supervised prediction, classification, regression, or forecasting on tabular/structured data (no target modeled)
pixel-precise spatial editing at an exact bounding box is required (use mask-conditioned inpainting instead)
hardware has <~20 GB VRAM at full precision without quantization
fine structural fidelity below the autoencoder's spatial compression factor is essential

children.name: DALL-E 1
children.diff_siblings: Unlike later multimodal transformers that use diffusion decoders or CLIP-guided priors, DALL-E 1 generates images purely autoregressively: it concatenates BPE text tokens with discrete image tokens produced by a dVAE and trains a 12B-parameter GPT-style transformer to predict the joint sequence token-by-token.
strengths: Unified sequence model — text and image share a single token vocabulary, so cross-modal attention emerges naturally without a separate alignment module.
dVAE compression reduces each 256×256 image to a 32×32 grid of 8192-codebook tokens, making the 12B-parameter autoregressive step computationally tractable.
Zero-shot compositional generalization: trained on 250M text-image pairs, it handles novel object-attribute combinations never seen verbatim during training.
weaknesses: Autoregressive image decoding is sequential (1024 tokens per image), making inference orders of magnitude slower than one-pass diffusion models.
Maximum output resolution is 256×256 px; fine spatial detail, text rendering, and photorealism fall well short of contemporaneous diffusion-based models.

CLIP reranking is required post-hoc to select plausible samples — the raw model generates many semantically inconsistent images, exposing the weak explicit text-image alignment of the autoregressive objective.
recommended_for: Research on discrete visual tokenization where downstream tasks require an interpretable, finite codebook of image patches (e.g., building retrieval or classification heads on top of dVAE tokens).
Low-resolution concept-to-sketch prototyping pipelines where 256×256 outputs are sufficient and a single unified sequence model simplifies the training stack.
not_recommended_for: Production image generation requiring 512×512 px or higher output, photorealistic detail, or legible rendered text — DALL-E 2/3 or diffusion models are strictly superior.
Latency-sensitive applications: sequential decoding of 1024 image tokens per sample cannot match the single-pass throughput of denoising diffusion or flow-matching models.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Ramesh, Pavlov, Goh et al. (OpenAI, 2021) in 'Zero-Shot Text-to-Image Generation' (arXiv 2102.12092), DALL-E 1 was named after the surrealist painter Salvador Dalí and the Pixar robot WALL-E, reflecting OpenAI's intent to blend artistic creativity with machine intelligence.

target.notes: Conditional generative model: produces 256x256 RGB images from a text prompt. No supervised scalar/class target; output is a joint sequence of BPE text tokens + 1024 discrete dVAE image tokens (8192-codebook). Density modeled autoregressively over the token sequence.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds of millions of text-image pairs to train (DALL-E 1: ~250M pairs); not trainable on small data. As a pretrained model, usable for inference/feature extraction without retraining.
data_regime.dimensionality: high-dimensional: 12B-parameter transformer over 1280-length token sequences.

features.interpretability: low — 12B-param autoregressive transformer; dVAE codebook gives a finite, somewhat interpretable discrete latent grid but generation logic is opaque.
features.notes: Inputs are paired (caption, image). Images compressed by a discrete VAE to a 32x32 grid of codebook indices; text tokenized with BPE. Modalities share a single vocabulary.

assumptions: Captions and images are semantically aligned in the training corpus.
A discrete codebook of 8192 tokens is sufficient to reconstruct images at 256x256 without major detail loss.
Joint text+image distribution is well-modeled by left-to-right autoregressive factorization.
loss: cross-entropy / negative log-likelihood over the joint discrete token sequence (text + image tokens)
dVAE trained separately with ELBO (reconstruction + KL / relaxed categorical)
CLIP score used post-hoc for sample reranking, not a training loss
contraindicated_when: Production image generation requiring >=512x512 resolution, photorealism, or legible rendered text — diffusion models (DALL-E 2/3, Stable Diffusion) are strictly superior.
Latency-sensitive serving: sequential decoding of 1024 image tokens per sample is far slower than single/few-pass diffusion or flow-matching.
Tasks needing a discriminative target (classification, regression, detection) — this is a generative sequence model, not a predictor.
Low-data or compute-constrained settings: cannot be trained from scratch without massive paired data and GPU clusters.

children.name: Segment Anything Model (SAM)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike multimodal transformers focused on classification or retrieval (e.g., CLIP), SAM is a specialized generative architecture that outputs segmentation masks based on spatial or, in later versions, text-based prompts.
strengths: Excellent zero-shot generalization to unseen objects and image domains without task-specific training.
Highly flexible 'promptable' interface, accepting points, boxes, and text to guide segmentation.
Produces high-quality, detailed object masks.
