weaknesses: Does not assign semantic labels to masks, identifying 'what' but not 'what kind'.
Performance can degrade on specialized domains (e.g., medical, aerial) and with low-contrast objects.
The Vision Transformer encoder is computationally expensive, making real-time application on edge devices challenging.
recommended_for: Accelerating data annotation and labeling for computer vision datasets.
Interactive image editing tools for object selection, removal, and manipulation.
not_recommended_for: Tasks requiring real-time video segmentation on resource-constrained hardware.
Applications that need semantic class predictions out-of-the-box (e.g., 'car', 'person').
children.curiosity: The model was trained on the SA-1B dataset, which contains over 1.1 billion segmentation masks across 11 million images, and was created using a human-in-the-loop process where the model itself helped assist annotators.

target.notes: Class-agnostic instance/region segmentation: outputs binary object masks, not semantic class labels. No probabilistic target distribution; mask quality scored by IoU. Use a downstream classifier/detector to attach semantic labels.

data_regime.rows: zero-shot at inference, no task-specific training data required; fine-tuning a specialized domain needs hundreds to thousands of annotated masks
data_regime.dimensionality: high-dimensional pixel input (ViT-B/L/H image encoder)
needs: large labeled data only if fine-tuning

features.interpretability: low - deep ViT encoder, mask output is spatial but the embedding space is opaque
features.notes: Promptable: accepts point, box, or (later variants) text prompts as spatial guidance. RGB images; encoder cost dominated by ViT, heavy for real-time/edge.

assumptions: objects are visually distinguishable by appearance/edges (degrades on low-contrast boundaries)
input domain resembles natural images (degrades on medical, aerial, microscopy without fine-tuning)
a meaningful prompt is available to localize the target
loss: focal loss + dice loss on mask logits
IoU prediction (mask quality regression) for ambiguity-aware mask ranking
contraindicated_when: semantic class labels are required out-of-the-box
real-time video segmentation on resource-constrained hardware
specialized non-natural-image domains with no fine-tuning budget
tasks needing pixel-precise masks on low-contrast or heavily occluded objects without prompts

children.name: Whisper
children.diff_siblings: It is a weakly-supervised encoder-decoder Transformer specialized for robust, multilingual, and multitask speech-to-text processing, trained on a massive and diverse dataset of 680,000 hours of web-collected audio.
strengths: High accuracy and robustness to accents, background noise, and technical language.
Performs multilingual transcription (99 languages) and translation into English within a single model.
Zero-shot generalization to diverse datasets and domains without task-specific fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Can 'hallucinate' text, especially during silent periods or with non-speech audio.
Does not perform speaker diarization (identifying 'who spoke when') natively.
Performance is lower for low-resource languages that were underrepresented in the training data.
recommended_for: General-purpose automatic speech recognition (ASR) and transcription.
Translating speech from multiple languages directly into English text.
not_recommended_for: Low-latency, real-time streaming applications without specialized adaptations.
Natively identifying or separating different speakers in a single audio file.
children.curiosity: The model was trained on 680,000 hours of 'weakly supervised' audio data collected from the web, a scale and diversity that enabled its robust zero-shot performance.

target.notes: Sequence-to-sequence model: maps audio waveform (log-Mel spectrogram input) to a token sequence (transcribed or English-translated text). Output is discrete text tokens, not a numeric target distribution.

data_regime.rows: pretrained off-the-shelf; zero-shot inference needs no labeled data. Fine-tuning a low-resource language benefits from hundreds+ hours of transcribed audio
data_regime.dimensionality: fixed 30s audio windows (chunked/padded), 80-channel log-Mel features
needs: GPU for practical inference latency on larger checkpoints (small/medium/large)
pretrained weights (not trained from scratch in typical use)

features.interpretability: low: deep encoder-decoder Transformer, opaque acoustic-to-text mapping
features.notes: Input is raw audio resampled to 16 kHz, converted to log-Mel spectrogram. No tabular/numeric/categorical features.

assumptions: input is speech audio within roughly 30s segments (longer audio must be chunked)
language present is among the ~99 supported; quality degrades for low-resource/underrepresented languages
non-speech or silent audio can trigger hallucinated text

contraindicated_when: low-latency real-time streaming is required without specialized adaptation
speaker diarization (who spoke when) or source separation is needed natively
input is non-speech audio (music, environmental sound classification)
target task is tabular prediction, classification of numeric features, or any non-audio modality

target.notes: Family node spanning self-supervised representation (CLIP-style contrastive, masked modeling) and supervised heads. Many uses are retrieval/embedding (no target) or generation; when a label exists it is typically a classification head (VQA answer over a closed vocabulary, multiclass) or free-form text decoding. Not a tabular regressor.

data_regime.rows: needs large paired multimodal corpora for pre-training (millions to billions of image-text/audio-text pairs); fine-tuning needs tens of thousands of paired examples minimum, below which cross-modal attention stays under-trained
data_regime.dimensionality: high-dimensional raw inputs (pixels, tokens, spectrograms) embedded into shared latent space; p>>n at the raw level, handled by learned encoders
needs: pretrained backbone (CLIP/ViLBERT/FLAVA/BLIP) strongly preferred over training from scratch

features.interpretability: low: cross-modal attention maps offer some token-region alignment introspection, but the fused representation is opaque
features.notes: Inputs are two or more raw modalities (text, image, video frames, audio); requires aligned/paired data so each modality conditions attention over the other. Modality-specific tokenization/patching and normalization required.

assumptions: modalities are semantically paired and aligned in the training data (mismatched pairs degrade contrastive learning)
sufficient pre-training scale to close the modality gap; small corpora leave a persistent gap and weak token-level alignment
task genuinely requires joint reasoning across modalities, not just late fusion of independent unimodal predictions
loss: contrastive / InfoNCE (CLIP-style image-text alignment)
masked language modeling
masked image modeling
image-text matching (binary cross-entropy)
cross-entropy for VQA/classification heads

fewer than tens of thousands of paired multimodal examples available
queries demand precise compositional or spatial grounding and only a global dot-product fusion model (CLIP) is available
low-latency or low-compute deployment with no GPU budget
no paired/aligned multimodal data exists (only separate unimodal corpora)

children.name: Time Series Transformers
children.diff_siblings: Unlike text or vision Transformers, Time Series Transformers replace token-level attention with temporal patch embeddings or decomposition-based attention (autocorrelation) to capture periodicity and trend structure that standard positional encodings cannot encode.
strengths: Parallel processing of all time steps simultaneously enables training on sequences orders of magnitude faster than LSTMs on modern hardware
PatchTST-style patching reduces sequence length by a factor equal to the patch size, cutting attention complexity from O(L²) to O((L/P)²) while preserving local temporal context
Channel-independent embedding in models like PatchTST allows a single set of Transformer weights to generalize across all variates, reducing overfitting on high-dimensional multivariate inputs
weaknesses: Vanilla self-attention is O(L²) in memory and compute, making raw application to sequences longer than ~1000 steps prohibitively expensive without architectural modifications like ProbSparse or patching
Positional encodings designed for language (sinusoidal or learned) carry no concept of calendar periodicity, requiring domain-specific modifications to model seasonality correctly
Require substantially more training data than LSTMs or TCNs to avoid underfitting; on short datasets (hundreds of observations), simple linear models frequently outperform Transformer variants
recommended_for: Long-horizon multivariate forecasting (e.g., 720-step ahead electricity or weather prediction) where capturing long-range cross-variate dependencies justifies the architectural complexity
Large-scale time series datasets (tens of thousands of series) where channel-independent Transformers can amortize weights across series and exploit GPU parallelism fully
not_recommended_for: Short univariate series with fewer than a few thousand observations, where linear or tree-based models achieve lower MSE with far less compute and no risk of attention collapse
Low-latency edge inference scenarios where the quadratic memory footprint and multi-head attention overhead exceed hardware constraints even after patching optimizations
children.curiosity: The Informer (Zhou et al., 2021), the first widely adopted time-series Transformer, received the AAAI-21 Outstanding Paper Award for its ProbSparse self-attention that reduced complexity from O(L²) to O(L log L), enabling forecasting horizons of 48 h on hourly electricity data that were intractable with vanilla Transformers.

children.name: PatchTST
children.diff_siblings: Unlike other Time Series Transformers that tokenize individual time steps or full variates, PatchTST segments each univariate channel into fixed-length overlapping subseries patches and treats each patch as a token, combining this with strict channel independence so a single shared Transformer processes every variate separately.
strengths: Patching reduces the attention map from O(L²) to O((L/P)²) quadratically, enabling look-back windows up to 1024 steps without the memory cost that defeats vanilla Transformers on long sequences.
Each patch encodes a local semantic window (e.g., 16 time steps) rather than a single point, giving the self-attention mechanism meaningful sub-series context instead of noisy per-step tokens.

Channel independence makes the model directly transferable to self-supervised pre-training: the same encoder pre-trained on one variate can be fine-tuned on a different number of channels without architectural changes.
weaknesses: Channel independence ignores inter-variate correlations by design, so it underperforms channel-mixing models on datasets where variables are causally or statistically coupled (e.g., weather stations with strong spatial dependence).
Patch size and stride are fixed hyperparameters that must be tuned per dataset; a poor choice fragments meaningful seasonal patterns or merges distinct events into the same token.
The linear projection head assumes a fixed forecast horizon set at training time, requiring a full retrain to produce forecasts of a different length.
recommended_for: Long-horizon univariate or weakly-coupled multivariate forecasting (horizon ≥ 336 steps) on datasets like ETTh1/ETTm2 where channel independence holds and long look-back windows carry predictive signal.

Self-supervised pre-training on large unlabeled time series corpora followed by fine-tuning on a small labeled target dataset, exploiting the channel-independent masked-patch pre-training scheme introduced with the model.
not_recommended_for: Multivariate forecasting where cross-variate dependencies are the primary signal (e.g., traffic sensor grids or financial portfolios with known correlation structure), since channel independence discards that information entirely.

Short look-back, low-resource settings where the quadratic-reduction benefit of patching is negligible and simpler linear models (e.g., DLinear) match accuracy with far lower compute and no hyperparameter tuning.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Nie et al. (ICLR 2023) in 'A Time Series is Worth 64 Words', the paper showed that a vanilla Transformer with patching and channel independence outperformed all prior Transformer-based forecasters, prompting a broader reassessment of whether attention mechanisms or simple linear mappings were responsible for gains attributed to Transformers in earlier time-series benchmarks.

target.notes: Multi-step point forecasting of one or more continuous-valued series. Forecast horizon is fixed at training time by the linear projection head; changing horizon length requires retraining.

data_regime.rows: needs long sequences and thousands+ of windows; benefits from very long look-back (up to ~512-1024 steps). Underpowered datasets favor simpler linear baselines.
data_regime.dimensionality: channel-independent: scales to many variates by sharing one encoder across channels, but does not model cross-channel dependence
needs: sufficient training windows for the Transformer to learn
optional: large unlabeled corpus for self-supervised masked-patch pre-training

features.interpretability: low; attention over patch tokens is opaque, no closed-form coefficients
features.notes: Operates on regularly-sampled, evenly-spaced numeric series; each univariate channel is segmented into fixed-length overlapping subseries patches. Patch size and stride are dataset-specific hyperparameters that must be tuned. Standard instance normalization (per-series mean/var) of inputs assumed.

assumptions: series are regularly sampled at a fixed frequency with no large gaps
predictive signal is concentrated within-channel (channel independence) rather than across channels
long look-back actually carries signal for the target horizon
chosen patch size/stride aligns with the data's seasonal/event structure
forecast horizon known and fixed at training time
loss: mean squared error (squared error)
mean absolute error (L1)
masked-patch reconstruction loss for self-supervised pre-training
contraindicated_when: cross-variate dependencies are the dominant signal (e.g., traffic sensor grids, correlated financial portfolios, spatially-coupled weather stations) -> channel independence discards that information
short look-back / low-resource settings where simple linear models (DLinear) match accuracy at far lower cost
irregular, event-driven, or sparsely-sampled series
very short or noisy series with too few windows to train a Transformer
the deployment requires variable / on-the-fly forecast horizons without retraining
probabilistic / quantile forecasts are required (native head is point-forecast only)

children.name: iTransformer
children.diff_siblings: Unlike siblings that embed temporal patches or raw time steps as tokens and apply attention across the time axis, iTransformer inverts the roles: each variate (channel) becomes the token, so self-attention operates across variates to capture inter-series correlations, while the FFN encodes temporal patterns within each series independently.
strengths: Directly models multivariate correlations via attention over variate tokens, making it effective when inter-variable dependencies (e.g., correlated sensor readings) drive forecast accuracy.
Scales favorably with high-dimensional inputs: attention operates over the number of variates, not the sequence length, so quadratic cost grows with channels rather than with lookback window size.

Longer lookback windows consistently improve accuracy because each variate token aggregates the full input series into one representation, avoiding the performance degradation vanilla Transformers suffer at longer contexts.
weaknesses: Temporal ordering within a series is handled entirely by the FFN after attention, not by the attention mechanism itself, so fine-grained sequential dependencies (e.g., abrupt local spikes) may be poorly captured.
Performs poorly on univariate or low-dimensional datasets where there are no meaningful inter-variate correlations to attend to, yielding no advantage over simpler models.
The whole-series variate token discards local temporal locality, making it less suited than patch-based models (e.g., PatchTST) for series with rapid, short-duration fluctuations.
recommended_for: High-dimensional multivariate forecasting (e.g., traffic sensor networks with 200+ channels) where inter-variable correlations are strong and the lookback window is long (336–720 steps).

Scientific or industrial monitoring where each measured variable (temperature, pressure, flow rate) has a distinct physical meaning and cross-variable relationships are the primary forecasting signal.
not_recommended_for: Univariate time series (single channel) such as a single stock price or a single weather station reading, where the variate-level attention provides no useful signal.

Highly non-stationary or rapidly fluctuating series (e.g., high-frequency electricity spot prices with sudden spikes) where local temporal context within short windows is critical and global series aggregation loses the necessary detail.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Liu et al. (2024) and accepted as an ICLR 2024 Spotlight, iTransformer achieves its gains without modifying any Transformer module — it reuses the standard attention and FFN unchanged, simply transposing the input so that time and variate dimensions are swapped before tokenization.

target.notes: Multivariate point forecasting over a future horizon; jointly predicts all channels. Native objective is mean (not full predictive distribution).

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of time steps; deep model that overfits short series
data_regime.dimensionality: shines with high channel count (tens to hundreds of variates); attention cost is quadratic in number of variates, not in lookback length, so long lookbacks (336-720 steps) are cheap and beneficial

features.interpretability: low; attention maps over variates give some cross-series correlation insight but the model is a black box
features.notes: Each variate becomes a token (inverted attention); requires multiple numeric channels. Standard normalization/instance-norm per series expected.

assumptions: Forecast signal is driven by inter-variate correlations rather than fine-grained local temporal dynamics
Series are roughly stationary or normalizable; whole-series aggregation into one token assumes no critical short-window detail
Enough channels exist for cross-variate attention to be meaningful
loss: mean squared error (MSE)
mean absolute error (MAE)
contraindicated_when: Univariate or low-dimensional series (no cross-variate structure to exploit)
Highly non-stationary series with abrupt local spikes where short-window temporal locality is critical
Small datasets (insufficient data to train a deep Transformer)
Probabilistic/quantile forecasts required (native model outputs point estimates)

children.name: DeepAR (Amazon)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike attention-based Transformers (TFT, Autoformer), DeepAR uses an LSTM autoregressive loop that feeds the previous step's sampled output back as input at each decoding step, outputting parametric likelihood distributions (Gaussian, Negative Binomial) rather than point or quantile forecasts.
strengths: Trains a single global model across thousands of related series simultaneously, letting sparse series borrow statistical strength from the full corpus
Outputs full predictive distributions (e.g. Negative Binomial for count data) rather than point estimates, calibrating uncertainty directly from the likelihood
Learns scale-invariant representations via input normalization per series, handling electricity demand alongside web traffic counts in one model without manual scaling
weaknesses: Cold-start series with few historical observations get poor forecasts because the LSTM encoder has little context to condition on
Autoregressive decoding accumulates errors over long horizons since each step depends on the previous sampled value, degrading accuracy for multi-step-ahead windows
Produces no variable-importance scores or attention weights, making it opaque compared to TFT or Autoformer when stakeholders need to understand which covariates drive a forecast
recommended_for: Retail or e-commerce demand forecasting with thousands of SKUs sharing seasonal patterns but varying sales volumes, where a global model reduces per-series fitting cost
Probabilistic energy or web-traffic forecasting where decision-makers need full quantile ranges (P10–P90) to size capacity buffers, not just a single expected value
not_recommended_for: Single isolated time series with no related series to train on, where the global-model assumption provides no advantage over ARIMA or Exponential Smoothing
Forecasting tasks requiring interpretable covariate attribution (e.g. regulated financial forecasting), since DeepAR offers no built-in explanation of which inputs shaped the output
children.curiosity: Introduced by Salinas, Flunkert, Gasthaus, and Januschowski (arXiv 2017, published in International Journal of Forecasting 2020), DeepAR was deployed at Amazon scale to replace hundreds of hand-tuned per-product ARIMA models with a single neural model, reducing median absolute percentage error by over 15% on internal retail datasets.

target.notes: Outputs a parametric predictive distribution per future step; likelihood family is chosen to match the target (Negative Binomial / Poisson for non-negative counts like unit sales, Gaussian/Student-t for real-valued series). Native probabilistic forecasting, not point or pinball-quantile.

data_regime.rows: needs a panel of many (hundreds to thousands+) related series; per-series history can be short since strength is borrowed across the corpus
data_regime.dimensionality: scales with number of series and covariates; not p>n regime
needs: large collection of related time series

features.interpretability: low - LSTM with sampled-output feedback gives no variable importance or attention weights
features.notes: Per-series input scaling/normalization is built in, so heterogeneous-magnitude series train jointly without manual scaling. Categorical series identity handled via learned embeddings; supports static and time-varying covariates.

assumptions: The many series are related enough that global pooling of patterns transfers across them
Each series has enough conditioning history (cold-start series forecast poorly)
The chosen likelihood family adequately describes target dispersion (e.g. Negative Binomial for overdispersed counts)
loss: negative log-likelihood of the chosen parametric distribution (Gaussian/Student-t/Negative-Binomial/Poisson)
probabilistic quantile ranges derived by Monte Carlo sampling of the autoregressive decoder
contraindicated_when: single isolated series with no related cohort (classical ARIMA/ETS is simpler and competitive)
interpretable covariate attribution is required (use TFT instead)
very long forecast horizons where autoregressive sampling compounds error
only a handful of short series with no cross-series structure to exploit

children.name: TCN (Temporal Convolutional Network)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike attention-based siblings (Informer, Autoformer, PatchTST), TCN replaces the self-attention mechanism entirely with stacked dilated causal 1D convolutions and residual blocks, achieving O(n) complexity per layer instead of O(n²).
strengths: Dilated convolutions double the receptive field with each layer (dilation d=1,2,4,...,2^k), reaching thousands of time steps without proportional parameter growth.
Causal padding guarantees no future leakage by construction, eliminating the need for masking tricks required in decoder-side transformers.
Parallelizes fully across the time axis during training — unlike RNNs and unlike autoregressive decoders — because convolutions have no sequential state dependency.
weaknesses: Receptive field is fixed at architecture definition time (determined by kernel size × dilation depth); handling sequences longer than the design horizon requires rebuilding the network.

Captures only local convolutional patterns and cannot model non-adjacent cross-timestep interactions the way global self-attention can, limiting performance on series with irregular long-range dependencies.
Lacks an explicit mechanism to model inter-variable relationships in multivariate settings — each channel is convolved independently unless cross-channel mixing layers are added manually.
recommended_for: High-frequency sensor or ECG streams (1 kHz+) where O(n²) attention is computationally prohibitive and short-to-medium temporal patterns (up to ~1 000 steps) dominate the signal.
Industrial anomaly detection on fixed-length sliding windows, where the deterministic receptive field maps cleanly to a known fault horizon and training throughput matters.
not_recommended_for: Very long time series (tens of thousands of steps) with dependencies that span the entire sequence, where the fixed receptive field would need an impractically deep stack of dilated layers to cover.
Multivariate forecasting tasks where inter-series correlations are the primary predictive signal (e.g., traffic networks), since TCN has no built-in cross-variable attention.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Bai, Kolter, and Koltun (2018) in 'An Empirical Evaluation of Generic Convolutional and Recurrent Networks for Sequence Modeling', the paper showed that a plain TCN outperformed LSTMs and GRUs on most of the 10 sequence modeling benchmarks tested, directly challenging the then-dominant assumption that recurrence was necessary for sequence tasks.

target.notes: Sequence model for forecasting (regression head) or sequence classification/anomaly detection; target is a function of an ordered temporal window. Distribution-agnostic (loss defines output assumptions).

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of windows/sequences to fit conv filters; benefits from long contiguous series
data_regime.dimensionality: scales to long sequences in O(n) per layer; receptive field fixed at build time by kernel_size x dilation depth (~up to ~1000 steps practically)
needs: GPU for training (parallel across time axis)

features.interpretability: low - stacked dilated causal convolutions are a black box
features.notes: Inputs are evenly-spaced sequences; channels convolved independently unless cross-channel mixing added. Normalize/scale inputs. Causal padding prevents future leakage by construction.

assumptions: dependencies fall within the fixed receptive field (no critical long-range interactions beyond design horizon)
regular fixed-interval sampling (no irregular timestamps / missingness)
predictive signal is local/short-to-medium-range temporal pattern, not non-adjacent cross-timestep interaction
in multivariate settings, inter-series correlation is secondary (no native cross-variable mixing)
loss: squared error / MAE for forecasting
log-loss / cross-entropy for sequence classification
any differentiable custom loss (architecture-agnostic head)
contraindicated_when: very long series (tens of thousands of steps) with whole-sequence dependencies requiring impractically deep dilation stacks
multivariate forecasting where inter-series correlation is the primary signal (e.g. traffic networks) - prefer attention/graph models
irregularly sampled or event-timestamped data
tiny datasets where simpler classical models (ARIMA, exponential smoothing) suffice

children.name: Informer
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Autoformer (which replaces attention with autocorrelation) or PatchTST (which segments series into patches), Informer retains the encoder-decoder attention structure but replaces standard O(L²) self-attention with ProbSparse attention — sampling only the top-u 'active' queries via a KL-divergence sparsity criterion — and adds cascading self-attention distilling layers to halve the sequence length at each encoder stage.
strengths: ProbSparse self-attention reduces time and memory complexity from O(L²) to O(L log L), enabling multi-step forecasting horizons of 720+ steps that would be infeasible for vanilla Transformers
Generative-style decoder predicts the entire output sequence in a single forward pass rather than auto-regressively step-by-step, eliminating accumulated error propagation over long horizons

Self-attention distilling (stacked convolutional pooling between encoder layers) compresses long input representations, allowing the model to digest very long lookback windows without GPU memory overflow
weaknesses: ProbSparse sampling assumes attention scores follow a long-tail distribution; on irregular or non-stationary series this assumption breaks and sampled queries may miss critical dependencies

Later benchmarks (e.g., Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?, 2023) showed Informer is consistently outperformed by simple linear baselines (DLinear, NLinear) on standard LTSF datasets, suggesting its inductive biases are poorly matched to many real series
The generative decoder requires the target sequence length to be fixed at training time, making it inflexible for variable-horizon inference without retraining
recommended_for: Long-horizon multivariate forecasting (horizons 336–720 steps) on regular, high-frequency sensor or IoT streams where the input length far exceeds what vanilla Transformers can process in memory
Applications where inference latency matters and auto-regressive decoding is too slow, such as real-time grid load forecasting where the full 24-hour profile must be predicted in one shot
not_recommended_for: Short- to medium-horizon forecasting tasks (horizon < 96 steps) where simpler linear or MLP models match or exceed its accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost

Highly irregular or aperiodic financial tick data where the long-tail attention distribution assumption fails and the fixed-length generative decoder cannot adapt to variable-length prediction windows
children.curiosity: Introduced by Zhou et al. (AAAI 2021), Informer won the Outstanding Paper Award at AAAI 2021 — one of only two papers selected from over 9,000 submissions — making it the first time-series forecasting paper to receive that distinction at AAAI.

target.notes: Multi-step (long-horizon) forecasting of one or more continuous channels; generative decoder emits the entire horizon (e.g. 336-720 steps) in one pass, so the horizon length is fixed at train time.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of timesteps; designed for very long lookback windows (input length L large)
data_regime.dimensionality: handles multivariate input (many channels); benefits when L is large enough that vanilla O(L^2) attention is infeasible
needs: fixed prediction horizon at train time

features.interpretability: low; deep attention model, predictions not directly explainable
features.notes: Expects regularly-sampled, high-frequency series; channels should be standardized. Time covariates (calendar features) are fed as positional/temporal embeddings.

assumptions: attention scores follow a long-tail distribution so ProbSparse top-u query sampling captures the dominant dependencies (breaks on irregular/non-stationary series)
approximate stationarity / stable periodicity over the lookback window
regular, evenly-spaced sampling intervals
fixed output horizon length
loss: mean squared error
mean absolute error
contraindicated_when: short- to medium-horizon forecasts (horizon < 96) where DLinear/NLinear or simple MLP match or beat it at far lower cost
irregular, aperiodic, or non-stationary series (e.g. financial tick data) where the long-tail attention assumption fails
variable-horizon inference is required without retraining
small datasets or no GPU available
univariate short series where classical models (ARIMA/ETS) suffice

children.name: Autoformer
children.diff_siblings: Autoformer replaces the standard dot-product self-attention with an Auto-Correlation mechanism computed via Fast Fourier Transform over period-aligned sub-series, and embeds a series decomposition block (moving-average trend extraction) inside every encoder and decoder layer — neither of which appears in siblings like Informer (ProbSparse attention) or FEDformer (frequency-domain mixing).
strengths: Auto-Correlation aggregates sub-series aligned by periodicity, giving O(N log N) complexity while capturing long-range seasonal dependencies that point-wise attention misses.

Inline decomposition blocks continuously separate trend from seasonality during forward propagation, preventing trend leakage into the seasonal head and improving accuracy on periodic datasets like weather and energy.
Achieved 38% relative improvement over prior transformer baselines across six benchmarks at NeurIPS 2021, establishing a strong reference point for structured, periodic multivariate series.
weaknesses: Auto-Correlation assumes dominant periodic structure; on irregular or purely stochastic series (financial tick data, sensor noise) it offers no advantage over simpler linear baselines.
Moving-average trend extraction uses a fixed kernel size per layer, so it cannot adapt to series where trend frequency changes abruptly — rapid regime shifts are smoothed away.

Despite O(N log N) attention, the full encoder-decoder stack with decomposition blocks is outperformed on standard benchmarks by single-layer linear models (DLinear), questioning the added architectural complexity.
recommended_for: Long-horizon multivariate forecasting (720+ steps) on datasets with strong seasonal periodicity, such as hourly electricity consumption or daily weather variables where cyclic patterns repeat predictably.
Applications requiring interpretable trend-season separation, such as energy demand planning, where the decomposed trend output is itself a usable signal alongside the final forecast.
not_recommended_for: Non-stationary financial or high-frequency trading series where periodicity assumptions break down and the FFT-based Auto-Correlation finds spurious cycles in noise.
Short-horizon forecasting tasks or datasets without recurring seasonal structure, where the decomposition overhead and FFT alignment provide no benefit over a lightweight MLP or linear model.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Wu et al. (NeurIPS 2021), the Auto-Correlation mechanism exploits the Wiener-Khinchin theorem — the fact that the autocorrelation of a signal equals the inverse FFT of its power spectral density — to discover period-based dependencies in O(N log N) time, the same theoretical cost as a single FFT pass.

target.notes: Multivariate long-horizon forecasting; predicts L future steps (designed for 96-720+) jointly across channels. Real-valued targets; no native probabilistic/quantile output (point forecast).

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of timesteps; designed for long sequences and long output horizons
data_regime.dimensionality: handles multivariate (many channels) input; benefits from long lookback windows
needs: long contiguous time series with stable sampling rate

features.interpretability: medium: inline series-decomposition blocks expose a trend component that is itself a usable signal, but the Auto-Correlation attention is opaque
features.notes: Inputs should be regularly sampled and roughly stationary in seasonal structure; standard normalization per channel expected. Exogenous covariates only via concatenated channels.

assumptions: Series has dominant, stable periodic/seasonal structure that FFT-based Auto-Correlation can align
Sampling is regular and the period is approximately constant over the window
Trend frequency is slow relative to the fixed moving-average kernel (no abrupt regime shifts)
loss: mean squared error (L2)
mean absolute error (L1)
contraindicated_when: Non-periodic, purely stochastic, or high-frequency financial/tick series where Auto-Correlation finds spurious cycles in noise
Short horizons or small datasets where simple linear models (DLinear) or an MLP match/beat it at far lower cost
Abrupt regime shifts or non-stationary trend that the fixed-kernel decomposition smooths away
Irregularly sampled or heavily missing series
Probabilistic/quantile forecasts required (no native uncertainty output)

children.name: TimesNet
children.diff_siblings: Unlike sibling Transformers that apply self-attention directly over temporal tokens, TimesNet converts 1D time series into 2D tensors via FFT-detected periods, then processes intraperiod and interperiod variations jointly using 2D convolutional inception blocks instead of attention.
strengths: Single architecture handles five distinct tasks (long/short forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, classification) without task-specific redesign, because the 2D representation is task-agnostic.

FFT-guided period detection automatically identifies dominant cycles (daily, weekly, etc.) and reshapes the series accordingly, making periodicity an explicit structural prior rather than something the model must learn implicitly.
Inception blocks with multi-scale 2D kernels (1x1, 3x3, 5x5) capture temporal patterns at multiple granularities simultaneously without the quadratic attention cost scaling with sequence length.
weaknesses: FFT-based period detection assumes the series has clear, stationary dominant frequencies; aperiodic or irregularly-sampled series yield noisy period estimates that degrade the 2D reshape quality.

Differing period lengths produce feature maps of incompatible spatial sizes, preventing full parallelization across periods and increasing wall-clock time compared to uniform-token Transformers like PatchTST.

Does not model cross-variate dependencies explicitly — each channel is reshaped and processed independently, so it underperforms iTransformer on datasets where inter-variable correlations are the primary predictive signal.
recommended_for: Datasets with strong multi-scale periodicity (e.g., hourly energy consumption or traffic with daily and weekly cycles) where making period structure an architectural prior yields a direct accuracy gain.
Unified pipelines requiring a single backbone for heterogeneous time series tasks (forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection) without maintaining separate specialized models.
not_recommended_for: Highly aperiodic financial tick data or event-driven series where FFT finds no dominant frequencies, causing the 2D reshape to introduce meaningless structure.
Scenarios demanding very low latency inference at scale, because variable-size feature maps from multiple detected periods prevent the full parallelism that pure attention or linear models achieve.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Wu et al. (2023) at ICLR, TimesNet was motivated by the observation that 2D vision models were far more mature than 1D temporal models; reshaping time into 2D allowed the authors to directly reuse inception-style CNN advances from image recognition for time series analysis.

target.notes: Primarily multivariate/univariate continuous forecasting (long- and short-horizon); also supports imputation, anomaly detection, and full-sequence classification. No probabilistic output by default; emits point predictions.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of timesteps; deep model requires substantial training sequences
data_regime.dimensionality: handles multivariate channels but treats each channel independently; input length fixed via lookback window

features.interpretability: low; FFT-detected periods give some structural insight but inception-block features are opaque
features.notes: Series should be regularly sampled (uniform timestamps) since FFT period detection assumes fixed sampling interval; standard normalization per channel; benefits from stationary dominant frequencies.

assumptions: Series has clear, stable dominant periodicities detectable by FFT
Regular (uniform) sampling interval
Approximate stationarity of frequency content over the window
Per-channel modeling is adequate (no strong cross-variate coupling required)
loss: squared error / MSE (forecasting, imputation)
MAE
cross-entropy (classification)
reconstruction error (anomaly detection)
contraindicated_when: Aperiodic or event-driven series (financial tick data, irregular events) where FFT finds no dominant frequency
Irregularly-sampled or unevenly-spaced timestamps
Cross-variate correlations are the main predictive signal (prefer iTransformer)
Very low-latency inference needs (variable-size period feature maps limit parallelism)
Small datasets where a linear/classical model (ARIMA, DLinear) suffices

children.name: TFT (Temporal Fusion Transformer)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike vanilla Time Series Transformers that apply self-attention directly to raw sequences, TFT fuses an LSTM encoder for local temporal processing with interpretable multi-head attention for long-range dependencies, and adds Gated Residual Networks with Variable Selection Networks to dynamically suppress irrelevant features and handle three distinct input types (static covariates, observed past, known future) in a single architecture.
strengths: Variable Selection Networks assign sparse, time-step-level importance weights to each input feature, providing built-in interpretability without post-hoc SHAP or LIME
Native support for known-future inputs (e.g., promotions, holidays) encoded separately from observed-past, which pure autoregressive models cannot exploit by design
Outputs calibrated quantile forecasts (e.g., P10/P50/P90) via quantile regression loss, enabling direct uncertainty quantification across multi-horizon horizons
weaknesses: Parameter count is roughly 4x that of an equivalent-depth vanilla Transformer, requiring GPUs with at least 16 GB VRAM or gradient checkpointing for training on long sequences
Variable Selection Networks and gating layers demand hundreds of training samples per series; performance degrades sharply on datasets with fewer than ~500 time steps per entity
Inference latency is high relative to linear or tree-based baselines because the LSTM and attention stacks run sequentially, making real-time low-latency deployment impractical
recommended_for: Retail demand forecasting with promotional calendars and store metadata, where known-future regressors and static covariates are abundant and probabilistic quantile outputs drive inventory decisions
Energy load or price forecasting over horizons of 24–168 hours where long-range periodic dependencies, weather covariates, and calibrated uncertainty intervals are all required simultaneously
not_recommended_for: Short univariate series (fewer than a few hundred observations) where the model's gating and attention mechanisms are data-hungry and simpler ARIMA or exponential smoothing methods generalize better

Latency-critical online inference pipelines (sub-10 ms) where the sequential LSTM encoder and multi-head attention stack introduce unacceptable computational overhead compared to lightweight linear models
children.curiosity: Introduced by Bryan Lim, Sercan O. Arik, Nicolas Loeff, and Tomas Pfister at Google Cloud AI (arXiv 2019, published in International Journal of Forecasting 2021), TFT outperformed N-BEATS by 7–14% in normalized quantile loss on electricity, traffic, and retail benchmarks, establishing it as a state-of-the-art multi-horizon forecasting baseline at the time of publication.

target.notes: Multi-horizon point and probabilistic forecasting; supports multiple entities/series jointly (global model). Quantile outputs make it natural for continuous demand/load; counts handled via quantile regression but no native count likelihood.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds+ of time steps per entity and ideally many entities; degrades below ~500 steps/series
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for rich multivariate covariates; Variable Selection handles many candidate features
needs: many covariates to justify the architecture

features.interpretability: medium-high: Variable Selection Networks give per-time-step feature importance and interpretable attention, unusual for deep forecasters
features.notes: Distinguishes three input classes: static covariates, observed-past inputs, and known-future inputs (calendars, promotions, holidays). Categoricals via learned embeddings; numerics typically scaled per series.

assumptions: enough history per series for gating/attention to learn (data-hungry)
informative covariates exist (static and/or known-future) to exploit
relationships across horizons are learnable from past patterns
loss: quantile/pinball loss (multi-quantile P10/P50/P90)
supports point losses (MSE/MAE) but quantile is the native design
contraindicated_when: short univariate series (few hundred obs) where ARIMA/ETS generalize better
sub-10ms latency-critical inference (sequential LSTM + attention overhead)
no useful covariates and a single simple series (architecture is wasted)
very small data / few entities (overfits gating and selection layers)

children.name: Chronos (Amazon)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike sibling time series transformers that use continuous embeddings or patch-based tokenization, Chronos repurposes a T5 encoder-decoder LLM verbatim — it quantizes scaled float values into a discrete vocabulary of 4096 bins and trains with cross-entropy loss, treating forecasting as next-token prediction over numeric tokens rather than regression over continuous outputs.
strengths: Zero-shot generalization across domains: pretrained on ~1 billion observations from 42 real and synthetic datasets, it matches or beats task-specific models on over 40 benchmarks without any fine-tuning.
Probabilistic forecasts by design: autoregressive sampling over the quantized vocabulary produces full predictive distributions (mean, quantiles, intervals) with no extra parametric assumption.
Model family covering resource constraints: five T5 variants from 8 M (Tiny) to 710 M (Large) parameters, plus Chronos-Bolt which achieves up to 250x faster inference at matched accuracy.
weaknesses: Strictly univariate: the tokenization scheme encodes a single scalar sequence — it cannot natively ingest exogenous regressors or multivariate covariate channels without architectural changes (addressed only in Chronos-2).

Quantization information loss: binning continuous values into 4096 uniform bins discards sub-bin precision; for series with very fine-grained variation (e.g., financial tick data) this degrades resolution.

Context-length bottleneck: the T5 self-attention quadratic cost limits practical context to a few hundred to ~2048 tokens, making it less suitable for very long historical dependencies without truncation or subsampling.
recommended_for: Demand forecasting across heterogeneous product catalogs where labeled history per SKU is scarce and zero-shot transfer from the pretrained model eliminates per-series model fitting.
Probabilistic energy load or weather forecasting pipelines that require calibrated uncertainty intervals without specifying a parametric distribution family.
not_recommended_for: Multivariate time series where leading indicators or related channels must inform the target forecast — the native architecture is univariate and adding covariates requires retraining.
High-frequency tick-level financial data where sub-bin price precision is critical and latency constraints rule out transformer inference overhead.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Ansari et al. (Amazon, 2024) in 'Chronos: Learning the Language of Time Series' (arXiv:2403.07815), the key insight was that no architectural change to T5 was needed — only replacing text tokenization with mean-scaled numeric quantization, showing that LLM cross-entropy training on discrete tokens transfers directly to probabilistic time series forecasting.

target.notes: Univariate scalar sequence forecasting. Produces full predictive distribution via autoregressive sampling over a 4096-bin quantized vocabulary; no parametric family assumed (mean, quantiles, intervals are sample-derived).

data_regime.rows: zero-shot: works even with scarce per-series history (short context of a few hundred to ~2048 points); pretrained on ~1B observations so no per-series training data needed
data_regime.dimensionality: single channel only (p=1 target series); cannot add exogenous regressors natively
needs: no labeled training data required (zero-shot foundation model)

features.interpretability: low: T5 LLM over quantized numeric tokens, black-box autoregressive forecasts
features.notes: Input is a single scaled+quantized numeric series; values binned into 4096 uniform bins (sub-bin precision lost). Context length capped ~2048 by quadratic self-attention.

assumptions: target is univariate with no required covariate/exogenous information
relevant dependencies fit within the bounded context window
sub-bin numeric precision is not critical (quantization tolerable)
series resembles the broad distribution of pretraining domains for good zero-shot transfer
loss: cross-entropy over quantized token vocabulary (next-token prediction)
yields probabilistic forecasts; evaluate with quantile/pinball loss, CRPS, WQL
contraindicated_when: multivariate forecasting where leading indicators / related channels must inform the target
exogenous regressors are essential (covariates require retraining/architecture change)
high-frequency tick-level data needing sub-bin precision
very long-range historical dependencies exceeding the context window
hard low-latency / CPU-only constraints where transformer inference overhead is prohibitive (mitigated by Chronos-Bolt)

children.name: TimeGPT
children.diff_siblings: Unlike PatchTST or iTransformer, which are trained from scratch on task-specific data, TimeGPT is a closed-weight foundation model pre-trained on over 100 billion data points across diverse domains, enabling zero-shot inference on unseen series via API without any fine-tuning.
strengths: Zero-shot forecasting across heterogeneous domains (finance, weather, IoT) with no training step required — inference is a single API call.
Supports conformal prediction intervals out of the box, providing statistically valid coverage guarantees without manual calibration.
Handles anomaly detection and forecasting in the same model, using reconstruction error from the encoder-decoder to flag outliers.
weaknesses: Closed-weight model accessible only via Nixtla's API — no self-hosting, full reproducibility, or inspection of weights is possible.
Zero-shot accuracy degrades on series with domain-specific seasonalities, frequencies, or exogenous covariates absent from pre-training data.
Univariate-channel processing by default: cross-variable dependencies are not modeled unless explicit multivariate extensions are used.
recommended_for: Rapid production forecasting where labeling time or training infrastructure is unavailable — e.g., retail demand for thousands of SKUs with cold-start items.
Anomaly detection on operational time series (IoT sensors, server metrics) where labeled anomalies are scarce and zero-shot inference suffices.
not_recommended_for: Highly regulated environments (healthcare, finance compliance) requiring full model auditability and self-hosted inference, ruled out by the closed-weight API-only access.

Series governed by strong exogenous variables unseen during pre-training (e.g., bespoke industrial process signals), where a task-specific model trained on in-domain data will consistently outperform zero-shot inference.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Garza and Mergenthaler-Canseco from Nixtla in October 2023 (arXiv:2310.03589), TimeGPT-1 was the first publicly available foundation model for time series, trained on a corpus larger than 100 billion data points spanning finance, healthcare, weather, and transport domains.

target.notes: Univariate point and probabilistic forecasting over a regular time index; also outputs anomaly flags via encoder-decoder reconstruction error. Handles multiple frequencies (hourly/daily/weekly/monthly). Cross-series covariates supported only via explicit exogenous/multivariate API extensions; default is per-channel univariate.

data_regime.rows: works with short history per series including cold-start items, since it is zero-shot and requires no per-series training; benefits from at least a few seasonal cycles of context
data_regime.dimensionality: scales to thousands of parallel series (e.g. many SKUs) cheaply because no fitting step is needed
needs: network access to Nixtla API (closed-weight, no self-hosting)
no GPU or training infrastructure on the user side

features.interpretability: low - closed foundation model, weights and internals not inspectable
features.notes: Consumes the raw historical series plus timestamps; no manual feature engineering or scaling required. Pre-trained on heterogeneous domains, so it generalizes best when the series resembles common patterns (finance, weather, IoT, retail demand).

assumptions: Target series' seasonality, frequency, and dynamics resemble patterns seen in the broad pre-training corpus
Behavior is driven mainly by endogenous history rather than bespoke exogenous signals unseen during pre-training
Stationary-enough regime within the forecast horizon (no unprecedented structural break)
loss: point forecast (trained for accurate conditional mean/median)
conformal prediction intervals for calibrated coverage (probabilistic forecasting)
reconstruction error for anomaly scoring
contraindicated_when: full auditability, reproducibility, or self-hosted/offline inference is required (regulated healthcare/finance) due to closed-weight API-only access
behavior is dominated by strong domain-specific exogenous variables absent from pre-training, where an in-domain task-specific model outperforms
series has highly idiosyncratic seasonality or sampling frequency unlike the pre-training distribution
cross-variable dependencies are central and only the default univariate channel mode is available

target.notes: Point forecasting of one or more continuous variates over a horizon; produces multi-step (often direct multi-horizon) outputs. Equispaced, regularly-sampled series assumed. Probabilistic variants emit quantiles or distributional params, but the base family targets the conditional mean.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of timesteps per series and/or many series; underfits on hundreds of observations where linear/tree models win
data_regime.dimensionality: scales well to high variate count via channel-independent embedding (PatchTST); long lookback L is the bottleneck, O(L^2) attention unless patched/sparsified

features.interpretability: low; attention weights are not faithful temporal-causal explanations
features.notes: Requires per-variate normalization (instance/RevIN) because attention is scale-sensitive and series drift; calendar/seasonality must be injected via temporal covariates or decomposition since language-style positional encodings carry no periodicity. Missing timestamps must be imputed/resampled to a regular grid first.

assumptions: regular, equally-spaced sampling on a common grid
sufficient history to learn long-range and cross-variate structure
future is driven by patterns learnable from past windows (no strong unprecedented regime shifts)
stationarity after normalization/decomposition; raw non-stationary trend hurts attention
loss: MSE / squared error (default)
MAE / L1
quantile / pinball loss for probabilistic variants
negative log-likelihood under an emitted distribution
MASE/sMAPE used for evaluation
contraindicated_when: short univariate series (hundreds of points) — linear (DLinear), ARIMA, or gradient-boosted trees give lower error with far less compute
irregular/unevenly-sampled or heavily-missing series without resampling
strong abrupt regime changes or non-recurring events with little precedent
low-latency or edge inference under tight memory budgets (quadratic attention footprint)

children.name: TabPFN
children.diff_siblings: It is a Transformer-based model specifically designed for small tabular classification, whereas its siblings focus on modalities like natural language, computer vision, or time series. It operates without requiring hyperparameter tuning by performing in-context learning on the provided training data in a single forward pass.
strengths: Extremely fast inference, often producing predictions in under a second on small datasets.
Requires no hyperparameter tuning, simplifying the modeling pipeline.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on small tabular classification tasks (typically <= 1000 samples), often outperforming tuned tree-based models.
weaknesses: The original version is limited to small datasets (e.g., <= 1000 rows, <= 100 features, <= 10 classes).
Primarily designed for classification; not applicable for regression tasks in its initial version.
Performance can degrade on datasets with high dimensionality or many categorical features.
recommended_for: Rapid prototyping and establishing strong baselines for small tabular classification problems.
AutoML pipelines where inference speed and zero-tuning are critical for small-scale data.
not_recommended_for: Large-scale datasets that exceed the model's context window (e.g., >10,000 samples).
High-dimensional datasets, as performance can be worse than simpler models.
children.curiosity: TabPFN is a Prior-Data Fitted Network (PFN) pre-trained on millions of synthetic datasets generated from structural causal models, allowing it to approximate Bayesian inference on a new dataset in a single forward pass.

target.notes: Original TabPFN is classification-only; outputs calibrated class posteriors approximating Bayesian inference over a synthetic prior of structural causal models. Regression is not supported in the v1 design.

data_regime.rows: best <= 1000 training samples; degrades / hits context limits beyond ~10000 rows
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n strongly preferred; <= 100 features, <= 10 classes in the original version

features.interpretability: low; a pre-trained Transformer doing in-context learning in one forward pass, no explicit fitted coefficients or splits
features.notes: Designed for low-to-moderate numeric features; many high-cardinality categoricals hurt performance. No per-dataset hyperparameter tuning required.

assumptions: The dataset resembles the synthetic prior TabPFN was meta-trained on (moderate-dimensional, structured tabular data)
Small sample/feature counts within the model context window
Features are not dominated by high-cardinality categoricals or extreme dimensionality
loss: log-loss / cross-entropy (approximate posterior predictive distribution); no per-dataset training objective since it is amortized in-context inference
contraindicated_when: Sample size or feature count exceeds the model's context budget (e.g. >10k rows, >100 features, >10 classes)
Target is continuous (regression) in the original version
High-dimensional or heavily categorical data where tuned gradient-boosted trees outperform
A regulatory/interpretability requirement demands an inspectable model

target.notes: Umbrella family. Output head is task-agnostic: softmax over a vocabulary for generation/seq2seq, class logits for classification/NER (token- or sequence-level), scalar/regression heads for tabular or forecasting, or no target at all for self-supervised pretraining (masked-token / next-token objectives that learn representations).

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ labeled when training from scratch (pretraining wants billions of tokens); with a pre-trained checkpoint, fine-tunes from hundreds to low-thousands of examples
data_regime.dimensionality: handles very high-dimensional sequential/token inputs; attention cost is O(T^2) in sequence length T, so naive use is impractical beyond ~4k tokens without sparse/linear-attention variants
needs: large labeled or unlabeled corpus (from scratch)

features.interpretability: low: distributed self-attention representations; attention weights are not faithful feature attributions
features.notes: Consumes tokenized/patchified sequences. No native order awareness, so position must be injected (positional encodings). Cross-attention unifies multi-modal inputs (image patches + text tokens) without architecture changes.

assumptions: relevant structure is expressible as relations between sequence/set elements
enough data (or transferable pretraining) to learn local/order patterns the architecture does not encode as an inductive bias
sequence length kept within the quadratic-attention compute/memory budget
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss (classification, next-token, masked-token)
label-smoothed cross-entropy (translation/generation)
sequence-to-sequence teacher-forcing likelihood
contrastive / self-supervised objectives (representation pretraining)
squared error for regression/forecasting heads
contraindicated_when: low-data tabular regression/classification (<~5k rows) with no suitable pre-trained checkpoint: gradient-boosted trees or MLPs generalize better
strong local/translation-invariant structure with limited data (small-image vision, short n-gram text) where CNNs/RNNs inject the right inductive bias more sample-efficiently
very long sequences without sparse/linear attention, where O(T^2) memory is prohibitive
tight-latency or low-memory edge inference, where a minimum viable Transformer is far heavier than an equivalent CNN/RNN

children.name: 2.5 State Space Models (SSM)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Transformers (which use full pairwise attention with quadratic complexity) and RNNs (which process tokens strictly sequentially), SSMs parameterize sequence dynamics as a continuous-time linear system (x'(t) = Ax(t) + Bu(t)) that can be computed either as a recurrence at inference or as a global convolution during training, achieving linear time complexity without sacrificing long-range dependency modeling.
strengths: Linear O(N) inference cost: the recurrent form processes each new token in constant time and constant memory, unlike Transformers whose KV-cache grows with sequence length.

Effective long-range memory: HiPPO-initialized state matrices (S4, Gu et al. 2021) compactly encode the entire input history in a fixed-size latent state, allowing the model to reach dependencies across tens of thousands of tokens without gradient vanishing.

Hardware-efficient training via parallel scan: the convolutional form of the SSM kernel enables fully parallel training on GPUs with the same throughput as a CNN, avoiding the sequential bottleneck of plain RNNs.
weaknesses: Weak content-based retrieval: the fixed-size state cannot selectively "look up" a specific past token by content; tasks requiring exact recall of arbitrary positions (e.g., copying a random key from a long context) are structurally harder than for attention.

Sensitive matrix initialization: stability and expressiveness depend heavily on the parameterization of the state matrix A; naive random initialization leads to vanishing/exploding gradients, requiring structured initializations (HiPPO, diagonal-plus-low-rank) that add implementation complexity.

Limited in-context learning: pure SSM language models consistently underperform equivalently sized Transformers on few-shot ICL benchmarks, likely because ICL requires dynamic, input-dependent weight-like behavior that a fixed linear recurrence cannot easily approximate.
recommended_for: Very long sequences (>8 k tokens) where quadratic attention memory is prohibitive, such as genomic DNA classification, hour-long audio waveform modeling, or continuous sensor streams from IoT devices.

Edge or real-time inference where memory and latency are constrained, since the recurrent SSM form processes each step in O(state_size) time and O(state_size) memory regardless of sequence history length.
not_recommended_for: Tasks requiring precise retrieval of specific past tokens by content (e.g., multi-hop question answering over long documents, or associative recall), where attention's explicit key-value lookup gives a structural advantage.

Small, short-sequence datasets (e.g., tabular time series with fewer than ~100 steps per sample), where the overhead of structured matrix parameterization yields no benefit over a simple LSTM or 1-D CNN.
children.curiosity: The foundational S4 architecture was introduced by Albert Gu, Karan Goel, and Christopher Re (2021) in 'Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces'; its state matrix is initialized using the HiPPO-LegS polynomial projection framework, which Gu et al. had derived the prior year to prove that certain structured matrices optimally compress continuous input history into a fixed-size state.

children.name: S4 (Structured State Spaces)
children.diff_siblings: S4 parameterizes the state transition matrix A as a diagonal-plus-low-rank (DPLR) structure initialized via HiPPO theory, enabling exact diagonalization and reducing the recurrence to a Cauchy kernel computable in O(N log N), unlike other SSMs that rely on approximations or dense matrix representations.
strengths: Solves Path-X (sequence length 16,384) on Long Range Arena where all prior SSMs and Transformers fail, demonstrating genuine capture of dependencies spanning tens of thousands of steps.
Training via convolution mode yields O(L log L) complexity over sequence length L, matching Transformer throughput while avoiding the O(L²) memory bottleneck of attention.
HiPPO-based initialization gives the A matrix a principled mathematical grounding for polynomial approximation of history, making training stable without careful tuning of the recurrent dynamics.
weaknesses: State-space parameters (A, B, C) are fixed across all input positions, so S4 cannot perform content-based gating — it treats every token identically regardless of its value, which Mamba later addressed with selective parameterization.

DPLR diagonalization requires working in the complex domain and applying correction terms; implementing correctly is non-trivial and numerically sensitive, limiting accessibility compared to attention-based models.
Underperforms Transformers on standard language modeling benchmarks (e.g., perplexity on The Pile), where in-context retrieval and content-dependent attention matter more than long-range compression.
recommended_for: Raw audio and speech classification tasks with sequences of 8,000–100,000+ samples, where temporal dependencies span seconds and neither RNNs (vanishing gradient) nor Transformers (quadratic cost) are viable.

Time-series forecasting or biosignal modeling (ECG, EEG) where the signal is dense, regularly sampled, and global structure over thousands of steps must be captured without positional encoding engineering.
not_recommended_for: Natural language tasks requiring associative recall or copying specific tokens from context (e.g., question answering over documents), where the fixed-parameter state cannot selectively retain rare tokens.
Settings where pre-trained Transformer checkpoints (BERT, GPT family) are available for fine-tuning, since S4 has no ecosystem of pre-trained weights and would require full training from scratch.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Gu, Goel, and Ré (ICLR 2022, Oral), S4 was the first model to successfully solve the Path-X task in the Long Range Arena benchmark — a binary classification over sequences of length 16,384 that every prior architecture, including Transformers, scored at chance level (50%).

target.notes: Sequence-to-label (classification) or sequence-to-sequence head bolted on the SSM backbone; the model itself is a sequence encoder, so target type depends on the head. No inherent target distribution assumption.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of labeled sequences for the deep variant; benefits from very long individual sequences (L from ~1k to 100k+ steps)
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for extreme sequence length L where attention's O(L^2) is infeasible; handles modest feature channels per step

features.interpretability: low: latent linear state-space dynamics with HiPPO-initialized complex (DPLR) parameters, not human-readable
features.notes: Inputs should be dense, regularly sampled, single time-step granularity (raw audio samples, biosignals, pixels-as-sequence). No positional encoding needed; the recurrence encodes order. Irregular sampling or missing steps break the fixed-step convolution kernel.

assumptions: dependencies are captured by a fixed (input-independent) linear state-space recurrence — parameters do not gate on token content
sequence is regularly sampled at a constant step so the discretized SSM kernel is valid
relevant structure is long-range/global rather than sparse content-based retrieval of specific tokens
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss for classification
squared error for regression/forecasting heads
contraindicated_when: task requires associative recall, copying, or selective retention of specific rare tokens (use selective SSMs like Mamba, or attention)
natural-language modeling where content-dependent attention and in-context retrieval dominate (Transformers outperform)
pretrained checkpoints would shortcut training — S4 has no pretrained-weight ecosystem
sequences are short (L small), where a Transformer's quadratic cost is a non-issue and attention is simpler
data is irregularly sampled or has missing timesteps without resampling

children.name: Mamba
children.diff_siblings: Unlike S4 and other linear time-invariant SSMs, Mamba makes the state-space parameters B, C, and the discretization step Δ explicit functions of the input at each position (S6 selective scan), enabling data-dependent gating without attention; a hardware-aware parallel associative scan run in GPU SRAM compensates for the loss of convolution-based computation.
strengths: Linear-time O(L) inference in sequence length L, with recurrent inference that avoids KV-cache growth — directly contrasting the O(L²) memory cost of full attention at long contexts.
Input-dependent selection allows the model to dynamically suppress irrelevant tokens and propagate relevant state across thousands of positions, a property absent in time-invariant SSMs like S4.
5x higher throughput than comparably sized Transformers at sequence lengths above 2K tokens due to the hardware-aware scan that keeps intermediate state in SRAM rather than HBM.
weaknesses: Cannot natively perform exact content-based lookup across arbitrary positions — tasks requiring precise copying or induction heads (e.g., in-context learning) are structurally harder than for attention.
The fixed-size hidden state imposes a hard compression bottleneck: information not captured during the forward scan is permanently lost, unlike Transformer KV-caches that retain all tokens.

The selective scan's data-dependent parameters break the LTI convolution shortcut, requiring a custom CUDA kernel; deploying Mamba on hardware without that kernel (e.g., TPUs, edge MCUs) is non-trivial.
recommended_for: Long-sequence autoregressive language modeling (context > 8K tokens) where GPU memory for KV-caches becomes the binding constraint and throughput matters more than exact retrieval.
Streaming time-series or audio processing where the recurrent form provides O(1) per-step inference and the selective gate naturally filters irrelevant temporal segments.
not_recommended_for: Retrieval-heavy tasks requiring the model to locate and copy a specific verbatim substring from a long context (e.g., document key-value retrieval benchmarks), where attention's exact lookup is structurally superior.
Small datasets or short sequences (< 512 tokens) where the efficiency advantage disappears and the custom CUDA dependency adds deployment overhead without benefit.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Albert Gu and Tri Dao (2023) in 'Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces' (arXiv:2312.00752); the name S6 for the selective scan derives from it being the sixth iteration in the structured SSM lineage (S1–S4, then H3, then S6/Mamba), and the original model matched GPT-3-scale Transformer perplexity on The Pile while running at 5x the throughput.

target.notes: Autoregressive next-token/next-step prediction over discrete tokens (multinomial over vocabulary) or continuous sequence values; also usable as a sequence encoder backbone with task-specific heads. Target type follows the head, not the SSM core.

data_regime.rows: needs large training corpora (thousands+ long sequences); advantage only materializes at sequence length L > 2K and grows with context
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for very long L (8K-1M+ tokens); fixed-size recurrent hidden state means memory is O(1) in L at inference

features.interpretability: low: data-dependent state-space gating is opaque, no attention map to inspect
features.notes: Operates on ordered sequences (tokens, audio frames, genomic bases, time steps); requires a fixed sampling/tokenization. Not for tabular i.i.d. rows.

assumptions: signal is sequential/ordered with meaningful long-range temporal dependencies
relevant information can be compressed into a fixed-size recurrent state during a single forward scan
sufficient data and GPU compute to train a deep sequence model
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss for autoregressive token prediction
squared error for continuous sequence regression
any differentiable sequence objective via task head
contraindicated_when: task requires exact content-based retrieval or verbatim copying from arbitrary positions (attention is structurally superior)
sequences are short (< 512 tokens) so the O(L) efficiency advantage vanishes
deployment target lacks the custom CUDA kernel (TPU, edge MCU, CPU-only)
data is tabular/i.i.d. with no sequential structure
small dataset where a Transformer or classical sequence model trains adequately

children.name: Hyena / RetNet / RWKV
children.diff_siblings: Unlike SSMs such as Mamba that use selective state-space recurrences, this family replaces attention with distinct primitives: Hyena uses implicitly parametrized long convolutions interleaved with data-controlled gating; RetNet introduces a multi-scale retention mechanism with three equivalent computation forms (parallel, recurrent, chunkwise); and RWKV reformulates attention as a linear time-decay weighted sum, making it expressible as a true RNN at inference time.
strengths: Sub-quadratic or linear sequence complexity: Hyena runs 100x faster than attention at length 64K; RetNet and RWKV achieve O(1) per-step inference cost by collapsing context into a fixed-size hidden state.
Training parallelism preserved: RetNet's parallel retention form and RWKV's time-parallel WKV operator allow full GPU utilization during training, unlike vanilla RNNs that must unroll sequentially.

Constant memory footprint at inference: RWKV and RetNet maintain a fixed-size recurrent state regardless of sequence length, enabling deployment on memory-constrained hardware without KV-cache growth.
weaknesses: Weaker in-context retrieval than softmax attention: the linear or exponential-decay weighting in RetNet and RWKV cannot perfectly replicate the sharp, arbitrary-position attention pattern that transformers use for copying or lookup tasks.

Hyena's implicit long-convolution kernels are harder to interpret and tune than explicit state-space matrices; hyperparameter sensitivity to kernel parametrization can degrade performance on short sequences.

Recurrent hidden state is a lossy compression: all three architectures trade exact context access for efficiency, causing degradation on tasks requiring verbatim recall of tokens far back in the sequence.
recommended_for: Autoregressive language model inference at scale where KV-cache memory is the bottleneck — RWKV and RetNet deliver O(1) memory per step, enabling longer effective batch sizes on fixed GPU memory.
Long-document processing (>32K tokens) where quadratic attention is computationally prohibitive — Hyena's convolutional approach and RetNet's chunkwise form scale linearly with sequence length.
not_recommended_for: Tasks requiring precise associative recall or multi-hop lookup over a long context (e.g., needle-in-a-haystack retrieval), where softmax attention's exact position-specific weighting is necessary.

Short sequences (<512 tokens) with abundant compute, where the architectural overhead of these alternatives yields no efficiency benefit and standard transformers achieve higher quality with less tuning.
children.curiosity: Hyena was introduced by Poli et al. (2023) at Stanford and shown to match Transformer perplexity on The Pile while being 2x faster than FlashAttention at sequence length 8K and 100x faster at 64K, purely through implicit long convolutions without any attention operation.

target.notes: Autoregressive next-token prediction over discrete vocabulary; categorical cross-entropy over sequences. Applies to any long ordered token stream, not only NL text.

data_regime.rows: needs large-scale token corpora (billions of tokens) for competitive LM quality; pretraining regime
data_regime.dimensionality: very high effective parameter count; designed for sequence length 32K-256K+ where attention is quadratic

features.interpretability: low: implicit long-convolution kernels (Hyena) and decayed recurrent states are opaque
features.notes: Tokenized discrete sequences; primary differentiator from siblings is per-step O(1) inference memory (no growing KV-cache) and sub-quadratic training cost at long context.

assumptions: Predictive signal is dominated by smooth/decaying long-range structure that a fixed-size recurrent state or implicit convolution can compress without exact per-position recall
Sequence length is large enough that quadratic attention is the actual bottleneck
loss: autoregressive cross-entropy / log-loss over next token
language-modeling perplexity
contraindicated_when: Task requires exact associative recall or multi-hop lookup over long context (needle-in-a-haystack, verbatim copying) where softmax attention's sharp position-specific weighting is needed
Short sequences (<512 tokens) with ample compute, where standard transformers reach higher quality with less tuning
Tabular, low-dimensional, or small-n problems with no sequential/temporal structure

target.notes: Sequence-to-sequence family: supports autoregressive next-token/next-step prediction, per-step labeling, and whole-sequence classification. Target depends on the head; the backbone learns sequence representations.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of sequences; deep nets do not regularize well on small data
data_regime.dimensionality: scales to extremely long sequences (10k-1M+ steps) at linear O(N) cost; state size is a fixed hyperparameter independent of sequence length
needs: long sequences to justify over LSTM/1D-CNN

features.interpretability: low; learned latent state dynamics are not directly inspectable
features.notes: Operates on ordered sequences (audio waveforms, DNA, token streams, sensor signals). Inputs typically embedded/tokenized; benefits from regular, densely sampled sequences.

assumptions: data has meaningful sequential/temporal structure with long-range dependencies
fixed-size latent state can summarize relevant history (no need for exact content-based recall of arbitrary past tokens)
stable structured parameterization of the state matrix (HiPPO / diagonal-plus-low-rank) for well-behaved gradients
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss (autoregressive LM, classification)
squared error (continuous sequence regression/forecasting)
any differentiable sequence objective via task head
