strengths: Photorealistic novel-view synthesis with view-dependent effects (specular highlights, reflections) from only sparse posed images
Encodes geometry and appearance as a continuous, compact 3D representation, often beating photogrammetry on thin structures and low-texture surfaces
Real-time rendering once fitted (3D Gaussian Splatting reaches 1080p at over 100 fps)
weaknesses: Per-scene optimization with no inherent generalization: each new scene must be fit from scratch
Heavy compute and memory cost (NeRF training takes hours to days; Gaussian splats need roughly 500 MB to 1.5 GB per scene)
Struggles with dynamic, deformable, or large unbounded scenes and is prone to aliasing and floater artifacts
recommended_for: Free-viewpoint VR/AR capture and digital twins of real environments from casual photo or video sets
High-fidelity 3D reconstruction for cultural heritage, product visualization, and robotics/SLAM scene mapping
not_recommended_for: Generating novel, never-seen objects or scenes from a prompt or noise (use Diffusion or GANs instead)
Real-time reconstruction of fast dynamic scenes or single-image-to-3D under tight latency and storage budgets
children.curiosity: NeRF was introduced by Mildenhall et al. (2020); 3D Gaussian Splatting by Kerbl et al. (2023) replaced the slow MLP ray-marching with rasterized anisotropic 3D Gaussians, won Best Paper at SIGGRAPH 2023, and enabled real-time radiance-field rendering.

children.name: 3D Gaussian Splatting
children.diff_siblings: Unlike implicit neural representations like NeRF which use a coordinate-based MLP to represent the scene, 3D Gaussian Splatting uses an explicit set of millions of 3D Gaussians that are directly rasterized, enabling much faster training and real-time rendering.
strengths: Enables high-quality, photorealistic novel view synthesis at real-time frame rates (often over 100 FPS).
Training times are significantly faster than most Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) variants.
The explicit point-based representation excels at capturing fine details and complex, thin structures.
weaknesses: Scene representation requires a large memory and storage footprint, often hundreds of megabytes or more.
Editing the scene by manipulating or removing objects is non-trivial due to the unstructured nature of the millions of Gaussians.
The explicit representation lacks a well-defined surface, making it difficult to use for geometric analysis or tasks requiring a mesh.
recommended_for: Creating digital twins and photorealistic fly-throughs of static scenes for VR/AR and virtual production.
Rapid 3D capture and visualization of objects and environments where rendering speed is critical.
not_recommended_for: Applications with strict memory or storage limitations due to large file sizes.
Projects requiring precise geometric measurements, editing, or analysis typically performed on 3D meshes.
children.curiosity: The technique's real-time performance is achieved through a custom differentiable rasterizer that projects and sorts the 3D Gaussians onto the 2D image plane for efficient rendering and gradient backpropagation.

target.notes: Not a predictive/supervised model. Fits an explicit scene representation (millions of anisotropic 3D Gaussians with position, covariance, opacity, spherical-harmonic color) to reconstruct a single static scene; outputs are rendered RGB images for novel viewpoints, not predictions on tabular targets.

data_regime.rows: dozens to a few hundred posed input photos of one scene; per-scene optimization, not a dataset-wide trained model
data_regime.dimensionality: scene parameterized by ~0.1M-5M+ Gaussians; representation is hundreds of MB
needs: multi-view images of the same static scene
accurate camera poses + sparse point cloud (typically from COLMAP/SfM)

features.interpretability: low; scene is an unstructured cloud of Gaussian primitives with no surface/mesh, hard to edit or measure geometrically
features.notes: Requires known/estimated camera intrinsics and extrinsics; sensitive to pose accuracy. Assumes calibrated overlapping views with sufficient parallax.

assumptions: Scene is static (no moving objects or lighting changes across captures)
Camera poses are accurate (errors propagate as floaters/blur)
Sufficient multi-view coverage and parallax for the regions to be rendered
Roughly consistent illumination across input images
loss: photometric reconstruction loss (L1 on rendered vs ground-truth pixels)
D-SSIM structural similarity term
differentiable tile-based rasterization enables gradient-based optimization with adaptive densification/pruning of Gaussians
contraindicated_when: dynamic/deformable scenes or large lighting variation
memory/storage is tightly constrained (representation is large)
a watertight mesh or precise geometric measurements are required
few input views, poor camera-pose estimates, or low parallax
extrapolating far outside the captured camera trajectory

children.name: NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike methods that produce explicit 3D representations like meshes or point clouds, NeRF uses a deep neural network to learn an implicit, continuous volumetric representation of a scene, encoding both geometry and view-dependent appearance.
strengths: Renders photorealistic, high-resolution novel views with complex geometry and view-dependent effects like reflections and translucency.
Represents scenes in a continuous, compact format (a few megabytes for the network weights) without explicit 3D geometry.
Can handle complex, non-Lambertian surfaces and fine details that are challenging for traditional photogrammetry.
weaknesses: Extremely slow training and rendering times for the original model, often taking hours or days to train per scene.
Requires a large number of input images with accurately known camera poses to avoid artifacts.
The learned scene representation is not easily editable or composable, and lighting is 'baked in'.
recommended_for: High-quality novel view synthesis for static scenes.
3D scene reconstruction from a collection of 2D images for applications in VR/AR and content creation.
not_recommended_for: Real-time rendering applications (without significant modifications or newer variants like Instant-NGP).
Scenes with dynamic elements, changing lighting, or for which precise, editable mesh extraction is the primary goal.
children.curiosity: The original NeRF paper from ECCV 2020, co-authored by Ben Mildenhall and others, received a Best Paper Honorable Mention and sparked a wave of research in neural rendering.

target.notes: Not a predictive model over a tabular target. Optimizes a per-scene reconstruction objective: given a set of posed 2D images, learns a continuous 5D function (x,y,z,theta,phi) -> (RGB, density) for novel-view synthesis. Output is rendered pixel radiance, not a labeled prediction.

data_regime.rows: per-scene fit, not dataset-driven: needs tens to ~100+ multi-view images of one static scene with accurate camera poses (typically from SfM/COLMAP)
data_regime.dimensionality: small MLP (millions of params) overfit to a single scene; no train/test generalization across scenes in the vanilla formulation
needs: hours of per-scene optimization (vanilla NeRF; faster variants like Instant-NGP exist)

features.interpretability: low: scene encoded as opaque MLP weights; geometry and view-dependent appearance are implicit, not an editable mesh
features.notes: Inputs are calibrated multi-view RGB images. Uses positional/frequency encoding of 3D coordinates and viewing direction to let the MLP represent high-frequency detail; volumetric rendering integrates color/density along camera rays.

assumptions: Scene is static during capture (no moving objects)
Lighting is fixed; illumination is baked into the learned radiance
Camera poses are known and accurate; pose error causes blur/ghosting artifacts
Sufficient, well-distributed multi-view coverage of the scene
loss: photometric reconstruction loss (squared error between rendered and observed pixel colors over sampled rays)
contraindicated_when: real-time rendering is required (vanilla NeRF; needs accelerated variants)
scene is dynamic, deformable, or has changing lighting
camera poses are unknown or noisy
only sparse/few input views are available
an explicit, editable, or composable 3D mesh/point cloud is the deliverable
relighting or scene editing is needed (lighting is baked in)

target.notes: Not a predictive estimator over a labeled target. Fits a single 3D scene from posed 2D images; the learned function maps a query ray/3D point + view direction to radiance/color/density, optimized to reconstruct held-in views, not to predict an outcome variable.

data_regime.rows: per-scene fit from tens to a few hundred posed images; no cross-scene training set needed (no generalization either)
data_regime.dimensionality: input is dense pixel observations of one scene; quality scales with view coverage and overlap, not with sample count in a tabular sense
needs: accurate camera poses / intrinsics (typically from SfM e.g. COLMAP)
minutes to hours of per-scene optimization
100s of MB to ~1.5 GB storage per fitted scene (3DGS)

features.interpretability: low for the learned weights (MLP radiance field) but the fitted representation is a directly inspectable/renderable 3D field; Gaussian splats are explicit primitives
features.notes: Requires multi-view 2D images with known/estimated camera poses and sufficient baseline and overlap. View-dependent appearance (specularity) is captured via the view-direction input.

assumptions: scene is static during capture (rigid geometry; non-rigid/dynamic motion needs deformable or 4D variants)
camera poses and intrinsics are accurate; pose error directly corrupts geometry
adequate multi-view coverage with overlapping baselines; sparse or co-located views cause floaters and holes
consistent illumination and exposure across views (varying lighting violates the static-radiance assumption)
bounded or well-parameterized scene extent (unbounded scenes need contraction/anti-aliasing variants)
loss: photometric reconstruction loss (per-pixel L1 / L2 / MSE between rendered and observed images)
D-SSIM / perceptual terms (common in 3D Gaussian Splatting)
regularizers on density/opacity, geometry, or splat count; evaluated via PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS
contraindicated_when: you need to generate novel, never-observed objects/scenes from a prompt or noise (use Diffusion or GANs)
no reliable camera poses are available and SfM fails (textureless, repetitive, or wide-baseline captures)
scene is dynamic, deformable, or fast-moving and only standard static variants are available
single-image or few-image input with no multi-view coverage
tight latency/storage budget for training (per-scene optimization and large splat files are costly)
very large unbounded environments where artifacts and aliasing dominate

target.notes: Umbrella family for models of the data distribution p(x) (or joint p(x,y)). Goal is to estimate/sample the density, not predict a label; supervision is typically absent. Conditional variants accept a label/prompt as input to steer generation, but the learned object is still a distribution over outputs, not a point estimate.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands to millions of unlabeled examples; modern variants (diffusion, large autoregressive) require very large corpora to reach realism
data_regime.dimensionality: built for high-dimensional structured data (images, audio, text, molecules) where p>n in raw pixel/token space; learns a compact latent manifold

features.interpretability: low: learned latent space and likelihoods are not directly interpretable; sample quality is judged perceptually or via proxy metrics
features.notes: raw high-dimensional inputs with strong local/spatial/sequential structure that the model exploits; not aimed at small tabular feature vectors

assumptions: the training set is a representative i.i.d. sample of the target distribution to be synthesized
enough data and capacity to cover the modes (otherwise mode collapse / dropped modes)
the quantity of interest is distributional fidelity / plausibility, not semantic or factual correctness
loss: maximum likelihood / negative log-likelihood (autoregressive, normalizing flows)
evidence lower bound (ELBO) for latent-variable models (VAEs)
adversarial / min-max objectives (GANs)
denoising score matching / variational diffusion loss
reconstruction error used for likelihood-based anomaly scoring
contraindicated_when: a precise deterministic input->output mapping is needed (tabular regression, standard classification) where discriminative models converge faster and more reliably
outputs must be factually/physically guaranteed correct (model optimizes distributional fit, not correctness)
data is scarce or low-dimensional tabular, so a simple density estimator or discriminative model suffices
strict low-latency inference budgets clash with multi-step sampling of diffusion/autoregressive variants

children.name: 2.7 Autoencoders
children.diff_siblings: Autoencoders learn compressed latent representations by training an encoder-decoder pair to minimize reconstruction error on the input itself — no adversarial signal, no diffusion process, no sequential modeling — making the learned bottleneck directly inspectable and usable for downstream tasks.
strengths: Anomaly detection without labeled anomalies: reconstruction error spikes naturally for out-of-distribution inputs, requiring only normal-class training data.
Tractable, single-objective training (reconstruction loss only), avoiding the instability of adversarial games (GANs) or the long inference chains of diffusion models.
The encoder alone is a useful artifact: it maps any new input to a fixed-size latent vector, enabling clustering, retrieval, and transfer learning independently of the decoder.
weaknesses: Standard (deterministic) autoencoders do not model a probability distribution over the latent space, so naive sampling from it produces incoherent reconstructions — generative use requires VAE or similar extensions.
Reconstruction loss (MSE/BCE) biases the model toward blurry, averaged outputs because it penalizes pixel-wise deviation, not perceptual or structural fidelity.
Bottleneck dimensionality is a brittle hyperparameter: too small discards discriminative features; too large allows the network to copy the input without learning useful structure.
recommended_for: Unsupervised anomaly detection in tabular or sensor data where only normal examples are available (e.g., industrial fault detection, fraud screening), using reconstruction error as the anomaly score.

Representation learning as a pretraining step for labeled tasks with limited data — the encoder pretrained on large unlabeled corpora produces features that fine-tune faster than random initialization.
not_recommended_for: High-fidelity image or audio synthesis where sample quality is the goal: GANs and diffusion models consistently outperform autoencoders on perceptual metrics (FID, IS) for generation tasks.

Sequence modeling of text or time series with long-range dependencies, where architectures with explicit temporal structure (Transformers, LSTMs) capture order information that a bottleneck encoder discards.
children.curiosity: The architecture was introduced by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams (1986) in 'Learning Internal Representations by Error Propagation' as a way to perform backpropagation without labeled targets, using the input as its own supervision signal.

children.name: Autoencoder Vanilla
children.diff_siblings: Unlike denoising, sparse, and variational autoencoders — which impose additional constraints (noise injection, sparsity penalty, or probabilistic latent space) — the vanilla autoencoder uses only mean squared reconstruction loss with a deterministic bottleneck, making it the unconstrained baseline of the family.
strengths: Interpretable bottleneck: the latent vector is a fixed-size deterministic embedding, making it straightforward to inspect or use as input to downstream classifiers.
Anomaly detection without labels: trained exclusively on normal data, it flags anomalies by thresholding reconstruction error — no annotated outliers required.
Architecture-agnostic encoder/decoder: the encoder and decoder can be replaced with CNNs, RNNs, or MLPs without changing the training objective, adapting naturally to the data modality.
weaknesses: Unstructured latent space: unlike VAEs, the latent space has no density guarantee, so interpolation or sampling between points produces undefined or degenerate outputs.
MSE reconstruction loss averages pixel/feature values, producing blurry or over-smoothed reconstructions on high-frequency data such as natural images.

Capacity sensitivity: if the bottleneck is too wide, the model learns a near-identity mapping and fails to compress; too narrow and it discards semantically important variance — both require manual tuning.
recommended_for: Unsupervised anomaly detection on continuous, low-to-medium dimensional tabular data (e.g., network intrusion logs, sensor readings) where only normal examples are available for training.
Non-linear dimensionality reduction as a preprocessing step for downstream clustering or classification when PCA's linear constraint is insufficient and a compact deterministic embedding is needed.
not_recommended_for: Generative tasks requiring novel sample synthesis: the unregularized latent space produces incoherent outputs when sampled randomly — use a VAE or GAN instead.
High-resolution image reconstruction where perceptual fidelity matters: MSE loss blurs fine textures and edges, and the deterministic bottleneck cannot model multi-modal output distributions.
children.curiosity: The architecture traces directly to Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams (1986), who used a symmetric encoder-decoder network trained with backpropagation to learn compressed internal representations without supervision — predating the term 'autoencoder' itself, which was popularized later by the community.

target.notes: Unsupervised; trained to reconstruct its own input. No labels. Reconstruction error doubles as an anomaly score when trained only on normal data.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ to learn a useful nonlinear encoding; small n overfits to near-identity
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; bottleneck width must be < intrinsic data dimension to force compression
needs: unlabeled data (or normal-only data for anomaly detection)
GPU helpful but not required for tabular/MLP variants

features.interpretability: medium: latent bottleneck is a fixed-size deterministic embedding usable downstream, but individual latent dims are not semantically disentangled
features.notes: Inputs should be scaled/normalized (e.g. min-max or standardize) for stable MSE training. Continuous features fit naturally; categorical needs encoding.

assumptions: meaningful structure is low-dimensional and nonlinear (otherwise PCA suffices)
for anomaly detection: training set is clean/normal so high reconstruction error indicates outliers
bottleneck capacity is tuned to compress rather than memorize an identity map
loss: mean squared reconstruction error (default)
binary cross-entropy reconstruction for [0,1]-scaled inputs
contraindicated_when: novel sample generation is required (unregularized latent space samples degenerately; use VAE/GAN)
high-frequency/high-resolution image fidelity matters (MSE produces blurry reconstructions)
the data relationships are linear and a compact deterministic projection suffices (PCA is simpler and cheaper)
labeled supervised prediction is the goal (use a discriminative model)

children.name: Denoising Autoencoder (DAE)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Variational Autoencoders (which impose a probabilistic latent space) or Sparse Autoencoders (which add sparsity regularization), the DAE trains by minimizing reconstruction loss between the output and the ORIGINAL clean input, given a stochastically corrupted version as input — forcing the encoder to learn the data manifold by undoing deliberate perturbations (Gaussian noise, masking noise, or salt-and-pepper).
strengths: Corruption-as-regularization prevents the encoder from learning a trivial identity mapping without needing an explicit regularization term in the loss function.
Learns feature representations that capture statistical dependencies between input dimensions, since masked features must be inferred from surviving ones.
Compatible with both dense and convolutional architectures, and can be stacked (SDAE) to pre-train deep networks layer by layer in an unsupervised fashion.
weaknesses: Noise type and intensity are critical hyperparameters: too little corruption allows identity-mapping, too much destroys the signal — both degrade representation quality.
The learned representations are tied to the corruption distribution used during training and generalize poorly to noise types not seen at training time.
Does not produce a structured, sampleable latent space, making it unsuitable for generation or interpolation between data points without additional modifications.
recommended_for: Image restoration pipelines where inputs are known to contain a specific, characterizable noise process (e.g., sensor noise in medical imaging or satellite imagery).
Unsupervised pre-training of deep feature extractors on unlabeled data before fine-tuning on a downstream classification task with limited labeled examples.
not_recommended_for: Generative tasks requiring sampling or interpolation in latent space, where a VAE or GAN provides a structured probabilistic framework the DAE lacks.
Scenarios where the noise distribution at inference time is unknown or highly variable, since the reconstruction quality degrades sharply when the corruption regime differs from training.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Vincent, Larochelle, Bengio, and Manzagol at ICML 2008, the DAE was one of the first principled methods to show that a deliberately corrupting-then-reconstructing objective produces representations superior to a standard autoencoder; Vincent (2011) later proved that training a DAE with Gaussian noise is mathematically equivalent to score matching of the data density.

target.notes: Self-supervised reconstruction; no external label. Trains to map a stochastically corrupted input back to the original clean input. Outputs a learned representation (encoder) and/or a denoised reconstruction (decoder), not a prediction of a labeled target.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of unlabeled examples for stable representation learning
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for high-dimensional inputs (pixels, raw signal); learns p>>1 dependencies via reconstruction
needs: a characterizable corruption process matched to deployment noise

features.interpretability: low; learned latent codes are distributed and not semantically axis-aligned
features.notes: Inputs should be scaled/normalized to a fixed range so the chosen corruption (Gaussian, masking, salt-and-pepper) is well-calibrated. Corruption type and intensity are the key hyperparameters and must mirror inference-time noise.

assumptions: data lies on a lower-dimensional manifold recoverable by undoing perturbations
corruption distribution at inference matches the one used in training
input dimensions carry exploitable statistical dependencies (so masked features are inferable from survivors)
loss: reconstruction error between output and clean input: squared error (Gaussian inputs) or cross-entropy / Bernoulli log-loss (binary or [0,1]-scaled inputs)
contraindicated_when: generative sampling or smooth latent interpolation is required (no structured probabilistic latent space; use VAE or GAN)
inference-time noise is unknown or highly variable versus training corruption
labeled supervised prediction is the actual goal and no pretraining stage is wanted
data is low-dimensional or tabular with few correlated features, where manifold reconstruction offers little benefit

children.name: VQ-VAE (Vector Quantized VAE)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike standard VAEs (continuous Gaussian latent space) and beta-VAEs (scaled KL regularization), VQ-VAE maps encoder outputs to the nearest vector in a learned discrete codebook, producing integer token sequences instead of continuous distributions.
strengths: Discrete bottleneck eliminates posterior collapse: the decoder cannot bypass the codebook, forcing every code index to carry information
Latent sequences are directly compatible with autoregressive priors (PixelCNN, Transformers), enabling high-fidelity generation without a separate continuous prior
Compression ratio is explicit and controllable via codebook size K and spatial downsampling factor, giving precise rate-distortion trade-off at design time
weaknesses: Codebook collapse: gradient updates concentrate usage on a small subset of the K vectors, leaving most embeddings unused unless restarts or EMA updates are applied
Quantization is non-differentiable; the straight-through estimator introduces gradient bias, making training sensitive to codebook learning-rate and commitment-loss weight
Two-stage training required: the VQ-VAE must be fully trained before fitting the autoregressive prior, doubling training cost and preventing end-to-end joint optimization
recommended_for: High-resolution image tokenization pipelines where downstream Transformer models (e.g., DALL-E, MaskGIT) consume discrete visual tokens of fixed vocabulary size
Speech codec and waveform modeling where audio is quantized into discrete units for language-model-based TTS or voice conversion
not_recommended_for: Tasks requiring smooth interpolation in latent space (e.g., style transfer, latent arithmetic), where the discrete grid creates discontinuous jumps between codes
Small datasets (fewer than ~50k samples): the codebook needs sufficient coverage to avoid collapse, and scarce data leaves many embeddings unreachable
children.curiosity: Introduced by van den Oord, Vinyals, and Kavukcuoglu (NeurIPS 2017) in 'Neural Discrete Representation Learning'; they showed that a 64x spatial-compressed discrete code with a 512-entry codebook was sufficient to reconstruct intelligible speech, motivating the entire line of discrete-token generative models.

target.notes: Self-supervised autoencoder; reconstructs its own input. No external label. Learns a discrete latent code, not a predictive target.

data_regime.rows: needs tens of thousands+ (recommend >50k); codebook coverage degrades on small data, leaving most embeddings unused
data_regime.dimensionality: built for high-dimensional structured signals (images, audio waveforms/spectrograms); not for low-dim tabular vectors
needs: two-stage training: train VQ-VAE, then fit autoregressive prior (PixelCNN/Transformer) on the discrete tokens

features.interpretability: low: latent is a grid of integer codebook indices with no inherent semantics
features.notes: Inputs should be spatially/temporally structured (pixel grids, audio frames). Downstream consumers treat the integer code map as a token sequence.

assumptions: Data has local spatial/temporal structure a convolutional encoder-decoder can compress
Codebook size K and downsampling factor are chosen to give enough capacity to cover the data manifold
Discrete latent grid is acceptable; reconstruction tolerates quantization error
loss: reconstruction error (squared error / MSE for continuous inputs)
codebook/VQ loss (L2 between encoder output and chosen codebook vector, via stop-gradient)
commitment loss (beta-weighted, keeps encoder near its assigned code)
straight-through estimator for the non-differentiable quantization step
EMA codebook updates as a common alternative to the VQ loss term
contraindicated_when: smooth/continuous latent interpolation or latent arithmetic is required (style transfer, attribute morphing) — discrete codes jump discontinuously
dataset is small (<~50k samples) — codebook collapse, many unreachable embeddings
data is low-dimensional tabular without spatial/temporal locality
a single end-to-end differentiable model is required — the two-stage prior fitting prevents joint optimization
the goal is a calibrated probabilistic density over a continuous latent (use a standard/continuous VAE instead)

children.name: Sparse Autoencoder
children.diff_siblings: Unlike denoising autoencoders (which enforce robustness via input corruption) and variational autoencoders (which impose a probabilistic prior on the latent space), Sparse Autoencoders enforce sparsity directly on hidden unit activations via an L1 penalty or KL divergence term, so only a small fraction of neurons fire for any given input.
strengths: Learns interpretable, disentangled features because each hidden unit specializes in a narrow subset of inputs rather than all neurons encoding everything jointly.
The sparsity regularizer reduces co-adaptation between neurons, acting as implicit regularization that lowers overfitting on small labeled datasets without dropout.
Overcomplete architectures (more hidden units than inputs) are viable because sparsity prevents trivial identity solutions, enabling richer feature dictionaries.
weaknesses: The sparsity target (rho) and penalty weight (beta) are sensitive hyperparameters: wrong values cause dead neurons or representations that ignore sparsity entirely.
KL-divergence sparsity requires computing mean activations over mini-batches, making training stateful and incompatible with very small batch sizes.
Does not model the data distribution, so it cannot generate new samples — unlike VAEs — limiting its use to discriminative or retrieval tasks.
recommended_for: Unsupervised feature extraction from high-dimensional fixed-size inputs (e.g., image patches, spectrograms) where interpretable, sparse feature dictionaries are needed for downstream classifiers.
Mechanistic interpretability of large language models: fitting a sparse autoencoder on LLM residual-stream activations to decompose polysemantic neurons into monosemantic features (Anthropic, 2023).
not_recommended_for: Generative tasks requiring sampling from a structured latent space (images, audio synthesis), where VAEs or diffusion models are the correct architecture.
Sequential or variable-length inputs (text, time series of arbitrary length) where the fixed-size bottleneck and lack of temporal structure make reconstruction unstable.
children.curiosity: Andrew Ng formalized the Sparse Autoencoder with KL-divergence sparsity in Stanford's CS294A lecture notes (2011), showing that adding a penalty that drives each neuron's mean activation toward a target rho (e.g., 0.05) forces the network to learn sparse codes analogous to those found in the mammalian visual cortex.

target.notes: Unsupervised representation learning; reconstructs its own fixed-size input. No external label/target. Learned sparse codes feed downstream supervised models, anomaly scoring, or interpretability analysis.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of unlabeled examples to learn a stable feature dictionary; sparsity acts as implicit regularization so it tolerates smaller sets better than unregularized nets
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for high-dimensional fixed-size inputs; overcomplete latent (hidden > input) is viable because sparsity blocks the identity solution
needs: mini-batches large enough to estimate mean activations when using KL-divergence sparsity

features.interpretability: high for the learned latent: each unit specializes on a narrow input subset, yielding near-monosemantic/disentangled features (used to decompose polysemantic LLM activations)
features.notes: expects fixed-length dense vectors (image patches, spectrograms, activation vectors); inputs should be scaled/normalized. Not suited to variable-length or sequential inputs without a separate sequence encoder.

assumptions: useful structure in the data is sparse: each example is explained by a small subset of latent factors
inputs are fixed-size and roughly i.i.d.; reconstruction loss matches the input's scale (e.g. MSE assumes Gaussian-ish continuous inputs, cross-entropy for [0,1] pixels)
batch statistics are representative enough to estimate target activation rho
loss: reconstruction error (squared error / MSE, or binary cross-entropy for bounded inputs) plus a sparsity penalty: L1 on activations or KL divergence between target rho and mean activation
contraindicated_when: generative sampling from a structured latent is required (use VAE / diffusion)
inputs are sequential or variable-length (text, arbitrary-length series) where a fixed bottleneck destabilizes reconstruction
the underlying representation is dense rather than sparse, so the sparsity prior fights the data
very small batch sizes make KL-divergence mean-activation estimates unreliable

children.name: Contractive Autoencoder
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Denoising Autoencoders (which achieve robustness by corrupting inputs stochastically) and Sparse Autoencoders (which penalize activation magnitude), the Contractive Autoencoder adds an explicit analytic penalty on the Frobenius norm of the encoder's Jacobian matrix, directly forcing the learned representation to be insensitive to infinitesimal input perturbations.
strengths: Learns representations that are locally invariant to irrelevant input directions while preserving variation along the data manifold, yielding geometrically meaningful latent spaces.
Penalty is computed analytically from the Jacobian (no stochastic corruption needed), making the regularization deterministic and stable across training runs.
Empirically produces better transferable features for downstream classification than Denoising Autoencoders on the same architectures, as shown by Rifai et al. (2011) on MNIST and CIFAR benchmarks.
weaknesses: Jacobian Frobenius norm computation scales as O(h * d) per sample (h hidden units, d input dimensions), making training substantially more expensive than other regularized autoencoders on high-dimensional inputs such as raw images.

The analytic penalty applies only to the encoder; the decoder receives no contraction constraint, leaving reconstruction gradients free to counteract the regularization if lambda is not carefully tuned.
Provides no probabilistic latent space, so it cannot be used as a generative model or for structured sampling, unlike Variational Autoencoders.
recommended_for: Unsupervised pre-training of feature extractors for tabular or moderate-dimensional data (e.g., gene expression arrays with ~10,000 features) where stable, manifold-aligned representations matter more than generation.
Anomaly detection on sensor or industrial time-series where the Jacobian penalty encourages the encoder to ignore noise directions and cluster normal operating modes tightly in latent space.
not_recommended_for: High-resolution image data (e.g., 224x224 RGB inputs) where computing the full Jacobian per batch becomes computationally prohibitive and VAEs or DAEs offer better cost-quality trade-offs.
Tasks requiring generative sampling or latent space interpolation, since the CAE latent space has no defined prior distribution and cannot guarantee meaningful points between learned codes.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Rifai, Vincent, Muller, Glorot, and Bengio at ICML 2011 ('Contractive Auto-Encoders: Explicit Invariance During Feature Extraction'), the paper demonstrated that the CAE penalty is the analytic, deterministic counterpart to the stochastic corruption used in Denoising Autoencoders: both methods push the model to learn the tangent directions of the data manifold, but CAE does so by directly penalizing the Jacobian's Frobenius norm rather than averaging over noise samples.

target.notes: Unsupervised representation learning / dimensionality reduction; trained on reconstruction, no label or response variable.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ for stable representations; standard SGD minibatch training
data_regime.dimensionality: best for moderate input dimensionality; Jacobian Frobenius penalty costs O(h*d) per sample, so scales poorly as input dimension d grows
needs: GPU helpful but not mandatory for moderate-d inputs

features.interpretability: low; latent codes are learned, not directly interpretable, though geometrically aligned to the data manifold
features.notes: Inputs should be scaled/normalized (typically [0,1] or standardized) since the encoder Jacobian penalty is sensitive to input scale. Suited to dense moderate-dimensional vectors (e.g. ~10k-feature gene arrays), not raw high-resolution images.

assumptions: Data lies on a lower-dimensional smooth manifold and meaningful variation is local
Irrelevant variation lies in directions the encoder can be made insensitive to via the Jacobian penalty
Regularization strength lambda is well tuned relative to reconstruction loss, since the decoder is unconstrained
loss: reconstruction error (squared error / cross-entropy on inputs) plus Frobenius-norm penalty on the encoder Jacobian (contractive penalty)
contraindicated_when: High-resolution image inputs where per-batch full Jacobian computation is prohibitive (prefer DAE/VAE)
Generative sampling or smooth latent interpolation is required, since the latent space has no prior distribution
A probabilistic/structured latent space is needed (use a VAE instead)

target.notes: Self-supervised: trained to reconstruct its own input, no external label. Reconstruction error doubles as an anomaly score (one-class). Encoder output is used downstream (clustering, classification, retrieval).

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of (unlabeled) examples to learn a useful manifold; small-n overfits the bottleneck
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for high-p input (images, sensors, high-dim tabular); learns nonlinear low-dim embedding
needs: GPU for image/audio scale (tabular trains on CPU)

features.interpretability: low — the latent bottleneck is dense and not individually meaningful; only reconstruction error and embedding geometry are inspectable
features.notes: Inputs must be scaled to the output activation's range (e.g. [0,1] for sigmoid+BCE, standardized for linear+MSE). Categorical inputs need embedding/one-hot first.

assumptions: normal/in-distribution data dominates training when used for anomaly detection (reconstruction error only flags OOD if the model never learned to reconstruct anomalies)
the data lies on a lower-dimensional manifold that a fixed bottleneck can capture
bottleneck width is well-chosen: too small loses signal, too large lets the net copy the input identity-style
loss: mean squared error (continuous/standardized inputs)
binary cross-entropy (inputs scaled to [0,1])
masked/denoising reconstruction loss (denoising AE)
contraindicated_when: the goal is high-fidelity generative sampling — MSE/BCE reconstruction yields blurry, averaged outputs; use VAE, GAN, or diffusion
you need a proper probabilistic latent for sampling/density — a deterministic AE has no distribution over latent space (use a VAE)
long-range sequence dependencies matter — a fixed bottleneck discards order; use Transformers/LSTMs
labeled anomalies are abundant — a supervised classifier will outperform reconstruction-error scoring
n is small or data is low-dimensional and roughly linear — PCA or simpler outlier methods are cheaper and as effective

children.name: 2.8 Graph Neural Networks (GNN)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike CNNs (which assume a fixed-grid topology) and RNNs (which assume a sequential chain), GNNs operate on arbitrary graph structures by iteratively aggregating node representations from variable-size, unordered neighborhoods via message passing.
strengths: Native relational inductive bias: nodes accumulate multi-hop neighborhood context without hand-crafted graph features, because the message-passing layers directly encode edge connectivity.
Permutation invariance by design: aggregation functions (sum, mean, attention) are order-agnostic, so node predictions are stable regardless of how the adjacency matrix is stored or indexed.

End-to-end property prediction on molecules: treating atoms as nodes and bonds as edges, a single forward pass yields a differentiable molecular fingerprint that captures 3-D topology without requiring explicit feature engineering.
weaknesses: Over-smoothing with depth: after roughly 4–6 message-passing layers, node embeddings converge toward indistinguishable vectors because repeated neighborhood averaging erases local structure.

Quadratic memory on dense graphs: full-graph training stores the entire adjacency matrix and all intermediate node embeddings in GPU memory, making billion-edge graphs impractical without mini-batch sampling heuristics.

Bounded expressive power: standard message-passing GNNs are at most as powerful as the 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman graph isomorphism test, so they cannot distinguish certain pairs of non-isomorphic graphs (e.g., regular graphs of the same degree).
recommended_for: Molecular property prediction where data is naturally graph-structured (atoms as nodes, covalent bonds as edges) and the target property depends on local chemical substructures — e.g., solubility or binding affinity from SMILES datasets of 10k–1M compounds.

Transaction fraud detection in financial networks where accounts and transfers form a heterogeneous graph with thousands to millions of nodes, and fraud rings manifest as dense subgraph patterns invisible to tabular classifiers.
not_recommended_for: Independent tabular records with no relational structure: if entities have no meaningful pairwise connections, constructing an artificial k-NN graph introduces noise without relational signal and adds engineering overhead.

Very deep propagation requirements on sparse graphs: when the task needs information from nodes more than 5–6 hops away (e.g., diameter-spanning dependencies in large social networks), over-smoothing degrades performance and standard GNNs fail to propagate signal reliably.
children.curiosity: The foundational GNN model was introduced by Scarselli et al. in 'The Graph Neural Network Model' (IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks, 2009), which proved that GNNs can approximate any function satisfying unfolding equivalence on graphs — predating the convolutional reformulation by Kipf and Welling (2017) by eight years.

children.name: GCN (Graph Convolutional Network)
children.diff_siblings: GCN applies spectral graph convolution via a symmetric normalized adjacency matrix (D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}), giving each neighbor uniform weight after degree normalization — unlike GAT (learned attention weights), GraphSAGE (learnable aggregator with inductive sampling), or GIN (sum aggregator tuned for maximum expressiveness).
strengths: Scales linearly with the number of edges, making full-batch training on medium citation graphs (e.g., Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed) tractable without sampling
Simple two-layer architecture achieves strong semi-supervised node classification using very few labeled nodes (as few as 20 per class) by propagating label information through graph structure
Symmetric normalization (D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}) prevents gradient explosion on high-degree hubs, stabilizing training on heterogeneous degree distributions
weaknesses: Over-smoothing: stacking more than 2-3 layers causes node representations to converge toward a uniform value, collapsing discriminative information
Transductive only: requires the full adjacency matrix at training time, so adding new nodes at inference demands retraining or approximation
Uniform neighbor weighting ignores edge semantics — a node connected to a noisy neighbor is penalized equally as one connected to a highly relevant neighbor
recommended_for: Semi-supervised node classification on homophilic citation or social graphs (e.g., predicting paper category from sparse labels + co-citation links) where the graph is fully observed and fits in memory
Link prediction tasks on static knowledge graphs where the structural proximity captured by spectral convolution correlates strongly with the target relation
not_recommended_for: Large-scale inductive settings where new nodes arrive at inference time (e.g., dynamic user graphs in production recommendation systems), as GCN cannot generalize to unseen adjacency
Heterophilic graphs where connected nodes belong to different classes (e.g., predator-prey biological networks), because degree-normalized averaging blurs rather than sharpens class boundaries
children.curiosity: Introduced by Kipf and Welling (2017) in 'Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks' (ICLR 2017), the paper derived the layer-wise propagation rule as a first-order approximation of spectral convolutions based on Chebyshev polynomials, reducing the original O(n^2) spectral computation to O(|E|) linear complexity in the number of edges.

target.notes: Primarily semi-supervised node classification (label per node) and link prediction (binary edge existence). Target is per-node or per-edge, not per-row-iid. Also usable for unsupervised node embedding (target none).

data_regime.rows: works on small-to-medium graphs (thousands to ~100k nodes) in full-batch; transductive, must hold full adjacency + features in memory
data_regime.dimensionality: node feature dim p typically 100s-1000s; effective signal comes from graph structure not just p
needs: GPU helpful but full-batch on medium graphs runs on CPU
node feature matrix (or identity/structural features if none)

features.interpretability: low: spectral convolution mixes neighbor signals across layers, individual feature attribution is opaque
features.notes: Requires an adjacency matrix; raw tabular rows without relational edges cannot use it. Features are propagated and averaged over neighborhoods; degree normalization (D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}) handles skewed degree distributions.

assumptions: Homophily: connected nodes tend to share labels/properties; violated on heterophilic graphs
Graph is fully observed and static at training time (transductive)
Uniform neighbor relevance after degree normalization (no edge-importance weighting)
Shallow depth (2-3 hops) suffices; deep stacks cause over-smoothing
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss for node classification
binary cross-entropy or contrastive/negative-sampling loss for link prediction
contraindicated_when: No relational/graph structure exists (plain i.i.d. tabular data) — use a tabular model instead
Inductive setting with new nodes arriving at inference (use GraphSAGE)
Heterophilic graphs where neighbors have differing classes
Need to weight neighbors by relevance or edge semantics (use GAT)
Very deep propagation needed across many hops (over-smoothing collapses representations)
Graph too large to fit full adjacency in memory without sampling

children.name: GAT (Graph Attention Network)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike GCN (fixed symmetric normalization) and GraphSAGE (fixed aggregation per sample), GAT computes a learned attention coefficient for each directed edge via a shared neural network, allowing each node to assign non-uniform, data-dependent importance to its neighbors during aggregation.
strengths: Adaptive neighbor weighting: attention scores are computed from node features at each forward pass, so the model focuses on structurally relevant neighbors without any modification to the graph topology.
Inductive capability: the attention function operates on node feature pairs, not on precomputed graph-level matrices, so a trained GAT generalizes directly to unseen nodes and entirely new graphs.

Multi-head attention reduces variance: running K independent attention heads and concatenating (or averaging) their outputs stabilizes training and increases the effective representational capacity without adding graph-level parameters.
weaknesses: Attention computation scales quadratically with neighborhood size: for high-degree nodes the O(|N_i|^2) cost per head becomes a bottleneck on dense or power-law graphs.

Assumes homophily: the local softmax normalization tends to wash out signals from dissimilar but informative neighbors, degrading accuracy on heterophilic graphs where connected nodes belong to different classes.
Over-smoothing accumulates with depth: stacking many GAT layers causes node representations to converge to indistinct averages, limiting effective depth to 2-3 layers for most benchmarks.
recommended_for: Citation or social network node classification where edges connect semantically similar entities and the graph fits in GPU memory (e.g., Cora, Citeseer: ~3k nodes, sparse adjacency).

Molecular property prediction on small-to-medium graphs (10-100 atoms per molecule) where different atoms have varying relevance to the target property and inductive generalization across compounds is required.
not_recommended_for: Web-scale graphs with millions of high-degree nodes (e.g., product co-purchase graphs), where full-neighborhood attention per node exceeds GPU memory and mini-batch approximations discard the very edges attention was designed to weight.

Graphs with strong heterophily (e.g., fraud detection networks where fraudsters connect to legitimate nodes), where local softmax attention systematically under-weights the dissimilar neighbors that carry the discriminative signal.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Veličković et al. (ICLR 2018, arXiv:1710.10903), GAT was the first GNN to apply masked self-attention directly on graph edges; on the Cora benchmark it achieved 83.0% accuracy, outperforming GCN by 1.5 percentage points while using no eigendecomposition or pre-computed graph Laplacian.

target.notes: Node-level (classification/regression on each node), edge-level (link prediction), or graph-level (graph classification/regression via pooling) targets. Semi-supervised setting: only a fraction of nodes labeled. Can also produce unsupervised node embeddings (target none).

data_regime.rows: node classification works on small transductive graphs (~3k nodes, e.g. Cora/Citeseer); inductive use needs many graphs or labeled nodes
data_regime.dimensionality: node feature dim arbitrary; effective depth limited to 2-3 layers (over-smoothing)

features.interpretability: medium: attention coefficients per edge are inspectable and indicate which neighbors a node attends to, but the learned representation itself is opaque
features.notes: Requires graph topology plus per-node feature vectors. Attention computed from node-feature pairs, so it is inductive and generalizes to unseen nodes/graphs. Per-head cost scales with neighborhood size (O(|N_i|) edges per head), expensive on high-degree/power-law graphs.

assumptions: Homophily: connected nodes tend to be similar/share labels; local softmax attention under-weights informative dissimilar neighbors on heterophilic graphs
Informative graph structure: edges carry signal relevant to the target
Neighborhoods fit in memory for full-neighborhood attention; mini-batch sampling discards edges attention was meant to weight
Shallow propagation suffices (2-3 hops); deep stacks over-smooth
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss (node and graph classification)
squared error (node/graph regression)
link-prediction objectives (e.g. negative-sampling BCE on edge scores)
contraindicated_when: Strong heterophily (e.g. fraud networks where fraudsters connect to legitimate nodes); discriminative signal lives in dissimilar neighbors that softmax attention suppresses
Web-scale graphs with millions of high-degree nodes where full-neighborhood attention exceeds GPU memory
No meaningful graph/relational structure exists (tabular data with no edges) - use standard tabular models
Long-range dependencies requiring many hops, where over-smoothing destroys node distinctness

children.name: GraphSAGE
children.diff_siblings: Unlike GCN (which requires the full adjacency matrix and is inherently transductive) and GAT (which attends over all neighbors), GraphSAGE learns parameterized aggregator functions (mean, LSTM, or max-pooling) over a fixed-size randomly sampled neighborhood, making it the only approach in this family that generalizes inductively to completely unseen nodes at inference without retraining.
strengths: Inductive generalization: a single trained model produces embeddings for nodes never seen during training, enabling deployment on dynamic graphs where new nodes appear continuously.
Neighborhood sampling caps the per-node receptive field to a fixed budget (e.g., 25 first-hop, 10 second-hop neighbors), keeping mini-batch memory and compute constant regardless of hub-node degree.
Choice of aggregator (mean, LSTM, max-pool) lets practitioners trade off symmetry, sequential expressiveness, and training capacity for the specific graph structure at hand.
weaknesses: Uniform random sampling ignores neighbor informativeness, introducing high gradient variance — more sophisticated importance-sampling methods (FastGCN, VR-GCN) partially solve this at additional implementation cost.
Practical depth is limited to 2-3 hops before mini-batch sizes explode exponentially, constraining the model's ability to capture long-range structural dependencies.

The concatenate-then-linear aggregation treats all sampled neighbors with equal implicit weight, making GraphSAGE less expressive than attention-based siblings (GAT) on heterophilic graphs where only a subset of neighbors is informative.
recommended_for: Web-scale evolving graphs (e.g., Pinterest recommendation, Reddit user classification) where new nodes arrive after training and the graph has millions of nodes with rich node features.
Protein-protein interaction networks requiring out-of-sample generalization across organisms: train on one set of species, infer embeddings for proteins from a new species with no retraining.
not_recommended_for: Small, static, fully-observed graphs (e.g., Cora, Citeseer with ~2 000 nodes) where the transductive overhead of GCN is negligible and spectral methods have richer theoretical guarantees.

Graphs with extremely high-degree hubs and no node features (pure structure), where uniform sampling produces highly variable neighborhood representations and the absence of features leaves the aggregators with little signal.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Hamilton, Ying, and Leskovec (NeurIPS 2017), GraphSAGE was validated at Pinterest scale on a graph of 3 billion nodes and 18 billion edges, where it ran in real-time recommendation under the name PinSage — the first industrial deployment of an inductive GNN at that scale.

target.notes: Supervised node classification (binary/multiclass) or link prediction; also runs unsupervised to learn node embeddings (target=none) via a graph-based loss. Target is attached to graph nodes/edges, not i.i.d. rows.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of nodes; designed for large/web-scale graphs (millions of nodes); overkill on small static graphs
data_regime.dimensionality: consumes node feature vectors of arbitrary p; neighborhood sampling caps per-node compute regardless of degree
needs: moderate-to-large labeled node set for supervised mode

features.interpretability: low: learned aggregator embeddings are opaque, no per-feature coefficients
features.notes: Requires node feature matrix; aggregators (mean/LSTM/max-pool) operate over sampled neighborhoods. Performs poorly with no node features (pure structure). Inductive: generalizes to unseen nodes without retraining.

assumptions: homophily / locally smooth signal — informative neighbors are near (1-3 hops); weaker on heterophilic graphs
node features carry signal; degrades when features are absent or uninformative
fixed-size sampled neighborhood is representative — uniform sampling adds gradient variance on high-degree hubs
short-range dependencies suffice; 2-3 hop depth limit misses long-range structure
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss for node classification
unsupervised graph loss: encourage proximate nodes to have similar embeddings, negative sampling for distant nodes
link prediction objectives (e.g. dot-product + cross-entropy on sampled edges)
contraindicated_when: small, static, fully-observed graphs (~thousands of nodes, e.g. Cora/Citeseer) where transductive GCN suffices
graphs with no node features (pure structure) and high-degree hubs
strongly heterophilic graphs where only a subset of neighbors is informative (prefer GAT)
tasks needing long-range / global structural dependencies beyond 2-3 hops
non-graph tabular/i.i.d. data with no relational structure

children.name: GIN (Graph Isomorphism Network)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike GCN (mean aggregation) and GraphSAGE (mean/max pooling), GIN uses a sum-based injective aggregation with a learned MLP — provably reaching the expressive upper bound of the 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman test, which no other standard message-passing GNN achieves.
strengths: Provably maximally expressive among neighborhood-aggregation GNNs: sum aggregation preserves the full neighbor multiset, unlike mean/max which collapse non-isomorphic structures into identical embeddings.

MLPs as update functions (instead of linear layers) guarantee the per-layer transformation is injective, making graph-level representations theoretically non-collapsing for any pair 1-WL can distinguish.
Consistently strong on graph classification benchmarks (MUTAG, COLLAB, RDT-B): empirically matches or surpasses GCN and GraphSAGE on tasks where whole-graph structure drives the label.
weaknesses: Inherits the 1-WL ceiling: cannot distinguish certain regular graphs (e.g., two non-isomorphic 3-regular graphs with identical degree sequences) that require higher-order WL tests to separate.
Higher risk of overfitting in small-graph datasets because the MLP aggregator has more parameters than a simple linear GCN layer, requiring careful regularization and tuning.
The learnable epsilon parameter interacts subtly with the MLP; in practice its value often collapses near zero, and the theoretical benefit over a fixed epsilon = 0 is rarely observed empirically.
recommended_for: Graph-level classification over molecular graphs (e.g., property prediction on MUTAG or biochemical assay datasets) where distinguishing structural isomers from identical degree-sequence graphs matters.
Social-network or citation-graph benchmark tasks (COLLAB, REDDIT-BINARY) where whole-graph topology — not just node-level features — determines the target label.
not_recommended_for: Node-level regression or link prediction tasks where the injectivity guarantee at the graph-readout level provides no advantage and simpler GCNs generalize better with lower parameter count.

Graphs that require distinguishing beyond 1-WL equivalence classes (e.g., strongly regular graphs, CFI graphs), where GIN produces identical embeddings and higher-order k-GNN or NGNN variants are necessary.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Xu, Hu, Leskovec, and Jegelka (ICLR 2019, arXiv:1810.00826), GIN was the first GNN accompanied by a formal proof that any injective, sum-aggregating message-passing network is as powerful as the 1-WL isomorphism test — and that no standard message-passing GNN can exceed this bound.

target.notes: Primarily graph-level classification (one label per whole graph). Adaptable to graph-level regression with a continuous readout head, but the expressivity advantage is designed for discriminating graph structure for classification.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds to thousands of labeled graphs; sum-aggregation MLPs overfit on small graph datasets without strong regularization
data_regime.dimensionality: scales with number of nodes/edges per graph and node-feature dimension; benefits from many graphs to learn the injective aggregator
needs: GPU recommended for training over large graph batches

features.interpretability: low: learned MLP aggregators and pooled graph embeddings are opaque
features.notes: Inputs are graphs with node features (and optionally edge features); discrete/categorical node attributes work well as the multiset-preserving sum aggregation distinguishes neighbor compositions. Node features should be encoded numerically; benefits from meaningful node attributes but can operate on structure alone.

assumptions: Label is driven by whole-graph topology / substructure, not just node-local features
Distinguishing power required does not exceed 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman equivalence (cannot separate non-isomorphic graphs that 1-WL cannot, e.g. regular graphs with identical degree sequences)
Sufficient labeled graphs relative to MLP parameter count to avoid overfitting
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss for graph classification
squared error if used with a regression readout
contraindicated_when: Node-level prediction, link prediction, or node regression (graph-readout injectivity gives no benefit; simpler GCN/GraphSAGE generalize better)
Tasks requiring discrimination beyond 1-WL (strongly regular graphs, CFI graphs) where higher-order k-GNN variants are needed
Small graph datasets where the extra MLP parameters overfit relative to a linear GCN layer
Non-graph tabular, sequence, image, or text data

children.name: MPNN (Message Passing Neural Network)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike GCN (fixed spectral averaging), GraphSAGE (sampled neighborhood aggregation), or GAT (attention-weighted neighbors), MPNN is a unifying abstract framework where both the message function M_t and the node update function U_t are arbitrary learnable functions, allowing explicit edge features to be incorporated into each message computation.
strengths: Explicit edge feature support: bond type, distance, or any pairwise attribute enters M_t directly, giving the model richer structural information than adjacency-only architectures
Unifying framework: GCN, GGNN, and Interaction Networks are all special cases of MPNN, so any improvement to one can be reinterpreted and applied within this abstraction

State-of-the-art on molecular property prediction: the enn-s2s variant achieved chemical accuracy on 11 of 13 QM9 targets when introduced, outperforming prior DFT-based approximations at a fraction of the compute
weaknesses: Over-squashing: messages from distant nodes get compressed into fixed-size vectors through graph bottlenecks, causing information loss for tasks requiring long-range structural context
Expressivity bounded by 1-WL test: cannot distinguish non-isomorphic graphs that fool the Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement, limiting its power on highly symmetric graphs
Quadratic edge complexity: incorporating full pairwise edge features across dense graphs (e.g., fully connected molecular graphs) scales as O(E) per layer, becoming prohibitive for large molecules
recommended_for: Molecular property prediction on small-to-medium graphs where bond type, distance, and chirality must be encoded as edge features (e.g., QM9 energy and quantum chemical target regression)
Drug discovery pipelines predicting bioactivity from 2D/3D molecular graphs, where the rich edge-feature mechanism captures both topology and geometry
not_recommended_for: Large-scale social or citation graphs with millions of nodes and sparse homogeneous edges, where simpler GCN or GraphSAGE aggregations are faster and edge features add no benefit
Tasks requiring global graph-level reasoning over distant node pairs, where over-squashing across many hops causes critical structural signals to vanish before reaching the readout
children.curiosity: Introduced by Gilmer, Schoenholz, Riley, Vinyals, and Dahl at ICML 2017, the MPNN framework was not presented as a novel architecture but as a unifying formalism: the authors showed that six prior GNN variants (including GGNN, Interaction Networks, and Molecular Graph Convolutions) were all special cases of the same message-passing equation, then used this insight to design enn-s2s, which set a new state-of-the-art on the QM9 quantum chemistry benchmark.

target.notes: Graph/node/edge-level prediction. Originally graph-level regression of molecular/quantum properties (QM9); also node classification, graph classification, and link prediction. Target lives at node, edge, or whole-graph level depending on readout.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of labeled graphs (or one large graph with many labeled nodes); supervised deep model, data-hungry
data_regime.dimensionality: scales with number of edges E per layer; O(E) message computation makes dense/fully-connected graphs (e.g. large molecules) expensive

features.interpretability: low; learned message and update functions are opaque, though edge-feature attribution is more inspectable than adjacency-only GNNs
features.notes: Input is graph-structured: node features, edge features (bond type, distance, chirality, any pairwise attribute), and connectivity. Key advantage over GCN/GraphSAGE/GAT is native edge-feature ingestion into the message function M_t.

assumptions: Relational/graph structure carries the predictive signal (relevant info is in topology + node/edge attributes)
Relevant interactions are local / few-hop; long-range dependencies suffer from over-squashing through graph bottlenecks
Target graphs are distinguishable under 1-Weisfeiler-Leman refinement (cannot separate WL-equivalent non-isomorphic graphs)
Edge features are informative; if edges are homogeneous, the framework's extra capacity yields no benefit over simpler aggregators
loss: squared error / MAE for property regression
cross-entropy / log-loss for node and graph classification
any differentiable task loss via learnable M_t, U_t, and readout
contraindicated_when: Large-scale homogeneous graphs (millions of nodes, sparse uniform edges) where GCN/GraphSAGE are faster and edge features add nothing
Tasks needing global reasoning over distant node pairs (many hops) where over-squashing erases structural signal before readout
No meaningful edge attributes available, removing MPNN's core advantage
Highly symmetric graphs requiring expressivity beyond the 1-WL test
Non-relational tabular data with no natural graph structure

children.name: HAN (Heterogeneous Attention Network)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike homogeneous GNNs that treat all nodes and edges as one type, HAN operates on heterogeneous graphs by converting them into multiple homogeneous subgraphs via manually defined meta-paths, then applying a two-level hierarchy of attention — node-level within each meta-path subgraph, semantic-level across meta-paths — to jointly learn neighbor importance and meta-path importance.
strengths: Hierarchical attention (node-level + semantic-level) lets the model learn both which neighbors matter and which meta-paths are most informative for a given task, without requiring manual weighting.

Handles multiple node and edge types natively, making it directly applicable to heterogeneous information networks such as academic graphs (author-paper-venue) without flattening the graph into a single relation type.
Semantic-level attention produces interpretable weights per meta-path, allowing practitioners to inspect which relation types (e.g., co-authorship vs. co-citation) the model relies on most.
weaknesses: Meta-paths must be defined manually by domain experts before training; poor meta-path selection leads to suboptimal embeddings, and exhaustive enumeration is combinatorially expensive on large schemas.

Node-level attention uses a global shared weight vector rather than local pairwise comparison, so the model cannot distinguish relative importance between two specific neighbors — only aggregate neighbor salience.
Ignores intermediate nodes along a meta-path (uses only start and end nodes), discarding relational context that methods like MAGNN explicitly encode.
recommended_for: Node classification or link prediction on academic or biomedical heterogeneous graphs where multiple, well-understood relation types exist (e.g., ACM paper-author-subject graphs with 3+ meta-paths).
Drug-drug interaction prediction on knowledge graphs where entities are of heterogeneous types (drugs, proteins, diseases) and meta-paths encode biologically meaningful indirect relations.
not_recommended_for: Graphs with a single node/edge type (homogeneous graphs), where the meta-path mechanism adds complexity without benefit compared to standard GAT or GraphSAGE.
Domains where domain expertise to define valid meta-paths is unavailable, since automatic meta-path discovery is not part of HAN and erroneous meta-paths degrade performance.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Wang et al. (WWW 2019) in 'Heterogeneous Graph Attention Network' (arXiv:1903.07293), HAN was the first work to apply hierarchical attention to heterogeneous graphs and demonstrated that semantic-level attention weights align with human intuition — on the ACM dataset, the paper-author meta-path consistently received higher attention than paper-subject when predicting paper topic.

target.notes: Primary tasks are transductive/semi-supervised node classification (cross-entropy over labeled nodes) and link prediction on heterogeneous graphs; embeddings can also be produced unsupervised. Target lives on graph nodes/edges, not on i.i.d. rows.

data_regime.rows: operates on a single (or few) graph(s); needs enough labeled nodes per class for supervised attention to learn, but works in semi-supervised regime with a small labeled fraction
data_regime.dimensionality: scales with number of nodes/edges and number of meta-paths; per-meta-path subgraph aggregation makes cost grow with meta-path count and neighborhood density
needs: graph-structured heterogeneous data with multiple node/edge types
node feature vectors per node type

features.interpretability: medium: semantic-level attention yields per-meta-path importance weights that are inspectable; node-level attention is coarser (shared weight vector, not pairwise)
features.notes: Requires a heterogeneous information network with typed nodes/edges and per-node feature vectors; different node types may have different feature spaces (type-specific projection). Meta-paths must be specified a priori.

assumptions: graph is heterogeneous with >=2 node/edge types and >=2 meaningful meta-paths
useful meta-paths are known and correctly specified by domain experts
relational signal between meta-path endpoints carries the task-relevant information (intermediate nodes on the path are ignored)
homophily/relational smoothness along meta-paths so attention-weighted neighbor aggregation is informative
loss: softmax cross-entropy (node classification)
link-prediction / contrastive objectives for edges
unsupervised embedding objectives
contraindicated_when: graph is homogeneous (single node/edge type) — standard GAT/GraphSAGE is simpler and as good
no domain expertise to define valid meta-paths, or schema is too large for tractable meta-path enumeration
task needs fine-grained pairwise neighbor discrimination (node-level attention uses a global shared vector)
intermediate-node context along paths matters (prefer MAGNN or relation-aware models like R-GCN/HGT)
data is tabular/i.i.d. with no relational/graph structure

target.notes: Family covers node-level (classification/regression over nodes), edge-level (link prediction), and graph-level (whole-graph classification/regression) targets. Unsupervised/self-supervised variants produce node/graph embeddings with target=none. Target type is task-defined, not model-defined.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of labeled nodes/edges/graphs; full-graph training feasible up to ~10^5-10^6 nodes, beyond that requires neighbor/subgraph sampling (GraphSAGE-style mini-batching)
data_regime.dimensionality: handles high-dim node feature vectors; scaling is dominated by edge count and neighborhood fan-out, not feature p

features.interpretability: low: learned node embeddings from stacked message passing are opaque; attention weights (GAT) give partial edge-importance attribution only
features.notes: Requires a relational structure as input (edges must carry real signal). Node/edge features benefit from standardization; supports heterogeneous node/edge types and edge attributes in extended variants.

assumptions: Homophily / meaningful local neighborhood structure: predictive signal is assumed to live in multi-hop neighborhoods; on strongly heterophilous or random-edge graphs standard message passing underperforms
Edges encode genuine relational dependence (not artificially imposed)
Relevant signal is reachable within a few hops (depth limited by over-smoothing, ~2-6 layers)
loss: cross-entropy / log-loss (node & graph classification)
binary cross-entropy with negative sampling (link prediction)
squared error (node/graph regression)
contrastive / self-supervised objectives for unsupervised embeddings
contraindicated_when: records are i.i.d. tabular with no real pairwise relations (a fabricated k-NN graph adds noise, not signal)
task requires long-range propagation beyond ~5-6 hops on sparse graphs (over-smoothing erases local structure)
graph is billion-edge scale without a sampling/partitioning strategy (quadratic memory on dense full-graph training)
distinguishing fine graph structure that exceeds 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman expressive power (e.g., regular graphs of equal degree)
very small labeled data where a simpler tabular model on engineered graph features suffices

children.name: 2.9 Specialized Architectures
children.diff_siblings: Unlike sibling categories built around a single dominant inductive bias (spatial locality in CNNs, sequential state in RNNs, global attention in Transformers), Specialized Architectures groups models that replace or augment the standard feedforward/backprop stack with fundamentally different computational primitives — routing networks, dynamic systems, part-whole hierarchies, or energy minimization — each tailored to a structural property of the problem rather than a general-purpose signal-flow pattern.
strengths: Models here exploit strong structural priors — e.g., Capsule Networks preserve part-whole pose relationships that pooling destroys, yielding viewpoint robustness without data augmentation

Mixture-of-Experts achieves parameter scaling without proportional compute cost by activating only a sparse subset of expert modules per token, enabling trillion-parameter models on fixed FLOPs budgets
Neural ODEs parameterize depth as a continuous variable solved by an ODE solver, giving adaptive computation depth at inference and exact log-likelihood in generative settings
weaknesses: Training stability is harder than standard architectures: dynamic routing (CapsNets) and expert load balancing (MoE) require auxiliary losses or careful initialization to avoid mode collapse or expert starvation
Inference latency is unpredictable in solver-based or routing-based models — ODE solvers add variable overhead, and MoE routing adds communication cost in distributed settings
Small research communities per sub-architecture means fewer pretrained checkpoints, standardized frameworks, and empirical best practices compared to CNNs or Transformers
recommended_for: Problems with known geometric or relational structure not captured by grid or sequence assumptions — e.g., 3D pose estimation, molecular property prediction on graphs, or physics simulations where the governing equations are known up to parameters
Extreme-scale language or multimodal models where total parameter count must exceed active compute per forward pass — MoE routing enables this decoupling directly
not_recommended_for: Standard image classification or NLP tasks with abundant labeled data, where well-tuned CNNs or Transformers deliver better accuracy-per-engineering-hour with far more mature tooling

Production systems requiring strict inference latency SLAs, since solver-based (Neural ODE) and routing-based (MoE with all-to-all communication) architectures introduce variance that is difficult to bound at the 99th percentile
children.curiosity: Capsule Networks were introduced by Sabour, Frosst, and Hinton (2017) in 'Dynamic Routing Between Capsules' (NeurIPS), with Hinton arguing that the CNN's use of max-pooling to achieve translation invariance actively discards the precise spatial relationship between features — a design flaw he called 'a sin' in a 2014 talk — and that capsules with dynamic routing were the principled fix.

children.name: PINN (Physics-Informed Neural Network)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike purely data-driven specialized architectures (e.g., neural operators, graph networks), PINNs encode governing PDEs directly into the loss function as residual terms evaluated at collocation points, enabling mesh-free training without labeled simulation data and making them the only architecture in this group that can solve both forward PDE problems and inverse parameter-identification problems within the same framework.
strengths: Solves inverse PDE problems (recovering unknown parameters or boundary conditions from sparse observations) without re-deriving adjoint equations — the physics residual and data mismatch are minimized jointly.
Mesh-free: collocation points are sampled in continuous space, so there is no mesh-generation step and irregular or high-dimensional domains cost no extra mesh overhead.
Requires very few labeled observations when the governing equations are known, because the PDE constraint acts as a strong regularizer across the entire domain.
weaknesses: Fails or converges slowly on high-frequency and multi-scale solutions (spectral bias of MLPs causes the network to under-represent sharp gradients); standard architectures need ad-hoc spectral or domain-decomposition workarounds.
Each PDE instance (new geometry, boundary condition, or parameter value) requires full retraining from scratch — the model learns one solution, not a solution operator.

Loss landscape is ill-conditioned: competing physics-residual and boundary-condition terms create gradient pathologies; weighting these terms is problem-specific and has no general automated strategy.
recommended_for: Forward and inverse problems in fluid mechanics or heat transfer governed by known PDEs (Navier-Stokes, Burgers, Poisson) where labeled simulation data are scarce but equation form is certain.

Parameter identification from sparse sensor measurements in physical systems (e.g., inferring viscosity or diffusivity fields from a handful of point observations) where re-meshing for each candidate parameter would be prohibitive.
not_recommended_for: High-throughput scenarios requiring many PDE evaluations across varying parameters or geometries (e.g., design optimization sweeps) — retraining cost per instance makes FEM or neural operators far cheaper.
Purely data-driven prediction tasks with no known governing equation, where a standard deep learning architecture trained on labeled data will converge faster and generalize better.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Raissi, Perdikaris, and Karniadakis (Journal of Computational Physics, 2019), the PINN framework built on their 2017 'hidden physics models' work and showed that automatic differentiation through a neural network's own computation graph is sufficient to enforce PDE constraints — no discretization of the differential operator is ever needed.

target.notes: Target is a continuous field u(x,t) satisfying a known PDE/ODE, not a labeled response. Supervision comes primarily from the physics residual at collocation points plus optional sparse boundary/initial/observation data. Also used for inverse problems: jointly recovering unknown PDE parameters/fields alongside the solution.

data_regime.rows: works with very few or zero labeled observations when the governing equations are known; the PDE residual replaces labeled data as the supervision signal
data_regime.dimensionality: mesh-free, handles irregular and moderately high-dimensional spatial domains; one trained network represents a single PDE instance (geometry + BCs + parameters)
needs: known governing differential equations (PDE/ODE form must be specified)
