automatic differentiation framework for residual computation
domain knowledge to set boundary/initial conditions and residual weighting

features.interpretability: medium: outputs are physical fields with mechanistic meaning, but the network weights and learned solution are opaque
features.notes: Inputs are spatial/temporal coordinates (x, y, z, t) sampled at collocation points; inputs should be normalized to a bounded domain. Performance is sensitive to collocation point density and sampling strategy.

assumptions: the governing differential equation and its form are known and correct
the true solution is smooth enough for an MLP to represent (no sharp shocks/high-frequency content without specialized variants)
boundary and initial conditions are accurately specified
residual and data-mismatch loss terms can be balanced into a well-conditioned objective
loss: composite loss: PDE residual (collocation) + boundary-condition + initial-condition + optional data-mismatch terms, typically squared (L2)
for inverse problems, data misfit on sparse observations minimized jointly with the physics residual
contraindicated_when: no known governing equation (purely data-driven task) — use standard supervised deep learning
solution has high-frequency, multi-scale, or shock/discontinuous features (spectral bias causes failure without ad-hoc fixes)
many PDE evaluations across varying geometries/parameters are needed (design sweeps) — per-instance retraining makes FEM or neural operators far cheaper
abundant high-fidelity labeled simulation data already exist, removing the need for physics regularization

children.name: AlphaFold2
children.diff_siblings: Unlike other specialized architectures that use standard transformer blocks on a single representation, AlphaFold2 processes two coupled data streams simultaneously — a Multiple Sequence Alignment (MSA) representation and a residue-pair representation — fused through 48 Evoformer blocks with triangle self-attention that enforces geometric consistency across residue triplets.
strengths: Achieves median backbone RMSD under 1Å on CASP14 targets, surpassing all prior methods by a margin that made the competition effectively solved
Triangle attention in the Evoformer encodes physical constraints (distances must satisfy triangle inequality) directly into the architecture, not as a post-processing step
Outputs per-residue confidence scores (pLDDT) and predicted aligned error (PAE) that reliably distinguish well-folded regions from disordered loops without requiring experimental validation
weaknesses: Prediction quality degrades sharply for proteins with fewer than ~30 homologous sequences in the MSA, making it unreliable for novel or highly divergent proteins
Predicts a single static ground-state structure and cannot model conformational ensembles, fold switching, or intrinsically disordered regions that sample multiple states
Inference requires constructing deep MSAs via homology search (e.g., JackHMMER against UniRef90), adding substantial preprocessing time and storage compared to sequence-only models like ESMFold
recommended_for: Structural genomics pipelines where thousands of bacterial or eukaryotic proteins with moderate sequence conservation (>30 homologs) need 3D coordinates for downstream docking or annotation
Drug discovery target identification when the protein has a known fold family and a static structure is sufficient to identify binding pockets via tools like FTMap or Fpocket
not_recommended_for: Proteins that undergo large-scale conformational changes upon ligand binding or are known fold-switchers, since AlphaFold2 returns only the lowest free-energy conformation
Orphan viral proteins from novel pathogens with no detectable homologs, where MSA depth falls below ~10 sequences and pLDDT scores become unreliable indicators of true structure
children.curiosity: Introduced by Jumper et al. at DeepMind (Nature, 2021), AlphaFold2 won CASP14 with a median GDT_TS score of 92.4 — so far above second place (GDT_TS ~75) that the assessors described it as a solution to the 50-year-old protein folding problem.

target.notes: Structured prediction of 3D atomic coordinates (per-residue backbone/side-chain positions) from an amino-acid sequence; not a tabular regression/classification target. Auxiliary outputs are per-residue confidence (pLDDT) and a residue-pair predicted aligned error (PAE) matrix.

data_regime.rows: Single-instance inference per protein; no user training set. Pretrained on PDB (~170k structures) plus self-distillation on large unlabeled sequence sets.
data_regime.dimensionality: Inputs are L residues (typically tens to ~1000s); memory and compute scale roughly quadratically in L (pair representation L x L), so very long chains/complexes are constrained.
needs: deep MSA from homology search (JackHMMER/HHblits against UniRef/BFD)
large sequence/structure databases for the MSA pipeline

features.interpretability: low — end-to-end deep network (48 Evoformer blocks + structure module); pLDDT/PAE give confidence calibration but not mechanistic explanation.
features.notes: Primary signal is co-evolutionary covariation extracted from a multiple sequence alignment, supplemented by structural templates. Effective input is the MSA depth and quality, not the single sequence alone.

assumptions: Sufficient MSA depth: >~30 homologs needed; quality degrades sharply below that and is unreliable below ~10 sequences
Protein adopts a single dominant ground-state fold (lowest free-energy conformation)
Co-evolutionary contact signal is present and informative in the alignment
Static structure is biologically meaningful for the question being asked
contraindicated_when: Orphan / novel / highly divergent proteins with few or no detectable homologs (shallow MSA)
Proteins requiring conformational ensembles, fold switching, or large ligand-induced conformational changes (returns one static state)
Intrinsically disordered regions that sample multiple states
Sequence-only / low-latency settings where building deep MSAs is infeasible (consider sequence-only folders like ESMFold)
Tasks that are actually tabular target prediction — this is a structural-biology model, not a general predictor

children.name: Neural ODE
children.diff_siblings: Unlike other specialized architectures that stack discrete layers, Neural ODE parameterizes the derivative of the hidden state with a neural network and integrates it using a numerical ODE solver, making depth continuous rather than a fixed integer count.
strengths: Constant memory cost during training: the adjoint sensitivity method computes gradients by solving a second ODE backward in time, independent of the number of solver steps.
Adaptive computation per input: the ODE solver automatically adjusts step size based on local truncation error, spending more evaluations on complex regions of the input.
Naturally handles irregularly sampled time series: the latent state can be queried at any real-valued time point without imputation or binning, unlike RNNs that require fixed discrete steps.
weaknesses: ODE flows are homeomorphisms, so the learned mapping must be topologically equivalent to the identity; this prevents the model from representing functions whose trajectories must cross in latent space.
Slow wall-clock training: each forward pass calls an adaptive ODE solver (e.g., Dormand-Prince RK45) with multiple function evaluations, making it 2-10x slower than an equivalent-capacity ResNet.

Vanishing influence of past states: because the dynamics are autonomous and Lipschitz-constrained, the effect of early initial conditions decays over long integration intervals, limiting long-range dependency capture.
recommended_for: Irregularly sampled clinical or sensor time series (e.g., ICU vitals recorded at non-uniform intervals) where the model must interpolate or extrapolate to arbitrary future time points without data imputation.
Continuous normalizing flows for density estimation tasks where exact log-likelihood is required and invertibility must be guaranteed analytically via the ODE uniqueness theorem.
not_recommended_for: High-throughput classification tasks on fixed-resolution images (e.g., ImageNet) where a standard ResNet delivers equivalent accuracy at a fraction of the inference latency.

Sequences with long-term discrete dependencies (e.g., document-level NLP) where the topological constraint of ODE flows prevents the model from learning the necessary non-homeomorphic input-output mappings.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Chen, Rubanova, Bettencourt, and Duvenaud at NeurIPS 2018, the paper showed that the adjoint sensitivity method — originally developed for optimal control in the 1960s by Pontryagin — reduces the memory cost of backpropagation through an ODE solver from O(L) in the number of solver steps to O(1).

target.notes: Most natural fit is modeling continuous-time latent dynamics: regress a state trajectory and query it at arbitrary real-valued times. Also used as a density estimator (continuous normalizing flow) with no labeled target. Less suited to discrete-target classification.

data_regime.rows: needs thousands+ of trajectories/sequences to fit the dynamics network well
data_regime.dimensionality: moderate latent/state dimension; cost scales with solver evaluations, not depth

features.interpretability: low; learned vector field is a black-box neural net, though the ODE/dynamical-system framing aids physical inspection
features.notes: Excels with irregularly/non-uniformly sampled time series: state can be evaluated at any t without imputation or binning. Inputs should be scaled; the autonomous vector field assumes stationary dynamics.

assumptions: The input-output map is a homeomorphism (topologically equivalent to identity): ODE flows cannot represent mappings whose latent trajectories must cross
Dynamics are Lipschitz-continuous so the solution exists and is unique (enables exact-likelihood CNF and the adjoint method)
Underlying process is well-described by smooth continuous-time dynamics rather than abrupt discrete jumps
loss: squared error / Gaussian NLL on reconstructed or forecast trajectories
exact log-likelihood via instantaneous change-of-variables (continuous normalizing flow density estimation)
ELBO when used as the decoder of a latent-ODE VAE for generative time-series modeling
contraindicated_when: Target mapping is non-homeomorphic (trajectories must cross), e.g. document-level NLP with long discrete dependencies
Fixed-resolution image classification where a ResNet matches accuracy at far lower inference latency
Long-range dependency tasks: Lipschitz-constrained autonomous dynamics let early initial-condition influence decay over long integration intervals
Latency-critical inference: adaptive solvers (e.g. Dormand-Prince RK45) run 2-10x slower than equivalent-capacity discrete nets

children.name: Matrix Factorization (Collaborative SVD)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike NMF (which enforces non-negativity) or ALS (which optimizes for implicit feedback via weighted least squares), Collaborative SVD factorizes the explicit rating matrix into user and item latent factor vectors trained by SGD, minimizing regularized squared error on observed ratings only.
strengths: Learns compact k-dimensional latent representations that capture taste-genre associations without requiring explicit feature engineering on items or users
SGD training scales to millions of observed ratings by updating only on non-missing entries, avoiding the O(n*m) cost of filling the full sparse matrix
Straightforwardly incorporates per-user and per-item bias terms (b_u + b_i) that absorb systematic rating tendencies, measurably reducing RMSE versus pure dot-product factorization
weaknesses: Suffers complete cold-start failure: a new user or item with zero ratings has no latent vector and cannot receive or generate predictions without a fallback strategy
Captures only linear interactions between latent factors; cannot model higher-order or non-linear user-item affinities that deep models handle natively
Requires explicit numerical ratings as supervision signal; binary or implicit feedback (clicks, plays) demands reformulation to ALS or BPR, where plain SVD degrades significantly
recommended_for: Movie or product rating platforms (e.g., 1-5 star scale) with millions of user-item pairs but high sparsity (~99%), where SGD-based MF consistently outperforms neighborhood methods on RMSE
Offline batch recommendation pipelines where interpretable low-rank structure (k=50-200 factors) and fast dot-product scoring at inference time are operational requirements
not_recommended_for: Applications with frequent new-user or new-item arrivals (e.g., news feeds, live auctions) where cold-start coverage is critical and content features must be exploited from day one
Implicit feedback datasets (streams, clicks, purchases without ratings) where the absence of a rating is not the same as a zero and ALS with confidence weights or BPR is the correct formulation
children.curiosity: Koren, Bell, and Volinsky (2009) showed in their IEEE Computer paper that SVD-based matrix factorization was the foundation of the winning BellKor solution in the Netflix Prize, achieving over 10% RMSE improvement versus Netflix's own Cinematch baseline on 100 million ratings.

target.notes: Predicts explicit user-item ratings (e.g. 1-5 stars) on observed entries of a sparse rating matrix. Target is the rating value; trained only on non-missing cells. Not for implicit/binary feedback without reformulation (ALS/BPR).

data_regime.rows: needs many observed interactions (tens of thousands to millions of ratings); shines under high sparsity (~99% missing)
data_regime.dimensionality: factorizes a large users x items matrix into low rank k (typically 50-200 latent factors)
needs: many repeat interactions per user and per item to estimate latent vectors

features.interpretability: medium: latent factors are abstract but bias terms (b_u, b_i) and dot-product scores are inspectable; factors are not semantically labeled
features.notes: Inputs are essentially (user_id, item_id, rating) triples; no side features. Pure ID-based, so it cannot exploit content/content features and gives no signal for unseen ids.

assumptions: rating matrix is approximately low-rank (taste/genre structure captured by k factors)
user-item interaction is linear in latent factors (dot product); no higher-order or non-linear affinities
missingness is informative only as 'unobserved', not as a zero rating
every user and item to be scored has at least some training ratings
loss: regularized squared error (RMSE/MSE) on observed entries with L2 penalty on user/item factors and bias terms, optimized by SGD
contraindicated_when: frequent new users or items (cold start): no latent vector exists, predictions impossible without fallback
implicit feedback (clicks, plays, purchases) where absence != zero rating; use ALS with confidence weights or BPR instead
rich side/content features are available and must drive recommendations from day one (use content-based or hybrid/factorization-machine models)
non-linear or higher-order user-item interactions dominate (use neural collaborative filtering / deep recommenders)
very few interactions per user/item, making latent factors unidentifiable

children.name: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike monolithic specialized architectures (e.g., CNNs, RNNs, or dense Transformers), MoE replaces fixed feed-forward layers with N independent expert sub-networks and a learned gating network that routes each input (or token) to only the top-k experts, decoupling total parameter count from per-sample computational cost.
strengths: Sparse activation enables models with hundreds of billions of parameters to run at the same FLOP cost as a much smaller dense model, since only k of N experts fire per token.
Each expert specializes on a distinct region of the input distribution, allowing a single model to handle heterogeneous data (e.g., different languages or domains) without a shared bottleneck layer.
Scales parameter count independently of training compute: doubling the number of experts doubles capacity while leaving per-token FLOPs unchanged.
weaknesses: All expert weights must reside in memory simultaneously at inference, so GPU VRAM requirements match the full parameter count even though only a fraction of weights are active per token.
Expert collapse: the router tends to concentrate traffic on a few experts early in training; preventing this requires auxiliary load-balancing losses that add a sensitive hyperparameter.
Communication overhead between GPUs scales with the number of experts under expert-parallelism, making distributed training significantly more complex than for equivalent dense models.
recommended_for: Large-scale language model pretraining where total parameter capacity must be maximized on a fixed compute budget — e.g., training a 100B-parameter model with the effective FLOPs of a 10B dense model.
Multi-domain or multilingual tasks where input heterogeneity benefits from learned specialization, such as a single model serving both code and natural language with distinct expert routing.
not_recommended_for: Memory-constrained inference deployments (edge devices, single consumer GPUs) where all expert weights must be loaded even if only 1–2% are active per forward pass.
Small datasets or narrow single-domain tasks where the router cannot learn meaningful specialization and the auxiliary load-balancing loss destabilizes training without capacity benefit.
children.curiosity: The foundational MoE concept was introduced by Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan, and Hinton (1991) in 'Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts' (Neural Computation, vol. 3); the modern sparse variant used in LLMs — top-k gating with noisy logits for load balancing — was formalized by Shazeer et al. (2017) in 'Outrageously Large Neural Networks.'

target.notes: Architectural pattern, not tied to a target type; in practice used as the feed-forward block of large autoregressive/seq2seq Transformers, so the effective target is next-token prediction over a large multinomial vocabulary. Can be adapted to regression/classification heads but the value proposition is capacity scaling, not a specific likelihood.

data_regime.rows: needs very large corpora (billions+ of tokens); router specialization fails to emerge on small/narrow datasets
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for very high effective capacity (10s-100s of billions of parameters); decouples parameter count from per-token FLOPs
needs: large GPU VRAM (full parameter count must be resident at inference even with sparse top-k activation)

features.interpretability: low; learned gating routes tokens to experts with no semantically guaranteed specialization, and the sparse routing adds opacity over an already opaque dense Transformer
features.notes: Operates on learned token embeddings; benefits most when the input distribution is heterogeneous (multilingual, multi-domain, code+NL) so distinct experts can specialize.

assumptions: Input distribution is heterogeneous/multimodal enough that learned per-expert specialization is meaningful
Training data and compute are large enough for the router to learn a stable, balanced routing policy
Auxiliary load-balancing loss is tuned to prevent expert collapse (router concentrating on few experts)
loss: cross-entropy / next-token log-loss of the host model
auxiliary load-balancing / router z-loss to spread token traffic across experts (sparsely-gated MoE)
contraindicated_when: Memory-constrained or edge/single-GPU inference: all expert weights must be loaded despite only k-of-N firing per token
Small or narrow single-domain datasets: no specialization signal, and load-balancing loss destabilizes training without capacity benefit
Compute is the binding constraint rather than parameter capacity: a dense model of equivalent active FLOPs is simpler with comparable quality
Low-latency single-stream serving where expert-routing communication overhead dominates

target.notes: Umbrella family; target type is inherited from the chosen sub-architecture rather than the category. MoE wraps any supervised head (typically multiclass token prediction); Neural ODEs serve continuous regression, density estimation, and continuous-time series; PINNs target continuous PDE solution fields; CapsNets target image multiclass; energy-based and memory-augmented models are often used unsupervised or as generative/representation modules with no fixed target.

data_regime.rows: thousands+ generally; MoE and large-scale variants need very large corpora to amortize parameter count; PINNs are an exception (learn from governing equations plus few collocation/boundary points, so they tolerate sparse or no labeled data)
data_regime.dimensionality: handles high-dimensional structured inputs (images, sequences, graphs, spatiotemporal fields); not aimed at tabular p>n problems
needs: substantial engineering for training stability and serving

features.interpretability: low overall; the structural prior can be inspectable (CapsNet pose vectors, MoE expert routing, PINN physical residuals) but the learned mapping is opaque
features.notes: Choice is driven by a known structural property of the data — part-whole/pose geometry (CapsNets), sparse conditional computation at scale (MoE), continuous-depth/known dynamics (Neural ODE, PINN), external memory/algorithmic reasoning (NTM/MANN), or energy-landscape modeling (EBM). Inputs typically require the same normalization as standard deep nets.

assumptions: The problem genuinely carries the structural property the sub-architecture encodes (e.g., meaningful part-whole pose for CapsNets, known governing equations for PINNs); a wrong prior wastes capacity and hurts accuracy versus a generic CNN/Transformer
Training budget allows auxiliary losses and tuning (load-balancing for MoE, routing agreement for CapsNets) needed to avoid expert starvation or routing collapse
For solver-based models the dynamics are sufficiently smooth/well-conditioned for the ODE solver to integrate stably
loss: task loss of the wrapped head: cross-entropy/log-loss for classification, squared error for regression

auxiliary objectives specific to the architecture: MoE load-balancing/router-z loss, CapsNet margin loss, EBM contrastive divergence / score-matching energy loss, PINN physics residual + boundary/initial-condition loss, Neural ODE adjoint-based likelihood
contraindicated_when: Standard image or NLP task with abundant labels and no special structure — a well-tuned CNN or Transformer gives better accuracy per engineering hour with mature tooling
Strict tail-latency SLAs in production: ODE-solver overhead and MoE all-to-all routing make 99th-percentile latency hard to bound
Small datasets without a usable structural/physical prior, where the added training instability and scarce pretrained checkpoints outweigh any inductive-bias gain
Tabular data — none of these primitives target low-dimensional mixed numeric/categorical tables

children.name: 2.10 Transfer Learning (Deep)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike other deep learning paradigms that train a model from scratch on a target task, Transfer Learning reuses weights from a model pretrained on a large source dataset, initializing the target network from a learned representation rather than random values, so the optimization starts close to a useful solution.
strengths: Drastically reduces labeled data requirements on the target task — ImageNet-pretrained CNNs reach competitive accuracy on domain-specific datasets with as few as a few hundred labeled examples, because low-level features (edges, textures) are reused directly.
Cuts training time by orders of magnitude: fine-tuning a pretrained ResNet-50 for a new 10-class task converges in minutes on a single GPU versus days of training from scratch.
Acts as a strong regularizer — pretrained weights encode structural priors from millions of examples, reducing overfitting on small target datasets compared to random initialization.
weaknesses: Negative transfer: when source and target domains are dissimilar (e.g., natural images to medical X-rays), pretrained features can hurt more than random initialization, with no reliable automatic detector for this mismatch.

Catastrophic forgetting during aggressive fine-tuning — updating all layers on a small target dataset can overwrite general representations, destroying the transferable knowledge the pretraining provided.

Tight coupling to source-domain biases: a model pretrained on ImageNet inherits its class imbalances and visual biases, which propagate to the target task unless explicitly corrected with domain-adaptation techniques.
recommended_for: Image classification or object detection with fewer than 10,000 labeled target examples, where a large pretrained backbone (ResNet, EfficientNet) is fine-tuned on domain-specific images such as satellite imagery or medical scans.

NLP tasks like sentiment analysis or named-entity recognition on specialized corpora, where a pretrained language model (BERT, RoBERTa) is fine-tuned, leveraging general linguistic representations to reach strong performance with limited task-specific annotations.
not_recommended_for: Tasks where the source and target domains are fundamentally dissimilar in input structure — for example, transferring from natural-image CNNs to time-series sensor data, where convolutional spatial priors are irrelevant and training from scratch is more principled.

Production scenarios requiring full model interpretability or strict auditability of every learned feature, since pretrained weights encode implicit knowledge from a large external dataset whose content may be unknown or proprietary.
children.curiosity: The formal framework for transfer learning was established by Pan and Yang in their landmark 2010 IEEE TKDE survey, which defined source and target domains, tasks, and the three canonical settings (inductive, transductive, unsupervised) — a taxonomy still used unchanged in the literature today.

children.name: Fine-tuning
children.diff_siblings: Unlike feature extraction (which freezes all pretrained weights) or adapter tuning (which inserts small trainable modules), fine-tuning unfreezes and updates the pretrained network's own parameters end-to-end on the target task, allowing every layer to shift its representations.
strengths: Higher ceiling accuracy than frozen-feature approaches when source and target domains are similar, because all layers can specialize to the target distribution.
Flexible layer-wise control: early layers can be frozen while later, task-specific layers receive larger learning rates, concentrating adaptation where the domain gap is greatest.
Works across modalities and architectures — the same gradient-based update procedure applies to CNNs on images, Transformers on text, and audio encoders, requiring no architectural changes.
weaknesses: Catastrophic forgetting: updating all weights can overwrite generalizable pretrained representations, especially with a large learning rate or a small target dataset.
Requires careful hyperparameter tuning (per-layer learning rates, unfreezing schedule) — wrong settings cause either underfitting (too frozen) or representational collapse (too aggressive).
Computationally expensive relative to feature extraction: full backward passes through the entire pretrained model are needed even when only the final layers change meaningfully.
recommended_for: Medical imaging classification with moderate-sized labeled datasets (hundreds to low thousands of images) where the source domain (e.g., ImageNet) differs enough from X-rays or histology slides that frozen features lose discriminative power.

Domain-specific NLP tasks (sentiment, legal classification) where a pretrained language model has strong priors but the vocabulary and style diverge enough from the pretraining corpus to require weight updates throughout the network.
not_recommended_for: Scenarios with very few target examples (fewer than ~50 per class) and a large pretrained model, where frozen feature extraction or few-shot methods generalize better and fine-tuning risks overfitting.
Continual learning pipelines where the model must sequentially learn multiple tasks without forgetting previous ones, because unconstrained fine-tuning erases earlier task representations.
children.curiosity: Yosinski et al. (NeurIPS 2014) provided the first systematic quantification of layer transferability in deep networks, showing that early convolutional layers learn general Gabor-like filters transferable across any dataset, while layers 6-7 of AlexNet become so task-specific that fine-tuning them — rather than freezing — is necessary to recover full performance on a new domain.
keywords: fine-tune pretrained model on my data

target.notes: Procedure, not a target-specific model: inherits the target type of whatever pretrained backbone/head is adapted (classification, regression, generation, sequence labeling). Target distribution is determined by the chosen output head, not by fine-tuning itself.

data_regime.rows: best in the small-to-moderate labeled regime (hundreds to low thousands per class); below ~50 examples/class prefer frozen feature extraction, adapters/LoRA, or few-shot
data_regime.dimensionality: handles extreme p>>n via the pretrained prior; raw input is high-dimensional (pixels, tokens) and the backbone supplies the inductive bias
needs: source-target domain similarity for best transfer

features.interpretability: low - end-to-end deep network with millions+ updated parameters; no coefficient-level explanation
features.notes: Operates on raw or backbone-native inputs; preprocessing must match the pretraining pipeline (tokenizer, normalization stats, input resolution). Per-layer/discriminative learning rates and an unfreezing schedule are the key levers.

assumptions: source and target domains are related enough that pretrained representations transfer (negative transfer if domains are disjoint)
target labels are reliable; full-parameter updates amplify label-noise overfitting on small sets
a single target task at a time (sequential unconstrained fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting)
loss: any differentiable task loss of the attached head: cross-entropy / log-loss for classification, squared error for regression, token-level / autoregressive NLL for sequence and generation tasks
optionally combined with regularization toward pretrained weights (e.g. L2-SP, EWC) to limit forgetting
contraindicated_when: very few labeled target examples (<~50/class) with a large backbone - overfits; use feature extraction, adapters/LoRA, or few-shot instead
continual / multi-task learning without forgetting constraints - unconstrained updates erase prior tasks
no domain gap from the pretrained model - frozen feature extraction is cheaper for equal accuracy
no compute budget for full backward passes through the backbone
source and target domains are unrelated, where transfer provides no useful prior

children.name: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike full fine-tuning (which updates all weights) or adapter layers (which insert new modules between transformer blocks), LoRA freezes the pretrained weights entirely and injects two small trainable matrices A and B whose product BA approximates the weight update delta W, with rank r << min(d_in, d_out), so zero new parameters are added to the inference graph once the matrices are merged back.
strengths: Zero inference latency: adapter matrices are merged into the frozen weights before deployment (h = W0x + BAx collapses to a single matmul), unlike bottleneck adapters which add sequential modules at runtime.

Drastic parameter reduction: adapting GPT-3 175B requires training only ~4.7M parameters (rank-4 on attention projections) versus 175B for full fine-tuning, enabling fine-tuning on a single consumer GPU.
Composable and swappable: multiple LoRA checkpoints can be stored cheaply (~10 MB each) and swapped at runtime on a shared frozen base, supporting multi-task serving without reloading the full model.
weaknesses: Rank r must be chosen manually; too low a rank underrepresents complex task shifts (LoRA recovers only ~90-95% of full fine-tuning quality on high-resource tasks), while too high a rank risks overfitting and approaches full fine-tuning cost.
Applied naively to attention layers only (Q, V projections), LoRA underperforms substantially compared to including MLP layers, making module selection a non-trivial tuning decision.

The low-rank assumption breaks when the target task requires a high-intrinsic-dimension weight shift (e.g., large domain shift from natural language to code in a model with no code pretraining), where rank-deficient updates are structurally insufficient.
recommended_for: Instruction-tuning or domain adaptation of large pretrained transformers (7B-70B) on a single GPU: the rank-4 to rank-16 decomposition cuts trainable parameters by 1000x while preserving most of the pretrained representation.
Multi-tenant LLM serving where dozens of task-specific adapters share one frozen base model: each LoRA checkpoint is ~10-50 MB, enabling hot-swapping without reloading multi-gigabyte weights.
not_recommended_for: Tasks requiring large weight shifts from a weakly related pretraining distribution, where the low-rank constraint actively prevents the model from acquiring the necessary representational capacity.
Small models (under ~100M parameters) where the overhead of designing and tuning rank and alpha hyperparameters outweighs the memory savings of full fine-tuning on modest hardware.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Hu et al. (2021) at Microsoft Research in 'LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models' (arXiv:2106.09685), the method drew directly from Aghajanyan et al.'s finding (2020) that pretrained model updates lie in a low intrinsic dimension, empirically validating that rank-4 adapters on GPT-3 match full fine-tuning on several benchmarks.

target.notes: Not a model itself but a fine-tuning technique; the downstream target is whatever the base transformer is adapted to (text generation, classification, etc.). Target type is inherited from the task, not from LoRA.

data_regime.rows: works with modest labeled data (hundreds to tens of thousands of examples); the frozen base supplies most knowledge, so it shines in low-to-mid-resource adaptation rather than from-scratch training
data_regime.dimensionality: operates on large pretrained transformers (typically 100M-70B+ params); irrelevant for small models
needs: GPU (single consumer/mid GPU is the point; QLoRA enables 4-bit base to fit even tighter)
task-relevant pretraining in the base for the low-rank shift to suffice

features.interpretability: low; it is a weight-update parameterization, not an interpretable model
features.notes: Two tunable hyperparameters dominate fit: rank r (4-64 typical) and scaling alpha; module selection (attention Q/V vs also MLP) materially affects quality. Adapters merge into base weights for zero added inference latency.

assumptions: the required task-specific weight update has low intrinsic rank (delta W approximable by BA with r << min(d_in,d_out))
the pretrained base already covers a distribution close to the target task
the chosen rank and target modules capture the needed adaptation capacity
contraindicated_when: the target task demands a high-intrinsic-dimension weight shift from a weakly related pretraining distribution (low-rank constraint blocks needed capacity)
the base model is small (<~100M params), where full fine-tuning is cheap enough to make LoRA's hyperparameter tuning overhead not worth it
you need maximum achievable quality on a high-resource task (full fine-tuning typically recovers the last few percent LoRA leaves on the table)
there is no suitable large pretrained base to adapt

children.name: Prompt Engineering
children.diff_siblings: Unlike adapter tuning, prefix tuning, prompt tuning, and LoRA — which all introduce trainable parameters or modify internal model representations — prompt engineering adapts a frozen pretrained model purely through crafted natural-language instructions or examples in the input, requiring zero gradient updates.
strengths: Zero compute cost for adaptation: no training loop, no GPU memory overhead beyond inference — the same frozen model handles any new task by changing only the input text.

Immediately transferable across tasks and models: a well-structured few-shot prompt (Brown et al., 2020) can match fine-tuned baselines on classification, translation, and QA without any labeled training set.
Fully interpretable control surface: every behavioral constraint is explicit human-readable text, making auditing and iterative refinement straightforward compared to opaque weight deltas.
weaknesses: Hard performance ceiling on complex reasoning: even with chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022), prompting consistently underperforms fine-tuned models on tasks requiring deep domain adaptation or precise structured output.
Context-window bound: all demonstrations, instructions, and retrieved context must fit within the model's token limit, which caps the number of examples and the complexity of the task description.

Brittle to phrasing and ordering: output quality is sensitive to minor wording changes, example ordering, and prompt length, making reliable reproducibility difficult without systematic prompt optimization.
recommended_for: Rapid prototyping on NLP tasks (classification, summarization, QA) where labeled training data is scarce and a pretrained LLM is already available — few-shot examples in the prompt eliminate the data-collection bottleneck.

Multi-task pipelines where a single deployed model must handle heterogeneous tasks at inference time, since switching tasks requires only swapping the prompt rather than loading a different fine-tuned checkpoint.
not_recommended_for: Tasks demanding consistent, highly structured output (e.g., strict JSON schema extraction or code generation with complex constraints) where fine-tuning on domain examples achieves reliably lower error rates.

Latency-critical production systems with token budgets: large few-shot prompts substantially increase input token count, raising inference cost and latency compared to a fine-tuned model that encodes task knowledge in weights.
children.curiosity: The modern formalization of prompt engineering as a transfer paradigm emerged from Brown et al. (2020) in 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners', which showed that GPT-3 (175 billion parameters) could match or exceed fine-tuned BERT-scale models on several benchmarks using only in-context examples — with no weight updates.

target.notes: Not a trained estimator; adapts a frozen LLM via input text. Targets are whatever the LLM emits as text: free-form generation, classification labels, extracted spans, QA answers. No fitted target distribution; no calibrated probabilities.

data_regime.rows: no training set required; operates per-inference with 0 to ~tens of in-context examples (few-shot), bounded by context window
data_regime.dimensionality: not applicable; task knowledge supplied as natural-language examples, not as a feature matrix
needs: inference compute only — no GPU training loop
prompt iteration / evaluation harness rather than labeled training data

features.interpretability: high — every behavioral constraint is explicit human-readable instruction/example text, fully auditable, no opaque weight deltas
features.notes: Inputs are natural-language tasks plus optional demonstrations; numeric/tabular/image data must be serialized to text. Sensitive to phrasing, example ordering, and demonstration count.

assumptions: a sufficiently capable pretrained LLM already encodes the relevant task/domain knowledge
task, instructions, demonstrations, and retrieved context all fit within the model's token limit
the task is expressible in natural language and tolerant of phrasing/ordering brittleness
contraindicated_when: strict structured output is required (exact JSON schema, constrained code) where fine-tuning yields reliably lower error
complex multi-step reasoning or deep domain adaptation where fine-tuned models clearly outperform even with chain-of-thought
latency- or cost-critical serving with tight token budgets (large few-shot prompts inflate input tokens)
high-reproducibility needs without systematic prompt optimization, given brittleness to wording and example order
calibrated probabilistic predictions or quantified uncertainty are needed

children.name: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike fine-tuning, adapters, or prompt tuning — which all encode new knowledge into model weights — RAG keeps the base LLM frozen and instead appends retrieved passages from an external corpus at inference time, making its knowledge store updatable without retraining.
strengths: Knowledge can be updated by modifying the document corpus alone, with no gradient step or redeployment of model weights.
Retrieval provides traceable, citable passages, making it possible to verify exactly which source drove a given answer.
Reduces hallucination on factual queries because the generator is grounded in retrieved text rather than relying solely on parametric memory.
weaknesses: Answer quality is bounded by retrieval quality: if the relevant document is not retrieved (wrong embedding, stale index, chunking mismatch), the generator has no fallback and may confabulate.
Adds substantial infrastructure overhead — vector database, embedding pipeline, chunking strategy, and retrieval tuning — compared to pure parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods.
Multi-hop questions requiring synthesis across several documents degrade significantly, as the retriever is not trained to chain evidence across multiple passages.
recommended_for: Enterprise Q&A over frequently updated internal documentation (policies, product specs) where retraining on every update is infeasible.
Open-domain factual question answering over large corpora (e.g., medical literature, legal databases) where citation and auditability of the source passage are required.
not_recommended_for: Tasks requiring stylistic or behavioral adaptation (tone, format, domain jargon internalization), where fine-tuning or adapter methods embed the desired behavior more reliably.
Low-latency inference pipelines with strict SLA requirements, since retrieval adds a network round-trip and vector search step before generation begins.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Lewis et al. (NeurIPS 2020), RAG was the first framework to treat document retrieval as a latent variable and marginalize over retrieved passages using a Dense Passage Retriever (DPR) jointly with a BART seq2seq generator, establishing the retrieve-then-generate pattern now ubiquitous in LLM applications.
keywords: ground llm responses in your own data
answer questions from pdfs and documents
context injection for large language models

target.notes: Not a statistical estimator over a labeled target. It is an inference-time architecture that conditions a frozen generative LLM on retrieved text; the 'output' is free-form natural language, not a fitted distribution over a response variable.

data_regime.rows: no training set required for the core pattern (base LLM and embedder are pretrained); needs a corpus of documents large enough to contain answers but small/large is fine since it is non-parametric retrieval
data_regime.dimensionality: operates on dense embedding vectors (typically 384-3072 dims) indexed in a vector store; scales to millions of passages

features.interpretability: medium-high for provenance: retrieved passages are citable and auditable so you can trace which source drove an answer; the generator's internal reasoning remains opaque
features.notes: Inputs are unstructured documents (PDF, HTML, knowledge bases) chunked into passages and embedded. Performance is highly sensitive to chunk size, embedding model choice, and index freshness.

assumptions: The answer-bearing passage is actually present in the corpus and retrievable by the embedding similarity metric (retrieval recall is the binding constraint)
Queries are answerable from a small number of independently relevant passages rather than requiring multi-hop synthesis across many documents
Document corpus is reasonably clean and chunkable; semantic similarity in embedding space aligns with relevance to the query
contraindicated_when: The task is a structured prediction problem (regression/classification over tabular, numeric, count, or time-series targets) rather than open-ended text generation
Goal is stylistic/behavioral adaptation (tone, format, jargon internalization) which lives in weights, not retrievable facts; fine-tuning/adapters fit better
Answers require multi-hop reasoning chaining evidence across many documents, which single-shot retrievers handle poorly
Strict low-latency SLA, since retrieval adds a vector-search round-trip before generation
The knowledge is static and small enough to internalize via fine-tuning, making the retrieval infrastructure unjustified overhead

target.notes: Umbrella deep-learning paradigm, not a task family. Target type is inherited from the downstream head attached to the pretrained backbone (classification, regression, detection, segmentation, sequence labeling). Equally applicable to representation/feature-extraction with no explicit target.

data_regime.rows: Designed for the small-to-moderate labeled-target regime (hundreds to low tens of thousands); its core value disappears once the target set is large enough to train from scratch. Requires a large source dataset, but that is supplied via the pretrained weights, not by the user.
data_regime.dimensionality: Handles extreme raw input dimensionality (pixels, tokens) because the pretrained backbone reduces it to a learned low-dimensional representation; effective p>n on the target task since most parameters are frozen or weakly updated.
needs: GPU (lighter than full training; feature-extraction mode can run on CPU)
a pretrained backbone whose source domain matches the target modality

features.interpretability: low: predictions rest on opaque pretrained weights encoding unknown/proprietary source-domain knowledge; not auditable feature-by-feature.
features.notes: Requires input preprocessing to match the backbone's pretraining pipeline (resolution, normalization statistics, tokenizer/vocabulary). Source and target must share input structure/modality for the priors to transfer.

assumptions: Source and target domains share transferable low/mid-level structure (the marginal feature distributions are related); strongly violated domains cause negative transfer.
Target task is a specialization of, or compatible with, the representation learned during pretraining.
Input modality and preprocessing match the backbone's pretraining regime.
loss: any differentiable downstream objective on the attached head: cross-entropy / log-loss, squared error, detection/segmentation losses, contrastive losses
optionally discriminative/layer-wise learning rates, layer freezing, and regularization toward pretrained weights to limit catastrophic forgetting
contraindicated_when: source and target domains are fundamentally dissimilar in input structure (e.g., natural-image CNN to tabular or raw sensor time-series), where spatial/linguistic priors are irrelevant and from-scratch training is more principled
no suitable pretrained backbone exists for the modality
target labeled data is already abundant enough that from-scratch training matches or exceeds fine-tuning
full feature-level interpretability or strict auditability of all learned knowledge is required
the task is small structured/tabular data where shallow models (gradient boosting, linear/GLM) dominate

children.name: 2.11 MLP-based Forecasting
children.diff_siblings: Unlike RNN/LSTM-based models that process sequences recurrently and Transformer-based models that use self-attention, MLP-based forecasting flattens lag windows into fixed-length feature vectors and applies fully-connected layers along the temporal dimension — avoiding sequential state and quadratic attention complexity.
strengths: Faster training than Transformers: no O(T²) attention computation, making long-horizon runs feasible on commodity hardware
Competitive accuracy on univariate benchmarks — N-BEATS (a pure MLP stack with residual connections) beat the M4 competition winner by 3% without hybrid components
Interpretable decomposition possible: the N-BEATS interpretable variant constrains basis functions to trend and seasonality, producing human-readable components as a byproduct
weaknesses: Requires manual lag selection: the input window must be fixed at training time, so the model cannot adapt to variable-length dependencies without retraining
No built-in handling of irregular timestamps or missing values — inputs must be regularly sampled and pre-imputed
Flattening the temporal window destroys positional order implicitly; the model must re-learn temporal structure from co-occurrence patterns rather than from explicit sequence modeling
recommended_for: Univariate or low-dimensional multivariate forecasting on regularly sampled data (e.g., hourly energy demand, monthly retail sales) where training speed and interpretability matter
M-competition-style point forecasting tasks with thousands of independent series, where global MLP models trained across series (e.g., N-BEATS) outperform per-series statistical methods
not_recommended_for: Irregularly sampled clinical or IoT time series with frequent missing observations, where recurrent or attention-based models with masking handle gaps natively
Very long sequences (>10 000 steps) where the flattened input vector becomes impractically large and CNNs or Transformers with hierarchical pooling are more parameter-efficient
children.curiosity: Introduced by Oreshkin, Carpov, Chapados, and Bengio (2019) in 'N-BEATS: Neural Basis Expansion Analysis for Interpretable Time Series Forecasting' (ICLR 2020), N-BEATS was the first pure deep-learning model — using only stacked fully-connected blocks with residual links, no recurrence or convolution — to surpass both statistical ensembles and the hybrid ES-RNN winner of the M4 competition.

children.name: N-BEATS
children.diff_siblings: Unlike other MLP-based forecasters that operate on flat fully-connected layers, N-BEATS uses a doubly-residual stacking of blocks where each block outputs a backcast (removing what it explains from the input) and a forecast, with basis expansion constraining interpretable variants to polynomial (trend) and Fourier (seasonality) bases.
strengths: Interpretable configuration decomposes output into explicit trend (polynomial basis) and seasonality (Fourier basis) components without post-hoc analysis
Purely MLP-based with no recurrence or convolution — trains faster than RNN/LSTM families and avoids vanishing gradient issues in deep stacks
Doubly-residual connections let each block specialize on residual signal, enabling very deep architectures (30+ layers) without degradation
weaknesses: Designed exclusively for univariate forecasting — multivariate use requires flattening variables into the batch dimension, losing cross-series dependency modeling
Requires a fixed lookback window length set as a hyperparameter; poor window selection leads to missing long-range seasonal patterns or including irrelevant history
Computationally heavier than its direct successor N-HiTS, which achieves lower error with 54% fewer parameters and 1.26x faster training on the same benchmarks
recommended_for: Univariate demand or energy forecasting where additive trend + seasonality decomposition must be auditable by non-technical stakeholders
M-competition-style point forecasting tasks with hundreds of independent series at fixed horizons, where a single generic model must generalize across series without covariates
not_recommended_for: Multivariate forecasting problems where interactions between simultaneous signals (e.g., multiple sensor streams) drive predictive accuracy
Very long-horizon forecasting with irregular or multiple seasonality periods, where N-HiTS hierarchical interpolation handles multi-scale patterns more efficiently
children.curiosity: Introduced by Oreshkin, Carpov, Chapados, and Bengio (ICLR 2020), N-BEATS outperformed the M4 competition winner by 3% using no time-series-specific feature engineering — a first for a purely deep learning approach on that benchmark.

target.notes: Univariate point forecasting only: predicts a fixed-length future horizon from a fixed lookback window of a single series. No native probabilistic/distributional output; multivariate or covariate-driven targets are not modeled (extra series go into the batch dimension, losing cross-series dependence).

data_regime.rows: needs many observations per series and/or many series; M-competition-style pools of hundreds of independent series let the generic config generalize without covariates
data_regime.dimensionality: input dimension = lookback window length (hyperparameter); no exogenous features

features.interpretability: medium-high in interpretable config: doubly-residual blocks with polynomial (trend) and Fourier (seasonality) basis expansion decompose the forecast into auditable additive components without post-hoc analysis; generic config is low interpretability
features.notes: Consumes raw lagged values of one series; no manual feature engineering required. No support for static or time-varying covariates.

assumptions: Lookback window length is well chosen to capture relevant seasonal/long-range patterns
Series dynamics are stable enough that a fixed-horizon, fixed-window mapping generalizes
Forecast is well approximated by additive trend + seasonality (interpretable config) for the decomposition to be meaningful
loss: squared error / MSE
MAE
MAPE / sMAPE (common in M-competition setups)
contraindicated_when: Multivariate forecasting where interactions between simultaneous signals drive accuracy
Forecasts must be conditioned on exogenous covariates or static metadata
Probabilistic/quantile forecasts are required (no native predictive distribution)
Very long horizons with irregular or multiple seasonalities (N-HiTS is more efficient and accurate)
Very short series with little history per series

children.name: N-HiTS
children.diff_siblings: Unlike N-BEATS, which uses fixed-resolution basis expansions, N-HiTS adds MaxPool-based multi-rate input sampling per stack and hierarchical linear interpolation of outputs, forcing each stack to specialize in a distinct temporal scale and enabling efficient long-horizon extrapolation with fewer parameters.
strengths: Long-horizon accuracy: hierarchical interpolation enforces output smoothness across stacks, reducing MSE by up to 17% at 720-step horizons compared to Transformer baselines
Parameter efficiency: achieves N-BEATS-level accuracy with 54% of the parameters and 1.26x faster inference due to coarser interpolation grids at lower-frequency stacks

Multi-scale decomposition by design: MaxPool kernels with increasing sizes force lower stacks to capture slow trends and higher stacks to refine short-term residuals, without any explicit decomposition preprocessing
weaknesses: Fixed sampling rates: MaxPool kernel sizes are static hyperparameters set before training, so the model cannot adapt its temporal resolution to non-stationary or irregularly sampled series
Univariate by architecture: multivariate support is achieved only by flattening the input tensor, discarding inter-variable relationships that Transformer or graph-based models capture natively
Sensitive hyperparameter space: stack count, pooling kernel sizes, and interpolation ratios interact in non-obvious ways, requiring careful grid search to avoid degenerate scale assignments
recommended_for: Long-horizon univariate forecasting (e.g., 96-720 steps) on periodic signals such as hourly electricity demand or daily weather variables, where hierarchical scale decomposition captures both trend and seasonality reliably

Resource-constrained production environments requiring fast inference over many independent series (e.g., thousands of SKUs in retail), where N-HiTS's reduced parameter count and fixed-graph architecture outperform heavier attention-based models
not_recommended_for: Short-horizon forecasting (1-10 steps) where the hierarchical interpolation overhead brings no accuracy benefit and simpler MLP or ARIMA baselines are competitive at lower cost

Multivariate problems with strong cross-variable dependencies (e.g., sensor fusion in autonomous systems), where flattening variables loses relational structure that models with explicit channel mixing exploit
children.curiosity: Introduced by Challu, Olivares, Oreshkin, Garza, Mergenthaler, and Dubrawski (AAAI 2023, arXiv 2201.12886), N-HiTS was the first MLP-based model to report a 25% average accuracy improvement over Transformer architectures on the long-horizon Exchange, Weather, and ETT benchmarks, directly challenging the then-dominant assumption that attention mechanisms were necessary for state-of-the-art time series forecasting.

target.notes: Univariate by architecture; produces direct multi-step point forecasts over a fixed horizon. Multivariate only via flattening, which discards cross-variable structure. No native probabilistic output unless paired with a quantile loss.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds to thousands of observations per series; performs best with long histories that expose multiple seasonal cycles. Trains across many series (global model)
data_regime.dimensionality: designed for many independent univariate series (e.g. thousands of SKUs); not for high cross-channel dimensionality
needs: sufficient history relative to forecast horizon

features.interpretability: medium: hierarchical stacks decompose output into interpretable trend/seasonal-scale components, but individual interpolation weights are opaque
features.notes: Requires evenly spaced timestamps; static MaxPool kernels assume a fixed sampling rate. Inputs typically scaled/normalized per series. Exogenous covariate support is limited compared to attention-based forecasters.

assumptions: Series sampled at a fixed, regular frequency
Approximate stationarity of seasonal/trend structure across the lookback and horizon (fixed sampling rates cannot adapt to non-stationary regimes)
Forecast target decomposes into distinct temporal scales (trend + multi-rate residuals)
Horizon and lookback windows fixed at training time
loss: MAE / squared error (MSE) for point forecasts
MAPE / sMAPE
pinball / quantile loss for probabilistic multi-horizon forecasts
contraindicated_when: Short-horizon forecasting (1-10 steps), where simpler MLP/ARIMA baselines match it at lower cost
Multivariate series with strong cross-variable dependencies (flattening loses relational structure)
Irregularly sampled or strongly non-stationary series where fixed MaxPool rates misalign with the underlying dynamics
Very short histories that cannot fill the lookback window
Need for native uncertainty/full predictive distribution beyond quantile heads

children.name: NNAR (Neural Network AutoRegression)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike N-BEATS and N-HiTS — which learn basis expansions over a fixed lookback window — NNAR uses explicit autoregressive lag inputs (p past values) as raw features to a single-hidden-layer MLP, making it the direct nonlinear analogue of AR(p) rather than a residual block architecture.
strengths: Handles nonlinear lag dependencies that linear ARIMA cannot capture, using the same NNAR(p,k) lag-selection logic as AIC-optimal AR(p)
Seamlessly extends to seasonal series via NNAR(p,P,k)[m], adding P seasonal lags without any manual decomposition step
Ensemble averaging of 25 independently initialized networks reduces variance from random weight initialization, improving forecast stability over a single run
weaknesses: Single hidden layer with sigmoid activations limits capacity relative to deep architectures; cannot model very long-range dependencies beyond the specified lag window
Results are non-deterministic across runs due to random weight initialization, making exact reproducibility require fixing the random seed explicitly
Provides no native prediction intervals; simulation-based intervals (bootstrapped residuals) are computationally expensive and undercover in the presence of model misspecification
recommended_for: Monthly or quarterly economic/demand series with moderate nonlinear seasonality where ARIMA underfits and a lightweight R-native solution is required (e.g., nnetar on retail sales with m=12)
Short univariate series (n < 500) where deep architectures overfit but nonlinear lag interactions are suspected, leveraging NNAR's AIC-based automatic lag selection
not_recommended_for: High-dimensional multivariate forecasting where cross-series relationships matter — NNAR accepts only univariate input and ignores covariates by default
Long-horizon probabilistic forecasting requiring calibrated intervals, where models such as DeepAR or TFT produce proper distributional outputs natively
children.curiosity: Rob Hyndman introduced the nnetar() function implementing NNAR in version 4.0 of the R forecast package (2013), making it one of the first neural-network forecasters embedded in a mainstream statistical forecasting library; the NNAR(p,k) notation was deliberately chosen to mirror ARIMA(p,d,q), with the analogy that NNAR(p,0) is a nonlinear AR(p) without stationarity constraints.

target.notes: Univariate point forecasting. Predicts future values of a single numeric series from its own p lagged values (and P seasonal lags for NNAR(p,P,k)[m]); no exogenous covariates by default.

data_regime.rows: suited to short series, n<500; deep forecasters overfit there. Upper-bounded by single-layer capacity, not data volume.
data_regime.dimensionality: strictly univariate; feature dimension = number of selected lags (p, optional P), kept small
needs: fixed random seed for reproducibility (ensemble of ~25 random-init nets is non-deterministic)

features.interpretability: low: single-hidden-layer MLP over lag inputs is a black box vs AR(p), though lag structure (p,P) is explicit and AIC-selected
features.notes: inputs are raw lagged observations; scaling/normalization of the series helps sigmoid-activation training. Direct nonlinear analogue of AR(p).

strictly linear dynamics where ARIMA is simpler, deterministic, and equally accurate
long, high-volume series where deep sequence models exploit capacity NNAR lacks

Target type depends on the head; the differentiator is raw high-dimensional input, not target distribution. No parametric target-distribution assumption.

children.name: 3. Classical Statistics
children.diff_siblings: Unlike ML (which optimizes a loss function empirically) and Deep Learning (which learns hierarchical representations end-to-end), Classical Statistics grounds every model in explicit distributional assumptions and produces closed-form estimates with known sampling distributions, enabling formal inference on parameters rather than just prediction.
strengths: Formal uncertainty quantification: confidence intervals and p-values follow analytically from the assumed data-generating process, not from resampling heuristics.
Small-sample validity: methods such as the t-test and ANOVA were designed for n in the tens, where neural networks and gradient boosting are unreliable.
Regulatory and scientific interpretability: coefficients carry causal-narrative weight and satisfy audit requirements in clinical trials, econometrics, and epidemiology.
weaknesses: Distributional assumptions (normality, homoscedasticity, linearity) are strong and, when violated, invalidate inference even when point predictions look reasonable.
Manual feature engineering and interaction specification are required; the framework has no mechanism to discover nonlinear structure automatically.
Predictive accuracy plateaus well below that of ensemble or deep methods on high-dimensional, high-n problems where the assumption-driven structure is a constraint rather than a benefit.
recommended_for: Clinical trials and epidemiological cohort studies where the estimand is a causal effect size (e.g., hazard ratio, odds ratio) and regulatory bodies require interpretable, assumption-transparent models on samples of hundreds to low thousands.
Economic and social-science research where the goal is to test a pre-registered hypothesis about a specific coefficient under controlled experimental or quasi-experimental conditions.
not_recommended_for: Image, audio, or text prediction tasks where the input is raw high-dimensional data and no closed-form feature representation of the signal exists.

Production ranking or recommendation systems requiring retraining on millions of observations per day, where iterative gradient-based optimization of flexible models dominates both accuracy and throughput.
children.curiosity: The foundational framework of Classical Statistics was largely established between 1920 and 1935 by Ronald A. Fisher, who introduced maximum likelihood estimation (1922), analysis of variance (1925), and the design of experiments (1935), creating the inferential scaffold on which nearly all subsequent parametric methods rest.

children.name: 3.1 Structural Equations (SEM)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike path analysis (observed variables only) or confirmatory factor analysis (measurement model only), SEM simultaneously estimates a measurement model (latent constructs from indicators) and a structural model (directional regression paths among those latent constructs) within a single covariance-based framework.
strengths: Separates measurement error from structural relationships, so path coefficients are not attenuated by indicator unreliability as they would be in plain regression.
Tests complex theories with multiple mediators and latent variables in a single model fit, rather than requiring a chain of separate regressions whose errors compound.
Provides global fit indices (CFI, RMSEA, SRMR) that quantify how well the entire hypothesized covariance structure matches the observed data.
weaknesses: Requires multivariate normality and a sample of at least 200 observations (often 10–20 per estimated parameter); smaller samples yield unstable parameter estimates and inflated fit indices.
The model must be identified (more known covariances than free parameters), and misspecification of the measurement structure silently biases all structural paths.
Covariance-based SEM captures only linear, first-order relationships; nonlinear effects or interaction terms among latent variables require extensions that are rarely used in practice.
recommended_for: Psychometric and social-science research where theoretical constructs (e.g., 'customer satisfaction', 'cognitive load') are unobservable and must be inferred from multiple survey items, and directional hypotheses among those constructs need simultaneous testing.

Mediation analysis with latent variables — e.g., testing whether organizational commitment mediates the effect of leadership style on employee performance, while accounting for measurement error in all three constructs.
not_recommended_for: Exploratory studies where the researcher has no prior theory specifying which indicators belong to which latent factor and which structural paths exist; EFA or regularized regression are more appropriate for discovery.

Small datasets (n < 100) or purely observed-variable problems with no latent constructs, where standard multiple regression or path analysis achieves the same result without the identification constraints and distributional assumptions of SEM.
children.curiosity: Sewall Wright introduced path analysis — SEM's direct ancestor — in 1918 to decompose correlations among bone measurements in rabbits into direct and indirect causal effects; Karl Jöreskog unified path analysis with confirmatory factor analysis into the modern LISREL framework in 1970, making latent-variable structural models computationally tractable for the first time.

children.name: SEM (Structural Equation Modeling)
children.diff_siblings: Full SEM is the only framework in this family that jointly estimates a measurement model (latent variables from observed indicators via CFA) and a structural model (directed paths among those latents) in a single covariance-structure optimization, whereas siblings such as Path Analysis operate only on observed variables and CFA addresses measurement alone.
strengths: Simultaneous estimation of measurement error and structural paths prevents attenuation bias that plagues observed-variable regression, making latent-variable coefficients more accurate.
Global fit indices (RMSEA, CFI, SRMR) test the entire implied covariance matrix against sample data, allowing falsification of the theoretical model rather than just individual coefficients.
Supports bidirectional (non-recursive) relationships and correlated residuals, enabling richer theory testing that standard regression or path analysis cannot represent.
weaknesses: Requires large samples — typically 200+ observations — because maximum-likelihood estimation of the full covariance matrix becomes unstable with fewer cases, especially in models with many latent indicators.
Model fit can be improved by post-hoc modification indices (freeing residual covariances, adding paths) that risk overfitting and capitalization on chance, undermining the confirmatory rationale.

Identification constraints (each latent needs a scale anchor, sufficient indicators, and no empirical under-identification) make model specification technically demanding and easy to get wrong silently.
recommended_for: Psychometric scale validation where constructs such as depression or brand loyalty are measured by multiple Likert items and researchers must account for measurement error before testing relationships between constructs.

Longitudinal panel studies modeling latent growth curves — intercept and slope as latent variables — to decompose between-person differences from within-person change trajectories across 3+ time points.
not_recommended_for: Exploratory research with no prior theory about which indicators load on which factors, since SEM is confirmatory by design and fit indices will be misleading when the factor structure is data-driven.
Small samples (n < 100) or datasets with many free parameters relative to observations, where ML estimation yields biased standard errors and fit statistics lose interpretability.
children.curiosity: The LISREL framework that formalized full SEM was introduced by Karl Jöreskog (1973), who showed that the general covariance structure model unifies factor analysis and simultaneous-equation econometric models under a single matrix algebra, enabling maximum-likelihood estimation of both measurement and structural parameters in one step.

target.notes: Models the covariance/mean structure among observed continuous indicators; no single response variable. Multiple endogenous latents/observed outcomes estimated jointly. ML estimation assumes multivariate normality of indicators; ordinal/Likert items require WLSMV/DWLS or polychoric correlations.

data_regime.rows: needs large samples; 200+ typical, n<100 yields biased SEs and fit stats; rule-of-thumb 5-20 cases per free parameter
data_regime.dimensionality: p (indicators) modest; model must be identified (each latent needs >=2-3 indicators and a scale anchor); high p inflates parameters and destabilizes ML
needs: multiple observed indicators per latent construct

features.interpretability: high — coefficients are interpretable structural paths and factor loadings tied to a specified theory; global fit indices (RMSEA, CFI, TLI, SRMR) falsify the whole model
features.notes: Indicators commonly Likert/survey items; reflective vs formative measurement must be specified. Categorical indicators need polychoric correlations + WLSMV estimator.

assumptions: correct a priori specification of measurement and structural model (confirmatory, not exploratory)
multivariate normality of continuous indicators under ML estimation
linear relationships among latents and between latents and indicators
model identification (sufficient indicators, scale anchors, no empirical under-identification)
no major omitted variables/paths (mis-specification biases all estimates)
independent observations unless multilevel SEM is used
loss: maximum-likelihood discrepancy between sample and model-implied covariance matrix (default)
weighted least squares / WLSMV / DWLS for categorical-ordinal indicators
robust MLR / Satorra-Bentler corrected fit for non-normal data
generalized/unweighted least squares variants
contraindicated_when: sample is small (n<100) or free parameters are large relative to n
no prior theory about factor structure or directed paths (use EFA/exploratory methods instead)
goal is pure predictive accuracy on a single outcome rather than testing a measurement+structural theory
single-indicator constructs with no way to model measurement error
strongly non-normal or sparse categorical data without appropriate estimator
model fit is achieved only via post-hoc modification indices (overfitting/capitalization on chance)

children.name: CFA (Confirmatory Factor Analysis)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike path analysis (which models regressions among observed variables) and full SEM (which combines measurement and structural models), CFA is purely a measurement model — it specifies a priori which observed indicators load on which latent factors and estimates that fixed pattern by maximizing the likelihood of the observed covariance matrix.
strengths: Hypothesis-driven: lets the researcher impose a theoretically derived factor structure and formally test it against data via chi-square and fit indices (RMSEA, CFI), rather than letting structure emerge arbitrarily.
Enables rigorous validity testing: convergent validity (high loadings on the intended factor) and discriminant validity (low cross-loadings) are quantified simultaneously within a single model.

Measurement invariance testing: the same CFA model can be compared across groups (configural → metric → scalar invariance) to verify that a construct is measured equivalently — a prerequisite for meaningful group comparisons.
weaknesses: Chi-square fit test is highly sensitive to sample size; with N > 400 virtually any model yields a significant misfit, forcing reliance on approximate indices whose cutoffs (e.g., RMSEA < 0.06) are themselves debated.

Model is fully confirmatory: if the pre-specified structure fits poorly, modifying it by freeing parameters post-hoc inflates Type I error and capitalizes on chance — requiring a fresh validation sample.

Assumes multivariate normality and continuous indicators; ordinal Likert-scale data (common in surveys) requires polychoric correlations and WLSMV estimation, which many practitioners omit, biasing loadings upward.
recommended_for: Scale validation in psychology or social sciences: a researcher proposes that 12 items measure 3 latent constructs and uses CFA to confirm the structure, estimate factor loadings, and report RMSEA/CFI before using the scale in further analyses.

Multi-group measurement invariance: comparing latent mean differences (e.g., anxiety scores) across clinical vs. control groups, where metric and scalar invariance must be established before the comparison is meaningful.
not_recommended_for: Early-stage instrument development with no prior theoretical structure, where EFA is more appropriate for discovering how items cluster without imposing a predefined pattern.

Purely predictive pipelines (regression, classification): CFA adds no predictive machinery — it tests measurement structure, not outcome relationships, making it irrelevant when the goal is minimizing prediction error.
children.curiosity: Introduced by Karl Jöreskog in 'A General Approach to Confirmatory Maximum Likelihood Factor Analysis' (Psychometrika, 1969), who showed that fixing any subset of the factor loading matrix and estimating the remaining parameters by maximum likelihood yields a large-sample chi-square test of the imposed restrictions — the first rigorous statistical test of a pre-specified factor structure.
keywords: test if items measure a latent construct

target.notes: Not a predictive model. CFA is a measurement model that tests a hypothesized latent-factor structure against an observed covariance matrix; there is no outcome variable being predicted.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds+ observations; common heuristics ask for N>200 or 5-10 cases per estimated parameter; chi-square misfit becomes near-certain at N>400
data_regime.dimensionality: p = number of observed indicators, modest (typically 5-50 items); factor structure (which indicators load on which latent factors) must be specified a priori from theory
needs: fully observed item-level data (no derived features)

features.interpretability: high: estimated factor loadings, residual variances, and inter-factor correlations map directly to a substantive measurement theory
features.notes: Indicators assumed continuous and multivariate normal for ML estimation; ordinal Likert items require polychoric correlations with WLSMV/DWLS estimation instead of treating them as continuous (which biases loadings upward)

assumptions: multivariate normality of indicators (for ML estimation)
continuous indicators (else polychoric/WLSMV needed)
correct a priori specification of which items load on which factors
linear relationships between indicators and latent factors
