children.name: EFA (Exploratory Factor Analysis)
children.diff_siblings: Unlike CFA, which tests a researcher-specified factor structure against data, EFA imposes no prior constraints on factor-variable assignments and lets the correlation matrix itself reveal which latent dimensions best explain shared variance.
strengths: Requires no a priori factor structure: the loading pattern emerges entirely from the data's covariance, making it suitable for early-stage instrument development.
Rotation methods (Varimax for orthogonal, Oblimin for oblique) allow the solution to be transformed into the most interpretable simple structure without changing model fit.
Communality estimates isolate shared variance from unique and error variance, giving a cleaner latent-factor signal than PCA, which absorbs error into components.
weaknesses: Factor retention decisions (scree plot, parallel analysis, Kaiser criterion) are subjective and different rules often yield different numbers of factors on the same data.
Requires large samples: stable factor loadings typically need at least 5-10 observations per variable, and low communalities destabilize solutions in small datasets.
Produces no fit indices or hypothesis tests, so there is no formal way to confirm whether the recovered structure is correct or merely one of many equivalent rotations.
recommended_for: Scale construction in psychology or social sciences where the dimensional structure of a new questionnaire (e.g., 20-item personality inventory) is unknown and must be discovered from item intercorrelations.

Biomedical data reduction where many correlated clinical measures (lab panels, symptom checklists) are suspected to reflect a smaller set of underlying syndromes with no theory yet specifying which items belong together.
not_recommended_for: Datasets where a theoretically motivated factor structure already exists and the goal is to test its fit: CFA within a full SEM framework is the correct tool for confirmatory purposes.
High-dimensional settings with many more variables than observations (e.g., genomics with p >> n), where the correlation matrix is singular or ill-conditioned and EFA extraction fails numerically.
children.curiosity: Charles Spearman introduced factor analysis in 1904 ('General Intelligence, Objectively Determined and Measured', American Journal of Psychology) to argue that all cognitive abilities share a single underlying factor g, making EFA one of the oldest multivariate techniques in the behavioral sciences.

target.notes: Unsupervised latent-variable model. No response variable; estimates latent common factors from the observed covariance/correlation matrix.

data_regime.rows: needs large samples; rule of thumb 5-10 observations per variable and N>200 for stable loadings; low communalities require even more
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n required; the variable correlation matrix must be non-singular and well-conditioned. Fails in p>>n.
needs: multiple correlated continuous indicators (typically 3+ per expected factor)

features.interpretability: high; factor loadings + rotation (Varimax/Oblimin) yield interpretable simple structure mapping items to latent constructs
features.notes: Designed for interval/continuous indicators; ordinal Likert items handled via polychoric correlations. Variables should be linearly correlated and ideally multivariate normal for ML extraction. Requires standardization implicit in correlation-matrix input. Variables with near-zero correlation to all others contribute nothing.

children.name: 3.2 Count and Proportion Models
children.diff_siblings: While other Classical Statistics branches model continuous outcomes (regression) or time-to-event data (survival analysis), Count and Proportion Models specialize in discrete, bounded response variables — non-negative integers or rates in [0,1] — using GLM link functions (log for counts, logit for proportions) that respect the distributional constraints of Poisson, negative binomial, and binomial families.
strengths: Poisson and negative binomial GLMs provide unbiased coefficient estimates and correct standard errors for count outcomes without requiring transformation, unlike log-transforming and applying OLS which introduces retransformation bias.

The negative binomial dispersion parameter explicitly captures overdispersion (variance > mean), a near-universal feature of real count data such as hospital admissions or insurance claims, where Poisson assumptions would underestimate standard errors.

Beta regression and logistic-family models for proportions respect the [0,1] boundary by construction, avoiding nonsensical predictions outside that range that linear probability models routinely produce.
weaknesses: Zero-inflated count data (e.g., species abundance surveys with structural zeros) require a two-component mixture model (zero-inflated Poisson or hurdle model) — standard Poisson and NB fits fail diagnostically under excess zeros.

Proportion models based on the binomial family assume a known denominator (number of trials); when the denominator varies substantially and is itself uncertain, model calibration degrades and quasi-binomial or beta regression adjustments are needed.

Count GLMs assume independence of events within the observation window; correlated counts (e.g., repeated measures per subject, spatially clustered events) require random-effects or GEE extensions, adding model complexity.
recommended_for: Epidemiological rate modeling where the outcome is a raw event count (disease cases per district) with a known exposure offset — Poisson or negative binomial regression directly estimates incidence rate ratios across covariates.

Survey or ecological studies reporting proportions with a fixed sample size denominator (e.g., proportion of seedlings surviving per plot) — binomial GLM with logit link yields odds ratios and confidence intervals with correct coverage.
not_recommended_for: Continuous positive outcomes such as monetary expenditure or reaction time, which may look count-like but are truly real-valued — gamma or log-normal regression fits the distribution far better and avoids discretization artifacts.

High-dimensional settings with hundreds of predictors and complex interactions, where regularized methods (elastic net, gradient boosting) provide better predictive accuracy than maximum-likelihood GLMs whose variance-bias tradeoff is suboptimal without penalization.
children.curiosity: Poisson regression was formalized as part of the Generalized Linear Model framework introduced by Nelder and Wedderburn (1972) in their landmark Royal Statistical Society paper, which showed for the first time that Poisson, binomial, and Gaussian regression all share the same iteratively reweighted least squares fitting algorithm, unifying count and proportion modeling under a single theoretical roof.

children.name: Negative Binomial
children.diff_siblings: Unlike Poisson regression (which forces variance = mean), Negative Binomial adds a free dispersion parameter alpha that lets variance grow as mu + alpha*mu^2, explicitly modeling unobserved heterogeneity across observations.
strengths: Handles overdispersion without misestimating standard errors: the extra parameter alpha absorbs between-subject heterogeneity that Poisson assumes away, keeping inference calibrated.
Direct maximum-likelihood estimation of alpha alongside regression coefficients, so overdispersion is quantified and testable (likelihood-ratio test vs. Poisson).
Naturally produces heavier right tails than Poisson, matching empirical count distributions in biology, epidemiology, and insurance claim data.
weaknesses: Fails when zeros are structurally excess beyond what the overdispersion parameter can explain; a Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial is then required.
MLE of the dispersion parameter alpha is numerically unstable for very small samples or weakly overdispersed data, sometimes failing to converge.
Assumes a specific variance-mean relationship (quadratic); data with a different variance structure (e.g., power-law tails) may still be misspecified.
recommended_for: Hospital readmission counts per patient over a year, where patient-level frailty creates variance well above the mean (classic overdispersion scenario).
Species abundance counts per survey plot in ecology, where rare-species heterogeneity inflates variance relative to the Poisson assumption.
not_recommended_for: Count outcomes dominated by structural zeros from a separate zero-generating process (e.g., non-anglers in a fishing survey), where a hurdle or ZIP/ZINB model is more appropriate.
High-dimensional predictor settings with small n, where estimating the additional dispersion parameter alongside many regression coefficients increases instability and overfitting risk.
children.curiosity: Introduced as a statistical model for accident proneness by Greenwood and Yule (1920) in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society (vol. 83, pp. 255-279), making it one of the earliest compound-distribution models applied to heterogeneous count data.

target.notes: Non-negative integer counts with overdispersion (Var > mean). Models variance as mu + alpha*mu^2 (NB2); free dispersion parameter alpha estimated by MLE. Reduces to Poisson as alpha->0.

data_regime.rows: needs hundreds+; alpha MLE unstable on very small n or weak overdispersion (may fail to converge)
data_regime.dimensionality: p<n preferred; extra dispersion parameter aggravates instability when p approaches n

features.interpretability: high: GLM with log link, coefficients are interpretable as multiplicative rate ratios (exp(beta)); alpha quantifies overdispersion
features.notes: Supports exposure/offset term (log exposure) to model rates per unit time/population. Standard GLM scaling/encoding conventions apply.

assumptions: Conditional mean follows log-linear form in predictors
Variance follows quadratic mean relationship Var = mu + alpha*mu^2 (NB2); misspecified if true variance is e.g. power-law or linear-overdispersion (NB1)
Independent observations (no within-cluster correlation unless modeled)
No excess structural zeros beyond what overdispersion explains
